question: A country is worried its own shoemakers cannot compete with cheaper shoes coming in from another country. So the government puts a big extra tax on every foreign shoe that crosses the border. That way local shoemakers can charge higher prices without losing all their customers to the imports. What is the special name economists use for this kind of border tax on imports?
answer: A tariff
choices: A tariff
A subsidy
A minimum wage
A quota
context: A tariff is a tax on imports. The July Monarchy applied heavy tariffs on iron, textiles, and grain to protect French producers. Bastiat's Economic Sophisms (1845, 1848) is the classical satirical field guide to the protectionist arguments that defended those tariffs in the Chamber. Source: http://davidmhart.com/liberty/Papers/Bastiat/EconomicSophisms/Hart_BastiatsSophismsAug2011.html.

question: A government tells its citizens that any jobless person can come get a guaranteed wage, and the government will pick the job for them. It sounds generous, but the money has to come from somewhere. What is usually the biggest hidden cost of a program like this?
answer: The government has to tax everyone else a lot to pay them all
choices: The government has to tax everyone else a lot to pay them all
The jobless people refuse to accept any work
Foreign countries buy fewer of the country goods
Interest rates automatically drop to zero
context: Louis Blanc (1811-1882) had published L'Organisation du travail (The Organization of Labor) serially in 1839, arguing that only the state could remedy unemployment through 'social workshops' organized craft by craft. In February 1848 he joined the Provisional Government and pushed the decree that created the National Workshops. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Blanc.

question: Imagine a national government makes a bold promise: any citizen who is out of work can sign up for a state-paid job, no questions asked, with wages coming from taxes. Within a few months, 100,000 people have signed up — but the government has only lined up real productive work for a small fraction of them. Digging holes and filling them back in doesn't count. The rest are put on the payroll anyway. What is the built-in problem with a program like this?
answer: There is not enough real work, so most enrolled people are paid to do very little
choices: There is not enough real work, so most enrolled people are paid to do very little
Everyone finds a real job matched to their skills
The program pays for itself right away
Fewer people sign up than expected
context: The National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) opened in late February 1848 and grew past 100,000 enrollees by May. The treasury could not pay them for real work, and wages became a straight welfare payment. Louis Blanc had originally wanted them run as producer cooperatives; the actual implementation, under minister Marie, was mostly digging and hauling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Workshops.

question: Imagine a big city government decides to hire 100,000 people to do busywork -- raking leaves, filing papers, painting benches -- and pays them out of the city budget. This lasts a few years, then the money runs out and the program is shut down all at once. Those 100,000 people wake up the next morning with no paycheck. What usually happens in the streets right after?
answer: The suddenly unpaid workers riot, because their income has been cut off
choices: The suddenly unpaid workers riot, because their income has been cut off
Everyone quietly finds new jobs the next day
Business owners protest the closure
Prices drop across the city
context: The June Days (Journees de Juin, June 23-26, 1848) followed the closure of the National Workshops and were suppressed by General Louis-Eugene Cavaignac with heavy casualties. Louis Blanc, tainted by his association with the workshops, fled to England, where he lived in exile for 22 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Workshops.

question: The French anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon published his most notorious book in 1840. Asked in its title 'What Is Property?', Proudhon delivered a three-word French answer that became one of the most-quoted lines in 19th-century political thought: 'la propriete, c'est le ______.' Fill the blank.
answer: vol
choices: vol
roi
dieu
peuple
context: Proudhon's Qu'est-ce que la propriete? (1840) delivered the famous line 'la propriete, c'est le vol' -- 'property is theft.' Proudhon was the first thinker to call himself an anarchist, and he became Bastiat's most sustained French debate opponent. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Pierre-Joseph-Proudhon.

question: In October 1849 Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and Frederic Bastiat began a public debate in Proudhon's newspaper La Voix du Peuple. It ran roughly weekly through March 1850 -- fourteen letters back and forth. Proudhon wanted his Bank of the People to lend at zero cost. What was Bastiat defending against Proudhon's scheme?
answer: That interest is the market price of time-preference and cannot be legislated to zero
choices: That interest is the market price of time-preference and cannot be legislated to zero
That the state should replace private banks with a single central bank of issue
That labor unions should set wages by industry-wide bargaining
That gold coinage should be replaced with government paper money
context: Proudhon pushed his Banque du Peuple as an issuer of interest-free credit ('credit gratuit'). Bastiat defended interest as the real market price paid for the use of savings over time. Proudhon collected the letters as Interet et principal; Bastiat published his version, augmented by a fourteenth reply, as Gratuite du credit (1850). Source: https://praxeology.net/FB-PJP-DOI-IV-2b.htm.

question: In October 1845 the French writer Bastiat published a mock petition. He signed it as if he were French candle-makers begging their government to shut every window, skylight, and shutter. The petition said a foreign rival was ruining their trade unfairly. Which rival did the petition name?
answer: The sun
choices: The sun
British gaslight
American whale oil
Belgian coal-tar lamps
context: The Petition of the Candlemakers (Petition des fabricants de chandelles) demands protection from the unfair competition of the sun. Bastiat's target was every real protectionist argument then live in the French Chamber -- that any foreign competitor with a natural advantage was somehow 'unfair' to French industry. Source: https://mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition-0.

question: In 1840 the French writer Étienne Cabet published a novel called Voyage en Icarie about a perfect communist republic where everyone shared everything and no one owned private property. Readers loved it. In 1848 Cabet actually led about 500 followers across the Atlantic to Texas and then Illinois to build a real Icaria on American soil. Dozens of similar small communist colonies sprang up across the 1800s United States. What happened to most of these experiments in real life?
answer: They fell apart within a few years from fighting and shortages
choices: They fell apart within a few years from fighting and shortages
They grew into huge successful cities within twenty years
They were shut down by the US government for being illegal
They still run today as the largest farms in Illinois
context: Etienne Cabet (1788-1856) published Voyage en Icarie in 1839, then led the Icarian emigration in 1848; the settlement eventually landed at Nauvoo, Illinois after the Mormons had abandoned it. Fourier (phalansteres) and Saint-Simon (industrial technocracy) were the earlier utopian-socialist generation whose ideas fed into the 1848 moment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Cabet.

question: In 1848 two German thinkers, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, were living as exiles in London. Europe was boiling with worker uprisings that year, and a small group called the Communist League asked them to write a manifesto. In just twenty-three pages, Marx and Engels called on workers everywhere to unite and overthrow the owners of factories and land. It became the founding text of communism -- a movement that would later kill roughly 65 to 100 million people in the twentieth century. What is that pamphlet called?
answer: The Communist Manifesto
choices: The Communist Manifesto
The Wealth of Nations
The Prince
The Social Contract
context: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei in London in February 1848, the same month the February Revolution broke out in Paris. Marx's tradition was distinct from Louis Blanc's state-socialism, Proudhon's mutualism, and Cabet's utopianism, but it addressed the same crisis moment. Bastiat's 'The State,' September 1848, is his answer inside the French debate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Against Louis Blanc's National Workshops -- which the treasury paid for by drawing on tax revenue and borrowing -- Bastiat's essays kept pressing one specific reasoning move a modern reader can learn to spot. Which move did Bastiat press against the workshops?
answer: That every franc paid to a workshop enrollee had to be taken from another citizen who never saw the transfer
choices: That every franc paid to a workshop enrollee had to be taken from another citizen who never saw the transfer
That workers' cooperatives always outperform private firms in productivity
That the state should issue paper currency to fund public works directly
That property in land is theft but property in movable goods is legitimate
context: Bastiat's answer to the workshops was the seen/unseen move: the enrolled worker's wage is SEEN; the tax-payer's or lender's foregone spending is UNSEEN. This is the same transfer-recognition his 1848 essay 'The State' compressed into the 'great fiction' line. The reader can accept or reject the evaluation; the reasoning MOVE is the transfer-recognition. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: The countries that pump most of the world's oil -- Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, and their neighbors -- decide together to stop selling their oil to certain buyer nations. This kind of cut-off is called an embargo. Because the buyer countries still need oil to run their cars, trucks, and factories, what almost always happens to the price of oil for those buyers?
answer: They shoot way up
choices: They shoot way up
They stay the same
They drop
They double, then quickly return to normal
context: The 1973 Oil Crisis saw world oil prices roughly quadruple in a matter of months. The embargo formally ended March 1974 but prices remained substantially elevated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis.

question: A hurricane is coming and gas is already running short. The government orders every gas station: do not raise your gas prices, no matter what. Drivers rush over hoping to fill up at the normal price. What usually happens at the pumps next?
answer: Long lines form and pumps run empty faster
choices: Long lines form and pumps run empty faster
Everyone drives less on their own
New oil wells suddenly open near town
The gas stations start giving fuel away
context: Odd-even license-plate rationing rules meant drivers with odd-ending plates could only buy on odd-numbered dates; even-ending plates on even dates. Stations posted 'NO GAS' signs when empty. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: In 1973 and 1974, Americans waited in lines an hour long just to buy gasoline. Many blamed the oil embargo by OPEC (the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries), when Arab nations cut off shipments to the United States. But free-market economists, following Milton Friedman, pointed at a US government policy first set by President Nixon in 1971. It legally kept gas prices from rising to match the drop in supply, so stations ran dry instead of just charging more. What was that policy?
answer: Federal price ceilings on gasoline
choices: Federal price ceilings on gasoline
The 55-mph national speed limit
Federal excise taxes on gasoline
The Alaska Pipeline delay
context: Nixon-era gasoline price ceilings were already in force before the embargo. The ceiling prevented the pump price from rising to clear the market; the resulting shortage was rationed by queuing. Without the ceiling, prices would have risen sharply and lines would not have formed. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: In October 1973, Arab oil-producing countries cut off oil sales to nations that had helped Israel in the Yom Kippur War. In America, Britain, and France, cars stretched in mile-long lines at gas stations for weeks. But two European countries had no lines at all -- their pumps stayed full, though their prices were much higher than everywhere else. Which pair of countries is the standard textbook example?
answer: West Germany and Switzerland
choices: West Germany and Switzerland
France and Italy
Norway and Denmark
Britain and Ireland
context: West Germany and Switzerland had no price controls and no lines during the 1973-74 shock. Prices rose sharply, demand adjusted, supply cleared. The US had controls and lines. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: The 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught that every policy has two sides -- the Seen (its obvious effects) and the Unseen (the hidden costs everyone forgets). In 1974, the American economist Murray Rothbard published an essay called 'The Energy Fiasco' about America's long 1973 gasoline lines, when federal price controls held pump prices artificially low. Using Bastiat's frame, what did Rothbard call the Seen and the Unseen of those price controls?
answer: Seen: the low pump price. Unseen: hours in line, imports not brought in at a loss, deliveries not made
choices: Seen: the low pump price. Unseen: hours in line, imports not brought in at a loss, deliveries not made
Seen: OPEC greed. Unseen: US oil imports rising
Seen: rising gas taxes. Unseen: falling road maintenance
Seen: consumer thrift. Unseen: producer overproduction
context: Rothbard's Bastiatian argument: the low pump price is what people saw; what was hidden was the time-cost paid in the line, the private importers unwilling to bring in gasoline at a loss, and the deliveries that did not happen. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: In 1945 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that a market runs on knowledge spread across millions of ordinary people. A family choosing tomatoes at a grocery store makes thousands of small decisions -- what price is fair, what tastes good, what they can afford. Together those decisions signal farmers what to plant next season. Now imagine a small government office in the capital tried to replace all those choices with one central plan. What would most likely go wrong first?
answer: The office would guess wrong about what people actually want, leading to shortages and waste
choices: The office would guess wrong about what people actually want, leading to shortages and waste
Shoppers would prefer being told what to buy
Farmers would grow exactly the right amount because their instructions would be clearer
Grocery stores would run more smoothly with simpler prices
context: Free to Choose (PBS 1980, tie-in book by Milton and Rose Friedman) devoted a segment to the 1973-74 gasoline lines as an illustration of price-ceiling shortages. Source: freetochoosenetwork.org.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, in his 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen,' taught that every policy has an obvious effect and a hidden effect. In the 1970s, Austrian economists like Murray Rothbard used that idea to sharpen the case against price ceilings. They argued a price cap does not really remove the cost of a scarce good -- the government just converts one kind of cost into another kind, which most shoppers do not notice. What conversion do the Austrian economists name?
answer: Money-costs converted into time-costs paid in line
choices: Money-costs converted into time-costs paid in line
Money-costs converted into transportation-costs
Money-costs converted into gasoline-quality-costs
Money-costs converted into environmental-costs
context: The ceiling converts what would have been a money-cost (buyer pays higher price, seller collects it) into a time-cost (buyer pays hours in line, no seller collects). The cost is not eliminated -- and no producer receives the payment. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: In 1971 President Richard Nixon set a legal ceiling on the price of American oil, and his successors Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter kept the caps in place. Long gas lines formed at pumps across the country and stayed for years, even after the 1973 Arab embargo ended. Then in January 1981, on his first day in office, President Ronald Reagan signed an executive order that scrapped the oil price caps entirely. What happened to the gas lines after that?
answer: They disappeared quickly as producers could sell at real market prices
choices: They disappeared quickly as producers could sell at real market prices
They stayed the same because rules do not change real behavior
They got much worse because prices spiked forever
They only ended when the government built more oil wells
context: Reagan's January 28, 1981 executive order lifted the remaining federal price controls on domestic crude oil. Within months, gasoline lines disappeared even though world prices remained elevated. Source: reaganlibrary.gov executive orders.

question: In 1979 the Iranian Revolution overthrew the Shah and cut off Iran's oil exports, sending world oil prices spiking for the second time in a decade. Gasoline lines came back to America -- but only to one state. California drivers waited hours at the pump; other states had no lines at all. Federal price controls from 1973 had been lifted, but California had done something different. Why was California the outlier?
answer: Its state price controls remained in force
choices: Its state price controls remained in force
Its refineries were destroyed by an earthquake
Its truck-driver strike blocked deliveries
Its harbor unions refused to unload tankers
context: California's 1979 lines returned because state-level price controls were still in force even as federal controls were unwinding. The natural experiment inside the US confirmed the price-ceiling-produces-lines mechanism a second time. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price that a seller is not allowed to charge above -- like gasoline capped at a low pump price. The 1973-74 American gas lines and the 1979 California repeat are the cleanest real-world case study of what a price ceiling actually produces. Austrian economists like Murray Rothbard drew a single sharp lesson from both episodes -- one that goes beyond just 'shortage.' Which lesson do they most often draw?
answer: The shortage under a ceiling is a shortage in space AND in time
choices: The shortage under a ceiling is a shortage in space AND in time
The shortage under a ceiling is offset by tariff reductions
The shortage under a ceiling improves consumer welfare
The shortage under a ceiling requires more central planning
context: The reasoning move: the shortage manifests both as empty pumps (space) and as hours of queueing (time). Removing the ceiling ends both instantly. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: Two friends in a big city talk about fixing traffic. Anna says the fix is easy -- put smart people in charge and let them plan it right. Ben shakes his head. He says no small group can ever know enough about all the drivers, all the streets, and all the daily changes to plan a whole city. What is Ben's cautious view called in one word?
answer: Skeptical
choices: Skeptical
Confident
Selfish
Angry
context: Thomas Sowell, A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles (William Morrow, 1987; revised editions 2002, 2007). Sowell developed the framework across a trilogy over the next twelve years. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 1987).

question: Some grown-ups believe that with the right rules and enough education, people can be made just about perfect. Other grown-ups believe that humans come with real, permanent limits -- selfishness, ignorance, weakness -- that no rulebook can fully erase. Many political fights come down to which of these ______ is correct.
answer: views of human nature
choices: views of human nature
election laws
tax brackets
foreign trade deals
context: Sowell chose 'visions' precisely because they are pre-analytical -- pictures of human nature that shape which policies feel obviously correct or obviously naive before any specific argument. Source: Sowell, Conflict of Visions (Morrow 1987), Chapter 1.

question: In 1987 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book called A Conflict of Visions. In it he argues that most political fights come down to two rival pictures of human nature -- one that sees people as fixed and flawed, one that sees people as endlessly improvable. He gave each picture a single one-word label. What is that pair of one-word labels?
answer: Constrained and unconstrained
choices: Constrained and unconstrained
Left and right
Progressive and conservative
Statist and libertarian
context: Sowell uses 'constrained' as the primary label (with 'tragic' as a synonym from within the tradition) and 'unconstrained' as the paired label (with 'utopian' as a critical synonym). He explicitly rejects a 'realistic vs idealistic' framing. Source: Sowell, Conflict of Visions (1987).

question: In his 1987 book Conflict of Visions, the American economist Thomas Sowell described two very different pictures of human nature. One picture says people are stuck with fixed limits -- knowledge is spread out among millions, self-interest does not go away, and good rules take a long time to build up through trial and error. Which view of human beings does Sowell say this is?
answer: A view that human nature has real limits we must work around
choices: A view that human nature has real limits we must work around
A view that people can be reshaped into anything by a smart plan
A view that self-interest can be trained out of people
A view that a small group of experts can plan a whole country
context: The constrained vision runs through Smith, Burke, the American Federalists, and Hayek. Politics in this vision is about designing rules to channel imperfect people -- not about identifying who has the right vision and empowering them. Source: Sowell (1987), Chapter 2.

question: In his 1987 book Conflict of Visions, the American economist Thomas Sowell mapped two rival views of human nature. The first, called the constrained vision, says people are basically fixed -- greed, envy, and short-sightedness never really go away, so wise rules and long tradition are needed to steer them. Sowell said Adam Smith, Edmund Burke, and the American Founders held this view. What is the opposite view usually called?
answer: The unconstrained vision — human nature is flexible and can be improved with new institutions
choices: The unconstrained vision — human nature is flexible and can be improved with new institutions
The invisible hand — markets guide selfish choices toward good outcomes on their own
The knowledge problem — no central planner can know what everyone actually wants
The tragedy of the commons — shared resources tend to be overused
context: The unconstrained vision runs through Godwin, the French Revolutionaries, John Kenneth Galbraith, and Rawls. Politics in this vision is about identifying who has the correct vision and empowering them to act. Source: Sowell (1987), Chapter 2.

question: In his 1987 book A Conflict of Visions, the American economist Thomas Sowell describes the 'constrained' view of human nature -- the picture in which people come with real, permanent limits that no policy can fully erase. He captured this view in a single short slogan that has become one of his most-quoted lines. It says every policy choice is a bargain between goods, never a pure fix. Which phrase captures the constrained view of politics?
answer: There are no solutions, only trade-offs
choices: There are no solutions, only trade-offs
The arc of history bends toward justice
Every child is a philosopher
The state is the moral agent of the community
context: The trade-offs slogan is Sowell's constrained-vision headline. It recurs across A Conflict of Visions (1987), The Vision of the Anointed (1995), and dozens of Sowell's shorter essays. Source: Sowell (1987); Sowell, The Vision of the Anointed (Basic 1995).

question: Thomas Sowell, the American economist behind A Conflict of Visions, often paired his 'no solutions, only trade-offs' slogan with a second short question. It refuses to let a reformer say 'this policy is bad' without naming the actual real-world option they'd prefer -- because every policy is measured against some alternative, never against a fantasy. What is that two-word question of Sowell's?
answer: Compared to what?
choices: Compared to what?
Who decides?
At what cost?
Which market?
context: 'Compared to what?' recurs across Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (1980), The Vision of the Anointed (1995), and Basic Economics (2000). It presses the constrained-vision comparative move against unconstrained-vision idealizations. Source: Sowell, Knowledge and Decisions (Basic 1980).

question: In 1987 the American economist Thomas Sowell published Conflict of Visions, laying out his idea of two rival visions of human nature -- the constrained (people have fixed limits) and the unconstrained (people can be reshaped by smart plans). Sowell then developed that framework into a trilogy of books over the following twelve years. In 1995 he published the second book, applying the utopian lens as a diagnostic to modern American social policy. What was that book's title?
answer: The Vision of the Anointed
choices: The Vision of the Anointed
The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Discrimination and Disparities
Intellectuals and Society
context: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic 1995) analyzed the unconstrained vision in operation across US social policy. It is the second book in the trilogy. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 1995).

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell started his conflict-of-visions series in 1987, arguing that thinkers split into two camps: the constrained (people have fixed limits) and the unconstrained (people can be perfected by wise planners). The second book, in 1995, was The Vision of the Anointed. Then in 1999 Sowell published the third book, which followed the unconstrained view all the way to its utopian endpoint and diagnosed the results. What did Sowell title that final volume?
answer: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
choices: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Applied Economics
Migrations and Cultures
Ethnic America
context: The Quest for Cosmic Justice (Free Press, 1999) analyzed the unconstrained vision's aspirations to remake outcomes to match a picture of ultimate fairness. It is the closing book in the trilogy. Source: simonandschuster.com (Sowell 1999).

question: Thomas Sowell's 1987 book A Conflict of Visions maps two rival pictures of human nature -- the constrained (people are fixed and flawed) and the unconstrained (people are endlessly improvable). The book carefully describes both views, traces them through named thinkers like Adam Smith and William Godwin, and applies them to specific policy debates. But it deliberately holds back on one final step. What does the book explicitly refuse to do?
answer: Declare either vision correct
choices: Declare either vision correct
Describe the visions in detail
Trace the visions through named thinkers
Apply the visions to specific policy debates
context: Sowell's methodological restraint: the book maps the disagreement without declaring which vision is right. Kids learn to RECOGNIZE which vision is speaking, not which is right. The bank replicates that restraint. Source: Sowell (1987), Introduction.

question: The economist Thomas Sowell's Conflict of Visions framework helps explain something puzzling: professional economists and grassroots activists often talk past each other on the exact same policy question, as if they're not even hearing each other. Sowell says both sides may know the facts equally well -- the disagreement runs deeper than that. What is the underlying source of the gap, according to Sowell?
answer: Each side operates from a different picture of what humans essentially are
choices: Each side operates from a different picture of what humans essentially are
One side has poor mathematical training
One side ignores empirical data on principle
One side is paid by wealthy donors and the other is not
context: The unconstrained-vision speaker sees trade-off talk as failure of will; the constrained-vision speaker sees solution talk as naive utopianism. Both are reasoning inside internally-coherent frameworks -- the gap is the pre-analytical vision, not the argument at the surface. Source: Sowell (1987), Chapters 4-6.

question: Sending an email costs your computer almost nothing, which is why spammers can blast out millions of emails a day for free. But imagine each email required your computer to solve a tiny math puzzle that takes half a second before it could send. For a normal person sending a few emails, that's nothing you'd even notice. What would happen to a spammer who sends millions a day?
answer: They could not afford to keep spamming -- the puzzles would take hours
choices: They could not afford to keep spamming -- the puzzles would take hours
Nothing would change -- spammers have faster computers
They would send twice as much spam
Regular users would stop being able to send email
context: Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997. SpamAssassin is a 2001 Bayesian filter; SPF is a 2003 email-authentication record; DomainKeys is a 2004 Yahoo predecessor of DKIM. None used proof-of-work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: Imagine every email you sent required your computer to solve a small puzzle that took half a second before it could go out. For a normal person sending twenty emails a day that's barely noticeable -- ten seconds of computer work spread across the day. Now imagine a spammer trying to blast out one million emails in a single day, one puzzle per email. Roughly how long would all that puzzle-solving take?
answer: Hours or days
choices: Hours or days
Half a second
A few minutes
Instantaneous
context: One puzzle costs milliseconds; a million puzzles multiply into hours or days on a spammer's hardware. Hashcash imposes no monetary fee or certificate; the asymmetry is pure CPU time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: In 1997 the British computer scientist Adam Back proposed a system called Hashcash to stop email spam. It made every sender's computer solve a puzzle before sending -- a puzzle that is expensive for a computer to solve but almost instant for the receiver to check. This asymmetric idea -- costly to produce, cheap to verify -- has a formal name in computer science, and it is the same idea Bitcoin later used to secure its blockchain. What is it called?
answer: proof-of-work
choices: proof-of-work
proof-of-stake
proof-of-authority
zero-knowledge proof
context: 'Proof-of-work' is the general name for an asymmetric puzzle (search-cost >> verification-cost) that predates Hashcash by a few years (Dwork & Naor 1993 used the term). Proof-of-stake, proof-of-authority, and zero-knowledge proofs are separate cryptographic ideas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: In 1997 the British cypherpunk Adam Back invented Hashcash. It made every email carry a small proof-of-work stamp -- a math puzzle the sender's computer had to solve first. Spammers who blast out millions of emails would find the puzzles far too expensive, while normal users would barely notice. One giant email provider in the mid-2000s tried Hashcash-style stamps as a spam filter, but it never spread everywhere because all email software would have needed to switch at the same time. Which mail service used them?
answer: Microsoft's mail servers
choices: Microsoft's mail servers
Google Gmail
Apple iCloud Mail
AOL Mail
context: Microsoft integrated Hashcash-style postmark stamps into its Exchange/Hotmail anti-spam stack (Penny Black project, 2003 onward). Google, Apple, and AOL relied on other filtering (Bayesian, reputation, DKIM) rather than PoW stamps. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: In 1997 the British cypherpunk Adam Back released Hashcash, which forced computers to burn a bit of real energy to send a message. His idea spread fast on cypherpunk mailing lists -- a scattered group of programmers dreaming up digital cash without banks. Around 1998, two of those builders each designed a digital-money system that leaned directly on Hashcash-style proof-of-work. A decade later, Bitcoin's 2008 white paper would build on both of their designs. Which two builders were they?
answer: Wei Dai (b-money) and Hal Finney (RPOW)
choices: Wei Dai (b-money) and Hal Finney (RPOW)
David Chaum (DigiCash) and Nick Szabo (bit gold)
Phil Zimmermann (PGP) and Eric Hughes (remailers)
Tim May (crypto anarchy) and John Gilmore (toad.com)
context: Wei Dai's b-money (Nov 1998) and Hal Finney's Reusable Proof-of-Work (RPOW, 2004) both cited Hashcash. DigiCash used blind signatures, not PoW; PGP is encryption; Tim May and John Gilmore ran the cypherpunk community infrastructure. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt; https://nakamotoinstitute.org/rpow/.

question: In October 2008 the pseudonymous programmer Satoshi Nakamoto published a white paper for Bitcoin. Its mining system borrowed an idea from Adam Back's 1997 project Hashcash: to add a new block of transactions, a computer must first do real work by solving a math puzzle that costs electricity. Miners around the world race to solve it. Why does building money on top of that puzzle-work idea create scarcity?
answer: Because each new coin costs real energy to mint, so no one can flood the network with cheap coins
choices: Because each new coin costs real energy to mint, so no one can flood the network with cheap coins
Because a government office limits how many coins can be issued each year
Because only rich people are allowed to buy the mining hardware
Because the coins are stored on paper that is hard to copy
context: Satoshi emailed Adam Back in August 2008 asking for comments on the draft, on the strength of Back's Hashcash paper. Back later published the exchange. Chaum, Szabo, and Ulbricht were not part of that pre-publication group; Ulbricht (a physics student in 2008) was still years away from founding Silk Road. Source: https://satoshi.nakamotoinstitute.org/emails/back/.

question: On October 31, 2008, an unknown figure named Satoshi Nakamoto quietly published a nine-page white paper titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' on a small cryptography mailing list. At the very end is a short references section listing eight earlier papers Satoshi drew on. One of them is Adam Back's 1997 Hashcash paper, which introduced the proof-of-work idea Bitcoin uses to secure blocks. Which numbered reference in Satoshi's paper is Hashcash?
answer: Reference 6
choices: Reference 6
Reference 1
Reference 3
Reference 8
context: Hashcash appears as Reference 6 in the Bitcoin white paper. Reference 1 is Wei Dai's b-money; Reference 3 is Haber & Stornetta's 1991 timestamping paper; the reference list ends at 8. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Bitcoin is an open network with no owner, no CEO, and no central foundation gatekeeping its code. The software is public, so any company or team anywhere in the world can build wallets, tools, and improvements for it without asking anyone's permission. Compare this to a normal app store, where one company decides who gets to build what. What does it mean, in practice, that any team can build for Bitcoin freely?
answer: Anyone can improve the network, and competing teams keep each other honest
choices: Anyone can improve the network, and competing teams keep each other honest
Only one official company is allowed to change the code each year
A Bitcoin foundation must approve every new feature before release
Governments choose which teams may work on the software
context: Adam Back co-founded Blockstream in 2014 and became its CEO; Blockstream contributes heavily to Bitcoin Core development and runs the Liquid sidechain. Chainalysis is a blockchain-analytics firm; Coinbase is an exchange; Ripple Labs runs the XRP payment network. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Back.

question: Hashcash was in production email systems for years before Bitcoin existed. When Satoshi later used the same proof-of-work primitive as the heart of Bitcoin's mining, the primitive was put to a very different second job than fighting spam. What core function did PoW take on in Bitcoin that it never played in Hashcash?
answer: settling network-wide agreement on the ordering of transactions
choices: settling network-wide agreement on the ordering of transactions
encrypting the contents of individual messages
authenticating the identity of the sender
compressing block-chain data for storage
context: In Hashcash, PoW just imposes a per-message cost. In Bitcoin, PoW plus the longest-chain rule is the consensus mechanism -- how thousands of nodes agree on the ordering of transactions without a central coordinator. Encryption, sender-authentication, and compression are separate technologies. Source: Nakamoto (2008) sec 4; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: A Bitcoin writer in 2026 looks back at the British cypherpunk Adam Back and his 1997 Hashcash. Before Hashcash, anything on a computer could be copied for free -- an mp3, a photo, a text file, a game. But Back's proof-of-work stamps forced real electricity to be spent to make one. The writer argues Hashcash was the first moment software showed one key economic trait that no earlier digital object had. Which trait does the writer name?
answer: digital scarcity: something expensive to produce and cheap to check
choices: digital scarcity: something expensive to produce and cheap to check
digital anonymity: transactions without identifying information
digital consensus: agreement among many nodes without a leader
digital irreversibility: a payment that cannot be reversed
context: Hashcash's specific contribution was making costly digital tokens verifiable at zero cost -- the first working demonstration of digital scarcity. Anonymity (blind signatures), consensus (Nakamoto's longest chain), and irreversibility (block confirmations) came from different later designs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash; Szabo's later 'shelling out' essay.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen built a mathematical model of how federal government offices grow over time. He argued they end up bigger and better-funded than the public they serve actually needs. His trick was to ask a simple question: what does each government office act like it is trying to make as large as possible, year after year? What did Niskanen say every bureau tries to maximize?
answer: Their bureau's budget
choices: Their bureau's budget
Voter approval
Judicial rulings
Congressional testimony
context: Niskanen's argument: salary, prestige, staff, and career prospects all correlate with agency budget, so career-motivated bureaucrats rationally push to expand it. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (Aldine-Atherton 1971).

question: After the September 11, 2001 terror attacks, the US Congress created a brand-new federal agency called the TSA (Transportation Security Administration) to search bags at every American airport. Twenty years later, in the 2020s, is the TSA smaller, bigger, or gone?
answer: Bigger -- new government agencies almost never shrink
choices: Bigger -- new government agencies almost never shrink
Smaller -- the crisis is over
Gone -- the law only lasted five years
The same size it was on day one
context: The TSA was created by Public Law 107-71, signed November 19, 2001. Founding staff about 30,000; by 2023 approximately 60,000 employees with an annual budget near $10B. Source: dhs.gov (TSA history).

question: The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was created after 9/11 to screen every US airport passenger and bag. In 2015 the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ran a secret test: undercover agents tried to sneak fake guns and bombs through TSA checkpoints across the country. When the results leaked to reporters, the number stunned Congress. What was the reported failure rate?
answer: About 95 percent
choices: About 95 percent
About 5 percent
About 30 percent
About 50 percent
context: The 2015 DHS OIG covert red-team test found TSA screeners missed approximately 95% of test contraband. A 2017 follow-up found little improvement. Results are sensitive to test conditions but were widely reported. Source: oig.dhs.gov (2015 covert testing summary).

question: In August 2022 the US Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act. Tucked inside was 80 billion dollars of new funding for the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the federal tax collector, spread across ten years. Most of the money was set aside not for computers but for hiring an army of new agents and support workers. Roughly how many new IRS hires did the law authorize?
answer: About 87,000
choices: About 87,000
About 8,000
About 800,000
About 500
context: The IRA authorized approximately 87,000 additional IRS hires over ten years, alongside $80B in supplemental funding. Later legislation and rescissions modified the totals; the initial authorization figure was 87,000. Source: irs.gov; cbo.gov (IRA scoring documents).

question: When a problem catches the country's attention, Congress often creates a new federal agency to fix it. Over the decades that follow, the agency's budget grows, its staff grows, and its offices grow. Think of the Department of Education, launched in 1979 to raise US school test scores, or the Department of Homeland Security, launched in 2002 to secure US airports. What often happens to the very problem each agency was created to solve?
answer: The problem does not clearly get better even as the agency grows
choices: The problem does not clearly get better even as the agency grows
The problem is solved within about ten years and the agency is closed
The agency shrinks steadily until it disappears
Congress hands the problem back to the states within a decade
context: The Department of Education Organization Act was signed by Jimmy Carter on October 17, 1979. Reagan campaigned to abolish the department in 1980 but the department survived and grew. Source: ed.gov (department history).

question: Between 1970 and 2010, the United States more than doubled its real per-student spending in public schools. In 1979 President Jimmy Carter created a new federal Department of Education to push that money and set new rules. When researchers measured reading and math scores on major national tests at the end of high school across all those years, what did they usually find?
answer: Scores stay roughly flat, even though spending has gone way up
choices: Scores stay roughly flat, even though spending has gone way up
Scores rise in perfect step with the extra spending
Scores double, matching the rise in per-student funding
Scores fall by about half within the first ten years
context: NAEP long-term-trend twelfth-grade reading and math scores changed very little from 1979 to 2019 despite decades of increased federal education spending. Source: nces.ed.gov (NAEP long-term-trend reports).

question: Since 2001 the Transportation Security Administration has grown to over 60,000 workers guarding US airports. Since its founding the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has grown into one of the largest tax offices on earth. Since 1979 the Department of Education has spent hundreds of billions of dollars trying to raise US test scores. Watching all three across the decades, what single pattern shows up in every one?
answer: Staff and budget grow while the results the agency should deliver do not clearly improve
choices: Staff and budget grow while the results the agency should deliver do not clearly improve
Staff and budget shrink whenever a new president takes office
The results triple every ten years no matter what
Congress shuts each agency down within twenty years
context: The recurring pattern across all three: growing staff, growing budget, and difficulty demonstrating proportional improvement on the metric the agency was created to move. Niskanen's model predicts exactly this. Source: Niskanen (1971); GAO agency performance reports.

question: Imagine a US government office where the yearly budget is set by how many workers it employs, not by anything it actually finishes or achieves. Public-choice economists like James Buchanan spent careers studying what this incentive creates. Over ten years, how does an office like this tend to change?
answer: It hires more people and finds new tasks so its budget keeps growing
choices: It hires more people and finds new tasks so its budget keeps growing
It shrinks its own staff to save taxpayer money
It closes down once its original job is finished
Its workers refuse promotions to keep the office small
context: James Q. Wilson, Bureaucracy: What Government Agencies Do and Why They Do It (Basic Books, 1989). Wilson analyzed observable, measurable outputs versus procedural rule-following as key determinants of agency behavior. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Q._Wilson.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen wrote a book arguing that government agencies naturally push to grow their own budgets, whether or not the extra money produces more real results. His public-choice framework gives citizens a specific test to run whenever an agency claims it needs more funding. What comparative test does Niskanen's framework demand?
answer: Show that the last ten percent of prior budget produced roughly ten percent of the output
choices: Show that the last ten percent of prior budget produced roughly ten percent of the output
Show that the agency's staff outnumber the affected industry's staff
Show that the agency's building is smaller than the average corporate headquarters
Show that the agency chief holds a doctorate in public administration
context: The marginal-cost / marginal-product test: if the last dollar of prior spending was well below its cost in output, adding more is even less likely to be worthwhile. Niskanen predicts agencies systematically resist any measurement scheme that would allow this comparison. Source: Niskanen (1971), Chapter 5.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen argued that government offices are run by people who want bigger budgets, more staff under them, and more power -- not by people who want to shrink the office they work in. Imagine a school district hires 100 workers to run its lunch program. Ten years later there are 400 workers, even though the number of kids eating lunch has not grown. A public-choice thinker following Niskanen would say the growth mostly reflects what?
answer: What the workers themselves want, not what the job actually needs
choices: What the workers themselves want, not what the job actually needs
A big rise in the number of kids eating school lunch
Workers being lazier than they used to be
New rules from a distant state agency
context: Niskanen's payoff: whenever budgets and headcounts grow while measurable output does not, the presumption should be that the growth reflects internal incentives, not rising external demand. The move is recognition, not a policy verdict. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971).

question: The American economist William Niskanen warned in 1971 that government offices tend to grow past what their real work requires. In December 2024, President-elect Donald Trump announced a new federal effort, led by Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy, to hunt for exactly that pattern -- bureaus that had bloated without doing more real work. Its short name was a joke on a popular internet meme about a Shiba Inu dog. What was the effort's full proposed name?
answer: The Department of Government Efficiency
choices: The Department of Government Efficiency
The Federal Streamlining Office
The Bureau of Bureaucratic Review
The Council on Public Administration Reform
context: The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) proposal was announced in December 2024 as a modern institutional attempt to apply Niskanen-style diagnosis to federal agency growth. The acronym echoed a viral meme. Source: contemporary press coverage 2024-25.

question: Imagine an insurance company that sells home-loan insurance to hundreds of banks across the country. If a single bank has a bad year and a few loans go bad, the insurer pays that bank and moves on. But suppose home loans start going bad everywhere at once — every state, every bank, all at the same time. What danger does the insurance company now face?
answer: The company runs out of money -- it sold more coverage than it could ever pay
choices: The company runs out of money -- it sold more coverage than it could ever pay
The company makes huge profits from all the new claims
The company gets more customers than ever before
Home prices go up automatically
context: American International Group, founded 1919, was one of the largest insurance companies in the world. Its Financial Products unit had written CDS coverage on hundreds of billions in mortgage-backed securities held by every major bank. Source: Grokipedia 'American International Group' (2026-09-05).

question: On September 15, 2008, the investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed and Wall Street panicked. The next day, September 16, the Federal Reserve made an emergency loan to a failing insurance giant called American International Group (AIG), which had promised to cover hundreds of billions of dollars in bad mortgage bets. In return, the Fed took nearly 80 percent of the company. How big was that first emergency loan?
answer: About 85 billion dollars
choices: About 85 billion dollars
About 8 billion dollars
About 300 billion dollars
About 15 billion dollars
context: The initial September 16 2008 commitment was $85 billion, later expanded to a total of $182 billion -- the largest single bailout in US history. Source: Grokipedia 'AIG bailout' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008, the US Federal Reserve announced an 85 billion dollar emergency rescue of the giant insurance company AIG (American International Group), which had bet wrongly on the American housing market. Over the following months the total commitment kept growing well beyond that first size. What was the peak commitment?
answer: About 182 billion dollars
choices: About 182 billion dollars
About 85 billion dollars
About 500 billion dollars
About 45 billion dollars
context: The $182 billion peak commitment is the largest single-firm government rescue in US financial history. It exceeded the entire TARP allocation used on the banks combined. Source: Grokipedia 'AIG bailout' (2026-09-05).

question: Historians looking back at the September 2008 rescue of the insurance giant AIG (American International Group) say the AIG bailout was really a rescue of another group of firms. AIG had sold credit default swap (CDS) insurance to big Wall Street banks, and those banks would have taken enormous losses if AIG had gone bust. Whose rescue was the AIG rescue really?
answer: AIG's counterparties -- the banks that had bought CDS protection from it
choices: AIG's counterparties -- the banks that had bought CDS protection from it
AIG's retail insurance policyholders
AIG's foreign subsidiaries in Asia
AIG's executive stockholders
context: AIG immediately used the loaned money to pay CDS collateral at 100 cents on the dollar to its counterparties. Every major dealer that had bought protection was made whole through the insurance conduit. Source: SIGTARP Report, October 2009.

question: In 2008, the giant US insurance company American International Group (AIG) had promised to pay Wall Street banks if their risky mortgage bets went bad. When those bets collapsed, the US government stepped in and made AIG cover every promise at full price, using taxpayer money. Which banks collected the biggest checks in that bailout?
answer: The biggest investment banks, the ones who had made the largest risky bets
choices: The biggest investment banks, the ones who had made the largest risky bets
Small local savings banks that never made risky bets
Foreign banks with no operations in the country
Only the banks that had already gone out of business
context: Goldman Sachs received about $12.9 billion in CDS collateral through AIG. Deutsche Bank received about $11.8 billion, Societe Generale about $11.9 billion, and Merrill Lynch about $6.8 billion. Source: SIGTARP Report, October 2009.

question: During the 2008 financial crisis, the US government bailed out AIG, a giant American insurance company on the brink of collapse. Congress set up a special watchdog office, the Special Inspector General for the Troubled Asset Relief Program (SIGTARP), to track where the bailout money actually went. In 2009 the SIGTARP report showed the AIG rescue was really a pipe that paid the big Wall Street banks in full -- 100 cents on the dollar. The man who led SIGTARP paid for that report in his career. Who was he?
answer: Neil Barofsky at SIGTARP
choices: Neil Barofsky at SIGTARP
Elizabeth Warren at the COP
Sheila Bair at the FDIC
Mark Calabria at the FHFA
context: Barofsky, the Special Inspector General for TARP, published a series of reports 2009-2011 documenting exactly how AIG's rescue moved money to Goldman, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch, and others. His book Bailout (2012) tells the story. Source: SIGTARP Reports 2009-2011.

question: In the 2000s, the American insurance giant AIG sold contracts called credit default swaps -- promises to pay out if certain mortgage bonds went bad. Because AIG carried a top AAA credit rating, no regulator made it set aside cash to back those promises. Then in September 2008, as the housing market cracked, AIG's credit rating was cut. Under the terms of its own contracts, what suddenly happened?
answer: The company owed billions in collateral overnight and could not pay
choices: The company owed billions in collateral overnight and could not pay
Nothing changed because credit ratings are only for show
The company was allowed to keep promising with no cash reserves
The government cancelled all the promises for free
context: AIG's counterparties had accepted its promise to pay without collateral, trusting the AAA rating. When rating agencies downgraded AIG in September 2008, collateral demands surged past what the firm could raise. Source: Grokipedia 'AIG Financial Products' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 the Federal Reserve rescued American International Group (AIG), a giant US insurance company that had covered hundreds of billions of dollars in risky mortgage bets and lost. The Fed poured 85 billion dollars into AIG to keep it alive rather than let it fail. Every other big Wall Street firm was watching closely. What lesson do those big firms take away from a rescue like that?
answer: Take even bigger risks next time, since the government will step in if they fail
choices: Take even bigger risks next time, since the government will step in if they fail
Never take any risk again, since the rescue was so painful
Ask the Fed for permission before every new bet
Trust that regulators can predict every future crisis
context: Geithner led the New York Fed 2003-2009 and personally designed the AIG rescue. He became Treasury Secretary under Obama in January 2009. Source: Grokipedia 'Timothy Geithner' (2026-09-05).

question: During a financial crisis, the government rescues a huge insurance company, saying it is to protect regular families' insurance. Later, people find most of the rescue money flowed straight through the company to big banks the insurance company owed. What is the 'unseen' part?
answer: The rescue money mostly went to the big banks, not to protecting regular policyholders
choices: The rescue money mostly went to the big banks, not to protecting regular policyholders
The insurance company's workers all lost their jobs anyway
Every branch office had to close within a year
Foreign banks refused to accept the rescue money
context: The AIG rescue was a bank bailout laundered through an insurance company -- avoiding the political optics of paying Goldman and Deutsche Bank directly while producing the same substantive result. Source: Barofsky, Bailout (2012).

question: Public-choice economists warn that when a government rescue is set up so voters cannot see who really gets the money -- like the 2008 AIG bailout that quietly paid off the big Wall Street banks holding AIG's insurance at 100 cents on the dollar -- two things tend to happen in the years that follow. What are they?
answer: Big risk-takers expect more rescues, and public trust in the government shrinks
choices: Big risk-takers expect more rescues, and public trust in the government shrinks
All future rescues fail to help anyone
Small banks always outperform big banks afterward
Regulators successfully stop all future risky bets
context: The AIG conduit worked in the moment but corroded institutional legitimacy over years. Every future risk-taker learned that political optics can be managed while counterparties get paid. Source: Barofsky, Bailout (2012).

question: From 1938 to 1978, the US Civil Aeronautics Board in Washington set the ticket prices for every American airline. An airline could not lower a fare without first asking this federal panel for permission. Who gained the most from this forty-year rule?
answer: The existing airlines -- they did not have to fear a cheaper competitor
choices: The existing airlines -- they did not have to fear a cheaper competitor
Passengers -- prices went down every year
New airline start-ups -- it was easy to open one
Airport janitors -- they got a raise
context: The Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938 created the authority that became the Civil Aeronautics Board in 1940. The CAB issued 'certificates of public convenience and necessity' specifying exact endpoints and stops, and set fares. The ICC regulated railroads and trucking, the FAA handled safety and air traffic, the FTC advertising and competition. Sources: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: From 1938 to 1978, a US agency called the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) decided which airlines could fly which routes and how much a plane ticket could cost. The Board never told the public this was a favor to the big established airlines. Instead it warned that letting anyone fly anywhere at any price would unleash one specific danger. Which danger did the Board name?
answer: Ruinous competition that would bankrupt carriers and strand small towns
choices: Ruinous competition that would bankrupt carriers and strand small towns
Crowded skies that air traffic controllers could not handle safely
Foreign carriers taking over the profitable American routes
Airlines cutting maintenance to survive on cheaper tickets
context: The CAB's stated purpose was to avert 'destructive' or 'ruinous' competition, keep the established trunk carriers solvent, and sustain service to smaller communities by cross-subsidy. Because the Board treated large price differences as destabilising, airlines competed on meals, seat width and schedules rather than fares. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: The Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) was the US agency that, from 1938 to 1978, decided which airlines could fly which US routes. Between 1950 and 1974, seventy-nine new companies applied to the CAB asking for permission to fly a US airline route. Each one hoped to break into the market and compete with the big established carriers. Of those seventy-nine hopeful applications, how many did the CAB approve?
answer: None of them
choices: None of them
Three of them
Eleven of them
Twenty-six of them
context: Between 1950 and 1974 the CAB received 79 applications from firms outside the domestic scheduled airline industry, and not one was granted; with minor exceptions the Board had not even set such applications for hearing since 1960. The protected 'trunk carriers' faced no new entrants for forty years. Source: Journal of Air Law and Commerce, vol. 41.

question: In the 1960s and 1970s, Pacific Southwest in California and Southwest in Texas sold tickets 30 to 60 percent cheaper than other airlines. Their planes flew fuller too. The Civil Aeronautics Board never stopped them. Why couldn't the Board touch them?
answer: Each flew only inside one state, so its business never reached the Board's authority
choices: Each flew only inside one state, so its business never reached the Board's authority
Each was owned by its own employees, an arrangement the Board's rules did not cover
Each carried mail under a contract that exempted its fares from Board review
Each used aircraft small enough to be classed as air taxis, which were exempt
context: The CAB regulated INTERSTATE air transport. PSA in California and Southwest in Texas flew only intrastate, escaping the Board entirely, and their fares ran roughly 30-60 percent below comparable regulated fares with higher load factors. The air-taxi exemption was real -- Part 298 covered aircraft under 30 seats -- but neither airline used it. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: Robert Timm ran the Civil Aeronautics Board until 1974. He set a rule that airlines should earn 12 percent on their money. Senator Ted Kennedy's team later asked the Justice Department to look at him for a gift he took from the airlines he oversaw. What was the gift?
answer: A golf holiday in Bermuda
choices: A golf holiday in Bermuda
A seat on a carrier's board of directors
Lifetime first-class travel for his family
A consulting fee routed through a trade group
context: Timm, CAB chair until 1974, prioritised ensuring scheduled airlines made a 12 percent return on investment and was caught accepting a Bermuda golf vacation from those airlines; Kennedy's subcommittee referred him to the Justice Department. Kennedy's 1975 hearings, with Stephen Breyer as counsel, publicised both this and the low intrastate fares. Source: Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: In 1977, President Jimmy Carter put Alfred Kahn in charge of the Civil Aeronautics Board. Kahn was a Cornell professor and lifelong Democrat who had written two books on how regulated markets work. He liked to say he could not tell one plane from another. He then said something about planes that stuck to him for life. What did he say they were to him?
answer: All just marginal costs with wings
choices: All just marginal costs with wings
Buses that happen to leave the ground
Tubes full of people and kerosene
The most protected machines in America
context: Kahn (1917-2010), author of The Economics of Regulation (1970-71) and called the father of airline deregulation, said: 'I can't tell one plane from the other. To me, they're all just marginal costs with wings.' A marginal cost is what one more unit -- here one more passenger on a flight already leaving -- actually adds to cost, and Kahn's point was that fares should track it. Source: Wikipedia 'Alfred E. Kahn'.

question: Under the Civil Aeronautics Board, flights to small towns had been paid for out of sight: passengers on busy trunk routes were charged above-competitive fares, and the surplus quietly covered the thin routes. When Congress ended fare control in 1978 that hidden transfer had nowhere left to hide, so Congress built a replacement. What did it create?
answer: The Essential Air Service programme, funded as a line in the federal budget
choices: The Essential Air Service programme, funded as a line in the federal budget
A rule obliging every major carrier to keep flying a quota of rural routes
A landing-fee rebate that small airports could offer to attract carriers
A rural air mail contract system administered by the Postal Service
context: Congress created Essential Air Service alongside the 1978 act to keep flights going to low-density airports formerly cross-subsidised under the CAB regime. The economics lesson is Bastiat's: the cost had always been paid, but by invisible passengers on other routes; deregulation did not abolish it so much as move it into daylight where a legislature has to vote on it. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'.

question: The Airline Deregulation Act cleared Congress by crushing margins -- 82 to 4 in the Senate, 356 to 6 in the House -- and President Carter signed it on October 24, 1978. The lopsided votes hid a long and bitter fight, and it is the identity of the losing side that economists still cite about the whole episode. Who fought hardest to keep the Board's controls?
answer: The established trunk airlines and the Air Line Pilots Association
choices: The established trunk airlines and the Air Line Pilots Association
The consumer movement, with Ralph Nader leading the opposition
The Federal Aviation Administration and the big airport authorities
The aircraft manufacturers, Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, together
context: The fiercest resistance came from the incumbent trunk carriers and ALPA -- the parties forty years of route protection had shielded -- which is Stigler's regulatory capture visible from the outside: an industry defending its regulator. ALPA lost, and low-fare, often non-union entrants eroded the wage premiums it had won. Nader in fact SUPPORTED deregulation, on the ground that CAB rules propped up monopoly. American Airlines chairman Albert Casey gave in with: 'If you're not going to protect us, get out of our way.' Sources: ALPA, 'From the Hill'; Cato, 'Alfred Kahn, 1917-2010'; Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'.

question: In 1963 a young New York economist named Murray Rothbard published his Austrian-school account of the 1929 to 1933 slump that had wrecked the American economy. He blamed the Federal Reserve, not free markets, for the crash and the depression. What did Rothbard title the book?
answer: America's Great Depression
choices: America's Great Depression
The Road to Serfdom
A Monetary History of the United States
The General Theory of Employment
context: Published by D. Van Nostrand of Princeton in 1963, 361 pages. Rothbard (1926-1995) was 37 when the book appeared. It became the definitive Austrian-school treatment of the 1929-33 downturn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America%27s_Great_Depression.

question: In 1963 the Austrian-school economist Murray Rothbard published a book called America's Great Depression. It re-examined the terrible economic slump of 1929 to 1933, when thousands of US banks failed and unemployment climbed to nearly a quarter of the workforce. Rothbard argued the free market was not to blame — two other culprits were. Which two did his account name?
answer: The Federal Reserve and President Hoover
choices: The Federal Reserve and President Hoover
Wall Street speculators and the gold standard
Consumer debt and rural bank failures
European war debts and immigration limits
context: Rothbard argued Fed credit expansion in the 1920s produced the boom that had to bust, and then Hoover's activist response after October 1929 turned what should have been a short liquidation into a decade-long depression. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: In his 1963 book America's Great Depression, the Austrian economist Murray Rothbard pinned the reckless 1920s credit boom -- the one that led straight to the 1929 stock market crash -- on one specific Federal Reserve official. Rothbard said this man had loosened American credit in the mid-1920s partly to help Britain hold gold, inflating the US stock bubble. Which Fed official did Rothbard blame?
answer: Benjamin Strong, Governor of the New York Fed
choices: Benjamin Strong, Governor of the New York Fed
Marriner Eccles, Chairman of the Board of Governors
Paul Warburg, founding member of the Federal Reserve Board
Andrew Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury
context: Rothbard singled out Strong as the dominant force at the Fed during the 1920s. Strong pushed easy credit in part to help Britain sustain the pound after Britain's 1925 return to gold at the pre-war parity, working closely with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: In late October 1929 the US stock market crashed. Weeks later, in November, President Herbert Hoover called the country's top factory owners to a series of meetings at the White House. Murray Rothbard's book America's Great Depression tells what Hoover pressed the industrialists to promise as unemployment began to rise. What did Hoover push them to promise?
answer: That they would not cut wage rates
choices: That they would not cut wage rates
That they would suspend all foreign lending
That they would sell their gold holdings to the Treasury
That they would freeze retail prices for one year
context: The centerpiece conference was November 21, 1929, with figures like Henry Ford and Pierre du Pont. Rothbard argued Hoover's high-wage policy blocked the labor-market adjustment that had ended earlier American depressions in eighteen months or less. Source: mises.org/online-book/progressive-era/15-herbert-hoover-and-myth-laissez-faire.

question: In 1920 the US economy fell into a sharp recession. Unemployment jumped to about 12 percent, and industrial output dropped roughly 17 percent -- a bust deeper than the early years of the Great Depression that came a decade later. President Warren Harding took an unusual path for a modern politician: instead of launching new spending programs, he cut the federal budget almost in half and let wages and prices fall to new levels. What happened next?
answer: The recession ends within about a year and a half as prices reset
choices: The recession ends within about a year and a half as prices reset
Unemployment stays at 12 percent for a full decade
The economy shrinks by another 17 percent the following year
Prices freeze in place and no one buys anything
context: The Harding administration slashed the federal budget as the 1920-21 slump deepened. Rothbard, and later Austrian writers, treated this 'forgotten depression' as the natural experiment showing that non-intervention produced a fast recovery, while Hoover's opposite response after 1929 produced the opposite result. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/forgotten-depression-1920.

question: In 1930, deep in the worst downturn the United States had ever seen, Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act. It slapped a huge extra tax on nearly every product coming into the country from abroad, promising to protect American workers. The same shape shows up every time a country tries this move during a recession. What do the other countries usually do next?
answer: They pass their own big tariffs on that country's exports, and world trade collapses further
choices: They pass their own big tariffs on that country's exports, and world trade collapses further
They cut all their tariffs to zero to keep trade flowing
They ignore it and keep buying that country's exports at the same rate
They send extra help to soften the effect on the recession
context: Signed June 17, 1930. Rothbard argued the tariff choked off foreign trade at precisely the moment the world economy needed liquidation and adjustment, spreading the American slump internationally. Source: millercenter.org/the-presidency/presidential-speeches/june-16-1930-message-regarding-smoot-hawley-tariff-act.

question: In 1932 President Herbert Hoover created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC), a brand-new federal agency whose whole job was to make giant emergency loans to banks and railroads that were about to fail. Several were saved from bankruptcy that year. But rescue programs like the RFC carry a long-run danger that plays out over the decades that follow. What is the main long-run risk?
answer: Firms take bigger risks in the future, expecting a rescue loan if they get in trouble
choices: Firms take bigger risks in the future, expecting a rescue loan if they get in trouble
Firms become more careful because the loans come with strict rules
Banks and railroads promptly refund the loans within one year
The government makes a profit large enough to end all taxes
context: Signed January 22, 1932. The RFC extended over a billion dollars in loans in its first six months. Roosevelt kept the agency and expanded it in 1933. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/reconstruction-finance-corporation.

question: A common school story about the Great Depression says President Herbert Hoover did nothing as the economy fell after the October 1929 stock crash, and only when Franklin Roosevelt took office in 1933 did the government finally step in with big programs. But historians like Murray Rothbard and Amity Shlaes, who look at the actual records of Hoover's four years in office, find what?
answer: The first president also ran big spending and price-support programs
choices: The first president also ran big spending and price-support programs
Neither president did anything until the 1940s war spending
The first president perfectly stayed out of the economy
The economy recovered fully before either president acted
context: Rothbard wrote that 'if we define New Deal as an antidepression program marked by extensive governmental economic planning and intervention, Herbert Clark Hoover must be considered the founder of the New Deal in America.' Amity Shlaes's 2007 book The Forgotten Man popularized this view. Source: mises.org/online-book/progressive-era/15-herbert-hoover-and-myth-laissez-faire.

question: A high-school textbook usually tells you the October 1929 stock-market crash caused the Great Depression. In his 1963 book America's Great Depression, the Austrian economist Murray Rothbard pressed back using a reasoning move from his school of thought known as Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT). ABCT focuses on how central banks like the Federal Reserve steer the boom-bust cycle by pumping cheap credit into a country. Which reasoning move does Rothbard press against the crash-caused-it story?
answer: The 1929 bust was the inevitable liquidation of Fed-created 1920s malinvestment, not itself the cause
choices: The 1929 bust was the inevitable liquidation of Fed-created 1920s malinvestment, not itself the cause
The crash was psychological panic that spread by newspaper coverage rather than by real economic forces
The crash was caused by insufficient consumer spending and could have been offset by fiscal stimulus
The crash reflected structural overproduction in American manufacturing outrunning global demand
context: ABCT holds that artificially cheap credit steers savings into projects that only look profitable while rates are suppressed. When rates normalize, those projects reveal themselves as malinvestment. On this reading the 1929 crash was the correction, not the disease. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: Murray Rothbard's book America's Great Depression, published in 1963, was not a stand-alone project. It grew directly out of a much larger treatise Rothbard had finished the year before -- a full Austrian-school economics textbook covering money, prices, production, and government intervention. Which larger 1962 Rothbard treatise was America's Great Depression written as a companion volume to?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
What Has Government Done to Our Money?
context: Man, Economy, and State was Rothbard's major economic treatise, published in 1962 by D. Van Nostrand with Volker Fund support. America's Great Depression, published one year later by the same house, applied its Austrian framework to a single historical case. Source: mises.org/austrian-economics-newsletter/interview-murray-rothbard-man-economy-and-state-mises-and-future-austrian-school.

question: A student compares two Fed-centered accounts of the 1929-1933 downturn. The Friedman-Schwartz 1963 Monetary History blames the Fed for CONTRACTING the money supply by roughly a third after the crash. Rothbard's 1963 monograph blames the Fed for a different failure mode across the whole preceding decade. Which failure mode does Rothbard blame?
answer: Expanding credit through the 1920s to support Britain's return to gold, producing the malinvestment that had to bust
choices: Expanding credit through the 1920s to support Britain's return to gold, producing the malinvestment that had to bust
Refusing to lend to solvent banks facing liquidity runs after October 1929
Failing to enforce the 1913 Federal Reserve Act's real-bills doctrine on member banks
Overpaying gold miners at the statutory dollar-per-ounce rate throughout the 1920s
context: Rothbard's account is a CAUSE-of-the-boom story; Friedman-Schwartz's is a CAUSE-of-the-post-crash-contraction story. Both blame the Fed but for opposite mechanisms. Rothbard traced the cheap-credit push to Benjamin Strong's cooperation with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman after Britain returned to gold in 1925 at the pre-war parity. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: In 1816, after the War of 1812, the US Congress chartered a giant private bank based in Philadelphia. Only this bank could print paper notes accepted nationwide, and only this bank could hold the US Treasury's money. Its powerful president from 1823 onward was Nicholas Biddle of Philadelphia. What was the bank called?
answer: The Second Bank of the United States
choices: The Second Bank of the United States
The First Bank of the United States
The Bank of New York
The Bank of Massachusetts
context: The Second Bank of the United States was chartered for a 20-year term in 1816 as the follow-on to Hamilton's First Bank (which had expired in 1811). Biddle ran it from 1823. Source: Grokipedia 'Second Bank of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1830s US President Andrew Jackson threw himself into a fight to kill the Second Bank of the United States, a giant national bank chartered by Congress and headquartered in Philadelphia. Jackson believed the Bank was controlled by a small circle of rich eastern shareholders and foreign investors. What danger was Jackson worried about?
answer: A small group having control over the whole country's money
choices: A small group having control over the whole country's money
The bank charging too little interest on loans
Foreign countries printing US dollars
The bank giving too many loans to poor farmers
context: Jackson won the 1828 election on a populist platform. His fight against the Bank became the defining political conflict of his two terms. Source: Grokipedia 'Andrew Jackson' (2026-09-05).

question: On July 10, 1832, Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to renew the Second Bank of the United States. It became one of the most famous vetoes in US history. His veto letter said Congress could not hand out special deals that shifted wealth in one direction. What did his letter say the Bank did?
answer: Made the rich richer and the potent more powerful
