question: A book on the 1929 stock crash blamed one particular Federal Reserve action during the 1920s. The Federal Reserve pushed interest rates artificially low to help foreign banks. What does Austrian economics say cheap central-bank credit does to an economy?
answer: It fuels a boom that ends in a crash as bad bets get exposed
choices: It fuels a boom that ends in a crash as bad bets get exposed
It permanently makes everyone richer with no downside
It has no effect on business decisions of any kind
It only touches prices, never the pattern of production
context: Strong ran the New York Fed 1914-1928 and drove the Fed's 1920s low-rate policy, partly to help Britain return to gold at the pre-war parity. Rothbard traced the boom to Strong's inflationary credit expansion and the 1929 collapse to its inevitable correction. Marriner Eccles chaired the Fed 1934-1948; Paul Warburg was a founding governor 1914-1918; William McChesney Martin chaired 1951-1970. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America%27s_Great_Depression.

question: A town builds too many empty office towers during a lending boom. When the boom ends, buyers won't touch them at boom-era prices. Austrian-school economists say: if the government now steps in and buys the empty towers at boom prices, what happens to the correction?
answer: The correction drags on, because bad projects are kept alive instead of cleared
choices: The correction drags on, because bad projects are kept alive instead of cleared
The correction ends quickly and demand fully returns
Deflation is prevented and prices stay stable
The length of the correction is unchanged
context: The Austrian argument is that a bust is DIAGNOSTIC as well as painful: the projects that fail are the ones that never should have been started, and liquidating them frees capital and labour for uses that DO reflect real time preferences. Keynesian stimulus -- keeping demand up for the malinvested projects -- protects them from liquidation and stretches the correction. Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) presses this reading of the 1930s: Hoover's and Roosevelt's interventions prolonged the depression they were supposed to cure. Source: mises.org/online-book/skyscraper-curse-and-how-austrian-economists-predicted-every-major-economic-crisis-last-century/chapter-24-what-wrong-abct.

question: The Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued that in a healthy market -- one where a central bank isn't meddling with interest rates -- borrowing costs would settle at a level where the total amount people want to save exactly equals the total amount businesses want to borrow for real projects like factories, farms, and new equipment. What is the technical name for that reference rate?
answer: The natural rate of interest
choices: The natural rate of interest
The federal funds rate
The prime rate
The Wicksellian target rate
context: Mises and Hayek inherit the 'natural rate' concept from the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell (Interest and Prices, 1898): it is the interest rate at which voluntary saving and voluntary investment would balance in the absence of monetary distortion. When the central-bank rate is BELOW the natural rate, credit expands beyond real saving and malinvestment follows. The federal funds rate is the Fed's actual operating target; the prime rate is a commercial bank benchmark; 'Wicksellian target' is not a standard term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: John Maynard Keynes wrote a famous 1936 book on the boom-bust cycle. He turned down the monetary story and instead pointed to a mental force at the wheel -- spontaneous urges to invest that swing between confidence and panic. Keynes gave those urges a memorable two-word name. Which name?
answer: Animal spirits
choices: Animal spirits
Bounded rationality
Rational expectations
Adaptive expectations
context: Keynes: 'Most, probably, of our decisions to do something positive... can only be taken as a result of animal spirits -- of a spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction.' The clash is direct: Austrians say the cycle is a MONETARY event with a specific institutional cause and a specific remedy (stop suppressing the rate); Keynes says it is a PSYCHOLOGICAL event with no simple institutional cause and a specific remedy (stabilise demand). Bounded rationality is Herbert Simon 1955; rational and adaptive expectations are 1960s-70s macro developments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_spirits_(Keynes).

question: In 2000, the American economist Thomas Sowell -- a former Marxist who had become a Chicago-school defender of free markets, then 70 years old -- published a book aimed squarely at a working adult who had never taken an economics class. Basic Books put it out. By 2015 it had gone through five editions and been translated into more than a dozen languages. What was the book called?
answer: Basic Economics
choices: Basic Economics
Free to Choose
Economics in One Lesson
The Wealth of Nations
context: Basic Economics grew across five editions from about 500 pages in 2000 to over 700 by 2015. Each new edition added case studies rather than abstract theory. Free to Choose was Milton and Rose Friedman's 1980 book; Economics in One Lesson was Henry Hazlitt's 1946 one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Thomas Sowell is an American economist trained at the University of Chicago. In 2000 he published Basic Economics, a book written to explain how economies work to readers who had never taken a class. Later editions run about 800 pages. One choice by Sowell makes his book stand out from every other economics textbook on the shelf. What is that choice?
answer: No graphs, no equations, no algebra anywhere in the book
choices: No graphs, no equations, no algebra anywhere in the book
Every chapter is written entirely in verse
The entire book is presented in dialogue form
Every example is drawn from ancient Rome
context: Sowell's earlier 1971 textbook 'Economics: Analysis and Issues' had used the traditional graph-and-equation format. Basic Economics was his conscious departure from that model, aimed at a working adult reader without prior training. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics (2000) uses real cases instead of math models. It draws on Ghana's rice farms, US rent control, apartheid South Africa's labor rules, Ireland's famine, and post-Soviet Europe. Rather than march through theories one at a time, Sowell groups his chapters a different way. How does the book group its chapters?
answer: Organization by institution -- Prices, Production, Work and Pay, Time and Risk, National, International
choices: Organization by institution -- Prices, Production, Work and Pay, Time and Risk, National, International
Organization by year of publication of the underlying research
Organization by geographic region only (Africa, Asia, Europe, Americas)
Organization alphabetically by economist name
context: Each chapter examines the institution through case studies, then returns repeatedly to the same handful of questions: What are the trade-offs? At what cost? Compared to what? What are the incentives? Who bears the unseen costs? Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: In 1932 the British economist Lionel Robbins wrote a famous definition of the field: economics is the study of how people use scarce resources that could serve many different needs. Because time, money, and effort are always limited but human wants are not, what kind of decision does Robbins's definition force on every person, every single day?
answer: A tradeoff -- picking one use means giving up others
choices: A tradeoff -- picking one use means giving up others
A calculation with a single correct answer
A random guess with no real consequences
A vote where the majority always gets more
context: Robbins's 1932 'An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science' put the scarcity-with-alternative-uses definition into the modern discipline's vocabulary. Sowell adopts and popularizes it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lionel_Robbins.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics (2000) is a long book — 800 pages, meant to be read across a summer. Fans often describe it as the broader version of an older short book from 1946, one so tight a reader can finish it in a single afternoon. That older book argued that policies must be judged by their unseen effects, not their good intentions. What was the older short book?
answer: Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson'
choices: Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson'
John Maynard Keynes's 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'
Friedrich Hayek's 'Prices and Production'
Ludwig von Mises's 'Bureaucracy'
context: Hazlitt (1946) built his book around a single lesson: consider the effect of a policy not only on those it obviously affects, but on all groups over the long term. Sowell's Basic Economics applies the same reasoning approach across scenes and institutions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: Thomas Sowell is an American economist at the Hoover Institution who writes plainly for ordinary readers. In 2000 he published 'Basic Economics,' a book with almost no charts or equations that explains prices, wages, and trade one clear paragraph at a time. Since that first edition it has become the book most often recommended as the first serious economics reading for a high schooler or a curious adult. What is one specific reason for that reach?
answer: It has been translated into eight or more languages and is widely used in home-school economics curricula
choices: It has been translated into eight or more languages and is widely used in home-school economics curricula
It is required reading in every US public high school by federal mandate
It is bundled free with every US passport issued since 2020
It has never been published in any language other than English
context: The no-graphs-no-equations design makes translation easier and makes the book accessible to students without a math background. Home-school networks, in particular, have used it as a primary economics text. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: In the 1800s England kept a set of laws called the Corn Laws — a big extra tax on wheat brought in from other countries. English landlords, who owned the wheat fields, loved the tax because it kept the price of their wheat high. But bread is made from wheat, and everyone eats bread every day. Who was hurt most by the tax?
answer: Poor families -- the tax makes bread more expensive every day
choices: Poor families -- the tax makes bread more expensive every day
The landlords -- they earn less on their wheat
Ship captains -- the harbor is less crowded
Nobody -- the tax just disappears
context: The Anti-Corn Law League, founded in Manchester by Richard Cobden and John Bright, was the classic 19th-century mass free-trade movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anti-Corn_Law_League.

question: In the 1840s two Manchester cotton merchants led a huge public campaign in Britain to repeal the Corn Laws — the tariffs that kept bread expensive and enriched landowners. They founded the Anti-Corn Law League, toured the country giving speeches, and won free trade for grain in 1846. Both men later became famous names in Parliament. Who was this pair?
answer: Richard Cobden and John Bright
choices: Richard Cobden and John Bright
William Gladstone and Benjamin Disraeli
Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington
Lord Palmerston and Lord John Russell
context: Cobden (1804-1865) and Bright (1811-1889) led the League from Manchester through seven years of relentless public campaigning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anti-Corn_Law_League.

question: In 1846 the British Prime Minister Sir Robert Peel pushed a bill through Parliament repealing the Corn Laws — the tariffs on imported grain that had kept the price of bread high for years. His own Conservative party was furious because rural landowners lost their protection from cheaper foreign grain. Peel had to resign four days later. What did his action show about tariffs?
answer: They can help a small group but hurt millions of ordinary buyers
choices: They can help a small group but hurt millions of ordinary buyers
They always help everyone in the country equally
They never split political parties
They automatically raise wages for workers
context: Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws on June 25, 1846 was the classic case study of a free-trade movement winning against a landed political interest. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Repeal_of_the_Corn_Laws.

question: In the 1840s the French economist Frederic Bastiat traveled across the Channel to England. There he watched a huge peaceful movement — the Anti-Corn-Law League led by Richard Cobden and John Bright — in which ordinary working families marched to demand an end to the tariffs on imported grain, so that a loaf of bread could cost less. Why did those poor English families want the tariffs gone?
answer: The tariffs made bread more expensive than it needed to be
choices: The tariffs made bread more expensive than it needed to be
The tariffs made grain farmers richer worldwide
The tariffs raised wages for factory workers
The tariffs stopped foreign wars
context: The League's headquarters and organizational base was Manchester; Bastiat traveled there in 1845 specifically to study its methods. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat traveled to England to study the Anti-Corn Law League, a mass movement led by Richard Cobden that fought to repeal the tariffs making bread expensive for ordinary families. Back home, Bastiat wrote a book introducing the League's campaign to French readers. The publisher Guillaumin put it out in Paris the same year. What is the book's short title?
answer: Cobden et la Ligue
choices: Cobden et la Ligue
Sophismes economiques
Harmonies economiques
La Loi
context: Cobden et la Ligue, ou l'agitation anglaise pour la liberte des echanges (Guillaumin, 1845) translated the League's speeches and pamphlets for French audiences. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In 1846 the French economist Frederic Bastiat, inspired by the British movement that had just repealed the Corn Laws, started his own free-trade league in the French port city of Bordeaux. He and his allies believed a tariff protects a few favored producers by making every buyer in the country pay more. What was the main argument these free-trade leagues made?
answer: Tariffs help a few producers a lot but raise prices for everyone else, so most people are worse off
choices: Tariffs help a few producers a lot but raise prices for everyone else, so most people are worse off
Tariffs make everyone richer because they protect the whole country
Tariffs are free of any hidden costs because the government keeps the money
Tariffs speed up the invention of new machines
context: The French Free Trade Association (Association pour la liberte des echanges) was founded in Bordeaux in February 1846 and expanded to Paris and elsewhere later that year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In the 1840s Frederic Bastiat and his allies at the French free-trade league launched a newspaper called Le Libre-Echange (Free Trade). Week after week they argued that tariffs — extra taxes stuck on foreign goods at the border — quietly hurt every ordinary buyer. Their favorite example: a tariff on foreign shoes. What is the main free-trade argument against a tariff on foreign shoes?
answer: Every family pays more for shoes so a few shoemakers can charge more
choices: Every family pays more for shoes so a few shoemakers can charge more
Tariffs create infinite jobs at no cost to anyone
Foreign shoemakers pay the tariff instead of local shoppers
Tariffs are always undone the next day by the mayor
context: Le Libre-Echange (November 1846 onward) was the movement's official periodical, edited by Bastiat during his most productive years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In the 1840s a group of thinkers from an English factory city — led by the cotton merchant Richard Cobden and the fiery orator John Bright — pushed hard for free trade and against tariffs on grain. Their campaign finally forced Parliament to repeal Britain's Corn Laws in 1846. History named this group after their industrial home city. What is their two-word name?
answer: The Manchester School
choices: The Manchester School
The Fabian School
The Chicago School
The Salamanca School
context: The Manchester School was the British counterpart to Bastiat's French free-trade tradition and gave English a shorthand for classical-liberal political economy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Manchester_School.

question: In February 1848 France overthrew King Louis Philippe and set up the Second Republic. One of the new government's first big acts was ending slavery in every French colony. The abolitionist Victor Schoelcher drafted the decree in Paris that April. What was the date of that order?
answer: April 27, 1848
choices: April 27, 1848
August 4, 1789
February 22, 1848
context: The abolition decree of April 27, 1848 covered Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana, and Reunion; it was the second and definitive French colonial abolition after Napoleon had reversed the first (1794) in 1802. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Abolition_of_slavery_in_France.

question: When a country ends slavery, the workers who were once forced to labor without pay become free to pick their own jobs, quit if they want, and keep the money they earn each week. Compared to forced labor under whips and chains, what does free labor tend to be over time?
answer: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
choices: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
Exactly the same -- pay and freedom do not affect effort
Less productive -- nobody works without being forced
Impossible -- no country has ever tried it
context: Victor Schoelcher (1804-1893) drafted and championed the April 27, 1848 decree. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Victor_Schoelcher.

question: During the French Revolution, France abolished slavery in its colonies in 1794. But eight years later a new French leader, trying to restore sugar profits from Saint-Domingue and other Caribbean holdings, brought slavery back. In 1802 he sent troops across the Atlantic to reimpose it by force. Who reversed that first end of slavery?
answer: Napoleon Bonaparte
choices: Napoleon Bonaparte
King Louis XVI
Robespierre
King Louis Philippe
context: Napoleon's 1802 reversal restored slavery in French colonies until Schoelcher's 1848 decree ended it definitively. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Abolition_of_slavery_in_France.

question: In February 1848 revolution swept France and toppled King Louis Philippe. Two months later, in April 1848, the new French republic held elections for a National Assembly. The economist Frederic Bastiat — famous for his free-trade pamphlets and his tale of the broken window — ran for a seat and won. Which French department elected him?
answer: Landes
choices: Landes
Paris
Bouches-du-Rhone
Nord
context: Bastiat represented Landes, his native southwestern department, in the Constituent Assembly from May 1848. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, famous for the broken-window parable, argued against slavery using his usual method: compare what people SEE with what they miss. Defenders of the plantation economy pointed to cotton output and Southern wealth. Bastiat pressed a deeper move — one about incentives on the plantation and about what forced labor does to a master's own character. Which argument did he press?
answer: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
choices: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
The abolitionist movement had no chance of political success
The Caribbean colonies were unprofitable regardless of the labor system
The moral case for slavery outweighed the economic case against it
context: Bastiat argued that the slave region SEES the free labor and its products but does not see the incentive-destroyed population, the strangled free-labor market, and the corrupted master class. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: In 1833 the British Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act, ending slavery across most of the British Empire. To get the law past the powerful plantation lobby, Parliament wrote it in a way that has stirred lasting debate. France used a version of the same model when it abolished slavery in 1848. What choice did the British Act make?
answer: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
choices: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
Compensating the freed slaves directly for years of unpaid labor
Confiscating the plantations and redistributing them to the freed slaves
Requiring the freed slaves to purchase their freedom over 20 years
context: The 1833 British Act paid GBP 20 million in compensation to former slave owners; freed slaves received an 'apprenticeship' period rather than direct compensation. This became the framework for later 19th-century abolitions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833.

question: In 1850, dying of tuberculosis in Rome, the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short pamphlet called The Law. In it he described how governments could take from some people to give to others while dressing the act in legal language. He walked through slavery, protectionism, and welfare with one running concept holding it all together. For Bastiat, slavery was the maximal case of that concept. Which concept did he use?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Natural monopoly
Diminishing returns
The margin of exploitation
context: The Law defines legal plunder as one person's labor or property being taken from them by legal force and given to another; slavery is its purest form. Source: bastiat.org/en/the_law.html.

question: Frederic Bastiat was a French economist and, in the last years of his short life, a member of the new French National Assembly created in 1848. Here is an accuracy note about him. The decree that abolished slavery in French colonies was signed on April 27, 1848, but the new National Assembly did not first meet until May 4, 1848. So Bastiat's actual voting record on slavery had a particular shape. Which characterization is correct?
answer: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
choices: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
He voted against the abolition decree because he opposed the Provisional Government
He drafted the abolition decree in his role as under-secretary of the Navy
He was absent from the Assembly for the entire 1848-1850 session
context: Sequencing: Bastiat elected April 23, decree April 27, Assembly opens May 4. He supported the abolition, had a decades-long antislavery record in print, and voted for the implementation and compensation measures the Assembly took up. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The Austrian School of economics — founded in 1871 by the Vienna professor Carl Menger — says value is subjective. Only people, each with their own tastes, can decide what one thing is worth to them. A hungry kid values a candy bar more than a kid who just finished lunch. So what does subjective value mean about the 'true' price of a candy bar?
answer: There is no single true price -- it is worth different amounts to different kids
choices: There is no single true price -- it is worth different amounts to different kids
A government committee can calculate the true price exactly
The true price is always one dollar
The true price is written on every candy bar's atoms
context: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action: A Treatise on Economics was published by Yale University Press on September 14, 1949. Mises had left Vienna for the Graduate Institute in Geneva in 1934 and emigrated to New York City in 1940 after the Nazi occupation of Europe closed in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: While living in Geneva, Ludwig von Mises wrote an early German version of what would become 'Human Action.' It came out in 1940. He spent most of the 1940s rewriting it, not just translating it, for readers in America. What was the 1940 German book called?
answer: Nationaloekonomie
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Kritik des Interventionismus
Grundprobleme der Nationaloekonomie
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens was published in Geneva in 1940. When Henry Hazlitt urged an English translation, Mises insisted on rewriting for the American audience -- the result was Human Action (1949). The other three titles are real earlier Mises books but not the direct precursor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: In 1920 Ludwig von Mises wrote a famous paper. Under socialism, no one owns the factories or the land or the machines, so there are no real market prices for them. Then planners have no reliable way to tell which projects are worth doing. What is the missing tool that socialism removes?
answer: Real market prices that reveal what things actually cost
choices: Real market prices that reveal what things actually cost
The freedom to buy imported goods
The right to hold elections
The number of workers in each factory
context: The 1920 paper appeared in the Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, volume 47, and was translated by S. Adler as 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth,' reprinted in the 1935 volume Collectivist Economic Planning that Friedrich Hayek edited. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: In September 1945, Friedrich Hayek published a short essay in The American Economic Review. It became one of the most-cited papers in modern economics. Its main claim: no central planner can gather all the small pieces of local knowledge held in millions of heads. What was the title?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
The Pretence of Knowledge
The Constitution of Liberty
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the September 1945 American Economic Review as a rebuttal to Oskar Lange's proposal for 'market socialism.' It was reprinted in Hayek's 1948 essay collection Individualism and Economic Order. The other three titles are real Hayek works from different decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: A school of economists called the Austrians — following Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, and Friedrich Hayek — argue that big economic downturns like the Great Depression are usually not caused by markets themselves going crazy. They point to something else instead, a policy choice made by a country's central bank. What do these Austrian economists say is the main cause of these financial crashes?
answer: Central banks pushing interest rates below where savings and borrowing would naturally meet
choices: Central banks pushing interest rates below where savings and borrowing would naturally meet
Farmers refusing to grow enough food during good years
Consumers being naturally too selfish to keep the economy stable
Small shopkeepers charging prices that are too fair
context: Murray Rothbard (1926-1995) published Man, Economy, and State in 1962 at age 36. The three distractors are all real Mises students from the New York seminar of the 1950s. Rothbard's book was commissioned by the Volker Fund as an accessible companion to Human Action; it grew into a full-scale rival treatise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: In 1946 the American journalist Henry Hazlitt — an editorial writer at the New York Times — published a short book called Economics in One Lesson. Hazlitt had read Frederic Bastiat's seen-and-unseen essays closely. He wanted to boil that whole method into a single rule any ordinary reader could apply to any policy debate. What is that one lesson?
answer: Look at the effect of a policy on every group, not just the group it is meant to help
choices: Look at the effect of a policy on every group, not just the group it is meant to help
Every policy helps every group equally over time
Only the visible effects of a policy ever really matter
Government spending is always free money for the country
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is a chapter-by-chapter extension of Bastiat's seen/unseen method, with Hazlitt explicitly acknowledging the debt in his preface. Hazlitt was also the New York Times economics columnist who first urged Mises to write an English successor to Nationaloekonomie -- the project that became Human Action. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/broken-window.

question: Joseph Schumpeter was an Austrian-born economist who taught at Harvard University in the 1930s and 40s. In his 1954 book 'History of Economic Analysis,' published after his death, he dismissed the French economist Frederic Bastiat with one short famous line. That line shut down mainstream university study of Bastiat for a whole generation. Which line did Schumpeter write?
answer: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
choices: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
Bastiat is the most dangerous socialist ever to have written in French.
Bastiat's Sophisms are the finest work of economics in the 19th century.
Bastiat and Marx must be read as complementary halves of a single vision.
context: Schumpeter's dismissal in History of Economic Analysis (published posthumously in 1954) discouraged academic economists from taking Bastiat seriously for decades. Rothbard's later Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995) was in part an explicit answer to Schumpeter, treating Bastiat as a genuine French classical-liberal theorist. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: Murray Rothbard was the American economist who carried the Austrian school forward after Ludwig von Mises. Before he died in 1995, Rothbard wrote a huge two-volume history of economic thought. The publisher Edward Elgar released it after his death. In it, Rothbard answered Joseph Schumpeter's put-down of Frederic Bastiat by treating Bastiat as a real theorist, not a mere pamphleteer. What was the book's title?
answer: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
choices: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
The Panic of 1819
context: Rothbard's two-volume An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought was published posthumously by Edward Elgar in 1995 (Rothbard died in January 1995). The book devotes serious attention to Bastiat and the wider French classical-liberal tradition -- an implicit rebuke of Schumpeter's 1954 dismissal. The three distractors are all real earlier Rothbard books. Source: https://mises.org/library/book/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought.

question: Three books form the spine of modern Austrian economics. Frederic Bastiat's 19th-century French essays came first. Ludwig von Mises's 1949 book 'Human Action' rebuilt the argument into a full system in English. Murray Rothbard's 1962 book 'Man, Economy, and State' made it more formal still. This is not just a genealogy of names — each book teaches the same one reasoning move applied more carefully. Which move is that shared analytic backbone?
answer: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
choices: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
That empirical macro-econometrics is the only rigorous form of economic knowledge
That all economic laws must be established through controlled laboratory experiments
That government spending stimulates growth by expanding aggregate demand
context: Mises's praxeology -- reasoning from the axiom that human action is purposive -- is the formal core of Human Action, and it inherits Bastiat's plain-language habit of tracing consequences past the seen effect to the unseen. Rothbard rebuilds the same method in Man, Economy, and State (1962). The reader can accept or reject Austrian conclusions; the reasoning MOVE is the seen/unseen chain of consequences. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: In 1840 a young French printer's apprentice named Pierre-Joseph Proudhon published a small book with the question 'What is property?' right on the cover. Proudhon was the first thinker to publicly call himself an anarchist. His answer to his own question — just three short words — became a famous slogan quoted for the next 200 years. Which one?
answer: 'Property is theft'
choices: 'Property is theft'
'Property is liberty'
'Property is order'
'Property is labour'
context: Proudhon (1809-1865) meant the phrase strictly of ABSENTEE property that draws rent or interest without labour, not of a workman's tools -- a distinction later socialists frequently blurred. The 1840 book was Qu'est-ce que la propriete? (What is Property?). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Pierre-Joseph Proudhon'.

question: In January 1849, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon started a lending group in Paris. It aimed to lend to workers at zero interest, using notes traded for members' goods. About 3,600 people signed up and put in around 18,000 francs. Then Proudhon was jailed and the group was shut down. What was it called?
answer: The Bank of the People
choices: The Bank of the People
The Society of the Rights of Man
The National Workshops
The Society of the Seasons
context: Proudhon's Banque du peuple was the concrete institutional test of his mutualist idea that competing lenders could organise credit gratuit -- interest-free lending -- outside the state and outside profit. Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux (National Workshops) were a different 1848 scheme; the Society of the Rights of Man and the Society of the Seasons were older republican secret societies. Source: recma.org 'Proudhon et la Banque du Peuple'.

question: From late 1849 into early 1850, Frederic Bastiat and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon traded long public letters. They argued whether it was fair to charge interest on a loan. Almost every letter ran in the same Paris paper, Proudhon's own daily, edited from his prison cell. Name the paper.
answer: La Voix du Peuple
choices: La Voix du Peuple
Le National
La Presse
Le Constitutionnel
context: La Voix du Peuple ran from October 1849 into the summer of 1850 as Proudhon's third and last major daily; he continued editing it from Sainte-Pelagie prison. Publishing the exchange in his OWN paper meant Bastiat argued in front of Proudhon's readership. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: Bastiat's central argument against interest-free lending was not that lenders deserved a reward or that borrowers were ungrateful. It was a claim about what price interest actually is. On his account, interest paid on a loan of 1,000 francs for a year is the price of exactly what?
answer: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
choices: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
The paperwork and risk of writing the loan
The borrower's expected profit from the loan
The scarcity of gold coin in the economy
context: A century before the Austrian school named it 'time preference', Bastiat had the argument's core: a lender is a person who does without his capital for a period; the interest compensates him for that period of doing without, not for any labour of lending. Paperwork, risk, and borrower profit are separate items. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Frederic Bastiat, the French economist, and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a French socialist thinker, argued in a series of open letters in 1849 about interest on loans. Proudhon wanted the law to force lenders to charge zero interest. Bastiat pressed him on a consequence he refused to accept: if the law forced interest to zero, Bastiat said, borrowers would not actually get cheap loans at all. Something worse would happen. What?
answer: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
choices: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
Only the wealthy would still be able to borrow, at higher secret rates
The state would have to nationalise every bank at once
Prices of all consumer goods would fall by about the old interest rate
context: The disappearance-of-lenders argument runs: at zero interest, savers cease to LEND -- they hold cash or hoard specie instead -- so the volume of loanable funds collapses toward nothing. This is the same reasoning modern economists use against binding usury caps. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was a French socialist writer best known for the slogan 'property is theft.' In his 1849 exchange with the French economist Frederic Bastiat, Proudhon insisted that ending interest on loans would not need the state to force anyone at all. In his ideal society, he claimed, a force inside the economy itself would drive the interest rate all the way to zero. Which mechanism did Proudhon propose?
answer: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
choices: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
A single state monopoly bank issuing paper money
Public shaming of anyone charging any interest at all
A universal tax on capital equal to the interest rate
context: Proudhon insisted his scheme was not coercive: multiply the number of mutual banks, let them compete for borrowers, and the rate would fall organically to zero. Bastiat rejoined that competition could push the rate down only to the value of time-preference itself, and no further. Source: praxeology.net Letter 13.

question: In 1850 Frederic Bastiat gathered the whole exchange with Pierre-Joseph Proudhon into a single book, published in Paris by the Guillaumin house. He gave the volume a title that ironically named Proudhon's own slogan for the scheme -- one French noun and its qualifier. What title?
answer: Gratuite du credit
choices: Gratuite du credit
Interet et principal
Contradictions economiques
Solutions du probleme social
context: Gratuite du credit -- literally 'Free Credit' or 'The Gratuity of Credit' -- was Proudhon's own slogan for the interest-free-lending idea, and Bastiat used it as the book's ironic title. Proudhon in turn published a rival edition of the same letters under his own preferred title Interet et Principal. Source: worldcat.org record 4078594.

question: In 1849 the French economist Frederic Bastiat and the French socialist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon printed a series of open letters in Paris arguing about whether lenders should be allowed to charge interest. By convention their debate is described as fourteen letters — the count in Bastiat's own Paris edition. In Proudhon's rival edition of the same debate, the letter count is different. How different?
answer: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
choices: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
Twelve letters -- Proudhon dropped both the opening piece and Bastiat's last
Fifteen letters -- Proudhon added a summary letter of his own
Ten letters -- Proudhon printed only his own contributions
context: The opening letter of the exchange was by C.F. Cheve, a Proudhon disciple; then twelve letters ran between Bastiat and Proudhon in strict alternation. Bastiat added a closing fourteenth letter (Letter 14) which Proudhon refused to answer, and Proudhon's Interet et Principal simply omitted it. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: Bastiat had told Proudhon in plain prose that interest is the price of time preference. That idea got its full formal statement in a multi-volume work called 'Kapital und Kapitalzins' (Capital and Interest). It came out in Innsbruck across the 1880s and 1890s. Which Austrian economist wrote it?
answer: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
context: Bohm-Bawerk's Kapital und Kapitalzins appeared in three parts between 1884 and 1889, with a second edition into the 1890s. He credited Bastiat as one of the nineteenth-century predecessors of the theory. Menger founded the Austrian school (1871) but did not write on interest at that length; Wieser worked on opportunity cost; Mises came a generation later. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Eugen Bohm von Bawerk'.

question: After the second world war the Austrian school of economics rebuilt itself in exile from Vienna. In 1949 its mature argument came back to English readers as the core chapter of a thousand-page book published in New York. Its author, a Viennese exile then teaching in the United States, treated time preference not as a quirk of capitalism, but as a basic feature of any person's choice between now and later. Which book was it?
answer: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
choices: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
The Road to Serfdom, by Friedrich Hayek
Man, Economy and State, by Murray Rothbard
The Theory of Money and Credit, by Ludwig von Mises
context: Human Action (Yale University Press, 1949) is Mises's systematic English treatise; its chapters on interest treat originary time-preference as an inescapable category of acting man. The Road to Serfdom (1944) was Hayek's political tract; Rothbard's Man, Economy and State came later (1962); Mises's Theorie des Geldes was much earlier (1912). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Ludwig von Mises'.

question: Picture a huge investment company on Wall Street in New York. Every single night it borrows enormous sums of money from other banks just so it can keep running the next day — that is how it pays its bills. One week the other banks all get scared about the company and refuse to lend to it. What is likely to happen to the company by Friday?
answer: It collapses -- it cannot last a few days without the borrowed money
choices: It collapses -- it cannot last a few days without the borrowed money
Nothing -- companies do not really need to borrow
It grows twice as big overnight
It quietly turns into a farm
context: Bear Stearns, founded in 1923, was heavily exposed to subprime mortgages and mortgage-backed securities. Its two internal hedge funds collapsed in July-August 2007, previewing the firm's own collapse eight months later. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2008 the American investment bank Bear Stearns was about to collapse. Over one weekend, the US government helped a healthier bank — JPMorgan Chase — buy Bear Stearns quickly for just $2 a share. Officials rushed to close the deal before Monday morning trading opened. Why does the government step in to arrange the sale?
answer: To keep the collapse from spreading and scaring every other bank
choices: To keep the collapse from spreading and scaring every other bank
To collect all the pens from the bank's desks
Because the government already owns the bank
To lower the price of coffee at the bank
context: JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, was the buyer. The Fed's involvement made the sale possible on a compressed timeline. Source: Grokipedia 'JPMorgan Chase acquisition of Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: Bear Stearns was a huge American investment bank based in New York. Over one weekend in March 2008 it collapsed as its lenders stopped renewing its overnight loans. That same weekend the larger bank JPMorgan Chase, with help arranged by the Federal Reserve, agreed to buy the wreckage. The first announced price per share was famously low — a fraction of the price Bear had traded at just days earlier. What was that first price, before shareholder lawsuits forced JPMorgan to raise it?
answer: Two dollars
choices: Two dollars
Ten dollars
Fifty cents
Twenty dollars
context: The initial Sunday-night announcement was $2 per share. Bear shareholders threatened lawsuits over the price; JPMorgan raised it to $10 the following week. The stock had traded at $172 fourteen months earlier -- a 99% loss for shareholders in a single weekend. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2008 the US Federal Reserve helped JPMorgan Chase buy the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns. To make JPMorgan agree, the Fed created a special company called Maiden Lane to take about $30 billion of Bear Stearns' worst mortgage loans off the books first. JPMorgan only had to buy the healthy parts. Who ended up owning those bad loans in the end?
answer: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
choices: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
The failing bank's original shareholders
The buyer paid full price for them
Foreign central banks
context: Maiden Lane LLC, named after the New York Fed's address, held $30 billion of Bear's worst mortgage-backed securities. The Fed took the assets off JPMorgan's books via a non-recourse loan. Source: Grokipedia 'Maiden Lane Transactions' (2026-09-05).

question: The March 2008 rescue set an important precedent about how failing investment banks would be handled. Shareholders and executives would suffer losses, but one specific group would be made whole. Who did the Fed rescue protect at 100 cents on the dollar?
answer: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
choices: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
Junior employees at the collapsing firm
Retail brokerage clients
Municipal pension funds holding the stock
context: The Bear precedent: shareholders got wiped out but creditors and counterparties were paid in full. This was designed to prevent a broader panic but also trained the market to expect similar rescues in future crises. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: When the US government rescued the investment bank Bear Stearns in 2008, critics warned that saving one big bank would make every other bank expect to be saved too. If a bank knows the Fed will catch it, it takes bigger risks — gambling with taxpayer money instead of its own. Market discipline weakens. Economists have a name for this failure mode, where insurance against a bad outcome makes the bad outcome more likely. What is it called?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Ricardian equivalence
Regulatory capture
context: Moral hazard is the classic problem where insurance against a loss weakens the incentive to avoid it. Applied to bank rescues: if creditors expect government to make them whole, they discipline banks less carefully. Source: Grokipedia 'Moral hazard' (2026-09-05).

question: After the Bear Stearns rescue in March 2008, everyone on Wall Street had watched the Federal Reserve broker a deal that made the failing bank's creditors and trading partners whole. Six months later, in September 2008, another huge New York investment bank, Lehman Brothers, was collapsing in the same way — its overnight lenders would not renew. What did Lehman's creditors and trading partners expect the Fed to do this time?
answer: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
choices: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
Let Lehman fail immediately to punish executive risk-taking
Nationalize Lehman directly under a special Treasury charter
Merge Lehman with Bank of America without Fed involvement
context: Markets had priced in the Bear precedent. When Lehman was allowed to fail on September 15 2008, the counterparty network priced in exactly the outcome the Bear rescue had trained them not to expect. The moral-hazard trap sprung the other way. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2008 the US Federal Reserve helped JPMorgan Chase buy the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns. Most Wall Street voices cheered the rescue as a save. But two well-known economists — one from the political left, one from the right — warned in real time that saving Bear would encourage even bigger risks at the next bank. Which two figures made this argument publicly in early 2008?
answer: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
choices: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
Paul Krugman on the left; Larry Kudlow on the right
Alan Blinder on the left; Milton Friedman on the right
Joseph Stiglitz on the left; John Taylor on the right
context: Roubini (NYU) and Schiff (Euro Pacific Capital) both publicly warned in spring 2008 that the Bear rescue was setting up worse crises. Both were widely dismissed at the time and vindicated within six months. Source: Grokipedia 'Nouriel Roubini' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2008 Bear Stearns rescue — when the US Federal Reserve backed JPMorgan Chase's fire-sale purchase of the collapsing investment bank — is now a textbook case in the Austrian School of economics. Austrians like Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, and Murray Rothbard argue that each rescue teaches the market to expect the next one. Which recognition move does this ladder press?
answer: Each rescue changes the expectations for the next crisis; the sudden removal of an expected rescue can cause the panic the earlier rescue was meant to prevent
choices: Each rescue changes the expectations for the next crisis; the sudden removal of an expected rescue can cause the panic the earlier rescue was meant to prevent
Rescues always work as intended and stabilize markets permanently
Rescues fail only when the Fed misprices the collateral for its loan
Rescues encourage moral hazard only when they involve foreign banks
context: The Bear rescue trained markets to expect the Lehman rescue; the September 15 Lehman failure violated that trained expectation. The Fed's discretionary rescue policy is not neutral -- each intervention writes the script for the next crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In the summer of 2007, two big hedge funds run inside the New York investment bank Bear Stearns were quietly collapsing. Bear's chairman, Jimmy Cayne, was reportedly at a national bridge tournament instead of managing the crisis. Less than a year later Bear itself failed. What lesson do critics draw from stories like this about the leaders of huge failing firms?
answer: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
choices: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
Card games improve executive decision-making under stress
Big banks always have perfect information about their own risk
Employees will always cover for a distracted boss
context: Jimmy Cayne, then Bear's chairman, was playing at a bridge tournament while the July 2007 collapse of Bear's internal hedge funds unfolded. The anecdote became emblematic of Wall Street executive detachment during the run-up to the crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'James Cayne' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1914 the United States created a central bank called the Federal Reserve, often just called 'the Fed.' Its main power is to change how much money is in circulation in the country. Suppose the Fed prints a lot of new money and hands it into the economy. What usually happens to the prices you see in the stores?
answer: Prices go up -- more money chasing the same goods
choices: Prices go up -- more money chasing the same goods
Prices stay exactly the same forever
Prices fall to zero
Prices change to a different color
context: Strong had been at the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting as president of Bankers Trust. He led the New York Fed from 1914 until his death in 1928. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Benjamin Strong Jr. led the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1914 until his death in 1928. He pioneered a Fed policy tool that is still central today. With it, the Fed buys US Treasury bonds from private banks, pushes new dollars of reserves into the banking system, and drives interest rates down. What is this tool called?
answer: Open market operations
choices: Open market operations
Reserve requirements
The discount window
Quantitative easing
context: Open market operations became the Fed's most important standing tool. Strong built the New York Fed's Open Market Committee into the operational center of American monetary policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Open market operation' (2026-09-05).

question: Benjamin Strong ran the Federal Reserve Bank of New York through most of the 1920s — the most powerful arm of the young American central bank. He became close personal friends with the man who ran the Bank of England from 1920 all the way to 1944. Their friendship shaped world money policy through the whole decade, including the run-up to the 1929 crash. Who was the Bank of England chief?
answer: Montagu Norman
choices: Montagu Norman
John Maynard Keynes
Winston Churchill
Hjalmar Schacht
context: Montagu Norman led the Bank of England for 24 years -- one of the longest tenures at any major central bank. His friendship with Strong shaped 1920s international monetary coordination. Source: Grokipedia 'Montagu Norman' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1925 Britain — under Chancellor of the Exchequer Winston Churchill — returned to the gold standard, tying the pound sterling back to a fixed weight of gold. Churchill chose a specific price for the pound. That price left the pound overvalued, caused painful deflation, and set off mass strikes and unemployment across British industry. John Maynard Keynes attacked the choice in a famous pamphlet. At what prewar rate did Britain return?
answer: The 1914 prewar parity of about $4.86 per pound
choices: The 1914 prewar parity of about $4.86 per pound
A 20% devaluation from prewar levels
A 10% appreciation above prewar levels
A floating market rate with no fixed peg
context: Britain's 1925 return to gold at the prewar parity, on Chancellor Churchill's decision, was economically painful. Strong agreed to help by keeping US rates low so gold would not flow from London to New York. Source: Grokipedia 'Return to gold' (2026-09-05).

question: In July 1927 Benjamin Strong, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, hosted a secret meeting on Long Island with three foreign central bankers. Days later the Fed cut its discount rate — the rate it charges when banks borrow from it — from 4% to 3.5%. The cut was meant to help Europe defend the gold standard. Which three foreign central bankers attended?
answer: Montagu Norman of Britain, Emile Moreau of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
choices: Montagu Norman of Britain, Emile Moreau of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
John Maynard Keynes of Britain, Rene Coty of France, and Konrad Adenauer of Germany
Winston Churchill of Britain, Georges Clemenceau of France, and Otto von Bismarck of Germany
Nicholas Biddle of Britain, Charles de Gaulle of France, and Otto von Habsburg of Germany
context: The July 1927 Long Island meeting brought together the heads of the four leading Western central banks. It produced the rate cut that Austrian economists later blamed for the final phase of the 1920s boom. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Benjamin Strong ran the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in the 1920s. In July 1927, after his secret Long Island meeting with three European central bankers, Strong pushed the Fed's discount rate down from 4% to 3.5%. In private, he reportedly described the cut using a distinctive alcoholic metaphor — an image of what the cheap money would do to the roaring stock market. Which phrase did he use?
answer: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
choices: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
A friendly nudge to the bond market
A helping shot for the London Fund
A quiet toast to European stability
context: The 'coup de whiskey' phrase is attributed to Strong via Adolph Miller's later Senate testimony. It captured the sense in which the rate cut was calculated to lift asset markets rather than to serve any narrow domestic policy purpose. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1963 the American economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published 'A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960.' In it they argued that the Federal Reserve's 1927 interest-rate cut helped inflate the stock-market bubble that popped in the 1929 crash. In Austrian economics, what does a fake-low interest rate — one held below where savings and borrowing would naturally meet — wrongly signal to a business owner deciding whether to build a factory?
answer: That people want to save more, so long-term projects look profitable
choices: That people want to save more, so long-term projects look profitable
That the economy is already at full production capacity
That the government wants prices to fall next year
That businesses should invest less than they normally would
context: Rothbard's 1963 book America's Great Depression built the Austrian case that the 1927 Strong-Norman coordination directly seeded the 1929 crash. Rothbard identified Strong as the pivotal Fed figure of the whole 1920s. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Rothbard's book America's Great Depression blamed the crash on the Fed's 1921-1929 credit expansion. After governor Benjamin Strong died in October 1928, no one was left to slow it. What did Austrians call the wasteful projects funded by that cheap credit -- projects doomed to fail once the boom ended?
answer: Malinvestment
choices: Malinvestment
Overproduction
Excess capacity
Speculation
context: M2 grew roughly 60% from 1921 to 1929, with much of the expansion coming during and after the 1927 easing. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In 1927 the American central bank — the Federal Reserve, led by Benjamin Strong of the New York Fed — pushed US interest rates down partly to help European economies struggling to hold the gold standard. Cheap money flooded into New York. Two years later, in October 1929, the American stock market crashed, kicking off the Great Depression. What do critics of the 1927 easing say those low rates did?
answer: They fueled a stock-market bubble that later burst
choices: They fueled a stock-market bubble that later burst
They cured European unemployment permanently
They prevented all future bank failures
They set the natural rate of interest
context: Adolph Miller, a Fed Board member 1914-1936, was the dissenter on the 1927 rate cut and later Senate witness against Strong's legacy. His testimony is the traceable source of the 'coup de whiskey' quote. Source: Grokipedia 'Adolph Miller' (2026-09-05).

question: The Strong-Norman coordination story of 1927 teaches one clear recognition move about central banks working together across borders. Which move does this ladder press?
answer: Coordinated easing among central banks to defend a fixed exchange rate can produce asset-price inflation in the country doing the easing, even when its own economy does not need easing
choices: Coordinated easing among central banks to defend a fixed exchange rate can produce asset-price inflation in the country doing the easing, even when its own economy does not need easing
International central-bank coordination is always fiscally neutral for the cooperating countries
Central banks never coordinate policy in secret
International cooperation always prevents financial crises
context: Strong cut US rates in 1927 to help Britain defend the pound. The unintended domestic consequence was a US stock-market bubble that broke in 1929. International cooperation solved one problem by creating another. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Imagine a big city like New York passes a law in 1975 freezing all apartment rents at a low price, locked there for five years. No landlord can raise rents, no matter what heating and repairs cost. A few years later, a young couple hunts for a brand-new apartment. What is likely to have happened to the number of new apartments being built?
answer: It drops -- builders will not build for a rent they cannot raise
choices: It drops -- builders will not build for a rent they cannot raise
It doubles -- the low price attracts many new builders
Nothing changes -- rent control has no effect on building
Only tiny apartments are built
context: Mietendeckel means 'rent lid' in German. The rule applied only inside Berlin, so neighboring Brandenburg municipalities kept market pricing -- creating a natural experiment economists rarely have. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: In 2020 the city of Berlin, Germany passed a law called the Mietendeckel -- a strict rent cap that froze rents on most apartments across the city. What made economists excited to study it was one clean feature: it applied inside Berlin only. Just outside the city line, in nearby towns like Potsdam, landlords could still charge market rents. That gave researchers a rare real-world experiment: same country, same year, one side capped, one side not. What was that special feature of the Berlin rent cap?
answer: It applied only within Berlin's city boundaries, so neighboring municipalities kept market pricing
choices: It applied only within Berlin's city boundaries, so neighboring municipalities kept market pricing
It applied to every German city simultaneously
It was enacted at the European Union level
It applied only to commercial (not residential) tenants
context: Economists at the ifo Institute in Munich and the DIW in Berlin used the border discontinuity to compare rental-market outcomes in Berlin against adjoining non-Berlin municipalities. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Suppose a big American city passes a new law that caps how much any landlord can charge for rent — say, no more than a fixed dollar amount per apartment per month. Within a few months, researchers count how many apartments are listed for rent inside the city and compare that number with listings in the towns just outside the city line. What do they usually find?
answer: Listings inside the city drop sharply while listings in the towns just outside rise
choices: Listings inside the city drop sharply while listings in the towns just outside rise
Listings rise in both places as landlords rush to comply
Listings stay unchanged everywhere
Listings fall in both places by the same amount
context: Landlords held units off the market, listed them as furnished shares (exempt from the freeze), or converted them to sale. The supply-shrinkage was the central empirical finding of the natural experiment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: A big city council, hoping to help renters, passes a law that freezes rents on every apartment already leased in the city. A year later, Maria -- a nurse moving in for a new hospital job -- searches the listings. She finds almost none available, and the few that are listed cost far more than before the freeze. Why did rents jump on the leftover listings?
answer: The freeze shrank the pool of listings, so movers now compete for the few left
choices: The freeze shrank the pool of listings, so movers now compete for the few left
The freeze had no effect on the rental market at all
The central bank quietly raised interest rates during the freeze
The city ordered landlords to raise prices on movers only
context: Applied Bastiat: seen benefit (protected sitting tenants) was real; unseen cost fell on the mover who now faced a smaller and more competitive market for the units that remained available. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Berlin's Mietendeckel rent freeze had been in force for about 15 months when, on April 15, 2021, Germany's highest court -- the Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe -- struck it down. The judges did not rule on whether the price cap was good or bad economics. They ruled on who had the legal power to make the rule at all. On what specific legal ground did the court strike the law down?
answer: Federalism -- rent regulation is a federal competence and the Berlin state lacked the authority
choices: Federalism -- rent regulation is a federal competence and the Berlin state lacked the authority
The freeze violated the human right to shelter under the Basic Law
The freeze violated European Union free-movement rules
The freeze violated Germany's post-1990 unification treaty with the East
context: The Court did not rule on the economic merits of the freeze; it ruled that the wrong level of government had enacted it. Retroactive rent had to be paid back by Berlin tenants who had been paying the frozen rate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Berlin's 2020 Mietendeckel rent cap only lasted about 15 months before Germany's Constitutional Court killed it in April 2021. But during those 15 months, economists watched exactly what happens when a big European city suddenly freezes rents: listings collapsed, new construction stalled, and landlords pulled apartments off the market entirely. Today, in almost every European housing economics class, that short experiment plays one specific role. What has the Berlin case become?
answer: The standard modern case study of rent-control-shock supply response
choices: The standard modern case study of rent-control-shock supply response
The standard modern case study of successful municipal rent regulation
The standard modern case study of European Union housing subsidies
The standard modern case study of central-bank interest-rate policy on rents
context: The combination of a real Western democracy, excellent economic statistics, a clean border discontinuity, and a fifteen-month before/after window makes the Berlin case a rare gift for empirical work on rent control. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Across history people have used all kinds of things as money -- gold coins in Rome, silver bars in China, cowrie shells in West Africa, wampum belts in North America, and giant round rai stones on the Pacific island of Yap. Very different objects, very different places. But every single one shared one trait that let it hold value over time. What was that trait?
answer: It was difficult to produce more of
choices: It was difficult to produce more of
It was universally beautiful to look at
It was easy to divide into small units
It was heavy enough to be hard to steal
context: Difficulty of production is the property that made gold, silver, and every other commodity money resist debasement. Easy-to-produce goods flooded markets and lost value; scarce goods held it. Source: Menger, Principles of Economics, 1871.

question: In 2009 an anonymous programmer known as Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin with one radical rule baked into the code: a hard cap on how many coins can ever exist. No central bank, no committee, and no future developer can raise it. The number is fixed forever by the protocol itself. That cap is a big reason Bitcoiners say it beats every government currency. What is that number?
answer: 21 million
choices: 21 million
1 billion
100 million
300 million
context: The 21-million-coin cap is coded into the reference client; the issuance curve halves every 210,000 blocks and terminates around the year 2140. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Carl Menger was a 19th-century Austrian economist and one of the founders of the whole Austrian school of economic thought. In his writings on money, Menger said money is not chosen because it is pretty, or small, or hard to break. Money wins out for one main reason: whatever a lot of people accept most easily in trade slowly becomes the money everyone uses. What one word names this feature of a good?
answer: Marketability
choices: Marketability
Divisibility
Portability
Durability
context: Menger's Principles (1871) grounds money in MARKETABILITY -- the depth of the network of would-be trading partners. High marketability historically correlated with difficulty of production. Source: mises.org/library/principles-economics.

question: Gold has been trusted as sound money for thousands of years because miners cannot suddenly flood the world with more of it. Every year new gold comes out of mines in South Africa, Australia, and Nevada, but that new supply is tiny compared to all the gold ever pulled from the ground and still sitting in vaults and jewelry. Austrian economists point to this slow growth as the gold standard's real strength. About what percentage does the world's total gold stock grow each year from new mining?
answer: About 1 to 2 percent
choices: About 1 to 2 percent
About 5 to 6 percent
About 10 to 12 percent
Effectively zero, at the geological limit
context: New annual mining runs about 1-2% of above-ground stock. This is why gold's 'issuance rate' has been the historical benchmark for a hard money against which every fiat currency was measured. Source: World Gold Council annual supply data.

question: Bitcoin is the digital money invented in 2009 by an anonymous person or group writing under the name Satoshi Nakamoto. Its computer code is written so that a total of exactly 21 million coins will ever exist — no additional units can be issued past that limit, ever. No previous form of money in history, not gold or silver or paper, has ever had a total upper bound written into it like this. What short phrase describes this property?
answer: Absolute scarcity
choices: Absolute scarcity
Relative scarcity
Digital fungibility
Cryptographic uniqueness
context: Gold is relatively scarce (~1-2% annual growth); Bitcoin is absolutely scarce (fixed upper bound). No prior commodity money has been absolutely scarce; even the tightest fiat central bank grows supply several percent yearly. Source: saifedean.com (Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard, 2018).

question: To measure how hard a form of money like gold or silver is to inflate, some economists take the total amount already in existence and divide it by how much fresh new supply is added each year through mining. A higher number means the money is harder to inflate, because the new yearly supply is small compared to what is already stored up in the world. What is this ratio called?
answer: Stock-to-flow
choices: Stock-to-flow
Price-to-earnings
Debt-to-equity
Money velocity
context: Ammous's argument: gold's stock-to-flow is about 60 (years of annual production to equal above-ground stock); Bitcoin's rises past gold after each halving and approaches infinity as issuance approaches zero around 2140. Source: saifedean.com/thebitcoinstandard.

question: Bitcoin was designed by Satoshi Nakamoto with a fixed rule: every 210,000 blocks -- about every four years -- the reward miners get for finding a block gets cut in half. This is called the halving. Because of it, the flow of new bitcoins slows down over and over until it basically stops. The stock-to-flow ratio, which compares all existing coins to the yearly new coins, keeps rising toward infinity. Around what year does Bitcoin's new-coin issuance reach effectively zero?
answer: About 2140
choices: About 2140
About 2050
About 2200
About 2100
context: The block-reward halves every 210,000 blocks (~4 years); after about 33 halvings the reward rounds to zero and issuance ends, around 2140. Miners then earn only transaction fees. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: An analyst writing under the pen name PlanB built a Bitcoin price model based on how much scarcer the coins get after each 'halving' — the moment when the reward paid to Bitcoin miners is cut in half. His model looked accurate for a few years after 2019, then missed badly starting in 2021 when the price failed to reach the level it predicted. What limit of a model fitted to past data does PlanB's Bitcoin miss reveal about its future predictions?
answer: A model that fits the past does not always predict the future
choices: A model that fits the past does not always predict the future
Price models are always exactly right forever after being published
Scarcity has nothing to do with a coin's price at any time
Only government-approved models can predict any market
context: 'PlanB' (pseudonym of a Dutch analyst) published the stock-to-flow price model in 2019; it forecast very high Bitcoin prices post-2021 halving. The model diverged sharply from reality after 2021. The MONETARY concept remains sound; the price model has not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock-to-flow.

question: Austrian-school economists -- thinkers like Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek's intellectual heirs -- argue Bitcoin's real point is not that it must become world money. Their argument is smaller and sharper: every past currency, from the Roman denarius to the US dollar, eventually lost value through one specific mechanism that Bitcoin's fixed 21-million cap makes impossible. Which mechanism does Bitcoin block?
answer: Debasement by the issuing authority
choices: Debasement by the issuing authority
Counterfeiting by private forgers
Loss of physical stock to warfare
Substitution by more convenient rival currencies
context: Roman denarius under Diocletian, medieval coin-clipping, Weimar mark 1923, every post-1971 fiat currency: the issuing authority has always been the debasement channel. Bitcoin's protocol removes that channel by making supply not-decidable by any actor. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: One school of Austrian-tradition economists argues that sound money must be genuinely difficult to produce more of, like gold or Bitcoin. This whole reasoning line traces back to a single foundational book published in 1871. Which book is the founding text of that tradition?
answer: Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
choices: Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
Ludwig von Mises's Theory of Money and Credit
Friedrich Hayek's Denationalisation of Money
Murray Rothbard's What Has Government Done to Our Money
context: Menger's Principles of Economics (Vienna, 1871) is the founding Austrian text on money's market emergence via marketability; every later Austrian monetary book (Mises 1912, Hayek 1976, Rothbard 1963) builds on it. Source: mises.org/library/principles-economics.

question: To spend bitcoin, your wallet must keep a huge secret number safe. That number is too long to memorize or copy by hand without errors. So every modern Bitcoin wallet turns it into a much friendlier backup -- a short list of ordinary English words you can write on paper and lock in a safe. What is that word-based backup called?
answer: a seed phrase of 12 or 24 English words
choices: a seed phrase of 12 or 24 English words
a QR code printed on plastic
a fingerprint scan
a nine-digit PIN
context: Bitcoin wallets convert the underlying 256-bit key into a mnemonic seed phrase -- typically 12 or 24 English words -- from which every derived key can be regenerated. QR codes are just visual encodings; biometrics and PINs are device unlocks, not the key material itself. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: Bitcoin wallets from every company -- Trezor, Ledger, and dozens of phone apps -- all build their word-list backups from the exact same short dictionary of common English words. That way, if one wallet dies, any other wallet in the world can read the same backup and restore your coins. That shared dictionary is fixed. How many words are on it?
answer: 2,048 words
choices: 2,048 words
500 words
10,000 words
12 words
context: The BIP-39 wordlist is exactly 2,048 English words (11 bits per word). 12 is the number of words in a short seed phrase, not the wordlist size. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/english.txt.

question: Bitcoin lets you memorize a special sequence of 12 or 24 English words, called a seed phrase. Those words alone unlock all of your coins from any computer, anywhere on Earth. Suppose you cross a national border with no wallet on you, no printed paper, and no phone — just the seed phrase memorized in your head. What can customs officers actually find?
answer: nothing — no search reveals the memorized words in your head
choices: nothing — no search reveals the memorized words in your head
border scanners can read memorized information
customs freezes coins tied to any traveler crossing a border
the network refuses to sign anything from the new country
context: A memorized seed phrase leaves no physical trace; the coins remain moveable from any internet-connected machine that can reconstruct the wallet. Contrast: gold triggers metal detectors, cash triggers currency-dog searches, bank balances can be frozen from any jurisdiction. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki; Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.).

question: When police search your house, they can seize the paper your seed phrase is written on. But if the phrase is only in your head -- memorized, never spoken -- American lawyers argue the state cannot force you to speak it out loud. One amendment to the US Constitution protects you from being made to testify against yourself, and it is the amendment defense lawyers cite in these crypto cases. Which amendment is it?
answer: the Fifth Amendment
choices: the Fifth Amendment
the First Amendment
the Fourth Amendment
the Second Amendment
context: The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination has been invoked in US courts to argue that compelling password disclosure is compelled testimony. First Amendment covers speech; Fourth covers search and seizure; Second covers arms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution.

question: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says nobody can be forced to give testimony against themselves. American courts have split on whether that protection covers a phone or laptop password. Some judges refuse to force someone to unlock a device. Other judges order it anyway, using a rule that says the state already knows the answer is on the device, so making the person unlock it reveals nothing new. What is that rule called?
answer: the foregone-conclusion doctrine
choices: the foregone-conclusion doctrine
the Miranda rule
the exclusionary rule
the plain-view doctrine
context: Some US courts have used the 'foregone-conclusion' doctrine to compel password disclosure when the state can show the material's existence, location and authenticity are already established. Miranda concerns warnings; the exclusionary rule bars illegally seized evidence; plain-view relates to warrantless observation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foregone_conclusion.

question: In 2013, a small team of Bitcoin developers wrote an open standard for recovering a wallet using a list of ordinary English words — a 12- or 24-word seed phrase. They published it for free, so any wallet company anywhere could use the same format without asking permission or paying a fee. Because so many companies adopted the same standard, users gained one big practical benefit. What is that main benefit for users?
answer: A user can move funds between wallet brands without losing access
