choices: A user can move funds between wallet brands without losing access
Only one company at a time can sell wallets that work with Bitcoin
Wallets built to the standard must pay a yearly fee to a foundation
Users can only recover a phrase if the original vendor still exists
context: BIP-39 authors: Marek Palatinus (Slush), Pavol Rusnak (Stick), Aaron Voisine, Sean Bowe -- 2013. Back, Dai, and Szabo are earlier cypherpunks not on the BIP-39 author list. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: A person owns a hardware Bitcoin wallet -- a small device that stores their secret key offline. It follows the open seed-phrase standard set in Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39 (BIP-39), meaning its backup is 12 or 24 plain English words. One morning the company that made the device announces it is closing forever: no more updates, no more support. The person feels a moment of panic, then realizes their coins are still safe. What can they do?
answer: Restore the phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard
choices: Restore the phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard
Nothing -- the coins are lost once the vendor turns off its servers
Wait for the largest surviving vendor to migrate the coins automatically
Convert the phrase into a new secret format before any other wallet reads it
context: BIP-39 phrases are portable across compliant wallets -- the whole design intent. No vendor server is involved in signing; migrations and format conversions are not needed. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: Every other form of money in history sits in a physical place: coins in a pocket, gold in a vault, dollars in a bank ledger. A person who memorizes their Bitcoin recovery phrase can hold their savings somewhere no earlier money has ever lived. Where?
answer: Inside their own memory, with no physical or digital trace outside their head
choices: Inside their own memory, with no physical or digital trace outside their head
Inside a special chip installed at each country's border
Inside a global vault run by the United Nations
Inside a ledger held by the International Monetary Fund
context: The novel property is that ownership can be reduced entirely to a memorized sequence of words in a human mind -- no border chip, UN vault, or IMF ledger is involved. Every prior monetary asset had a physical or ledger footprint outside the owner. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.).

question: A Bitcoin user can memorize a 12-word seed phrase — the master key that controls their coins — and carry nothing physical at all when crossing a border. A person holding gold sets off scanners. A person carrying cash gets flagged by currency-detection dogs. A person with bank balances can have their accounts frozen from a distant office. The memorized phrase blocks one specific kind of state action that the others do not. Which action does the memorized phrase block?
answer: seizure through physical search, currency detection, or remote account freeze
choices: seizure through physical search, currency detection, or remote account freeze
market-price volatility during the crossing
double-spending by a corrupt merchant on the far side of the border
conversion of the coins into a new format
context: Gold is heavy and detectable; cash is dog-searchable; bank balances can be frozen from any jurisdiction. A memorized phrase leaves no target for any of the three. Volatility, double-spend and format conversion are separate technical issues. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.); The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: A slick new website promises 1% interest every single day if you deposit your crypto with them. That grows $100 into more than $3,700 in a year -- thirty-seven times your money -- with no work and no risk. Even the safest US Treasury bond pays only about 4% for a whole year. When a crypto site promises 1% a day, what is that almost always a sign of?
answer: A scam -- no real business can pay that much
choices: A scam -- no real business can pay that much
A safe, boring savings account
A charity
A regular government bond
context: BitConnect was a supposed 'lending platform' launched in 2016 promising ~1% daily returns via a proprietary trading bot. Chainlink, Litecoin, and Cardano are separate cryptocurrency projects with different histories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BitConnect.

question: In 1920 an Italian immigrant in Boston named Charles Ponzi promised huge returns on international postal coupons. He had no real business behind the pitch. He paid early investors with money from new ones and paid commissions to anyone who brought in more depositors. The whole thing collapsed within a year and his name became the label for that whole trick. What is this scam called?
answer: a Ponzi scheme
choices: a Ponzi scheme
a hedge fund
a mutual fund
a public offering
context: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors from new investors' contributions and typically recruits through a pyramid of downstream depositors. Named for Charles Ponzi (1920). Hedge funds, mutual funds, and public offerings are legitimate structures. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponzi_scheme.

question: BitConnect was a crypto firm that promised depositors huge, steady returns generated by a mysterious 'trading bot' nobody could inspect. In January 2018, financial regulators in Texas and North Carolina told the firm to stop taking new money because the scheme looked like a classic Ponzi. Its coin crashed from about 400 dollars to nearly zero in a matter of days, wiping out families around the world. How much did depositors lose in all?
answer: about $2.4 billion
choices: about $2.4 billion
about $50 million
about $30 billion
about $200 million
context: Estimated depositor losses were about $2.4 billion. BitConnect founder Satish Kumbhani was indicted by the US Department of Justice in 2022 and remains a fugitive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BitConnect.

question: An even bigger fake-crypto scheme than BitConnect was run by a woman who called herself the 'Cryptoqueen.' She staged sold-out promo events at big venues and vanished with billions of dollars in 2017. What makes a scheme like hers a Ponzi and not a real investment?
answer: Old investors were paid with new investors' money, not real earnings
choices: Old investors were paid with new investors' money, not real earnings
The scheme mined real Bitcoin with special hardware
The scheme was audited by real accountants
Everyone got their money back at the end
context: Ruja Ignatova launched OneCoin in 2014 and marketed it worldwide as the Cryptoqueen. Elizabeth Holmes ran Theranos (unrelated blood-testing fraud); Cheung and Wojcicki are unrelated executives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin.

question: Ruja Ignatova, a Bulgarian-born businesswoman with a Frankfurt law degree, launched a coin called OneCoin around 2014 and sold it worldwide as the next Bitcoin. She held glitzy events at Wembley Arena in London, pulled in an estimated $4 billion from investors, and promised a revolutionary cryptocurrency. When investigators finally took OneCoin apart, they found one crucial piece missing that any real cryptocurrency must have. What did OneCoin lack?
answer: any working blockchain -- the ledger was just an internal database
choices: any working blockchain -- the ledger was just an internal database
any independent trading pair on any external exchange venue
any legally registered corporate address or filing history
any bug-bounty program or third-party security review
context: OneCoin had no blockchain; the 'ledger' was entries in an internal SQL database that Ignatova and her staff controlled. That means the entire operation was them typing numbers by hand. It had registered companies, celebrity appearances, and its own internal exchange rate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin; BBC 'The Missing Cryptoqueen' podcast.

question: OneCoin was a Bulgaria-based crypto project run by Ruja Ignatova, the self-styled 'Cryptoqueen,' who vanished in 2017. She sold OneCoin around the world as the next Bitcoin, but investigators later found no real blockchain behind it. Prosecutors in the US, UK, and Germany pieced together what investors had put in. Their number dwarfed the roughly $2 billion lost in the earlier BitConnect scam. What range do they give for OneCoin?
answer: roughly 4 to 15 billion US dollars
choices: roughly 4 to 15 billion US dollars
roughly 40 to 60 billion US dollars
roughly 100 to 200 million US dollars
roughly 500 million to 1 billion US dollars
context: OneCoin fundraising estimates range from $4B to $15B depending on the accounting; even the low end is larger than BitConnect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin; US DOJ indictments.

question: On October 25, 2017, US and German investigators were closing in on Ruja Ignatova, the Bulgarian-born founder of the OneCoin cryptocurrency scam that had taken an estimated $4 billion from investors around the world. That evening she boarded a Ryanair flight out of Sofia, Bulgaria -- and has not been seen in public since. Which country did that final Ryanair flight land in?
answer: Greece (Athens)
choices: Greece (Athens)
Germany (Frankfurt)
the United Arab Emirates (Dubai)
the United States (New York)
context: The last confirmed public sighting was her Sofia-to-Athens Ryanair flight on October 25, 2017; she vanished from Athens. Investigative reporters have pursued leads through several countries since. Source: BBC 'The Missing Cryptoqueen' podcast (2019).

question: By 2022, US federal prosecutors had spent years chasing Ruja Ignatova, the missing Bulgarian founder of the OneCoin cryptocurrency scam that stole an estimated $4 billion from investors worldwide. On June 30, 2022, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) publicly gave her a status that only a small handful of fugitives in American history have ever held. Which formal FBI listing did she receive that day?
answer: placement on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
choices: placement on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
a US federal indictment sealed under national-security law
an Interpol Blue Notice
designation as a specially designated national by the US Treasury
context: The FBI added Ignatova to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on June 30, 2022. Federal indictments against her had already been unsealed; other legal tools exist but the specific 2022 event was the Ten Most Wanted listing. Source: https://www.fbi.gov/wanted/topten/ruja-ignatova.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos is a Greek-British computer scientist who wrote Mastering Bitcoin, the standard technical book on the protocol. He and other longtime Bitcoin teachers push back hard whenever reporters lump every blockchain project under the single word 'crypto.' To them that word blurs a real distinction between Satoshi's original 2009 protocol and the thousands of later coins run by companies, foundations, or promoters. Which point do they insist reporters recognize?
answer: That Bitcoin -- a specific 2009 protocol with a proven fixed supply -- is not the same category of thing as most projects that call themselves 'crypto'
choices: That Bitcoin -- a specific 2009 protocol with a proven fixed supply -- is not the same category of thing as most projects that call themselves 'crypto'
That all cryptocurrency including Bitcoin should be regulated identically by financial authorities
That any project using a blockchain is legitimate regardless of its economics
That the SEC alone should decide which cryptocurrencies are legitimate
context: The Bitcoin-vs-crypto distinction (Antonopoulos, Ammous, Song) treats Bitcoin as a specific rule-bound engineering artifact; most 'crypto' projects have an issuer who can change the rules, which is what BitConnect and OneCoin exploited. Regulatory framings and blockchain-as-legitimizer are precisely the moves the distinction refuses. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.).

question: Charles Ponzi was an Italian immigrant in Boston who in 1920 promised huge returns from trading international postage coupons; instead he paid old investors with new investors' money, and the whole scheme collapsed within a year. When modern Austrian-tradition writers examine crypto scams like BitConnect (2016–2018) and OneCoin (2014–2017), they compare them directly to Ponzi's original 1920 fraud. Which historical claim about the pattern do they most often press?
answer: That the pattern of promising fixed high returns with a vague mechanism and paying them from new deposits is older than the technology it dresses in
choices: That the pattern of promising fixed high returns with a vague mechanism and paying them from new deposits is older than the technology it dresses in
That fraud of this specific shape was invented by the cryptocurrency industry and had no prior counterpart in twentieth-century finance
That government regulation of financial products reliably prevents Ponzi schemes if the enforcement budget is high enough
That Ponzi schemes structurally require a specific new financial technology to attract depositors and cannot succeed with older tools
context: The Austrian pattern-recognition argument treats BitConnect and OneCoin as a 1920 Ponzi rewrapped in 2016 clothing -- the technology is decoration; the structure is ancient. Government regulation did not prevent either; the technology did not create the Ponzi form (Ponzi himself had none). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponzi_scheme.

question: In old American towns, some places banned Sunday alcohol sales entirely. Church groups pushed for the ban because they believed drinking on Sunday was wrong. But illegal moonshine sellers also pushed for the ban — with legal stores closed on Sunday, thirsty buyers walked over to them instead, and the moonshiners made more money. Two very different groups quietly wanted exactly the same rule, for opposite reasons. What kind of coalition is this?
answer: Two very different groups quietly wanting the same rule for opposite reasons
choices: Two very different groups quietly wanting the same rule for opposite reasons
A single group united in one shared belief
A group that only cares about profits
A group that only cares about morals
context: Bruce Yandle spent 1982-84 as Executive Director of the FTC. His 1983 essay in Regulation magazine (Cato Institute) coined the 'Bootleggers and Baptists' framing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Yandle.

question: In 1983, the American economist Bruce Yandle wrote a short essay describing a strange pattern he kept seeing while working at the Federal Trade Commission. Over and over, two very different groups -- one moral, one out for profit -- quietly backed the same regulations for opposite reasons. Yandle gave the pattern a memorable two-word nickname that stuck in economics classes ever after. What was that nickname?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists
Preachers and Peddlers
Doctors and Dealers
Bosses and Buddies
context: The 1983 essay is titled 'Bootleggers and Baptists -- The Education of a Regulatory Economist'. The pairing has become one of the most-cited concepts in modern political economy. Source: cato.org (Regulation magazine 1983).

question: The classic example Bruce Yandle pointed to came from the American South. On Sundays, laws banned the sale of liquor. On the surface it looked purely moral, and one group of devout churchgoers loudly backed it as a moral crusade. But quietly, another group of criminals profited from the same ban, because they sold liquor illegally on Sundays with no legal competition to undercut them. Which two groups formed this famous unspoken coalition?
answer: Baptists (moral) and Bootleggers (profit)
choices: Baptists (moral) and Bootleggers (profit)
Doctors (moral) and Distillers (profit)
Preachers (moral) and Publishers (profit)
Pastors (moral) and Prosecutors (profit)
context: Southern Baptists supported Sunday liquor bans on moral grounds; bootleggers supported them because Sunday legal sales would compete with their illegal operations. The Baptists gave moral cover; the bootleggers supplied resources. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983).

question: In Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers-and-Baptists pattern, both groups back exactly the same regulation but for opposite reasons. The bootleggers get real profit -- with legal liquor stores forced to close on Sundays, their illegal Sunday sales face no competition and prices rise. What do the Baptists give the same rule in return that makes it politically safe for lawmakers to keep?
answer: Moral cover
choices: Moral cover
Legal defense
Election financing
Media coverage
context: The Baptists' visible moral rhetoric provided political legitimacy; the bootleggers' quiet profit interest supplied resources. Together the coalition was more effective than either could be alone. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983).

question: Bruce Yandle, an American economist, noticed that odd political coalitions form around new regulations: one group has money at stake, another has moral cover to give. A modern US example is city rules that tighten where Uber and Lyft can pick up passengers or what they can charge. Two very different groups usually show up together at city hall backing those tighter rules. Which pair?
answer: Taxi-medallion holders (economic) and pedestrian-safety advocates (moral cover)
choices: Taxi-medallion holders (economic) and pedestrian-safety advocates (moral cover)
Uber shareholders (economic) and consumer-rights groups (moral cover)
Ride-share drivers (economic) and disability advocates (moral cover)
Hotel operators (economic) and neighborhood groups (moral cover)
context: Taxi-medallion holders benefit economically from restrictions that raise the cost of ride-share entry. Pedestrian-safety and passenger-protection advocates provide moral cover. Yandle's pattern applied to a modern case. Source: mercatus.org ride-share studies.

question: Modern environmental regulations often look like a clean fight between green activists on one side and dirty industry on the other. But Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers-and-Baptists lens shows a hidden alliance underneath. Real environmentalists back a rule for the planet -- and a specific kind of business quietly cheers along, because the same rule crushes their competitors and locks in their own market share. Which kind of business most often plays that hidden bootlegger role in environmental fights?
answer: Domestic producers seeking barriers against foreign competitors
choices: Domestic producers seeking barriers against foreign competitors
Foreign producers seeking US market access
Public-utility monopolies seeking rate cuts
Insurance companies seeking premium hikes
context: Environmental rules that raise costs on all producers can disadvantage foreign competitors more than domestic ones (particularly under carbon-adjustment or content-labeling schemes). Domestic producers become the bootleggers behind the environmental moral coalition. Source: cato.org environmental economics.

question: America's most famous ban of all -- the 1919-1933 Prohibition of alcohol, written into the Constitution as the 18th Amendment -- is treated by economists as the biggest real-world example of Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers-and-Baptists pattern. Two very different groups pushed together to make Prohibition happen, then benefited together while it lasted. Which two groups actually formed the Prohibition alliance?
answer: Moralists and organized-crime beneficiaries
choices: Moralists and organized-crime beneficiaries
Farmers and factory owners
Suffragists and railroad barons
Immigrants and native-born citizens
context: Prohibition united moralists (temperance movements, WCTU, Anti-Saloon League) with organized-crime beneficiaries who would run the resulting black market. The 18th Amendment (1919) and the Volstead Act became the American case study. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States.

question: In 1983, the American economist Bruce Yandle wrote a short essay describing a strange political pattern he called 'bootleggers and Baptists' — the moral crusaders and the illegal booze sellers both quietly cheering the same Sunday liquor law. In 2014, Yandle published a full book-length expansion of that framework, co-authored with a modern American economist confusingly named Adam Smith (not the 1776 one). The Cato Institute released it. What is that 2014 book's title?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics
Public Choice for Ordinary People
The Economics of Coalitions
Regulation and Its Alternatives
context: The 2014 book (Cato Institute) extends the framework to modern regulatory cases across environmental policy, consumer protection, financial regulation, and more. Co-author Adam Smith is a modern American economist. Source: cato.org (Yandle + Smith 2014).

question: Bruce Yandle turned his Bootleggers-and-Baptists observation into a rule of thumb for reading political news. When a regulation has a clear moral reason on the surface and quiet backing from firms that will profit from it, look at which side does what in public. The moral (Baptist) side plays one specific public role, while the profit (bootlegger) side plays another quieter one. What role does the moral side play?
answer: The visible lobbying while the profit coalition supplies the resources
choices: The visible lobbying while the profit coalition supplies the resources
The private financing while the profit coalition takes the public credit
The economic analysis while the profit coalition provides the theory
The election donations while the profit coalition writes the laws
context: Yandle wrote that regulatory economists spend years learning to look past the moral rhetoric to identify the bootlegger. The moral side gets the microphone; the profit side gets the check. Recognition-not-verdict: the kid learns to spot the pattern. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983, 2014).

question: In the 1920s American South, two very different groups both fought to keep Sunday laws that banned liquor sales: devout Protestant churchgoers pushing for moral order, and illegal liquor sellers who feared legal Sunday competition would ruin their profits. Fifty years later, the American economist Bruce Yandle would name a whole coalition pattern after this odd pair. What two-word name did he give it?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists
Farmers and Foundries
Merchants and Ministers
Sailors and Saloonkeepers
context: Bruce Yandle, 'Bootleggers and Baptists -- The Education of a Regulatory Economist' (Regulation, May/June 1983). Baptists supported Sunday closing on moral grounds; bootleggers supported it because closed legal outlets meant Sunday drinkers had to buy from illegal suppliers. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983 reprint).

question: The Bootleggers-and-Baptists pattern is named for old US Sunday alcohol laws. Baptists preached against Sunday drinking on moral grounds. Bootleggers quietly loved the same law because it killed the legal Sunday competition and let them charge more. Their reasons for supporting the law were opposite. But for the pattern to fit at all, one thing had to match between the two groups. What must they share?
answer: Identical policy positions on the rule's specific design
choices: Identical policy positions on the rule's specific design
Identical philosophies of government
Shared electoral organization
Common demographic background
context: Yandle's insight: the moral coalition provides political cover; the commercial coalition provides funding and lobbying muscle. Both need identical detail-level policy to succeed. Source: Yandle, Regulation (1983).

question: In August 2022, California's air board banned the sale of new gasoline cars starting in 2035. Bastiat would have asked about the unseen: the strain on the grid, the mining supply chain, the low-income drivers priced out. What did Bastiat call these hidden effects that policymakers ignore?
answer: The Unseen
choices: The Unseen
The Seen
External benefits
Consumer surplus
context: California ACC II mandates that all new passenger vehicles sold in the state be zero-emission by 2035. About a dozen other states adopted the same target. Source: ww2.arb.ca.gov (Advanced Clean Cars II rulemaking).

question: In 2020, the state of California ordered that every new car sold in the state from 2035 onward must be a zero-emission electric vehicle — no more gasoline engines. Environmental groups cheered the rule as a victory for the climate. But the biggest established car makers — companies like GM and Ford — also cheered it and publicly said they supported the mandate. Why would huge, powerful car makers back a strict regulation like that?
answer: They can afford the switch, but smaller rivals cannot
choices: They can afford the switch, but smaller rivals cannot
Big carmakers always fight new rules
The rule bans them from selling any cars at all
The rule forces them to shrink their factories
context: Large incumbent automakers (GM, Ford, Stellantis) publicly backed the ACC II timeline. Their compliance capital is a moat: smaller automakers and independent parts suppliers who cannot afford the transition are the unrepresented losers. Source: reuters.com (2022 CARB rulemaking coverage).

question: The June 2018 Supreme Court ruling in South Dakota v. Wayfair allowed states to require out-of-state online sellers to collect state sales tax. Which category of business quietly supported the ruling as a way to raise compliance costs on smaller rivals?
answer: Large brick-and-mortar retailers and Amazon
choices: Large brick-and-mortar retailers and Amazon
Small independent Etsy sellers
State university bookstores
Rural post-office contractors
context: Wayfair was a classic Bootleggers-and-Baptists case: state revenue officials and 'level-playing-field' advocates (Baptists) with big-box retailers and Amazon (Bootleggers, since both already had physical nexus and were already collecting). Small e-commerce sellers now face 45+ state sales-tax regimes. Source: supremecourt.gov (Wayfair 585 US ___).

question: Starting with Colorado and Washington in 2012, many US states have legalized recreational marijuana. But those states added tight rules on the legal industry: only a few licenses granted, high sales taxes, and mountains of paperwork for growers and shops. In California in 2023, licensed stores were competing against unlicensed street dealers who paid no taxes at all. What share of the pot sold in the state that year was still from the illegal market?
answer: About two-thirds
choices: About two-thirds
About one-tenth
About one-third
Essentially none
context: California's licensed cannabis market has been repeatedly estimated to supply only about one-third of total consumption, with the illegal market preserving roughly two-thirds -- a structural gift to Bootleggers-and-Baptists coalitions of anti-drug advocates and licensed incumbents. Source: California DCC market reports; New Frontier Data.

question: In 1998 the four biggest US tobacco companies -- Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson, and Lorillard -- signed the Master Settlement Agreement with 46 state attorneys general. On paper it was a punishment for the tobacco industry. But economists later showed the settlement locked out new tobacco competitors and helped the big four keep market share, while states got a huge stream of tobacco money for decades. Which two coalitions ended up on the same side, despite opposite stated goals?
answer: Public-health advocates and the four largest tobacco companies
choices: Public-health advocates and the four largest tobacco companies
Tobacco farmers and cigarette retailers
State attorneys general and independent smoke shops
Advertising firms and pharmaceutical companies
context: The MSA locked in the Big Four tobacco companies' market share by imposing per-cigarette payments that made new entry prohibitively expensive. Public-health advocates got funding; Big Four got a moat. Source: naag.org (MSA 1998); Viscusi, Smoke-Filled Rooms (Chicago 2002).

question: In 1983, the American economist Bruce Yandle noticed something strange: two totally different groups often lobby for the same regulation for opposite reasons. On Sunday liquor bans, churchgoing teetotalers pushed for the ban on moral grounds, while illegal liquor sellers quietly supported the same law because it killed their legal competition. In 2014, Yandle teamed up with his grandson Adam Smith to expand this insight into a book for the Cato Institute, gathering modern cases from banking, green rules, and tobacco settlement deals. What did they title it?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists
The Political Economy of Regulation
The Captured Economy
Regulation Revisited
context: Adam Smith + Bruce Yandle, Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics (Cato Institute, 2014). Note: the Adam Smith here is a Johnson & Wales political scientist, not the 18th-century economist. Source: cato.org (2014).

question: Bruce Yandle, a Clemson University economist, wrote his famous Bootleggers-and-Baptists paper in 1983 after watching decades of US federal regulation. He wanted to teach students and policy analysts a specific mental habit: whenever an odd coalition of moral reformers and quiet business interests shows up backing the same new rule, do not just credit the moral story out front. Look one layer down. What should the analyst look for?
answer: A concentrated commercial beneficiary hiding behind the moral advocate
choices: A concentrated commercial beneficiary hiding behind the moral advocate
A single ideological cause explaining the whole coalition
A single geographic region driving the outcome
A hidden foreign influence campaign
context: The Yandle move: when moral rhetoric and commercial interest happen to align on identical policy detail, look for the commercial beneficiary. This is a diagnostic tool, not a policy verdict on the substantive goal. Source: Yandle, Regulation (1983); Smith + Yandle (Cato 2014).

question: A US town proposes a rule to ban a legal product. At the public hearing, the people who show up to argue for the ban include church groups — who oppose the product on moral grounds — and rival companies who quietly profit if their competitor is banned. Economist Bruce Yandle named this the 'bootleggers and Baptists' coalition after Sunday-liquor laws. What broader lesson about regulation does this pattern teach?
answer: Stated moral reasons rarely fully explain who really pushes for a rule
choices: Stated moral reasons rarely fully explain who really pushes for a rule
Moral supporters always deserve more trust than business supporters
Businesses should be banned from every regulatory debate
Only bipartisan coalitions ever produce good rules
context: The Yandle move applies to left, right, and non-partisan rules alike. The moral coalition may be sincere; the commercial coalition may be following naked incentive. What matters is the joint outcome. Source: Yandle, Regulation (1983).

question: In July 1944, with World War II almost won, delegates from 44 Allied nations gathered at a grand American hotel in the White Mountains of New Hampshire for 22 days. Their job was to design the money system that would run the world after the war ended. In which hotel did they meet?
answer: the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
choices: the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
the Waldorf Astoria in New York City
the Willard Hotel in Washington, DC
the Palmer House in Chicago, Illinois
context: The July 1-22, 1944 Bretton Woods Conference was held at the Mount Washington Hotel in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. The Waldorf, Willard and Palmer House were sites of other 20th-century political events but not the Bretton Woods Conference. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_Conference.

question: Under the 1944 Bretton Woods plan, every Allied currency was tied to the US dollar at a fixed exchange rate. In turn, the dollar itself was tied to gold at one specific fixed price set by law. Any foreign government could bring their dollars to the US Treasury and swap them for gold at that rate. What was the dollar-to-gold price per ounce?
answer: $35 per ounce of gold
choices: $35 per ounce of gold
$20 per ounce of gold
$100 per ounce of gold
$400 per ounce of gold
context: The Bretton Woods peg was $35 per ounce of gold. The classical US gold-standard price before Roosevelt's 1934 devaluation was ~$20.67; $100 and $400 are later 1970s prices after the peg broke. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied nations gathered at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design the postwar world money order. John Maynard Keynes led the British team; Harry Dexter White led the Americans. They agreed to peg currencies to the US dollar and the dollar to gold, and to set up two new global institutions to run the system. Which pair did the meeting create?
answer: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank
choices: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank
the United Nations and the World Trade Organization
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the European Central Bank
the Bank for International Settlements and the League of Nations
context: Bretton Woods created the IMF (for exchange-rate stability) and the World Bank (formally IBRD, for postwar reconstruction). The UN and WTO were established elsewhere; NATO and the ECB came much later; BIS predates Bretton Woods (1930) and the League of Nations was already dissolving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_Conference.

question: At the 1944 Bretton Woods meeting, Britain's top delegate was the famous economist John Maynard Keynes. Keynes pitched a rival plan against the American one. He wanted a truly global reserve money, run not by any single country but by a new 'International Clearing Union' that would settle trade balances between nations. What did Keynes name his proposed new currency?
answer: the Bancor
choices: the Bancor
the Euro
the Special Drawing Right
the ECU
context: John Maynard Keynes proposed the Bancor at Bretton Woods; the US design (Harry Dexter White's dollar anchor) was adopted instead. The Euro (1999) and ECU (1979) came from European monetary integration; SDRs (1969) were the IMF's much later reserve asset. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bancor.

question: In July 1944, delegates from 44 winning Allied nations gathered at a resort called Bretton Woods in New Hampshire to design a new world money system for after World War Two. They agreed to peg every major currency to the US dollar at a fixed exchange rate, and to peg the US dollar itself to gold at 35 dollars per ounce. What was the main goal of this arrangement?
answer: To keep exchange rates steady and stop countries from printing money without limit
choices: To keep exchange rates steady and stop countries from printing money without limit
To let each country's currency float freely against every other
To create a single world currency to replace all national money
To end all international trade for twenty years
context: Harry Dexter White drafted the winning US plan for Bretton Woods. Morgenthau was Treasury Secretary (his subordinate); Acheson was at State; Harriman was Ambassador to the USSR and later a Cabinet officer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Dexter_White.

question: Starting in 1995, the NSA began releasing files from a wartime program that had cracked Soviet cables. The files proved that Harry Dexter White, while helping design the postwar money system, had been a Soviet source. Which project's files showed this?
answer: the Venona project
choices: the Venona project
the Manhattan Project
Operation Paperclip
the Bletchley Park archive
context: Venona (public releases 1995-96) provided the strongest forensic evidence that White was a Soviet source (codenames 'Jurist' and 'Richard'). The Manhattan Project built the atomic bomb; Paperclip recruited German scientists; Bletchley Park broke Enigma. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venona_project.

question: A high US Treasury official helped design the world's postwar money system in 1944. Years later, testimony to Congress showed he had secretly worked for a foreign power. What hidden risk of letting a small group design the world's money does this Treasury official's story reveal?
answer: A few insiders with hidden agendas can steer rules that bind everyone else
choices: A few insiders with hidden agendas can steer rules that bind everyone else
Only elected representatives ever help design money systems
Every design decision was open to public vote from the start
Insiders always openly share every belief that they hold
context: Whittaker Chambers named White during 1948 HUAC testimony. Alger Hiss was the more famous Chambers-named State Department official; Bentley named other Soviet sources; Hoover was FBI Director, not a witness. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Dexter_White.

question: For 26 years after 1945 the US promised foreign governments they could trade paper dollars for gold at a fixed rate. In August 1971 a US president ended that promise on television one Sunday evening. What did that decision mean for the world's money?
answer: The dollar became a paper currency backed only by the government's word
choices: The dollar became a paper currency backed only by the government's word
Every family in America got a free bar of gold in the mail
The dollar was permanently pegged to silver instead
Every country in the world stopped using dollars overnight
context: Richard Nixon announced the closing of the gold window on August 15, 1971, formally ending Bretton Woods. Johnson expanded Great Society spending that stressed the peg; Kennedy died in 1963; Ford succeeded Nixon in 1974 after the peg had already broken. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: The Bretton Woods system, agreed at a New Hampshire resort in 1944, pegged the US dollar to gold at 35 dollars per ounce and every other major currency to the dollar. It ran for 27 years until President Richard Nixon closed the gold window in August 1971, because the US no longer had enough gold to cover the dollars it had issued. A historian summarizing that collapse presses one specific reasoning move about what the peg's design revealed from the very start. Which move does the argument make?
answer: That any peg that required the peg-setter to run fiscal deficits in its own currency was arithmetically doomed the moment those deficits exceeded gold reserves
choices: That any peg that required the peg-setter to run fiscal deficits in its own currency was arithmetically doomed the moment those deficits exceeded gold reserves
That the peg would have held indefinitely if postwar political leaders had shown more discipline about deficit spending and had chosen to defend the peg with fiscal restraint
That the peg was purely a matter of international communication and could have been sustained by careful rhetoric and coordinated central-bank statements to hold public confidence
That the peg was an accidental byproduct of postwar chaos rather than a deliberately designed monetary system and had no coherent architecture to defend once challenged
context: The Austrian argument (Rothbard, Ammous): the Bretton Woods gold-exchange standard collapsed by arithmetic. Once US dollar issuance outran gold reserves, the peg could not survive any test. The other options mistake the failure for discretion, rhetoric, or accident. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States; Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Austrian monetary historians distinguish between two related but different forms of gold-based money. In the classical version, used in Britain before 1914, ordinary citizens could walk into a bank and redeem paper money directly for gold coins. In a looser version, only foreign central banks could redeem dollars for gold, while ordinary citizens could not. The Bretton Woods system that ran from 1944 to 1971 was the second form, not the first. Which technical term captures what Bretton Woods actually was?
answer: a gold-exchange standard rather than a classical gold standard
choices: a gold-exchange standard rather than a classical gold standard
a bimetallic standard rather than a silver standard
a floating peg rather than a fixed peg
a currency board rather than a central bank
context: Bretton Woods was a gold-EXCHANGE standard: only foreign central banks could redeem dollars for gold, not ordinary citizens. A classical gold standard makes gold coins the actual circulating money. The other pairs address different distinctions. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_exchange_standard.

question: In 2009, four large rising economies decided to team up as a formal group: Brazil, Russia, India, and China. South Africa joined the club in 2010, giving the group five members spanning four continents. They meet regularly to coordinate on trade, banking, and world politics as a counterweight to the older G7. What short name do they go by?
answer: BRICS
choices: BRICS
G7
OPEC
APEC
context: The original 2009 BRIC grouping became BRICS in 2010 when South Africa joined. It is a coordination forum, not a treaty organization. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2001, the British economist Jim O'Neill at the bank Goldman Sachs noticed four large countries: Brazil, Russia, India, and China. Their economies looked ready to grow fast over the next 20 years, and he coined a snappy nickname for the group using the first letter of each country. What did those four countries share that made him bet on them?
answer: Huge populations and lots of room to catch up to richer countries
choices: Huge populations and lots of room to catch up to richer countries
They all spoke the same language
They all had winter Olympics that year
They all shared one central bank
context: Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill coined the term BRIC in a 2001 paper titled 'Building Better Global Economic BRICs.' The label described projected economic weight; the actual political group formed later. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS' (2026-09-05).

question: Jim O'Neill's 2001 BRIC group — Brazil, Russia, India, China — grew into a formal bloc called BRICS after South Africa joined in 2010. In 2024, the bloc admitted new members from the Middle East and Africa, including Iran, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates. Together the enlarged bloc wants to build a trading system independent of the US dollar. Why would these countries want a separate international system of their own?
answer: They fear the US could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them
choices: They fear the US could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them
Their people prefer paper money over any digital system
They want to share a single central bank with the US
They believe the dollar has too little inflation
context: The January 1 2024 expansion added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the UAE. The expanded group is often called BRICS+ and represents roughly 45% of global population and 35% of world GDP. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS+' (2026-09-05).

question: In February 2022, Russian troops invaded Ukraine. Within days the US, the European Union, the UK, and Japan froze the dollar and euro savings that Russia's central bank had parked in Western banks — money built up over years of oil and gas sales. The freeze shocked other countries around the world that had assumed their own foreign reserves were untouchable. About how much of Russia's savings was frozen?
answer: About 300 billion dollars
choices: About 300 billion dollars
About 30 billion dollars
About 3 trillion dollars
About 3 billion dollars
context: The February 2022 freeze of roughly $300 billion in Russian central-bank reserves was the largest such action in modern history. Non-Western reserve holders read the precedent and accelerated their interest in alternative payment rails. Source: Grokipedia 'Sanctions during the Russo-Ukrainian War' (2026-09-05).

question: After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the United States and its allies froze about 300 billion dollars of Russia's dollar reserves overnight. Russia and China responded by quickly moving their trade with each other away from dollars: they now pay each other in rubles and yuan, their own national currencies, instead. According to Chinese customs data, about what share of Russia–China trade now uses those two currencies?
answer: Over 90 percent
choices: Over 90 percent
About 20 percent
About 50 percent
Under 5 percent
context: Chinese customs data show over 90% of Russia-China trade now settles in ruble-yuan, up from a small fraction pre-2022. India began paying for Russian oil in rupees and UAE dirhams. Saudi Arabia signaled acceptance of yuan for some Chinese oil purchases at the 2023 Beijing summit. Source: Grokipedia 'De-dollarisation' (2026-09-05).

question: Since 2000 the dollar's share of world central-bank reserves has slipped from 71 percent to under 60, yet no rival currency has caught up. In the 1960s French finance minister Valery Giscard d'Estaing gave the dollar's status a famous name. What was it?
answer: Exorbitant privilege
choices: Exorbitant privilege
Special drawing right
Reserve arbitrage
Petrodollar recycling
context: IMF COFER data show dollar share of allocated reserves at roughly 58% in 2024, down from 71% in 2000. The trend is directional but slow; 88% of foreign-exchange transactions still have a dollar leg. Source: IMF Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves.

question: US federal debt now equals roughly a full year of everything the country makes. Ludwig von Mises warned that when governments can no longer tax enough to service their debt, they inflate their way out until the currency collapses. What did he call this final stage?
answer: The crack-up boom
choices: The crack-up boom
The liquidity trap
The Great Moderation
The deflationary spiral
context: US federal debt held by the public is roughly 120% of GDP in 2025, up from about 79% in 2019. The combination of high debt and demonstrated willingness to weaponize the dollar drives reserve diversification. Source: Congressional Budget Office 2025 Long-Term Budget Outlook.

question: After the United States froze Russia's dollar reserves in 2022, central bankers in other countries began asking a nervous question: what if our reserves get frozen next? Combined with worries about the rising US national debt, they responded by sharply increasing purchases of one specific neutral reserve asset that no other government controls. That accumulation hit a 55-year high in 2022 and stayed elevated through 2024. What did the central banks buy?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Bitcoin
Chinese sovereign debt
Swiss francs
context: World Gold Council data show central-bank gold purchases hit a 55-year high in 2022 at roughly 1,082 tonnes. The 2023 and 2024 totals remained above 1,000 tonnes each year -- historically extraordinary. Source: World Gold Council, Central Bank Gold Statistics.

question: Several large countries — including China, Russia, India, and Turkey — have started keeping less of their national savings in US dollars and more in physical gold. At the same time, US federal government debt has climbed past 34 trillion dollars and keeps rising every year. Austrian-tradition analysts, who track monetary trends carefully and are skeptical of unlimited money printing, read these two facts together. What do they say is most likely to happen?
answer: A slow shift toward neutral assets is starting, but the dollar isn't immediately replaced
choices: A slow shift toward neutral assets is starting, but the dollar isn't immediately replaced
The dollar will collapse within two years and be replaced by the Chinese yuan
A shared new currency will launch worldwide within twelve months
Gold will be dropped by every central bank as too old-fashioned
context: The Austrian read (Luke Gromen, Lyn Alden, Ammous): near-term dollar hegemony intact; long-term directional shift is real. Weaponized reserves plus rising sovereign debt drive rational holders toward assets no state can freeze. Source: Lyn Alden, Broken Money (2023).

question: Historians who study why great trading currencies lose their perch — the Venetian ducat, the Spanish dollar, the Dutch guilder, the British pound — notice a pattern. Rival economies are usually there in the background for a long time before the shift happens. What actually tips the change is rarely a war lost or a competitor rising. It is one habit the issuing country falls into. What reason do they name?
answer: The issuing country's own choices to overspend or freeze others' savings
choices: The issuing country's own choices to overspend or freeze others' savings
Being outcompeted by a bigger rival economy
Losing a major war to a smaller country
Being displaced by a new currency pegged to gold
context: The BRICS+ story is not really about the yuan or rupee. It is about the choices the US made -- freezing reserves, running large deficits -- that made non-Western holders want alternatives. The reserve-currency issuer is the primary driver of its own displacement. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: After a disaster destroys a city block, you often hear people say 'well, at least the rebuilding will boost the economy — think of all the jobs.' The French economist Frederic Bastiat called this the broken-window fallacy. The seen part is the construction work. The unseen part is what the money for rebuilding would otherwise have done. Why is the boost claim a mistake in reasoning?
answer: The money for rebuilding was going to be spent on other things people wanted
choices: The money for rebuilding was going to be spent on other things people wanted
Rebuilding creates unlimited new wealth from thin air
Rebuilding is illegal in most countries
The block was worthless before, so it is a pure gain
context: Krugman, then a new Times columnist and later the 2008 Nobel laureate in economics, wrote in the column: 'Now, all of a sudden, we need some new office buildings.' Friedman and Dowd wrote opinion columns on foreign policy and politics; Brooks joined the Times in 2003. Source: outsidethebeltway.com 'Paul Krugman: 9/11 Has Become An Occasion For Shame'.

question: In an 1850 essay, Frederic Bastiat told a story about a shopkeeper's son who breaks a window. Everyone sees the six francs paid to the glazier. But no one sees the six francs the shopkeeper would have spent on something else. What does the essay call that missing second purchase?
answer: That which is not seen
choices: That which is not seen
The dead-weight loss
The unpaid labour
The hidden surplus
context: The essay is titled Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas -- 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen'. Bastiat's move is that the six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or a book is the UNSEEN loss the disaster caused. Dead-weight loss is a much later diagram-based concept (Harberger, 1954). Source: oll.libertyfund.org, Bastiat, 'That Which is Seen'.

question: In August 2009, during the depths of the Great Recession, the US government offered to pay car dealers 3,500 or 4,500 dollars for each old, gas-guzzling car that a customer traded in for a newer, more fuel-efficient one. The dealers killed the old engine on the spot by pouring a sodium-silicate goo into it while it ran, seizing it forever. Then the whole car was crushed. What was the program called?
answer: Cash for Clunkers
choices: Cash for Clunkers
The Auto Rescue
The Detroit Bailout
The Green Fleet Programme
context: Its formal name was the Car Allowance Rebate System (CARS), enacted under Title XIII of the Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2009 and administered by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Auto Rescue and Detroit Bailout are informal names for the separate TARP-funded GM and Chrysler restructurings. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Car Allowance Rebate System'.

question: In summer 2009, the US government launched Cash for Clunkers, a program that paid people to trade in old gas-guzzlers for new cars. The old clunkers had to be destroyed on the spot, their engines wrecked with sodium silicate so they could never drive again. The $3 billion budget ran out in only 55 days, from July 1 to August 24. About how many cars did the program force to be scrapped?
context: NHTSA's final figure was 677,081 vehicles scrapped under CARS, at a total voucher cost of about $2.85 billion of the $3 billion authorised. The other three numbers are plausible fleet-size distractors from the same era. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Car Allowance Rebate System'.

question: French economist Frederic Bastiat's famous 1850 essay 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen' taught that every policy has a visible effect and an invisible cost you have to think hard to notice. Analysts at the Cato Institute and Mises Institute applied his method to the 2009 Cash for Clunkers program, which pulled hundreds of thousands of working used cars off the market to be crushed. They found a specific unseen cost. On whom did that cost fall hardest?
answer: Lower-income buyers priced out of the shrunken used-car market
choices: Lower-income buyers priced out of the shrunken used-car market
New-car dealers left with exhausted showroom inventories
Municipal fleet managers rebuilding patrol-car reserves
Long-haul freight carriers rebuilding tractor-cab fleets
context: Roughly 677,000 vehicles pulled out of the used-car supply pushed prices at the low end higher, hitting the buyers whose only option is a used car under a few thousand dollars. Dealers, fleet managers and freight carriers were largely unaffected -- their vehicle classes were not the ones being scrapped. Source: cato.org 'Cash for Clunkers: Dumbest Program Ever?'.

question: In 2013 the Brookings Institution released a study by the American economists Ted Gayer and Emily Parker checking whether Cash for Clunkers had actually boosted the US economy in 2009. They compared car sales in the program window with what buyers would have done in the months just after. Their finding cut hard against the program's fans. What did they conclude the vouchers had mostly done?
answer: Pulled forward car purchases that would have happened anyway within a few months
choices: Pulled forward car purchases that would have happened anyway within a few months
Created a lasting increase in the total US vehicle fleet's fuel economy
Prevented a wave of car-dealer bankruptcies in the summer recession
Transferred purchasing power from urban to rural households
context: Gayer and Parker's Brookings paper found the surge in July-August 2009 sales was largely offset by a corresponding fall over the following months, and that both the stimulus and the environmental benefit were far smaller than official estimates. The other three claims were made at the time but did not survive the data. Source: brookings.edu 'Cash for Clunkers Evaluation Policy Brief' (Gayer 2013).

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a famous essay called 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen.' He used the story of a boy breaking a shop window to teach a rule about wealth: the glazier's new sale is visible, but the suit the shopkeeper cannot now afford is invisible. Today, after a hurricane wrecks a coastal town, some TV pundits say 'at least the storm will boost the economy through all the rebuilding.' What is the hidden flaw in that cheerful argument?
answer: The money and time spent rebuilding could have built something new instead
choices: The money and time spent rebuilding could have built something new instead
Storms really are the best way to grow a nation's wealth
Rebuilding creates goods that would never have existed otherwise
Only insurance companies benefit, so the argument fails only for them
context: Boudreaux, a former president of the Foundation for Economic Education, co-founded Cafe Hayek with Russ Roberts in 2004 and writes the recurring 'Quotation of the Day' invoking Bastiat. Cowen writes Marginal Revolution; Caplan writes at EconLog; Boettke works chiefly on Austrian scholarship. Source: cafehayek.com.

question: Russell Roberts is the host of the popular economics podcast EconTalk and a research fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution. In 2008 he wrote an economics novel set around a fictional earthquake that hits Palo Alto, California, using the story to teach Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen idea in the form of a family drama about supply, prices, and hidden costs. What is the novel called?
answer: The Price of Everything
choices: The Price of Everything
The Choice
The Invisible Heart
How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life
context: The Price of Everything (Princeton University Press, 2008) uses a post-earthquake supermarket to show how sharply rising prices coordinate the movement of bottled water and generators to where they are most needed -- Bastiat's method dramatised. The Choice (2006) and The Invisible Heart (2001) are Roberts's other novels; How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life is his 2014 non-fiction. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Russ Roberts'.

question: During World War Two the official measures of the American economy — what today is called gross domestic product (GDP) — shot up because the government was building tanks, ships, and planes at a furious pace. In the 1990s, the American economic historian Robert Higgs looked past those wartime headline numbers to what regular families actually experienced day to day. What did his research show?
answer: Everyday goods for regular families barely improved from Depression levels during the war
choices: Everyday goods for regular families barely improved from Depression levels during the war
The government's war spending was smaller than peacetime spending had been
Business investment kept growing during the war as fast as before it
Unemployment stayed above ten percent throughout every war year
context: Higgs's point is that GDP counts what is SPENT, including tanks and shells; what an ordinary American could actually buy at home -- meat, sugar, tires, gasoline, new cars -- was under strict rationing, and real private per-capita consumption sat near 1938-39 levels until demobilisation. The other three claims are false. Source: eh.net review, 'Depression, War, and Cold War' (Higgs).

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat opened his essay 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' with the story of a shopkeeper's son breaking a window. Bystanders comforted the shopkeeper by pointing out the glazier would now be paid — supposedly boosting the economy. Bastiat's broken-window section closes with a compressed four-word refutation, in French, of every later 'disaster-as-stimulus' claim. Which four words?
answer: 'Destruction n'est pas profit'
choices: 'Destruction n'est pas profit'
'Luxe n'est pas richesse'
'Spoliation n'est pas industrie'
'Echange n'est pas vol'
context: The full French sentence reads 'briser, gaspiller, dissiper, n'est pas encourager le travail national; ou plus brievement: destruction n'est pas profit.' The other three phrases are Bastiat-style constructions, not attested lines from the broken-window passage; only the answer is the essay's own closing formula. Source: bastiat.org 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas'.

question: An economist argues that most of the extra pay a college graduate earns is not really from things learned in class. Instead, it comes from the diploma itself sending a message to employers: 'I can finish hard, boring things.' The degree acts like a flag waved at hiring managers, not proof of new skills. What is this idea called?
answer: Signaling
choices: Signaling
Inflation
Rent control
Free trade
context: Bryan Caplan (b. April 8, 1971) took his Princeton PhD in 1997 under Gene Grossman and is a professor at GMU and Mercatus senior fellow. Source: bcaplan.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Caplan.

question: The George Mason economist Bryan Caplan argues in his book The Case Against Education that a college degree helps a graduate mostly by SIGNALING — proving to employers that the person is smart, patient, and willing to sit through boring classes — rather than by teaching real job skills. If that story is right, students face one obvious choice. What will people spend a lot of money to get?
answer: The degree itself -- even if the actual classes taught nothing useful
choices: The degree itself -- even if the actual classes taught nothing useful
Only the things learned in class, never the paper degree
Nothing to do with school at all
Only a PhD, never a bachelor's
context: Bryan Caplan, The Case Against Education: Why the Education System Is a Waste of Time and Money (Princeton UP, 2018). Source: press.princeton.edu (Caplan 2018).

question: The American economist Bryan Caplan noticed something odd in the labor-market numbers. A student who drops out one single class short of a diploma earns much less over a working life than a graduate with the exact same credits and grades. The physical paper — the sheepskin — appears to be worth tens of thousands of dollars all by itself. Economists have a special name for this earnings jump right at the diploma line. What is it called?
answer: The sheepskin effect
choices: The sheepskin effect
The credential trap
The Peter principle
The reservation-wage gap
context: The sheepskin effect: substantially higher earnings for degree-holders than for those with the same coursework but no completed credential. It is a classic empirical marker consistent with signaling. Source: Jaeger + Page, Review of Economics and Statistics (1996).

question: Bryan Caplan is an economist at George Mason University in Virginia. In his 2018 book The Case Against Education, he argues that most of college's payoff comes from signaling — the diploma itself — not from real learning. He points to the 'sheepskin effect' (the last course before graduating pays much more than earlier courses) and to how little most adults actually remember from class years later. What is his main policy recommendation?
answer: Cut education subsidies
choices: Cut education subsidies
Free college for all
More STEM funding
Extend the school year
context: Caplan's book-length estimate is that ~80% of the college wage premium is signaling. It is heterodox even among economists sympathetic to public choice; treat as Caplan's specific claim, not a settled number. Source: Caplan (2018), Chapter 6.

question: In 2007 the American economist Bryan Caplan published a book arguing that voters hold systematically slanted views about the economy — biased against markets, against foreigners, against saving. Because a single vote almost never changes the outcome of a big election, holding a wrong belief at the ballot box costs the voter nothing personally, so wrong ideas persist. What is the book's title?
answer: The Myth of the Rational Voter
choices: The Myth of the Rational Voter
The Vision of the Anointed
Rational Ignorance
Democracy and Its Critics
context: Bryan Caplan, The Myth of the Rational Voter: Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies (Princeton UP, 2007). Source: press.princeton.edu (Caplan 2007).

question: Bryan Caplan of George Mason University coined a specific two-word term for a puzzle he saw in politics: voters hold systematically wrong views about economics and policy because they bear essentially no personal cost from doing so, unlike consumers who bear the cost of their wrong shopping choices. Caplan's term is distinct from the economist Anthony Downs's earlier 1957 phrase 'rational ignorance.' What did Caplan call his own idea?
answer: Rational irrationality
choices: Rational irrationality
Structural bias
Systemic error
Cognitive drift
context: Caplan's 'rational irrationality' extends Downs 1957. Downs said voters rationally do not INFORM themselves; Caplan adds that voters rationally do not THINK CLEARLY, because clear thinking on politics is personally costly and privately worthless. Source: Caplan (2007), Chapter 4.

question: Bryan Caplan, an American economist at George Mason University, wrote a popular parenting book with Basic Books in 2011. Using twin studies and adoption studies from behavioral genetics, he argues that parents shape their adult children far less than most parents assume. Its title makes a specifically optimistic case for having a larger family. What is the exact title of that 2011 book?
answer: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids
choices: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids
The Nurture Assumption
Nurture Shock
The Parent Trap
context: Bryan Caplan, Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids (Basic Books, 2011). Draws on twin-adoption studies and Judith Rich Harris's Nurture Assumption (Free Press 1998). Source: basicbooks.com (Caplan 2011).

question: Imagine a wheat farmer in a poor country who grows about $500 worth of crops each year using an ox and hand tools. That exact same worker, moved to a rich country with tractors, paved roads, and reliable electricity, could earn about $40,000 doing similar work. What economic idea does this huge productivity gap between the two places show?
answer: That where a person works, not just effort, sets what they can produce
choices: That where a person works, not just effort, sets what they can produce
That workers everywhere produce roughly the same value
That richer countries owe poorer ones direct payments
That trade always hurts the poorer country
context: Bryan Caplan + Zach Weinersmith, Open Borders: The Science and Ethics of Immigration (First Second, 2019). Standard economic-gains-from-trade case for free migration, presented in graphic-novel format as a popularization experiment. Source: firstsecondbooks.com (Caplan 2019).

question: Imagine a booming American city like San Francisco makes it very hard to build new houses — endless permits, strict zoning, neighborhood vetoes on every project. For twenty years, almost no new homes go up. Meanwhile, tech jobs pull thousands of new residents into the city every single year, all looking for somewhere to live. Basic supply-and-demand reasoning gives a clear answer. What happens to home prices?
answer: They go way up, because supply cannot keep up with demand
choices: They go way up, because supply cannot keep up with demand
They fall, because building slows down
They stay flat, because people leave the city
They swing wildly with no clear pattern
context: Bryan Caplan + Ady Branzei, Build Baby Build: The Science and Ethics of Housing Regulation (Cato Institute, 2024). Argues for sweeping housing-supply reform on affordability, mobility, and welfare grounds. Source: cato.org (Caplan + Branzei 2024).

question: Caplan's rational-irrationality argument is a specific extension of an earlier public-choice claim from Anthony Downs. Downs argued that voters spend little effort studying issues, because any single vote is extremely unlikely to matter. What did Downs call that pre-Caplan claim?
answer: Rational ignorance
choices: Rational ignorance
Rational apathy
Political myopia
Structural confusion
context: Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (Harper 1957): voters rationally choose not to inform themselves because the private return on political knowledge is essentially zero. Caplan extends this from ignorance to irrationality. Source: Downs (1957); Caplan (2007).

question: Bryan Caplan is a tenured economics professor at George Mason University. Unusually for a working academic, he writes nonfiction graphic novels — full comic books drawn by illustrator Zach Weinersmith — to teach economics topics like open borders and housing policy. Academic prose reaches other academics and mostly stops there. What problem does the graphic-novel form solve that plain academic writing cannot?
answer: Reaching general readers who do not read academic prose
choices: Reaching general readers who do not read academic prose
Meeting APA citation standards
Substituting for peer review in economics
Replacing the referees of academic journals
context: Popularization is the specific problem. Caplan's graphic-novel books on open borders and housing deregulation are aimed at readers who would never open a Princeton UP monograph, extending public-choice arguments to a wider audience. Source: Caplan blog Bet On It; interviews 2019-24.

question: In his 2018 book The Case Against Education, the American economist Bryan Caplan argued that most of college is signaling — showing employers you are smart, diligent, and willing to jump through hoops — rather than actually building useful skills. If Caplan is largely right, that changes what happens when taxpayers pump money into college through grants, subsidized loans, and state-funded universities. What follows for taxpayers paying for college?
answer: Subsidies pump up signals without producing corresponding productive skills
choices: Subsidies pump up signals without producing corresponding productive skills
Subsidies create additional productive skills proportional to enrollment
Subsidies always reduce total educational credentials issued
Subsidies convert signals to human capital by definition
context: Caplan's payoff: if degrees mostly SIGNAL that a student is smart, conscientious, and conformist, then subsidizing more degrees inflates the signal without increasing the underlying trait. The wage premium erodes as more people hold the same signal. Source: Caplan (2018), Chapter 12.

question: In a big election with millions of ballots cast, one single vote almost never decides the outcome. So being wrong at the ballot box — voting from confused ideas about the economy — costs the individual voter nothing personally. The American economist Bryan Caplan uses this fact to ask a sharp follow-up question. What does it suggest about the average voter's views on the economy?
answer: They can be pretty wrong, because being wrong at the voting booth costs nothing
choices: They can be pretty wrong, because being wrong at the voting booth costs nothing
They are always perfectly correct on every economic issue
They are decided by a computer program
They exactly match the top experts' views
context: Bryan Caplan, Princeton-trained economist at George Mason University, is the author. The Myth of the Rational Voter (Princeton UP, 2007) extends Downs's rational-ignorance to 'rational irrationality'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Caplan.

question: In 2007 the American economist Bryan Caplan published a book with the subtitle 'Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies.' Its main title starts with the words 'The Myth of the' and ends with a two-word noun phrase about voters. What is the full title of that 2007 book?
answer: The Myth of the Rational Voter
choices: The Myth of the Rational Voter
The Case Against Democracy
The Voter's Fallacy
The Ignorance Trap
context: The Myth of the Rational Voter: Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies (Princeton UP, 2007). Caplan's argument: voters are not just uninformed but systematically wrong on economic questions in identifiable ways. Source: press.princeton.edu.

question: In his 2007 book The Myth of the Rational Voter, the George Mason economist Bryan Caplan compared surveys of ordinary US voters against surveys of trained economists across left, right, and center. He found that voters share four systematic biases about the economy that economists — regardless of party — do not share. Which pair are two of those four?
answer: Anti-market and anti-foreign biases
choices: Anti-market and anti-foreign biases
Anti-tax and anti-immigrant biases
Anti-Congress and anti-Fed biases
Anti-education and anti-labor biases
context: The four biases: (1) anti-market, (2) anti-foreign, (3) make-work, (4) pessimistic. Anti-market: voters underestimate market benefits. Anti-foreign: voters underestimate trade gains. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: In his 2007 book The Myth of the Rational Voter, the American economist Bryan Caplan identified four systematic biases voters hold about the economy. The third one is that voters treat jobs as valuable in themselves — the more work required, the better — rather than valuing jobs for what those jobs actually produce. Cutting a wasteful position looks bad to voters even when it saves resources. What is Caplan's name for this third bias?
answer: Make-work bias
choices: Make-work bias
Job-security bias
Employment worship
Career preservation
context: Make-work bias: voters treat job counts as ends in themselves rather than as means to produce goods. It underlies opposition to labor-saving technology, automation, and free trade. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: In his 2007 book The Myth of the Rational Voter, the American economist Bryan Caplan identified four systematic biases voters hold about the economy. The fourth bias is that voters consistently overestimate how bad current economic conditions are, and how much worse things are getting compared to the past. Caplan pointed to survey after survey showing voters expecting decline even during booms. What is Caplan's name for this fourth bias?
answer: Pessimistic bias
choices: Pessimistic bias
Nostalgic bias
Negative-news bias
Doom-shift bias
context: Pessimistic bias: voters systematically overestimate how bad the economy is and how fast things are worsening. It underlies persistent 'the economy is bad' polling results even during expansions. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: In 1996 the Washington Post, the Kaiser Family Foundation, and Harvard University together sponsored a big paired survey. They asked the same set of economic questions to ordinary American voters and to PhD economists, then compared the two groups' answers side by side. The American economist Bryan Caplan later used this survey as his main data source in The Myth of the Rational Voter. What is the short abbreviated name for that survey?
answer: SAEE
choices: SAEE
GSS
ANES
PISA
context: The Survey of Americans and Economists on the Economy (SAEE, 1996) was conducted for the Washington Post with Kaiser Family Foundation and Harvard collaboration. Across dozens of questions, the systematic public-versus-economist gap tracked Caplan's four biases. Source: kff.org SAEE.

question: The George Mason economist Bryan Caplan uses the phrase 'rational irrationality' to explain why voters keep believing wrong things about the economy — that trade destroys jobs on net, that immigrants shrink the pie, that market prices are arbitrary — even after those beliefs are corrected. A single vote in a national US election almost never decides the outcome. So one simple calculation makes it rational for a voter to keep a comforting wrong belief. Why does it make sense for them to do that?
answer: The private cost of one wrong belief is essentially zero
choices: The private cost of one wrong belief is essentially zero
Political leaders always correct voter mistakes
News media always deliver accurate information
Public education successfully teaches economics
context: The private cost of holding an economically wrong belief is essentially zero because the belief influences one vote out of tens of millions. Consumers with wrong beliefs about products suffer directly; voters do not. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: In The Myth of the Rational Voter, the American economist Bryan Caplan draws a sharp contrast between two arenas in which people hold economic beliefs. In one arena, a wrong belief costs the believer real money out of their own pocket — so they think carefully before acting. In the other arena, one wrong choice affects the individual almost not at all — so they can afford to be lazy or biased. What is that contrast?
answer: Consumers pay for wrong beliefs about products; voters do not pay for wrong beliefs about policy
choices: Consumers pay for wrong beliefs about products; voters do not pay for wrong beliefs about policy
Investors pay for wrong beliefs about stocks; workers do not pay for wrong beliefs about jobs
Homeowners pay for wrong beliefs about maintenance; renters do not pay for wrong beliefs about landlords
Producers pay for wrong beliefs about markets; distributors do not pay for wrong beliefs about supply
context: Caplan's central contrast: a consumer who buys a bad product suffers directly; a voter who supports a bad policy pays essentially nothing individually. Democracies systematically choose bad policies because voter beliefs face no discipline. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: The public choice school of economics was born in the 1960s under the Nobel laureate James Buchanan and his colleague Gordon Tullock. Over the following decades one American university became its main institutional home, with a faculty roster including Peter Boettke, Alex Tabarrok, Tyler Cowen, and Bryan Caplan. That same university today runs the Mercatus Center think tank and hosts the Marginal Revolution economics blog. Which American university is it?
answer: George Mason University
choices: George Mason University
Harvard University
Yale University
Stanford University
context: The GMU-Buchanan-Tullock tradition includes Peter Boettke (Austrian-tradition), Alex Tabarrok (co-founder of Marginal Revolution), and Tyler Cowen (also Marginal Revolution, GMU chair). All are Caplan's colleagues. Source: gmu.edu economics department.

question: For much of the 20th century, economists modeled politicians and bureaucrats as pure public servants trying to maximize social welfare. James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock argued this was silly. Politicians want votes and re-election, bureaucrats want bigger budgets, voters want handouts — all pursuing self-interest the same way people do in markets. The whole branch of economics that studies this became standard. What is it called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Monetary policy
International trade
Labor economics
context: James M. Buchanan of George Mason University was announced as the 1986 sole laureate on October 16, 1986. The prize put public-choice theory on the world academic map. Source: nobelprize.org (Buchanan 1986).

question: In 1986 the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to James Buchanan, a Tennessee-born economist who taught at George Mason University in Virginia. The citation was carefully worded to name his central idea rather than pin him to the 'public choice' school label he was famous for founding. What did the official citation say the prize was for?
answer: The contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making
choices: The contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making
The empirical study of federal fiscal policy
The macroeconomic foundations of economic growth
The mathematical formalization of equilibrium theory
context: The 1986 citation was carefully general to name the analytical move rather than the school-name 'public choice'. Source: nobelprize.org (1986 press release).

question: On December 8, 1986, James Buchanan stood in Stockholm to give the Nobel lecture that traditionally follows the award ceremony. He was 67.
