By then he had spent decades arguing that political fights over any single tax rate miss the deeper question — what rules make those fights possible in the first place. He put that whole idea into the title of his lecture. What was it called?
answer: The Constitution of Economic Policy
choices: The Constitution of Economic Policy
The Calculus of Consent
Public Finance in Democratic Process
Cost and Choice
context: 'The Constitution of Economic Policy' (December 8, 1986, Stockholm) argued that economic policy should be evaluated by the rules governing choices, not just by outcomes of individual choices. Published in AER March 1987. Source: nobelprize.org (Buchanan lecture 1986).

question: The public choice school of economics, founded in the 1960s by the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, studies voters, elected politicians, and government bureaucrats the same way regular economics studies shoppers and business owners. It uses the same core tool: people respond to incentives. What is the new idea public choice adds specifically about people who work in government?
answer: Politicians and bureaucrats respond to incentives just like everyone else
choices: Politicians and bureaucrats respond to incentives just like everyone else
Politicians always act only for the public good
Voters carefully study every bill before elections
Government agencies never grow beyond their original mission
context: Buchanan was based at George Mason University's Center for Study of Public Choice at the time of his 1986 Nobel. He had moved from Virginia Tech in 1983. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Buchanan.

question: Public-choice economists, in the tradition of the Nobel laureate James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, treat politicians, regulators, and career bureaucrats as normal humans who chase rewards — reelection, bigger budgets, personal influence, comfortable careers — just like everyone else in the economy. Many rival economists strongly dislike this framing. Why do they object so much to public choice's view of government workers?
answer: It removes the assumption that officials always act for the public good
choices: It removes the assumption that officials always act for the public good
It ignores how markets actually set prices
It only applies to small local governments, not national ones
It refuses to use any mathematics
context: Samuelson reportedly complained the prize was for political science -- which, if true, was exactly the point Buchanan had been making since 1962: the artificial disciplinary wall between economic analysis of markets and of politics was itself the mistake. Source: widely reported anecdote.

question: The British economist Ronald Coase pointed out something simple. If two people could always negotiate a deal for free, they would work out any small dispute over noise or pollution on their own. In the real world, though, negotiating costs time, effort, and lawyers. Coase called this friction a transaction cost. What does this cost help explain?
answer: Why firms exist, and why laws about who owns what matter so much
choices: Why firms exist, and why laws about who owns what matter so much
Why interest rates always rise during winter
Why every worker in the world earns the same wage
Why governments must set every price by law
context: Ronald Coase won the 1991 Nobel for transaction-cost economics. His 1937 paper 'The Nature of the Firm' and 1960 paper 'The Problem of Social Cost' anchored much of what public-choice and new-institutional economics built. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: By the 1990s a research tradition called 'new institutional economics' — asking how the rules of the game shape prosperity — had already won three Nobel Prizes: James Buchanan for public choice in 1986, Ronald Coase for transaction costs in 1991, and Douglass North for economic history in 1993. In 2009 a fourth laureate in this same tradition won the prize for showing how real communities can self-govern shared resources — grazing lands, fisheries, irrigation canals — without either state ownership or privatization. Who was she?
answer: Elinor Ostrom
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Esther Duflo
Claudia Goldin
Anne Krueger
context: Elinor Ostrom (Indiana University) won the 2009 Nobel (shared with Oliver Williamson) for her analysis of governance of the commons. She was the first female laureate in economics. Source: nobelprize.org (Ostrom 2009).

question: In the US Senate, a senator is deciding how to vote on a big spending bill. The bill would build a new bridge in his home state that helps a small group of local businesses a lot. It would also cost every US taxpayer a few dollars each. Public-choice economists — the school of Mancur Olson and James Buchanan — say senators often vote yes on bills shaped like this one. Why?
answer: The benefits are focused on a few, while the costs are spread thin over many
choices: The benefits are focused on a few, while the costs are spread thin over many
Voters everywhere always want more spending, so he obeys them
The senator does not understand the true cost of the bill
Federal law forces him to vote yes on any spending request
context: Gordon Tullock had co-authored The Calculus of Consent (1962) with Buchanan and pioneered rent-seeking analysis in 1967. His never receiving a Nobel became a persistent complaint among public-choice scholars. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Tullock.

question: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics has honored four economists in what is sometimes called the 'institutions matter' lineage: James Buchanan in 1986, Ronald Coase in 1991, Douglass North in 1993, and Elinor Ostrom in 2009. They studied constitutions, property rights, legal systems, and rules for sharing common resources like fisheries. All four owe a debt to one analytical move that Buchanan pioneered decades earlier. What was that move?
answer: Taking institutions seriously as objects of economic analysis
choices: Taking institutions seriously as objects of economic analysis
Formalizing rational-expectations models mathematically
Building general-equilibrium computer simulations
Applying game theory to industrial organization
context: Buchanan's Virginia-school move: the rules of the game are as much a subject for economic analysis as the play within the rules. Coase's transaction costs, North's institutions, and Ostrom's commons all extend that analytical stance. Source: nobelprize.org economics laureates.

question: The Nobel-winning American economist James Buchanan liked to say: 'Don't argue over who gets the ball at recess today -- sit down and write the rules for who gets the ball every day.' Buchanan built a whole field of study around choosing the rules themselves, not each single decision. What did he call the study of the rules themselves?
answer: Constitutional political economy
choices: Constitutional political economy
Positive political science
Behavioral macroeconomics
Institutional public finance
context: Constitutional political economy: the right level for political-economic analysis is not the individual policy choice but the rules that govern how such choices are made. Buchanan pioneered the term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_economics.

question: James Buchanan, the American Nobel-winning founder of public choice economics, pointed out that arguing whether a specific tax should be 20 percent or 25 percent turns every new law into a fresh political fight, with lobbyists and rent-seekers lining up each time. He wanted the debate moved to a different level entirely — one step up from any single policy. Where does he want to move it?
answer: The rules governing how policy is made
choices: The rules governing how policy is made
The individual voter's preferences
The Fed's monetary policy
The federal budget process
context: Buchanan's move: analyzing whether a constitutional rule should require a supermajority to raise taxes relocates the debate to a level where interest-group pressure operates differently. Rules bind both majority and minority in ways particular policy debates cannot. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: James Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize for founding public choice, the study of politicians as self-interested actors rather than saints. A year earlier, in 1985, Buchanan teamed with the Australian economist Geoffrey Brennan to write the standard modern textbook on why constitutions and firm rules must bind government policy instead of trusting officials' goodwill. What is that book called?
answer: The Reason of Rules
choices: The Reason of Rules
The Calculus of Consent
The Limits of Liberty
Cost and Choice
context: The Reason of Rules: Constitutional Political Economy (Cambridge University Press, 1985) is the standard modern statement. Brennan (Australian philosopher-economist) was Buchanan's most important later co-author. Source: cambridge.org (Brennan + Buchanan 1985).

question: In their 1985 book The Reason of Rules, the American economists James Buchanan and Geoffrey Brennan argued that people should choose the rules of the political game while pretending they do not know their own future spot in life — whether they will end up rich or poor, powerful or ordinary. That way the rules stay fair for whoever ends up where. What did Buchanan call this thought-experiment framing?
answer: The veil of uncertainty
choices: The veil of uncertainty
The Rawlsian curtain
The choice horizon
The Hobbesian mist
context: The 'veil of uncertainty' is Buchanan and Brennan's device (adapted from Rawls's veil of ignorance): constitutional rules agreed to when the choosers do not know their future position bind both majority and minority. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: In 1977 the American economist James Buchanan, founder of public choice, joined Richard Wagner to publish a book blaming John Maynard Keynes for teaching politicians they could safely spend far more than they taxed. Buchanan and Wagner said this Keynesian license had wrecked one specific old rule of American fiscal policy. Which shift did they target?
answer: The dissolution of the balanced-budget norm and the ratchet upward of deficits
choices: The dissolution of the balanced-budget norm and the ratchet upward of deficits
The gold-standard collapse and pure fiat
The Bretton Woods currency-peg system
The rise of federal income taxation
context: Democracy in Deficit: The Political Legacy of Lord Keynes (Academic Press, 1977) argued that the old constitutional norm of balanced budgets had disciplined politicians for a century. Once Keynes's General Theory legitimized deliberate deficit spending, the norm dissolved and deficits ratcheted upward. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_in_Deficit.

question: James Buchanan's 1977 book with Richard Wagner, Democracy in Deficit, did not just attack this or that particular budget shortfall. Buchanan said American politicians had crossed a bigger line, that an old constitutional habit had quietly died, and that every future deficit was the downstream result. What was the older rule Buchanan said had been lost?
answer: The old constitutional norm of balanced budgets
choices: The old constitutional norm of balanced budgets
The gold-standard convertibility rule
The Fed's independence from Treasury
The Senate's supermajority rule for tax hikes
context: Buchanan's move: individual deficits are not the problem; the erosion of the RULE that had disciplined all politicians is. Once the norm dissolved, the political incentive structure changed permanently. Source: Buchanan + Wagner, Democracy in Deficit (1977).

question: The whole public-choice tradition, the study of politicians and voters as self-interested actors, traces back to a 1962 book by the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. It applied basic economic reasoning to the design of constitutions themselves, showing why simple majority rule alone is not enough to protect a minority. This founding book is remembered as the birth of the field. What was it called?
answer: The Calculus of Consent
choices: The Calculus of Consent
The Reason of Rules
The Limits of Liberty
Cost and Choice
context: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy (University of Michigan Press, 1962) is the founding text of public-choice economics. Buchanan and Tullock introduced the constitutional-versus-post-constitutional distinction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Calculus_of_Consent.

question: In their 1985 book The Reason of Rules, the American economists Geoffrey Brennan and James Buchanan argued that a country is better off picking clear rules that everyone follows — like a posted speed limit — than letting individual officials decide the right choice one case at a time. Their argument turned on how ordinary people plan their lives and how power gets abused when discretion is wide. Why is a fixed rule better than case-by-case discretion?
answer: Fixed rules limit favoritism and let people plan ahead
choices: Fixed rules limit favoritism and let people plan ahead
Officials always make wiser choices than any rule can
Rules only work for small towns, not big countries
Case-by-case choices are always faster to make
context: Geoffrey Brennan (Australian National University philosopher-economist) co-authored The Power to Tax (1980) and The Reason of Rules (1985) with Buchanan. Source: philosophy.cass.anu.edu.au.

question: Before a coach picks teams for kickball, everyone agrees on how score will be kept. Once teams are picked, each side knows how the rules will help or hurt them. A public-choice thinker asks: judge each rule from before-you-know-your-team, not after. What does this move do to the argument?
answer: It moves the debate from picking winners to picking fair rules
choices: It moves the debate from picking winners to picking fair rules
It reduces every choice to a single number
It applies only to changes in a country's constitution
It makes every policy choice look equal
context: The constitutional-political-economy move: from OUTCOMES (is this policy good?) to CONSTRAINTS (would we have consented to the rules that produced it, behind the veil of uncertainty?). This is the mature analytical stance Buchanan is remembered for. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: A fisherman on a lake has two choices for feeding his family this month. He can wade in and grab fish by hand, which he can do all day starting now. Or he can spend a full day weaving a net, catch nothing that day, and then catch many more fish per day for the following weeks. The Austrian school gave the second method a name -- longer path now, more output later. What is it called?
answer: Roundabout production
choices: Roundabout production
Marginal utility
Spontaneous order
Comparative advantage
context: Boehm-Bawerk's word for longer, more indirect production processes -- using tools to make tools to make consumer goods -- was 'roundabout production' (German Produktionsumweg). The extra day spent on the net produces far more fish over the following weeks; the extra season spent making a plough produces far more grain the next season. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Bohm-Bawerk's Roundaboutness' (https://www.fff.org/explore-freedom/article/bohm-bawerks-roundaboutness-why-the-longest-path-to-wealth-is-usually-the-shortest/).

question: In 1884 an economist in the Austrian school began publishing a giant three-volume work on the theory of interest — why lenders charge, why borrowers pay, and why the whole system of paying for time exists at all. The second volume in 1889 laid out his own original answer, later known as the 'time-preference' theory of interest. Who was this Austrian economist?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
context: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk published 'Kapital und Kapitalzins' in three volumes: Volume 1 in 1884, Volume 2 in 1889, Volume 3 posthumously in 1921. Menger was his teacher; Wieser his brother-in-law; Mises his student a generation later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Capital and Interest' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest).

question: In the 1800s Karl Marx claimed that interest and profit were stolen from workers by capitalists. Later, in Vienna, the Austrian economist Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk pushed back hard. He said interest is real payment for something the saver actually gives up. When a person hands over money today so someone else can use it, they postpone all the things they could have enjoyed with that money right now. What is the saver being paid to do?
answer: To wait
choices: To wait
To supervise
To take risk
To organize
context: Boehm-Bawerk's answer to Marx: production takes TIME, and someone must release present resources so that future output can exist. That someone is the saver, and interest is the market price paid to persuade him to wait. It is not stolen from the worker; it is compensation for the postponement of consumption. Source: Capitalism Magazine, Ebeling on Boehm-Bawerk (https://capitalismmagazine.com/2016/02/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-refuter-marxism-theorist-economics-capitalism/).

question: In 1889 the Austrian economist Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk asked why people value a loaf of bread today more than the same loaf next year. He listed three reasons: you might die before next year; your needs and tastes might change by then; and a good on hand right now can be put to work to create even more goods. He said these three reasons together explain what?
answer: Interest
choices: Interest
Profit
Rent
Wages
context: The three grounds Boehm-Bawerk offers in Volume 2 -- expectation of future prosperity, systematic underestimation of future wants, and the technical superiority of longer production processes -- are his positive theory of INTEREST specifically, the price the market pays for the postponement of consumption. Rent, profit, and wages are separately theorised elsewhere in the Austrian tradition. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: A person could spend $100 today on candy, or lend it for a year and get back $105 instead. Some economists say the $5 extra is the reward for one specific thing. What is that thing?
answer: Waiting — the person delayed enjoying the money for a year
choices: Waiting — the person delayed enjoying the money for a year
Producing — the money itself worked in a factory
Stealing — the money was taken from another worker
Voting — the person supported the correct political party
context: Nassau William Senior (1790-1864), Oxford's first Drummond Professor of Political Economy, is the name Boehm-Bawerk associates in Volume 1 with the abstinence theory of interest -- the view that interest rewards the saver for the self-denial of postponing consumption. Ricardo and Mill worked mainly within cost-of-production and productivity accounts; Marshall came later. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Boehm-Bawerk asked people to notice a simple fact about how things get made. A fisherman weaves a net before he catches fish. A farmer builds a plow before he plants grain. A factory sets up its line before it ships a car. What one feature of making things is he pointing to?
answer: That production takes time
choices: That production takes time
That production yields joint products
That production faces diminishing returns
That production requires cooperation
context: The insight the whole Positive Theory rests on: production is a process across TIME, not an instant. Because the saver must release resources today for output that will only exist next month or next year, and because people prefer present to future goods, someone must be paid a premium to bridge the wait. Interest is the market price of that time gap. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Boehm-Bawerk gives interest three separate grounds in Volume 2. Ground one is that people expect the future to be more prosperous than the present, so a future good is worth less to them now. Ground two is that people are shortsighted and systematically underestimate their future wants. Ground three was the most controversial, because it implies positive interest rates would exist even if grounds one and two failed. What does ground three appeal to?
answer: The technical superiority of longer production processes
choices: The technical superiority of longer production processes
The moral virtue of self-denial by the saver
The bargaining power of capitalists over workers
The state's legal enforcement of debt contracts
context: Ground three -- the technical superiority of longer, more roundabout production methods -- is Boehm-Bawerk's most disputed claim. It says that even without shortsightedness or expected prosperity, more roundabout methods yield more output per unit input, so waiting is intrinsically worth something. The American economist Frank Fetter later argued ground two (time preference) does all the real work and ground three is redundant; John Bates Clark defended a rival pure-productivity account. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: Suppose someone offers you a choice. Take $10 today, or wait exactly one year and take $10 then. The amount is identical. Almost every person alive picks today. Austrian economists gave this ordinary human habit a name -- time preference -- and built their whole theory of interest on it. What economic idea does this preference show?
answer: People value goods and money in the present more than the same amount in the future
choices: People value goods and money in the present more than the same amount in the future
People cannot count amounts of money over time
The price of goods always drops in a year, so today's dollar buys more
Waiting one year makes no real difference to anyone
context: Frank A. Fetter (1863-1949), an American Austrian, argued that time preference (ground two) is the whole explanation of interest and that Boehm-Bawerk's technical-productivity ground three is dispensable. John Bates Clark went the other direction and defended a pure productivity-of-capital theory; Irving Fisher tried to combine productivity and impatience; Knut Wicksell developed the natural-rate concept in a different direction. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: A modern socialist argues that interest paid to a saver is unearned income. The saver did no labor — the money simply sat in an account and grew. In his 1889 book 'Capital and Interest' the Austrian economist Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk answered exactly this charge from Karl Marx head-on. Without appealing to risk or entrepreneurship, how did his answer go?
answer: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
choices: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
The saver takes on the risk that the borrower will default, and interest is the premium compensating that risk
The saver exercises entrepreneurial judgment about which projects deserve capital, and interest is the reward for that judgment
The saver enjoys legal protection under contract law, and interest is the state-enforced return on lawful lending
context: The clean Boehm-Bawerkian move: production takes time; someone must release today's resources for tomorrow's output; that release is what the saver contributes; the interest payment is the market price of that contribution. Risk, entrepreneurship, and legal enforcement are separate real phenomena but they answer different questions -- this specific question is about where interest itself comes from, and the answer is time-preference plus waiting. Source: Capitalism Magazine, Ebeling on Boehm-Bawerk (https://capitalismmagazine.com/2016/02/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-refuter-marxism-theorist-economics-capitalism/).

question: A central bank forces interest rates down to zero. Austrian economists warn that interest rates aren't just any old price -- they measure something specific about how people trade what they have now for what they can have later. Which price does a zero-rate policy actually distort?
answer: The price of time itself -- how much people value goods now versus later
choices: The price of time itself -- how much people value goods now versus later
The value of the dollar against foreign money
The wages paid to workers who make exports
The price tag on things people buy on credit
context: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory, developed by Mises and Hayek on the Boehm-Bawerkian foundation, treats the interest rate as the price of time -- the price coordinating how much of today's resources get released for tomorrow's output through more roundabout production. Forcing that price down artificially misleads entrepreneurs into starting more roundabout projects than real savings can complete; when the bust arrives the malinvested projects have to be liquidated. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: In 1962 the American economist Milton Friedman published a book that grew out of lectures he had given at Wabash College in Indiana in 1956. His wife Rose helped shape the manuscript into plain English for general readers. It went on to sell more than half a million copies and spread free-market ideas to a wide audience. What was the book's title?
answer: Capitalism and Freedom
choices: Capitalism and Freedom
Free to Choose
A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
context: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962). Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo25839091.html.

question: In 1962 the American economist Milton Friedman published a slim book called Capitalism and Freedom. He argued that two kinds of freedom, the freedom to trade and produce and the freedom to vote and speak, are tightly linked but only in one direction. One kind of freedom is the ground the other stands on. Which link does the book argue for?
answer: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
choices: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
Political freedom always suffices for economic freedom
Economic freedom is irrelevant to political freedom
Political freedom is a sufficient condition for economic freedom
context: Friedman's move: once government controls the means of employment, the media, and the currency, dissent cannot be sustained -- the dissenter cannot eat. Economic freedom is necessary though not sufficient for political freedom. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 1.

question: In 1962 the American economist Milton Friedman published Capitalism and Freedom, a slim book packed with proposals that sounded strange at the time. Several of its ideas later became normal US policy over the following decades. But one item in the list below was never in Friedman's 1962 book. Which one was not in it?
answer: Universal single-payer health insurance
choices: Universal single-payer health insurance
School vouchers for parents
The negative income tax
An all-volunteer military
context: Friedman proposed vouchers, NIT, all-volunteer army, floating exchange rates, and drug decriminalization in the 1962 book. Universal single-payer health insurance is the Canadian model and was not part of Friedman's proposal package. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962).

question: In the late 1960s the American economist Milton Friedman argued that the US military draft should be ended and replaced with an all-volunteer force. In a famous hearing before a presidential commission, General William Westmoreland complained he did not want to command 'an army of mercenaries.' Friedman shot back one sentence that stopped the general cold. What did Friedman say?
answer: 'Would you rather have an army of slaves?'
choices: 'Would you rather have an army of slaves?'
'Would you draft your own children?'
'Is your own salary not a wage?'
'Who defends the mercenary's family?'
context: Congress let the induction authority expire in 1973, ending the American peacetime draft. Friedman had proposed abolishing the draft in Capitalism and Freedom (1962). Source: history.army.mil (draft history).

question: Imagine a shopper walks into a large supermarket and picks her own items freely from thousands of choices — bread, milk, apples, whatever her family actually wants — spending her weekly grocery budget however she likes. Now imagine that instead, a small committee of nutrition experts in an office chose everyone's groceries for them, with the same budget at the same store. What would most likely happen?
answer: Many shoppers would get food they did not want, and shelves would be full of things no one bought
choices: Many shoppers would get food they did not want, and shelves would be full of things no one bought
Shoppers would be happier because they would not have to think
Grocery stores would run out of nothing, ever
Farmers would grow exactly the right amount because instructions would be clearer
context: Milton + Rose Friedman, Free to Choose: A Personal Statement (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1980), with companion PBS series in ten episodes. It was the best-selling nonfiction book of 1980 in the United States. Source: pbs.org (Free to Choose archive).

question: In 1980 Milton and Rose Friedman filmed a ten-episode PBS television series called Free to Choose. They shot it on location in Hong Kong, Chicago, Washington, and other cities so viewers could see for themselves how free markets work in the real world. They also released a companion book with the same title. Where did that book rank on US book sales for its year of publication?
answer: Best-selling nonfiction book of 1980
choices: Best-selling nonfiction book of 1980
Best-selling children's book of 1980
Best-selling paperback fiction of 1980
Best-selling academic textbook of 1980
context: Free to Choose was the best-selling nonfiction book of 1980 in the United States. The PBS series reached millions of viewers and became a curriculum staple. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998), memoir chapter on Free to Choose.

question: Friedman's book Free to Choose was translated into more than a dozen languages. According to his memoirs, it was smuggled into one particular bloc of countries in illegal underground translations. It influenced later economic reformers there. Which region was that?
answer: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
choices: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
Central African republics
Southeast Asian dictatorships
Latin American military regimes
context: Free to Choose was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in samizdat translations. Vaclav Klaus later credited the book as an intellectual source of Czechoslovakia's post-1989 economic reforms. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Milton Friedman, the American economist and later 1976 Nobel laureate, is best known for the school-voucher proposal that appears in his 1962 book 'Capitalism and Freedom.' But the voucher idea actually first appeared five years earlier, in a stand-alone essay Friedman published in 1955 inside an academic volume edited by Robert A. Solo. Which 1955 essay was that?
answer: The Role of Government in Education
choices: The Role of Government in Education
The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
A Monetary and Fiscal Framework
The Methodology of Positive Economics
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education' (in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest, Rutgers UP 1955). The voucher proposal was collected into Capitalism and Freedom (1962). Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: In August 1971 President Nixon closed the US gold window and let the dollar float, ending the Bretton Woods fixed-exchange-rate system. Friedman had been recommending this move since 1953 in his essay 'The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates.' What did the resulting international monetary regime become?
answer: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
choices: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
A permanent gold-based monetary system
A single global fixed-rate regime
Complete abolition of national currencies
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 closing of the gold window ended dollar-gold convertibility; the international regime shifted to floating major-currency exchange rates by 1973. Friedman had argued the case since 1953. Source: Friedman, 'The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates' (1953, in Essays in Positive Economics).

question: Milton Friedman's 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom argued for ideas that sounded radical at the time -- an all-volunteer army, a negative income tax, school vouchers, floating exchange rates, and the end of licensing rules that kept people out of trades. Decades later, historians looked back with a striking observation. Which one-sentence summary best captures why the book still matters?
answer: Many proposals that seemed eccentric in 1962 later became mainstream policy
choices: Many proposals that seemed eccentric in 1962 later became mainstream policy
None of its proposals were ever tried anywhere
It advocated returning to a nineteenth-century gold standard exclusively
It called for immediate abolition of all federal agencies
context: The all-volunteer military (1973), floating exchange rates (1971-73), and state-level voucher programs (1990s-2020s) all trace to Capitalism and Freedom proposals that were dismissed as eccentric at the time. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: In 1871 in Vienna, an Austrian professor named Carl Menger published a book called 'Principles of Economics' that started a whole new school of economic thought. His big idea was that the value of a thing depends on how much a person wants it, not on how much labor went into making it. What did his group of followers become known as?
answer: The Austrian School
choices: The Austrian School
The Chicago School
The Keynesian School
The Marxist School
context: Carl Menger (1840-1921), the founder of the Austrian School, published 'Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre' (Principles of Economics) in 1871 while still working in the prime minister's press office; the book won him a Vienna chair in 1873. Wieser and Boehm-Bawerk were his students; Mises a generation later still. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger: The Founding of the Austrian School' (https://mises.org/articles-interest/carl-menger-founding-austrian-school).

question: In the early 1870s three economists working separately in three different countries — Carl Menger in Vienna, William Stanley Jevons in Manchester, and Leon Walras in Lausanne — all landed on the same big idea at almost the same time. Value comes from how useful the last extra bit is to the buyer, not from the labor put into making it. What is this shared breakthrough called?
answer: The marginal revolution
choices: The marginal revolution
The classical synthesis
The Keynesian revolution
The monetarist counter-revolution
context: Menger's Principles (1871), Jevons's Theory of Political Economy (1871), and Walras's Elements of Pure Economics (1874) all worked out marginal-utility subjective value theory within a few years of each other, an event later known as the 'marginal revolution.' The Keynesian revolution came in the 1930s; monetarism was Milton Friedman's later counter to it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginal revolution' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_revolution).

question: In 1876 the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph hired the top economist at the University of Vienna to serve as private tutor to his teenage son, Crown Prince Rudolf, on a long educational tour through Europe. That same professor had just published a book five years earlier that founded what would become the Austrian school of economics. What did he say makes a good valuable?
answer: What each buyer personally wants and how much of it they already have
choices: What each buyer personally wants and how much of it they already have
The amount of labor used to make it
The cost of the raw materials
A price set by government experts
context: Menger tutored Crown Prince Rudolf of Habsburg -- the only son of Emperor Franz Joseph and heir to the throne -- from 1876 to 1878. Franz Ferdinand was Rudolf's cousin and the eventual heir after Rudolf's death; Karl I became emperor in 1916; Otto was a different Habsburg. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger, Crown Prince Rudolf, and the Marginal Revolution That Never Was' (https://mises.org/mises-wire/carl-menger-crown-prince-rudolf-and-marginal-revolution-never-was).

question: Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian school of economics, taught at the University of Vienna during the 1870s and 1880s. Two of his brightest students went on to write almost the entire next chapter of Austrian thought — covering capital theory, the imputation of value from goods to factors, and the definitive refutation of Marx's labor theory of value. The two young men also happened to marry a pair of sisters. Who are they?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
Israel Kirzner and Murray Rothbard
Joseph Schumpeter and Otto Bauer
context: Menger's two most important direct students were Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk (capital theory, Marx refutation) and Friedrich von Wieser (imputation, opportunity cost); the two were brothers-in-law, having married sisters. Mises and Hayek were the third and fourth generation; Kirzner and Rothbard the fifth; Schumpeter and Bauer were students of Boehm-Bawerk not Menger. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Carl Menger, the Austrian economist who founded the Austrian school in Vienna in the 1870s, did not come to the field through math or engineering. His formal training was in law. In 1867 he took his doctorate at the oldest university in Poland, in a city famous for its medieval royal castle on a hill above the Vistula river. Which university was that?
answer: Jagiellonian University in Krakow
choices: Jagiellonian University in Krakow
Charles University in Prague
Humboldt University in Berlin
University of Vienna
context: Menger took his doctorate in jurisprudence at Jagiellonian University in Krakow in 1867, then joined the Austrian civil service. Charles University in Prague was where he studied earlier; Humboldt in Berlin was the leading German university of the era but not his; Vienna was where he later held his chair. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Menger's civil-service job before he became famous involved reading daily commodity reports for the Austrian prime minister's press office. That work produced the founding insight of the Austrian school. The old textbook idea that price reflects labor put into a good did not match real trading. What did Menger say determines price instead?
answer: The subjective usefulness of the last unit to each individual consumer
choices: The subjective usefulness of the last unit to each individual consumer
The average number of labor hours embodied in the good
The long-run natural rate of return on invested capital
The state's ability to enforce a fair-price statute
context: Menger's Principles (1871) replaced the classical labor-cost account of value with marginal utility -- price emerges from individual consumers each valuing the LAST unit of a good by its subjective usefulness to them. Labor-hours-embodied was Marx's version; natural-rate-of-return was Ricardo's cost-of-production account; fair-price statutes were medieval scholastic doctrine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Principles of Economics (Menger book)' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book)).

question: Two friends stand together in line at a food truck in the park. One buys a taco because he loves them. The other passes because he does not care for tacos at all. The taco costs the same price and is made of the same ingredients for both boys. Carl Menger and the Austrian school in Vienna built a whole theory of prices on what this everyday moment shows. What idea does the scene demonstrate?
answer: Value is subjective -- it depends on the person, not the object itself
choices: Value is subjective -- it depends on the person, not the object itself
Value is fixed by the cost of making the item
Value is set by how long the item takes to eat
Value is the same for everyone in the same line
context: Rudolf and Vetsera died at the Mayerling hunting lodge on the night of 29-30 January 1889; the murder-suicide displaced Rudolf's cousin Franz Ferdinand as heir (who was himself assassinated at Sarajevo in 1914, triggering the First World War). Menger, deeply affected by his former pupil's death, withdrew further into scholarship. Schoenbrunn was the imperial summer palace; Ischl the emperor's holiday town; Belvedere Franz Ferdinand's Vienna residence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf%2C_Crown_Prince_of_Austria).

question: Carl Menger, the founder of the Austrian school of economics, had a son also named Karl Menger, born in Vienna in 1902. The younger Menger became a famous mathematician in his own right, contributing to dimension theory and joining the Vienna Circle of philosophers around the 1930s. A well-known three-dimensional fractal — a cube endlessly hollowed by smaller and smaller cubes — was named after him. What is the fractal called?
answer: The Menger sponge
choices: The Menger sponge
The Sierpinski triangle
The Mandelbrot set
The Cantor dust
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) -- son of the Austrian-school founder -- was a mathematician of the Vienna Circle who defined the Menger sponge, the 3-D fractal you get by iteratively removing the central subcube of every cube. The Sierpinski triangle (Waclaw Sierpinski, 1915) and Cantor dust (Georg Cantor, 1883) are older; the Mandelbrot set (Benoit Mandelbrot, 1980) is later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Karl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Menger).

question: In 1892 Menger wrote a famous essay, second only to his 1871 Principles. It shows how money grows out of barter with no government behind it. Traders spot which goods are most widely accepted, and slowly settle on the most tradeable one. What was the essay's German title?
answer: Ueber den Ursprung des Geldes
choices: Ueber den Ursprung des Geldes
Untersuchungen ueber die Methode
Die natuerliche Werthlehre
Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems
context: Menger's 1892 essay 'Ueber den Ursprung des Geldes' ('On the Origins of Money') is his second most-cited work and the Austrian foundation for the theory that money emerges spontaneously from barter as traders converge on the most SALEABLE commodity. 'Untersuchungen ueber die Methode' (1883) was his methodological work; 'Der natuerliche Werth' (1889) was Wieser's; 'Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems' (1896) was Boehm-Bawerk's Marx refutation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian school of economics, spent decades building one of the largest private economics libraries in nineteenth-century Europe — thousands of rare books, pamphlets, and periodicals. After his death in Vienna in 1921, his family sold the entire collection abroad rather than keep it in Austria. It survives today, catalogued together as the Menger Library. Which university now houses it?
answer: Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo
choices: Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo
Harvard University in Cambridge
Cambridge University in England
Chicago University in Illinois
context: Menger's private economics library, one of the largest in Europe, was sold by his heirs to Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo after his 1921 death; the collection is still catalogued there as the 'Menger Library.' Harvard, Cambridge (England), and the University of Chicago all built major economics libraries in the same era but not from Menger's holdings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: In 1980 US gasoline prices had jumped very high after the second oil shock. American oil companies were earning extra profits just because pump prices had risen so much. President Jimmy Carter and Congress passed a brand-new tax to grab that extra money from the oil producers. What is the general name for a tax on unusually large profits like that?
answer: A windfall tax
choices: A windfall tax
A tariff
A sales tax
A property tax
context: The Crude Oil Windfall Profit Tax Act was signed in Carter's last year in office. Reagan campaigned against the tax in the 1980 election and eventually got it repealed in 1988. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: In 1980 US President Jimmy Carter signed the Crude Oil Windfall Profit Tax. Politicians sold it as a way to take back 'unfair' profits US oil companies were supposedly making at the pump. The higher oil prices, though, had come from one dramatic event in the previous year, 1979, that cut off a huge share of the world's oil supply almost overnight. Which event was it?
answer: The Iranian Revolution and the second oil crisis
choices: The Iranian Revolution and the second oil crisis
The collapse of the Bretton Woods system
The Yom Kippur War oil embargo
The Alaskan pipeline completion
context: The 1979 revolution overthrew the Shah and disrupted Iranian oil exports; world crude went from about $15/barrel in 1978 to over $35 by 1981. The Carter administration argued domestic producers should not keep the price increase as pure profit. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1979_oil_crisis.

question: In 1990 the Congressional Research Service, the nonpartisan agency that studies policy questions for the US Congress, released a report on Jimmy Carter's 1980 Crude Oil Windfall Profit Tax. The economists wanted to know one thing. What had the tax actually done to US oil production during the 1980s? Their finding surprised almost no Austrian or free-market economist. What did the report find?
answer: Domestic production fell by roughly 3 to 6 percent and imports rose by similar amounts
choices: Domestic production fell by roughly 3 to 6 percent and imports rose by similar amounts
Domestic production rose by roughly 30 percent
Domestic production was unaffected either way
Domestic production fell by roughly 50 percent
context: The tax raised the effective cost of producing each additional barrel of US oil, so marginal wells were not drilled. The country supposedly worried about energy independence produced less domestic oil as a result. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: In 1985 a US senator from Texas complains on the Senate floor that the 1980 Windfall Profits Tax on oil companies has cost his state's oil patch thousands of jobs. An economist in the Bastiat tradition — the French tradition of naming both what is seen and what is unseen — pushes back with a specific reasoning move about the barrels that never came out of the ground because the tax made them unprofitable to drill. Which move is he pressing?
answer: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue -- the undrilled barrels and unhired workers are the unseen cost
choices: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue -- the undrilled barrels and unhired workers are the unseen cost
The tax is a Keynesian aggregate-demand stimulus that raises drilling investment
The tax is a Coasean bargaining solution that internalizes drilling externalities
The tax is a Pigovian correction that equates marginal social benefit and marginal social cost
context: A tax on the return to production at the margin reduces production at the margin. Applied Bastiat: the seen is oil-company profit recovery for the public; the unseen is domestic supply that never enters the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: In the early 1980s the US federal government slapped a large new tax on domestic oil companies, projecting tens of billions of dollars in revenue over its lifetime. In response, oil companies pumped less and drilled fewer new wells because each barrel now paid a smaller net return. By the time Congress repealed the tax in 1988, it had collected only a small fraction of the projected revenue. What lesson does this show?
answer: Taxes change behavior, so the money collected is often much less than planned
choices: Taxes change behavior, so the money collected is often much less than planned
Big taxes always collect exactly what the government predicts
Oil companies cannot lower their production even if taxed
The tax must have been too small to affect anything
context: By the mid-1980s world oil prices had collapsed to below the tax's base-price threshold, so it was collecting almost nothing. Reagan had campaigned against the tax in 1980 and the repeal completed a signature deregulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: The idea of a 'windfall tax' — a special extra tax on companies enjoying unusually high profits — keeps coming back. It was proposed on US banks after the 2008 financial crisis, on drug companies during the 2020 pandemic, and imposed on North Sea oil firms under the UK's 2022 Energy Profits Levy, signed by then-Chancellor Rishi Sunak. Each time, one classic question in the tradition of Frederic Bastiat returns. Which question is it?
answer: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
choices: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
What is the highest tax rate the affected industry can bear before bankruptcy?
How does the tax score under the Congressional Budget Office static model?
How much revenue will the tax collect in its first fiscal year?
context: The Bastiat pattern: measure the seen benefit against the unseen response. Any tax on the reward for producing during a shortage removes some of the incentive to produce during the crisis when society most needs it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Windfall_tax.

question: On June 24, 2009 US President Barack Obama signed the Car Allowance Rebate System, nicknamed 'Cash for Clunkers.' Buyers got a $3,500 to $4,500 rebate for trading in a working older car for a more fuel-efficient new one. Before the dealer received the rebate, the trade-in had to be destroyed a very specific way so it could never be resold. Which method wrecked the engines?
answer: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
choices: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
Draining the fuel tank and towing the car to a landfill for compaction
Removing and melting the catalytic converter, then junking the shell
Shipping the vehicle intact to a licensed scrapyard for parts recovery
context: The mandate that engines be seized with sodium silicate (liquid glass) was written to keep the trade-ins from being resold as running cars; some 690,000 running vehicles were destroyed this way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Allowance_Rebate_System.

question: In 2009, during a big recession, the US government under President Barack Obama paid people to trade in their old fuel-guzzling cars for new fuel-efficient ones. The dealer scrapped the old car and the buyer got a discount toward the new one. The program had a catchy nickname using 'cash' for money and a slang word for a beat-up old car. What was that nickname?
answer: Cash for Clunkers
choices: Cash for Clunkers
Homes for Heroes
Trade for Tomorrow
Drive for America
context: Signed June 24 2009, the program ran July-August 2009 and burned through its $3B appropriation faster than expected. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Allowance_Rebate_System.

question: In 2009 the US government ran a program called Cash for Clunkers. It paid people to trade in working used cars so those cars could be smashed and scrapped, supposedly to help sell new ones and boost the economy. Back in 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat had already warned about this exact mistake in a famous parable about destruction being called wealth. Which Bastiat argument does Cash for Clunkers match?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The negative railway
The candlemakers' petition
The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: Bastiat's broken-window: destruction of a usable good is not creation. Cash for Clunkers spent $3B destroying about 690,000 usable cars to make the subsidized new-car sale look like fresh economic activity. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: In 2009 the US Cash for Clunkers program destroyed about 690,000 running used cars. Most were in the affordable price range that low-income families and college students actually shop for. With that many cheap cars taken off the market in a single summer, Austrian economists predicted an obvious result. What happened to used-car prices in the year after the program ended?
answer: Used-car prices rose about 10%
choices: Used-car prices rose about 10%
New-car prices fell about 10%
Fuel prices rose about 10%
Auto-insurance premiums fell about 10%
context: Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index for 2009-10 showed a roughly 10% jump in used-car prices, pricing out the very households the auto-stimulus was said to help. Source: manheim.com/used-vehicle-value-index (2010 press releases).

question: In 2013 two economists at the Brookings Institution in Washington, Ted Gayer and Emily Parker, published a study analyzing the 2009 Cash for Clunkers program. They found that most of the 'new' car sales the program appeared to generate would have happened anyway within six to nine months — buyers had simply moved their purchases forward in time to grab the rebate. What did Gayer and Parker call this effect?
answer: Pulled-forward sales
choices: Pulled-forward sales
Aggregate multiplier
Rationing tax
Deadweight loss
context: Gayer & Parker (Brookings, October 2013) estimated the program pulled forward about 380,000 vehicles, generated no long-run net jobs, and produced CO2 savings at $91-$301 per ton -- well above the EPA's own social cost of carbon. Source: brookings.edu/articles/cash-for-clunkers-an-evaluation-of-the-car-allowance-rebate-system.

question: In the summer of 2009, as new-car sales collapsed after the financial crisis, the US federal government launched a program called Cash for Clunkers. It paid Americans up to $4,500 to trade in older cars, which dealers then had to destroy, so buyers would purchase newer and more fuel-efficient vehicles. One US cabinet department wrote the rules and processed the paperwork for wrecking each car. Which department ran it?
answer: The Department of Transportation
choices: The Department of Transportation
The Department of Commerce
The Environmental Protection Agency
The Department of Energy
context: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, inside DOT, administered the CARS Act rebate and destruction certification; final DOT figures put new-vehicle sales under the program at 677,842. Source: nhtsa.gov/cars-allowance-rebate-system.

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat warned that every policy has what is seen -- the shiny result -- and what is unseen -- the hidden cost most people miss. Cash for Clunkers in 2009 made the seen benefit obvious: a new car in the buyer's driveway. Austrian and Chicago-school critics kept pointing at a group of unseen victims the program hurt directly. Name that group.
answer: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
choices: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
Auto-parts manufacturers whose supply contracts came under EPA review
Insurance companies whose collision policies subsidized the rebate
Foreign auto brands excluded from the eligibility criteria
context: Destroying 690,000 vehicles in the $1,500-$4,500 range is destroying exactly the price band low-income buyers actually shop; used-car prices rose accordingly. This is Bastiat's UNSEEN victim: the low-income family that no longer finds a cheap running car. Source: cato.org/commentary/cash-clunkers-textbook-example.

question: Cash for Clunkers, said Austrian and Chicago-school critics, is the modern working example of the case laid out in a classic book-length restatement of Frederic Bastiat's argument about 'what is seen and what is not seen.' The book was written in 1946 by the American financial journalist Henry Hazlitt, who worked at Newsweek and the New York Times. Which 1946 book anticipated the whole critique?
answer: Economics in One Lesson
choices: Economics in One Lesson
The Road to Serfdom
Free to Choose
Human Action
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is the seen/unseen method in modern American English; every 21st-century commentator applying it to Cash for Clunkers is applying Hazlitt's chapter on public-works make-work. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Frederic Bastiat's rule from 1850 says every government spending program has one visible benefit and many invisible costs. Cash for Clunkers in 2009 cost US taxpayers about $3 billion. Beyond the 690,000 destroyed cars and the priced-out used-car buyers, Austrian economists point to a much larger loss -- a broader resource-allocation loss most people never think about. What is that loss?
answer: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
choices: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
The additional carbon emissions from the mandated new-car manufacturing
The regulatory-compliance staff the auto dealers had to hire to process claims
The tax revenue foregone on the salvage value of the destroyed trade-ins
context: Every $3B of federal spending had to come from a taxpayer or a lender; that money's alternative use is the Bastiat UNSEEN. The seen is the DOT sales figure; the unseen is the private consumption and investment that never happened. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: In 1977 three men joined forces in San Francisco to start a libertarian think tank. One was a young organizer named Ed Crane. One was a Kansas oil billionaire. One was the fiercest free-market economist of his generation. Later the group moved to Washington DC and grew into one of the country's most influential public-choice and free-market policy hubs. Which three men founded it?
answer: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
choices: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
William Buckley, Milton Friedman, and Barry Goldwater
James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Douglass North
Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, and Wilhelm Ropke
context: Crane served as founding president, Koch was the principal early funder, and Rothbard was the intellectual leader. The institute relocated to Washington DC in 1981. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute takes its name from a series of political essays published in London newspapers between 1720 and 1723. The two English authors wrote under the pen name 'Cato,' after the Roman republican senator Cato the Younger who resisted Julius Caesar. Their letters attacked corruption and defended liberty, and they helped inspire America's revolutionary generation. Who were the two English authors?
answer: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon
choices: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon
Alexander Hamilton and James Madison
John Locke and John Stuart Mill
Edmund Burke and Adam Smith
context: 'Cato's Letters' were published in London and reprinted heavily in the American colonies, where they influenced the founders. Hamilton and Madison wrote The Federalist Papers as Publius, a different pen-name project. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato%27s_Letters.

question: In 1981 the Cato Institute's founding intellectual leader was pushed out after a bitter dispute with the co-founders over strategy and personnel. He responded by founding a rival think tank in 1982 with Lew Rockwell. Who was he, and what did he found?
answer: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
James Buchanan, who founded the Center for Study of Public Choice
Milton Friedman, who founded the Free To Choose Network
Friedrich Hayek, who founded the Mont Pelerin Society
context: The Mises Institute (Auburn, Alabama, 1982) took a more radical Austrian direction than Cato, which pursued a Washington-focused policy engagement. The split defined two wings of the modern American libertarian movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen published 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government,' arguing that the people running government agencies behave much like business owners. They try to grow their agency's budget and staff, because a bigger agency means better pay, more prestige, and more political influence for the people at the top. Why does Niskanen's insight matter for how we think about government?
answer: It predicts that agencies will keep expanding whether or not the underlying problem gets fixed
choices: It predicts that agencies will keep expanding whether or not the underlying problem gets fixed
It proves government workers are lazier than private workers
It shows every agency will shut itself down within ten years
It means agencies never need any oversight
context: Niskanen was best known for his 1971 book 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government,' a foundational public-choice analysis of bureaucratic behavior. His long chairmanship shaped Cato's public-choice orientation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: In 2012 the Cato Institute, the Washington DC free-market think tank, got tangled in a legal fight with two of its own founding backers -- two wealthy brothers from Kansas who ran a huge private industrial company. For a few tense months the dispute briefly threatened Cato's political independence and made national news. What happened?
answer: Charles and David Koch sued Cato in a fight over board control; the case was settled and Cato remained independent
choices: Charles and David Koch sued Cato in a fight over board control; the case was settled and Cato remained independent
The US Department of Justice charged Cato with tax fraud; the case was dismissed
The Ludwig von Mises Institute sued Cato for trademark infringement over the name 'Cato'
Congress subpoenaed Cato's donor list under the Foreign Agents Registration Act
context: The dispute concerned Cato's board structure. Under the settlement, Ed Crane was succeeded as president by former BB&T CEO John Allison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute is often compared to two older free-market groups. The Foundation for Economic Education, run by Leonard Read, began in New York in 1946 and focused on educating the general public. The Mont Pelerin Society, chaired by Friedrich Hayek, began in Swiss mountain resorts in 1947 as a private scholarly network. What made Cato, founded in 1977, different from both of them?
answer: Day-to-day policy influence in Washington -- Congressional testimony, staffer events, and studies aimed at real legislation
choices: Day-to-day policy influence in Washington -- Congressional testimony, staffer events, and studies aimed at real legislation
General-public educational outreach through pamphlets and lectures
Private scholarly networks meeting biennially in Swiss mountain resorts
Formal academic training programs granting master's and doctoral degrees
context: The Foundation for Economic Education (Leonard Read, 1946) focused on general educational outreach; the Mont Pelerin Society (Hayek, 1947) organized scholarly networks. Cato uniquely aimed at the real-time DC policy process. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: In Washington DC a research group named after the Roman republican senator Cato the Younger -- the same historical figure celebrated by America's Founding Fathers as a symbol of resistance to tyranny -- has grown into a main home where free-market and public-choice economists publish their work on taxes, regulation, and monetary policy. What is the think tank called?
answer: The Cato Institute
choices: The Cato Institute
The Brookings Institution
The Ford Foundation
The Federal Reserve
context: Distinct from Public Choice (the disciplinary flagship founded by Tullock in 1966), the Cato Journal aims to bridge scholarly work with policy-oriented readership. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: In December 1989 the people of Romania rose up in the streets against their long-time ruler, Nicolae Ceausescu, who had held total power in the country since 1965. Shops had been empty for years, secret police were everywhere, and heat and electricity were rationed to a few hours a day so the regime could pay off foreign debt. His government fell in about a week and he was executed on Christmas Day. What kind of government were the Romanians throwing off?
answer: A communist dictatorship
choices: A communist dictatorship
A constitutional monarchy
A parliamentary democracy
A free-market republic
context: Nicolae Ceausescu ruled Socialist Romania from 1965 as party general secretary. His wife Elena served as effective co-ruler. Both were tried and shot on December 25, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Ceausescu.

question: Nicolae Ceausescu, the communist dictator of Romania, ordered a giant palace project built in central Bucharest during the 1980s to house the Communist Party's ruling bodies. It became the world's second-largest office building by floor area. To make room, a huge stretch of the old city was flattened, taking 26 historic churches with it. What is the enormous building called today?
answer: The Palace of the Parliament
choices: The Palace of the Parliament
The Casa Batlló
The People's Ministry
The Ceausescu Museum
context: Built as Casa Poporului (House of the People), 365,000 square meters, using 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. It now houses Romania's Parliament. It remains one of the heaviest and most expensive buildings ever constructed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_the_Parliament.

question: In October 1966 the communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu ordered his government in Romania to ban both abortion and birth control across the entire country. Both had been legal since 1957. Ceausescu wanted to force the birthrate up and grow the population by government order. The law came in a single decree that Romanians still remember today by its number. What number does the decree go by?
answer: Decree 770
choices: Decree 770
Decree 100
Decree 1000
Decree 512
context: Decree 770, October 2, 1966. Unmarried women and childless couples over 25 paid a special tax; birth rates jumped from 14.3 to 27.4 per 1,000 within a year. The state proved unable to house the resulting babies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_770.

question: Decree 770 in Romania forbade women from having abortions or using contraception. It ran for over twenty years under the communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and produced hundreds of thousands of unwanted children. In 1990, after Ceausescu was overthrown and executed, foreign reporters walked into Romanian state buildings for the first time and put the crisis on Western television. What did they find?
answer: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
choices: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
A mass wave of infant mortality on farms
Widespread hunger among rural schoolchildren
A polio outbreak in three major cities
context: By 1989 roughly 100,000 children were in Romanian state institutions. Western television footage after 1990 showed severe neglect and drove international adoption reform for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_orphans.

question: In the 1980s the Romanian communist government under Nicolae Ceausescu launched a program called 'systematization' that bulldozed thousands of small farming villages across the country. Families were forced out of their traditional houses and pushed into identical concrete apartment blocks in bigger towns, so they could be moved closer to state-run factories. Why is a top-down plan like that typical of central planning?
answer: One small group decides how everyone should live, ignoring what people actually want
choices: One small group decides how everyone should live, ignoring what people actually want
The plan carefully asks each family which house they prefer
Prices in a free market always cause the same result
The plan lets villages vote on whether to be demolished
context: Sistematizare demolished over 40,000 Bucharest buildings alone during the 1980s to make room for the Centrul Civic. Villages across Romania were slated for erasure under the policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematization_(Romania).

question: In late 1989 a Romanian pastor was about to be evicted by the communist government. People in his town crowded the streets to protect him. Within days the protests spread across the whole country and toppled the regime. What does the Romanian crowd's cascade reveal about how quickly public obedience to a dictator can collapse once people see others daring to protest?
answer: Public obedience can vanish very quickly once people see others daring to protest
choices: Public obedience can vanish very quickly once people see others daring to protest
Dictators keep their power forever because no one ever dares protest
Uprisings only succeed if a foreign army invades on the same day
Communist governments are always more popular than they appear
context: Timisoara protests defending Laszlo Tokes on December 16, 1989 spread across the city and were met with lethal force. Within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: In communist Romania, Nicolae Ceausescu had ruled as a harsh dictator for 24 years. On December 21, 1989, he ordered a mandatory rally at the Central Committee balcony in Bucharest to show the country he was still in charge. State television carried the speech live to every home. Then, mid-sentence, he lost control of the crowd for the very first time. What did the crowd do?
answer: Booed him live on state television
choices: Booed him live on state television
Threw stones at the balcony
Chanted Ceausescu's name louder
Sang the national anthem
context: The recording of Ceausescu's stunned face as the crowd's boos rose is preserved. Within four days he had fled by helicopter, been captured, tried, and shot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: Nicolae Ceausescu ruled communist Romania as a brutal dictator for 24 years, running a secret-police state and starving his own people to pay off foreign debt. In December 1989, as the Berlin Wall's fall spread revolution across Eastern Europe, Romanians rose up and captured him and his wife Elena. A short military tribunal found them guilty and they were shot by firing squad on a holiday date many still remember. Which date?
answer: December 25, 1989
choices: December 25, 1989
January 1, 1990
December 31, 1989
November 30, 1989
context: The Christmas Day execution at Targoviste military barracks makes Ceausescu the only communist leader shot during the 1989 collapse. The military tribunal proceeding lasted about an hour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Nicolae_and_Elena_Ceausescu.

question: Throughout the 1980s Nicolae Ceausescu, the communist dictator of Romania, decided he would pay off every dollar of his country's foreign debt no matter the cost to his people. He shipped Romanian grain, meat, and fuel abroad to earn hard currency while shops at home emptied out. Winter after winter, families waited in cold apartments for whatever the state chose to allow. What everyday hardship did his debt-paydown force on Romanian families?
answer: Electricity blackouts and food rationing
choices: Electricity blackouts and food rationing
Universal barter for basic goods
State confiscation of home appliances
Mandatory sale of family land
context: Ceausescu personally decided to pay off Romania's foreign debt at all cost. The 1980s saw scheduled blackouts, chronic queues for meat, sugar, and cooking oil, and gasoline severely rationed while agricultural goods were exported for hard currency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania.

question: Twentieth-century communist regimes around the world -- East Germany with its Stasi, the Soviet Union with its KGB, Albania with its Sigurimi, Romania with its Securitate under Nicolae Ceausescu -- all built one particular kind of institution to defend the state from its own people. Even in small countries it grew enormous relative to the population, with paid officers and vast networks of neighborhood informants. What kind of institution was it?
answer: A secret-police force with a wide informant network
choices: A secret-police force with a wide informant network
A free-press bureau to publish citizen complaints
A voluntary labor union free of state control
A church-run charity for the poor
context: Securitate (Departamentul Securitatii Statului) was Romania's secret police 1948-1989. Its file archive was opened after the revolution under a series of transparency laws; the National Council for the Study of the Securitate Archives (CNSAS) still processes access requests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitate.

question: In about 35 US states, plus Washington DC, hospitals cannot just build new buildings or buy expensive scanners on their own. First they must get government approval by proving there is 'need' for the extra capacity. Public-choice economists call this rule a classic protection racket, because it lets existing hospitals block newer, cheaper competitors before they even open. What is the rule called?
answer: Certificate of Need
choices: Certificate of Need
Medicare Advantage
Stark Law
HIPAA
context: Certificate of Need (CON) laws vary by state but share the core requirement: state approval before adding capacity. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Certificate_of_need.

question: In many US states, a hospital cannot build a new wing or buy an MRI scanner without first getting a special permission slip from state regulators, called a Certificate of Need. Backers of these laws give one main reason for keeping them on the books. What reason is usually given?
answer: Duplicative healthcare investment
choices: Duplicative healthcare investment
Insurance fraud
Prescription drug abuse
Foreign medical school competition
context: Advocates argue CON prevents duplicative capacity and concentrates patients at higher-volume facilities. The empirical record does not bear out the cost-reduction claim. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Certificate_of_need.

question: Under Certificate of Need laws, any person or company that wants to build a new hospital in about 35 US states must first attend a formal state hearing and prove there is 'need' for the extra beds. When a proposal comes in, one particular group almost always shows up in force to argue against it -- to swear the state does not need any more hospital capacity at all. Who shows up?
answer: The hospitals already there, who don't want the competition
choices: The hospitals already there, who don't want the competition
Patients hoping the new hospital will lower prices
Home nursing groups
State insurance officials
context: The incumbent-veto mechanism: existing hospitals routinely file objections to competitor CON applications, delaying approvals by years or defeating them entirely. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: In much of the United States, a hospital cannot open unless a state board first hands out a paper called a Certificate of Need (CON). To get one, the builder must prove the area truly "needs" another hospital. Economists have compared states that use these CON rules to states that scrapped them. Compared to the no-rule states, what do CON states have?
answer: Fewer hospitals per person and higher prices
choices: Fewer hospitals per person and higher prices
More hospitals and lower prices
The same number of hospitals but happier patients
Better ambulance response times
context: Matthew Mitchell's Mercatus Center work is the leading modern empirical case against CON regimes. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: In many US states, a law called Certificate of Need (CON) says a new hospital can open only if a state board rules the area "needs" one. At the hearing, the existing hospitals in town are invited to speak — and they usually argue against the newcomer. Year after year, applications get denied by boards where the incumbents have a loud voice. What tends to happen to prices and choices over time?
answer: Fewer hospitals open, fewer scanners get bought, prices go up
choices: Fewer hospitals open, fewer scanners get bought, prices go up
More hospitals open and prices fall as new ones compete
Hospital count stays the same but wait times drop sharply
Rural areas gain more clinics because the board favors them
context: CON states show fewer hospitals per capita, fewer MRI machines per capita, and higher per-service prices -- the opposite of the stated 'lower costs from consolidation' rationale. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: Existing hospitals in a US state can often show up at a state hearing and block a rival hospital's application to open. In 1971, the American economist George Stigler published a famous paper explaining why regulators end up serving the industries they are supposed to police, rather than the public. What is the argument called?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Comparative advantage
context: George Stigler's 1971 'Theory of Economic Regulation' (Bell Journal) is the founding theoretical statement of regulatory capture: regulators come to serve the industries they regulate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Regulatory_capture.

question: In many US states, a company that wants to open a new home-health-care office must first appear before a state board and prove there is enough 'need' for its services. Under the rule, called a certificate-of-need law, the home-health companies already in business get to show up at the hearing and argue against letting the newcomer in. What does this kind of rule mostly end up doing?
answer: It protects the businesses already in the market from new competition
choices: It protects the businesses already in the market from new competition
