It lowers prices for patients by adding more providers
It guarantees each new company a share of the market
It stops fraud by making applicants pay a filing fee
context: IJ's Bogdanchik case argues Kentucky's home-health CON regime violates the 14th Amendment's protection of the right to earn a living. Source: ij.org/case/kentucky-home-health-care.

question: In 1978, in a poor village called Xiaogang, eighteen Chinese farmers met at night and signed a secret agreement. Under Mao's collective farming they had been starving. Now each family would work its own plot, hand a set amount of grain to the government, and quietly keep any extra for themselves. What happened to how much food they grew?
answer: It shot up -- they grew far more than before
choices: It shot up -- they grew far more than before
It stayed exactly the same
It fell because they got lazy
It only rose for one year
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed the December 1978 secret pact. The contract is preserved in Beijing's National Museum of Modern Chinese History. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: For decades, Chinese farming was run by big communes where everyone worked the land together and shared whatever was grown. Harvests were poor and hunger was common. Starting in 1978, the Communist Party let each farm family take charge of a set piece of land. Every household owed the state a fixed amount of grain, but any extra harvest they could keep or sell. What was this plan called?
answer: The Household Responsibility System
choices: The Household Responsibility System
The Free Farming Program
The Village Enterprise Reform
The New Rural Charter
context: Jiating lianchan chengbao zeren zhi (Household Responsibility System) was legalized nationwide by 1983. It restored the family plot and let households keep above-quota production. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: In late 1978, eighteen farmers in the tiny Chinese village of Xiaogang met in secret at night and signed a contract to divide the government's collective land into family plots and farm them privately. They knew that under Maoist law they could be executed for it, so they even pledged to raise each other's children if it went wrong. Life on the old commune had left their families in one steady condition, even though everyone worked every day. What condition?
answer: Chronic hunger despite constant work
choices: Chronic hunger despite constant work
Chronic surplus with no market
Chronic under-employment on rich land
Chronic conscription for army service
context: Xiaogang villagers had been sending members to beg for food in other counties for decades under the commune system. The famine memory of 1959-61 was still living. The life-and-death contract was a rational response to a chronic shortage economy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: In 1978 the eighteen farmers of Xiaogang village in China signed a secret contract to abandon the government's collective commune and farm their own family plots. Within a single year the risk paid off so heavily that local officials could not hide the harvest anymore. About what multiple did their grain output rise in that first year?
answer: About six times
choices: About six times
About twenty percent
About fifty percent
About a hundred times
context: Xiaogang's grain output rose roughly six-fold in one year under the household contract. The neighboring villages watched, imitated, and the practice spread county by county before official legalization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: In 1978 China's Communist Party changed the rules for farmers. Before, everyone worked a big commune and turned everything over to the state; harvests were poor. Under the new plan, called the Household Responsibility System, each family had to meet a state grain quota — but anything extra they grew, they could keep or sell in the market. Over the next six years grain output jumped about a third. What was the main reason?
answer: Farmers now had a reason to work harder and grow more, because the extra was theirs
choices: Farmers now had a reason to work harder and grow more, because the extra was theirs
The government sent new tractors and fertilizer to every village
Weather across China was unusually good for six straight years
The state simply raised the quota each year
context: Lin's 1992 China Economic Review paper 'Rural Reforms and Agricultural Growth in China' decomposed the growth. About half came from the incentive-restoration, not from fertilizer, weather, or better seed. Lin later served as World Bank Chief Economist 2008-12. Source: China Economic Review 1992.

question: After 1978, China's new Household Responsibility System let farmers keep any grain left over once they had delivered a set amount to the government. Families that produced extra ate better and got richer, so they worked much harder than farmers under the old collective rules, who had labored for a flat share. Economists have a name for this kind of incentive — the right to keep whatever is left after obligations are paid. What is it called?
answer: The residual claim
choices: The residual claim
The dual mandate
The Kaldor-Hicks compensation
The Coase invariance
context: The residual claim -- the right to keep whatever is left after fixed obligations -- gives the actor sharp incentive to increase output and improve technique. This is the load-bearing move behind private property in economic theory. Source: mises.org/library/residual-claim.

question: After Mao Zedong's death, China's new leader Deng Xiaoping quietly backed the Household Responsibility System, the reform pioneered by the eighteen farmers of Xiaogang village who broke the commune in secret in 1978 to farm their own plots. Deng defended letting farmers work for themselves with a famous saying about a cat. What was the phrase?
answer: It does not matter whether the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
choices: It does not matter whether the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
The eagle sees what the sparrow misses
The camel walks where the horse cannot
The tiger and the lion share the same forest
context: Deng's black-cat-white-cat saying (revived from a 1961 speech) became the shorthand slogan of Reform and Opening. Empirical results trump ideological purity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: In 1920 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published an essay arguing that a socialist state could never plan an economy well, because without real market prices the planners had no way to compare costs. Sixty years later, China's own Communist Party admitted the commune system had failed — market prices for grain and goods beat central orders. Austrian economists call this a natural experiment. Whose 1920 argument does it prove right?
answer: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
choices: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
John Maynard Keynes on effective demand
Karl Marx on primitive accumulation
Alfred Marshall on partial equilibrium
context: Mises's 1920 argument that socialist commonwealths cannot calculate rationally without market prices was empirically confirmed at the largest possible scale by the Chinese state's own reforms. Same land, same farmers, radically more output when prices returned. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The 1978 secret contract that eighteen Xiaogang farmers signed under a kerosene lamp, the crumbling paper with their red thumbprints that risked their lives to break Mao's commune system, is now treated as a national treasure of modern China. The physical document itself is on display today. Where is it kept?
answer: The National Museum in Beijing
choices: The National Museum in Beijing
The village schoolhouse in Xiaogang
The Ministry of Agriculture in Beijing
The Shanghai Museum
context: The original life-and-death contract is displayed in Beijing's National Museum of Modern Chinese History. It marks the practical starting point of Reform and Opening. Source: national museum catalog.

question: After 1978 China let farmers keep any grain grown above a state quota, in what became known as the Household Responsibility System. The same land, the same farmers, and the same seeds suddenly produced far more grain than they ever had under collective farming — the only change was who got to keep the surplus. For the socialist calculation debate, this became a two-word slogan Austrian economists love to point at. What is that two-word phrase?
answer: Incentives matter
choices: Incentives matter
Growth is exogenous
Central planning succeeds
Land quality dominates
context: 'Incentives matter' is the compressed lesson of the Chinese agricultural reform, taught in every introductory economics course. It captures the incentive-recognition side of the calculation debate. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: In 1937 the British economist Ronald Coase, then only 26 years old, published a short paper in the journal Economica asking a strange question: why do companies exist at all, if open markets can coordinate everything through the price system? That single paper later helped him win the 1991 Nobel Prize in Economics. What was the paper called?
answer: The Nature of the Firm
choices: The Nature of the Firm
The Problem of Social Cost
The Federal Communications Commission
The Marginal Cost Controversy
context: Ronald Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (Economica, November 1937). Coase was 26 and had done most of the thinking as a 21-year-old undergraduate on a US scholarship trip in 1931-32. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Coase 1937).

question: In 1931 a young English student named Ronald Coase used a traveling scholarship to tour America's giant new industrial firms. He wanted to see with his own eyes why so much work was organized inside huge companies instead of by open markets, the puzzle he would spend his whole career solving. On the trip he visited the famous Detroit carmaker of his day. Which carmaker did he visit?
answer: Ford
choices: Ford
General Electric
American Tobacco
US Steel
context: Coase's Cassel Scholarship US visit included Ford in Detroit, US Steel, and other integrated firms. Watching those hierarchies is what led him to ask why the firm existed rather than the market coordinating everything through prices. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: In 1937 a young British economist named Ronald Coase asked a puzzling question. If free-market prices work so beautifully at guiding people, why do big companies exist at all? Why does Ford hire a full-time worker on salary instead of paying a fresh freelancer for every screw turned, every letter typed, every meeting held? Coase said companies exist for one reason. Which?
answer: Because using the market for every tiny task has its own hidden costs
choices: Because using the market for every tiny task has its own hidden costs
Because governments make it illegal to hire freelancers
Because workers refuse to be paid by the task
Because companies get big tax breaks that freelancers don't get
context: Coase's key move: using markets is costly (finding partners, negotiating, monitoring, enforcing). When those costs exceed the costs of managing inside a firm, hierarchies replace market transactions. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: In his 1937 paper, the British economist Ronald Coase gave a rule for how big a company should grow. A firm keeps taking on new tasks in-house — cleaning, accounting, deliveries — until doing one more job inside starts to cost as much as just paying an outsider to do it. At that point it stops growing. What sets the company's size?
answer: The point where doing it inside costs the same as buying it from outside
choices: The point where doing it inside costs the same as buying it from outside
The point where it hires its one-thousandth worker
The point where payroll tax drops below ten percent
The point where paperwork staff match production staff
context: Coase's boundary condition: the firm grows until the marginal in-house transaction cost equals the marginal market transaction cost. Cheaper in-house transactions are absorbed; cheaper market transactions are outsourced. Source: Coase, Economica (1937), section III.

question: Ronald Coase's 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm asked why firms exist and gave a simple answer: doing every trade through the open market has hidden costs, from writing contracts to finding partners to checking that quality is honest. Decades later economists built a whole subfield on this single insight, and they named it after the very variable Coase had put at the center of his story. What is the standard modern name for the field?
answer: Transaction cost economics
choices: Transaction cost economics
General equilibrium theory
Behavioral economics
Public finance
context: Transaction cost economics (or New Institutional Economics) grew directly out of Coase 1937. Oliver Williamson's 2009 Nobel-winning work on 'markets and hierarchies' extends the framework substantially. Source: Williamson, Markets and Hierarchies (Free Press 1975).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase pointed out that when a company hires an outside firm to do a job, it isn't just paying the sticker price. Someone has to find the right supplier, write and sign a contract, watch the work to make sure it's done right, and argue in court when things go wrong. All of that takes time and lawyers. What do economists call these extra costs?
answer: Transaction costs
choices: Transaction costs
Fixed costs
Sunk costs
Marginal costs
context: Oliver Williamson shared the 2009 Nobel with Elinor Ostrom, cited for his work on the economic governance of the firm. Source: nobelprize.org (2009 Economic Sciences).

question: In 1937 the British economist Ronald Coase argued that big companies exist because using the free market has hidden costs — searching, contracting, monitoring. Today, cheap global shipping and the internet have slashed those costs. Modern tech giants like Apple now design chips in California but hire Taiwanese factories to build them. What shift has followed?
answer: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
choices: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
A move from outsourced supply chains toward vertical integration
A move from stock ownership toward partnership structures
A move from public listing toward private ownership
context: Apple in the 1980s made much of its hardware in-house; Apple in the 2000s+ largely designs in-house and manufactures through contract firms like Foxconn. Falling market transaction costs move the firm boundary outward. Source: Baldwin + Clark, Design Rules (MIT 2000).

question: In 1991 the British economist Ronald Coase won the Nobel Prize in Economics. His citation named two papers — one from 1937 titled "The Nature of the Firm", which explained why companies exist at all, and one from 1960 that reshaped how economists think about pollution, noise, and neighborly disputes. What did the 1960 paper analyze?
answer: The problem of social cost -- externalities and property rights
choices: The problem of social cost -- externalities and property rights
The efficiency of central-bank monetary policy
The distribution of income across households
The theory of international trade under quotas
context: 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960). The 1991 Nobel citation names both 1937 and 1960 as the key contributions. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: In 1937 the British economist Ronald Coase published "The Nature of the Firm", a paper that changed how economists study any industry. When analysts look at a deal — say, a car company buying steel — Coase's framework tells them to ask one key comparative question every time. What is that question?
answer: Why is this transaction organized inside a firm rather than through the market
choices: Why is this transaction organized inside a firm rather than through the market
How large is the industry's marketing budget
Which continent produces the most output
Which political party currently regulates the industry
context: Coase's move: for every transaction, ask why it is organized the way it is. The answer is always the relative transaction cost of the two arrangements. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: Ronald Coase, the British economist who would later win a Nobel Prize, wrote his famous 1937 paper 'The Nature of the Firm' while he was still in his twenties. He credited his undergraduate professors, especially Arnold Plant, for making him skeptical of the socialist central-planning ideas fashionable in 1930s Britain. Where did the young Coase earn his undergraduate degree in commerce?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Cambridge
The University of Chicago
Harvard University
context: Coase took his BCom at the London School of Economics (1932). His US Cassel Scholarship trip in 1931-32 provided the empirical observations behind Nature of the Firm. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: In 1960 the British economist Ronald Coase published one of the most famous papers in all of economics. It changed how people thought about problems like factory smoke drifting onto a neighbor's laundry — the paper argued the real question is who owns the right to the clean air, and whether the two sides can bargain. What was the paper called?
answer: The Problem of Social Cost
choices: The Problem of Social Cost
The Nature of the Firm
The Federal Communications Commission
The Marginal Cost Controversy
context: Ronald Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960). Its argument reframed the whole economics of externalities. Source: chicagounbound.uchicago.edu (Coase 1960).

question: A steel factory on the edge of town blows thick black smoke into the neighborhood next door. The families there start getting bad coughs and sore lungs, but the factory owner does not pay any of their doctor bills. Economists have a special one-word name for a cost like that — a cost the owner never pays because it lands on other people. What do they call it?
answer: An externality
choices: An externality
A subsidy
A windfall
A dividend
context: Arthur Pigou (1877-1959) had argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) that pollution should be corrected by government tax. Coase said the Pigouvian analysis was incomplete because it treated the causation as one-directional. Source: Pigou (1920); Coase (1960).

question: Ronald Coase, a British economist writing in 1960, looked at a factory whose smoke bothered its neighbors. He argued something people found strange: the harm actually flowed in both directions. Yes, the smoke hurt the neighbors — but a total ban on the smoke also hurt the factory owner, who could no longer produce and sell goods. What does that idea of reciprocal harm mean here?
answer: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
choices: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
The neighbor is legally required to endure the pollution
The neighbor loses standing to sue in federal court
The factory automatically owes triple damages
context: Coase's move: the economic question is not who is at fault. It is which use of the resource creates more value. Both parties have legitimate uses; a rule imposes costs on whichever party is prevented from its use. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960).

question: In his 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost", the British economist Ronald Coase told a story about a rancher whose cattle kept wandering onto a neighbor farmer's crops. Coase argued that if the rancher and farmer can talk cheaply and strike a deal — either the rancher pays for a fence, or the farmer pays the rancher to fence — one outcome always shows up. Which one?
answer: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
choices: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
The rancher always keeps the cattle
The farmer always keeps the crops
Both parties abandon their land
context: The initial rights determine WHO PAYS in the bargain; they do not determine the final resource allocation if transaction costs are low enough for the parties to negotiate. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960), section IV.

question: A rancher lets his cows wander into a neighbor's wheat field and trample it. Instead of a lawsuit, the two can talk and cut a deal -- the rancher pays for the damage, or the farmer accepts a fence. Economists say that when talking is cheap and easy, the two sides find a good outcome no matter which one the law protects. What is this idea usually called?
answer: The Coase theorem
choices: The Coase theorem
The tragedy of the commons
The invisible hand
The prisoner's dilemma
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase Theorem' in his 1966 textbook Theory of Price. Coase himself argued the textbook version was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase, who won the 1991 Nobel Prize, argued that when people can cheaply talk and cut deals, they can often solve pollution and property disputes on their own without a court or law. Many readers misread him as saying government is never needed at all. But Coase himself was careful. He had a specific real position for the case when talking is very costly, say between hundreds of affected neighbors. What was his real view then?
answer: Government action may be worth it, but the government's own costs of acting must be counted too
choices: Government action may be worth it, but the government's own costs of acting must be counted too
Nothing can be done and the parties must live with the harm
The market always still finds a fix on its own
Only judges, never lawmakers, may step in
context: Coase's actual argument in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: when private bargaining is too costly, government intervention may be superior -- provided the analysis honestly counts the transaction costs of government administration too. Source: Coase, The Firm, the Market, and the Law (Chicago 1988).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase argued that pollution and overfishing get solved best by giving people clear rights that they can trade. Instead of governments barking hard rules, let firms buy and sell the right to emit or catch. In the 1990s and 2000s, two big trading systems inspired by Coase took off around the world. Which pair?
answer: Tradeable pollution permits and individual transferable fishing quotas
choices: Tradeable pollution permits and individual transferable fishing quotas
Purely command-and-control emission limits and moral suasion
Federal ownership of all polluting facilities
Complete abolition of private industry
context: The 1990 US SO2 cap-and-trade Acid Rain Program, EU ETS (2005), and Iceland + New Zealand fisheries individual transferable quotas all trace their intellectual pedigree to Coase 1960. Source: Ellerman + Joskow, Markets for Clean Air (Cambridge 2000).

question: Ronald Coase's 1960 paper on property and pollution inspired another famous economist to study how real villages manage shared resources. She looked at Swiss mountain pastures, Spanish irrigation systems, Turkish fisheries, and Nepali forests, showing communities could govern their commons for centuries without a government or a private market running things. Her 1990 book became the standard reference on the topic. Which book is it?
answer: Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons
choices: Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons
Kenneth Arrow's Social Choice and Individual Values
James Buchanan's Calculus of Consent
Douglass North's Structure and Change in Economic History
context: Ostrom's Governing the Commons (Cambridge UP 1990) draws directly on Coase's institutional-analysis framework, extending it from two-party bargaining to many-party self-governance of common-pool resources. Source: Ostrom (1990); Coase (1960).

question: Ronald Coase, a British-born economist, wrote just two short papers that became world-famous: 'The Nature of the Firm' in 1937 and 'The Problem of Social Cost' in 1960. Together they run about 60 pages. In 1991 the Royal Swedish Academy awarded him the Nobel Prize in Economics, citing those two papers as the basis. What idea did the Academy say they had earned him recognition for?
answer: The significance of transaction costs and property rights for institutional structure
choices: The significance of transaction costs and property rights for institutional structure
The mathematical foundations of general equilibrium
The theory of comparative advantage in international trade
The empirical measurement of national income
context: The 1991 Nobel citation named Coase 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Both 1937 and 1960 papers are the pillars. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase, in his 1937 paper on firms and his 1960 paper on social cost, kept warning fellow economists about a bad habit. Too many analysts, he said, would compare a messy real-world market to a perfect textbook government, or a messy real-world government to a perfect textbook market — and then declare a winner. Which sentence best captures the honest rule Coase demanded?
answer: Never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative
choices: Never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative
Always favor markets over any form of state action
Always favor state action over any form of markets
All externalities disappear if you draw the diagram correctly
context: Coase's move: compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms. Firms, markets, private bargains, and government all have their own transaction costs. Honest comparative institutional analysis counts them all. Source: Coase, The Firm, the Market, and the Law (Chicago 1988).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase's 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost" gave rise to what textbooks call the Coase theorem — often taught as "if bargaining is costless, initial ownership doesn't matter." But Coase himself thought the textbook version was a misreading of what he actually said. Which version does Coase's own writing endorse?
answer: Transaction costs are high in the real world, so initial rights matter enormously
choices: Transaction costs are high in the real world, so initial rights matter enormously
Externalities disappear in every real market regardless of institutions
Government intervention is never justified for any externality
Property rights should be assigned to whichever party is wealthier
context: Coase in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: the zero-transaction-cost world of the textbook Coase Theorem does not exist. In the real world, transaction costs are high, so initial rights and institutional design matter enormously. Source: Coase (1988).

question: The United States taxes imported shoes at very different rates. Cheap plastic and canvas sneakers that a working family buys are hit with tariffs of 15% to 20%. Fancy leather dress shoes that a rich family buys are hit with tariffs of only 5% to 8%. The government collects the tariff, but the higher store price is passed on to shoppers. Which group pays more of this tax?
answer: Low-income households
choices: Low-income households
High-income households
Both income groups equally
Only foreign-based importers
context: Because low-income households spend a larger share of income on the tariffed low-end goods, they bear a disproportionately higher effective burden. Source: usitc.gov/tariff_affairs/tariff_databases.

question: In the United States, a tariff on imported shoes and cheap clothes makes those things cost more at the store. Say a rich family earns $200,000 a year and a poor family earns $30,000. Both need shoes and shirts and pants, and both buy them. The extra dollars they pay from the tariff hit the poor family's budget very differently. Which family loses a bigger SHARE of its income to that extra tariff cost?
answer: The poor family
choices: The poor family
The rich family
Both families lose the same share
Neither family loses anything
context: Ed Gresser's 'Toughest on the Poor: America's Flawed Tariff System' (PPI, 2002) is the definitive empirical treatment of tariff incidence across US household-income quintiles. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: In the 2000s, the American trade researcher Edward Gresser studied who really pays the United States tariff bill. He compared how much of their income the poorest fifth of American families spent on tariffs to how much the richest fifth spent. Even though rich families spend more dollars, poor families spend a much bigger share of what they earn. As a share of income, how many times bigger was the poorest fifth's tariff bill?
answer: 3 to 4 times
choices: 3 to 4 times
1.1 to 1.2 times
10 to 15 times
About 30 times
context: Bottom-quintile households pay roughly 3-4x the top-quintile burden as a share of income; the schedule targets specifically the goods the poor buy most. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: Thomas Sowell, the American economist and longtime Stanford scholar, wrote a popular textbook called Basic Economics for readers with no math. In it he tackles the political claim that tariffs, taxes charged on imported goods, protect American workers. Sowell says there is a hidden twist in that claim which the tariff supporters do not admit. What does he say?
answer: The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are taxing them the most
choices: The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are taxing them the most
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are helping them the most
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are unrelated to consumer prices
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are always wealthy foreigners
context: Sowell's Basic Economics distills the incidence result: protectionism sold as pro-worker functions economically as a regressive consumption tax hitting working-class families most. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Anna is faster than Ben at both baking cookies and drawing signs. It might still pay for Ben to make the signs while Anna bakes, then trade. What is the economics word for the idea that trade helps both sides even when one person is better at everything?
answer: Comparative advantage
choices: Comparative advantage
Absolute advantage
Diminishing returns
Economies of scale
context: Ricardo's 1817 Principles of Political Economy and Taxation formulated comparative advantage; every tariff that overrides it necessarily leaves both trading nations poorer. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comparative_advantage.

question: When the United States puts a tariff on imported shirts, the price at the store goes up, and the American who buys the shirt pays extra. The tariff doesn't hit wages or company profits directly — it hits the shopper at the register. In economic terms, this behaves much like one specific kind of tax. Which category of tax does a tariff most closely resemble?
answer: A consumption tax
choices: A consumption tax
A payroll tax
A corporate income tax
A capital gains tax
context: A tariff raises the domestic price of the imported good and is paid, in economic incidence, by the domestic consumer -- like a targeted sales tax. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tariff.

question: The United States tariff schedule taxes cheap shoes and cheap clothes at much higher rates than fancy versions of the same goods. This lopsided pattern wasn't a one-time policy — it built up over decades of tariff bills in Congress. Which mechanism best describes how the schedule came to look this way?
answer: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
choices: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
The World Trade Organization mandates the pattern
Federal statute requires 20% rates on all consumer goods
Foreign governments retaliated against US textile exports
context: The schedule is not accidental. Producers of low-end goods (footwear, apparel) had the strongest incentive to lobby for protection and the tariff schedule reflects their trade-lobby lawyers' work. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: In a growing number of US states, an ordinary adult can carry a concealed handgun for self-defense without any government permit at all. There is no fee, no application, no mandatory training class, just carry. Supporters call it a return to the original meaning of the Second Amendment. What is this no-permit rule called?
answer: Constitutional carry
choices: Constitutional carry
May-issue permitting
Shall-issue permitting
Open-carry only
context: As of 2024 about 27 US states allow constitutional carry (no permit required); the other extreme was 'may-issue' at official discretion, largely struck down by the Bruen decision. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Concealed_carry_in_the_United_States.

question: If robbers know some homes might have someone armed inside, some robbers will be less likely to break in. If they know for sure NO homes are armed, they may be MORE likely to try. What econ idea says people change their behavior based on the risks they face?
answer: Incentives change behavior
choices: Incentives change behavior
Prices always rise over time
Money is a social construct
All punishments are equal
context: John Lott's More Guns, Less Crime (Chicago, 1998; 3rd ed. 2010) is the most-cited empirical work on the effects of concealed-carry laws. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: A US state used to require heavy paperwork and thousands of dollars in fees before a person could carry a concealed handgun for self-defense. Then the state passed a law that lowered the fees and cut the paperwork way down. Researchers checked who signed up for the new easier permits. One specific group registered in much higher numbers than before. Which group?
answer: Lower-income and minority families who live in high-crime neighborhoods
choices: Lower-income and minority families who live in high-crime neighborhoods
Retired military officers
Suburban homeowners
College-educated professionals
context: Lower fees and non-discretionary issuance disproportionately raised permit uptake among lower-income and minority residents, who tend to live in higher-crime neighborhoods and cannot rely on rapid police response. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: On June 23, 2022, the US Supreme Court struck down New York state's may-issue concealed-carry law, which had let officials refuse a carry permit unless the applicant proved a special need. The Court ruled that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry firearms in public, not only at home. Gun-rights supporters call the case a landmark on par with Heller. What is its short name?
answer: Bruen
choices: Bruen
Heller
McDonald
Rahimi
context: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022), majority opinion by Justice Clarence Thomas, invalidated may-issue regimes requiring 'proper cause'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: In June 2022 the US Supreme Court ruled in a case called New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen that states could no longer make people prove a "special need" to get a concealed-carry permit. States that had used that rule to keep permits rare — like New York, New Jersey, and California — didn't want to give up. Instead of ending restrictions, they shifted to a different set of tools. Which set?
answer: Higher fees, extensive training requirements, and sensitive-place restrictions
choices: Higher fees, extensive training requirements, and sensitive-place restrictions
Age limits raised to 30 for all applicants
Federal preemption of local permitting entirely
Direct federal ownership of all firearms in the state
context: Restrictive states shifted from discretionary denial to cost-based and geography-based restriction after Bruen. The Bastiat move: the SEEN policy changed; the UNSEEN restriction on the low-income permit-seeker did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: The 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught a method he called the seen and the unseen: hunt for the person harmed but never counted, the victim invisible in the official numbers. Applied to a state's gun-permit fees and paperwork, Bastiat's method surfaces a specific class of person that government statistics on gun policy leave out entirely. Which class does the method make visible?
answer: The victim who could not afford the fee and was disarmed against her attacker
choices: The victim who could not afford the fee and was disarmed against her attacker
The firearm dealer who lost a small-caliber sale
The state licensing office that lost fee revenue
The insurance company that paid a smaller premium
context: The seen: revenue-generating fees and training requirements. The unseen: the woman being stalked who could not afford the $400+20-hours barrier and could not lawfully carry for self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: In 1995, a paper called 'Armed Resistance to Crime: An Examination of the Prevalence and Nature of Self-Defense with a Gun' appeared in the Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology and shook the American gun-control debate. The authors surveyed US households and estimated Americans use guns defensively about 2.2 million times a year — far more often than they use guns to commit crimes. Gun-control groups dispute the number to this day. Which pair of criminology researchers wrote it?
answer: Gary Kleck and Marc Gertz
choices: Gary Kleck and Marc Gertz
John Lott and David Mustard
Franklin Zimring and Gordon Hawkins
David Hemenway and Deborah Azrael
context: Kleck and Gertz's estimate of ~2.2 million annual defensive gun uses in the US is contested but remains a widely-cited figure in the empirical literature on self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Defensive_gun_use.

question: In May 1984, one of the biggest banks in the United States nearly failed. It had loaded up on bad loans to oil and gas drillers in Oklahoma and Texas, and when oil prices crashed the loans went bad. Depositors around the world began yanking their money out by the billion. To stop the panic, the US government stepped in with a huge rescue. Which bank was it?
answer: Continental Illinois National Bank
choices: Continental Illinois National Bank
First Chicago
Citibank
Manufacturers Hanover
context: Continental Illinois had about $40 billion in assets at the time of its 1984 crisis -- roughly $120 billion in 2026 dollars. It had bought energy loans from the failed Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma in 1982. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: In May 1984, Chicago's giant Continental Illinois bank started to collapse. In the old days, a bank run meant crowds of ordinary savers lining up at the teller windows to grab their cash. But this run was different — big companies and foreign banks yanked their money out by electronic wire, without anyone walking through the door. What is this new kind of run called?
answer: A wholesale run
choices: A wholesale run
A retail run
A silent run
A commercial run
context: A wholesale run happens over telecommunications rather than at teller windows. It moves orders of magnitude faster than a classic retail run. Continental Illinois was the first major US bank collapse to be primarily wholesale-driven. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank run' (2026-09-05).

question: In May 1984, a giant American bank in Chicago called Continental Illinois was about to fail after big loans went bad. The US government stepped in with a huge rescue. Federal officials promised to protect every single account at the bank, even the ones far above the usual insurance limit of one hundred thousand dollars. Big depositors got everything back. What is this kind of rescue called?
answer: A too-big-to-fail bailout
choices: A too-big-to-fail bailout
A private-sector rescue
An orderly bankruptcy
A depositor-loss event
context: At the time, FDIC insurance covered up to $100,000 per depositor. Extending protection above that cap for a specific bank was a discretionary expansion of the guarantee. It set a precedent that shaped every major US bank rescue since. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 1984, US Comptroller of the Currency Todd Conover went before a House banking committee to explain the Continental Illinois rescue. He told lawmakers there was a specific group of large American banks that the federal government would never allow to fail, no matter what. Which group did he name?
answer: The 11 largest US banks
choices: The 11 largest US banks
The 3 largest money-center banks
The 25 largest banks by branch count
The 5 largest investment banks
context: Comptroller C.T. Conover's September 19 1984 testimony was the first time a federal regulator used the phrase 'too big to fail' publicly to describe a policy commitment. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 1984, US Comptroller of the Currency Todd Conover spoke to a House banking committee about why Washington had bailed out Continental Illinois. To explain why the rescue had been necessary, he described a group of huge banks with four short words. That phrase became famous and is still used today for giant banks the government refuses to let collapse. What was the phrase?
answer: Too big to fail
choices: Too big to fail
Systemic risk exception
Lender of last resort
Money-center backstop
context: Comptroller Conover's 1984 testimony gave 'too big to fail' its policy meaning. The phrase was later popularized by Congressman Stewart McKinney and became the shorthand for the moral-hazard structure of modern banking regulation. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: After the 1984 Continental Illinois rescue, mergers among big American banks sped up dramatically, and small banks were bought or squeezed out. By 2020, just four giants — JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup — dominated the industry. How did the four largest US banks' combined share of all deposits change from 1984 to 2020?
answer: From about 10% of deposits to over 45%
choices: From about 10% of deposits to over 45%
From about 30% of deposits to about 40%
From about 20% of deposits to about 22%
From about 50% of deposits to about 55%
context: The four largest US banks held about 10% of deposits in 1984. By 2020 they held over 45%. The Continental Illinois precedent created an incentive for the biggest banks to take larger risks -- upside privatized, downside socialized. Source: Grokipedia 'Concentration in the banking industry' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian school of economics and public-choice thinkers have long criticized the 1984 Continental Illinois rescue. They argue the bailout taught giant banks a specific lesson that changed how those banks made loans for decades afterward. Once the precedent was set, big banks came to expect a particular kind of federal protection whenever they got into trouble. What did large banks learn from the 1984 rescue?
answer: Regulators would protect uninsured depositors and creditors in a crisis, so larger risks were now safer to take
choices: Regulators would protect uninsured depositors and creditors in a crisis, so larger risks were now safer to take
Regulators would strictly enforce capital requirements to prevent future rescues
Regulators would break up any bank that grew above a specific size
Regulators would nationalize any bank that engaged in risky lending
context: This is the moral-hazard structure of every subsequent bailout episode -- LTCM 1998, Bear Stearns 2008, TARP 2008, SVB 2023. All extended the Continental Illinois precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Moral hazard' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) is a US agency that promises to pay back deposits if a bank fails. It was created in 1933 after the Great Depression bank runs. Austrian and free-market economists worry the promise causes what they call moral hazard — banks feel bolder about risky loans because someone else covers the downside. Why would government-backed deposit insurance push banks to take bigger risks?
answer: The bank keeps profits from big bets, but taxpayers cover the loss if it fails
choices: The bank keeps profits from big bets, but taxpayers cover the loss if it fails
The bank has no risk any more, so there is no reason to lend at all
Depositors punish risky banks by moving their money quickly
Banks are forced by law to make risky loans every year
context: The FDIC took majority ownership of Continental Illinois in 1984 and gradually reduced its stake. Bank of America completed the acquisition in 1994. The name Continental Illinois disappeared from American banking. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1984 Continental Illinois, then the seventh-largest bank in America, nearly collapsed after huge oil-and-gas loans went bad. Rather than let it fail, US regulators rescued every single depositor, including the wealthy ones the law was never supposed to cover. Economists later argued that this one-time emergency rescue quietly set a lasting rule for every bank that came after. Which reasoning move does the story teach?
answer: A discretionary exception granted once becomes a structural precedent that shapes every future risk-taking decision in the sector
choices: A discretionary exception granted once becomes a structural precedent that shapes every future risk-taking decision in the sector
Emergency exceptions are always time-limited and never generalize
Discretionary exceptions can be revoked at any time without political cost
Bank rescues never influence the behavior of banks that were not directly rescued
context: The 1984 above-cap protection was framed as an exception. Every subsequent major rescue extended the pattern until 'too big to fail' was a well-understood implicit guarantee. The 2023 SVB extension of full protection was the direct heir of the 1984 precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1984 US regulators rescued Continental Illinois, then America's seventh-largest bank, and paid off every depositor, including the wealthy ones the law did not cover. Austrian economists drew a harder lesson from the episode: bailing out only the biggest banks changes the behavior of every big bank afterward. Which reasoning move do the Austrians press?
answer: Regulation that guarantees the biggest banks against failure is itself a subsidy that drives ever-greater concentration in the sector
choices: Regulation that guarantees the biggest banks against failure is itself a subsidy that drives ever-greater concentration in the sector
Regulation always reduces concentration in the banking sector
Bank consolidation has no relationship to deposit-insurance policy
Deposit insurance protects small banks preferentially over large ones
context: The Austrian point: too-big-to-fail is not just moral hazard for the biggest banks; it is an active subsidy over their smaller competitors. Depositors rationally prefer the guaranteed bank. Consolidation is the mechanical result. Source: Selgin, Bagehot's Legacy (Cato commentary, 2013-2020).

question: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 set the current US federal tax rate on company profits. What is that current federal rate?
context: The 2017 TCJA cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 21%; the tax applies to C-corporation profits and is separate from personal income tax paid on dividends and capital gains. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: Milton Friedman was a famous American economist who won the Nobel Prize for his work on money. He liked to remind people of a simple truth: a company is not a person, so a company cannot really pay a tax — only people can. When the government puts a tax on a company, one of three groups of real people always ends up paying it in the end. Which three groups?
answer: Workers, customers, or owners of the company
choices: Workers, customers, or owners of the company
Robots, computers, or buildings
The mayor, senators, and judges
Only foreign investors, never Americans
context: Friedman's line summarizes the incidence point: a corporation is a legal fiction and every dollar of tax comes from a real human's pocket -- a consumer, a worker, or a shareholder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: When economists study taxes, they use the word 'incidence' for who really feels the bite. Legal incidence is the person or company the law says has to pay the money. But once prices, wages, and rents adjust to the tax, someone else may actually lose the income. Economists call that second, real-world kind of incidence by its own name. What is the name for who really loses income from a tax?
answer: Economic incidence
choices: Economic incidence
Distributional incidence
Marginal incidence
Progressive incidence
context: Statutory vs economic incidence: the check-writer is often not the party whose income is reduced. This distinction is the analytic core of tax-policy analysis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tax_incidence.

question: Frederic Bastiat, the 19th-century French economist, taught readers to look past the obvious and ask who really bears a tax. Modern Bastiat-style economists apply the same test to the US corporate income tax. Congress writes the bill to the company, but a big share of the cost quietly flows to one particular group in the form of smaller earnings. Which group takes the largest hit through smaller paychecks?
answer: Workers via lower wages
choices: Workers via lower wages
Retirees via smaller Social Security checks
Foreign investors via US border tariffs
Landlords via higher property tax
context: Empirical research (Suarez Serrato and Zidar, AER 2016; CBO 2012 distributional update) shows a large share of the corporate income tax is ultimately borne by workers through lower wages. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: Economists studying corporate taxes noticed something surprising: when a country raises the tax on its companies, wages for workers often fall the most. The reason is a gap between the two main things a business uses to produce goods — money (capital) and workers (labor). One of these two production factors can flee the country easily to escape a tax. The other is stuck at home. Which asymmetry does the corporate tax exploit?
answer: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
choices: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
Labor is more mobile internationally than capital
Capital and labor are equally mobile
Neither capital nor labor moves across borders
context: Mobile capital's after-tax return is set by world markets; when the US taxes capital, mobile capital exits or requires a compensating gross return, and the burden shifts to less-mobile labor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: In 2016 the American Economic Review published a paper called 'Who Benefits from State Corporate Tax Cuts?' Using detailed local-labor-market data from every US state, it worked out whether workers, land owners, or shareholders really bear the cost when states raise or cut the corporate tax. It became the standard modern reference on tax incidence. Which pair of economists wrote it?
answer: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
choices: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
David Card and Alan Krueger
Anthony Atkinson and Thomas Piketty
context: Suarez Serrato and Zidar, 'Who Benefits from State Corporate Tax Cuts? A Local Labor Markets Approach with Heterogeneous Firms' (AER, 2016), is the workhorse modern study of state corporate-tax incidence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: When economists study who really bears the corporate income tax, part of the burden always falls on capital owners — the people who own shares in the taxed company. One important group of shareholders is almost never mentioned in political debates, even though it holds enormous amounts of stock indirectly through workers' retirement plans. Which frequently-overlooked group holds shares broadly through retirement accounts?
answer: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' retirement savings
choices: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' retirement savings
Wealthy hedge-fund managers exclusively
Foreign sovereign wealth funds exclusively
The Federal Reserve's balance sheet
context: The shareholder class is not only 'the rich' -- large pools of public-employee and private-sector pension fund savings hold corporate equity, so the incidence that falls on capital hits ordinary retirement accounts too. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: On September 7, 2021, one small Central American country made history by becoming the very first nation to accept Bitcoin as real money, standing right beside the US dollar in every store and paycheck. The young millennial president who pushed the law through was famous for his bold style and modern image. Which country was it, and who was its president?
answer: El Salvador, under Nayib Bukele
choices: El Salvador, under Nayib Bukele
Argentina, under Alberto Fernandez
Panama, under Laurentino Cortizo
Honduras, under Xiomara Castro
context: Bukele announced the plan at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference in Miami. Same-day September 7 the government launched the Chivo Wallet and issued each adult citizen a $30 Bitcoin allocation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: In 2021 the small Central American country of El Salvador, led by President Nayib Bukele, made a bold move: it declared Bitcoin — the digital currency invented in 2009 — to be 'legal tender' alongside the US dollar. El Salvador was the first country in the world to do this. But what does the phrase 'legal tender' actually mean for a money inside a country?
answer: Stores and businesses are legally required to accept it as payment
choices: Stores and businesses are legally required to accept it as payment
Only the government is allowed to spend it
It can only be used to pay taxes
It is worth more than any other money in the world
context: President Faustin-Archange Touadera signed the law, but the country had scant electricity infrastructure, low smartphone penetration, and IMF opposition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cryptocurrency_in_the_Central_African_Republic.

question: Deep in central Africa is a country called the Central African Republic. In April 2022 its government surprised the world by making Bitcoin legal tender alongside the country's regular currency, becoming only the second nation ever to accept Bitcoin, after El Salvador. But the new law lasted less than a year — parliament repealed it in early 2023. In which month did they reverse it?
answer: March 2023
choices: March 2023
September 2024
January 2025
August 2022
context: The reversal made the CAR experiment the shortest sovereign Bitcoin adoption in history. Lack of a reliable electricity grid, low smartphone penetration, and IMF opposition were the cited reasons. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cryptocurrency_in_the_Central_African_Republic.

question: In 2023, Argentines fed up with runaway inflation and a bloated bureaucracy elected a libertarian economist as president. At his campaign rallies, Javier Milei stormed on stage waving a real chainsaw over his head while crowds cheered. The chainsaw was a prop for something specific he had promised to do to the government once in office. What did the chainsaw stand for?
answer: Slashing the government's spending and cutting whole agencies
choices: Slashing the government's spending and cutting whole agencies
Cutting down forests to sell the timber
Breaking apart a big state-owned oil company
Ending trade with neighboring countries
context: Milei was inaugurated December 10, 2023. He has praised Bitcoin as 'the return of money to the private sector' and legalized Bitcoin-denominated contracts, though he has not made Bitcoin legal tender. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Javier_Milei.

question: Bhutan is a tiny Buddhist kingdom tucked into the Himalayan mountains between India and China. Its economy is small, but the country is rich in one thing — vast reserves of clean, cheap electric power from the rivers running down its mountains. Around 2019, while other countries argued over whether to embrace Bitcoin, Bhutan quietly did something very different from El Salvador or Argentina. What has Bhutan been doing since about 2019?
answer: Mined Bitcoin using its hydroelectric power and accumulated one of the world's largest sovereign Bitcoin reserves
choices: Mined Bitcoin using its hydroelectric power and accumulated one of the world's largest sovereign Bitcoin reserves
Banned Bitcoin entirely and criminalized possession
Made Bitcoin its sole legal tender, replacing the ngultrum
Issued a state-backed stablecoin as an alternative to Bitcoin
context: 2024 disclosures revealed Bhutan holds an estimated 13,000+ BTC. The mining is run through Druk Holding & Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund. The scale, on a population of 700,000, is proportionally very large. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Bhutan.

question: In 2021 El Salvador, a small country in Central America, made Bitcoin legal money: citizens could pay bills, taxes, and shop with it. Big banking groups like the IMF pressured President Nayib Bukele to reverse the law, warning of 'risks to financial stability.' Bitcoin supporters said the real reason ran deeper — a specific feature of Bitcoin that central bankers cannot copy. Which feature made them uneasy?
answer: No central bank controls its supply -- it cannot be inflated by policy
choices: No central bank controls its supply -- it cannot be inflated by policy
Bitcoin is much easier for governments to tax than dollars
Bitcoin transfers slow down the country's phone service
Bitcoin is printed only by a private company in New York
context: The IMF cited financial-stability risks and monetary-policy independence concerns in each case. Its consistent stance is a factual pattern the ladder teaches without moralizing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: A high-school student asks which of the three national Bitcoin experiments (El Salvador legal tender, Argentina under Milei, Bhutan sovereign mining) was 'the right way' to engage with Bitcoin. A Hayekian economist declines to pick a single winner. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Recognizing that different tradeoffs (infrastructure needs, deregulation without mandate, energy-into-savings) suit different national circumstances
choices: Recognizing that different tradeoffs (infrastructure needs, deregulation without mandate, energy-into-savings) suit different national circumstances
Insisting that only central-bank digital currency can be legitimate national money
Declaring that any state Bitcoin engagement is always successful regardless of context
Concluding that only the largest economies can adopt any new monetary technology
context: The CAR reversal warns that infrastructure prerequisites matter as much as legal declarations. Milei's legal-friendliness lets adoption grow organically. Bhutan converts stranded hydro energy into a portable savings asset. Different national situations, different fits. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan is home to only about 700,000 people, but by 2024 it had built one of the largest Bitcoin stashes owned by any government in the world. It did this by using its huge hydroelectric dams to run Bitcoin mining computers year after year, quietly and out of the news. The mining was not run by an ordinary ministry but by one specific arm of the Bhutanese state. Which arm ran the mining?
answer: The country's sovereign wealth fund
choices: The country's sovereign wealth fund
The army's engineering corps
A joint venture with the Bank of China
The foreign ministry directly
context: Druk Holding & Investments (DHI) is Bhutan's state investment vehicle. The mining uses hydroelectric power from Bhutan's mountain rivers -- energy that would otherwise be exported or wasted, converted into a portable, hard-cap asset. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Bhutan.

question: In March 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit the United States hard. People rushed to grocery stores for masks, hand sanitizer, and toilet paper, and prices started climbing fast as shelves emptied. Most state governments responded by making it illegal for stores to sell these emergency goods for more than their old, pre-pandemic prices. What are these laws called?
answer: Anti-price-gouging laws
choices: Anti-price-gouging laws
Emergency purchase laws
Wartime supply laws
Federal restraint laws
context: Anti-price-gouging statutes existed in most US states before 2020 and were activated as emergencies were declared. Enforcement agencies threatened fines and jail terms in March-April 2020. Source: NCSL.org state-by-state summary.

question: A hurricane slams Florida. Stores run out of bottled water. What water is left suddenly costs $10 a bottle instead of $2. Buyers are angry and call it price gouging. But free-market economists like Thomas Sowell say the high price is actually doing something useful for the whole state. What useful thing does the higher price do?
answer: It signals sellers to rush more water to Florida fast
choices: It signals sellers to rush more water to Florida fast
It punishes buyers for no reason
It hides the shortage from everyone
It makes water disappear entirely
context: Michael Munger, political-science and economics professor at Duke, has written and podcast repeatedly about the Shepperson-generators case. His EconTalk episodes on price gouging are widely cited. Source: sites.duke.edu/munger.

question: In September 2004, Hurricane Frances slammed into Florida, knocking out electric power for whole counties. A Kentucky man named John Shepperson watched the news and decided to help — and to make some money. He rented a big truck, loaded it up back home in Kentucky, and drove 600 miles south to a Florida county where nothing had power. What did he load into the truck to sell?
answer: 19 generators
choices: 19 generators
500 gallons of gasoline
100 chainsaws
50 portable radios
context: Shepperson bought 19 generators in Kentucky and drove them to a Florida county after Hurricane Frances. He planned to sell them at approximately double the retail price. Source: Michael Munger, EconTalk (2007).

question: In 1996 Hurricane Fran knocked out power across the American South. John Shepperson, a Kentucky man, saw the news, bought 19 electric generators, rented a truck, and drove them into the disaster zone. He offered them for sale at about double what he had paid — enough to cover his costs, his time, and his risk in making the trip. But local 'anti-price-gouging' laws forbid selling at unfairly high prices during an emergency. What happened to Shepperson?
answer: He was arrested and the generators were confiscated
choices: He was arrested and the generators were confiscated
He sold out within an hour to grateful buyers
He was given a permit to operate a temporary market
Local authorities helped him distribute them
context: Florida police arrested Shepperson under the state's anti-price-gouging law and confiscated the generators. His family did without power, the Florida county went without generators, and the incentive-signal was clear to any other Kentucky entrepreneur. Source: Michael Munger case discussion.

question: Frédéric Bastiat was a French economist in the 1840s who taught readers a habit of thought: whenever the government makes a rule, look for what is 'seen' — the obvious surface result everyone points to — and also for what is 'unseen' — the harm hidden behind it. Apply his move to the anti-price-gouging law that punished the generator seller John Shepperson. The seen part is the low, comfortable price the law forces on any generator that is actually sold. What is the unseen part?
answer: Every entrepreneur who does not drive supplies to a disaster area because the reward has been criminalized
choices: Every entrepreneur who does not drive supplies to a disaster area because the reward has been criminalized
The producers whose profits rise from the ceiling
The government's tax revenue from the fine imposed
The neighboring state's competing anti-gouging law
context: Bastiat's method: the ceiling looks fair (SEEN); the hidden cost is the surge of supply that the price signal would have called forth (UNSEEN). Criminalizing the reward silences the signal and prolongs the shortage. Source: bastiat.org.

question: In early 2020 masks and gloves were suddenly scarce. Most US states had laws banning "gouging" -- charging much more than normal in a crisis. A few states quietly did not enforce those laws, and shelves refilled faster there. What is the most likely reason?
answer: Higher prices told sellers to rush more supply in, and told buyers not to hoard
choices: Higher prices told sellers to rush more supply in, and told buyers not to hoard
The state government secretly shipped extra masks to those stores
The federal government forced factories in those states to run overtime
Shoppers in those states just needed fewer masks
context: Tennessee briefly waived enforcement on PPE gouging in 2020. Steven Horwitz and other economists documented that unwaived states saw longer shortages. The natural experiment matched the Bastiatian prediction. Source: mercatus.org COVID studies 2020.

question: Michael Munger is an American economist at Duke University who has spent decades studying what happens when governments ban 'price-gouging' during hurricanes and other disasters. In case after case he found that the high price is what pulls extra supplies from far away — trucks driving through the night with generators, water, and ice. Munger boils the whole lesson into one short, memorable slogan about the role of high prices during an emergency. What is his slogan?
answer: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
choices: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
The market always clears eventually
Consumers pay whatever the seller demands
Regulation is the answer to shortages
context: Munger's framing: the high price is the market's shout to producers and importers 'HERE, RUSH SUPPLY HERE'; the anti-gouging law silences the shout and prolongs the shortage. Source: EconTalk, Munger episodes on gouging.

question: Thomas Sowell is an American economist, born in 1930, whose textbook Basic Economics is read in classrooms around the world. In that book, Sowell tells the story of John Shepperson — the Kentucky man arrested for selling hurricane-relief generators at about double his cost. Sowell uses the case to point at a deeper mistake he says every anti-price-gouging law commits. In his framing, what is the reasoning error at the heart of those laws?
answer: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
choices: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
They ignore consumer welfare entirely
They assume unlimited government resources
They confuse macroeconomic and microeconomic scales
context: Sowell's move: the high price is information about scarcity, not evidence of bad character. The law that criminalizes the messenger destroys the message the market was trying to send. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Duke University economist Michael Munger argues that anti-price-gouging laws do not just punish the arrested seller who charges high prices in an emergency. He says the real cost of the law falls on a hidden, unseen group. Following the classic Bastiat argument about 'the seen and the unseen,' Munger names the group of would-be helpers who now know they will not be rewarded, and might even be jailed, for driving supplies into a disaster zone. Which group actually bears the real cost of the price ceiling?
answer: Future entrepreneurs who now know they will not be rewarded for driving supplies to emergencies
choices: Future entrepreneurs who now know they will not be rewarded for driving supplies to emergencies
Government inspectors doing enforcement
The insurance industry paying out claims
Local elected officials facing recall
context: The reasoning move's most powerful step: the visible arrest teaches every future entrepreneur that the risk of driving supplies to a disaster area will not be rewarded. Supply-response permanently degrades. Source: Munger on price gouging.

question: A Category 4 hurricane rips through the US Gulf Coast and knocks out the electric grid for a week. Gas stations run dry and generator prices shoot up. Local news calls it 'gouging,' angry customers demand price controls, and a few sellers face public shaming. A free-market economist in the Bastiat tradition argues the higher price is not the villain — it is quietly doing an important job that helps end the shortage faster. What job is that?
answer: Telling suppliers from far away that trucks and generators are worth rushing in
choices: Telling suppliers from far away that trucks and generators are worth rushing in
Making sure only rich buyers can get any goods
Forcing every competitor to lower their prices
Locking prices at their pre-storm level
context: Prices signal both scarcity (to buyers, to conserve) and profit opportunity (to sellers, to bring more supply). Ceilings that suppress the signal degrade both responses. This is the operating mechanism behind every emergency-supply anti-gouging analysis. Source: mercatus.org, mises.org.

question: In 2008 an unknown person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin whitepaper and mined the first coins, then disappeared without ever showing a face. Over the years many people have claimed to actually be Satoshi. Experts have a simple test they ask any claimant to perform to prove the identity. What do they ask the person to do?
answer: Move some of Satoshi's original bitcoins as a signature
choices: Move some of Satoshi's original bitcoins as a signature
Show a valid passport under that name
Post a video filmed in Japan
Recite the whole Bitcoin whitepaper by heart
context: Craig Steven Wright, born 1970, is the Australian computer scientist who claimed the Satoshi identity from 2015 until a UK court rejected the claim in 2024. Dan Kaminsky was the security researcher who exposed one of Wright's 'proofs'; Antonopoulos is a Bitcoin educator. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: For about ten years an Australian computer scientist named Craig Wright told reporters and courts he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the mysterious creator of Bitcoin. One quick test using Satoshi's own private cryptographic keys could have settled the whole question in minutes — but Wright never did it. Which single act would have proved his claim?
answer: signing a message with a known Satoshi private key
choices: signing a message with a known Satoshi private key
publishing a photograph of Satoshi
producing a birth certificate from Japan
moving one Bitcoin from a random address
context: A cryptographic signature made with one of Satoshi's known keys is a five-second, unforgeable proof. A photograph or birth certificate proves nothing about key control; moving Bitcoin from a random address proves nothing about Satoshi's addresses. Wright has never produced a valid signature. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Craig Wright, an Australian computer scientist, gathered a private group of reporters in London and told them he could prove he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the inventor of Bitcoin. He walked them through a cryptographic demonstration that looked convincing at the time. Within hours, other Bitcoin developers examined his work online and exposed it as a fake. Why couldn't Wright's trick hold up once outside experts looked at it?
answer: Bitcoin proofs can be checked openly by anyone with a computer
choices: Bitcoin proofs can be checked openly by anyone with a computer
The reporters recorded him confessing later
Satoshi came online personally to deny the claim
A government agency ran a background check on him
context: Dan Kaminsky (1979-2021), a well-known security researcher, publicly explained within hours that Wright's 'proof' was a copy-pasted old Satoshi signature rather than a fresh sign. Buterin created Ethereum; Antonopoulos is an educator; Satoshi is the missing party being impersonated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Instead of stepping back after his 2016 demonstration was exposed, Craig Wright doubled down. He co-founded a Bitcoin altcoin that broke away from Bitcoin Cash in 2018, whose ticker symbol carried his identity claim in its very name. Which altcoin did he help launch?
answer: Bitcoin Satoshi's Vision (BSV)
choices: Bitcoin Satoshi's Vision (BSV)
Litecoin (LTC)
Ripple (XRP)
Ethereum Classic (ETC)
context: BSV split from Bitcoin Cash in November 2018 and made 'Satoshi's Vision' part of its name -- an identity claim embedded in the ticker. Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee), Ripple (2012, Chris Larsen and Jed McCaleb), and Ethereum Classic (2016 fork) are unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_SV.

question: For years, an Australian computer scientist named Craig Wright loudly claimed he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the mysterious inventor of Bitcoin. In March 2024, a UK court finally ruled on his claim after a judge spent months studying his documents. A group of Bitcoin developers and open-source companies had banded together and sued him, hoping to stop his threats of lawsuits against the Bitcoin community. Which court case gave the ruling?
answer: COPA v Wright
choices: COPA v Wright
Kleiman v Wright
Wright v Bitcoin Core
Wright v Twitter
context: The Crypto Open Patent Alliance (COPA) brought the London High Court action; Mr Justice Mellor issued the March 14, 2024 ruling. Kleiman v Wright was the earlier Florida case (2018-21) over disputed early Bitcoin holdings; the other cases are hypothetical or minor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright#COPA_v._Wright.

question: Craig Wright, an Australian, spent years telling the world he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the inventor of Bitcoin. In 2024 the High Court in London tried the question, and Justice James Mellor ruled against him. The judge used unusually blunt language about the technical papers and emails Wright had brought as proof of his identity. What did the judge conclude Wright had done with those documents?
answer: The man had forged and backdated them
choices: The man had forged and backdated them
The man had forgotten crucial details under stress
The proof was scattered but real
The man had refused to answer any questions about them
context: Mr Justice Mellor found that Wright had forged and backdated his documents; many showed forensic evidence of manipulated fonts and metadata inconsistent with claimed dates. Wright testified extensively; the ruling was not about incomplete or forgotten details but affirmative fabrication. Source: COPA v Wright judgment, 20 March 2024.

question: Someone claims to have invented Bitcoin and starts suing programmers who add to its free open-source code. To defend against these lawsuits, several Bitcoin companies pool money for a shared legal fund. What kind of problem are they trying to solve together?
answer: A cost too big for one small developer, but cheap when split across many
choices: A cost too big for one small developer, but cheap when split across many
A shortage of programmers willing to work on Bitcoin
A rule that forces all software to be secret and paid
A tax on running any computer that mines Bitcoin
context: COPA (Crypto Open Patent Alliance, launched 2020) was founded and heavily funded by Jack Dorsey's Square (renamed Block in 2021), which held Bitcoin on its balance sheet and pledged its Bitcoin patents. Tesla briefly held Bitcoin but is not a COPA founder; Palantir and Meta are unrelated. Source: https://open-crypto.com/about.

question: For more than a decade Craig Wright, an Australian, told reporters, investors, and courts that he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the inventor of Bitcoin — yet he never produced the simple cryptographic proof the real Satoshi could give in seconds. Bitcoin developers say there is one obvious test the community can run on anyone who claims to be Satoshi. What is the easiest test they can use?
answer: Ask him to sign a message using a private key from the earliest Bitcoin blocks
choices: Ask him to sign a message using a private key from the earliest Bitcoin blocks
Take his word because no one else has stepped forward
Check if he owns a lot of expensive computer hardware today
Look up his college degrees in computer science
context: The Kleiman v Wright jury (December 2021) awarded roughly $100 million against Wright's W&K Info Defense Research firm. The verdict declined to affirm Kleiman was Satoshi's partner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: An Australian computer scientist named Craig Wright spent years telling the world he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the mysterious creator of Bitcoin. In March 2024, in a UK court case called COPA v Wright, the judge ruled he was not — the evidence, the judge said, had been forged. A group of Bitcoin developers had banded together to sue him after he threatened them with lawsuits. What happened to Wright afterwards?
answer: He was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
choices: He was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
He was awarded his legal costs by the court
He was granted permission to keep publishing as Satoshi
He was appointed to a Bitcoin standards committee
context: Following the March 2024 ruling, the court held Wright in contempt for repeated post-judgment claims and referred aspects of his conduct for possible criminal-prosecution consideration (perjury and forgery). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Bitcoin teachers who write about the Craig Wright saga — the Australian who falsely claimed for years to be Satoshi Nakamoto, the inventor of Bitcoin — often press one central reasoning move about identity in a cryptocurrency system. Wright pointed to old writings, public speeches, and legal papers to back up his claim. Those teachers argue he could never provide the one thing that would actually count as proof in Bitcoin's world. Which reasoning move does that argument make?
answer: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only meaningful identity claim in a system whose entire security model rests on private-key signatures
