choices: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only meaningful identity claim in a system whose entire security model rests on private-key signatures
That the courts alone should adjudicate who Satoshi is
That academic credentials and public speaking are the correct grounds for accepting an identity claim
That anonymous founders should be legally required to reveal themselves
context: The Bitcoin argument (Antonopoulos, Song, Kaminsky) is that in a system built on private-key signatures, the only relevant proof of any 'is-Satoshi' claim is a fresh signature -- courts and credentials cannot substitute for the primitive the system is built on. Legal-adjudication, credentialing, and forced-doxxing responses are precisely what the argument rejects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: For over thirty years, communist Cuba had been kept afloat by billions of dollars in yearly aid from the Soviet Union. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, that aid vanished almost overnight. From 1990 to 1994, life on the island grew extremely hard — food, fuel, and electricity all ran short, and hunger spread across the country. What did the Cuban government call this time?
answer: The Special Period in Time of Peace
choices: The Special Period in Time of Peace
The Great Leap Forward
The Cultural Revolution
The New Economic Policy
context: In Spanish, 'Periodo Especial en Tiempo de Paz.' The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and its subsidy to Cuba (fuel at below-world-market prices, guaranteed sugar purchases at above-world prices) ended essentially overnight. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: During Cuba's Special Period, the years from 1990 to 1994 after Soviet aid dried up, food shortages grew so severe that public-health researchers ran studies on how much weight ordinary Cubans lost. Calorie intake fell sharply and the average adult grew visibly thinner. Medical journals later reported a range for the average weight loss during those crash years. What was the reported range?
answer: Between 5 and 25 pounds
choices: Between 5 and 25 pounds
Between 1 and 3 pounds
Between 50 and 100 pounds
Essentially no change
context: Per-capita daily caloric intake fell from roughly 3,100 kcal in 1989 to roughly 1,900 kcal in 1993. The Special Period is one of the few modern rich-data natural experiments in what a fully price-controlled economy does when hit by a supply shock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: During Cuba's Special Period, from 1990 to 1994 after Soviet aid stopped, meat almost disappeared from ration books in the capital city of Havana. Journalists and researchers later documented that one particular group of city animals nearly vanished during these years, because hungry residents had started catching and eating them. Which group of animals nearly disappeared from Havana?
answer: Urban cats and dogs
choices: Urban cats and dogs
Domesticated cattle
Chickens on state farms
Racing pigeons
context: Some pets were eaten; many others starved or were abandoned. Zoo animals faced similar pressure. The pet-population collapse became one of the visible human-scale markers of how deep the caloric shock had gone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: After the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 cut off billions in yearly aid, Cuba's communist government kept most of its price controls and ration books in place — but quietly opened two small doors to markets so people could survive. Slowly the economy recovered, thanks to these two tiny reforms that were huge by Cuban standards. Which two openings were they?
answer: Small city vegetable plots plus legal self-employment, and letting people use US dollars
choices: Small city vegetable plots plus legal self-employment, and letting people use US dollars
Full price freedom and selling off all state factories
Leaving the socialist bloc and joining the North American free trade zone
Returning all farms and buildings to the families that owned them before 1959
context: The recovery lever was NOT more planning; it was permitting Cubans to grow and sell food and hold dollars. Where the market was let in, calories followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: A high-school student asks a Mises-influenced economist why Cuba's caloric collapse of 1990 to 1993 is such a useful case for judging central planning. When the Soviet Union fell in 1991, its billion-dollar-a-year food and oil subsidy to Cuba disappeared almost overnight, and Cuban calorie intake crashed from about 3,000 down to 1,900 a day. The analyst points to one specific feature that makes this a rare natural experiment. Which feature?
answer: The Soviet subsidy simply vanished while everything else (planning apparatus, US embargo, weather) stayed constant
choices: The Soviet subsidy simply vanished while everything else (planning apparatus, US embargo, weather) stayed constant
The US Congress passed a new embargo law timed to the Soviet collapse
A drought and locust plague coincided with the Soviet withdrawal
Cuba's rainfall changed dramatically during the period
context: The US embargo had been in place since 1962; weather was normal; the planning apparatus was retained. The subsidy loss isolates central planning's ability (or inability) to adapt to a supply shock. This is Mises's 1920 calculation-debate prediction played out in body-weight units. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cuba%E2%80%93Soviet_Union_relations.

question: By 1993 the Cuban people were in what the government called the 'Special Period in Time of Peace.' The Soviet Union had collapsed two years earlier, ending the sugar-for-oil subsidy that had propped up Cuba's centrally-planned economy. The average Cuban had lost about a third of the calories in a normal daily diet, and hunger stalked the island. Fidel Castro — the communist ruler since 1959 — gave a series of public speeches that year finally acknowledging the caloric collapse. What did he blame for the shortage?
answer: The US trade embargo, not the retained central-planning apparatus
choices: The US trade embargo, not the retained central-planning apparatus
Local Cuban corruption and mismanagement
The Soviet Union's decision to end the subsidy
Climate change and rainfall patterns
context: The embargo had been in place since 1962; the collapse was specifically timed to the 1991 subsidy loss. The rhetorical move blamed a constant factor for a variable outcome. The 1993 recovery began precisely when Cuba legalized the organoponicos and self-employment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: In 1982 an American computer scientist named David Chaum invented a clever math trick he called a 'blind signature.' A bank could digitally stamp a coin without seeing which coin it was stamping. Later, when someone spent that coin at a store, no one could trace the payment back to who had first withdrawn it. What was Chaum trying to protect for the customer?
answer: The buyer's privacy
choices: The buyer's privacy
The bank's profit
The store's inventory
The government's tax records
context: David Chaum invented blind signatures in 1982. Diffie co-invented public-key cryptography (1976); Rivest is the R in RSA; Merkle developed hash trees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Chaum.

question: In 1989 the American cryptographer David Chaum started a company called DigiCash to sell his invention: private digital cash that could be spent online without banks or governments tracking who paid whom. Chaum believed the big banks and big stores would rush to sign up. Instead, the banks moved slowly, only a handful of shops joined, and by the late 1990s DigiCash ran out of money and shut down. Why was it so hard to get people to switch?
answer: Cash and credit cards already worked well enough for most people
choices: Cash and credit cards already worked well enough for most people
The math didn't actually work
The government banned it worldwide
Nobody owned computers yet
context: DigiCash was founded in Amsterdam in 1989 and operated from there through the mid-1990s. Zurich, London, and Berlin were homes of other 1990s payment and cryptography ventures but not DigiCash. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In 1989 the American cryptographer David Chaum founded a company called DigiCash to build the world's first private digital money. His system used a clever math trick that let the bank check that a digital coin was real — that it had been properly issued and not spent twice — without the bank ever learning which person had received it. What is this cryptographic trick called?
answer: blind signatures
choices: blind signatures
ring signatures
Schnorr signatures
elliptic-curve signatures
context: Blind signatures (Chaum 1982) let a signer authenticate a message whose contents are hidden from them. Ring signatures (Rivest, Shamir, Tauman 2001) provide sender-anonymity from a group; Schnorr signatures are a different signing scheme; elliptic-curve is a mathematical family used by many signature schemes including Bitcoin's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_signature.

question: In the 1990s, a Dutch cryptographer named David Chaum built the first electronic cash system for the internet, called DigiCash. The math behind it was brilliant — payments were private and very hard to forge. But by 1998, DigiCash the company went bankrupt. The cypherpunk movement saw one deep design flaw in Chaum's system that they would spend the next decade trying to fix. What was that flaw?
answer: the system required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins
choices: the system required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins
the underlying blind-signature math was later found broken
the anonymity was only partial and revealed users to the bank
the coins could only be used inside the Netherlands
context: DigiCash's anonymity was strong but issuance still required a partnered bank; without one, no coins. That single trusted issuer became the point of failure. The blind-signature math held up; the design achieved bank-facing anonymity; DigiCash worked across borders. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In the 1990s David Chaum's small company DigiCash built the first working way to send private digital cash over the internet. Microsoft, then racing to launch Windows 95, offered him more than $100 million to bundle DigiCash into the new operating system. The deal collapsed in disagreements, but the price alone shocked observers. Why did the big software firms want this technology so badly?
answer: Private digital payments would let their users buy things online without a bank in the middle
choices: Private digital payments would let their users buy things online without a bank in the middle
Governments were already forcing every operating system to include a payment system
The technology could double the speed of their computers
The technology was needed to send email between different countries
context: Bill Gates and Microsoft reportedly offered David Chaum a nine-figure sum -- widely cited as either $100M or $180M -- to license DigiCash for Windows 95 integration. Chaum turned it down. Apple, Sun, and IBM had adjacent ambitions but did not make the specific DigiCash offer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In the mid-1990s, the American cryptographer David Chaum ran DigiCash, a Dutch company selling privacy-protecting electronic cash he had invented. Three big American firms wanted to buy his technology. Microsoft was the most famous, but two other giants also made offers -- one that made the leading web browser of the era, and one that ran a huge credit-card network. Chaum turned them both down. Which pair made the offers?
answer: Netscape and Visa
choices: Netscape and Visa
Netscape and MasterCard
AOL and American Express
Yahoo and Diners Club
context: In addition to Microsoft, Netscape (the dominant early web-browser company) and Visa made offers Chaum declined. MasterCard, AOL, Amex, Yahoo, and Diners Club are commonly asked about but were not the specific ones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: DigiCash, the Dutch electronic-cash company run by cryptographer David Chaum, went broke in November 1998 because its private digital money always needed a bank to issue it, and no bank ever fully signed on. That same month, a young cypherpunk -- one of a group of programmers who used cryptography to protect privacy from governments -- posted a new design for digital cash that needed no trusted bank at all, only a network of computers keeping a shared ledger. Which 1998 proposal was it?
answer: Wei Dai's b-money
choices: Wei Dai's b-money
Adam Back's Hashcash
Nick Szabo's bit gold
Hal Finney's RPOW
context: Wei Dai posted b-money on the cypherpunk list in November 1998 -- the same month DigiCash's bankruptcy filing. Hashcash was 1997; Szabo's bit gold was drafted 1998 (posted later); Finney's RPOW came in 2004. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: After David Chaum's DigiCash went bankrupt in November 1998, the cypherpunks -- a loose network of programmers who used cryptography to build privacy tools outside government control -- studied why brilliant math had not been enough. Thinkers like Wei Dai, Nick Szabo, and later the anonymous Satoshi Nakamoto (who launched Bitcoin in 2009) all drew the same lesson from that failure. Which reasoning move did they press about any digital cash that leans on a bank?
answer: even brilliantly-designed anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted, or shut down
choices: even brilliantly-designed anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted, or shut down
cryptography is inherently unsuited to money and every attempt at digital cash must always fail regardless of the design of the surrounding system
anonymous digital cash requires explicit government backing to succeed because private customers will never trust a purely mathematical monetary system
cash must be physical to be trusted; every attempt to build purely electronic money fails because ordinary users refuse to accept intangible balances
context: The DigiCash lesson (Dai, Szabo, Nakamoto) was that removing the trusted issuer was the central task -- because whoever ran issuance had a single point of business failure. The other options are the opposite of what the cypherpunks concluded. Source: Nakamoto white paper 2008 sec 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In 1990 the American cryptographer David Chaum founded DigiCash, one of the earliest digital-money companies. His system used clever math to let people spend digital coins privately, but every coin was issued by Chaum's own company. When DigiCash went bankrupt in 1998, every user's money froze. In 2008 an anonymous author called Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin paper. One close reader argues Satoshi did not merely improve DigiCash -- he removed the one piece that had killed it. What did Bitcoin design out that DigiCash could not survive without?
answer: the trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency
choices: the trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency
the requirement for cryptographic signatures on transactions
the concept of an anonymous unit of value
the concept of a fixed unit denominations
context: Bitcoin retains signatures, anonymous (pseudonymous) value units, and fixed denominations; the piece it removed is the trusted issuer -- issuance is by proof-of-work; validation is by a distributed network. Source: Nakamoto white paper 2008 sec 1-4.

question: David Chaum's DigiCash launched in the early 1990s with mathematics so clever that a bank could check a digital coin was real without learning who was spending it. Cryptographers praised the design, but by 1998 the company had filed for bankruptcy — customers never showed up, and the trust-based structure had a weakness that Bitcoin's decentralized design would later avoid entirely. Looking back at the collapse, economists press one big lesson about why brilliant cryptography was not enough. What is the claim?
answer: the operator of any trusted issuer, no matter how brilliant, can tank the whole project through ordinary business decisions
choices: the operator of any trusted issuer, no matter how brilliant, can tank the whole project through ordinary business decisions
the mathematics of blind signatures was fundamentally too slow for real commerce
the users of digital cash lacked the education to adopt any technology in the 1990s
the internet was too small to support any digital payment system before 2000
context: The DigiCash argument (Ammous, Antonopoulos, and Bitcoin historians) is that Chaum's turning down the Microsoft/Netscape/Visa offers -- an ordinary business choice -- was fatal to the whole system. The other options are widely-refuted alternative theories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: In 1973 an American economist published a famous book arguing that private firms and voluntary cooperation could handle jobs the government usually does -- police, courts, roads, even money. He was the son of the Nobel-winning free-market economist Milton Friedman, and he later taught law and economics at Santa Clara University. Who was he, and what was the book?
answer: David D. Friedman; 'The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism'
choices: David D. Friedman; 'The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism'
Milton Friedman Jr.; 'Free to Choose: A Personal Statement'
Rose Friedman; 'Two Lucky People: Memoirs'
Patri Friedman; 'The Seasteading Manifesto'
context: David Friedman was born February 12, 1945, the son of Milton and Rose Director Friedman. He took his PhD in theoretical physics (Chicago, 1971) before crossing into economics and law. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: Milton Friedman was the American economist who won the Nobel Prize and defended a small, limited government — police, courts, and the national defense, but not much more. His son David Friedman, born in 1945, grew up to be an economist too, but he ended up thinking about the state in a very different way than his dad did. What is the difference between the two Friedmans?
answer: David is an anarcho-capitalist (no state at all); Milton was a classical liberal (minimal state)
choices: David is an anarcho-capitalist (no state at all); Milton was a classical liberal (minimal state)
David is a democratic socialist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a monarchist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a technocratic centrist; Milton was a classical liberal
context: Milton Friedman defended a minimal state (national defense, courts, some social insurance). David Friedman argues no state is necessary at all, with all such functions in principle providable by competing private firms. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: David D. Friedman's 1973 book 'The Machinery of Freedom' asks how a society could work with no state at all. Instead of just arguing that government is bad, Friedman walks the reader through concrete mechanisms: how competing private courts could settle disputes, how rival police agencies might work, how privately-issued money could circulate, how roads could be paid for by the drivers who use them. What is his core move in the book?
answer: Describe HOW specific mechanisms would work and let the reader evaluate the design
choices: Describe HOW specific mechanisms would work and let the reader evaluate the design
Argue from natural rights that the state is inherently illegitimate
Prove mathematically that no state can ever be efficient
Chronicle historical cases of state failure without proposing alternatives
context: Friedman insists on institutional specifics rather than doctrinal claims. Chapters like 'How Would Private Law Enforcement Really Work?' walk through the contract-and-arbitration architecture with realistic edge cases. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: David Friedman and Murray Rothbard, two American thinkers in the twentieth century, both argued for anarcho-capitalism — a free market with no government at all. But they reached the same goal from opposite starting points. Rothbard argued from natural rights: every person owns himself, so any tax the state collects is theft. Friedman refused the rights-based argument and built his case on a completely different ground. What was Friedman's ground?
answer: Consequentialism -- anarcho-capitalism would produce better outcomes for most people most of the time
choices: Consequentialism -- anarcho-capitalism would produce better outcomes for most people most of the time
Natural rights -- the state inherently violates property rights
Divine command -- the state is forbidden by religious scripture
Aesthetic preference -- the state is inelegant as a system
context: Rothbard defended the same conclusion from natural rights (the state as an inherent violator of self-ownership). Friedman's consequentialist framing lets the reader compare outcomes without accepting the underlying rights premise. The distinction matters inside libertarian debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: The American economist and law professor David Friedman -- son of Nobel-winning Milton Friedman -- spent his career studying societies that solved disputes without a single central state. In 2019 he teamed up with two other scholars to publish a survey of real examples: Somali xeer, Icelandic saga law, Jewish rabbinical courts, Amish community rules, Roma kris, and many more. What was the book called, and who were his co-authors?
answer: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
choices: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
'Free to Choose,' with Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
'The Constitution of Liberty,' with Friedrich Hayek
'The Sovereign Individual,' with James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg
context: Peter Leeson is a George Mason University economist; David Skarbek is a Brown University political scientist. The book presents these historical cases as natural experiments in the decentralized private legal architecture 'The Machinery of Freedom' described in theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: The Friedmans are a three-generation American libertarian family. The grandparents, economists Milton and Rose Friedman, wrote 'Free to Choose' and Milton won the 1976 Nobel Prize in economics. Their son David wrote 'The Machinery of Freedom,' arguing for a society with no state at all. In 2008, David's own son took the family idea one step further and started a group aimed at building brand-new floating towns in international waters, beyond any single government's rules. What was the son's project?
answer: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
choices: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
Patri Friedman founded the Institute for Justice
Patri Friedman founded the Cato Institute
Patri Friedman founded the American Enterprise Institute
context: The Seasteading Institute proposes floating city-states on the high seas as a physical experiment in the polycentric governance David Friedman describes in theory. The Institute was funded early by Peter Thiel. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Patri_Friedman.

question: David D. Friedman's 1973 book 'The Machinery of Freedom' argued for a society run by private firms and voluntary cooperation rather than the state. When Friedman released the third edition of the book in 2014, he chose a distinctive way to distribute it that fit the book's own theme of removing gatekeepers -- something the 1973 first edition and 1989 second edition had not done. What was the specific change?
answer: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
choices: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
It was translated into every major world language simultaneously
It was published exclusively as an audio book
It was released only through university-press subscriptions
context: Consistent with the book's political stance, Friedman made the third edition freely downloadable. Any curious reader with internet access can read the complete text at no cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: In 1931 the United States Congress passed the Davis-Bacon Act. On any building project paid for by the federal government -- highways, schools, courthouses -- workers must be paid at least the local 'prevailing wage,' which in practice usually means the union rate for that area. How does that rule usually change the total cost of the building?
answer: It makes the project more expensive
choices: It makes the project more expensive
It makes the project much cheaper
It has no effect on cost
It cuts the cost in half
context: The Davis-Bacon Act 1931 (sponsored by Rep. Robert Bacon R-NY and Sen. James Davis R-PA) has been the AFL-CIO's core piece of federal-project protection for 90 years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: The Davis-Bacon Act is a 1931 US law that says any construction worker hired to build a federal project — a highway, a bridge, a courthouse — must be paid at least the 'prevailing wage' in that city. To find the prevailing wage, the US Department of Labor runs a survey of local pay rates. In most cities, that survey ends up using one specific wage as its default answer. Which wage is it?
answer: The union scale
choices: The union scale
The state minimum wage
The federal minimum wage
The Bureau of Labor Statistics median
context: The DOL wage-survey process defaults to the union scale in most metropolitan areas, making Davis-Bacon a de-facto union-wage protection on federally-funded projects. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: The Davis-Bacon Act of 1931 forces federal building projects to pay a 'prevailing wage,' which the Labor Department usually sets at the local union rate. Economists have measured how much extra this costs compared to state or private construction that pays normal market wages. Two well-known empirical studies found a fairly consistent premium. What did they find the extra cost to be?
answer: 10 to 15 percent
choices: 10 to 15 percent
1 to 2 percent
50 to 60 percent
0 percent (no premium)
context: A 10-15% cost premium on federal construction translates to roughly $100-180 billion on the $1.2 trillion 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act alone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: When the United States Congress debated the Davis-Bacon Act in 1931 -- the law requiring federal building projects to pay local union-scale wages -- several of the bill's backers were openly clear about a specific goal. They wanted to keep one group of lower-paid migrant workers off federal construction sites in the North during the Great Depression. Which group did the bill's backers name during the House debates?
answer: Southern Black workers
choices: Southern Black workers
European immigrant workers
West Coast Chinese workers
Mexican migrant workers
context: The 1931 debate shows sponsors explicit that the point was to keep Southern Black workers, who had been migrating north to compete for federal-project work at lower wages, off federal jobsites. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: During the 1931 House of Representatives debate on the Davis-Bacon Act -- the federal law requiring union-scale wages on government construction -- Congressman Robert Bacon of New York, the bill's co-sponsor, spelled out his explicit motive for excluding lower-wage migrant workers from federal building sites. His words later became infamous in histories of the law. Which line did Bacon speak on the House floor?
answer: Colored labor is being brought in to demoralize wage rates
choices: Colored labor is being brought in to demoralize wage rates
The southern states must build their own hospitals
Union labor is the only safe federal contractor
Immigration must be halted for national security
context: Bacon's 1931 House-floor statement is on the Congressional Record; the racial-exclusion motive was overt, and the Act retains that exclusionary effect even after the framing was dropped. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: The nineteenth-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to hunt for the hidden second side of any economic rule -- 'what is seen and what is not seen.' A bill passed for one visible reason often quietly transfers wealth from a large diffuse group to a small organized one. Apply that Bastiat lens to the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, which raises federal construction wages. One group wins big; a much larger group pays a little each. Which two-sided pattern is it?
answer: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
choices: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
Concentrated benefit to taxpayers, dispersed cost to unions
Uniform benefit and uniform cost across the population
Concentrated benefit to foreign contractors, dispersed cost to domestic firms
context: Mancur Olson's Logic of Collective Action (1965) explains the pattern: organized construction unions capture the concentrated benefit while every federal-project taxpayer bears a small share of the dispersed cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: The Davis-Bacon Act of 1931 is a US federal law that requires construction workers on government projects to be paid the local 'prevailing wage.' In practice, the Labor Department usually sets that at the union rate for the area, even when most local builders pay less. Free-market and public-choice economists have argued for decades against the law. What do these critics say it does?
answer: Raises the cost of every road, bridge, and school built with federal money
choices: Raises the cost of every road, bridge, and school built with federal money
Guarantees each project finishes ahead of schedule
Lowers wages for construction workers nationwide
Prevents corruption by state governors
context: Chris Edwards at Cato has published Policy Analyses on Davis-Bacon in the 2010s and 2020s calling for repeal. Source: cato.org/blog/davis-bacon-inflates-federal-construction-costs.

question: By the mid-1960s the United States was running deep into debt to fund two huge programs at once. The US dollar was pegged by law to gold at $35 per ounce under the postwar Bretton Woods system, and printing more dollars to pay for the spending was making that peg harder to defend. Foreign central banks began doubting the American promise. Which pair of programs was the drain on the dollar?
answer: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
choices: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
the Korean War and the Marshall Plan
the Cold War missile buildup and the Interstate Highway System
the Iraq War and the Bush tax cuts
context: The 1960s fiscal pressures came from Vietnam War spending and Johnson's Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty). Korea/Marshall Plan (1950s), missile buildup/highways (1950s), and Iraq/Bush tax cuts (2000s) are the wrong eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: In 1965 the president of France walked into a big press conference in Paris. After World War II the world's currencies were tied to the US dollar, and the dollar alone was tied to gold at $35 an ounce -- which meant America could print dollars almost as it pleased. He called that a 'huge unfair perk' for the US and announced that France would trade its own dollar reserves for real gold and ship the bars home. Which French leader was he?
answer: Charles de Gaulle
choices: Charles de Gaulle
Georges Pompidou
Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
François Mitterrand
context: Charles de Gaulle, French President 1959-69, made the February 1965 press conference challenging the dollar peg. Pompidou succeeded him; Giscard was his finance minister at the time; Mitterrand came to the presidency in 1981. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle.

question: The phrase 'exorbitant privilege' -- describing America's power to print the world's reserve currency and export its inflation abroad -- is often remembered as a 1965 line from French President Charles de Gaulle. In fact it was coined by de Gaulle's Finance Minister, a rising French economist who would himself become President of France in 1974. Which minister first came up with the phrase?
answer: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
choices: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
Charles de Gaulle
Jacques Chirac
François Mitterrand
context: Giscard d'Estaing coined 'exorbitant privilege' in his role as de Gaulle's finance minister; he later served as President 1974-81. De Gaulle used the phrase publicly but did not originate it. Chirac and Mitterrand were later French presidents unrelated to the coinage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: In the 1960s the French finance minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing coined a stinging phrase for the special advantage the United States enjoyed under the postwar dollar system: he called it the 'exorbitant privilege.' Because central banks all over the world had agreed to hold dollars as their main reserve currency, the US could do one thing that no other country in the world could do. What was the unfair edge?
answer: the US could import goods and pay in newly-printed dollars that other countries had to hold
choices: the US could import goods and pay in newly-printed dollars that other countries had to hold
the US could impose tariffs without any WTO review
the US could veto UN Security Council decisions
the US could station troops in foreign countries without permission
context: The asymmetry: the US paid for imports in dollars that were the world's reserve currency, so foreign banks accumulated dollar reserves -- effectively lending the US real goods in exchange for paper claims. Tariffs, Security Council vetoes, and troop stationing are separate political privileges. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: In 1965 President Charles de Gaulle of France opened a public campaign against the Bretton Woods system, which set the US dollar as the world's reserve currency at $35 per ounce of gold. To force the issue, France began cashing in some of its dollar reserves for actual gold from the US Treasury, making America defend the peg with real bullion. Roughly how much did France convert that first year?
answer: about $150 million
choices: about $150 million
about $2 billion
about $10 million
about $50 billion
context: France converted about $150 million of dollar reserves to gold in 1965. Larger conversions followed over the next several years; other central banks followed France's lead more quietly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: In the mid-1960s French president Charles de Gaulle demanded that France's dollar reserves be exchanged for physical gold bars and shipped back across the Atlantic. Those bars did not go straight to Paris -- they first sat in one of the world's largest gold vaults, dug 80 feet down into the bedrock of lower Manhattan, guarded around the clock. Which New York vault held that French gold?
answer: the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's gold vault at 33 Liberty Street
choices: the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's gold vault at 33 Liberty Street
Fort Knox in Kentucky
the New York Stock Exchange's basement vault
the West Point Mint
context: Foreign central-bank gold is held in the New York Fed's vault at 33 Liberty Street, dug into Manhattan bedrock. Fort Knox holds US-owned gold; NYSE has no gold vault; West Point Mint stores US bullion but does not warehouse foreign central-bank reserves. Source: https://www.newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/goldvault.html.

question: After World War II the world's currencies were tied to the US dollar, and the dollar itself was fixed at $35 for every ounce of gold. By the late 1950s private buyers in London were pushing gold's real market price above $35, threatening the whole arrangement. In 1961 eight Western central banks -- the United States, Britain, West Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Switzerland -- pooled their gold and sold into every private-market run to pin the price back down. What was this defensive pool called?
answer: the London Gold Pool
choices: the London Gold Pool
the Basel Gold Consortium
the Zurich Gold Compact
the Frankfurt Gold Alliance
context: The London Gold Pool (1961-68) coordinated 8 central banks (USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland). The other names are fabrications. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: In the 1960s eight Western central banks ran the London Gold Pool. Together they sold gold at $35 per ounce every time speculators pushed the free-market price higher, defending the Bretton Woods peg. France quit the Pool in June 1967, weakening the defense. Buying pressure on gold kept growing until the remaining Pool members -- led by the United States and the Bank of England -- finally gave up and dissolved the arrangement. When did the London Gold Pool end?
answer: March 17, 1968
choices: March 17, 1968
August 15, 1971
October 24, 1929
September 19, 1985
context: The London Gold Pool was dissolved March 17, 1968 after the remaining members had lost so much gold defending the peg that they gave up; a two-tier market emerged (official $35 for central banks, market price for private buyers). Nixon closed the gold window August 15, 1971; October 24, 1929 was Black Thursday; September 19, 1985 was the Plaza Accord. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: In March 1968 the London Gold Pool collapsed, and gold began trading at two different prices at the same time. Central banks could still redeem gold at the official $35 peg, while private buyers paid a separate market-determined price. What is this arrangement called in monetary history?
answer: a two-tier gold market
choices: a two-tier gold market
a bimetallic standard
a currency board
a fiat peg
context: A two-tier gold market means official ($35 for central banks) and free-market prices coexist. Bimetallism uses both silver and gold; a currency board pegs a national currency to a foreign one; 'fiat peg' is not a standard term. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: A Bastiat-style retelling of the 1965-68 gold drain argues that de Gaulle's redemption did not actually cause the peg to fail. It only revealed a peg that was already broken. What specific reasoning move does the argument make about the peg's condition before France tested it?
answer: That once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was arithmetically impossible to sustain and would break the moment any large holder tested it
choices: That once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was arithmetically impossible to sustain and would break the moment any large holder tested it
That the peg would have held indefinitely if France had shown more solidarity with the United States and had refrained from redeeming its dollar reserves for gold
That the peg's collapse was purely a matter of speculative attack by private market participants unrelated to the underlying arithmetic of US reserves against issuance
That the Bretton Woods peg was a political fiction that had never really existed in practice and only appeared to work because no country had tried to redeem before France
context: The Bastiat 'seen vs unseen' move: SEEN, a stable peg; UNSEEN, the arithmetic that once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was already dead and only needed testing. De Gaulle was the tester, not the cause. The other options misidentify the mechanism. Source: Rothbard; Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Imagine a small shop in a French town. A boy throws a rock, and the shopkeeper's front window shatters. A crowd gathers and someone says: 'Well, at least the glassmaker gets paid to fix it -- that's good for the economy!' In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote about this exact scene in a famous essay and said the crowd is missing something big. What is the crowd forgetting?
answer: The shopkeeper can't spend that money on shoes or bread now
choices: The shopkeeper can't spend that money on shoes or bread now
The kid actually paid for the window
The glassmaker gives the money back later
Broken windows never really happen
context: Bastiat died December 24, 1850 in Rome, at 49, of tuberculosis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, famous for essays like 'The Broken Window,' was dying of tuberculosis in 1850. Doctors sent him south to warmer weather. He spent his final months, September to December 1850, in an Italian city that at the time served as the capital of the Papal States under Pope Pius IX, and he died there on Christmas Eve. Which city was it?
answer: Rome
choices: Rome
Florence
Naples
Milan
context: Bastiat arrived in Rome in September 1850 hoping the warmer air would restore his failing throat and lungs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In the winter of 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat lay dying of tuberculosis in a sickroom in Rome. Even in his final months he kept working, correcting the page proofs of a big book he would not live to finish — his life's summary of how peaceful trade quietly builds a working society. What book was he correcting on his deathbed?
answer: Economic Harmonies
choices: Economic Harmonies
Economic Sophisms
The Law
Cobden and the League
context: Harmonies economiques, Bastiat's one attempt at a positive systematic theory, was being corrected and expanded from the sickroom right up to his death. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, writing in the 1840s, spent his days watching shopkeepers, farmers, and craftsmen trade in ordinary French markets. His last book was called Economic Harmonies, published in 1850. It argued that when many strangers freely buy and sell with each other, something surprising happens -- no single person or committee is in charge, yet the whole system works. What did Bastiat say emerges from all that free trading?
answer: A working system where each person's needs get met without a central planner
choices: A working system where each person's needs get met without a central planner
A guaranteed equal outcome for every worker
A total collapse into chaos
A slow drift into monopoly by the richest sellers
context: Prosper Paillottet, a close friend and Bastiat's chosen editor, prepared the expanded 1851 Economic Harmonies from Bastiat's manuscripts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat died in Rome on Christmas Eve 1850 during his final trip to Italy. Because Rome held France's own national Catholic church, he was buried inside a specific Renaissance-era church that still stands near Piazza Navona and serves French Catholics living in the city. The same church is also famous for holding three paintings by the Baroque master Caravaggio. What is the church's name?
answer: San Luigi dei Francesi
choices: San Luigi dei Francesi
Santa Maria del Popolo
Sant'Andrea della Valle
Santa Maria Sopra Minerva
context: San Luigi dei Francesi (Saint Louis of the French) is the French national church in Rome. A memorial plaque marks Bastiat's tomb inside. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Inside the church of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome hang three paintings by the Baroque master Caravaggio -- the Life of Saint Matthew, painted around 1600. Anyone can walk in off the street and see them for free. Yet if the paintings ever went to auction, they would sell for hundreds of millions of dollars. Free-market economists point to a scene like this to teach how markets set prices. What idea does this show about market value?
answer: Value comes from what people are willing to pay, not from whether it is being sold today
choices: Value comes from what people are willing to pay, not from whether it is being sold today
Value comes only from the cost of the paint and canvas
Nothing is valuable if you can see it without paying
Only items behind glass have any market value
context: Caravaggio's Contarelli Chapel cycle (The Calling, The Inspiration, and The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew), 1599-1600, in San Luigi dei Francesi, are among the most-visited paintings in Rome. Source: grokipedia.com/page/San_Luigi_dei_Francesi.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat lived exactly 49 years, dying of tuberculosis in Rome on Christmas Eve of 1850. In his final months, weak and coughing, he raced to finish one last essay. Its message: whenever a government spends, taxes, or bans something, do not stop at the visible effect that everyone points to -- follow the story further and count the hidden effects almost no one mentions. What is that essay's title?
answer: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
choices: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
The Law
Economic Sophisms
Economic Harmonies
context: Bastiat was born June 30, 1801 in Bayonne, France, and died December 24, 1850 in Rome. His enormous public output was compressed into the last five years of his life. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: For most of human history, families in almost every land were poor and often hungry. Then around the year 1800, in Europe and later in the United States, family incomes started to grow steadily year after year. Over the next 200 years, the average family in the West ended up about thirty times richer than their great-great-grandparents had been. What do historians usually call that huge jump?
answer: The Great Enrichment
choices: The Great Enrichment
The Great Depression
The Great Migration
The Great Awakening
context: Deirdre McCloskey (born September 11, 1942) is a Chicago-trained economic historian who taught at the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois at Chicago. Her Bourgeois Trilogy pressed the culture-of-innovation thesis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: Around 1800 something big changed and the Western world got a lot richer, fast. The American economic historian Deirdre McCloskey studied this jump for decades and argued the real change was not in tools, farmland, or savings. It was in what ordinary people believed about shopkeepers, inventors, and traders. Before 1700 most Europeans looked down on people 'in trade.' After 1800 something flipped. What changed?
answer: People started to respect them instead of looking down on them
choices: People started to respect them instead of looking down on them
People started to hate them and tax them harder
People stopped talking about them entirely
People sent all of them to jail
context: The Bourgeois Trilogy comprises The Bourgeois Virtues (2006), Bourgeois Dignity (2010), and Bourgeois Equality (2016), all from University of Chicago Press. Source: press.uchicago.edu (author page, Deirdre McCloskey).

question: The American economist Deirdre McCloskey spent decades writing a three-volume series called The Bourgeois Era, arguing that the modern explosion of wealth came from a change in how people talked about merchants and traders, not just from savings, technology, or new institutions. The University of Chicago Press published the middle volume, 'Bourgeois Dignity,' in 2010. Its subtitle presses a bold claim against the standard economist's story of why the modern world grew rich. What is that subtitle?
answer: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
choices: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
Institutions and the Wealth of Nations
The Cultural Origins of Capitalism
How the West Grew Rich
context: Bourgeois Dignity: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World (Chicago 2010). The provocation is that the standard economic inputs (capital, geography, institutions) do not account for the timing and place of the Great Enrichment. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo8474162.html.

question: The American economic historian Deirdre McCloskey spent twenty years writing a three-book set called the Bourgeois Trilogy to explain why the modern West got so rich. The third and final volume came out in 2016 from the University of Chicago Press with the main title 'Bourgeois Equality.' Its subtitle names the real driver of modern wealth right there on the cover. Which subtitle appears there?
answer: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
choices: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
The Rise of the Middle Class in Northwestern Europe
Merchants, Inventors, and the Industrial Revolution
Culture and Commerce Since 1600
context: Bourgeois Equality: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World (Chicago 2016). The subtitle is McCloskey's thesis in one sentence -- IDEAS about the merchant and inventor, not stocks of capital or formal rules, produced the modern world. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo22269023.html.

question: The American economic historian Deirdre McCloskey studied why the modern West got rich starting around 1800. She pointed to a specific cultural shift in Northwestern Europe -- especially in the Dutch Republic and England -- between roughly 1600 and 1800, and called it the missing ingredient in the standard growth story. During that shift, two kinds of people who had long been sneered at by aristocrats and clergy began to receive new moral respect. Which two?
answer: The merchant and the inventor
choices: The merchant and the inventor
The soldier and the magistrate
The scholar and the theologian
The landholder and the aristocrat
context: McCloskey argues that before roughly 1600, aristocratic and clerical cultures held merchants and inventors in contempt. After the shift, businesspeople acquired dignity, and millions of ordinary people started trying to invent things. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (2010), introduction.

question: The American economic historian Deirdre McCloskey wrote a three-book set arguing that the modern jump in Western wealth was not just from steam engines, empire, or piled-up savings. It came from a change in how society treated ordinary shopkeepers, inventors, and traders -- from sneering at them to admiring them. She picked one single word to name the missing piece. What word did she pick?
answer: Dignity -- treating regular business people with real respect
choices: Dignity -- treating regular business people with real respect
Property -- stronger legal ownership of land and tools
Machinery -- new steam and factory technology
Empire -- wealth pulled in from colonies
context: Bourgeois Dignity (2010) argues that once innovation and trade were DIGNIFIED in ordinary talk and public rhetoric, ordinary people started innovating in earnest. It is a rhetoric-and-culture story, not a capital-and-institutions story. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: The economist Deirdre McCloskey argues that Europe's Industrial Revolution took off because Europeans finally began to speak of merchants and inventors with dignity instead of scorn -- her 'bourgeois virtues' story. A student worries this culture story throws out property rights, contracts, and courts. But McCloskey's real view is more careful than that. Which statement best fits her stance on institutions?
answer: The cultural dignity of innovation COMPLEMENTS institutions rather than replacing them
choices: The cultural dignity of innovation COMPLEMENTS institutions rather than replacing them
Institutions are a purely illusory factor with no growth effect
Institutions matter only in societies that never industrialized
Institutional analysis should be abandoned in favor of pure rhetoric studies
context: McCloskey's move is to argue that the SAME capital and institutions that produced Ming stagnation produced British industrial takeoff -- because the CULTURE around the merchant differed. She adds a missing input, she does not remove the others. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Equality (Chicago 2016), preface.

question: Before Deirdre McCloskey became famous as an economic historian at the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois-Chicago, she wrote a short 1985 book that shocked her own field. In it, she looked at how professional economists actually persuade each other in journals — not with pure math and data, but with vivid metaphors, colorful little stories, and appeals to famous authorities. Which title did she give that book?
answer: The Rhetoric of Economics
choices: The Rhetoric of Economics
The Language of Growth
The Persuasion of Markets
Style in the Dismal Science
context: The Rhetoric of Economics (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985) opened the field of rhetorical study of economic writing and argued that economists persuade each other by narrative and metaphor as much as by proofs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: Deirdre McCloskey is an American economic historian who spent the 2000s and 2010s writing a three-book set called the Bourgeois Trilogy. Her books ask why the modern world got rich — why, after thousands of years of near-poverty, one corner of humanity in the 1700s and 1800s suddenly saw a thirty-fold jump in wealth. She sets up her puzzle with a pair of societies that had similar formal inputs — people, land, technology, trade — but wildly different results. Which pair best sharpens the puzzle?
answer: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
choices: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
Roman North Africa's decline versus medieval Italy's revival
Iberian empires' silver imports versus Dutch banking innovation
Ottoman guild economies versus Persian bazaars
context: McCloskey argues that Ming China had comparable capital, technology, and formal institutions to early-modern Britain -- but the culture around the merchant differed. Same inputs, different cultural legitimation, opposite outcomes. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: Bastiat wrote about the seen and the unseen in economics. McCloskey borrows that pattern for her growth story. She identifies one unseen factor that made the seen inputs (capital, institutions, geography) actually productive. Which factor does she name as the missing unseen?
answer: The cultural legitimation of the merchant-inventor
choices: The cultural legitimation of the merchant-inventor
The concentration of gold and silver bullion
The centralization of political authority in nation-states
The technical superiority of European engineering guilds
context: McCloskey's reasoning move: the SEEN is capital and institutions and geography; the UNSEEN is the cultural dignity of the merchant and inventor. Without that legitimation, the same seen inputs stagnate. With it, they compound into the Great Enrichment. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Equality (Chicago 2016).

question: Deirdre McCloskey calls it the Great Enrichment. Before 1800, most Europeans lived on about 3 dollars a day in modern terms -- the same as their great-grandparents, and their great-grandparents before them. In the two centuries since, real income per person in the countries that industrialized first has grown by roughly what factor?
answer: About 30-fold (3,000 percent)
choices: About 30-fold (3,000 percent)
About 3-fold (300 percent)
About 100-fold (10,000 percent)
About 3-fold, only in the richest cities
context: The 3,000-percent figure (roughly 30x) is the standard estimate from Angus Maddison and OECD historical statistics for real per-capita income growth in Western countries since 1800. McCloskey uses it as the puzzle to explain. Source: Maddison Project Database (2020 update); McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: In 1929 Joseph Stalin, the ruler of the Soviet Union, ordered the state to wipe out a whole class of Russian and Ukrainian farmers he called 'kulaks.' Their supposed 'crime' could be as small as owning one horse, hiring one farmhand, or storing a little extra grain. Soviet police and Red Army soldiers arrested them by the millions, shot many, deported the rest to labor camps in Siberia and Kazakhstan, and took their land for the state. About how many farmers were killed, starved, or shipped to camps?
answer: Several million
choices: Several million
A few hundred people
About twenty thousand people
None -- Stalin was bluffing
context: 'Kulak' (Russian for 'fist') was Soviet propaganda's label for any peasant slightly more prosperous than his neighbors. Stalin's December 27, 1929 speech to a conference of agrarian Marxists made kulak-status a target category for erasure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: In December 1929 Joseph Stalin gave a speech in Moscow that set Soviet farm policy for years. He targeted the kulaks -- peasants slightly wealthier than their neighbors, often just because they owned a few extra animals or a small plot of land. Stalin used a specific chilling phrase to describe what the Soviet state would do to them, and the phrase soon became notorious. What was it?
answer: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
choices: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
Correction of the peasant question
Reorganization of rural labor
Cleansing of the villages
context: The phrase 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class' (likvidatsiya kulachestva kak klassa) was delivered at the December 27, 1929 conference and formalized in a Politburo decree of January 30, 1930. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: On January 30, 1930 the Soviet Politburo -- the small ruling council of the Communist Party in Moscow -- turned Stalin's December 1929 call against the kulaks into official policy. The order sorted the wealthier peasant families of the Soviet countryside into three groups, each with a completely different fate. What were the three fates the Politburo assigned to those families?
answer: Executed, deported, or resettled locally
choices: Executed, deported, or resettled locally
Taxed, fined, or warned
Retrained, retained, or reassigned
Relocated, redistributed, or repatriated
context: The Politburo's January 30, 1930 decree sorted kulak families: category one shot, category two deported to the far north / Siberia / Kazakhstan, category three resettled locally on marginal land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: After the Soviet Politburo issued its anti-kulak order on January 30, 1930, the Soviet secret police carried out mass roundups of wealthier peasant families across the countryside. From 1930 to 1932 whole villages were loaded into cattle wagons and shipped east to labor settlements in Siberia, the Kazakh steppe, and the frozen far north of the Soviet Union. Roughly how many so-called kulaks were deported this way?
answer: About 2 million
choices: About 2 million
About 20,000
About 200,000
About 20 million
context: About 30,000 alleged kulaks were shot; about 2 million were deported to the far north, Siberia, and Kazakhstan; another 4-5 million were dispossessed of property and reassigned. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (Oxford UP, 2007).

question: Between 1930 and 1932 the Soviet state deported roughly two million so-called kulaks -- peasants slightly wealthier than their neighbors -- from their villages to labor camps in Siberia and the far north. The campaign is called dekulakization. It was more than a show of Marxist class war; it also served a very useful purpose for the collectivization drive that came right after, in which peasants were being forced to merge their private farms into state-run collective farms. What was that useful purpose?
answer: It removed the most experienced farmers so collective farms would face no organized resistance
choices: It removed the most experienced farmers so collective farms would face no organized resistance
It freed land for state ecological reserves
It provided cash reserves for industrial imports
It filled quotas for Red Army recruitment
context: The most competent farmers were destroyed because they were the most competent. The villages that remained had lost their most capable people BEFORE the 1932-33 famine hit -- a mechanism the Holodomor then exploited. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: In the early 1930s Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union carried out a campaign called dekulakization — forcibly seizing land from the more successful peasants and shipping millions of them, along with their families, into remote 'special settlements' in Siberia, the far north, and Kazakhstan. Building and running these settlements needed a Soviet agency willing to handle mass deportation and armed forced labor. Which agency was assigned the job?
answer: The OGPU (later the NKVD)
choices: The OGPU (later the NKVD)
The Red Army Corps of Engineers
The Ministry of Agriculture
The Comintern Executive
context: The OGPU (unified state political directorate, renamed NKVD in 1934) built 'special settlements' in Siberia and the Urals to hold deported kulak families. Winter 1931-32 death rates in these settlements ran to hundreds of thousands. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (2007).

question: During Stalin's collectivization drive of 1930 to 1932, local Soviet officials stretched the label 'kulak' -- originally meaning a slightly wealthier peasant -- so far that any villager who simply refused to join a collective farm could suddenly be tagged with it and deported to Siberia. Communist Party activists coined a specific term for the move of relabeling a stubborn peasant as a hidden class enemy. What did activists call this relabeling move?
answer: Unmasking someone as a kulak
choices: Unmasking someone as a kulak
Registering them as a class enemy
Naming them as a saboteur
Marking them for rectification
context: 'Unmasking' (razoblachenie) redefined kulak-status as anyone who resisted collectivization. The label became a catch-all administrative tool for eliminating opposition. Source: Fitzpatrick, Stalin's Peasants (1994).

question: Starting in 1929 the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin declared millions of hard-working Russian and Ukrainian farmers to be 'kulaks' -- enemies of the state -- just because they owned a little land, some tools, or a cow. Whole families were shot, starved, or shipped in cattle cars to labor camps in Siberia. The campaign had a name: dekulakization. What was Stalin's government really trying to accomplish?
answer: Force farmers off their land so the state could seize and run all farms
choices: Force farmers off their land so the state could seize and run all farms
Reward the most successful farmers with better land
Make sure every family had exactly the same size of farm
Move farmers closer to cities so they could work in factories
context: Lynne Viola's The Unknown Gulag (Oxford, 2007) uses newly opened OGPU archives to reconstruct the settlement system for deported peasants. Fitzpatrick, Conquest, and Applebaum work on adjacent Soviet-terror topics. Source: global.oup.com.

question: Between 1929 and 1932 Joseph Stalin's Soviet regime ran a campaign called dekulakization, which stripped the more skilled and productive peasants of their land and shipped them to Siberia. Ukraine — the empire's most fertile grain-belt — lost its best farmers first. Grain quotas set by Moscow stayed high anyway, so what remained in the villages was seized to meet them. By the winter of 1932-33 the countryside was hit by a catastrophe that historians say killed several million people. Which disaster did dekulakization set up?
answer: The Holodomor famine in Ukraine
choices: The Holodomor famine in Ukraine
The Great Terror purges
The 1937 nationalities operations
The Siege of Leningrad
context: With the most productive farmers gone, forced grain requisitions in 1932-33 stripped Ukrainian villages of their remaining food. The resulting famine killed several million Ukrainians. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught that every policy has visible effects everyone points to, and hidden effects almost no one talks about. Apply Bastiat's rule to Stalin's dekulakization -- the 1929-1933 Soviet campaign that killed, deported, or starved millions of the most skilled Russian and Ukrainian farmers. In Party newspapers the visible move was described as 'expropriating rich peasants for social justice.' What was the unseen cost that the villages paid in the years that followed?
answer: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
choices: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
A shortage of Party recruitment
An inflation in the price of textiles
A drop in industrial productivity in Moscow
context: The Bastiat move: the SEEN was 'redistributing kulak property'; the UNSEEN was the collapse of village agricultural knowledge (which farmer knew which fields, which seed variety, which threshing techniques) and the famine that used the resulting vulnerability. Source: mises.org/library/theft-of-a-nation-holodomor.

question: In 1976 the Austrian-British economist Friedrich Hayek published a short book called 'The Denationalisation of Money.' Its central idea was this: the government should not be the only one allowed to issue money. Private banks and firms could each print their own bills, and customers would freely pick whichever money kept its value best -- forcing every issuer to behave. What is this idea called?
answer: Currency competition
choices: Currency competition
Total price control
One-world central bank
Bartering only
context: Hayek (1899-1992) had won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics two years earlier, in 1974, sharing it with Gunnar Myrdal. The 1976 pamphlet was the most radical monetary proposal of his career. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: In 1976 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published a short book in London arguing that governments should give up their monopoly on printing money and let private issuers compete. His publisher was a small London think tank that the chicken farmer Antony Fisher had founded on Hayek's own advice years earlier. Which think tank put the book out?
answer: The Institute of Economic Affairs
choices: The Institute of Economic Affairs
The Cato Institute
The Adam Smith Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: The IEA, founded 1955, is Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank; Hayek personally counselled Antony Fisher to start it after Fisher read The Road to Serfdom. The Cato Institute (1977) and Adam Smith Institute (1977) did not yet exist. The Mont Pelerin Society is a scholarly society, not a publisher. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek was an Austrian-born economist who won the Nobel Prize in 1974 for his work on how markets carry information through prices. In 1976, watching inflation rip through the Western world, he wrote a short pamphlet arguing that the whole problem came from one place: governments hold a monopoly on printing money. He made a single bold proposal for what governments should do about that monopoly. What did he propose?
answer: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
choices: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
Return to a fixed exchange rate anchored on a single ounce of gold
Adopt a common global reserve currency issued by the International Monetary Fund
Delegate all monetary policy to an independent panel of academic economists
context: Hayek argued money is no different from any other good: competition between private issuers, checked by consumer choice, would supply it better than a state monopoly. The proposal was radical enough that even fellow Austrian economists mostly rejected it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek, the Austrian-born Nobel-winning economist, wrote a bold monetary pamphlet in 1976 arguing that governments should give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete for people's trust. The pamphlet's cover carried a long, formal title in the style of a classical treatise — naming both the reform Hayek wanted and the historical practice of many currencies circulating side by side. Which full title did the pamphlet carry?
answer: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
choices: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
The Constitution of Liberty: A Restatement of the Principles of a Free Society
The Fatal Conceit: A Study of the Errors of Socialism from Marx to the Present
Prices and Production: Four Lectures Delivered at the University of London
context: 'Concurrent currencies' referred to the historical episodes, such as pre-Civil-War American free banking or private banknote issuance in nineteenth-century Scotland, in which several currencies circulated together. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: In 1976 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published a short book called The Denationalisation of Money, arguing that governments should stop having a monopoly on money. His whole case rested on a claim about the historical record of every paper currency any government had ever issued as its own monopoly money. He said the record showed one clear pattern. What was it?
answer: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
choices: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
Every such currency has appreciated against gold across the twentieth century
Every such currency has stabilized once its central bank became independent
Every such currency has held value so long as its government retained a fiscal surplus
context: Hayek's examples ran from the Roman denarius under Diocletian to the Weimar mark of 1923 to modern post-war fiat currencies. His conclusion was that debasement is not a scandal but the predictable equilibrium of a monopoly issuer facing short-run political incentives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 book The Denationalisation of Money urged governments to give up their monopoly on money and let private issuers compete side by side. Readers asked the obvious question: if anyone can print money, how would competing private currencies stay honest? Hayek pointed to one specific discipline. Which force did he say would keep the issuers honest?
answer: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
choices: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
Government auditors inspecting each issuer's reserve ratios annually
International treaty obligations enforced through the World Bank
A gold-parity peg required by domestic constitutional law
context: Hayek's mechanism was identical to the market discipline any producer faces. Issuers whose currency lost purchasing power would see it refused in commerce, lose deposits, and fail; issuers who kept it stable would win business. No government auditor, treaty, or peg was needed. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/hayeks-plan-private-money.

question: An Austrian-tradition economist wrote a book saying governments should not be the only ones allowed to print money. Instead, private banks and companies could each issue their own currencies, and people could freely choose the best one. What outcome did he predict from that competition?
answer: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
choices: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
Prices would swing wildly and no trade could happen
One company would seize control and print even more money than governments
Every currency would collapse within a year
context: In the second edition Hayek added the speculation that a free monetary market would not sustain an unmanageable number of currencies but would converge on a limited number of stable standards. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: In 1976 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published 'The Denationalisation of Money,' arguing that private banks should be free to issue their own paper currencies and compete with each other for users. Even his fellow Austrian economist Murray Rothbard -- who agreed the government should not run the money supply -- drew a line right here. Rothbard wanted one more rule for any real free-market money. What did he require?
answer: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
choices: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
That the currency circulate only within a single sovereign jurisdiction
That the currency be issued exclusively by chartered depository institutions
That the currency be redeemable at par into government-issued specie
context: Rothbard remained a strict commodity-money advocate: free banking, yes, but the notes had to be redeemable claims on a real commodity such as gold. On this account Hayek's proposal for competing PAPER currencies with no commodity backing was more radical than Rothbard would go. Source: cameronharwick.com/writing/hayek-vs-rothbard-on-money.

question: A high-school student raises her hand in class and asks: 'The US government prints all the dollars right now, so why should we let different companies compete to supply money?' An Austrian economist in the tradition of Friedrich Hayek answers her: 'For the same reason we let many bakeries compete to sell bread, and many companies compete to sell phones.' What reason does he give?
answer: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
choices: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
Money is a natural monopoly that only one issuer can supply well
Only a central authority can measure the right amount of money
Bread and phones follow completely different economic laws
context: The Austrian methodological move: reject the special-pleading claim that money is uniquely unsuited to markets. Hayek argued the same competitive discipline that improves other goods would improve currency; the burden falls on defenders of the state monopoly to say why money is the exception. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Bitcoin, the digital currency launched in 2009 by the anonymous programmer Satoshi Nakamoto, was built to run without any government or bank. Its defenders, like the Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous, point to Friedrich Hayek's 1976 book The Denationalisation of Money as the grandfather of the project — competing currencies keeping each other honest. But Bitcoin uses one engineering trick Hayek could not have used in 1976. Which trick?
answer: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
choices: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
A gold-parity peg administered by an international clearinghouse
A one-to-one deposit-insurance guarantee from a sovereign issuer
A statutory reserve requirement enforced by domestic banking regulators
context: Hayek imagined competing private BANKS disciplined by consumer refusal to hold debased notes; Bitcoin, launched thirty-three years later by Satoshi Nakamoto, hard-codes the discipline into the protocol itself with a 21-million-coin cap and a halving schedule no operator can override. Ammous's 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard makes the intellectual-descent argument explicit; the European Central Bank has publicly noted the same theoretical lineage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In December 1978 the new paramount leader of China, Deng Xiaoping, turned the Communist Party away from Chairman Mao Zedong's strict command economy — where the state fixed every price and ran every farm. Deng let markets and real prices come back, first in farming, then in industry. Historians gave the whole program a two-word English name. What is it usually called?
answer: Reform and Opening
choices: Reform and Opening
The Great Leap
The Four Modernizations
The Cultural Revolution
context: Gaige kaifang -- Reform and Opening -- was launched at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee, December 18-22, 1978, under Deng Xiaoping. It ended pure central planning first in agriculture, then in industry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.

question: For decades under Chairman Mao Zedong, the Chinese state owned all the farms and factories and told each village and workshop exactly what to grow and make. After Mao died in 1976, a new leader named Deng Xiaoping took charge. Starting in 1978 he made big changes. Farmers could keep part of their crop and sell it. Some private shops could open. Foreign companies could build factories in special coastal zones. Compared to Mao's old rules, was Deng's China more central-planning or more market?
answer: More market
choices: More market
More central-planning
Exactly the same
Neither -- it banned all trade
context: Deng Xiaoping had been purged in 1966 and again in 1976. He returned to power in 1977 and by December 1978 had consolidated his faction's control. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: In the late 1970s the new leader of China, Deng Xiaoping, changed a big rule about farming villages. Before Deng, every village worked the fields together as one big commune and the state took all the crops. Under Deng's new rule, each family could keep or sell anything extra they grew above the state's quota. What happened to how hard the farmers worked?
answer: They worked much harder because they now got to keep the extra
choices: They worked much harder because they now got to keep the extra
They worked less because the pressure was off
It made no difference to their work
They stopped growing food and moved to cities
context: The Household Responsibility System (baochan daohu) tested in Anhui in late 1978 (informally in Xiaogang village) then rolled out nationally by 1982-83. Households farmed their own plots and sold surplus at market. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: In 1978, in a poor Chinese farming village called Xiaogang, eighteen peasant families secretly signed a contract dividing the commune's shared farmland into private family plots. Under Chairman Mao Zedong's rules this was illegal — the men knew they could be arrested or shot. Why did they take the risk?
answer: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew, not just the village as a whole
choices: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew, not just the village as a whole
To donate more grain to the state warehouse
To please the Communist Party leaders in Beijing
To attract tourists to their village
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed a secret agreement in December 1978 to divide land plots, pledging to raise each other's children if any were arrested.
