answer: Temporary government programs turn permanent once a group depends on the checks
choices: Temporary government programs turn permanent once a group depends on the checks
Emergency laws automatically expire on their published sunset date
Farmers ask Congress to end the program every time it comes up for renewal
Programs get smaller once the emergency they were built for has passed
context: The 'Farm Bill' is the general shorthand for the omnibus agricultural legislation Congress reauthorizes roughly every five years (most recently the 2018 Agriculture Improvement Act and its 2024 continuing resolution). The programs descend directly from the 1938 AAA. Source: usda.gov farm bill.

question: In 1933, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed an executive order telling every American to hand in their gold coins and gold bars to the government. In exchange, people got paper dollars. It became illegal for a normal citizen to keep the gold. Why would a government want everyone's gold locked up inside its own vaults?
answer: With gold locked up, the government could print more paper money without limit
choices: With gold locked up, the government could print more paper money without limit
Gold coins were too heavy to use
The government just wanted to give people nicer paper
Gold had become worthless
context: Executive Order 6102 required Americans to turn in gold at the official rate of $20.67 per troy ounce. It was signed under authority of the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 (a wartime law) as amended by the March 9 1933 Emergency Banking Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: In April 1933 President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102, which forced every American to hand in their gold coins, gold bars, and gold certificates to the federal government. The order was meant to stop 'hoarding' during the Great Depression. Anyone who refused and kept large gold holdings faced a serious punishment. What did they face?
answer: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
choices: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
A fine of $500 and community service
A tax surcharge of 20% on all income
Loss of voting rights for the remainder of Roosevelt's term
context: $10,000 in 1933 dollars is roughly $240,000 in 2026 dollars. Citizens could keep small amounts (up to $100 face value in coins) and coins of recognized numismatic value. Bulk holdings were confiscated. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: In April 1933 President Franklin Roosevelt had ordered Americans to hand in their gold at the old official price of $20.67 per ounce. Less than a year later, on January 31, 1934, Roosevelt signed a proclamation under the newly-passed Gold Reserve Act that reset the official gold price at a much higher figure. What was the new official rate?
answer: $35.00 per troy ounce
choices: $35.00 per troy ounce
$25.00 per troy ounce
$50.00 per troy ounce
$100.00 per troy ounce
context: The January 31 1934 proclamation raised the official gold price from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce -- a 40.94% devaluation of the dollar against gold. Anyone who had turned in gold the previous year could not buy it back at the new rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 1934 the US Congress passed the Gold Reserve Act, and President Franklin Roosevelt signed a proclamation cutting the dollar's fixed weight in gold from about 23.22 grains down to 13.71 grains — nearly in half. Millions of Americans still held dollars in their pockets and bank accounts from before the change. In simple terms, what did the rewrite do to every one of those dollars overnight?
answer: It made each dollar worth less in gold overnight
choices: It made each dollar worth less in gold overnight
It made each dollar worth more in gold overnight
It made the dollar stop working as money for a year
It gave every American a free gold coin
context: The Gold Reserve Act was signed January 30 1934. Roosevelt's proclamation raising the gold price to $35 followed the next day, January 31 1934. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 1934 President Franklin Roosevelt used the new Gold Reserve Act to cut the dollar's official gold weight nearly in half. Because the government had just seized private gold at the old price of $20.67 an ounce, and then set the new price at $35 an ounce, wealth shifted from ordinary savers who had held gold to the US Treasury. About how much of the gold savers' buying power was moved?
answer: Roughly 77% of the purchasing power of savers who had held gold
choices: Roughly 77% of the purchasing power of savers who had held gold
Roughly 15%
Roughly 5%
Roughly 200%
context: A $20.67 dollar bought only 59% of what a $35 gold ounce did -- an implicit 77% devaluation of purchasing power measured against the gold citizens had been forced to sell at the lower rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1933 and 1934 the US government took away private citizens' gold and then lowered the dollar's value against gold. Many contracts had promised payment "in gold." The Supreme Court decided by one vote to let the government break those promises. What did this ruling mean for savers?
answer: The government could reduce the real value of what it and others owed them
choices: The government could reduce the real value of what it and others owed them
The government now had to repay every gold contract in full
Private gold ownership was fully restored
Contracts written in dollars were no longer enforceable
context: The 1935 Gold Clause Cases (5-4) upheld the seizure and devaluation while declaring unconstitutional the government's abrogation of gold-clause obligations in its own bonds. But the Court also held that bondholders were not entitled to damages -- a limited victory that was in practice a full defeat. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Clause Cases' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102 making it illegal for private American citizens to own gold coins, bullion, or gold certificates. The ban stayed on the books for four decades, blocking ordinary Americans from holding real gold as savings. When was it finally repealed?
answer: December 31 1974, under President Gerald Ford
choices: December 31 1974, under President Gerald Ford
August 15 1971, under President Richard Nixon
January 20 1981, under President Ronald Reagan
October 3 2008, under President George W. Bush
context: Congress repealed the ban on private gold ownership effective December 31 1974. Americans could once again legally own gold bullion for the first time in over 40 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold ownership laws in the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: After President Franklin Roosevelt's 1933 Executive Order 6102 seized Americans' privately held gold, the federal government suddenly held massive amounts of bullion and needed a hardened place to keep it. In 1936 the US Treasury built a specific new fortress vault in Kentucky, on an Army base, for exactly that purpose. What is that facility called?
answer: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository
choices: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository
The New York Fed Vault
The Denver Assay Office
The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Vault
context: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository was completed in 1936 in Kentucky to house the seized gold. It remains one of the most secure facilities in the world and holds the majority of official US gold reserves. Source: Grokipedia 'United States Bullion Depository' (2026-09-05).

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to ask, for every policy, what is seen and what is unseen. Apply his lens to the 1933-34 gold episode: President Franklin Roosevelt's Executive Order 6102 seized Americans' gold at $20.67 an ounce, and his 1934 Gold Reserve Act then repriced gold at $35 an ounce. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures the structure of that combined seizure-and-devaluation?
answer: Seen: strengthening the banking system by preventing gold hoarding; Unseen: American middle-class savers who had prudently held gold were transferred wealth to the US Treasury via the devaluation
choices: Seen: strengthening the banking system by preventing gold hoarding; Unseen: American middle-class savers who had prudently held gold were transferred wealth to the US Treasury via the devaluation
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: full employment; Unseen: rising real wages
Seen: growing federal revenue; Unseen: shrinking bureaucratic overhead
context: The stated purpose was banking stability. The invisible mechanism was a targeted wealth transfer from the group that had chosen the specifically prudent monetary asset. Bastiat's frame fits the episode exactly. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In April 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102. It ordered Americans to hand over their gold coins and bullion to the government at $20.67 an ounce, and made private gold hoarding a federal crime punishable by prison. Once the gold was locked in Treasury vaults, the government revalued gold to $35 an ounce, wiping out a big chunk of every dollar's purchasing power overnight. What lasting recognition move does this 1933 seizure teach about state power over hard money?
answer: A determined state can criminalize private holding of hard money, seize existing holdings, and then devalue the currency at the new prices -- and this pattern has been used repeatedly across modern history
choices: A determined state can criminalize private holding of hard money, seize existing holdings, and then devalue the currency at the new prices -- and this pattern has been used repeatedly across modern history
States never take direct action against citizens' monetary choices
Democratic states are constitutionally unable to seize private property
Executive orders cannot legally override Article I Section 8 monetary powers
context: The 1933 US precedent is not unique. John Law tried to ban private gold ownership in 1720; the French Revolution imposed the death penalty for gold hoarding; multiple modern hyperinflators (Zimbabwe, Venezuela) have used similar mechanisms. The pattern is a standard tool. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold ownership laws by country' (2026-09-05).

question: During World War II, the US Federal Reserve -- America's central bank -- kept the government's borrowing costs artificially low. To do it the Fed bought huge amounts of government war bonds, essentially printing new dollars to lend to Washington. When the war ended in 1945, all those new dollars were still sitting in the American economy. What did that cause once wartime price controls came off?
answer: Rising prices as too much new money chased the same amount of goods
choices: Rising prices as too much new money chased the same amount of goods
Falling prices, since money was scarce
Nothing at all -- printing money never affects prices
A drop in government borrowing
context: The March 4 1951 Accord restored the Fed's independence to set monetary policy without pegging Treasury bond prices. Historians consider it the moment the modern independent Fed was born -- 38 years after the Federal Reserve Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1950s the head of America's central bank, William McChesney Martin, gave a famous speech about the Federal Reserve's job. He said the Fed's role was to 'take away the punch bowl just as the party gets going.' The punch bowl was his image for the cheap credit and easy money that make an economic party feel lively. What did Martin mean?
answer: The Fed should slow the flow of easy money before the boom turns into a crash
choices: The Fed should slow the flow of easy money before the boom turns into a crash
The Fed should serve free drinks at every meeting
The Fed should never do anything at all
The Fed should print more money during good times
context: Martin served as Fed chairman for nearly 19 years (April 1951 to January 1970) under presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: In April 1951 President Harry Truman needed a new Federal Reserve chairman. He picked William McChesney Martin, expecting Martin would be a loyal ally to the White House. There was an ironic twist: Martin had just spent months at the negotiating table hammering out the Fed-Treasury Accord -- the deal that finally freed the Fed from taking orders from Treasury. Martin had argued hard for one specific side of that Accord. Which side had he been on?
answer: The Treasury side
choices: The Treasury side
The Federal Reserve side
The Senate Banking Committee side
The Council of Economic Advisers side
context: Martin had negotiated the Accord as a Treasury official. Truman assumed a Treasury man would keep monetary policy accommodating to fiscal needs. Instead Martin became a fierce defender of Fed independence. Truman later said Martin 'double-crossed' him. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: On an October evening in 1955, Federal Reserve chairman William McChesney Martin stood in front of the New York Group of the Investment Bankers Association and reached for a memorable image to describe what the Fed does when the economy runs hot. His line became one of the most quoted metaphors in central banking history and shaped his career. Martin said the Fed's role was to be a specific figure at a party. Which figure?
answer: The chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up
choices: The chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up
The bartender who refuses to serve one more drink
The host who quietly turns down the music
The doorman who admits only sober guests
context: Martin's 1955 punchbowl metaphor became the classic description of anti-inflationary central banking. The Fed's job, he said, is to be unpopular precisely when the boom feels best. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1955 the Federal Reserve chairman William McChesney Martin Jr. told a room of bankers that the Fed's job was to 'take away the punchbowl just as the party gets going' — meaning raise interest rates to cool an overheating boom before inflation broke out. The line was so vivid that financial journalism turned it into shorthand for a specific Fed function. What function does 'take away the punchbowl' name?
answer: Restrictive monetary policy imposed against political pressure during an economic boom
choices: Restrictive monetary policy imposed against political pressure during an economic boom
Rate cuts that stimulate the economy during a recession
Emergency lending to specific failing banks
Coordinated policy with foreign central banks during a currency crisis
context: 'Take away the punchbowl' means: raise rates when everyone wants easy money because the party is fun. It captures the political-economy tension every anti-inflationary Fed chair faces. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: William McChesney Martin was the longest-serving chairman of the US Federal Reserve, running the central bank for nearly 19 years from 1951 to 1970. During that stretch he answered to five different American presidents in a row. Which sequence of five presidents covers his full tenure at the Fed?
answer: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
choices: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Ford
Roosevelt, Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson
Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, and Ford
context: Martin's tenure ran from April 1951 through January 1970. He served under five presidents across three decades -- the longest continuous Fed chairmanship in modern history. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: William McChesney Martin Jr. led the Federal Reserve as chairman from 1951 to 1970 — the longest run in Fed history. His father, William McChesney Martin Sr., had already held a specific earlier position inside the Federal Reserve System, making the Martins one of very few father-son central-banker pairs in US history. What was the father's role?
answer: First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
choices: First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
First chairman of the Federal Reserve Board
First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York
First president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston
context: William McChesney Martin Sr. was the first governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis when the Fed opened for business in 1914. His son led the whole system 37 years later. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Imagine a country that fights an expensive foreign war and launches big new welfare programs at the same time -- the way the United States did in the late 1960s under President Lyndon Johnson, funding both the Vietnam War and the Great Society. The government does not raise taxes to cover either bill. The central bank keeps interest rates low so the government's borrowing stays cheap. What does the country tend to get a few years later?
answer: High inflation
choices: High inflation
Low prices and a strong currency
A budget surplus
Falling wages across the board
context: LBJ's Great Society programs and Vietnam War spending combined to test Martin's resolve. He eventually gave in to some inflationary policy, contributing to the setup for the 1970s Great Inflation that Arthur Burns then made worse. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: During World War II the US Treasury needed cheap money to fund the war, so the Federal Reserve agreed to hold interest rates artificially low by buying whatever government bonds were needed. That arrangement only ended with the 1951 Fed-Treasury Accord, which restored the Federal Reserve's power to set interest rates on its own. The whole episode teaches a specific recognition move about wartime finance and monetary independence. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: During wars central banks lose their independence to fiscal financing; the reassertion of independence afterward is a political fight that must be won explicitly, not assumed
choices: During wars central banks lose their independence to fiscal financing; the reassertion of independence afterward is a political fight that must be won explicitly, not assumed
Central bank independence is automatic and does not require political defense
Wars have no effect on central-bank monetary policy
Fiscal deficits are always neutralized by market interest-rate discipline
context: The 1951 Accord was a political victory hard-won by insiders who understood the inflationary consequences of continued Treasury-bond pegging. Fed independence is not a natural equilibrium; it is a political achievement that must be actively maintained. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1955 the Federal Reserve chairman William McChesney Martin Jr. gave a famous speech saying the Fed's job is to 'take away the punchbowl just as the party gets going' — meaning it must raise interest rates and slow the economy right when Americans are enjoying the boom the most. What point does that image press about how central banks fight inflation?
answer: The Fed's most important tightening decisions are always politically unpopular precisely because they arrive just when everyone is enjoying the boom
choices: The Fed's most important tightening decisions are always politically unpopular precisely because they arrive just when everyone is enjoying the boom
The Fed's tightening decisions are always politically popular during booms
The public consistently supports early anti-inflationary action
The Fed's decisions are politically neutral because they are technical
context: The Martin insight explains why Burns caved to Nixon in 1971-72, why Greenspan avoided the 1996 warning follow-through, and why every subsequent chair has struggled with the same tension. Anti-inflationary policy is unpopular when it matters most. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1958 the American economist Leonard Read wrote a famous short essay called 'I, Pencil,' told from the point of view of a simple yellow pencil. Read argued that no single person on Earth knows how to make a pencil from scratch. The wood, graphite, rubber eraser, metal band, and yellow paint all come from different countries and thousands of different workers who have never met. What does Read say the pencil's story teaches?
answer: A free market coordinates millions of people without any central planner
choices: A free market coordinates millions of people without any central planner
One factory in the US makes every pencil in the world
Pencils are a government-run product
Making a pencil is the simplest job in the world
context: Leonard E. Read (1898-1983) founded the Foundation for Economic Education in March 1946 as the first American institutional home of the classical-liberal reading tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_for_Economic_Education.

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short book called The Law, published only months before his death. Bastiat argued that when governments take property from one group of citizens and hand it to another group, they betray their proper role and become an instrument of legal plunder dressed up in official paper. What did Bastiat say the law should do instead?
answer: Protect every person's life, freedom, and honestly-earned property
choices: Protect every person's life, freedom, and honestly-earned property
Distribute all property equally among the citizens
Set the price of every good sold in the country
Choose which jobs each citizen must do
context: La Loi (1850) as The Law, translated by Dean Russell, was the 1950 FEE edition that reintroduced Bastiat to English-language American readers. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Think of a simple yellow pencil. To make one, someone chops wood in Oregon, someone mines graphite, someone taps rubber trees for an eraser, someone smelts brass. Not a single person on Earth knows how to do all those jobs. What does this story teach?
answer: No one person could plan the whole economy
choices: No one person could plan the whole economy
Pencils should cost much more than they do
Only huge companies can make simple things
Governments make the best pencils
context: 'I, Pencil' has an ordinary pencil describe the millions of coordinated market actions -- lumbering, mining graphite, refining rubber, mining zinc for brass ferrules -- required to make it, illustrating that no single actor holds the whole recipe. Source: fee.org/resources/i-pencil.

question: A famous essay pointed out that not one single person on earth knows how to make a common wooden pencil from scratch. The wood, the graphite, the rubber, the paint, and the metal band all come from different places and people. What is the essay teaching about a market economy?
answer: Millions of people cooperate through prices without any single planner in charge
choices: Millions of people cooperate through prices without any single planner in charge
Pencils are so simple that anyone could make one alone
Only a central planner could organize something as complex as a pencil
Modern factories have made all the older skills useless
context: Free to Choose (PBS, 1980), hosted by Milton and Rose Friedman, built its second episode around 'I, Pencil'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: In an 1850 essay called 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen,' the French economist Frederic Bastiat told a small story that would echo through economics for two hundred years. A boy throws a rock and breaks a shopkeeper's window. Neighbors gather and shrug -- 'at least the glass-maker will get work now.' Bastiat said the neighbors had made a huge mistake in their reasoning. What were they failing to see?
answer: The money the shopkeeper spends on a window can no longer buy the shoes he had planned for
choices: The money the shopkeeper spends on a window can no longer buy the shoes he had planned for
The glass-maker was going to lose his job anyway
The window was already broken by the wind, not the boy
The shopkeeper had too many windows already
context: George B. de Huszar's 1964 FEE edition of Bastiat's Selected Essays on Political Economy became a standard American teaching text. Source: fee.org.

question: In 1946 the American journalist Henry Hazlitt published a short book called Economics in One Lesson. Hazlitt boiled the whole field down to a single rule he borrowed from the 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat. Every good economist, Hazlitt said, must follow this one rule when judging any policy. What is the rule?
answer: Look at both the seen and the unseen effects of any policy
choices: Look at both the seen and the unseen effects of any policy
Trust the government to set the right minimum wage
Print more money whenever people are out of work
Always tax imports to protect local jobs
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) was published the same year as FEE's founding and became the paired popular introduction to the tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued in his 1949 essay 'The Intellectuals and Socialism' that ordinary campaigning rarely changes a country's direction for long. What really matters, Hayek said, is what teachers, journalists, and writers accept as ordinary common sense -- because politicians eventually follow that consensus. Free-market think tanks, magazines, and student reading programs try to do something ordinary campaigning cannot. What is it?
answer: Slowly change what people take for common sense about how the economy works
choices: Slowly change what people take for common sense about how the economy works
Force politicians to obey a specific party leader
Pay voters directly for their votes each election cycle
Predict the exact price of stocks and bonds next year
context: FEE moved its offices to Atlanta, Georgia in the 21st century and continues its student-education mission from there. Source: fee.org.

question: In 1959 a young rebel named Fidel Castro marched into Havana and took control of Cuba. Once in power, he seized private farms, factories, and shops and put the government in charge of the whole economy -- deciding what got produced, who worked where, and who got paid. What is the system called where the government owns everything?
answer: Communism
choices: Communism
Free-market capitalism
Constitutional democracy
Traditional feudalism
context: Fidel Castro's July 26 Movement entered Havana on January 1, 1959. He served as Prime Minister from February 1959, First Secretary of the Cuban Communist Party from 1965, and President 1976-2008. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro.

question: In April 1980, six Cubans stole a city bus and crashed it through the iron fence of a foreign embassy in Havana, the capital of communist Cuba. They were begging for asylum from Fidel Castro's government. Furious, Castro pulled the Cuban police guarding the embassy -- and within 48 hours more than 10,000 desperate Cubans poured onto the embassy grounds asking to leave the country. Which foreign embassy was it?
answer: The Peruvian embassy
choices: The Peruvian embassy
The Spanish embassy
The Canadian embassy
The Mexican embassy
context: On April 1, 1980 six Cubans drove a bus through the Peruvian embassy gates in Havana. When Castro withdrew the Cuban security guards for 48 hours, 10,800 Cubans poured into the embassy grounds asking for asylum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: In 1980 the leader of a poor communist country briefly opened a harbor and told anyone who wanted to leave that they could sail to a nearby free country. Boats packed with families crossed the sea. What does this kind of mass escape tell you about that country's system?
answer: People were fleeing a system that had failed them
choices: People were fleeing a system that had failed them
The country had too many boats to store
The leader wanted to grow the population back home
The neighbors paid people to move in and work
context: Castro announced that Cubans who wished to leave could sail from Mariel harbor. From April through October 1980 about 125,000 Cubans crossed to Florida. Castro emptied several prisons and mental hospitals into the flow to embarrass the US. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: In 1980 the Cuban dictator Fidel Castro briefly opened the port of Mariel and told anyone unhappy with communist Cuba they could leave. From April to October that year, ordinary Cubans crowded onto boats and sailed north to Florida in what became known as the Mariel boatlift. About how many Cubans made it across?
answer: About 125,000
choices: About 125,000
About 12,500
About 1.2 million
About 15,000
context: About 125,000 Cubans left Mariel between April and October 1980. The exodus overwhelmed South Florida's absorption capacity and became a defining political event of the Carter presidency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, its huge subsidies of oil, food, and money to Cuba dried up almost overnight. Cuban dictator Fidel Castro's centrally-planned economy was left with almost no fuel, spare parts, or fertilizer. Cubans lost weight, blackouts became routine, and children were pulled from school to work fields with oxen. The Cuban government gave this long crisis a strangely soft-sounding official name. What did they call it?
answer: The Special Period
choices: The Special Period
The Ration Years
The Blockade Era
The Second Revolution
context: The 'Special Period in Time of Peace' (1990-95) saw Cuban GDP fall about 35 percent in three years and average daily calorie intake fall from ~2,900 to ~1,800. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Period.

question: During the summer of 1994, at the worst weeks of Cuba's post-Soviet economic slump under Fidel Castro, tens of thousands of desperate Cubans lashed together rafts from old truck tires, wooden pallets, and inner tubes. They pushed off from the beaches around Havana and tried to cross ninety miles of shark-filled open sea to Florida. Cubans called them balseros, or rafters. What does this desperate exodus tell you about how bad the shortages had become?
answer: The shortages were so severe that people risked their lives on the open sea to leave
choices: The shortages were so severe that people risked their lives on the open sea to leave
The Cuban government wanted people to leave and helped build the rafts
The Cubans had plenty of food but wanted to visit family
Florida offered free boats to anyone who wanted to come
context: 'Balseros' means raft-people. About 35,000 crossed to Florida in six weeks in 1994 aboard improvised rafts (balsas). The US shifted policy afterward to the 'wet foot / dry foot' rule that stood until 2017. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Cuban_rafter_crisis.

question: Armando Valladares was a young Cuban poet who refused to put a communist slogan on his desk at work. For that, Fidel Castro's government locked him away for 22 years. After his release he wrote a book called Against All Hope about what he had lived through in Cuba's prisons. Why did his book change many people's minds about Castro's government?
answer: It gave first-hand proof from someone who lived through it
choices: It gave first-hand proof from someone who lived through it
The government paid him to write it as an official story
It was written in a very old style that only scholars study
It won a medal from the United Nations that year
context: Armando Valladares was arrested in 1960 and released in 1982 after French intervention. His memoir Against All Hope (1985) documented the Cuban prison system for a global readership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armando_Valladares.

question: A country's new revolutionary government takes over all the big farms and factories. It puts a young fighter with no business or economics training in charge of the national bank. What tends to happen to the country's main crop output over the next few years?
answer: It collapses
choices: It collapses
It doubles because workers are more motivated
It stays exactly the same
It rises to world market prices
context: Ernesto 'Che' Guevara ran the National Bank of Cuba 1959-61 and the Ministry of Industry 1961-65. Cuban sugar output fell sharply during his industrial-diversification push. He left Cuba in 1965 and was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara.

question: After Fidel Castro's 1959 communist revolution seized businesses and farms across Cuba, waves of Cubans fled the island — first the middle class, then the 1980 Mariel boatlift, then the 1994 rafter crisis. By 2016 the number of Cubans living outside Cuba, plus their US-born children, had grown very large. Cuba itself has about 11 million people. What fraction of that number is the diaspora abroad?
answer: About a seventh (1.5 million)
choices: About a seventh (1.5 million)
About half (5 million)
About a hundredth (100,000)
About a fiftieth (200,000)
context: The 2010 US Census counted 1.79 million Cuban-Americans (immigrants plus US-born descendants), roughly a seventh of the island's population. Miami-Dade County alone had over 850,000. Source: US Census Bureau American Community Survey.

question: When the Soviet Union collapsed in December 1991, Cuba lost the enormous subsidies and cheap Soviet oil that had propped up its planned economy since the 1960s. Blackouts became routine, buses stopped running, and Cubans lost an average of twenty pounds each from food shortages. The government still insisted Cuba was a workers' paradise. Fidel Castro gave this long decade of hunger and rationing a strangely soft-sounding official name. What did he call it?
answer: The Special Period
choices: The Special Period
The Great Leap
The Rectification
The Struggle
context: Fidel Castro died November 25, 2016 at age 90. Raul Castro remained head of state until 2018 and party first secretary until 2021. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro.

question: In January 2009, after the 2008 financial crisis had thrown millions of Americans out of work, President Barack Obama's incoming economists Christina Romer and Jared Bernstein published a memo. It promised that if Congress passed a $787 billion stimulus law, US joblessness would stay below a specific rate. What rate did the memo predict?
answer: Below 8 percent
choices: Below 8 percent
Below 6 percent
Below 10 percent
Below 12 percent
context: The Romer-Bernstein memo of January 2009 ('The Job Impact of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan') published a chart showing unemployment peaking below 8%. In fact it reached 10.0% in October 2009, with ARRA fully in effect. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Recovery_and_Reinvestment_Act.

question: In January 2009 President Barack Obama's economists Christina Romer and Jared Bernstein predicted that if Congress passed the $787 billion stimulus law, the US jobless rate would stay under 8 percent. Congress passed the law that February. The jobless rate rose past 10 percent instead and stayed high for years. What is one honest lesson a kid should draw from that gap?
answer: Even smart experts often cannot predict what a whole economy will do
choices: Even smart experts often cannot predict what a whole economy will do
Government spending always works exactly as promised
The economy is easy to plan from Washington
Forecasts are always right if smart people make them
context: Christina Romer chaired the CEA; Jared Bernstein was Vice President Biden's chief economist. Their multiplier assumption of about 1.55 (each stimulus dollar raising GDP by $1.55) drove the under-8% forecast. Source: whitehouse.archives.gov (Romer-Bernstein memo, January 9 2009).

question: In 2009, in the middle of the Great Recession, President Barack Obama's economic advisers -- led by Christina Romer -- told the country that every $1 the government spent through the new stimulus law would grow the economy by about $1.55. Later independent studies found the real payoff was often less than $1, meaning the stimulus shrank the economy on net. What does that gap tell us about the original White House predictions?
answer: They were often too optimistic
choices: They were often too optimistic
They were far too pessimistic
They exactly matched later measurements
They were required by law to be conservative
context: The 1.55 multiplier assumption is what generated the sub-8% unemployment forecast; recalculated with standard New-Keynesian frictions and crowding-out, the same models produce multipliers in the 0.6-0.7 range. Source: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland, Journal of Economic Dynamics 2010.

question: The American economist Valerie Ramey studied enormous bursts of US federal spending during World War II and the Korean War, then measured what happens in ordinary peacetime. She found that in normal peacetime, every extra dollar the federal government spent produced less than a full dollar of new economic activity. What does that hint about ordinary federal spending?
answer: Government spending often does not pay for itself
choices: Government spending often does not pay for itself
Every dollar spent triples the economy
Only wartime spending is ever wasted
Peacetime spending always doubles wealth
context: Barro's estimate below 1 means: for every additional dollar of federal spending, private spending falls by MORE than the injected dollar, and total output rises by less than the dollar spent -- a net loss. Source: mercatus.org/publications/government-spending.

question: The 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to always ask a stubborn question: 'That dollar the government just spent -- where did it come from?' Any claim that government spending magically grows the economy by more than the dollar spent has to answer that question honestly. Bastiat's method names exactly three possible sources for a stimulus dollar. Which triple is the correct list?
answer: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
choices: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
Confiscated from a corporation, appropriated from foreign trade, or drawn from reserves
Levied on tariffs, extracted from monopoly rents, or issued as certificates
Deducted from savings, garnisheed from wages, or redistributed from land
context: Bastiat's method: whatever the government spends, that dollar came from a taxpayer's foregone consumption, a lender's foregone loan to a private borrower, or a printed dollar whose Cantillon-effect winners capture it before prices adjust. The SEEN is the road crew; the UNSEEN is the private capital that dollar would have financed. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: The American economist Valerie Ramey studied how much the US economy actually grows when the federal government spends one extra dollar in peacetime — on offices, gear, and salaries. Economists call that ratio the 'spending multiplier.' On average, across her peacetime data, how much did the economy grow for each extra dollar of federal spending?
answer: Less than one extra dollar
choices: Less than one extra dollar
About two extra dollars
About three extra dollars
About five extra dollars
context: Ramey's careful VAR estimates find defense multipliers of 0.6-1.1 depending on specification, and civilian peacetime multipliers below 1. Sub-1 means net crowding-out of private activity. Source: Journal of Economic Literature 49(3), 2011.

question: A town has a limited pool of savings that people are willing to lend. When the town government borrows a big chunk to build a new stadium, less is left for local shops and families to borrow. What is the standard name for private borrowers being pushed aside by heavy government borrowing?
answer: Crowding-out
choices: Crowding-out
Piling-on
Trickle-down
Overheating
context: 'Crowding-out' is the modern name for Bastiat's UNSEEN: the private investment the government's borrowing displaces. If crowding-out is large, the stimulus multiplier falls below 1. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowding_out_(economics).

question: In 2010, four American economists -- John Cogan, Tobias Cwik, John Taylor, and Volker Wieland -- published a paper in the Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control. They redid the Obama team's 2009 stimulus calculation but added standard real-world drag effects -- higher taxes later, private investment crowded out by government borrowing -- to the original 1.55 payoff model. What much smaller payoff number did their adjusted models produce?
answer: About 0.6-0.7
choices: About 0.6-0.7
About 1.3-1.4
About 2.0-2.2
About 2.8-3.0
context: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland showed the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 assumed away the crowding-out; realistic frictions bring the multiplier below 1. Source: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 34(3), 2010.

question: A town's mayor stands on the courthouse steps and announces, 'We will build a beautiful new bridge and put many good people to work!' A critic in the tradition of the 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat asks the same skeptical question every single time: before the bridge is built, before the first paycheck goes out, where does the money come from? What is the honest one-line answer to that question?
answer: Public works mean taxes on the people who would have spent that money elsewhere
choices: Public works mean taxes on the people who would have spent that money elsewhere
The bridge pays for itself because the workers spend their new wages in town
The Federal Reserve prints the money at no cost to anyone
Foreign banks lend the money and never ask to be paid back
context: Hazlitt's chapter 4 title, 'Public Works Mean Taxes,' compresses the whole Bastiat objection: the ribbon-cutting is seen; the tax that paid for it is unseen. Every 2009 ARRA critique is an application. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: The Bastiat objection to Keynesian public-works spending had a precedent in a 1932 letter to a British newspaper co-signed by four economists including F.A. Hayek, warning against Keynes-style deficit spending as a cure for the Depression. Which newspaper carried the letter?
answer: The Times of London
choices: The Times of London
The Manchester Guardian
The Daily Telegraph
The Financial Times
context: The October 19 1932 letter to The Times, signed by Hayek, T.E. Gregory, Lionel Robbins, and Arnold Plant, objected to Keynes's proposed public-works program on classical / Austrian grounds; Keynes and Pigou replied five days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynes-Hayek_letters.

question: In 1973 the American economist Murray Rothbard published a popular book called For a New Liberty. Its core idea was simple: keep the government small so that ordinary people are free to choose for themselves how they will live, work, worship, and trade. That whole worldview has a name. In one line, what is libertarianism?
answer: The belief that most decisions should be left to individuals rather than to governments
choices: The belief that most decisions should be left to individuals rather than to governments
The belief the government should own every business
The belief that everyone should live exactly the same
The belief that only royalty should decide anything
context: Macmillan editor Tom Mandel offered Rothbard the contract after reading his 1971 New York Times op-ed titled The New Libertarian Creed. The book, 327 pages in first edition, was Rothbard's first commercial book contract with a major trade house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: In 1973 the American economist Murray Rothbard published his most popular book with the Macmillan publishing house. The book laid out a complete libertarian vision of society -- private courts, private roads, no draft, no income tax -- and its subtitle was 'The Libertarian Manifesto.' What was its short main title?
answer: For a New Liberty
choices: For a New Liberty
The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
Power and Market
context: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto (Macmillan, 1973) was Rothbard's popular-audience movement statement, distinct from his systematic 1982 political ethics and his 1962 economic treatise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: In 1973 the American economist Murray Rothbard published his libertarian book For a New Liberty. The whole argument of the book rests on one central rule Rothbard called the non-aggression principle -- a moral line no person and no government is allowed to cross. Which rule does the book itself state?
answer: No person or group may aggress against the person or property of another
choices: No person or group may aggress against the person or property of another
Every person owes society a positive duty to reduce inequality where able
Government exists by the consent of the governed and rules only within that consent
The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right action
context: Rothbard called this the non-aggression axiom. He argued the whole libertarian program, on schools, roads, police, courts, and foreign policy, is what you get when you apply the axiom to state action as consistently as to private crime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: The American economist Murray Rothbard pushed further than most libertarians. He argued that people could live with no government at all — private firms would run the courts, the police, and even the roads, and every service would be paid for by voluntary choice rather than by tax. What is this stateless, purely free-market idea called?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism
choices: Anarcho-capitalism
Democratic socialism
Rule by kings
Government-run everything
context: Minarchism is the minimal-state position of Hayek and Milton Friedman. Classical liberalism dates to Adam Smith and the eighteenth century. Objectivism is Ayn Rand's philosophy. Rothbard's coinage set his position apart from all three by rejecting even a minimal state. Source: britannica.com/money/anarcho-capitalism.

question: In 1973 the American economist Murray Rothbard published his book For a New Liberty, defending an idea he called anarcho-capitalism -- a society with no state at all, only private property. Many parents hear the word and picture pure lawlessness. Rothbard pushed back with a specific answer to the obvious worry. Without any state, who does Rothbard say would handle police, courts, roads, and national defense?
answer: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
choices: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
Voluntary local militias governed by direct town-hall vote
A single elected but powerless minimal state of night-watchman scope
International arbitration panels enforcing global common law
context: Rothbard's central move: not the ABSENCE of law but the private-market PROVISION of it. The famous test case in the book is his chapter on private roads. Source: mises.org/library/book/for-new-liberty-libertarian-manifesto.

question: Nine years after his 1973 book For a New Liberty, the American economist Murray Rothbard published a longer and more philosophical work. It grounded libertarianism in the 17th-century English thinker John Locke's natural-rights tradition — the idea that every person owns their own body, labor, and property before any government exists. What is that 1982 book titled?
answer: The Ethics of Liberty
choices: The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
What Has Government Done to Our Money?
context: The Ethics of Liberty was published in 1982 by Humanities Press of Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey. If For a New Liberty was the popular manifesto, The Ethics of Liberty was the systematic treatise. A later edition (1998, NYU Press) carried an introduction by Hans-Hermann Hoppe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In 1974 the American thinker Robert Nozick published a famous libertarian book called Anarchy, State, and Utopia. He built his whole theory on an older idea he took from the English philosopher John Locke — the idea that people already own themselves, their labor, and what they earn, even before any government exists to hand out permissions. What is that older idea called?
answer: Natural rights
choices: Natural rights
Divine right of kings
Government-granted rights
Might makes right
context: Rothbard secularizes Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689): self-ownership, the labor theory of homesteading, and the strict limits on legitimate coercion. Rothbard drops Locke's theological grounding but keeps the natural-rights framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In 1973 the American economist Murray Rothbard released For a New Liberty, defending anarcho-capitalism -- a stateless society -- on grounds of natural rights and moral principle. That same year another American economist released a book called The Machinery of Freedom. It argued for the same stateless setup, but on practical results and cost-benefit reasoning rather than natural rights. Who wrote it?
answer: David Friedman, Milton Friedman's son
choices: David Friedman, Milton Friedman's son
Robert Nozick, Harvard philosopher
Hans-Hermann Hoppe, Rothbard's own student
Israel Kirzner, Austrian entrepreneurship theorist
context: David D. Friedman's The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism (Harper and Row, 1973) argued anarcho-capitalism on results-oriented grounds. The two 1973 manifestos, published within months of each other, defined the two branches of the modern anarcho-capitalist tradition, deontological (Rothbard) and consequentialist (Friedman). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: In 1974 the Harvard philosopher Robert Nozick published Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Nozick argued that a government should exist, but should only do three things: protect people from physical force, protect them from theft, and enforce broken contracts. No welfare programs, no post office, no public schools -- nothing else at all. A famous nickname is used for this very small kind of government. What is it called?
answer: A night-watchman state
choices: A night-watchman state
A total-planning state
A welfare state
A no-state anarchy
context: Nozick argued that a minimal state limited to protecting rights against force and fraud would arise from an anarchic starting point without violating anyone's rights, but that anything more would. Rothbard rejected the derivation and insisted the state itself is a rights-violation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy,_State,_and_Utopia.

question: The American economist Murray Rothbard's 1982 book The Ethics of Liberty spends most of its pages building his own natural-rights case for libertarianism, drawn from John Locke. Then, in Part IV, he turns critic and takes apart four other prominent theorists of liberty one by one — arguing each one's system fails to secure real freedom. Which four theorists does Rothbard critique in that Part IV?
answer: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
choices: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
Milton Friedman, James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Ronald Coase
John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, and Michael Sandel
Ayn Rand, Nathaniel Branden, Leonard Peikoff, and Tibor Machan
context: Rothbard reviews Mises's utilitarianism, Hayek's rule-of-law liberalism, Berlin's two-concepts-of-liberty essay, and Nozick's minimal-state derivation, and argues each falls short of a fully consistent libertarian position. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short essay called 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen.' In it he told the story of a boy who threw a rock and broke a baker's shop window. Some townspeople cheered, 'Good — this gives the glass-maker work!' Bastiat replied that they were forgetting something. What did he say they were forgetting?
answer: The shopkeeper cannot now buy shoes -- the shoemaker loses that sale
choices: The shopkeeper cannot now buy shoes -- the shoemaker loses that sale
The glass-maker gets richer for free
Broken things always help the economy
The boy's parents get a small tax refund
context: Bastiat was born in Bayonne on 30 June 1801 to a merchant family, orphaned by tuberculosis at nine, and raised by his grandfather on the family estate near Mugron. Bordeaux, Nantes and La Rochelle are the other three major French Atlantic ports of the period. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: The French thinker Frederic Bastiat lived quietly on his family farm in the town of Mugron, reading books about money and trade for twenty years. He was almost unknown until 1844, when a respected Paris economics journal printed his first paper — a defense of free trade against tariffs. Overnight he was famous across France. Which journal was it?
answer: Journal des Economistes
choices: Journal des Economistes
Revue des Deux Mondes
Le Constitutionnel
La Gazette de France
context: The Journal des Economistes was founded in 1841 by the Guillaumin house as the flagship of the French free-trade school. Bastiat's article 'The Influence of English and French Tariffs on the Future of the Two Peoples' appeared in the October 1844 issue. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In 1840s France, the economist Frederic Bastiat wrote his famous essays in short, plain French that a shopkeeper or a farmer could follow. Other economists of the day filled their pages with equations, graphs, and heavy academic jargon. Bastiat refused on purpose. He wanted regular readers -- not just professors -- to see through the traps in bad economic thinking. Which academic style did Bastiat deliberately refuse to use?
answer: Mathematical formalism
choices: Mathematical formalism
Historical narration
Satirical dialogue
First-person voice
context: Bastiat wanted his readers to be able to check the argument at each step without algebra. He used satirical dialogue (the Candlemakers' Petition), historical narration (the Sophisms), and first-person voice (Ce qu'on voit) freely; the one continental fashion he refused was the equation. Source: fee.org 'The Life of Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In 1840s Britain, a set of laws called the Corn Laws taxed imported grain so heavily that bread stayed expensive and poor families went hungry. Two Manchester factory owners -- Richard Cobden and John Bright -- founded the Anti-Corn Law League. Its members organized rallies, printed pamphlets, and gave speeches across the country to pressure Parliament to repeal the tax on foreign grain. What kind of movement was the Anti-Corn Law League?
answer: A free-trade movement
choices: A free-trade movement
A workers-only union
A movement to make bread illegal
A tax-raising campaign
context: Cobden's Anti-Corn Law League was founded in Manchester in 1838 and secured repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846. Bastiat visited England, met Cobden, and returned to Paris to build a French version of the League structure -- provincial chapters, a weekly paper, and public lectures. The Cobden Club came later (1866). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: After the 1848 revolution overthrew King Louis-Philippe of France, the French economist Frederic Bastiat was elected to the new National Assembly and re-elected the next year. He sat on the finance committee. Most of his speeches there attacked one particular political group whose ideas he believed would ruin the country. Which group did he mostly attack?
answer: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
choices: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
The legitimists of Henri de Chambord and Berryer
The Bonapartists of Louis-Napoleon and Persigny
The Orleanists of Thiers and the Duke de Broglie
context: Bastiat's parliamentary speeches, published in the Assembly journals of 1848-49, mostly opposed Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux and Proudhon's Bank of the People. He was not primarily engaged with the royalist, Bonapartist or Orleanist blocs. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In June and July 1850, dying of tuberculosis in Paris, Frederic Bastiat sent two short pamphlets to the printer in the space of a few weeks. Together they became the most-quoted pages he ever wrote and remain his two best-known short works. Name the pair.
answer: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
choices: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
Sophismes economiques and Petition des fabricants de chandelles
Harmonies economiques and Cobden et la Ligue
Propriete et loi and Capital et rente
context: La Loi (The Law) appeared in June 1850 and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen) in July 1850. The Sophismes had appeared as two earlier collections (1845, 1848); Harmonies was his unfinished positive treatise; Propriete et loi and Capital et rente were earlier short pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In the autumn of 1850 Frederic Bastiat's doctors sent him south, hoping the warm winter climate would ease his failing lungs. He travelled first to Pisa in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Which second Italian city did he then move to, and where he died on Christmas Eve?
answer: Rome
choices: Rome
Naples
Florence
Venice
context: Bastiat left Pisa for Rome in the late autumn of 1850 and lodged near the Piazza di Spagna. He died there on 24 December 1850 and is buried in the French national church of San Luigi dei Francesi. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Bastiat set out to answer the socialists on their own ground by showing that free exchange produces spontaneous cooperation rather than class conflict. He died before finishing the book, and only the first part appeared in his lifetime; editors later assembled the rest from his notebooks. What is the book called?
answer: Harmonies economiques
choices: Harmonies economiques
Cours d'economie politique
Traite d'economie politique
Principes d'economie politique
context: Harmonies economiques was Bastiat's attempt at a systematic positive doctrine, and he considered it the work he would be remembered for; only about half was in print at his death. Traite d'economie politique was Jean-Baptiste Say's 1803 textbook; Cours and Principes are common French treatise titles used by others. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: By Christmas Eve, 24 December 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat lay dying of tuberculosis in a rented room in Rome, only 49 years old. Friends kept vigil at his bedside. According to them, in his last hour he kept murmuring the same two-word French phrase over and over -- as if to remind them what he had spent his life defending in pamphlet after pamphlet. The phrase was:
answer: 'La verite, la verite'
choices: 'La verite, la verite'
'La liberte, la liberte'
'La justice, la justice'
'La patrie, la patrie'
context: The account of the deathbed scene comes from Prosper Paillottet, one of the editors of the posthumous Oeuvres completes, who was in the room. Bastiat had built his method around the discipline of not lying about consequences; the reported dying words -- 'the truth, the truth' -- were taken by his friends as the summary of that vocation. Legend, but well-attested. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Two economic concepts still standard in every modern textbook were introduced by Frederic Bastiat in the essays of 1848-1850. One is the parable of the broken window, which teaches the student to count what a policy destroys as well as what it creates. What is the OTHER concept?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Comparative advantage
Diminishing marginal utility
The velocity of money
context: Bastiat argued that every choice must be judged against the foregone alternative -- what the broken-window essay calls 'that which is not seen' -- and modern textbooks credit him with the first clear statement of opportunity cost. Comparative advantage is Ricardo (1817); marginal utility is Menger, Jevons and Walras (1871-74); the velocity of money goes back to the classical quantity theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In September 1970 The New York Times Magazine ran a short essay by the American economist Milton Friedman about what a business should really do. Friedman argued that a company's leaders should focus on running the company well and earning honest returns for the shareholders who owned it — not on chasing every fashionable social cause. The Times gave the essay a title that quickly became one of the most famous in business history. What title did they give it?
answer: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
choices: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
The Corporation as a Moral Agent
Ethics in the Marketplace
The Purpose of the Firm
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits' (New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970). Often called the Friedman Doctrine. Source: nytimes.com/1970/09/13/archives.

question: In September 1970 the American economist Milton Friedman wrote a famous essay in the New York Times Magazine titled 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits.' In it, Friedman said a company's executive really works for one specific group of people, and that group's interests set his job duties. Which group is it?
answer: The shareholders
choices: The shareholders
The customers
The federal government
The neighborhood community
context: Friedman: the executive is an employee of the shareholders and should generally maximize corporate profits within the rules of law and ethical custom. Any expenditure of shareholder money on the executive's own social projects is other people's money on his priorities. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (September 13, 1970).

question: In his 1970 New York Times essay on business, the American economist Milton Friedman drew a sharp line. He said a company's boss can spend his own paycheck on any cause he wants -- that is his own money to give away. But if the boss spends the company's money on a cause the owners never voted for, that is a very different matter. What is the boss free to do only with his own salary?
answer: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
choices: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
Deposit it in a personal bank account
Pay his personal income taxes
Buy shares in his own company
context: Friedman's careful distinction: private-individual charity is voluntary and comes from one's own money; corporate-resource philanthropy uses shareholders' money for the executive's own priorities without their consent. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: In his 1970 New York Times essay, the American economist Milton Friedman said a company executive is right to chase profit for the shareholders, but only inside certain limits. Friedman named two kinds of rules the executive must follow while doing his job. Which pair does he name?
answer: Both law and ethical custom
choices: Both law and ethical custom
Only the letter of federal statutes
Only the moral code of the CEO's church
Only quarterly earnings targets
context: Friedman's precise phrasing: the executive should run the business to make as much money as possible 'while conforming to the basic rules of the society, both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom.' He is not defending fraud or predation. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: In his famous 1970 New York Times Magazine essay, the American economist Milton Friedman warned that if the leaders of a company must serve their workers, their town, the environment, and the shareholders all at the same time, a serious problem shows up in how anyone can hold those leaders to account. What is the problem Friedman named?
answer: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
choices: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
They must consult a national advisory panel
They automatically qualify for federal subsidies
They lose access to corporate liability protection
context: Friedman's institutional-design point: multi-stakeholder mandates leave the executive without a specific principal to answer to. Any decision can be justified by naming which stakeholder it served. The shareholder-only mandate is disciplining precisely because it names one clear principal. Source: Friedman (1970); Jensen + Meckling, 'Theory of the Firm' (JFE 1976).

question: The 1970 New York Times Magazine essay by the American economist Milton Friedman was really the popular expansion of a single chapter he had written eight years earlier, in a 1962 book that laid out his whole case for free markets and limited government. The Times essay only shortened and sharpened that one chapter. Which 1962 book was it?
answer: Capitalism and Freedom
choices: Capitalism and Freedom
A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
Free to Choose
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 8, made the shareholder-primacy argument that the 1970 NYT essay condensed and popularized. Friedman had been making the argument for at least a decade before the magazine version. Source: Friedman (1962), Chapter 8.

question: In 1970 the American economist Milton Friedman wrote a famous essay in the New York Times Magazine arguing that a company's managers work for its shareholders -- the people who own the company -- and their job is to earn a profit within the rules. Today, Environmental, Social, and Governance investing (called ESG) asks corporations to steer profits toward social causes chosen by executives. Friedman's 1970 argument is the main intellectual pushback against ESG. In one phrase, what is his critique?
answer: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
choices: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
A regressive tax on middle-class households
A violation of federal antitrust law
An invitation to hostile foreign takeover
context: Classical-liberal critics of ESG apply the Friedman 1970 frame directly: fund managers directing corporate votes toward ESG goals are spending beneficiaries' assets to pursue the managers' own values without explicit consent. Source: Friedman (1970) as applied in Fink CEO-letter debates 2018-24.

question: In 1970 the American economist Milton Friedman argued that a company's one job was to make money for its shareholders — anything else was managers spending 'other people's money' on their own favorite causes. For decades that view dominated US business. Then in August 2019 the Business Roundtable, a Washington lobby group of nearly 200 top American CEOs, put out a Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation that publicly broke with Friedman's rule. How many CEOs signed the statement?
choices: About 50
context: The Business Roundtable's Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation (August 19, 2019) was signed by 181 CEOs and formally endorsed stakeholder capitalism over pure shareholder primacy. It was widely read as a direct response to renewed attention to the Friedman doctrine. Source: businessroundtable.org (August 2019).

question: On September 13, 1970, the American economist Milton Friedman published a short essay in the New York Times Magazine called 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits'. His worry was that a corporate executive who spends the company's money on his own favored social causes — without asking the shareholders who actually own the firm — is quietly acting as a self-appointed tax collector. The essay boiled that worry down to one memorable phrase. Which phrase is it?
answer: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
choices: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
Serving all masters at once
Building the corporate community
Protecting long-term brand value
context: The Friedman phrase focuses attention on WHOSE money is being spent and WHOSE priorities are being served. Even a well-meaning executive-imposed cause is a use of shareholder assets without shareholder mandate. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times essay argued that a company's only social duty was to make money for its shareholders. Decades later a wave of business school professors pushed back. Michael Porter of Harvard wrote about 'shared value.' Colin Mayer of Oxford wrote about the purpose of the firm. Rebecca Henderson of Harvard published Reimagining Capitalism. All three level the same charge at Friedman. What do they say his shareholder-only rule gets wrong about companies?
answer: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
choices: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
That the shareholder-only mandate should be criminalized federally
That the shareholder-only mandate applies only to European firms
That the shareholder-only mandate is unconstitutional under state law
context: The pro-stakeholder rebuttal, in various forms: attending to environmental, social, and community outcomes builds long-term corporate value that shareholder-narrow maximization misses. Friedman's response is that such considerations can be voluntarily adopted by shareholders themselves; executive imposition still lacks mandate. Source: Porter + Kramer, HBR (2011); Mayer, Prosperity (Oxford 2018); Henderson, Reimagining Capitalism (Public Affairs 2020).

question: In 1963 a huge 860-page economics book came out titled 'A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960'. It walked readers through a hundred years of American money and banking. Decades later, Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke called its chapter on the Great Depression the best account of the worst US economic disaster ever written. Who were the two economists who wrote the book together?
answer: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
choices: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow
John Maynard Keynes and Roy Harrod
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
context: Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research through Princeton University Press. It became one of the most influential economics books of the 20th century. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1963 the American economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published a huge history of US money. Chapter 7 -- 'The Great Contraction 1929-1933' -- argued that the Great Depression was mainly a money failure. Between 1929 and 1933 the M2 money supply (cash plus checking and savings deposits) shrank sharply while the Federal Reserve stood back and did nothing. By about what percent did M2 shrink in those four years?
answer: About 33 percent
choices: About 33 percent
About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
context: The M2 money supply contracted roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933. Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have prevented this by acting as lender of last resort during bank failures. It did not. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: The United States had about 25,000 commercial banks operating in 1929, each one holding neighbors' savings. Then between 1930 and 1933 the Federal Reserve allowed the money supply to shrink by about a third, and wave after wave of bank runs swept the country. Historians call this stretch the Great Contraction — the banking collapse at the heart of the Great Depression. How many American banks failed during those four years?
answer: About 9,000
choices: About 9,000
About 500
About 25,000
About 1,200
context: Roughly 9,000 US banks failed 1930-33 -- about a third of all banks. Each failure destroyed the deposits held there (no FDIC until 1933), further contracting the money supply. The Fed, chartered specifically to be lender of last resort, mostly stood aside. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: In their 1963 book on US money, the American economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued the Federal Reserve had made the Great Depression much worse. One key reason: in 1928 the strong leader who had guided the Fed for over a decade died suddenly. Without him the Fed splintered into feuding regional banks with no clear plan going into the 1929 crash. What did this leadership gap show?
answer: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
choices: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
Central banks always make the same choices no matter who leads
Only elected officials matter in economic policy
Committees always outperform any single leader
context: Strong died in October 1928, less than a year before the crash. His absence left the Fed without a dominant voice able to force the system into aggressive lender-of-last-resort action during the 1930-33 bank failures. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: In their 1963 book A Monetary History of the United States, the American economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz uncovered an internal Federal Reserve doctrine that had helped destroy the banking system in the early 1930s. According to this doctrine, the Fed should stand back and refuse to rescue banks it judged unsound -- letting them fail as a kind of purge. What is this rescue-averse Fed doctrine usually called?
answer: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
choices: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
The gold-standard doctrine
The Bagehot doctrine
The monetarist doctrine
context: The real-bills doctrine's liquidationist descendant held that the Fed should not lend to banks whose portfolios contained questionable loans -- exactly the banks needing rescue in 1930-33. The doctrine ensured the Fed refused to provide the liquidity that could have stopped the cascade. Source: Grokipedia 'Real bills doctrine' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 Ben Bernanke, then a Federal Reserve governor who had trained as an economic historian of the Great Depression, gave a speech in Chicago at a conference honoring Milton Friedman's 90th birthday. Bernanke closed by turning directly to Friedman and his co-author Anna Schwartz — the two economists whose 1963 book had blamed the Fed for turning a 1929 downturn into the Great Depression. What did Bernanke admit to them at the close of his speech?
answer: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
choices: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
You were partly right, we admit some errors were made
You were largely wrong, but your work provoked useful thinking
You were right about the mechanics but wrong about the ultimate cause
context: Bernanke's November 8 2002 speech at Friedman's 90th-birthday conference conceded institutional Fed responsibility for the Great Depression -- an extraordinary public admission that made the Friedman-Schwartz thesis officially accepted. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: The Austrian school of economics -- founded in Vienna by Carl Menger and later carried forward by Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek -- looks back at America's roaring 1920s and says the Federal Reserve's loose credit and easy money in those boom years were themselves the cause of the 1929 crash. Cheap loans drove up stocks and factories that would never have been built at real interest rates. In the Austrian view, the crash and the Great Depression that followed were what?
answer: The unavoidable hangover after an artificial boom
choices: The unavoidable hangover after an artificial boom
A random bad-luck event with no economic cause
A result only of tariffs, not money or credit
A normal year, no worse than any other
context: The Austrian addition: the 1929 bust was not just an accident that the Fed mishandled; it was the necessary correction of the malinvestment the Fed's own 1921-29 easing had produced. The two 1963 books agree that the Fed erred; they disagree about which decade's error was primary. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Milton Friedman won the Nobel; his coauthor Anna Schwartz never did -- even though their Monetary History of the United States remains the definitive American monetary history. Their book argued the Great Depression became a decade-long catastrophe because of one institution's mistake. Which one?
answer: The Federal Reserve
choices: The Federal Reserve
The US Treasury
The New York Stock Exchange
The Bank of England
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on monetary theory and consumption analysis. Schwartz's absence from the prize list is often cited as an example of the discipline's gender-biased recognition practices. Source: Grokipedia 'Anna Schwartz' (2026-09-05).

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz's 1963 book 'A Monetary History of the United States' argued that the Federal Reserve's tight-money policy from 1929 to 1933 turned an ordinary downturn into the Great Depression. For decades the Fed rejected that charge. Then in November 2002 Fed governor Ben Bernanke publicly agreed with the two authors and apologized on the Fed's behalf. What broader point about political economy does Bernanke's admission press?
answer: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
choices: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
Institutional acceptance of criticism has no effect on future policy
The Fed rarely acknowledges past errors publicly
Fed doctrine is entirely determined by whoever chairs the FOMC
context: The 2002 concession shaped Bernanke's own 2008 response (aggressive lender-of-last-resort action, massive QE). Austrian critics argue that by avoiding the 1930s error Bernanke created a different error -- long-lasting cheap money that seeded the 2020-24 inflation. Institutional learning has costs as well as benefits. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview at age 92, Anna Schwartz delivered a striking verdict on Ben Bernanke's crisis response. It effectively reversed the endorsement Bernanke had claimed six years earlier at Friedman's birthday party. What did she say about him?
answer: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
choices: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
That he was implementing exactly the policy she and Friedman had recommended
