That his response would restore price stability within one year
That she remained firmly in agreement with his approach
context: Schwartz's October 2008 Wall Street Journal interview sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response. Six years after Bernanke had claimed the Friedman-Schwartz mantle at the birthday party, the surviving coauthor publicly withdrew the endorsement. Source: Wall Street Journal (October 18 2008).

question: In March 1975 the American economist Milton Friedman took a six-day trip to a South American country. A private business group there had invited him. He met the country's military ruler for about 45 minutes and gave talks in the capital on how to stop the country's runaway inflation. Which country did Friedman visit?
answer: Chile
choices: Chile
Argentina
Peru
Brazil
context: Friedman visited Chile March 1975 at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He met Augusto Pinochet briefly and wrote one follow-up letter with monetary and economic recommendations. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: In the late 1970s Chile — the long, narrow country on South America's Pacific coast — was one of the poorest economies on its continent. A group of Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago, later nicknamed the Chicago Boys, pushed the government to cut price controls, open the country to foreign trade, and let private firms grow instead of being run from the capital. What happened to Chile's economy over the next twenty years?
answer: The country grew much richer over the next 20 years
choices: The country grew much richer over the next 20 years
The country immediately got much poorer
Nothing changed at all
Everyone left the country
context: 'The Chicago Boys' were about 25 Chilean economists trained at Chicago under a 1955-founded exchange with the Catholic University of Chile. Their leaders included Sergio de Castro (Finance Minister 1976-82) and Hernan Buchi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Boys.

question: In 1975 the American economist Milton Friedman flew to Santiago, Chile, and gave a lecture on how to stop runaway inflation. His trip caused an uproar back home because Chile was ruled by a military government that had seized power in a coup on September 11, 1973. Critics accused Friedman of advising a dictatorship; Friedman replied that an economist offering technical advice was no different from a doctor treating a sick patient. Who was the general in charge of Chile when Friedman visited?
answer: Augusto Pinochet
choices: Augusto Pinochet
Salvador Allende
Eduardo Frei
Juan Peron
context: Augusto Pinochet came to power in the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew the elected socialist president Salvador Allende. He ruled until 1990. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet.

question: After Milton Friedman's 1975 visit to Chile, some critics accused the American economist of endorsing Chile's military dictator, Augusto Pinochet. In a 1976 letter to Newsweek magazine, Friedman answered them with one specific phrase about the Chilean government -- flatly rejecting any personal endorsement of the regime. Which line matches what Friedman wrote?
answer: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
choices: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
A shining example of Latin American governance
The best hope for South American development
A necessary transitional phase toward liberty
context: In his 1976 Newsweek letter Friedman described the Pinochet regime as 'one that I have nothing but dislike for.' He compared his visit to a doctor treating a patient in a country whose government he disapproved of. Source: Friedman, Newsweek (1976); Two Lucky People (1998).

question: In 1975 the American economist Milton Friedman visited Pinochet's Chile and gave the government advice on fighting runaway inflation. American protesters accused him for years afterward of helping a dictator. But in 1980 Friedman also visited a much larger communist country and gave its leaders very similar free-market advice -- and almost no one protested that trip. Which country was it?
answer: Communist China
choices: Communist China
The Soviet Union
Vietnam
Cuba
context: Friedman visited China in 1980, meeting Chinese leaders including Zhao Ziyang. He argued the selective outrage over his Chile visit reflected a political double standard, since the China visit went uncontested. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Starting in 1975, a group of about twenty-five Chilean economists nicknamed the Chicago Boys -- because they had studied under Milton Friedman at the University of Chicago -- took over Chile's economic policy. They sold off state industries, cut tariffs, opened the country to global trade, and tamed runaway inflation. In 1973 about 45 percent of Chileans lived in poverty. What was Chile's poverty rate by 2010, after 35 years of these free-market reforms?
answer: About 10 percent
choices: About 10 percent
About 60 percent
About 40 percent
Essentially unchanged
context: Chilean poverty fell from ~45% (1973) to ~10% (2010) as measured by the Chilean national statistics agency and the World Bank. Chile went from poorest to richest per-capita economy in South America. Source: worldbank.org (Chile poverty and inequality data).

question: General Augusto Pinochet's own 1980 Chilean constitution required a special up-or-down vote after eight years to decide whether he could stay on for another presidential term. That vote came on October 5, 1988, when millions of Chileans went to the polls to answer a single Yes-or-No question about extending Pinochet's rule. What was the outcome of the vote?
answer: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
choices: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
Pinochet won and remained in power for another decade
The plebiscite was cancelled by the military
Pinochet abdicated before the vote was counted
context: The October 5, 1988 plebiscite voted Pinochet out. Free elections in December 1989 chose Patricio Aylwin as president; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Chilean_national_plebiscite.

question: In 1990 Chile returned to democracy after 17 years of military rule. During that time the Chicago Boys -- Chilean economists trained by Milton Friedman at the University of Chicago -- had reformed Chile's economy along free-market lines: privatized industries, low tariffs, open trade. The new elected governments were center-left. First the Christian Democrats took power, then Socialist-led coalitions. What did those elected left-leaning governments do about the Chicago Boys' free-market reforms?
answer: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
choices: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
They reversed nearly every reform within the first two years
They nationalized every privatized industry immediately
They abolished the central bank
context: Successor democratic governments in Chile substantially retained the market-economy framework across three decades of alternating center-left and center-right rule. Chile continued as the wealthiest South American economy per capita through the 2010s. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run macro data).

question: In 1976 the American economist Milton Friedman was invited to Stockholm, Sweden to accept one of the most prestigious awards in his field. Protesters showed up at the ceremony to denounce his 1975 visit to Pinochet's Chile, but Friedman gave his lecture anyway. Which specific Nobel award did Friedman win that year?
answer: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
The Nobel Peace Prize
The Nobel Prize in Literature
The Franklin Institute Bower Award
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economic Sciences 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Protests at the Stockholm ceremony centered on the Chile visit. Source: nobelprize.org (Friedman 1976).

question: After the American economist Milton Friedman advised Chile's finance ministers in 1975, critics used the Chile case to argue that free-market economics could not be separated from military dictatorship. Friedman rejected that link by pointing to a simple pattern in his own career of travels: he had also given advice and lectures in several other authoritarian countries during the Cold War, and had heard nothing like the same protests then. What was that pattern Friedman pointed out?
answer: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
choices: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
He refused ever to enter any country ruled by a dictator
He only visited democracies aligned with the US
He limited his travel exclusively to Western Europe
context: Friedman visited Communist China (1980), the Soviet Union, and Yugoslavia in earlier years, giving similar advice without generating comparable protests. He argued the selective outrage over Chile reflected political, not analytical, judgment. Source: Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Chile's economic story runs from 1973, when General Augusto Pinochet's coup ended democracy, through the Chicago Boys' free-market reforms of the late 1970s, past the October 1988 plebiscite that voted Pinochet out, and on into the 2010s under a series of elected governments. Economists often cite this whole stretch as a real-world natural experiment in what happens when a poor country switches to market rules. Which one-sentence summary is most accurate to that record?
answer: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
choices: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
Chile remained the poorest South American economy throughout the entire period
Chile experienced total economic collapse and mass emigration
Chile abandoned all market reforms within five years of democratization
context: The record: Chile in 1973 was the poorest large South American economy; by the 2000s it was the richest per capita; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful and free-market reforms were substantially retained by successor democratic governments. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run data).

question: In 1968 the American economist Milton Friedman gave a famous address to the American Economic Association. He warned that when a central bank prints extra money to push unemployment down, the trick works for a little while — but soon prices across the whole economy start rising and rising, and the jobs the printing was supposed to create do not last. What is that steady rise in prices called?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
Full employment
Barter
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (American Economic Review, March 1968), from his December 29, 1967 AEA presidential address. Source: jstor.org (Friedman AER 1968).

question: In his December 1967 presidential address to the American Economic Association — published in 1968 — the American economist Milton Friedman argued that the long-run US jobless rate is set not by central-bank money-printing but by real things in the economy: how long it takes workers to find new jobs, personal choices about work and family, and rules like the minimum wage. What did Friedman call this long-run floor for unemployment?
answer: The natural rate of unemployment
choices: The natural rate of unemployment
The equilibrium wage floor
The frictional threshold
The employment ceiling
context: Friedman's natural-rate hypothesis: there is a rate of unemployment determined by real, non-monetary factors. Monetary policy cannot push unemployment permanently below it; it can only produce temporary reductions at the cost of accelerating inflation. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: For years many economists believed a government could always trade a little more inflation for a little less unemployment. One skeptic in 1968 warned that in the long run this trade-off would break down. What did he say would happen to the trade-off over time?
answer: Collapse
choices: Collapse
Steepen sharply
Move upward for a decade
Remain constant forever
context: Friedman argued that once workers expected 4% inflation, they would demand 4% higher nominal wages, and unemployment would return to the natural rate -- with 4% inflation now baked in. The trade-off vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: In the late 1960s two American economists working separately -- Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps -- reached the same striking conclusion. No matter how much money a government printed to try to cut unemployment, the jobless rate always drifted back to a certain level built into the economy itself: how quickly people found new jobs, how many workers matched what employers needed, how flexible wages were. What is that built-in level of unemployment called?
answer: The natural rate of unemployment
choices: The natural rate of unemployment
The full-employment ceiling
The minimum-wage floor
The consumer price line
context: Edmund Phelps published 'Phillips Curves, Expectations of Inflation and Optimal Unemployment over Time' (Economica, August 1967) shortly before Friedman's AER paper. Phelps won the Nobel in 2006 specifically for this work. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Phelps 1967).

question: In the 1950s a New Zealand-born economist named A.W. Phillips drew a famous chart showing that when unemployment was low, wages tended to rise fast. Governments loved it — hire more workers, get more wages. Then in 1967-68 the American economist Milton Friedman and Columbia's Edmund Phelps updated the chart by adding one piece Phillips had left out: what workers and shoppers already believe prices will do next year. What is this missing piece called?
answer: Inflation expectations
choices: Inflation expectations
Federal deficit levels
International trade balances
Corporate tax rates
context: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve: workers demand nominal wages that account for expected inflation. Once expectations adjust, the trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman (1968); Phelps (1967).

question: In 1968 the American economist Milton Friedman warned that if the Federal Reserve tried to push unemployment below its natural floor by printing money year after year, the country would eventually face runaway price increases. Through the 1970s the Fed did roughly that, hoping to keep American jobs plentiful. By the year 1980, how high had the yearly jump in US consumer prices climbed?
answer: Over 13 percent
choices: Over 13 percent
About 1 percent
Over 30 percent
About half a percent
context: US CPI inflation ran ~2% in 1965, rising to ~13% by 1980. Unemployment did not fall permanently; both inflation and unemployment were high (stagflation) -- exactly what Friedman's 1968 address had predicted twelve years earlier. Source: bls.gov (CPI historical).

question: In the 1970s an American economy had high inflation (prices rising fast) and high unemployment (many out of work) at the same time. Older theory said one problem was supposed to push down the other. What one-word name did economists give this new mix?
answer: Stagflation
choices: Stagflation
Depression
Deflation
Recession
context: Stagflation (stagnation + inflation) is the name for the 1970s combination of high unemployment and high inflation. The word was coined by British politician Iain Macleod in 1965. It marked the failure of the stable-Phillips-curve consensus. Source: Grokipedia 'Stagflation.'

question: The American economist Milton Friedman argued that if a government tries to trick its way out of unemployment by secretly printing money and letting prices rise, the trick works only for a short time. Once workers and shopkeepers catch on and start demanding higher wages and prices to match the coming inflation, the surprise is gone. What happens to unemployment once people begin to expect the higher prices?
answer: It rises back to its natural level, only now with high inflation on top
choices: It rises back to its natural level, only now with high inflation on top
It stays permanently low forever
It falls all the way to zero
It becomes disconnected from prices entirely
context: Friedman received the 1976 Nobel 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Phelps received the 2006 Nobel specifically for the natural-rate work. Source: nobelprize.org.

question: Milton Friedman's 1968 natural-rate idea came with a warning for any central bank tempted to push unemployment permanently below its natural floor by printing money. Say the US Federal Reserve tried exactly that year after year, hoping to keep American jobs plentiful. What does natural-rate theory predict must happen?
answer: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
choices: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
Doing so requires only a one-time inflation shock
Doing so is impossible without changing the natural rate itself
Doing so imposes no long-run inflation cost at all
context: The accelerationist implication: if the Fed keeps trying to push unemployment below natural, it must keep raising expected inflation to keep workers surprised. 4% then 8% then 16% -- eventually the monetary system breaks down. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: Milton Friedman's 1968 address 'The Role of Monetary Policy' laid the groundwork for a specific rule that most developed-country central banks — the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, the European Central Bank — have followed since the early 1990s. Instead of chasing lower unemployment, they now publicly commit to holding one number steady. Which practice grew out of Friedman's address?
answer: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
choices: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
Fixed exchange rates against gold
Direct government spending controls
Complete abandonment of any monetary rule
context: Modern inflation targeting (New Zealand 1990, then dozens of countries) rests on the Friedman-Phelps insight: keep inflation expectations stable and the economy tends toward the natural rate. Wandering targets undermine expectations and produce accelerationist dynamics. Source: rbnz.govt.nz (New Zealand inflation-targeting history).

question: In 1974 the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek won the Nobel Prize in Economics for one central idea. Hayek argued that a whole modern economy — millions of workers, farms, factories, and shops — holds too many small local facts about prices, needs, and shortages for any government committee, no matter how smart, to ever gather in one place. What is the name for this idea?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The tax problem
The tariff problem
The lawyer problem
context: Friedrich August von Hayek (May 8, 1899 -- March 23, 1992). Mises was his teacher (born 1881); Menger founded the Austrian school in 1871 (born 1840); Rothbard was an American disciple (born 1926). Source: Wikipedia, Friedrich Hayek; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: In the 1920s in Vienna, Austria, a young economist named Friedrich Hayek regularly attended a famous private seminar held every other Friday night. The seminar was run by an older Austrian economist in his office at the Vienna Chamber of Commerce, and Hayek always said this man had taught him real economics. Who was Hayek's mentor?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Hayek attended Mises's Privatseminar (Mises-Kreis) in Vienna throughout the 1920s. Bohm-Bawerk (1851-1914) had died before Hayek's student years; Menger (1840-1921) was gone from teaching; Schumpeter was contemporary but not Hayek's teacher. Source: mises.org profile.

question: In 1931 a young Austrian economist named Friedrich Hayek was invited by the London School of Economics to give four lectures. The lectures grew into a famous short book called Prices and Production, arguing that cheap credit and easy money engineered by central banks create false booms in an economy that must end in painful busts. What kind of economic theory was Hayek presenting in those London lectures?
answer: A theory of the business cycle
choices: A theory of the business cycle
A theory of ocean tides
A theory of language origins
A theory of animal breeding
context: Robbins was building up LSE's economics department and had read a Hayek article on underconsumption theory. Keynes was at Cambridge (and Hayek's later intellectual opponent); Pigou also at Cambridge; Marshall had died in 1924. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A von Hayek (1899-1992) at LSE'.

question: In 1931 the young Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek was invited to London by Lionel Robbins to give a series of four public lectures on business cycles. The talks — later published as 'Prices and Production' — went so well that the university offered Hayek a permanent chair he held from 1931 until he left for the United States in 1950. Which British university housed the chair Hayek held during those years?
answer: London School of Economics
choices: London School of Economics
University of Cambridge
University of Oxford
University College London
context: The Tooke Chair, named for Thomas Tooke, was LSE's senior economic-statistics post. Cambridge was the Keynesian citadel Hayek argued against; Oxford and UCL had different appointments. Source: LSE History blog on Hayek at LSE.

question: In 1944, during the last year of World War II, the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek published a short book aimed at British and American readers. It warned that even a well-meaning government that tried to plan a whole economy from the top down would slowly gather power in ways that crushed personal freedom. What was the book's title?
answer: The Road to Serfdom
choices: The Road to Serfdom
Human Action
Man, Economy, and State
The General Theory
context: Published 1944, the book was a wartime bestseller in Britain and the United States. Human Action (1949) was Mises's magnum opus; Man, Economy, and State (1962) was Rothbard's; The General Theory (1936) was Keynes's. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: In 1950 Friedrich Hayek left Britain for the United States and settled at the University of Chicago. But there was a wrinkle: the university's famous economics department, then dominated by mathematical Keynesians, refused to hire him. Chancellor Robert Hutchins arranged a professorship for Hayek in a different interdisciplinary unit instead. Which Chicago unit made Hayek a professor?
answer: The Committee on Social Thought
choices: The Committee on Social Thought
The Cowles Commission
The Chicago Law School
The Booth School of Business
context: The economics department found The Road to Serfdom too politically radioactive; the William Volker Fund financed his chair on the Committee. The Cowles Commission was the mathematical-economics group; Booth (then GSB) and the Law School were separate schools. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: In April 1947, two years after World War II ended, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek gathered around forty classical-liberal scholars from Europe and America at a mountain resort in Switzerland. Central planning and socialism were fashionable everywhere in the postwar world, and Hayek feared the old tradition of free markets and limited government would die out. The scholars founded a society named after that Swiss mountain to keep the tradition alive. What was it called?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Fabian Society
The Cato Institute
The Institute of Economic Affairs
context: The founding meeting was April 1-10, 1947, at Mont Pelerin above Lake Geneva. The Fabian Society was the older British socialist group Hayek argued against; Cato (1977) and the IEA (1955) came later, both influenced by Mont Pelerin alumni. Source: Mont Pelerin Society, Friedrich Hayek page.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1944 book 'The Road to Serfdom', written in London while German bombs still fell on the city, argued that when a national government tries to plan the whole economy from the top — deciding what factories will make, what workers will earn, and what shops will sell — the country tends to slide in one clear direction over time, no matter how kind the planners' intentions. Which direction did Hayek warn about?
answer: Toward more and more control over people's daily lives
choices: Toward more and more control over people's daily lives
Toward higher and higher production of every good
Toward a permanent balance between labor and capital
Toward automatic equality of income
context: The committee paired Hayek and Myrdal deliberately to honor both traditions. Samuelson won in 1970, Kuznets in 1971, Leontief in 1973 -- neighboring but not co-laureates. Source: Wikipedia, Friedrich Hayek.

question: In December 1974 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek traveled to Stockholm to accept the Nobel Prize in Economics. In his prize lecture he turned on his own profession, warning that economists had copied the look of physics and chemistry -- their equations, their charts, their claims to precise prediction -- without the real underlying knowledge those methods require. What was the biting title Hayek gave the Stockholm lecture that mocked his own field?
answer: The Pretence of Knowledge
choices: The Pretence of Knowledge
The End of Laissez-Faire
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The General Theory of Second Best
context: Delivered December 11, 1974. 'The End of Laissez-Faire' was Keynes's 1926 essay; 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' was Hayek's 1945 American Economic Review paper (the same theme but a different work); the theory of second best was Lipsey and Lancaster 1956. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: In his final book, published in 1988 when he was 89 years old, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that morals, family, property, and the market grew slowly over thousands of years — a whole living order no small group of clever planners could redesign from scratch without breaking it. Trying to rebuild society by pure reason, he said, was a very specific mistake. What did Hayek name that mistake?
answer: The fatal conceit — believing reason can build from nothing what history took ages to grow
choices: The fatal conceit — believing reason can build from nothing what history took ages to grow
The knowledge problem — planners lack the local details that prices reveal
The utopian mirage — the idea that a perfect society is within easy reach
The rationalist error — the belief that anything old must be worth keeping
context: The Fatal Conceit (1988) was edited by W. W. Bartley III as the first volume of Hayek's Collected Works. The Sensory Order (1952) was his cognitive-psychology book; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected earlier essays; The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) was his methodology book. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A veteran economist rejects both "conservative" and "libertarian" as labels. He wants a name for defenders of old freedoms — free speech, jury trial, honest money — against planners on every side. Which broad economic idea does his tradition most defend?
answer: That prices, laws, and customs grew over centuries and cannot be redesigned from scratch
choices: That prices, laws, and customs grew over centuries and cannot be redesigned from scratch
That every generation should tear down its inherited institutions and start again
That the wisest person in the room should decide the price of bread
That elected officials always know more than the buyers and sellers themselves
context: Hayek explained the choice in the postscript to The Constitution of Liberty (1960), 'Why I Am Not a Conservative,' invoking Burke's use of the term. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Imagine it is Saturday morning. You have two ways to spend the next few hours: you can play video games at home, or you can walk down the block and mow lawns for twenty dollars an hour. If you choose to play games, you cannot at the same time earn that twenty dollars in lawn money. Economists have a name for the value of the best thing you gave up. What is that kind of cost called?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Sunk cost
Fixed cost
Marginal cost
context: Friedrich von Wieser (1851 Vienna - 1926 St. Gilgen) succeeded Menger at the University of Vienna in 1903 and held the chair until 1922. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: At a baseball card show, two collectors stop at the same booth. A rookie card for a shortstop lies on the table. The first collector loves the shortstop's team and offers $50 for the card on the spot. The second collector does not care about baseball at all and would pay only $2 for the exact same card. What does this simple scene show about the 'value' of a card?
answer: Value is not a fixed number -- it depends on what each person wants
choices: Value is not a fixed number -- it depends on what each person wants
Every card has one true price for every buyer
Only experts can say what a card is really worth
Value is decided by a government office
context: Paula Wieser's marriage to Eugen Boehm-Bawerk made Boehm-Bawerk Friedrich Wieser's brother-in-law. The two studied together as students and worked in parallel for the rest of their careers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser, one of the founding economists of the Austrian school of economics, returned to Vienna in 1903 to take over his brother-in-law Carl Menger's teaching chair. But before that homecoming, Wieser had spent nearly twenty years teaching economics in another Habsburg capital, at a German-language university that served the empire's German-speaking students inside a mostly Czech-speaking city on the Vltava River. In which city did Wieser teach for those two decades?
answer: Prague
choices: Prague
Berlin
Heidelberg
Budapest
context: Wieser held the chair at the German-language Charles University in Prague from 1884 until his 1903 move to Vienna. Prague was then the second university city of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In 1917, in the middle of World War I, Emperor Karl I of Austria-Hungary picked the famous Austrian-school economist Friedrich Wieser to join his imperial cabinet. Wieser was placed in charge of the branch that oversees trade, business, and industry across the empire. What is that cabinet branch usually called?
answer: Commerce
choices: Commerce
Foreign Affairs
War
Justice
context: Wieser served as Austro-Hungarian Minister of Commerce from August 30, 1917 to November 11, 1918, spanning the empire's collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A hungry man eats one apple, then a second, then a third. The pleasure the third apple gives him is less than the pleasure the first one did. Nineteenth-century economists needed a word for the extra usefulness of that LAST unit added. In 1884 a Vienna economist coined the German compound Grenznutzen for it -- and its English translation is now the load-bearing concept of modern price theory. Which term is the English translation of Wieser's 1884 coinage?
answer: marginal utility
choices: marginal utility
consumer surplus
producer surplus
elasticity of demand
context: Grenznutzen = MARGINAL UTILITY -- the value of the last (marginal) unit consumed, and the reason a thirsty man in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and nothing for the tenth. Alfred Marshall coined 'consumer surplus' and 'producer surplus'; 'elasticity of demand' is also Marshall. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In the Austrian city of Vienna in the late 1800s, the economist Friedrich von Wieser watched a farmer stare at his empty field in early spring. The farmer could plant wheat, or he could plant barley -- but not both on the same land. If he chose wheat, the real cost he paid was not the money he spent on seed. It was the barley crop he could have grown on that same field and now never would. Wieser coined a German word for exactly this idea -- Alternativkosten. The English translation is now standard in every economics textbook. What is the English name for the cost the farmer bears?
answer: opportunity cost
choices: opportunity cost
sunk cost
marginal cost
fixed cost
context: Wieser's Alternativkosten translates as OPPORTUNITY COST -- the value of the next-best alternative use foregone. Sunk cost is spent-and-unrecoverable; marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; fixed cost does not vary with output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In 1889 the Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser, working in Vienna, published a book called Natural Value. Older thinkers had said the price of a thing came from the labor hours or the raw material inside it. Wieser and his teacher Carl Menger argued something new: value is not baked into the object at all — each person judges a thing by how much they personally want it in the moment. What does this idea, called subjective value, say decides what a thing is worth?
answer: How much any one person values it right now
choices: How much any one person values it right now
The hours of labor it took to make
A government-issued official price list
The weight of its raw materials
context: Der natuerliche Wert (1889) was Wieser's more readable systematic restatement of Mengerian marginalism. For many 1890s German readers, Wieser -- not Menger -- was HOW they first met the theory. Karl Menger the mathematician was Carl Menger's son. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A steel mill makes train wheels using iron ore, coal, and skilled workers. The classical economists said the wheels' value came from adding up the labor in each part. The Austrian school flipped it: the wheels' value comes from what customers pay for a working train, and that value flows backward to the parts. In the Austrian view, where does value start?
answer: With the customer's use for the final product
choices: With the customer's use for the final product
With the hours of labor put into each part
With the amount of coal burned to smelt the iron
With the age of the machinery used
context: Wieser's IMPUTATION THEORY (Zurechnung) determines factor values by attributing back to each an appropriate share of the final product's utility -- a marginalist answer to the classical labor-theory question, from the top down. Arbitrage is exploiting price gaps; aggregation adds micro-quantities; depreciation reduces capital value over time. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In a famous 1945 essay called 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that no small group of government central planners can ever gather all the little local details -- who wants what, where, when, at what price -- that regular people and market prices already carry, minute by minute, through the whole economy. What did Hayek call this fundamental limit of central planning?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The paperwork problem
The counting problem
The tax problem
context: Hayek attended Wieser's Vienna seminars in the early 1920s; he later wrote a warm memorial essay on his old teacher. Friedman, Rothbard, and Kirzner were all Americans of the next generation. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: An economist watched horse-and-buggy makers lose out to cars, silent-film stars lose out to talkies, and typewriters lose out to home computers. He said the market's most important trait is exactly this sweeping-away of the old by the new. What two-word phrase did he coin?
answer: Creative destruction
choices: Creative destruction
Comparative advantage
Marginal utility
Rational expectations
context: Schumpeter was Wieser's Vienna student and always named the 1914 Social Economics as a formative influence on his own systematic ambitions. Boehm-Bawerk was Wieser's brother-in-law, not his student. Haberler and Machlup were later Vienna alumni. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser was born a commoner (plain 'Friedrich Wieser') but died a nobleman ('Friedrich von Wieser'). The particle 'von' was not birthright; it was awarded to him personally in 1917, the same year Kaiser Karl I put him in the cabinet and seated him in the upper chamber. Into which Austro-Hungarian body was Wieser seated on his 1917 ennoblement?
answer: the House of Lords
choices: the House of Lords
the Imperial Council
the Diet of Bohemia
the Reichsrat lower chamber
context: Wieser was elevated to hereditary nobility (Freiherr, Baron) in 1917 and appointed to the Austrian House of Lords (Herrenhaus) the same year, alongside his Ministry of Commerce cabinet role -- an unusually rapid political promotion for an academic. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: The Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, both trained in Vienna, argued that market prices are messages that carry hidden information about what is scarce and what people want. Say the price of a loaf of bread suddenly jumps up. What does that rising price tell buyers and sellers across the country?
answer: Bread is now more scarce OR more people want it -- so use less and make more
choices: Bread is now more scarce OR more people want it -- so use less and make more
Bread will always be expensive from now on
The baker is being greedy for no reason
Nothing at all -- prices carry no information
context: Fritz Machlup (1902-1983) took his Vienna doctorate in 1923 with Mises's help, joined the Privatseminar, and moved to America in 1933 as a Rockefeller research fellow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: In 1962 the Austrian-American economist Fritz Machlup, teaching at Princeton, wrote a famous book. It was the first serious attempt to count a whole invisible slice of the American economy that nobody had measured before — the making, sorting, and sharing of knowledge itself (schools, research labs, publishing, software). What was the book's title?
answer: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
choices: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
The Theory of International Trade
The Wealth of Nations
The Affluent Society
context: The 1962 Princeton book coined and measured what Machlup called the knowledge industry: schools, research and development, media, communication, and information services. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: In 1962 the economist Fritz Machlup published a book that added up schools, publishing, research, and media -- and showed a startling share of the US economy was already about producing and moving ideas. His figure launched a new field. What did he name this sector?
answer: The knowledge economy
choices: The knowledge economy
The service sector
The tertiary economy
The information age
context: Machlup's 29% estimate for 1958 was published fifteen years before 'the information economy' became a business-magazine cliche. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: After World War II many free-market thinkers worried that socialism was winning across Europe. In 1947 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek gathered around 40 scholars at a Swiss mountain village to found a private society for classical-liberal ideas. Fritz Machlup was one of the founding members, and the group still meets each year today. What is that society called?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Cato Institute
The Cobden Club
The Adam Smith Society
context: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded by Hayek in 1947 at Mont Pelerin, Switzerland; Machlup was a founding member and served as President 1966-1968. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: In 1966, after decades of work at Princeton and Johns Hopkins, Fritz Machlup was elected to the top professional office in economics — chosen by his fellow economists as their leader for the year. It is the highest honor an American economist can receive from peers. Which office was it?
answer: President of the American Economic Association
choices: President of the American Economic Association
Chair of the Federal Reserve
Director of the National Bureau of Economic Research
Chief Economist of the World Bank
context: Machlup's 1966 AEA presidency was a rare case of a Mises-trained Austrian reaching the summit of the American mainstream without abandoning his tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/American_Economic_Association.

question: Fritz Machlup was an Austrian-American economist who in 1962 wrote a groundbreaking study measuring how much of the US economy was based on knowledge industries -- schools, research, media, publishing, software. Later in life he expanded that study into a much larger project. Between 1980 and 1984, Princeton University Press published his eight-volume set on the same topic. What is the collective title of that eight-volume set?
answer: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
choices: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
Human Action
The Constitution of Liberty
A Monetary History of the United States
context: The eight-volume series was completed posthumously by Machlup's colleagues and remains the most exhaustive academic treatment of the knowledge-industry idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: Austrian economists argue that a country's trade deficit is not automatically bad news. When Americans buy foreign cars, phones, and coffee, dollars flow overseas — but the Americans did not lose anything. They chose the trade freely. What do those Americans get in return for the dollars going overseas?
answer: Goods they voluntarily chose to buy
choices: Goods they voluntarily chose to buy
Nothing at all
Only future debt payments
Guaranteed job losses
context: Machlup's academic path ran Buffalo (1935) - Johns Hopkins (1947) - Princeton (1960) - NYU (1971 until his death in 1983). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: In 1923 the young Fritz Machlup earned his doctorate at the University of Vienna. His advisor was the founding figure of the whole Austrian tradition — the economist who in 1920 had famously argued that a socialist state cannot rationally plan an economy, because without real market prices its planners have no way to compare costs. Who supervised the 1923 thesis?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Friedrich von Wieser
context: Machlup took his Vienna doctorate in 1923 under Mises and became one of the youngest members of the Mises Privatseminar. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: In November 2022 the world's second-biggest cryptocurrency exchange, headquartered in the Bahamas and run by a young American named Sam Bankman-Fried, suddenly froze customer withdrawals. Depositors could not get their money out. Days later the company filed for bankruptcy. What was its name?
answer: FTX
choices: FTX
Binance
Coinbase
Kraken
context: FTX, founded 2019 by Sam Bankman-Fried, filed for Chapter 11 on November 11 2022 after a run triggered by a CoinDesk leak about its sister trading firm Alameda Research. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: In 2022 the young American Sam Bankman-Fried ran a huge crypto trading firm called FTX. It later came out that he was secretly using customer deposits to make risky bets at a sister firm. FTX crashed, customers lost billions, and he was convicted of fraud. Bitcoin itself, the underlying network, kept running as usual. What does FTX's collapse — while Bitcoin kept running — actually show was the source of the failure?
answer: The problem was a dishonest company -- not Bitcoin itself
choices: The problem was a dishonest company -- not Bitcoin itself
Bitcoin failed as a currency
All crypto companies always steal money
Governments were behind the collapse
context: Sam Bankman-Fried, MIT-educated, worked at Jane Street before founding Alameda Research (2017) and then FTX (2019). Arrested in the Bahamas December 12 2022. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: In the early 2020s a big crypto exchange called FTX -- run by a young man named Sam Bankman-Fried -- had a sister trading firm called Alameda Research, run by his close friend Caroline Ellison. When Alameda lost huge bets on risky trades, FTX secretly took its own customers' Bitcoin and dollar deposits and quietly used them to cover Alameda's losses, without ever telling the customers. What kind of act was that?
answer: Fraud
choices: Fraud
Charity
Insurance
A refund
context: Alameda Research, founded by SBF in 2017, was FTX's linked market-making and prop-trading arm. Its balance-sheet reliance on FTT triggered the November 2022 run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alameda_Research.

question: At its peak, the crypto exchange FTX -- run by Sam Bankman-Fried -- paid to put its name on the Miami Heat's basketball arena and hired stars like the quarterback Tom Brady and the basketball legend Shaquille O'Neal to promote the exchange in TV ads. Months later, in November 2022, FTX collapsed and was exposed as a fraud that had used customer deposits to cover its sister firm's losses. Why do risky firms buy stadium names and celebrity ads?
answer: It buys the appearance of trust before people ask hard questions
choices: It buys the appearance of trust before people ask hard questions
The advertising department is required by law
It saves them money on their office rent
It cuts their electricity bill significantly
context: FTX bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's arena in a 2021 19-year, $135M deal. The naming reverted after the bankruptcy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaseya_Center.

question: In November 2022 the crypto exchange FTX collapsed after a leaked balance sheet showed its sister firm, Alameda Research, was propped up by huge piles of FTT — a token FTX had simply invented and printed itself. A real reserve is supposed to be something the exchange cannot conjure into existence on demand. Why is an exchange counting its own made-up token as its main asset unsafe?
answer: The token's value depended on the exchange staying alive, so it was not a real reserve
choices: The token's value depended on the exchange staying alive, so it was not a real reserve
Tokens are not allowed to be counted for tax purposes
The government requires reserves in paper only
Digital tokens weigh too much to store
context: FTT was FTX's own exchange token. Alameda's balance sheet holding its sister exchange's own token as its largest asset was the market signal that led competitor Binance to announce it would sell its FTT holdings -- and that triggered the run. Source: coindesk.com (November 2 2022 report).

question: In November 2022 the crypto exchange FTX looked shaky because its biggest reserve was FTT, a token FTX had invented itself. A larger rival exchange, Binance, publicly announced it would dump every FTT coin it held. Trust cracked overnight. What happened right after Binance's announcement?
answer: Customers rushed to pull their money out in a run
choices: Customers rushed to pull their money out in a run
The government printed more tokens to help
The token doubled in value the same day
Nothing changed for the next six months
context: Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao's November 6 2022 announcement that Binance would sell its FTT holdings after the CoinDesk leak triggered mass customer withdrawals from FTX; the run began within hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: A crypto exchange promises its customers in writing: your deposits are held safe in separate accounts, and you can withdraw your coins at any time. Behind the scenes the owner is quietly moving customer money out of those accounts and into his own trading firm to cover losses it took on bad bets. When customers finally try to pull their coins out, the vault is empty. In finance and law, what is this called?
answer: Commingling customer funds with the firm's own trading
choices: Commingling customer funds with the firm's own trading
A legal short-term loan customers agreed to
Standard fractional-reserve banking
An audited overnight sweep account
context: The commingling-and-use of customer funds was the criminal act; it is the same failure mode as Mt Gox (2014) and MF Global (2011). Every exchange collapse of this shape has taught the same lesson: not your keys, not your coins. Source: cnbc.com (FTX bankruptcy filings coverage).

question: Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, was convicted on all seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy on November 2, 2023. On March 28, 2024 the federal judge Lewis Kaplan handed down his sentence in a Manhattan courtroom. What was the sentence?
answer: Twenty-five years in federal prison
choices: Twenty-five years in federal prison
Life in federal prison
Ten years in federal prison
Five years in federal prison and a fine
context: Kaplan's 25-year sentence covered wire fraud, securities fraud, and money-laundering conspiracy. FTX creditors were later paid back close to dollar-value on their claims by the bankruptcy estate, but of course missed the Bitcoin appreciation over the recovery years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried, the FTX founder later convicted of fraud, publicly told reporters and donors that his personal ethics came from a specific philosophical movement. Its stated aim was 'do the most good possible with your resources' — earn a lot of money and give it away to whichever causes save the most lives per dollar. What was that movement called?
answer: Effective altruism
choices: Effective altruism
Rational optimism
Longtermism
Utilitarian pragmatism
context: SBF had been publicly associated with 'effective altruism' since his Jane Street days; his stated ethic was that he would earn as much as possible and give it away. He then stole billions from his own customers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism.

question: You buy Bitcoin through a big online exchange. Your coins sit in the exchange's account, not on your own device — you just trust their website to say how much is "yours." Then the exchange freezes withdrawals and admits it lost the funds. Which Bitcoin slogan compresses the lesson?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Verify, do not trust
One computer, one vote
Do your own research
context: Every FTX customer who had trusted the exchange lost access; every customer who had self-custodied was untouched. The slogan predates FTX by years and got its clearest 21st-century test in November 2022. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Cold_storage.

question: Imagine the US Congress sets up a new safety agency to watch over the country's car makers -- crash tests, seat belts, emission rules. Over time the agency hires former car-industry lobbyists as staff and starts writing rules that mostly help the three biggest car makers, while burdening smaller rivals with paperwork. What is it called when watchdog agencies end up quietly serving the very industry they were meant to police?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Consumer surplus
Market discipline
Free enterprise
context: George Stigler (1911-1991) won the 1982 Nobel in economic sciences for his work on industrial structure and regulation. The 1971 paper is his most-cited contribution. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stigler.

question: In 1971 the American economist George Stigler at the University of Chicago published a landmark paper called 'The Theory of Economic Regulation.' It argued that government rules meant to protect the public from big business often end up serving that industry instead. The paper ran in an academic journal funded by Bell Labs, the AT&T research arm. Which journal ran it?
answer: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science
choices: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
The Journal of Political Economy
The American Economic Review
context: The Bell Journal (Spring 1971, volume 2 issue 1) published Stigler's paper. The journal is now the RAND Journal of Economics. Source: jstor.org (Stigler, Bell Journal 1971).

question: In his 1971 paper, the American economist George Stigler flipped the usual civics-class story about regulation. Instead of the government protecting the public from powerful industries, he said, regulation is 'acquired by the industry' — the firms lobby for the rules, shape them, and quietly run them. He said the rules are mostly run for what goal?
answer: For that industry's benefit
choices: For that industry's benefit
For the consumer's protection
For technological progress
For national security
context: The exact phrasing: 'As a rule, regulation is acquired by the industry and is designed and operated primarily for its benefit.' Stigler documented this pattern across occupational licensing, trucking, and utilities. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal Spring 1971.

question: Imagine Congress passes a new rule -- say, a sugar-import tariff -- that hands a small group of big American sugar producers millions of extra dollars each year. To pay for it, every regular family's grocery bill quietly rises by about $2 a year for candy, cereal, and soda. The sugar companies hire lobbyists and fight hard to keep the rule. Most families never even notice. What word describes the shape of those tiny per-family costs?
answer: Dispersed
choices: Dispersed
Delayed
Voluntary
Advertised
context: Stigler's concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern: a few firms gain a lot, millions lose a little each, so the concentrated side is worth organizing around and the dispersed side is not. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: Imagine a US state is debating a new law that says nobody may work as an interior designer until they first pass a difficult exam and pay a yearly fee for an official state license. This blocks would-be newcomers from just hanging out their own shingle. Which group will show up most eagerly at the state capitol to support the new licensing law?
answer: Established interior designers already in the field
choices: Established interior designers already in the field
Consumers who hire interior designers
New people hoping to enter the profession
State enforcement staff
context: Occupational licenses raise incumbents' incomes by restricting entry, so incumbent designers gain and future entrants lose. Stigler documented this pattern across barbers, morticians, accountants, and dozens of other licensed trades. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: In 1965 the American economist Mancur Olson published a book called The Logic of Collective Action. He built a careful model of how different groups fight to shape a new government rule to their own advantage — some groups tiny with millions of dollars at stake, other groups huge with only a few cents per person at stake. In Olson's model, which kind of group usually wins that fight?
answer: A small, well-organized group with a lot to gain from the rule
choices: A small, well-organized group with a lot to gain from the rule
The largest group of shoppers who each save a few cents
Brand-new workers who have not yet entered the field
The general public through town-hall votes
context: Sam Peltzman, 'Toward a More General Theory of Regulation' (Journal of Law and Economics, 1976), generalized Stigler's insight into a formal model in which regulators balance pressure from multiple interest groups. Source: jstor.org (Peltzman 1976).

question: The American economist George Stigler had a theory that when a state creates a board to regulate an industry, the board slowly ends up working for that industry instead of the public. To test it, he pulled years of rate rulings from state utility boards across the country — the panels that set the prices power and gas companies could charge. Which side did those boards keep favoring?
answer: The regulated utilities themselves
choices: The regulated utilities themselves
Residential ratepayers
Industrial customers
State treasuries
context: Stigler's electricity-rate case studies showed regulated rates systematically higher than they would have been under competition -- benefiting utility shareholders at consumer expense. Source: Stigler + Friedland, Journal of Law and Economics (1962) and Stigler 1971.

question: In 1887 the US Congress created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first big federal regulatory agency, to police the railroads. Later Congress also gave it power over trucking. Over the years the commission set the rates and routes trucking firms were allowed to use — and it quietly protected established truckers by making it very hard for new rivals to enter the market. When an agency that was supposed to police an industry ends up serving that industry instead, what is that pattern called?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Free-market competition
Antitrust enforcement
Consumer protection
context: The ICC had regulated interstate trucking rates and routes since the Motor Carrier Act of 1935. Stigler's analysis anticipated the 1980 Motor Carrier Act deregulation. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: George Stigler's work on regulatory capture — showing that industries end up controlling their own regulators — drove a big policy shift in Washington during the late 1970s. In 1978 President Carter signed a law freeing one industry to set its own routes and fares, and in 1980 he signed a matching law that freed the freight haulers of the interstate highways. Which two transport industries did those laws deregulate?
answer: Airlines and trucking
choices: Airlines and trucking
Railroads and shipping
Broadcasting and telephony
Banking and insurance
context: The Airline Deregulation Act (October 24, 1978, Carter) and Motor Carrier Act (July 1, 1980, Carter) were direct policy responses to Stigler-Peltzman capture analysis. Alfred Kahn led the airline deregulation as CAB chairman. Source: brookings.edu (transportation deregulation history).

question: Stigler's 1971 paper reframed a policy debate that had been mostly moral. Where welfare economics had asked 'what regulation SHOULD society want?', Stigler applied an economic method that asked a different question. Which question did his analytical move press?
answer: What regulation do interest groups actually DEMAND, and what does government SUPPLY?
choices: What regulation do interest groups actually DEMAND, and what does government SUPPLY?
What regulation would maximize national income under central planning?
What regulation would emerge from a Rawlsian veil of ignorance?
What regulation would satisfy median-voter theorem predictions?
context: Stigler's move: treat regulation as a PRODUCT with a market of its own. Industries demand it; politicians supply it in exchange for votes, contributions, and future employment. The public-interest justification is often a story told afterwards. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971), section II.

question: A high-school student asks how to test regulatory-capture theory. Stigler's own 1971 paper offered a specific empirical case where the theory made a distinctive prediction that public-interest theory did not. Which case did he treat as his sharpest test?
answer: Occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes without measurable quality gains
choices: Occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes without measurable quality gains
Antitrust litigation always benefits the largest firms
Central bank independence produces lower inflation
Minimum-wage laws reduce urban crime
context: If licensing existed to protect consumers, quality should rise sharply relative to unlicensed states. Stigler and later Morris Kleiner found instead that incumbent wages rose and quality effects were small or nonexistent -- the pattern predicted by capture theory. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: A mayor of a large American city promises voters more parks during his campaign. He also very much wants to be re-elected. So instead of putting the new parks in the poorer neighborhoods that need them most, he places them in swing districts where active voters will thank him at the ballot box. A whole branch of economics studies politicians as ordinary people chasing their own goals, just like this mayor. What is that branch called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Behavioral economics
Welfare economics
Game theory
context: Gordon Tullock (born February 13, 1922, Rockford, Illinois; died November 3, 2014) took a JD from Chicago in 1947 and never earned a PhD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Tullock.

question: Picture the boss of a large government office. He wants more staff, more prestige, and more power. So every year he asks the legislature for a bigger budget — even in years when there is less real work to do. In good years and bad, the office almost never volunteers to shrink itself. What does this repeating behavior show about how large government offices tend to act over time?
answer: They try to grow themselves, not shrink
choices: They try to grow themselves, not shrink
They shrink when work drops
They always spend less than they receive
They only follow what voters want
context: Tullock served in the US Foreign Service 1947-1956, with postings in Tianjin (during the Communist takeover), Hong Kong, and Korea. He later credited the experience with teaching him more about political incentives than any economics course. Source: Tullock, Selected Works (Liberty Fund, 2004).

question: The American economists Gordon Tullock and James Buchanan met at the University of Virginia in the late 1950s. They wanted to use economic tools — self-interest, trade-offs, incentives — to study politics itself, not just markets. In 1962 they wrote a founding book of the new field they called public choice. What was the title of the book they wrote together that year?
answer: The Calculus of Consent
choices: The Calculus of Consent
The Logic of Collective Action
Bureaucracy and Representative Government
The Politics of Bureaucracy
context: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy (University of Michigan Press, 1962) is Buchanan-Tullock's founding text. Tullock arrived at Virginia in 1958. Source: press.umich.edu (Calculus of Consent).

question: In 1966 the American economist Gordon Tullock founded a new academic journal for a field he and his co-author James Buchanan had helped invent. The field studied politicians, voters, and bureaucrats as ordinary people chasing rewards — votes, budgets, careers — not as saints working only for the common good. Tullock and Buchanan argued this changed how you should read almost every government decision. What is the name of that field?
answer: Public Choice
choices: Public Choice
Public Relations
Political Science
Ancient History
context: Tullock founded 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making' in 1966 and renamed it Public Choice in 1968. He edited it for more than three decades. Source: springer.com/journal/11127.

question: In 1965 the American economist Gordon Tullock, a co-founder of public choice theory, wrote a short book. It applied cold economic thinking to government offices, showing how bureaucrats actually behave day to day: boosting their careers, expanding their agencies, and guarding turf against rival departments. What did he call the book?
answer: The Politics of Bureaucracy
choices: The Politics of Bureaucracy
Bureaucracy and Representative Government
Autocracy
The Logic of the Law
context: The Politics of Bureaucracy (Public Affairs Press, 1965) was Tullock's application of economic reasoning to bureau behavior. William Niskanen's 1971 Bureaucracy and Representative Government built directly on it. Source: mises.org (Tullock, Politics of Bureaucracy PDF).

question: A country creates a small number of valuable government permits that let only a few companies do a certain kind of business. Firms then spend huge amounts of money lobbying for those permits instead of making better products. What is this behavior called?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Free trade
context: Tullock's 1967 paper introduced the idea; Anne Krueger's 1974 paper on Indian import licenses gave 'rent-seeking' its modern name. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: One branch of economics looks at politicians and officials as people who follow incentives. They chase votes, bigger budgets, and job perks, just like anyone else. It does not just assume they always act for the public good. What is this branch called?
answer: Public-choice economics
choices: Public-choice economics
Behavioral economics
Monetary economics
Development economics
context: Tullock and Buchanan moved the Center for Study of Public Choice to George Mason University in 1983. Tullock retired from GMU in 2008. Source: mercatus.org (Tullock biographical note).

question: The public-choice tradition applies economics to politicians and asks a hard question about dictators. To hold on to power, does a dictator really need to please the great mass of ordinary people — or does he only need to keep a small inner ring of insiders very well rewarded? Thinkers like Bruce Bueno de Mesquita answer the second. Why must a dictator keep that small inner group so happy?
answer: If the insiders (soldiers, courtiers) turn on him, he falls
choices: If the insiders (soldiers, courtiers) turn on him, he falls
The wider public actually chooses dictators in secret votes
Dictators only need popular songs written about them
Insiders never have any real power once a dictator is picked
context: Autocracy (Kluwer Academic, 1987) extended the public-choice framework to dictatorships. Tullock argued dictators face the same rational-actor incentives as democratic politicians, only within different constraints. Source: springer.com (Autocracy 1987).

question: In 1986 the American economist James Buchanan won the Nobel Prize in economics for helping found public-choice theory — the study of politicians and bureaucrats as self-interested actors. Much of that theory had come from a 1962 book, 'The Calculus of Consent,' that Buchanan co-wrote with his close colleague Gordon Tullock. But when the Nobel was awarded, Tullock was pointedly left out. Tullock later made a famous bitter quip about the snub. What was it?
answer: Being co-author of the Calculus of Consent apparently did not count
choices: Being co-author of the Calculus of Consent apparently did not count
The Nobel committee had confused public choice with social choice
The Foreign Service ruined his chances by delaying his degree
He should have insisted on the PhD after all
context: Tullock expected to share every public-choice-related Nobel and never won one. He was famously acerbic about the 1986 omission; the quote is well-attested by GMU colleagues. Source: Kliemt + Boettke, obituaries in Public Choice (2015).

question: Before he ever wrote a word of economics, the American scholar Gordon Tullock spent almost ten years as a US State Department diplomat, posted in China and Korea. He later said that watching officials scheme, dodge, and cut deals inside a real working government taught him more than any textbook he ever cracked. What did he say his Foreign Service post taught him?
answer: More about political incentives than any economics course could have
choices: More about political incentives than any economics course could have
The importance of Keynesian aggregate-demand management
The mathematical foundations of general equilibrium
That bureaucracy could not be modeled economically
context: In his autobiographical essays Tullock repeatedly credited Tianjin, Hong Kong, and Korea postings with teaching him how real bureaucracies actually work -- the raw material for his later economics of politics. Source: Tullock, Selected Works vol. 1 (Liberty Fund 2004).

question: Watch any big economy over many decades. It grows steadily through a stretch of good years, then suddenly crashes into a bad slump where factories close and workers lose their jobs, and then it slowly climbs back up. The same rising-and-falling shape repeats over and over across the centuries. What do economists call this pattern of good times and bad?
answer: The business cycle
choices: The business cycle
A price shock
A trade balance
A tax rebate
context: Gottfried Haberler (1900-1995), a Vienna doctorate under Wieser and Mises and a Mises-Kreis member, was commissioned by the League of Nations to write the standard cross-theory survey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: In 1937 the Austrian-American economist Gottfried Haberler wrote a big survey book for the League of Nations in Geneva. It walked patiently through every major theory of why economies boom and then bust. The two-word main title of the book named the peak and the trough of the trade cycle themselves. What was the title?
answer: Prosperity and Depression
choices: Prosperity and Depression
Boom and Slump
Growth and Contraction
Expansion and Recession
context: Prosperity and Depression: A Theoretical Analysis of Cyclical Movements (Geneva, 1937) became the standard reference book on business-cycle theories for a generation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Prosperity_and_Depression.

question: In the 1930s and 1940s, Nazi and Soviet dictators had taken over Vienna and much of Central Europe. Many Austrian-trained economists — including Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, and Fritz Machlup — fled to the United States. What kind of economic ideas did most of these Austrians bring with them?
answer: Free markets and skepticism of central planning
choices: Free markets and skepticism of central planning
Full government control of all industries
Higher tariffs on every import
Bigger central banks with more power
context: Haberler emigrated to the United States in 1936 and held his Harvard chair until retiring in 1971. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: In 1937 the Austrian-American economist Gottfried Haberler's book Prosperity and Depression surveyed every serious theory of the business cycle for the League of Nations. Strict Austrians like his old Vienna teacher Ludwig von Mises were unhappy with how he handled it. They saw Haberler's approach as a first step toward compromising with mainstream economics. What was Haberler's move?
answer: He treated the Austrian theory as one theory among several equally worth surveying
choices: He treated the Austrian theory as one theory among several equally worth surveying
He refused to include the Austrian theory in the survey at all
He argued the Austrian theory alone was correct and dismissed all others
He translated the Austrian theory into full Keynesian aggregate-demand language
context: By presenting Austrian ABCT alongside Mitchell, Keynes, Schumpeter and the classical purely-real theories without a strong methodological commitment, Haberler softened the strict Austrian position. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Prosperity_and_Depression.

question: In 1933 the Austrian-American economist Gottfried Haberler wrote a book on international trade. He took David Ricardo's old 1817 idea of comparative advantage — that each country should make what it is relatively best at — and reworked its foundations in a way Austrian economists could accept, without leaning on labor-hours as the measuring stick. What was Haberler's key change?
answer: Comparative advantage restated using opportunity cost
choices: Comparative advantage restated using opportunity cost
Comparative advantage restated using labor-hours
Comparative advantage restated using capital-labor ratios
Comparative advantage restated using the Cobb-Douglas function
context: Der internationale Handel (1933) reformulated Ricardo's original labor-theory formulation into the modern opportunity-cost version taught in trade textbooks today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: Gottfried Haberler was an Austrian-born economist who had come to America and taught at Harvard. In 1947 he was among a small group of scholars who met at a Swiss village near Lake Geneva to defend classical liberalism after World War II. Friedrich Hayek called the meeting. Ludwig von Mises, Fritz Machlup, and a young Milton Friedman were also there. What did the group name the society they founded?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Cobden Club
The Fabian Society
The Royal Economic Society
context: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded by Hayek in April 1947; Haberler was among its founding members and remained a lifelong participant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: Gottfried Haberler, the Austrian-born economist who had taught international trade at Harvard for decades, retired in 1971. He wanted to keep writing pamphlets attacking wage-and-price controls, inflation, and trade barriers. So he moved to Washington, D.C., and joined a free-market think tank there. Which think tank did Haberler join?
answer: The American Enterprise Institute
choices: The American Enterprise Institute
The Brookings Institution
The Peterson Institute
The Heritage Foundation
context: Haberler moved to AEI after his Harvard retirement in 1971 and wrote there until near his death in 1995. His policy convictions stayed classical-liberal even as his theoretical framework had softened. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: Gottfried Haberler was a young Austrian economist in 1920s Vienna who would later become famous for his 1936 book on business cycles and international trade. But at the time he was still a graduate student in the University of Vienna's small circle of Austrian economists, finishing his doctorate there in 1925. His two doctoral advisors were both giants of the founding generation of the Austrian school -- the men who had built the school up after Carl Menger. Which pair advised him?
answer: Friedrich von Wieser and Ludwig von Mises
choices: Friedrich von Wieser and Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger and Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
Joseph Schumpeter and Hans Mayer
context: Haberler took his Vienna doctorate under Wieser and Mises and joined the Mises Privatseminar. Wieser had been Menger's direct successor at Vienna. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank in Washington, D.C. It controls interest rates and manages the US dollar. The President picks the person who runs it, called the chairman. But the President's pick cannot start work right away. First one part of Congress has to vote yes on the pick. Which body has to approve the choice?
answer: The Senate
choices: The Senate
The Supreme Court
The House of Representatives
The state governors
context: Greenspan took the Fed chair on August 11 1987. He was well-known for his admirer's relationship to Ayn Rand -- he had been a member of her Collective in the 1950s and contributed essays to her 1966 book Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 19, 1987 — a day later called 'Black Monday' — the US stock market lost more than 22 percent of its value in a single trading day. It was the biggest one-day fall in the market's history. When millions of investors panic and rush to sell all at once, prices can collapse in a matter of hours. What is this kind of collapse called?
answer: A market crash
choices: A market crash
A hedge fund
A dividend
A price ceiling
context: October 19 1987 -- Black Monday -- saw the Dow fall 22.6% in a single trading day. It remains the largest single-day percentage decline in Dow history, exceeding even the worst individual days of 1929 and 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Black Monday (1987)' (2026-09-05).

question: In the mid-1980s, the financial engineers Hayne Leland, John O'Brien, and Mark Rubinstein sold big Wall Street investors a new computer-driven strategy. If stock prices began to fall, their software automatically sold stock-index futures very fast to lock in gains before losses got worse. On October 19, 1987, when many firms' computers all sold at once, the market fell far harder than the designers expected. What was that strategy called?
answer: Portfolio insurance
choices: Portfolio insurance
Buy-and-hold investing
Long-term index saving
Slow dividend collecting
context: Portfolio insurance -- developed by Berkeley academics Hayne Leland and Mark Rubinstein -- used dynamic hedging with futures to protect portfolios from downside. In practice, during a sharp decline, the strategy triggered cascading sell orders that amplified the crash. Source: Grokipedia 'Portfolio insurance (finance)' (2026-09-05).

question: On Monday, October 19, 1987 -- 'Black Monday' -- the US stock market crashed nearly 23 percent in a single day. It was the biggest one-day drop in Wall Street history. The next morning, October 20, the new Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan -- who had taken the job only two months earlier -- issued a one-sentence public statement to reassure investors. Within days, the market calmed. What did the statement say?
answer: The Fed was ready to serve as a source of liquidity to support the economic and financial system
choices: The Fed was ready to serve as a source of liquidity to support the economic and financial system
The Fed would raise interest rates to defend the dollar
The Fed would suspend all open market operations pending review
The Fed would close the Discount Window until markets recovered
context: Greenspan's Fed statement of October 20 1987 committed to unlimited liquidity to prevent cascading bank failures from margin-call liquidations. Rates were cut. Markets stabilized within days. Source: federalreserve.gov (statement October 20 1987).

question: In August 1987 a new chair took charge of the US Federal Reserve — America's central bank. Just two months later, on October 19, the stock market crashed 22 percent in a single day. Within hours the new chair had slashed interest rates and pumped cash into the banking system to steady asset prices. Every time markets dropped hard afterward, the Fed did the same thing. Investors and traders gave that whole rescue pattern a nickname. What is it called?
answer: The Greenspan put
choices: The Greenspan put
The Bernanke floor
The Volcker call
The Yellen safety net
