context: The 'Greenspan put' is an options-market metaphor. A put option protects the holder against downside. Markets learned in 1987 that the Fed would provide that protection whenever asset prices fell sharply. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: After the massive stock crash of October 1987, President Ronald Reagan quietly created a small group of top financial officials — the Working Group on Financial Markets — to meet whenever markets were in crisis. Austrian-tradition critics argue that when the government props up asset prices during scary drops, it teaches investors the wrong lesson and makes the whole system riskier. What is the lesson investors learn from repeated rescues?
answer: That a bailout is likely, so they can safely take bigger risks
choices: That a bailout is likely, so they can safely take bigger risks
That saving is always better than spending
That stock prices never fall for very long
That foreign investors will soon disappear
context: The Working Group on Financial Markets -- created by executive order in March 1988 after Black Monday -- was quickly nicknamed the 'Plunge Protection Team' in financial press. It coordinates emergency responses across the Treasury, Fed, SEC, and CFTC. Source: Grokipedia 'Working Group on Financial Markets' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 19, 1987, a day called Black Monday, the US stock market fell 22.6 percent in a single session. Alan Greenspan, the new Federal Reserve chairman, quickly promised the Fed would lend cash to any bank that needed it. Stock prices bounced back within weeks. From an Austrian and moral-hazard view, that rescue taught investors a lasting lesson that shaped the next twenty years. Which lesson did the market learn?
answer: The Fed would step in during major declines, creating the risk-taking incentive that drove the 1990s dot-com and 2000s housing bubbles
choices: The Fed would step in during major declines, creating the risk-taking incentive that drove the 1990s dot-com and 2000s housing bubbles
Portfolio insurance was too dangerous and would never be used again
Cash equities would trade only between 9:30 AM and 4:00 PM Eastern
The Fed's discount window would no longer accept commercial paper
context: The 1987 intervention 'worked' brilliantly in the short run. Its long-run effect was to train markets to price in Fed backstops, encouraging progressively larger risk-taking. The 1987 template is the parent of every subsequent bubble. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 19, 1987, a day called Black Monday, the S&P 500 index of the biggest US companies crashed 22.6 percent in one day. The index had peaked at record highs the month before. After the crash, investors kept asking one question — how long would it take the S&P 500 to climb back to its September 1987 peak? The recovery time became a well-known figure in market history. How long did that recovery take?
answer: About two years
choices: About two years
About six months
About five years
About fifteen years
context: The S&P 500 recovered its pre-Black Monday level within about two years. The rapid recovery was itself part of the 'Greenspan put' lesson -- crashes that appear catastrophic in the moment could be reversed quickly if the Fed acted decisively. Source: Grokipedia 'Black Monday (1987)' (2026-09-05).

question: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, US stocks crashed 22.6 percent in one day. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan quickly pledged that the central bank would lend to any struggling firm. Markets rebounded within weeks. Austrian economists later pointed to that rescue to teach a recognition move about the tension between calming markets right now and creating dangerous risk-taking later. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: A rescue that succeeds brilliantly in the short run can teach markets exactly the wrong risk-taking lesson for the long run
choices: A rescue that succeeds brilliantly in the short run can teach markets exactly the wrong risk-taking lesson for the long run
Rescues always fail to stabilize markets
Short-run and long-run effects of rescues are always aligned
Markets never learn from prior rescue precedents
context: The 1987 intervention was a technical success. Its cost was expectational, arriving over years as markets priced in the implicit Fed backstop for every subsequent decline. The tension between short-run stabilization and long-run moral hazard is the deepest problem in discretionary central-bank policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve chairman during the 1987 crash was Alan Greenspan. He would later be called 'the Maestro' for cutting interest rates every time markets got shaky. But his intellectual past made that later policy record look surprising. Before joining the Fed in 1987, Greenspan had been closely tied to a hard-money, individualist movement in New York — and had even written for its newsletter. Which movement was it?
answer: Ayn Rand's Objectivist circle and his 1966 essay Gold and Economic Freedom
choices: Ayn Rand's Objectivist circle and his 1966 essay Gold and Economic Freedom
The Chicago-school monetarist movement led by Milton Friedman
The Austrian-school movement led by Ludwig von Mises
The MIT-based Keynesian mainstream
context: Greenspan had contributed 'Gold and Economic Freedom' to Rand's 1966 book Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, defending the gold standard. His shift to a discretionary Fed chair who orchestrated the Greenspan put is one of the most striking intellectual reversals in American economic policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank. Its main tool is setting a target for short-term interest rates, which controls how expensive it is to borrow money. When the Fed wants people and firms to borrow more and spend more, it lowers rates. But when prices are climbing too fast and the Fed wants to slow the borrowing, what does it do to interest rates?
answer: It raises interest rates
choices: It raises interest rates
It prints new bills for everyone
It shuts down banks
It cancels all loans
context: Greenspan served under Reagan, Bush 41, Clinton, and Bush 43. His nickname 'The Maestro' captured the cult of technocratic control that surrounded him at his peak. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: After the dot-com bubble crashed in 2000 and 2001, wiping out trillions in technology-stock wealth, the Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan responded by cutting the federal funds rate — the price banks charge each other for overnight loans. It had stood at 6.5 percent in December 2000. Cut after cut brought it steadily down. By June 2003 it had reached a historic low, and the Fed held it there for a full year. What was that floor rate?
answer: 1 percent
choices: 1 percent
3 percent
0 percent
0.25 percent
context: The 1% federal funds rate held from June 2003 through June 2004 -- at the time the lowest US policy rate in 46 years. Cheap credit flowed into interest-rate-sensitive sectors, especially housing. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve held its main interest rate near 1 percent for a long stretch of the early 2000s, making credit unusually cheap. Mortgages became much easier to get. For decades before, US home prices had grown at about the same pace as normal inflation. But in hot markets like California, Florida, and Nevada, something very different started happening. What was it?
answer: Home prices rose 10-15% per year
choices: Home prices rose 10-15% per year
Home prices fell as builders overbuilt
Home prices held flat as buyer demand softened
Home prices rose only in high-tech cities
context: Coastal metros saw double-digit annual price gains through 2004-2006. Mortgage originators wrote enormous volumes of subprime loans -- no-doc 'liar loans,' 2/28 adjustable-rate mortgages, negative-amortization products -- to feed the demand. Source: Grokipedia 'United States housing bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: In the mid-2000s two big lenders wrote most of the risky mortgages that fueled the American housing boom. One was Angelo Mozilo's California firm, at the time the largest home lender in the whole country. The other was a giant subprime lender based in Orange County, California, run by Roland Arnall. Which two lenders led that market?
answer: Countrywide and Ameriquest
choices: Countrywide and Ameriquest
Wells Fargo and Bank of America
Washington Mutual and Wachovia
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
context: Countrywide (Mozilo) and Ameriquest were the largest subprime originators through the mid-2000s boom. Both failed or were absorbed during 2007-2008 as the underlying loans defaulted at accelerating rates. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 27, 2005, the Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan gave a much-noticed speech to an industry group in Washington, DC. He brushed off warnings that a nationwide housing bubble was forming. He admitted some local 'froth' in home prices was possible, but insisted no nationwide bubble was likely. Which industry group hosted the speech?
answer: American Bankers Association
choices: American Bankers Association
National Association of Realtors
Mortgage Bankers Association
American Enterprise Institute
context: Greenspan's October 27 2005 ABA speech argued that housing markets were fundamentally local and heterogeneous, so a coordinated national bubble was unlikely. Two years later the national market entered the collapse that triggered the Global Financial Crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: In the early 2000s the Federal Reserve, led by chairman Alan Greenspan, kept interest rates unusually low to fight the aftershock of the dot-com bust. Austrian economists warned as early as 2003 that this was inflating a shaky housing boom. They pointed to a specific idea from Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek's business-cycle theory to explain why the bust was inevitable. Which idea did they name?
answer: Artificially low interest rates cause capital to be misallocated into interest-sensitive sectors, and the bust is inevitable when the underlying savings do not exist
choices: Artificially low interest rates cause capital to be misallocated into interest-sensitive sectors, and the bust is inevitable when the underlying savings do not exist
Rapid deflation forces creditors to seize collateral en masse
Foreign capital inflows always cause housing bubbles
Full employment always triggers wage inflation
context: Austrian business-cycle theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929): rates set below the natural rate mislead entrepreneurs into long-duration projects (like housing) that the real savings pool cannot sustain. When the mismatch resolves, the malinvestment liquidates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Between 2003 and 2007 the US housing market boomed and Wall Street celebrated. But three voices in the Austrian tradition kept warning that a bust was coming. One shouted about it on the CNBC business channel. One raised it during Congressional hearings on Capitol Hill in Washington. One wrote about it at the Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama. Which trio is usually cited?
answer: Peter Schiff on CNBC, Ron Paul in Congress, and Mark Thornton at Mises
choices: Peter Schiff on CNBC, Ron Paul in Congress, and Mark Thornton at Mises
Larry Summers, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Nouriel Roubini
Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Alan Blinder
context: Schiff's CNBC appearances 2005-07 predicting the collapse are widely circulated on YouTube ('Peter Schiff was right' compilations). Ron Paul warned in congressional hearings; Mark Thornton wrote at mises.org. All three were dismissed at the time. Source: Grokipedia 'Peter Schiff' (2026-09-05).

question: Alan Greenspan retired from the Federal Reserve in early 2006 after nearly twenty years as chairman. Two years later, in fall 2008, the housing bubble he had helped inflate collapsed and the global financial crisis exploded. Congress called him to testify in October 2008 about what had gone wrong. There Greenspan made a striking admission about his own long-held view of how the economy works. What did he say he had found?
answer: A flaw in his worldview about how markets self-regulate
choices: A flaw in his worldview about how markets self-regulate
That interest-rate policy had no effect on housing prices
That subprime lending had been entirely responsible without any Fed role
That the crisis had been predicted only by leftist economists
context: Greenspan's October 23 2008 testimony to the House Oversight Committee: he had found 'a flaw' in his belief that self-interested bankers would protect their institutions from ruin. The admission stunned Congress. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian school of economics — most famously Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek — teaches a specific recognition move about central banking. When a central bank like the Federal Reserve holds interest rates below the level that would naturally balance saving and borrowing for years at a time, the Austrians say a predictable pattern follows in the real economy. Which pattern does the Austrian ladder press here?
answer: Cheap credit misallocates capital into interest-sensitive sectors; the bust that follows is not a market failure but the correction of the earlier distortion
choices: Cheap credit misallocates capital into interest-sensitive sectors; the bust that follows is not a market failure but the correction of the earlier distortion
Central banks always time interest-rate cuts correctly
Housing markets are immune to interest-rate policy because they are local
Deregulation is the sole cause of asset-price bubbles
context: The Austrian read of 2000-2008: the 2007-09 crash was the necessary liquidation of the malinvestment the 2003-06 cheap credit had produced. The bust was the market working, not failing. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In 1966, a young private-sector economist named Alan Greenspan wrote an essay in Ayn Rand's Objectivist newsletter. In it he argued explicitly for a return to a gold-based monetary system and warned that fiat paper money would let governments quietly steal savings through inflation. Decades later Greenspan would chair the Federal Reserve, which manages exactly the fiat system he once opposed. What was the title of that 1966 essay?
answer: Gold and Economic Freedom
choices: Gold and Economic Freedom
The Case for a Sound Dollar
Monetary Policy in a Free Society
The End of Fiat Money
context: Greenspan's 1966 essay is one of the sharpest short defenses of the gold standard ever published. He abandoned that view when he took the Fed chairmanship in 1987. The gap between the 1966 Greenspan and the 2003-06 Greenspan is one of the most striking intellectual reversals in American economic policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: Long ago a king in Europe found that his country's pure gold coins were too expensive to make. To save money, he ordered his royal mint to mix cheap tin into every new coin. People at the market weighed the new coins in their hands and noticed at once that they felt lighter and duller than before. Soon every family was hiding its older, purer gold coins at home and only spending the cheap new ones. The English merchant Thomas Gresham described the pattern in the 1500s. What is the pattern called?
answer: Bad money drives out good
choices: Bad money drives out good
Supply and demand
Deadweight loss
The invisible hand
context: Thomas Gresham advised Elizabeth I on the crown's finances and founded the Royal Exchange in London in 1571. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Gresham.

question: Thomas Gresham was an English merchant advising Queen Elizabeth I in the 1500s. He noticed something about coins that people would later boil down to just six short words. The saying tells what happens when two coins have the same face value but are made of different metals — one worth more than the other. What is the six-word saying?
answer: Bad money drives out good
choices: Bad money drives out good
Supply creates its own demand
The invisible hand allocates capital
Inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
context: The formulation, later shortened to 'bad money drives out good,' is Gresham's core observation about circulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: In old England, two shillings both count as money worth one shilling apiece by law. But one is made of full silver. The other has been secretly cut with cheap metal and is only half silver. Gresham's Law predicts a smart spender will do the same thing at every checkout with those two coins jingling in his pocket. What does he do?
answer: Pays with the half-silver coin and keeps the full-silver coin
choices: Pays with the half-silver coin and keeps the full-silver coin
Pays with the full-silver coin and keeps the half-silver coin
Pays with whichever coin is nearest to hand
Melts both coins into a single new shilling
context: The rational spender unloads the worth-less coin and retains the worth-more coin. Merchants receive only debased coin; full-silver coins get hoarded, melted for bullion, or exported. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Long before Sir Thomas Gresham, the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus advised Prussia's rulers on coinage. His 1526 treatise Monetae cudendae ratio described how debased coins drive better coins out of circulation. By what name is this monetary law taught today?
answer: Gresham's Law
choices: Gresham's Law
Say's Law
Copernicus's Law
Menger's Law
context: Copernicus's Monetae cudendae ratio (1526) noted that when better coin is introduced, the old is not withdrawn but hoarded. He beat Gresham by 34 years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Monetae_cudendae_ratio.

question: Around the year 1360 the French bishop Nicole Oresme wrote a short book about coins called De Moneta. He noticed a simple rule at the royal mint. If a king puts less gold in each new coin but declares it worth the same as the old, purer coins, what will people do with the older, purer coins they still have?
answer: People hide them and only spend the cheap new ones
choices: People hide them and only spend the cheap new ones
People burn them for fuel
People pass them around freely alongside the new ones
People melt them all into jewelry the next day
context: Nicole Oresme's De Moneta (about 1360) preceded Gresham's 1560 letter by roughly 200 years. The observation, in short, is far older than the name attached to it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nicole_Oresme.

question: The rule 'bad money drives out good' was first written down by the medieval French bishop Nicole Oresme in the 1300s. Two centuries later the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus wrote it out again. Later still an English merchant, Sir Thomas Gresham, gave the rule its lasting name. Three people in three different countries all found the same pattern. Why do you think that happened?
answer: The rule describes a real pattern that repeats whenever coins are debased
choices: The rule describes a real pattern that repeats whenever coins are debased
They all read the same secret book from ancient Greece
Their kings paid each of them to say it
The rule was made up and passed on as a joke
context: Macleod's 1858 book The Elements of Political Economy attached Gresham's name to the maxim. Naming honors are downstream of who happens to publish the compilation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Dunning_Macleod.

question: For most of American history, US dimes and quarters were made of real silver, and you could weigh them to check. But in 1965 the US Congress passed a Coinage Act that changed the recipe. From that year on, dimes and quarters were made from a copper-nickel sandwich instead. Which metal did the 1965 Coinage Act remove from newly minted dimes and quarters?
answer: Silver
choices: Silver
Gold
Zinc
Bronze
context: The Coinage Act 1965 removed silver from dimes and quarters and clad them in copper-nickel; Americans quickly pulled the pre-1965 silver coins out of pocket circulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Coinage_Act_of_1965.

question: Before 1965, US dimes and quarters were made of 90 percent silver — real bullion coins. That year Congress passed the Coinage Act, which replaced them with cheaper copper-nickel 'clad' coins that had no silver in them at all. Within a few years, the older pre-1965 silver coins had almost completely vanished from cash registers and pocket change. Gresham's Law — bad money drives out good — names the mechanism. What did Americans do with the silver coins?
answer: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
choices: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
They deposited them at the Federal Reserve to be re-issued
They mailed them to the US Treasury for silver certificates
They exchanged them at banks for the new clad coins
context: The classic modern instance of Gresham's Law: as soon as the copper-nickel dime and quarter appeared, ordinary savers pulled pre-1965 silver coins from change and kept them for their metal value. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Gresham's Law says bad money drives out good — spenders hoard the high-value coins and pay everywhere with the low-value ones. But the law depends on one very specific legal condition being in force. Without that condition, people would simply price the two coins differently in the market and the mechanism would not fire at all. Which legal condition must be present?
answer: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
choices: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
One coin is manufactured by a foreign mint
The economy is under a fixed gold standard
The central bank is targeting a specific inflation rate
context: The law's engine is legal-tender equality: only when the state forces the two coins to trade at the same face value will spenders unload the worth-less coin and hoard the worth-more one. Without that fiat equality, they would simply trade at their true weights. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Bitcoin was invented in 2009 by an unknown creator using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. It is money that lives only on computers — no government prints it. Instead of a bank keeping the ledger, hard math puzzles running on thousands of computers around the world keep track of who owns what. What is the general name for money like Bitcoin, which runs on computers and math?
answer: Cryptocurrency
choices: Cryptocurrency
A stablecoin
A stock
A treasury bond
context: Hal Finney (1956-2014) was a cryptographer at PGP Corporation who had spent the 1990s and 2000s writing PGP's encryption code. His January 11 2009 tweet: 'Running bitcoin.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney was an early computer scientist and one of the very first people besides the mysterious Satoshi Nakamoto to run the Bitcoin software when the network went live. On January 11, 2009 -- just days after Bitcoin started -- Finney posted a two-word tweet describing what his own computer was doing at that moment. Those two words became famous in Bitcoin history. What did the tweet say?
answer: Running bitcoin
choices: Running bitcoin
Mining bitcoin
Testing bitcoin
Downloading bitcoin
context: 'Running bitcoin.' Finney was the second-ever Bitcoin node operator, running the software days after Satoshi's own machine started the network. Source: twitter.com/halfin (January 11 2009).

question: In late 2008 an anonymous coder using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a paper describing a new digital money called Bitcoin. In January 2009 Satoshi launched the network and mined the very first block. A few days later Satoshi sent 10 coins to another programmer, Hal Finney, in California. It was the first time Bitcoin ever moved between two different people. Why was that small transfer so important?
answer: It proved the new digital money actually worked as designed
choices: It proved the new digital money actually worked as designed
It made both programmers instantly rich forever
It was declared legal currency by the United States
It replaced credit cards worldwide within a month
context: Block 170 contains the first Bitcoin transaction between two distinct parties (Satoshi to Finney, 10 BTC). Every earlier transaction had been Satoshi mining and paying himself. Source: blockchain.info/block-height/170.

question: Before Bitcoin existed, a California programmer named Hal Finney spent years building tools that scrambled emails so only the person with the right secret key could read them. If a government agency intercepts a scrambled message, it just sees random gibberish. What is this scrambling of digital messages called?
answer: Encryption
choices: Encryption
Advertising
Downloading
Copying
context: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), designed by Phil Zimmermann and developed at PGP Corporation, was Finney's day job through the 1990s and 2000s. He wrote much of the code behind PGP as journalists and dissidents relied on it worldwide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy.

question: Hal Finney was the second person ever to run the Bitcoin software and received the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009. Later that same year Finney was diagnosed with a nerve disease. It slowly took away his ability to move his arms and legs. By 2013 he could only type by tracking his eyes across a screen. Which disease did Finney have?
answer: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
choices: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Parkinson's disease
Multiple sclerosis
Huntington's disease
context: ALS -- Lou Gehrig's disease -- progressively paralyzed Finney. His 2013 bitcointalk.org essay 'Bitcoin and Me' was typed with eye-tracking software when almost all voluntary movement was gone. Source: bitcointalk.org (Bitcoin and Me, 2013).

question: Hal Finney was one of the very first Bitcoin developers. He ran the second Bitcoin node ever set up and received the first person-to-person bitcoin transaction, sent to him by Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009. In 2013, slowly dying of ALS, Finney wrote an essay for the bitcointalk.org forum that told the whole story — running the node, getting that first transfer, and watching Bitcoin grow while his body failed him. What did he title the essay?
answer: Bitcoin and Me
choices: Bitcoin and Me
Running Bitcoin
The First Node
Notes from a Cryptographer
context: 'Bitcoin and Me' (bitcointalk.org, March 19 2013) is Finney's own account of everything from the first mailing-list post to his ALS diagnosis. It reads as a plain first-person history from inside the earliest Bitcoin community. Source: bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=155054.

question: An early cypherpunk programmer worked on a digital cash idea long before Bitcoin existed. The unsolved problem in his design was that his system still needed one central trusted server. Why is a single trusted server a big weakness for a would-be currency?
answer: If that server is taken down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks
choices: If that server is taken down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks
It always makes the currency more valuable
It has never caused any real system to fail
It is exactly what Bitcoin uses today
context: Alcor (Scottsdale, Arizona) performed Finney's cryopreservation; Finney had been a long-term life-extension advocate. Bitcoin was one of many long-view bets in his life. Source: alcor.org (case report A-2643).

question: Hal Finney was a California computer scientist and one of the earliest Bitcoin pioneers. In 2004, four years before Bitcoin existed, he published a paper called Reusable Proofs of Work. Later Satoshi Nakamoto would cite it as a direct source in the Bitcoin white paper. Finney also gave his system a short catchy acronym in that paper. What short name did Finney give his system?
answer: RPOW
choices: RPOW
HashCash
b-money
bit gold
context: RPOW (Reusable Proofs of Work), 2004, built on Adam Back's earlier hashcash and pushed the idea toward a spendable digital token. Satoshi cited RPOW as prior art in the Bitcoin white paper. Source: rpow.net.

question: For years Hal Finney, the California cypherpunk and Bitcoin developer who received the very first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009, was one of a small handful of people accused of secretly being Satoshi himself. But two independent lines of evidence rule out that theory. Which pair of evidence closes the case?
answer: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
choices: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
His documented US citizenship, plus the fact that Satoshi's writing style was clearly non-American
His public retirement announcement, plus his stated preference for gold-backed money over digital cash
His employer's NDA obligations, plus his lack of interest in cryptographic proofs
context: Finney explicitly denied being Satoshi. Timing evidence: he was training for a marathon and posting run-times during periods Satoshi was posting emails elsewhere; forensic-text analysis has not matched. Source: newyorker.com (Andy Greenberg profile, 2014).

question: Hal Finney was a longtime California cypherpunk who had worked on encryption and digital cash for a decade before Bitcoin. In the Bitcoin community he is remembered as the first person besides Satoshi Nakamoto to grasp clearly what Bitcoin was going to become. What specific technical role did Finney play in the very first weeks of the Bitcoin network in January 2009?
answer: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
choices: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
He wrote the first Bitcoin exchange to trade coins for dollars
He mined the very first block, the genesis block, before Satoshi did
He edited the final draft of the Bitcoin white paper for Satoshi
context: Satoshi's own machine was Bitcoin node 1; Finney's was node 2, running January 11 2009. He received the first person-to-person transaction on Block 170 the following day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Adam Back is a British computer scientist and one of the most important cypherpunks. In 1997 he built a system called Hashcash. It asked every email sender to attach a small proof-of-work stamp — a math puzzle solution — to slow down spammers who send millions of messages at once. But each Hashcash stamp had a strict limit compared to real money. What was that limit?
answer: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
choices: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
Each stamp had a fixed expiration date measured in seconds
Each stamp required a live connection to a central bank server
Each stamp was only redeemable on Microsoft-issued hardware
context: Hashcash proved you had done real computational work, but the stamp was spent after one use. Making stamps transferable required solving double-spending -- the same problem Bitcoin later solved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hashcash.

question: Adam Back's 1997 Hashcash used proof-of-work stamps that could only be spent once. In 2004 a California coder named Hal Finney took the idea further. He built a system where each proof-of-work stamp became a token you could pass to a friend, who could pass it again to someone else, and so on. What did Finney name his new system?
answer: Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW)
choices: Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW)
The Lightning Network
The Merkle Chain
The Cypherpunk Ledger
context: The cryptographer was Hal Finney. The RPOW acronym stands for Reusable Proofs of Work (plural of 'proof'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: In 2004, four years before Bitcoin, the California cypherpunk Hal Finney built a digital cash system called Reusable Proofs of Work. Each token was a proof-of-work stamp that a person could pass to a friend. But Finney faced a hard problem — how do you stop a token holder from copying and spending the same token twice? What architectural choice did Finney make to solve that double-spend problem?
answer: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
choices: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
A blockchain distributed across thousands of independent nodes
A cryptographic zero-knowledge proof stored on every user's device
A quorum vote among the top 21 stamp holders
context: Finney ran the server himself on an IBM 4758 secure coprocessor, whose signed open-source code could be audited. But the trusted server was still a single point of failure. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Before Bitcoin, one early digital-cash design used special tamper-proof server hardware so users could trust the server was running honest code. Bitcoin took a totally different route to trust. What does Bitcoin trust instead of a special piece of hardware?
answer: A public network of computers all checking each other
choices: A public network of computers all checking each other
One giant government-run server in Washington
A single billionaire's private data center
The honor system between anonymous strangers
context: The 4758 was a tamper-resistant special-purpose chip designed for cryptographic key storage. Finney used it to prove the RPOW server code was the audited version -- but the trusted-server architecture itself remained a weakness. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: In the 1990s the American cryptographer David Chaum built DigiCash, the first serious attempt at digital cash. Payments were routed through a single trusted server that used strong math to keep them private. Chaum himself admitted the design had one weakness that no amount of tamper-proof hardware could fix — the same weakness that Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was built to remove. What was that weakness?
answer: A single server that could be shut down or corrupted
choices: A single server that could be shut down or corrupted
The cost of buying computers
The size of individual payments
The language of the software code
context: This is the weakness Satoshi's proof-of-work + longest-chain rule solved four years later -- consensus without a trusted third party. Finney's own public writings had named the problem he could not solve. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Before 2008, digital-cash inventors could not solve one problem: how to make sure the same digital coin isn't spent twice, without trusting a central server that could freeze your money or shut down. What did the 2008 Bitcoin white paper invent to solve this?
answer: A public ledger that many strangers keep in sync using proof-of-work
choices: A public ledger that many strangers keep in sync using proof-of-work
A single trusted bank server run by a well-known company
A rule that every user must physically hand coins to each other
A promise from world governments to never seize digital money
context: One of the earliest public traces of anyone besides Satoshi running the Bitcoin software. Finney had downloaded the software the day after Christmas 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Bitcoin, the first decentralized digital currency, was launched by the anonymous inventor Satoshi Nakamoto on January 3, 2009. Just nine days later, on January 12, Satoshi sent the very first person-to-person Bitcoin transfer to the American cryptographer Hal Finney. The transaction was recorded in block 170 of the new blockchain. How much Bitcoin did that first transfer move?
answer: 10 BTC
choices: 10 BTC
50 BTC
100 BTC
context: Block 170 was the first Bitcoin transaction between two people (rather than a miner's block reward paying itself). Finney had answered Satoshi's forum post volunteering to test the network. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Bitcoin's rules are written into code that nobody can quietly change. One of those rules says: about every four years, the reward that miners receive for adding a new block of transactions is automatically cut in half. This slowly shrinks the number of new Bitcoin created, on a schedule everyone can see decades in advance. What is this scheduled event called?
answer: The halving
choices: The halving
The retarget
The airdrop
The fork
context: The halvings occurred in November 2012 (50 to 25 BTC per block), July 2016 (25 to 12.5), May 2020 (12.5 to 6.25), and April 2024 (6.25 to 3.125). The schedule caps the total supply at 21 million. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_halving.

question: Since Bitcoin's launch in January 2009, its price has climbed in a rough four-year rhythm. Each cycle tends to end in a big bull-market peak roughly a year after each halving of the mining reward. Traders and analysts have marked five such peaks so far across Bitcoin's history. Which sequence gives the approximate peak prices in the right years?
context: Each peak followed a halving by roughly 12-18 months, until the 2024-25 cycle, which peaked faster (about 8 months after the April 2024 halving) partly due to spot ETF flows. Source: grokipedia.com/page/History_of_Bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin has moved in a rough four-year rhythm ever since it began in 2009. First a hard crash after the peak. Then a quiet stretch of buying near the low. Then a slow rise as people notice again. Then a wild spike before the next crash. This repeating boom-and-bust shape looks a lot like an older economic pattern first described in the early 1900s. Which classic pattern does the Bitcoin cycle match?
answer: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
choices: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
The permanent-income consumption smoothing hypothesis of Milton Friedman
The animal-spirits investment theory of John Maynard Keynes
The productivity-growth model of Robert Solow
context: Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT) treats booms and busts as monetary phenomena rather than psychological ones. Bitcoin's cycles have been interpreted as this shape applied to a monetary asset in an early-adoption phase. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: In 2018 a Palestinian-American economist published a book that made the Austrian-school case for Bitcoin as sound money. He argued that Bitcoin's built-in halving schedule — where the reward given to miners is cut in half every four years — forces a hard-money discipline that no government can break. The book has become one of the most influential works in the whole Bitcoin world. Who wrote it, and what is it called?
answer: Saifedean Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard
choices: Saifedean Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard
Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan
Peter Thiel, Zero to One
Michael Lewis, The Big Short
context: Ammous made the argument that Bitcoin's programmatic supply schedule and its historical price cycles fit an Austrian monetary framework. Vijay Boyapati (The Bullish Case for Bitcoin) and Lyn Alden made related arguments. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In 2019 an anonymous analyst writing under the name 'PlanB' published a Medium post claiming he could predict Bitcoin's price using only its halving schedule — the built-in event that cuts new Bitcoin supply in half roughly every four years. He fit a mathematical curve to past prices and drew it into the future. What was his model called, and how has it held up since?
answer: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
choices: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
The stock-to-flow model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024
The Elliott wave model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024
The efficient-markets model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
context: PlanB's model became famous during the 2020-21 bull market but has failed as a forecast since. The Austrian recognition move survives -- past cycles are real -- but the specific PlanB quantitative claim did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: The 2024-25 Bitcoin cycle broke $100,000 in December 2024, only about eight months after the April 2024 halving. Prior cycles had taken 12-18 months to peak. A specific new source of demand introduced in January 2024 helps explain the compressed timing. What was it?
answer: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, approved by the SEC on January 10, 2024
choices: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, approved by the SEC on January 10, 2024
Widespread retail adoption of a new El Salvador wallet app
A Chinese central-bank purchase program for Bitcoin reserves
A European Central Bank digital-currency swap facility
context: Spot Bitcoin ETFs let institutional and retail buyers hold Bitcoin exposure through ordinary brokerage accounts. Inflows in early 2024 totaled tens of billions of dollars and preceded the December 2024 six-figure breakthrough. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_exchange-traded_fund.

question: Bitcoin has had roughly four-year price cycles since 2012, with each big rally coming near a halving — the built-in event that cuts new Bitcoin supply in half. A first-time Bitcoin holder in 2025 asks whether this past pattern guarantees another four-year peak is on the way. What is the honest analytical answer?
answer: The past cycles are real observations, but the 2024-25 cycle already broke the pattern -- past patterns do not guarantee future ones
choices: The past cycles are real observations, but the 2024-25 cycle already broke the pattern -- past patterns do not guarantee future ones
The pattern is mathematically certain and holders can time purchases from the halving date
The pattern was refuted by the stock-to-flow model and Bitcoin is now in permanent decline
The pattern only applies to gold, not to Bitcoin, so no forecast is possible
context: Recognizing the historical shape is teachable; treating it as a guaranteed forecast is not. The 2024-25 cycle compressed the timing and added spot-ETF demand as a structural factor prior cycles lacked. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: The American economist Murray Rothbard argued that even courts, roads, and police could be run by private firms competing with each other — no government at all, just companies selling protection and dispute-resolution to willing customers. What is this radical idea called?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism
choices: Anarcho-capitalism
Central planning
Fascism
Mixed economy
context: Hoppe was born September 2, 1949 in Peine, West Germany; joined Rothbard at UNLV in 1986; taught there until retiring in 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: In 2001 the German-American Austrian economist Hans-Hermann Hoppe published his best-known book. In it he argues that a hereditary king plans better for the long run than a modern elected leader, because the king owns the country while a president only rents it for a term. What is the book's title?
answer: Democracy: The God That Failed
choices: Democracy: The God That Failed
The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
The Road to Serfdom
context: Democracy: The God That Failed (Transaction Publishers, 2001) is Hoppe's best-known book and the flagship of his controversial-within-Austrian argument. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: A young Central European scholar in the 1970s went to graduate school under one of the leading left-wing philosophers of his day. He read Marx carefully and, for years, thought his teacher was right. Then, after watching how socialist governments actually ran their economies and reading free-market thinkers like Friedrich Hayek, he changed his mind about many things. Later in life he became a well-known defender of free markets. What does this personal story show?
answer: People can change their political views over time
choices: People can change their political views over time
No one ever changes their political views
Only elections change what people believe
Teachers always convince students of their own views
context: Hoppe's PhD in philosophy (Frankfurt, 1974) was supervised by Habermas, then the leading exponent of Frankfurt-School critical theory. It is an unusual training path for an Austrian economist. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe is a German-born Austrian-school economist and libertarian philosopher who taught for years at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. In 2006 he founded an annual libertarian conference called the Property and Freedom Society. It meets every summer at a specific Turkish coastal resort town on the Aegean Sea, where Hoppe spends part of the year. What is the town?
answer: Bodrum
choices: Bodrum
Istanbul
Antalya
Izmir
context: The Property and Freedom Society, founded by Hoppe in 2006, meets each year in Bodrum, Turkey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Property_and_Freedom_Society.

question: In his 2001 book Democracy: The God That Failed, Hans-Hermann Hoppe compares a hereditary king with an elected president. Both hold power over a country, but Hoppe says one weighs tomorrow against today very differently than the other. He builds his whole argument on one economic idea about how each ruler values the future. Which idea anchors his case?
answer: Time-preference of the officeholder
choices: Time-preference of the officeholder
Marginal-utility of the median voter
Nash equilibrium of party competition
Coase bargaining across constitutional layers
context: Hoppe's argument turns on time-preference: how heavily an officeholder weighs the present against the future, given his tenure horizon. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe, a German libertarian philosopher trained in the Austrian tradition, wrote a controversial 2001 book called Democracy: The God That Failed. In it he compared the incentives of two very different rulers -- a hereditary king who passes his kingdom on to his heir, and an elected politician who holds office for a fixed short term. Hoppe used one clear analogy from ordinary property life to show how differently the two treat the country they govern. Which analogy captures his point?
answer: A monarch owns the country; a democratic politician rents it
choices: A monarch owns the country; a democratic politician rents it
A monarch leases the country; a democratic politician homesteads it
A monarch mortgages the country; a democratic politician insures it
A monarch inherits the country; a democratic politician sub-lets it
context: Owner-vs-renter is Hoppe's core analogy: an owner protects the long-term value of an asset; a renter has an incentive to extract before the lease expires. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: In Democracy: The God That Failed, Hans-Hermann Hoppe argues that a hereditary king, who owns his kingdom outright, handles government debt differently than a president who holds office for only a fixed elected term. Because the king treats the country as his family's long-term property, he cares about its future revenue. What does Hoppe's argument predict the elected leader will do about public borrowing?
answer: He borrows heavily against future taxpayers he will not answer to
choices: He borrows heavily against future taxpayers he will not answer to
He avoids borrowing to keep his term's balance sheet clean
He borrows only from citizens who voted for him
He borrows against his own private estate rather than the state's
context: In Hoppe's incentive analysis a term-limited politician is rewarded for pulling forward spending and pushing costs onto successors and their taxpayers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: The German libertarian philosopher Hans-Hermann Hoppe developed a famous line of reasoning in the 1980s that he called 'argumentation ethics.' It goes like this: the very moment two people begin to argue with each other at all, each is already using their own voice, their own body, and their own time to make the case. Nobody can consistently argue that they do not own the very things they must use to argue with. So arguing itself, Hoppe said, quietly assumes each person owns something. What does the argument say each person must own?
answer: Their own body
choices: Their own body
A share of the state
A patch of common land
The other person's attention
context: Hoppe's argumentation-ethics move (1988) claims performative contradiction: to argue at all, one must already exercise property in one's own body. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Argumentation_ethics.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe's Democracy: The God That Failed split the Austrian school — the tradition of Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, Murray Rothbard, and Friedrich Hayek that stresses market prices and individual choice. Two Austrians accept much of Hoppe's incentive analysis of politicians but reject his anti-democratic conclusion. Which pair is most often cited?
answer: Peter Boettke and Joseph Salerno
choices: Peter Boettke and Joseph Salerno
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz
Larry Summers and Jason Furman
context: Boettke (George Mason) and Salerno (Pace, later Mises Institute) are prominent modern Austrians who engage Hoppe's incentive analysis critically without endorsing his political conclusion. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: Long before Democracy: The God That Failed made him famous, the Austrian economist Hans-Hermann Hoppe wrote a 1989 book that laid out his praxeological ethics — an argument for private property that starts from the logic of purposeful human action itself — as a defense against socialism. What is that earlier book?
answer: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism
choices: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism
The Economics and Ethics of Private Property
The Great Fiction
Getting Libertarianism Right
context: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism (Kluwer, 1989) is Hoppe's systematic praxeological-ethics treatise, four years before The Economics and Ethics of Private Property (Kluwer, 1993). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: Imagine a country where the government has abolished markets and prices. One central planning office in the capital must guess, each year, how many shoes, coats, tractors, and pencils the whole country should make. But without prices set by buyers and sellers, the office has no way to know what people actually want, or how scarce each material really is. Ludwig von Mises made this challenge famous in the 1920s. What is this hard problem called?
answer: The calculation problem
choices: The calculation problem
The free-rider problem
The trolley problem
The bank-run problem
context: Hayek, teaching at LSE since 1931, assembled and edited the volume Collectivist Economic Planning (Routledge, 1935) to bring the German-language debate into English. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In 1920, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had argued that a fully socialist economy could never rationally set prices -- without private markets, planners had no way to know what things were really worth. In 1935, Mises's younger colleague Friedrich Hayek edited a book for Routledge in London that gathered essays on this calculation debate from several economists on both sides. Its main title was two words followed by a colon and a longer subtitle. What was the main title?
answer: Collectivist Economic Planning
choices: Collectivist Economic Planning
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Prices and Production
context: Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism, edited by F. A. Hayek (Routledge, 1935). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In 1935 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek edited an English-language collection called Collectivist Economic Planning. Its centerpiece was the very first English translation of a 1920 German essay that few English-speaking economists had ever read — an essay arguing that a socialist economy without market prices cannot rationally allocate resources. Whose essay was newly translated?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Ludwig von Mises's Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
Karl Marx's Critique of the Gotha Program
Vilfredo Pareto's Manual of Political Economy
Leon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics
context: S. Adler's translation of Mises's 1920 essay became the volume's centerpiece; before 1935 the argument had circulated only in German-language economic journals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In 1908, Italian economist Enrico Barone wrote a famous math paper called 'The Ministry of Production in the Collectivist State.' He argued that a planning board could in theory set every price in an economy — if it could just solve millions of equations at once. Later Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises pointed out something Barone had missed. What was the real, practical problem with the plan?
answer: No planner could ever gather all that information in time
choices: No planner could ever gather all that information in time
The equations worked perfectly whenever tried
Computers turned out to be too fast for it
Prices set themselves without any effort
context: Enrico Barone's 1908 essay outlined an equilibrium theory of a planned economy that Lange would later develop; Barone was actually closer to the eventual market-socialist reply than to Mises's position. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In his 1935 collection Collectivist Economic Planning, Friedrich Hayek wrote two of his own essays to bracket the translated centerpiece by Ludwig von Mises. The opening essay covered the debate's origins. The closing essay surveyed what German-language economists in the 1920s had already written on socialist calculation. What is the closing survey's short title?
answer: The Present State of the Debate
choices: The Present State of the Debate
The Nature and History of the Problem
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretense of Knowledge
context: Hayek's two 1935 contributions were 'The Nature and History of the Problem' (introduction) and 'The Present State of the Debate' (survey of the 1920s German-language exchanges). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In a 1920 German essay, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued that a socialist government which has taken over all the factories faces a hidden problem. Suppose the planners have to decide how much steel to send to making trucks, versus tractors, versus bridges. Mises said they cannot rationally make the choice. Why not?
answer: Without private buyers and sellers, there are no market prices to guide the choice
choices: Without private buyers and sellers, there are no market prices to guide the choice
Because paperwork always gets lost in transit
Because factories never keep records of any kind
Because steel simply cannot be measured
context: Lange's 'On the Economic Theory of Socialism' Parts I and II (Review of Economic Studies, 1936-1937) is the founding market-socialist reply to Mises and to the 1935 Hayek volume. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek spent the 1930s and 1940s writing essays on two connected ideas -- that a socialist central planner cannot calculate prices without a market, and that no single mind can ever gather the scattered local knowledge that markets pool automatically. In 1948 the University of Chicago Press collected his most important essays on these themes into a single book. What is the book's title?
answer: Individualism and Economic Order
choices: Individualism and Economic Order
The Constitution of Liberty
Law, Legislation and Liberty
The Sensory Order
context: Individualism and Economic Order (Chicago, 1948) collects Hayek's 1930s-1940s essays, including 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) and 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Individualism_and_Economic_Order.

question: The American writer Henry Hazlitt wrote a newspaper column about economics for twelve years. He kept pounding one idea, borrowed from the Frenchman Frédéric Bastiat. To judge a rule, don't just look at who it helps now. Look at everyone it affects — including the people you can't easily see. What is this idea usually called?
answer: The seen and the unseen
choices: The seen and the unseen
Supply and demand
The invisible hand
The zero-sum game
context: Henry Hazlitt (1894-1993) had already edited economics at The Nation before the NYT job; he left the Times in 1946 for a Newsweek column he kept for twenty years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hazlitt.

question: Imagine a weekly business magazine that has kept the same economics writer for twenty straight years. The editors print what readers actually want to read, and any reader can cancel his subscription any day and take his money elsewhere. What system, built on voluntary buying and selling, keeps this magazine trying hard to please its readers?
answer: Market competition
choices: Market competition
Central planning
A government subsidy
A price ceiling
context: Hazlitt's 'Business Tides' column ran in Newsweek from 1946 to 1966; Milton Friedman later took a similar Newsweek slot in 1966, calling Hazlitt the model. Source: mises.org/library/portrait-henry-hazlitt.

question: In 1946 the American economist Henry Hazlitt published a short, plain-spoken book on economics that would sell over a million copies and never go out of print. He dedicated it on the title page to Frédéric Bastiat, a French pamphleteer who had died almost a hundred years earlier and whose 'seen and unseen' method Hazlitt was carrying forward. Which book was it?
answer: Economics in One Lesson
choices: Economics in One Lesson
Man vs. the Welfare State
The Failure of the New Economics
The Foundations of Morality
context: First issued by Harper & Brothers in 1946, then Arlington House in 1979; the dedication reads 'To Frederic Bastiat, 1801-1850.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: Henry Hazlitt's 1946 book 'Economics in One Lesson' teaches readers to look past the costs everyone can see and hunt for the ones the eye misses. Hazlitt dedicated the book to Frédéric Bastiat, a French pamphleteer from the 1840s whose short essays first used the 'seen and unseen' method. That method has one big lesson to teach. What is it?
answer: Always look for the hidden cost of any policy
choices: Always look for the hidden cost of any policy
Money spent is always money well spent
Only visible spending matters at all
Hidden costs are always tiny
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' is the essay Economics in One Lesson expands, chapter by chapter, into a mid-20th-century American application. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: In his 1946 book 'Economics in One Lesson,' the American writer Henry Hazlitt boils the whole subject down to one rule. Don't just look at what a new policy does today for one favored group. Look at what it does later for every group in the economy. Hazlitt had learned this rule from the French pamphleteer Frédéric Bastiat. What mistake is the rule warning against?
answer: Judging a policy only by its short-term help to one favored group
choices: Judging a policy only by its short-term help to one favored group
Reading old newspaper stories about the economy
Buying anything not made in your own country
Studying charts written before you were born
context: Every remaining chapter is a worked example of 'the one lesson' applied to a specific New Deal or postwar policy (public works, price fixing, tariffs, minimum wage). Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: In 1946, the same year Economics in One Lesson came out, Henry Hazlitt and Leonard Read started America's first free-market think tank. It sat in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Which group did they found?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education
The Cato Institute
The Mises Institute
The Reason Foundation
context: FEE (1946) predates Cato (1977), the Mises Institute (1982), and Reason Foundation (1978); Read was president, Hazlitt sat on the founding board. Source: fee.org/about/our-history.

question: In 1959 Henry Hazlitt published a book-length reply to John Maynard Keynes, working chapter by chapter through Keynes's 1936 General Theory and answering each argument in order. Which Hazlitt book was that?
answer: The Failure of the New Economics
choices: The Failure of the New Economics
Man vs. the Welfare State
The Way to Will Power
The Great Idea
context: The 1959 book is the closest thing to a full Austrian-tradition rebuttal of the General Theory, section by section; Hazlitt also edited The Critics of Keynesian Economics (1960), an anthology of every major published critique. Source: mises.org/library/failure-new-economics.

question: In 1946 the American journalist Henry Hazlitt published Economics in One Lesson, a plain-English guide to markets that became one of the best-selling economics books ever. Friedrich Hayek — the Austrian Nobel laureate and champion of free markets — praised it in a single two-word verdict that later editions proudly printed on the cover. Which two-word verdict did Hayek deliver?
answer: A brilliant performance
choices: A brilliant performance
A useful contribution
A necessary reminder
A worthy attempt
context: John Chamberlain gave it the Wall Street Journal review; F.A. Hayek's 'a brilliant performance' has adorned the back cover of most editions since. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson takes a French pamphleteer's 1850 essay and turns it into a mid-20th-century American book. The essay it restates was written by a dying tuberculosis patient months before his death. Which essay did Hazlitt restate?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
The Wealth of Nations
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Principles of Political Economy
context: Bastiat published the essay in July 1850 and died that December. Hazlitt's book applies its seen/unseen method to public works, tariffs, minimum wage, rent control, and every other 1946 American policy in turn. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Milton Friedman and Ron Paul both told beginners to start with Economics in One Lesson. For generations, American libertarians read it as their first book on how markets work. What single method does the book teach a reader to use on any proposed policy?
answer: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
choices: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
Sum the private benefits and subtract them from the private costs the sponsors disclose in advance
Compare the proposed policy against a randomly-selected historical policy of the same category
Accept the sponsors' stated aggregate multiplier and evaluate against that benchmark
context: This is Hazlitt's 'one lesson' verbatim from chapter 1: extend the analysis in TIME (past the immediate effect) and in SCOPE (past the visible group). Every remaining chapter applies it. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Deflation means prices fall over time. Next year, a dollar buys more than today. That sounds nice, but it can hurt jobs, because people wait to buy, hoping prices drop again. What happens to workers when nobody buys anything?
answer: Businesses lay off workers
choices: Businesses lay off workers
Wages rise quickly
Rent goes way up
New factories open
context: Bernanke was a Fed governor from 2002 to 2005, then Council of Economic Advisers chair in 2005-06, then Fed chair from February 2006. The 2002 speech previewed nearly every unconventional tool he later deployed. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 the Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke gave a speech about fighting deflation — the danger of prices actually falling year after year. He borrowed a wild teaching image the economist Milton Friedman had first used in a 1969 essay to show one way a central bank could push new money straight into an economy. What was the teaching image?
answer: Dropping money from a helicopter
choices: Dropping money from a helicopter
Burying coins in bottles for people to dig up
Sending cheques to every household
Buying every unsold house in the country
context: Friedman used the helicopter image in his 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' as a pedagogical device -- not as policy advocacy. Bernanke's citation converted the device into a proposed toolkit. Source: Grokipedia 'Helicopter money' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2002 the economist Ben Bernanke, later chair of America's Federal Reserve, gave a speech joking that a central bank could always fight deflation by dropping money from a helicopter. He was quoting a 1969 essay by Milton Friedman that first painted the helicopter picture. The nickname 'Helicopter Ben' stuck to Bernanke for the rest of his career. What is Friedman's essay called?
answer: The Optimum Quantity of Money
choices: The Optimum Quantity of Money
A Program for Monetary Stability
The Role of Monetary Policy
Free to Choose
context: Friedman's 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' used the helicopter as a thought experiment for a one-time increase in the money stock. Bernanke's 2002 reuse of the image gave him a nickname that outlasted his tenure. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2002, Ben Bernanke was a Federal Reserve governor -- he would later become Fed chairman in 2006, just before the 2008 crash. That year he gave a now-famous speech titled 'Deflation: Making Sure It Doesn't Happen Here.' It listed the unusual tools a central bank could still use once short-term interest rates had already been cut all the way to zero. Which large-scale asset-purchase tool headed his list?
answer: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
choices: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
Buying gold bullion at fixed prices
Selling foreign-currency reserves against domestic bonds
Issuing zero-coupon perpetual bonds directly to the public
context: The 2002 speech listed buying long-term Treasuries, buying agency debt, buying foreign government bonds, and (in extreme cases) directly funding tax cuts by printing. All but the last were deployed 2008-14. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke's November 2002 speech, 'Deflation: Making Sure It Doesn't Happen Here,' listed a menu of unusual tools a central bank could reach for when short-term interest rates were already near zero. Nearly every tool on that list was deployed between 2008 and 2014 under three named Federal Reserve programs. Which trio corresponds to what Bernanke had previewed?
answer: QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist
choices: QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist
TARP, PDCF, and PPIP
SLR, GSIB, and TLAC
SDR, IMF SDR-A, and SDR-B
context: QE1 (November 2008-March 2010, $1.75T), QE2 (November 2010-June 2011, $600B), Operation Twist (September 2011-December 2012), and QE3 (September 2012-October 2014) implemented in reality what Bernanke had merely sketched in 2002. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 the Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke gave a speech titled 'Deflation: Making Sure It Doesn't Happen Here.' Its core argument was a bold claim about what a certain kind of central bank can always do to fight falling prices, no matter how low interest rates have already been pushed. What was Bernanke's claim?
answer: A central bank with a fiat currency can always create money at zero marginal cost
choices: A central bank with a fiat currency can always create money at zero marginal cost
A central bank must always coordinate with the fiscal authority
A central bank cannot inflate without abandoning its inflation target
A central bank must convert to a gold standard to maintain credibility
context: The core Bernanke claim: unlike a gold-backed central bank, a fiat central bank faces no natural limit on money creation. The only constraint is political will. This was reassurance to markets facing deflation risk; it was warning to Austrians. Source: Grokipedia 'Fiat money' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 the Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke gave a speech saying central banks with fiat currency can always create more money to fight deflation. Austrian-tradition critics — economists in the Mises-Rothbard line who oppose central-bank money printing — attacked the speech in real time as a blueprint for eventual currency debasement. Which trio is usually cited as those critics?
answer: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
choices: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Larry Summers
Alan Greenspan, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz, and Karl Brunner
context: Murphy at the Mises Institute, Schiff on television, and commodities investor Jim Rogers all publicly warned that a fiat central bank willing to buy anything creates the conditions for eventual currency crisis. Source: mises.org/library/robert-p-murphy (2002-2010 articles).

question: Exactly six years after his November 2002 deflation speech, Ben Bernanke — now the Federal Reserve chair — launched, in November 2008 during the financial crisis, the first Fed program to buy long-dated Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities at unprecedented scale, expanding the central bank's balance sheet by hundreds of billions of dollars. What was that first program called?
answer: QE1
choices: QE1
TARP
TALF
MMLF
context: QE1, launched November 25 2008, initially bought $600 billion of mortgage-backed securities and $300 billion of Treasuries. It grew from there. The 2002 speech now reads as the most accurate preview of Fed crisis policy ever given -- everything Bernanke said the Fed could do, he did. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In his November 2002 deflation speech, Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke admitted one power a central bank with a fiat currency can always use. Austrian critics called it 'monetary financing of fiscal policy' — the central bank paying for the government's spending by simply creating new money. What specific action did Bernanke say a central bank could always take?
answer: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
choices: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
Freeze all commercial bank deposits by decree
Impose negative interest rates on retail savings
Suspend all foreign-exchange transactions overnight
context: The speech acknowledged that a fiat central bank could in extremis monetize a tax cut. Critics said this was the door to 'helicopter money' in the literal sense: government spending funded directly by the printing press, bypassing bond markets. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: Ben Bernanke's 2002 Federal Reserve speech, 'Deflation: Making Sure It Doesn't Happen Here,' walked through the tools the Fed could deploy in a future crisis at the zero interest-rate bound. Six years later, during the 2008 financial crash -- with Bernanke now Fed chairman -- the Fed did almost exactly what the 2002 speech had described. Austrian and public-choice economists point to this pattern as a specific recognition move about how central bankers signal what they will actually do. Which move does the 2002 speech teach?
answer: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
choices: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
Central bank speeches are cheap talk and rarely predict actual future policy
Central banks always follow through on rate cuts announced in advance
Central bank crisis toolkits are never used because they exist to reassure
context: Read carefully, the 2002 speech told a listener exactly what would happen if a large financial crisis struck. Six years later it did, and the toolkit was deployed. Austrians took the speech seriously; most others did not. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: One book argues a bottle of water is worth more to a thirsty hiker in the desert than to someone standing by a river. So a thing's value depends on who wants it and when. What is this idea about value called?
answer: Subjective value
choices: Subjective value
Labor theory of value
Fixed pricing
A price ceiling
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics (Yale University Press, 1949), roughly 881 pages. Socialism (1922, English 1936), The Theory of Money and Credit (1912), and Bureaucracy (1944) were the earlier Mises books it drew together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Ludwig von Mises, an Austrian economist who fled the Nazis and settled in New York City, published his masterwork in English in 1949. The book was called Human Action, and it built all of economics up from a single starting axiom about people. Mises opened Human Action with a seven-word sentence and said the whole rest of the treatise rested on it. Which sentence begins the book?
answer: Human action is purposeful behavior.
choices: Human action is purposeful behavior.
In the long run we are all dead.
The proper study of mankind is man.
There is no such thing as society.
context: The line is the opening of Chapter I, Section 1 -- and the axiom from which the entire treatise is deduced. The Keynes line, Pope line, and Thatcher line were all real but from other authors. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: One economist said economics is like geometry: start from an obvious truth about people, then reason step by step. No lab tests needed. He rejected the opposing view that economics should copy physics and test ideas with real-world data. What is that opposing view called?
answer: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
choices: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
Scholasticism, which grounds economics in medieval theology
Historicism, which denies any general economic laws at all
Mercantilism, which measures national wealth by the trade balance
context: Mises's target was the mid-20th-century positivist program (later associated with Milton Friedman's 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics') that wanted economics to work like physics -- form hypotheses, test them statistically, discard the failed ones. Praxeology instead deduces laws from the action axiom and uses history only to illustrate. Historicism was the OLDER German quarrel with Menger; mercantilism was pre-Smithian; scholasticism belonged to an earlier era. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: In his 1949 masterwork Human Action, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argues that only one kind of thing in the world actually chooses — an individual human being with his own aims. Markets, societies, and whole economies, he says, are the outcome of many such individual choices, planned by no one from above. What does Mises call this basic rule of economic thinking?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Methodological holism
Methodological pluralism
Methodological monism
context: 'The market' does not act; only Alice at the fruit stall and Bob at the cash register act. A price, a boom, a shortage are the aggregate outcome no individual planned. Methodological holism (the whole society acts as a unit) was the position Mises rejected; the other two are unrelated terms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action was not first written in America. While living in exile in Geneva in 1940, Mises had already published a long German-language version of the same sweeping treatise, which he later rewrote and expanded in English after fleeing to New York. What was the title of that earlier 1940 German book?
answer: Nationaloekonomie
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Gemeinwirtschaft
Kapital und Kapitalzins
Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens (Union, Geneva, 1940) was completed in the spring of 1940, weeks before the fall of France. Mises rewrote and expanded it into English as Human Action. Gemeinwirtschaft (1922) was his book on socialism; Kapital und Kapitalzins was Boehm-Bawerk; Grundsaetze was Menger's 1871 founding text. Source: mises.org/library/book/nationalokonomie-theorie-des-handelns-und-wirtschaftens.

question: Chapter 26 of Ludwig von Mises's 1949 book Human Action folds in a much older argument he had first made in a 1920 German journal essay — the essay that opened the twentieth-century debate over whether a fully socialist economy could work at all. Which older Mises argument does Chapter 26 grow into?
answer: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
choices: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
That business cycles are caused by central-bank credit expansion
That the value of money regresses back to a prior barter demand
That interest rates reflect the community's time preference
context: Mises's 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' became Chapter 26 of Human Action ('The Impossibility of Economic Calculation Under Socialism'). The credit-expansion theory of the cycle became Chapter 20; the regression theorem for money is Chapter 17; the time-preference theory of interest is Chapter 19. Each has its own chapter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: The Austrian-school economist Ludwig von Mises fled Vienna in 1940 and came to America. New York University gave him an office and a title but no salary — his out-of-favor free-market views were not fashionable in the academy. For twenty-four years his paycheck came instead from the William Volker Fund, a private foundation set up by a rich businessman. What is this way of funding out-of-favor scholars called?
answer: Private philanthropy
choices: Private philanthropy
Government grant funding
Student tuition
Corporate advertising
