question: After the 2005 US Supreme Court ruling in Kelo v. City of New London — which let cities seize private homes and hand them to private developers — more than 40 US states passed new laws restricting that power. In public-choice economics this reversal is unusual. Homeowners were a spread-out victim group, and normally concentrated interests like developers beat dispersed victims. Yet here the dispersed side won. What made that reversal possible?
answer: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
choices: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
The federal government abolished eminent domain entirely
Insurance companies refused to insure any seized property
The Supreme Court reversed itself in a follow-up case
context: IJ served as the selective-incentive engine (documentation, model legislation, media) that turned diffuse public concern into effective 45-state legislative action. This is Olson's own solution to the collective-action problem in action. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo advocacy history).

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow proved something strange using math. When a group has to combine many people's votes into one shared ranking of choices, some rule of fairness -- like 'no dictators' or 'if everyone prefers A over B, the group must too' -- has to break. There is no way to keep every fair rule at once. What did Arrow prove could not be done?
answer: A perfectly fair way to combine everyone's votes
choices: A perfectly fair way to combine everyone's votes
A perfectly efficient factory
A perfectly free market
A perfectly balanced budget
context: Kenneth Arrow (1921-2017) won the 1972 Nobel jointly with John Hicks. He was 51 -- then the youngest economics Nobel. His doctoral book Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951) contained the impossibility result. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Arrow.

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow published a short book based on his doctoral paper at Columbia University. Inside was his famous proof: no voting system can combine everyone's votes into a group choice and keep every fairness rule at once. The title named two things at once -- the group side of choosing and the person side. What is the book called?
answer: Social Choice and Individual Values
choices: Social Choice and Individual Values
General Equilibrium and Welfare
The Theory of Voting Systems
Preferences and Aggregation
context: Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951; second edition 1963). The book launched the modern field of social-choice theory. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (2012 reprint of the second edition).

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow published a math result later called Arrow's impossibility theorem. It laid down a short list of common-sense fairness rules for any voting method and asked whether all of them could be met at once. One rule stated: if every single voter prefers option A over option B, then the group's overall ranking must also put A over B. What is this basic requirement called?
answer: Pareto efficiency (or unanimity)
choices: Pareto efficiency (or unanimity)
Independence of irrelevant alternatives
Non-dictatorship
Universal domain
context: Arrow's five criteria include unanimity (if all voters rank A above B, so does the group), independence of irrelevant alternatives, universal domain, transitivity, and non-dictatorship. The theorem proves no method satisfies all simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963).

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow proved that no voting system can meet every fairness rule at once. One of the rules he listed says that no single voter should be able to set the group outcome no matter what everyone else picks -- one person cannot rule the whole vote. What is that rule called?
answer: Non-dictatorship
choices: Non-dictatorship
Anonymity
Neutrality
Monotonicity
context: The non-dictatorship condition rules out any voting method that always follows one specified voter. Arrow proved that dropping this condition is the only way to make the other criteria consistent -- which is why the theorem is so provocative. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Three friends vote on pizza toppings: pepperoni, cheese, or mushrooms. Even simple voting rules can end up giving strange results where no clear winner appears. What does math actually say about a perfect voting rule that is always fair for every group?
answer: No such perfect voting rule exists
choices: No such perfect voting rule exists
One exists only when there are exactly three voters
Ranked-choice voting solves every possible case
It works only if every voter is completely honest
context: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem: for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives, no method can satisfy the five fairness criteria simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow proved that no voting system can meet every fairness rule at once -- but the result kicks in only when the group is choosing between enough options. With only two choices on the ballot, plain majority rule works fine and no paradox appears. What is the smallest number of options where the problem starts?
answer: Three
choices: Three
Two
Five
Seven
context: With only two alternatives, majority rule satisfies every Arrow criterion. The impossibility applies for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives. The classic Condorcet paradox is a three-voter, three-option case. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: In 1957 the American economist Anthony Downs described a pattern that shows up again and again in real elections. Picture two candidates running for class president. Most kids at the school want moderate rules -- no extreme changes either way. Both candidates only care about winning the most votes, so each has to decide where to stand on the issues. Where do the two candidates usually end up standing?
answer: Right in the middle, to appeal to the average voter
choices: Right in the middle, to appeal to the average voter
At the far left, to stand out from the crowd
At the far right, to stand out from the crowd
Refusing to state their views at all
context: Duncan Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making' (Journal of Political Economy, 1948), showed that if preferences are single-peaked on one dimension, majority rule picks the median voter's preferred option. It is the narrow exception to Arrow's impossibility. Source: jstor.org (Black 1948).

question: In his 1951 doctoral thesis at Columbia University in New York, the American economist Kenneth Arrow proved a famous mathematical result. No voting system, he showed, can turn each individual voter's ranked picks into a fair group choice while meeting a short list of basic fairness rules all at the same time. Arrow later won the 1972 Nobel prize partly for this proof. What is the idea called?
answer: Arrow's impossibility theorem
choices: Arrow's impossibility theorem
The median voter theorem
The invisible hand principle
The efficient markets hypothesis
context: John Hicks and Kenneth Arrow shared the 1972 Nobel 'for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory.' Source: nobelprize.org (1972 Economic Sciences).

question: In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow published his impossibility theorem. He proved mathematically that when three or more voters rank three or more options, no voting method can combine their individual rankings into one coherent group ranking without breaking a basic fairness rule. Arrow's result was a bombshell for democratic theory. It suggested that a phrase heard every election night to justify the winner names no coherent object at all — the aggregate simply does not exist. Which phrase does Arrow's mathematics dissolve?
answer: The will of the people
choices: The will of the people
The consent of the governed
The public interest
The rule of law
context: If different voting methods produce different winners from the same voter preferences, there is no method-independent 'will of the people' waiting to be discovered. The winner is jointly produced by voters AND the aggregation rule. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (Freeman 1982).

question: Kenneth Arrow's 1951 impossibility theorem showed that no voting method can fairly turn individual preferences into a single group preference. Public-choice economists like James Buchanan, who founded that school in the 1960s, drew a lesson: if there is no method-free way to find 'the will of the people,' then the rules that pick the method must matter enormously. Which set of choices does Arrow's theorem give added weight to?
answer: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
choices: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
The particular slate of candidates matters more than the rules
Party discipline can substitute for any voting-method choice
Judicial review can always correct impossibility results
context: James Buchanan built on this insight: rules that determine HOW votes are aggregated do not merely process a preexisting will; they partly DEFINE what the aggregate looks like. Constitutional political economy takes the rules-choice question with new seriousness. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (1982).

question: In the 1970s an Austrian-school economist named Israel Kirzner, working in New York City, wrote about what makes an entrepreneur different from anyone else. An entrepreneur, Kirzner said, is someone who spots a chance to make money that everybody else has missed — a shop nobody has opened in a certain neighborhood yet, or a product nobody has thought to build. What is the key skill Kirzner said an entrepreneur has?
answer: Alertness to opportunities others miss
choices: Alertness to opportunities others miss
Having the most money to invest
Being the best at math
Knowing the government well
context: Israel Kirzner (b. February 13, 1930), Competition and Entrepreneurship (University of Chicago Press, 1973). Kirzner was a student of Ludwig von Mises at NYU. Source: press.uchicago.edu (Kirzner 1973).

question: The Austrian economist Israel Kirzner published his 1973 book Competition and Entrepreneurship. He wanted to settle a debate about what an entrepreneur really is. Frank Knight said the entrepreneur is mostly a risk-taker. Joseph Schumpeter said he is mostly an inventor of new products. Kirzner disagreed with both. What did he say the entrepreneur really is?
answer: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
choices: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
Someone who assembles the largest possible capital
Someone who lobbies government for protective regulation
Someone who monopolizes an existing market
context: Kirzner separates alertness from Knight's risk-bearing and Schumpeter's creative-destruction innovation. The entrepreneur perceives an opportunity in the flow of prices and technology that competitors with the same information failed to see. Source: Kirzner, Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago 1973).

question: The Austrian economist Israel Kirzner taught that an entrepreneur is someone alert to profit opportunities others walk right past. Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997 and led the launch of the iPhone in June 2007. His rivals BlackBerry, Nokia, and Motorola dominated the phone market at the time, and all three kept their old designs. In Kirzner's terms, what did Jobs see that his rivals did not act on?
answer: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
choices: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
That mobile phones should be limited to voice calls only
That physical keyboards would dominate for the next thirty years
That personal computers should replace all mobile devices
context: Jobs saw the integration opportunity. Touchscreens (LG Prada 2006), music players (Apple's iPod since 2001), and phones (Nokia, BlackBerry, Motorola) all existed. The Kirznerian alertness was seeing they could combine. BlackBerry's Jim Balsillie publicly derided the iPhone in 2007. Source: Isaacson, Steve Jobs (Simon & Schuster 2011).

question: In 2002 the South-African-born entrepreneur Elon Musk sold his stake in PayPal and used the money to start a rocket company called SpaceX. NASA, Boeing, and Lockheed Martin had all missed one specific chance for 40 years — every one of their rockets was thrown away after a single flight, like burning a jetliner after landing it once. Musk built SpaceX to chase what they had missed. What was that chance?
answer: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
choices: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
Traditional expendable rockets built cheaper offshore
Government-funded space colonies on Mars
Suborbital tourism using balloons
context: The launch industry had assumed rockets were disposable for decades. Musk's insight was that per-launch cost drops dramatically if the first stage lands and is reused. Falcon 9's first successful landing was December 21, 2015. Source: spacex.com (Falcon 9 mission archive).

question: When Elon Musk founded the rocket company SpaceX in 2002, the space industry treated every rocket as one-use — flown once and dropped in the ocean. Musk bet that rockets could land upright and fly again, cutting launch costs dramatically. By the mid-2020s SpaceX had proved him right by landing and reusing its Falcon 9 first-stage boosters many times over. About how many such first-stage landings and reuses had SpaceX done by that point?
answer: Over 300
choices: Over 300
About 10
About 30
About 3,000
context: By 2024 SpaceX had landed and reused Falcon 9 first stages over 300 times, some individual boosters twenty times or more. It has driven launch prices down substantially and captured most of the commercial launch market. Source: spacex.com (launch archive).

question: The Austrian economist Israel Kirzner argued that great entrepreneurs are people alert to opportunities the market has left open. On July 5, 1994, Jeff Bezos founded Amazon out of a garage in Seattle. He picked a single product category to start with rather than opening a general store. In Kirzner's view, what made this category the perfect launch point for a large online retailer?
answer: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
choices: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
Books have the highest per-unit profit margins in all of retail
Books face no competition from physical bookstores
Books are exempt from state sales tax on federal statute
context: Bezos's Kirznerian alertness: books were the perfect starting product for internet-scale retail. No physical bookstore could stock the long-tail catalog. Chain bookstores had the same information but did not move decisively online. Source: Stone, The Everything Store (Little Brown 2013).

question: Israel Kirzner emigrated from Britain and enrolled at New York University in the 1950s. There he found an older Austrian economist who ran the famous NYU Friday-night seminar and had written a huge 1949 treatise on human action. Kirzner became this teacher's most devoted student, and later carried his method into a whole new generation of Austrian economists. Who was the teacher?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Carl Menger
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
context: Ludwig von Mises taught at NYU from 1945 to his death in 1973. Kirzner was among his most prominent students and inherited the Austrian entrepreneurship-and-market-process tradition. Source: mises.org (Mises + Kirzner biographical materials).

question: The Austrian economist Israel Kirzner spent his career at New York University explaining what entrepreneurs actually do — spotting profit opportunities other people walked past. Many Austrians thought he deserved a Nobel Prize in economics for that work. He never got one. But in 2006 he did win a major international prize dedicated specifically to entrepreneurship research, funded by the Swedish government. Which prize did he win in 2006?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
The Presidential Medal of Freedom
The Templeton Prize
context: Israel Kirzner received the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research (Swedish Entrepreneurship Forum) in 2006 for his lifetime work. He is widely regarded as the leading Austrian theorist of the entrepreneurial function. Source: e-award.org (Kirzner 2006 laureate).

question: Israel Kirzner's Austrian framework asks one specific question about any successful company founder — Jeff Bezos at Amazon, Elon Musk at SpaceX, Steve Jobs at the iPhone. The technology was available to dozens of competitors. So was the capital. So were the engineers. Something else was not. Kirzner tells the analyst to focus the whole question on that missing piece. What does the Kirzner framework tell you to ask about the founder?
answer: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
choices: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
How much capital did the founder inherit from family
Which lobbying firm secured the founder's early contracts
How many patents did the founder personally hold
context: Kirznerian analysis: technology and capital are usually accessible to many; alertness is not. The reason a new firm succeeds where competitors failed is usually a specific perception of an integration or application others considered impossible. Source: Kirzner (1973), Chapter 2.

question: Austrian economists offered three different pictures of what an entrepreneur really is. Israel Kirzner said an entrepreneur is alert to opportunities others miss. Frank Knight said an entrepreneur is someone who bears true uncertainty about the future. Joseph Schumpeter said an entrepreneur invents new combinations that destroy old industries. Real founders like Elon Musk or Steve Jobs mix all three moves. What is the teaching value of pulling the three theories apart when we study a single founder?
answer: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
choices: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
It proves one of the three theories is always correct
It refutes the other two theories permanently
It replaces the need to look at any actual data
context: The point is not that a founder is 'a Kirznerian' or 'a Schumpeterian' in every action. The point is that different moves within a founder's career fit different theories: Bezos's book-choice was Kirznerian alertness; Musk's Mars ambition is Schumpeterian innovation; both took Knightian risks. Source: Kirzner (1973); Schumpeter (1911); Knight (1921).

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek pointed out a simple fact about modern economies: the knowledge needed to run one — who wants what, who can make it, what materials are near, what tools are broken, what a neighbor's harvest looks like this year — is scattered across millions of ordinary people going about their lives. No single office, computer, or planning agency ever holds it all. From that fact, what follows?
answer: No small group of planners can know enough to run the whole economy
choices: No small group of planners can know enough to run the whole economy
The government should hire more economists
Only computers can plan an economy
People should stop specializing at all
context: Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions with Basic Books in 1980; it ran 422 pages in hardcover and won that year's Law and Economics Center Prize. Stigler, Becker and Friedman were all Chicago colleagues of his, which is why they make honest distractors. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Knowledge_and_Decisions); Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: In 1980 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book called Knowledge and Decisions. Sowell built the whole book on a single article that the Austrian economist F.A. Hayek had written in September 1945 for the American Economic Review. Hayek's article argued that market prices carry scattered information no central planning office could ever gather on its own — the baker knows the bakery, the farmer knows the field. Which Hayek article was it?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretence of Knowledge
Economics and Knowledge
The Road to Serfdom
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review 35(4), September 1945. 'Economics and Knowledge' is his 1937 lecture, 'The Pretence of Knowledge' his 1974 Nobel lecture, and The Road to Serfdom the 1944 book. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' and 'Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Tin grows scarce -- maybe a mine floods, maybe a new use for it is found -- and the price rises. Manufacturers in a dozen industries economize on tin; none ever learns which cause it was. F.A. Hayek built his 1945 argument on this example, and Sowell built Knowledge and Decisions on Hayek's. What does Hayek say no central planning board could manage here?
answer: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
choices: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
Proving in advance that the scarcity was real and not a speculator's rumour
Keeping its own officials honest once tin was valuable enough to bribe over
Matching the speed with which foreign factories would switch to substitutes
context: Hayek's point is not that planners are stupid but that the knowledge is not theirs to have: it exists only as millions of particular circumstances of time and place. The price is not a summary of that knowledge -- it is the only form in which it can travel. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hayek' and 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: Thomas Sowell is an American economist trained at the University of Chicago who wrote dozens of books on economics, race, and public policy. In a 2018 interview near his 88th birthday, an interviewer asked which of his own books he was proudest of. Sowell picked a short, easy-to-read 1987 book — not one of his huge economics textbooks. Which book did he name as his personal favorite?
answer: A Conflict of Visions
choices: A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
Intellectuals and Society
Basic Economics
context: Sowell to Reason, November 26 2018: Knowledge and Decisions 'certainly was at the time, and it's certainly among the books that I'm proudest of now,' but his 'own personal favorite is Conflict of Visions, which is perhaps a third of the size and more readable.' Source: Reason, 'Thomas Sowell Returns' (https://reason.com/2018/11/26/thomas-sowell-returns/).

question: Thomas Sowell's 1980 book Knowledge and Decisions had rested its entire case on one 1945 essay by the Austrian economist F.A. Hayek about how market prices carry information no central office could gather. In December 1981, Hayek — then 82 years old and seven years past receiving the 1974 Nobel prize in economics — took up Sowell's book himself in the pages of the American libertarian magazine Reason. What did Hayek do there?
answer: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
choices: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
Objected in a letter to the editor that his 1945 essay had been flattened into slogans
Listed it among ten books he wished that he had written himself before the war
Warned readers that Sowell had confused his 1945 essay with Mises's 1920 one
context: Hayek's review ran in Reason, December 1981, under exactly that title. He wrote that Sowell had expanded admirably on his original concepts and made them clear to lay readers, with examples of economic activity drawn from the real world. Sources: Reason, December 1981 (https://reason.com/1981/12/01/the-best-book-on-general-econo/); Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: In the autumn of 1973 the pump price of American gasoline was held down by federal ceilings while queues at filling stations ran for hours. Oregon's Governor Tom McCall had no power to move the price, so he changed the rule about who could fill up -- the first state scheme of its kind, and other states soon copied it. What was Oregon's rule?
answer: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
choices: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
Every registered household received a coupon book good for a fixed number of gallons
The first two hours of every morning were reserved for commercial and farm vehicles
Each station auctioned off its remaining supply to the highest bidders at opening time
context: Oregon adopted odd-even rationing in the autumn of 1973, Governor Tom McCall urging stations to sell by the last digit of the plate. It is the clean illustration of Sowell's point: stop the price from rationing scarce gasoline and something else must ration it -- a queue, a coupon, a calendar. Source: Grokipedia, 'Odd-even rationing' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Odd-even_rationing) and '1970s energy crisis'.

question: The Law and Economics Center gave its 1980 prize to Knowledge and Decisions, calling the book a landmark work. The citation did not praise it in general terms; it named one specific thing the book had helped its readers understand. What did the committee name?
answer: The differences between the market process and the process of government
choices: The differences between the market process and the process of government
The reasons wage and price controls had failed in every decade since 1940
The drift of American courts away from the intentions of the Constitution's framers
The gap between what academic economists publish and what voters actually believe
context: The Law and Economics Center called Knowledge and Decisions a landmark work, chosen 'because of its cogent contribution to our understanding of the differences between the market process and the process of government.' Sources: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions); ContemporaryThinkers.org, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Through the winter of 1973-74 American drivers queued for hours at filling stations, and much of the coverage treated those queues as proof that the oil had simply run out. National inventories in fact remained adequate. Washington had capped the price of domestic oil and refined products. On Sowell's account, what did that cap do?
answer: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
choices: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
Moved the shortage from the pump back to the refinery, where it could be managed out of public sight
Raised the cost of hoarding so sharply that drivers ran their tanks down to fumes before refilling
Concentrated the loss on the oil companies while spreading the gain thinly across every single driver
context: The 1973 Arab embargo was a real supply shock -- crude went from about $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Sowell's argument is not that the controls caused the shortage but that they made it far worse: with the price frozen, refiners had little reason to produce more, drivers little reason to buy less, and hoarding paid. Source: Grokipedia, '1970s energy crisis' (https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s_energy_crisis) and 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: In his 1980 book Knowledge and Decisions, the American economist Thomas Sowell warned that modern societies face a growing split. Real hands-on knowledge — the kind held by farmers, tradesmen, and shopkeepers who deal with the world directly every day — gets pushed aside, Sowell said, by abstract theory about how society ought to work, held by planners and intellectuals far from the action. What gap does Sowell describe in his book?
answer: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
choices: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
Between what a government promises at election time and what it can actually afford to pay for later
Between the wealth held by a country's oldest households and the wealth held by its youngest ones
Between the speed at which a society's technology changes and the speed at which its laws get rewritten
context: Sowell's framing worry is a widening gap between firsthand knowledge and decision-making authority: the further a decision travels from the person who knows the particulars, the more it must run on somebody's general theory instead. Source: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: A student sums up Knowledge and Decisions as 'markets good, government bad.' Sowell's actual structure is different: he takes markets with their prices and profits, elected legislatures with their votes and lobbying, and courts with their rules of evidence, and runs every one of them through the same single test. What is that test?
answer: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
choices: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
Whether the people who designed the process meant well by those it would govern
How thinly the process spreads its costs and how narrowly it piles up its benefits
Which rival process would otherwise do the same job, and how badly it would do it
context: This is why the book is not a market-versus-state pamphlet: Sowell asks the identical question of every institution, markets included, and the answers come out different by institution rather than by team. The other three choices are real analytic moves too -- Sowell's own 'compared to what?', Mancur Olson's dispersed costs and concentrated benefits, and Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A college admits a student through a racial preference into a program where most classmates arrived far better prepared. Sowell argued this hurts the very students it was meant to help. He is clear his complaint is not about the students' ability. What does he say the admissions office never actually checks?
answer: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
choices: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
Whether this particular student's own high school was underfunded next to its neighbours
Whether the programme's faculty would end up marking this student harder than the others
How many students from the same background that programme had already admitted before
context: Sowell calls this mismatch. It grew out of what he saw teaching at Cornell in the late 1960s, where students admitted under preferences were disproportionately on academic probation -- not, he argued, because they could not do college work, but because the fit was wrong. He made the case at book length in Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study (Yale University Press, 2004). Note carefully what the argument is and is not: it is a claim about what admissions data can and cannot tell you, not a claim about who deserves a place. Sources: H-Net Reviews, DasGupta on Sowell, 'Affirmative Action Around the World'; Claremont Review of Books, Sowell, 'The Perversity of Diversity'.

question: The Black American economist Thomas Sowell wrote a plain-language textbook called Basic Economics, meant for anyone with no training in the subject. His very first rule fills the opening chapter: every choice you make means giving up the best thing you did not choose. Choosing college gives up years of a paycheck. Choosing a movie gives up sleep. Economists have one name for that giving-up cost. What is it called?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Sunk cost
Fixed cost
Marginal cost
context: Basic Books published it. Sowell followed it in 2001 with 'The Einstein Syndrome: Bright Children Who Talk Late.' The subject was well outside his usual economics beat and became his most personal work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Thomas Sowell, the Black American economist, is best known for books on economics and race. But he also spent years researching bright children who begin speaking unusually late — kids often mislabeled as autistic or slow. What drove him into that unrelated topic, and eventually into writing the book Late-Talking Children, was a specific event in his own household. What was it?
answer: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
choices: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
Sowell's own younger brother had been misdiagnosed as deaf
Sowell had witnessed a neighbor's child undergo similar mislabeling
Sowell had been asked to consult by a Stanford developmental clinic
context: When John was young, doctors and specialists variously diagnosed him as autistic, mentally retarded, or hearing-impaired -- all of which turned out to be wrong. John talked late and grew into a highly intelligent adult with a technical career. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell's own son John talked late as a small child. Sowell started studying other families with late-talking kids and saw a pattern. The children who talked late but were bright often had sharp math and music skills, and their relatives were often engineers, musicians, or scientists. Sowell named this cluster after a famous physicist who himself did not speak in full sentences until age three. What did he call the pattern?
answer: The Einstein Syndrome
choices: The Einstein Syndrome
The Turing Pattern
The Newton Cluster
The Feynman Presentation
context: Albert Einstein was reported to have been a late talker (his family said he did not speak in sentences until about age 3). The 2001 book carried the name in its title: 'The Einstein Syndrome: Bright Children Who Talk Late.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: After his own son talked late, the American economist Thomas Sowell wrote two books arguing that late-talking bright children were being over-diagnosed. Sowell said the professionals who evaluate these kids — pediatricians, speech therapists, and special-education programs — were not neutral judges. Their whole industry, he argued, ran on a specific incentive that pushed toward labeling. What incentive did he point to?
answer: Institutions had incentives to categorize children into named conditions with named interventions and named funding
choices: Institutions had incentives to categorize children into named conditions with named interventions and named funding
Institutions had a legal obligation to diagnose all children with a specific developmental syndrome
Institutions had a financial incentive to refuse to diagnose any child under age 5
Institutions had no diagnostic incentive of any kind
context: Sowell's argument is a Hayekian knowledge-problem move applied to a medical-institutional case. No single specialist could see the pattern because it crossed specialties, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded diagnosis-and-treatment over watchful waiting. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell built much of his life's work around a warning: big government programs run by distant experts, however well-meaning, tend to make problems worse instead of better. Sowell traced the failure not to bad character and not to bad intentions, but to a specific structural fact about knowledge itself. What is his main reason distant experts so often fail?
answer: They lack the specific local knowledge that people on the ground actually have
choices: They lack the specific local knowledge that people on the ground actually have
They secretly do not care about the people they are trying to help
They are almost always dishonest about their own motives
They rely too much on old-fashioned technology
context: Camarata's academic research provided a scholarly counterpart to Sowell's more accessible books. His own 'Late-Talking Children' (Broadway, 2014) drew on his Vanderbilt clinical practice. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell spent most of his career applying free-market reasoning to economics, race, and history. Late in life, prompted by his own late-talking son, he wrote two books on late-talking children. Those books took a specific reasoning move from the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek — one Sowell had long used on markets — and applied it to pediatric medicine. What is the core reasoning move that carried over?
answer: The knowledge-problem move: no single specialist could see the cross-specialty pattern, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over waiting
choices: The knowledge-problem move: no single specialist could see the cross-specialty pattern, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over waiting
The revealed-preference move: parents' choice of schools reveals their true valuation of education
The comparative-advantage move: economies specialize according to relative production costs
The efficient-markets move: all public information is instantly priced in
context: The same Hayekian analytical style Sowell applies to economic-policy questions carries over to a medical-institutional question. The books are often the first Sowell book recommended to non-economists because they show his method on a subject no one has a political axe about. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: In his seventies, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek wrote a three-volume set on rules, freedom, and the limits of what lawmakers can actually do well. Volume 1 came out in 1973 and Volume 3 in 1979. Its title lists three linked ideas that begin with the letter L. What is the whole three-book set called?
answer: Law, Legislation and Liberty
choices: Law, Legislation and Liberty
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Individualism and Economic Order
context: Law, Legislation and Liberty, Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1973 / 1976 / 1979. The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is a distinct earlier single-volume work; The Road to Serfdom (1944) is the wartime polemic; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected essays. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: The Austrian economist F.A. Hayek drew a famous picture to explain how societies get order. Think of a gardener, Hayek said, who plans and lays out every flower in a garden by hand. Then think of a forest, where every tree finds its own spot without any planner at all. Both a garden and a forest have order, in their own way. Hayek gave a special name to the kind of order the forest has. What kind of order does the forest have?
answer: A grown order that no one designed on purpose
choices: A grown order that no one designed on purpose
A hierarchical order commanded from the top
A random order with no pattern at all
A legal order backed by government force
context: Kosmos (grown) versus taxis (made) is Hayek's central pair -- a forest is a kosmos, a garden is a taxis. Hierarchical command is a species of taxis; randomness is Hayek's opposite of both; legal codification is legislative taxis. Source: Knowledge Problem blog, 'Hayek on Order: Cosmos and Taxis'.

question: The Austrian-British economist Friedrich Hayek won the 1974 Nobel Prize in economics. He gave a special name to systems that grow up on their own without any single designer — things like human language, English common law, and the market itself. No one plans them. They come from countless people acting on their own decisions and following local customs. What two-word phrase does Hayek use for such orders?
answer: Spontaneous order
choices: Spontaneous order
Central planning
Constructivist rationalism
Positive liberty
context: Hayek's canonical Kosmos examples of spontaneous order: language, the common law, market prices, and cultural norms. Central planning is the opposite; constructivist rationalism is the intellectual error Hayek attacks; positive liberty is Isaiah Berlin's concept, not Hayek's. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: Laws can grow in two very different ways. In one, a group of experts sits down and writes every rule in a big code book, and courts apply the code word for word. In the other, judges decide real disputes case by case, and later judges follow the earlier rulings, so rules build up over centuries from actual court fights. Friedrich Hayek admired the second kind for the same reason he admired markets — no single designer, lots of local knowledge. Which country is famous for the second kind?
answer: English common law
choices: English common law
Continental civil-code law
Roman imperial edicts
Islamic sharia jurisprudence
context: Common law grows precedent by precedent through judicial decision, without any single legislator; continental codes (Napoleonic Code 1804 and its successors) are deliberate taxis; Roman edicts and sharia have their own histories but are not Hayek's paradigm of a Kosmos-legal-order. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: The Austrian-British economist Friedrich Hayek wrote a three-volume work on law and freedom during the 1970s. In its second volume he went after a phrase people often use about market outcomes — poverty, unequal wages, who ends up rich or poor. Hayek called the phrase a category mistake, because a market has no single author to praise or blame, so its results can't be just or unjust the way a person's actions can. Which phrase did he target?
answer: Social justice
choices: Social justice
Economic freedom
Political liberty
Public reason
context: Hayek's argument: justice is a property of intentional individual conduct; the distribution that emerges from millions of separate voluntary acts is un-designed, so calling it 'just' or 'unjust' misapplies the concept. Economic freedom, political liberty, and public reason are terms Hayek uses positively or neutrally. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Volume 2.

question: F.A. Hayek was an Austrian economist who won the Nobel Prize in 1974. In his book Law, Legislation and Liberty he argued that the phrase 'social injustice' makes a category mistake: you can only call something unjust if a person chose it. To make the point he described a simple everyday scene where a natural event ruins someone's plans — nobody chose it, so nobody can be blamed. Which scene does Hayek pick?
answer: A rainstorm ruining a picnic
choices: A rainstorm ruining a picnic
A wolf carrying off a lamb
A river flooding a farmer's field
A rockfall blocking a mountain path
context: Hayek's picnic-and-rainstorm illustration: no one designed the weather to spoil your afternoon, so calling it 'unjust' misuses the concept of justice; his claim is that market outcomes are analogous. The wolf-and-lamb is Aesop and La Fontaine; river and traveler examples belong to other authors. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Volume 2.

question: In 1767 the Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson wrote a famous line that F.A. Hayek later quoted often: important things like language, money, and law are 'the result of human action, but not of human design.' The point is that these systems weren't planned by anyone — they grew over time from countless everyday choices. What does the phrase teach about how good social systems actually come about?
answer: They grow up from many small everyday choices, without any one person planning the whole thing
choices: They grow up from many small everyday choices, without any one person planning the whole thing
A wise ruler must sit down and design them from the top
They need central experts to keep them working properly
Only a written national constitution can ever create them
context: The exact phrase comes from Part III of Ferguson's 1767 Essay: nations 'stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design.' Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776); Hume died 1776; Hutcheson was Smith's teacher but did not coin this phrase. Source: Online Library of Liberty, Adam Ferguson quote page.

question: F.A. Hayek, the Austrian-born Nobel economist, wrote a three-volume book called Law, Legislation and Liberty between 1973 and 1979. Volume 3, published in 1979, is his most political. He worried that plain majority-rule democracies were drifting away from stable general laws and toward day-to-day politicking, ruining the rule of law. To slow the drift, he proposed a specific constitutional change. What change does he propose?
answer: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
choices: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
A single-chamber assembly directly elected by universal proportional franchise
The abolition of parliament in favor of binding national referenda on major questions
The devolution of central authority to autonomous chartered city-states of Swiss size
context: Hayek's design: a rule-making chamber elected on a long, lifetime-scale franchise to insulate it from short-term political pressures, and a separate government-making chamber on ordinary franchises -- an explicit bicameral proposal to protect the rule of law from majoritarian drift. Source: University of Chicago Law Review, review of Volume 3.

question: F.A. Hayek, the Austrian economist and Nobel laureate, warned about a specific intellectual mistake. Someone looks at a slowly grown social pattern — human language, English common law, market prices — and treats it as if it were a machine that a clever committee could sit down and redesign from scratch. Hayek gave that mistake a name. What did he call it?
answer: Constructivist rationalism — the belief that reason can build a society from scratch
choices: Constructivist rationalism — the belief that reason can build a society from scratch
Methodological individualism — explaining groups by starting from persons
Analytical positivism — the view that only measurable claims count
Evolutionary skepticism — the doubt that old customs still fit new problems
context: Constructivist (or naive) rationalism is Hayek's label for the mistake of thinking that reason can design social institutions from scratch, as against evolutionary rationalism which recognizes tested-through-time rules. Methodological individualism is a separate Austrian commitment; analytic positivism belongs to the Vienna Circle Hayek argued against. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: F.A. Hayek published Volume 2 of his trilogy Law, Legislation and Liberty in 1976, subtitled 'The Mirage of Social Justice.' Five years earlier, a Harvard professor had put out a huge book that made 'social justice' the central topic in modern political philosophy. Hayek wrote Volume 2 partly to answer it. Which 1971 book was that?
answer: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
choices: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
Anarchy, State, and Utopia by Robert Nozick
The Open Society and Its Enemies by Karl Popper
The Concept of Law by H. L. A. Hart
context: Rawls's A Theory of Justice (Harvard, 1971) put social justice at the center of Anglophone political philosophy; Hayek's 1976 argument is the counter-tradition's reply. Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) was itself a reply to Rawls; Popper (1945) and Hart (1961) are earlier works Hayek shared intellectual ground with. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: The Hungarian-British scientist Michael Polanyi noticed something strange about real experts. A doctor spots appendicitis in seconds but cannot fully write down what tells her. A carpenter knows how to steady a warped board but cannot put every finger position into words. Polanyi named this kind of knowledge — real, usable, and passed on by practice, but almost impossible to write into a manual. What did he call it?
answer: Tacit knowledge — real skill you cannot fully write down
choices: Tacit knowledge — real skill you cannot fully write down
Analytic proof — a claim demonstrated step by logical step
Explicit rules — a written instruction anyone can follow
Formal theory — a general model with clearly stated axioms
context: Michael Polanyi (1891-1976), in Personal Knowledge (1958) and The Tacit Dimension (1966), argued that we know more than we can tell -- a claim Hayek treated as complementary to his own case that dispersed knowledge cannot be aggregated by a central planner. Popper, Berlin, and Russell were contemporaries in Hayek's circle but on other questions. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty; standard secondary literature on Hayek and Polanyi.

question: On September 15, 2008, the giant American investment bank Lehman Brothers suddenly declared bankruptcy after 158 years in business. Its collapse shocked the world overnight, froze the credit markets, and revealed that many big banks had been making very risky home loans and hiding the risk. What huge event did the Lehman failure help kick off?
answer: The 2008 financial crisis
choices: The 2008 financial crisis
The Great Depression
The 1970s oil crisis
The dot-com bubble
context: Lehman Brothers filed at 1:45 AM on September 15 2008 with $639 billion in assets, primarily mortgage-backed securities and commercial real estate. The S&P 500 fell 4.7% that day. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: A big bank's CEO gets paid huge cash bonuses every year his risky bets pay off. But if those same bets go wrong and the bank collapses, he still keeps every bonus he was already paid. And if the government even bails the bank out with taxpayer money, he pays no real price at all. Economists have a name for this situation, where one person takes the risk but other people pay if it goes wrong. What is this risk-taking problem called?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Opportunity cost
Sunk cost
Deflation
context: Fuld led Lehman from 1994 through the 2008 collapse. His stock holdings represented most of his personal wealth. When Lehman shares went to zero, roughly $450 million of his paper wealth was destroyed. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Fuld' (2026-09-05).

question: Lehman Brothers was a 158-year-old Wall Street investment bank. Through the summer of 2008 its share price kept falling and its CEO Dick Fuld tried to save the firm by selling it to a bigger buyer. Two specific rescuers came to the table — one in July and one in early September — and both walked away, leaving Lehman to file bankruptcy on September 15. Which pair of potential buyers walked away?
answer: Korea Development Bank in July and Bank of America in early September
choices: Korea Development Bank in July and Bank of America in early September
Wells Fargo in July and Deutsche Bank in September
HSBC in June and Barclays in August
Citigroup in July and Nomura in September
context: Korea Development Bank walked away in July over price. Bank of America talks collapsed in early September when a better opportunity to buy Merrill Lynch presented itself. Both losses left Lehman without an exit. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 the giant investment bank Lehman Brothers was failing. Over one desperate weekend in New York, the U.S. Treasury Secretary and the Chair of the Federal Reserve met with the bosses of the biggest Wall Street banks. The two officials tried to arrange a private rescue so Lehman would not collapse — and failed. Who were the two officials in that room?
answer: Hank Paulson and Ben Bernanke
choices: Hank Paulson and Ben Bernanke
Robert Rubin and Alan Greenspan
Tim Geithner and Janet Yellen
Jack Lew and Jerome Powell
context: Paulson (former Goldman Sachs CEO, now Treasury Secretary) and Bernanke (Fed chair) worked with New York Fed president Tim Geithner over that weekend. The private-rescue attempt failed when the strongest candidate buyer walked away. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 the huge American investment bank Lehman Brothers was hours from failing. A British bank, Barclays, was ready to buy Lehman and rescue it. At the last minute the US Treasury said it would not put taxpayer money behind any guarantee of Lehman's bad loans. Barclays now faced all the risk alone if the trades went bad. What did Barclays most likely do next?
answer: Walked away, since it now bore all the risk alone
choices: Walked away, since it now bore all the risk alone
Bought the bank anyway just to be a hero
Sued the American government for damages
Offered to double its purchase price
context: Barclays was the last serious buyer standing. British regulators refused to bless the deal without a US backstop, and Paulson would not provide one. Barclays walked away on Sunday, September 14. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: On September 15, 2008, the huge American investment bank Lehman Brothers failed. The next day a big money-market fund called the Reserve Primary Fund revealed that it had owned Lehman's short-term debt — now worthless — and its share price fell below one dollar. Savers had always trusted money-market funds to sit steady at a dollar per share. What did nervous savers do next?
answer: They rushed to pull their money out of other money-market funds
choices: They rushed to pull their money out of other money-market funds
They ignored the news and kept saving as usual
They bought more shares to average their price down
They asked the fund manager for a personal refund
context: The Reserve Primary Fund held over $700 million in Lehman commercial paper. It broke the buck on September 16 2008, triggering a broad run on money-market funds and forcing the Treasury to guarantee the whole sector. Source: Grokipedia 'Reserve Primary Fund' (2026-09-05).

question: After the crisis, Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson and Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke each wrote memoirs defending their decision not to rescue the investment bank Lehman Brothers in September 2008. Both men argued they had no real choice — a specific legal rule, they said, kept the Fed from lending to Lehman that weekend. What did they claim the constraint was?
answer: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
choices: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
The Fed was prohibited by the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act
The Fed needed prior congressional approval for the specific loan
The Fed's charter forbade any loan to an investment bank
context: Paulson and Bernanke both maintained that Lehman lacked the good collateral required under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act. Whether this claim was accurate has been sharply disputed by later historians. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: When a huge bank makes bad bets and starts to fail, the central bank sometimes lets it collapse and sometimes steps in with a taxpayer-backed rescue. Austrian-school critics say every rescue teaches banks around the country a dangerous lesson: they can gamble bigger next time, since the government will cover the losses. Economists have a name for that dangerous lesson. What is it?
answer: Moral hazard — taking bigger risks because someone else will cover the loss
choices: Moral hazard — taking bigger risks because someone else will cover the loss
Sunk-cost fallacy
Diminishing returns
Adverse selection
context: Larry Ball's The Fed and Lehman Brothers (Cambridge, 2018) built on years of archival research to argue that the collateral was adequate and the Fed's refusal was a political choice, not a legal necessity. Source: Grokipedia 'Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2008 the US Federal Reserve helped rescue the investment bank Bear Stearns, sending Wall Street a message that big firms would be saved. Six months later, in September 2008, the Fed refused to rescue Lehman Brothers and Lehman collapsed. The Lehman decision is the most debated single Fed action of the modern era. Austrian critics argue the Bear-to-Lehman shift proves a specific point about market expectations. Which point do they press?
answer: Markets had priced in a rescue based on Bear; the sudden removal of that expectation caused the panic that followed
choices: Markets had priced in a rescue based on Bear; the sudden removal of that expectation caused the panic that followed
The Fed's refusal to lend was economically correct and stabilized markets
Lehman's collapse was unrelated to the earlier Bear precedent
Only fiscal policy could have prevented the September 2008 panic
context: The March Bear rescue trained counterparties to expect similar treatment for Lehman. When the trained expectation was violated overnight, the panic that swept the system was exactly the outcome the earlier rescue had trained people not to expect. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012).

question: In September 2008 the U.S. Federal Reserve chose not to rescue the investment bank Lehman Brothers, and Lehman fell into the biggest bankruptcy in American history. Just six months earlier the same Fed had brokered a rescue of the smaller bank Bear Stearns. Austrian critics say the whole pattern — some banks saved, some not, all at the Fed's discretion — teaches a specific lesson about central-bank rescues. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: Discretionary rescues alter market expectations, and the alteration itself becomes a source of future instability
choices: Discretionary rescues alter market expectations, and the alteration itself becomes a source of future instability
Discretionary rescues always stabilize markets in the long run
Discretionary rescues are neutral because markets absorb them quickly
Discretionary rescues are effective only when applied uniformly to every failing firm
context: The Bear-then-Lehman sequence shows the trap: rescue creates expectation, non-rescue violates expectation, both generate systemic effects. Discretionary policy is not a neutral fallback -- each intervention rewrites the script for the next crisis. Source: Selgin, Money: Free and Unfree (2017).

question: Bitcoin is a digital money whose main record chain adds one new block every ten minutes. Each block holds only a few thousand payments — fine for big transfers, but too slow and too expensive for buying a cup of coffee. To fix small everyday payments, engineers built something new on top of the main Bitcoin chain. What was that?
answer: A second layer for fast small payments
choices: A second layer for fast small payments
A totally separate cryptocurrency
A permission slip from the government
A single huge central computer
context: Lightning is a layer built on top of Bitcoin, not a separate cryptocurrency. Base-layer Bitcoin remains the settlement rail; Lightning handles the fast, cheap, off-chain payments. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Bitcoin's main blockchain can only handle a few transactions per second, which makes small everyday payments slow and expensive. In January 2016 two developers published a paper describing the Lightning Network — a second layer on top of Bitcoin that would let people send fast, cheap payments through private payment channels without writing every single transaction onto the main chain. Who were the two authors of that founding paper?
answer: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja
choices: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja
Vitalik Buterin and Gavin Wood
Nick Szabo and Wei Dai
Adam Back and Hal Finney
context: The paper proposed payment channels secured by Bitcoin smart contracts. The mainnet went live in March 2018 with implementations from Lightning Labs (LND), Blockstream (c-lightning), and ACINQ (Eclair). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: The Lightning Network is a fast-payment system built on top of Bitcoin. Two people who want to trade a lot on Lightning start with one step on the main Bitcoin chain, where they lock up funds together. Then they can send payments back and forth off-chain, as many as they want. At the end, they settle the running total back on the main chain. What is that setup step called?
answer: Opening a payment channel with a funding transaction
choices: Opening a payment channel with a funding transaction
Broadcasting a proof-of-stake attestation
Registering with the Federal Reserve
Purchasing a Bitcoin ETF share
context: The funding transaction commits Bitcoin to a two-party multisignature address. Off-chain updates rebalance the split without touching the chain. When the channel closes, only the final balance is settled on-chain. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: The Lightning Network sits on top of Bitcoin and lets two people who share a payment channel send money back and forth instantly at almost no cost. Channels get more powerful when they link up. Alice has a channel with Bob. Bob has a channel with Carol. Alice can now pay Carol through Bob, even though she has no direct channel with Carol. What does Bob get for passing the payment along?
answer: A small routing fee, paid by the sender to each intermediary along the path
choices: A small routing fee, paid by the sender to each intermediary along the path
A block reward paid out of Bitcoin's monetary base
A transaction subsidy from the Lightning Labs company
An interest charge added to Carol's balance at settlement
context: Routing fees are voluntary market prices set by each node. The network structure depends on nodes with well-funded channels making themselves available for routing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: A small Central American country in 2021 declared Bitcoin an official money alongside the US dollar. Merchants had to accept it, and the government made a phone wallet so people could pay for lunch with almost no fee. What is the term for money the government officially accepts for paying debts and taxes?
answer: Legal tender
choices: Legal tender
Reserve currency
Fiat money
Central bank money
context: The wallet was called Chivo. Same-day the government issued each adult citizen a $30 Bitcoin allocation to encourage adoption. The rollout had bugs but demonstrated Lightning at national retail scale for the first time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: Bitcoin's main network is slow — worldwide it can only settle a few big transactions per second. So developers built a second layer on top that bundles tiny payments together and settles them cheaply and quickly. What is the name of Bitcoin's fast, low-fee payment layer?
answer: The Lightning Network
choices: The Lightning Network
The Merkle Tree
The Mempool
The Proof-of-Stake Ledger
context: Mallers appeared alongside President Nayib Bukele at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference where the legal-tender law was announced. Strike allowed US-El Salvador remittances via Lightning at negligible cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Mallers.

question: A high-school student in 2025 buys a $2 coffee in San Salvador using a Bitcoin app on her phone; the transaction settles in under a second for a fraction of a cent. A Hayekian economist notes that the Lightning Network solves a specific problem that a central authority could not have solved by fiat. Which problem?
answer: How to preserve auditable Bitcoin settlement while enabling coffee-sized payments no central rate-setter could price
choices: How to preserve auditable Bitcoin settlement while enabling coffee-sized payments no central rate-setter could price
How to eliminate all fees on international wire transfers by legislative decree
How to guarantee a fixed exchange rate between Bitcoin and the US dollar
How to compel merchants worldwide to accept a single national currency
context: Lightning fees are set by node operators competing for routing volume, not by any central body. Bitcoin's settlement layer stays fully auditable. The design is analogous to how the internet has TCP/IP at the base and higher-level protocols on top. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: In the 1990s an American hedge fund called Long-Term Capital Management was launched by famous math experts, including two economists who had won the Nobel Prize. They used very complex math models to make trades. In 1998 the fund suddenly collapsed and needed a giant rescue. What lesson did that teach the world?
answer: Complex math models don't guarantee safety in markets
choices: Complex math models don't guarantee safety in markets
Only Nobel winners should run hedge funds
All hedge funds always fail eventually
Government funds are always safe
context: LTCM's founder team included Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who had won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on options pricing (the Black-Scholes model). Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: Imagine a hedge fund uses one dollar of its own money plus twenty-seven dollars borrowed from banks to buy twenty-eight dollars of assets. Small gains become big wins — but small losses become disasters, because the fund still owes back all the borrowed money to the banks. What is this borrowed-money strategy called?
answer: Leverage
choices: Leverage
Inflation
Arbitrage
Diversification
context: LTCM held roughly $125 billion in positions against only $4.7 billion in capital -- a leverage ratio of about 27 to 1 (and much higher when derivative exposures were counted). For four years (1994-97) the strategy produced spectacular returns of 40%+ annually. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: A big trading firm bet that two nearly identical bonds would drift back to the same price. In 1998 a large country suddenly stopped paying its debts, panic spread across world markets, and the two bond prices moved far apart instead. What happened to the trading firm?
answer: It nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to prevent wider damage
choices: It nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to prevent wider damage
It doubled its money because prices moved exactly as expected
It quietly closed with no losses and moved to a new office
It bought the country's debt and forgave it as charity
context: The Russian government defaulted on August 17 1998, devaluing the ruble and defaulting on domestic debt. The resulting flight to quality made LTCM's leveraged spread bets go against them across every desk. Source: Grokipedia '1998 Russian financial crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: On September 23, 1998, the New York branch of the US Federal Reserve called the heads of 14 big Wall Street banks into one room. A famous hedge fund called Long-Term Capital Management was about to fail and drag the banks down with it. The banks agreed to pool their own money — not taxpayer money — to buy the fund out and unwind its trades quietly. How big was the rescue?
answer: About $3.6 billion
choices: About $3.6 billion
About $700 million
About $30 billion
About $250 million
context: The $3.6 billion September 23 1998 rescue was entirely privately funded. Each of the 14 banks contributed and took a stake in the fund's positions, unwinding them slowly over months. No federal money was used, but the Fed's coordination power was central. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 1998 the huge Connecticut hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management was collapsing after Russia defaulted on its debt, and its counterparty banks stood to lose billions. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York — whose president has traditionally handled Wall Street crises for the Fed — quietly summoned the big bank chiefs into a conference room and pushed them to organize a private rescue. Who was the New York Fed president who ran that coordination?
answer: William McDonough
choices: William McDonough
Timothy Geithner
William Dudley
E. Gerald Corrigan
context: William McDonough led the New York Fed 1993-2003. Peter Fisher ran the actual operation of coordinating the private banks. The rescue was a formative moment in Fed practice of coordinating rescues without directly using federal funds. Source: Grokipedia 'William McDonough' (2026-09-05).

question: Long-Term Capital Management was a hedge fund run out of Connecticut. It had no depositors, no branches, no small savers to protect — nothing the Federal Reserve is legally supposed to backstop. Yet in September 1998, as LTCM collapsed, the New York Fed still summoned the biggest Wall Street banks and pushed them to bail LTCM out. The Fed gave one specific reason for stepping in. What did the Fed say justified it?
answer: LTCM's counterparty banks were so exposed that a disorderly unwind could cascade into the banking system
choices: LTCM's counterparty banks were so exposed that a disorderly unwind could cascade into the banking system
LTCM held over $10 billion in FDIC-insured deposits
LTCM's Nobel-laureate advisors deserved public defense
LTCM's collapse would trigger a Russian government invasion of Ukraine
context: The 1998 justification: LTCM's counterparties (the 14 banks that would organize the rescue) were also its potential victims. A disorderly unwind of $125 billion in leveraged positions could damage them enough to trigger a broader crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1998 the US central bank helped organize a rescue of a giant private investment fund that had lost billions on risky bets. Critics said the rescue sent a bad message: from now on, risky private investors — not just regular banks — would expect a safety net. What is the term for the danger that a rescue teaches players to take even bigger risks next time?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Sunk-cost fallacy
Diminishing returns
context: The LTCM precedent extended too-big-to-fail protection beyond commercial and investment banks to any purely private vehicle sufficiently interconnected with the banking system. The 2008 AIG rescue and 2008 money-market fund guarantees extended the pattern further. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 1998, a giant American hedge fund called Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) was collapsing after billions in bad bets, and Wall Street feared it would drag other banks down with it. The billionaire investor Warren Buffett phoned in a private offer to buy LTCM's bad positions with his own money -- no taxpayers, no Federal Reserve. The deal fell through, and the Fed organized a rescue by other banks instead. Free-market critics wish the private offer had gone through. Why do they prefer private buyouts over government-led rescues?
answer: Private buyouts do not teach big firms that the government will always save them next time
choices: Private buyouts do not teach big firms that the government will always save them next time
Private buyouts always pay much more money than government rescues do
Government rescues are always against federal law
Private investors have unlimited money to spend
context: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, together with AIG and Goldman Sachs, offered $250 million for LTCM's positions in early September 1998. The offer would have wiped out the LTCM partners entirely. Negotiations broke down; the Fed rescue came days later. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: A hedge fund is run by two economists who share a Nobel Prize for pricing risk with elegant math. Their models say a market move as big as 1998's cannot happen in a thousand years. It happens the very next summer, and the fund nearly collapses. What did the math miss?
answer: Rare events are not as rare as models built on calm years suggest
choices: Rare events are not as rare as models built on calm years suggest
Nobel Prizes prove a model is correct in every market
Only unregulated funds ever lose their investors' money
The Federal Reserve can always predict the next crisis
context: Scholes and Merton won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for the Black-Scholes options-pricing model. Less than a year later, the fund they advised was near-insolvent. It is one of the most-cited coincidences in modern finance. Source: Grokipedia 'Myron Scholes' (2026-09-05).

question: When a huge lender fails, the government bails it out to "protect the whole system." Then a huge insurance company. Then a huge investment fund. Each rescue is called "just this once." What pattern does this teach about who ends up protected from failure?
answer: The circle of firms treated as too big to fail quietly grows over time
choices: The circle of firms treated as too big to fail quietly grows over time
Only small commercial banks ever get government protection
The government can protect big firms while still keeping others cautious
Private funds never receive help from federal regulators
context: The LTCM pattern extended through AIG (2008), the Reserve Primary Fund (2008), and eventually to any entity whose failure would cascade into the banking system. The Continental Illinois principle grew steadily across categories over four decades. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian school of economics teaches that the worth of a thing isn't fixed by its ingredients or its production cost. It depends on who wants the thing, when they want it, and why. A cold water bottle in the desert is worth a lot; the same bottle sitting in your fridge is worth much less. What is this idea called?
answer: Subjective value
choices: Subjective value
Fixed cost
Objective price
Central pricing
context: Ludwig Lachmann (1906-1990) taught at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg from 1948 and became the leading voice of what is now called radical-subjectivist Austrian economics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Ludwig Lachmann was an Austrian-school economist teaching in South Africa in the 1950s. In 1956 he published a short but important book arguing that a factory's machines, a farmer's tractors, and a bakery's ovens are all different tools with different uses -- capital is not one big lump of 'stuff' that can be totaled up. What short title did Lachmann give this book?
answer: Capital and Its Structure
choices: Capital and Its Structure
The Theory of Money and Credit
Human Action
Prices and Production
context: Capital and Its Structure (Bell, London, 1956) argued that a lathe is not a truck is not a factory building, and that aggregating them into a single 'K' hides the actual complementarities the cycle disrupts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Ludwig Lachmann, an Austrian-school economist writing in the 1950s, published Capital and Its Structure in 1956. In it he pushed back against a habit mainstream economists had picked up: treating every drill, oven, tractor, and truck in a country as one giant number the textbooks called K. Lachmann said this trick hid the real story of how different tools fit together. Which idea did he attack?
answer: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
choices: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
That capital is always privately owned
That capital depreciates at a constant rate
That capital is measured in labor-hours
context: The heterogeneous-capital claim: because specific goods have specific complementarities, adding them into aggregate K erases the very structure that matters to production and to booms and busts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: In the 1970s a new school of thought called 'rational expectations' argued that business owners can basically calculate the future using probability, as if tomorrow were a solvable math problem. Ludwig Lachmann, an aging Austrian-school economist who had known both Mises and Hayek, disagreed sharply. He said tomorrow is not a math problem -- it is genuinely open, and different business owners will guess about it in different ways. Which view did Lachmann defend against rational expectations?
answer: The future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs form different expectations
choices: The future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs form different expectations
The future is a well-defined probability distribution known to all entrepreneurs
The future is known perfectly through central-planner announcements
The future is irrelevant because entrepreneurs only respond to present prices
context: Lachmann invoked Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between measurable risk and genuine uncertainty; there is no such thing as 'the' rational expectation of a market participant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Austrian economists and post-Keynesians like George Shackle and Ludwig Lachmann argue the economic future is not just risky like a dice roll. Dice have known odds. The future is genuinely unknown because new inventions, new companies, and new choices have not happened yet — no odds can be honestly assigned to what does not yet exist. If they are right, what does that mean for ten-year economic forecasts?
answer: They are basically guesses and should not be trusted like weather reports
choices: They are basically guesses and should not be trusted like weather reports
They are perfectly accurate if the model has enough data
They only work inside communist economies
They only work during wartime
context: 'From Mises to Shackle: An Essay on Austrian Economics and the Kaleidic Society' (JEL, 1976) argued the tradition should follow Shackle's radical-uncertainty picture rather than any equilibration story. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig Lachmann taught for decades at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa. In a 1976 essay he pushed the Austrian school to its most radical position — markets are never in equilibrium, plans and expectations constantly shift, and the whole pattern reshuffles like a child's toy tube full of colored glass. Borrowing a word from the British economist George Shackle, Lachmann gave this restless picture of markets a two-word label. Which phrase became the name for his position?
answer: The kaleidic society
choices: The kaleidic society
The knowledge economy
The spontaneous order
The equilibrium constellation
