context: 'Kaleidic' -- from kaleidoscope -- captures Lachmann's picture of markets in constant pattern-shifting flux, as opposed to any tendency toward stable equilibrium. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: The Austrian school of economics — Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, and their students — argues that a modern economy is far too complex for any small group of central planners to run well. Their attack is not on planners' character or motives. They point instead to a specific structural problem about information itself that they say makes real central planning impossible. Which problem do they identify?
answer: No small group can gather all the knowledge scattered across millions of buyers and sellers
choices: No small group can gather all the knowledge scattered across millions of buyers and sellers
Central planners are always personally lazy and dishonest
Computers are not yet powerful enough to run the calculations
Ordinary workers refuse to follow any orders from the government
context: The NYU Austrian program under Kirzner and Rothbard was the principal American training ground for the modern tradition; Lachmann's visiting stint made him one of its senior figures. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Max Weber was a German sociologist writing around 1900. In his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) he argued that the values a culture teaches — hard work, thrift, honesty in trade, keeping your word — shape how well its markets grow, on top of any laws or natural resources. What broad claim is he making?
answer: Culture and shared habits shape a market as much as its rules do
choices: Culture and shared habits shape a market as much as its rules do
Only written laws matter — culture is only decoration
Only natural resources decide how rich a country becomes
Markets grow at the same speed everywhere regardless of habit
context: The Legacy of Max Weber (1971) applied Austrian ideas about individual choice under uncertainty to Weberian action-theory sociology. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises taught that free-market prices carry two kinds of information at once. Prices tell us what people actually want to buy. Prices also tell us what things really cost to make. In a communist economy where the state sets prices and there is no free market, what goes wrong for the central planners?
answer: Planners can't tell what is scarce or what people really need
choices: Planners can't tell what is scarce or what people really need
Factories run out of workers to hire
People stop having children
The government becomes too popular
context: Mises (1881-1973) fled Vienna via Geneva in 1934 and Europe in 1940. Hayek left Vienna for London in 1931, not New York; Schumpeter had moved to Harvard in 1932 with a full professorship; Machlup emigrated in 1933 and held paid chairs at Buffalo, Johns Hopkins, and Princeton. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises was an Austrian economist who spent his career warning that no government committee could ever gather enough information to run an economy from the top. He said the knowledge planners need -- who wants what, how much people will pay, what is cheap or scarce -- never sits in one office. In a free market, Mises said, that knowledge comes from one everyday place. Where does it come from?
answer: Prices set by millions of buyers and sellers making their own choices
choices: Prices set by millions of buyers and sellers making their own choices
Government surveys once a year
University economics departments
News reports on TV
context: Mises was born in Lemberg, then the capital of Austrian Galicia -- today Lviv, western Ukraine's largest city. The city was Polish (Lwow) between the wars, Soviet after 1945, and Ukrainian since 1991. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises was an Austrian economist who studied at the University of Vienna and earned his doctorate there in 1906. The two teachers who shaped him most were the founder of the Austrian School of economics and that tradition's greatest capital theorist. Which pair taught the young Mises?
answer: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
Alfred Marshall and Arthur Pigou
Leon Walras and Vilfredo Pareto
context: Menger (1840-1921) had founded the school with his 1871 Principles of Economics; Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) developed the theory of capital and interest and demolished the Marxian labor theory of value. Marx and Engels were Vienna's ideological opponents, not teachers; the other two pairs were English and Franco-Italian schools respectively. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises never held a paid university chair in Vienna. From around 1909 for the next 25 years his real day job was chief economist at a big Vienna organization that spoke for Austrian businesses and lobbied the government on their behalf. The University of Vienna only granted him an unpaid lecturer title. Which organization actually paid his salary?
answer: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce
choices: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce
The Austro-Hungarian National Bank
The University of Vienna
The Austrian Ministry of Finance
context: The Kammer fuer Handel, Gewerbe und Industrie (Chamber of Commerce, Trade and Industry) paid Mises to draft economic policy briefs on tariffs, labor law, and monetary reform. He held his unpaid University of Vienna Privatdozent title from 1913 to 1938 in parallel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: From 1920 to 1934 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises ran a private economics seminar in his Vienna office every other Friday night for 14 years. His most famous student, Friedrich Hayek, would go on to win the 1974 Nobel Prize. Hayek's central insight was that market prices carry information — facts scattered across millions of buyers and sellers — that no single central planner could ever gather in one place. What is this idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The marginal utility problem
The employment problem
The trade balance problem
context: Hayek (1899-1992) attended the Vienna seminar throughout the 1920s and shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal. Schumpeter (1883-1950) belonged to an older Vienna cohort and never received a Nobel (he died 19 years before the prize was created). Machlup and Morgenstern also attended the seminar but neither won a Nobel; Morgenstern is better remembered for co-authoring the 1944 Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with von Neumann. Source: mises.at/en/denker/ludwig-von-mises.

question: In 1920, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published a paper attacking the whole idea of full socialism. His argument was economic, not moral. In a fully socialist system, the state owns every factory, farm, and tool. Since these things are never bought and sold on a real market, they have no real prices. Mises said that without those prices, central planners face an impossible problem when they try to decide what to produce and how. What was his key reason?
answer: Without real prices, planners cannot tell which uses of resources create the most value
choices: Without real prices, planners cannot tell which uses of resources create the most value
Workers get lazy when everyone earns the same wage
Inflation always makes long-term planning impossible
Central bankers can never agree on interest rates
context: Margit Sereny (1890-1993) had been a Hamburg actress before her first marriage; she met Ludwig in Vienna in 1925 and married him in 1938 as Nazi pressure closed in. She wrote the 1976 memoir 'My Years With Ludwig von Mises' (Arlington House) and helped Lew Rockwell found the Mises Institute in 1982. The other three names are inventions. Source: mises.org/library/book/my-years-ludwig-von-mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises was an Austrian economist. In 1927, back in Vienna, he founded a small research group funded by the American Rockefeller Foundation. Over the next decade Mises and his colleagues — including a young F.A. Hayek — worked on a single question there: why capitalist economies swing between boom and bust. What was the group called?
answer: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
choices: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
The Vienna School of Political Economy
The Austro-Hungarian Monetary Union
The Kreditanstalt Research Bureau
context: The Oesterreichisches Institut fuer Konjunkturforschung was directed by Mises's young protege Friedrich Hayek from its founding; Hayek's monthly reports on the American boom made his name in Britain and led to Lionel Robbins's 1931 invitation to the LSE. The other three are inventions or unrelated institutions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises was an Austrian economist who fled Europe in World War II and died in New York in 1973. Nine years after his death, an American organizer named Lew Rockwell opened a research institute in Mises's name. It had the backing of Mises's widow Margit, Murray Rothbard, Henry Hazlitt, and Ron Paul. Which Alabama town has been its home since October 1982?
answer: Auburn
choices: Auburn
Tuscaloosa
Birmingham
Montgomery
context: Llewellyn H. Rockwell Jr. founded the Mises Institute in October 1982 and placed it in Auburn, home of Auburn University, whose economics department at the time had several Austrian-friendly faculty. Tuscaloosa is Alabama's other main university town; Birmingham is the largest city; Montgomery is the state capital. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/story-mises-institute.

question: Mises rejected the label 'economist' as too narrow for his method. He held that economics was only one branch of a wider deductive science of purposeful human action, and he preferred to describe himself using its Greek-derived name. Which self-description did Mises prefer?
answer: praxeologist
choices: praxeologist
monetarist
microeconomist
econometrician
context: Praxeology (from Greek praxis, action) was Mises's own coinage for the general science of purposive action; economics is the best-developed branch of it. Monetarism was Milton Friedman's Chicago-school program; microeconomist and econometrician are 20th-century academic labels Mises specifically resisted. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: In 1962, a 36-year-old American economist named Murray Rothbard published a massive two-volume, thousand-page book that presented the entire Austrian-school system -- human choice, prices, capital, money, business cycles -- as one connected theory. It became the standard Austrian textbook for the next generation of students. What is Rothbard's 1962 treatise called?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
Human Action
Individualism and Economic Order
Principles of Economics
context: Published 1962 by D. Van Nostrand of Princeton, New Jersey, in two volumes running 987 pages. Human Action (1949) is Mises's own treatise; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) is Hayek; Principles of Economics (1871) is Menger. Source: Wikipedia, Man, Economy, and State.

question: In 1962, the American Austrian economist Murray Rothbard published a huge treatise called Man, Economy, and State. But the project had started smaller. A donor foundation had first asked Rothbard to write a shorter textbook version of an earlier 1949 Austrian classic that most college students found too dense. Whose earlier book was he originally asked to turn into a textbook?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action
choices: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action
Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom
Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest
context: The William Volker Fund gave Rothbard the assignment in the mid-1950s. Under his hand the textbook grew into a full original treatise. Road to Serfdom (1944) is a political tract, not a treatise; Menger 1871 and Bohm-Bawerk 1884-89 predate the assignment. Source: FEE, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State at 50'.

question: After World War Two, most American colleges liked central planning and Keynesian economics. Big commercial publishers turned down manuscripts by free-market writers like Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, and Murray Rothbard. A quiet donor group called the William Volker Fund stepped in and paid to print those books anyway. Why does a story like this matter for the world of ideas?
answer: It lets unpopular ideas find an audience without needing official approval
choices: It lets unpopular ideas find an audience without needing official approval
It guarantees any funded book will become a bestseller
It forces universities to hire only free-market thinkers
It makes the government pay for every economics book ever printed
context: The Kansas-City-based Volker Fund, run by Luhnow after 1947, was the single largest financier of American classical-liberal scholarship in the postwar decades. The three larger foundations funded almost exclusively mainstream progressive research. Source: Gary North, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State: A Memoir', Mises Institute.

question: In 1962, the American economist Murray Rothbard published his massive Austrian treatise Man, Economy, and State. He opens the book with a chapter called The Fundamentals of Human Action, and every later chapter builds on it. Rothbard was following his teacher Ludwig von Mises in refusing to start economics from statistics or equations. What is the starting move that opening chapter makes?
answer: It takes as its axiom that human beings act -- consciously choosing means to reach chosen ends -- and deduces economic law from there
choices: It takes as its axiom that human beings act -- consciously choosing means to reach chosen ends -- and deduces economic law from there
It gathers price-and-quantity time series and infers regularities by statistical induction
It postulates a representative agent maximizing utility subject to a budget constraint
It begins with the equilibrium condition that aggregate supply equals aggregate demand
context: This is the Misesian method Rothbard calls praxeology: the science of human action, developed by deduction, not by econometric induction. The other three describe mainstream methodological rivals -- positivism, neoclassical utility maximization, and Keynesian aggregate equilibrium. Source: FEE, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State at 50'.

question: Murray Rothbard, the young American Austrian-school economist, finished writing his two-volume treatise Man, Economy, and State in the late 1950s. When the publisher, D. Van Nostrand, prepared the 1962 first edition for printing, they made one big change to the manuscript: they thought a specific stretch of it was too politically hot for a scholarly economics book. What did the publisher ask Rothbard to do?
answer: That the final eight chapters -- the systematic analysis of government intervention -- be cut before printing, as too politically radical
choices: That the final eight chapters -- the systematic analysis of government intervention -- be cut before printing, as too politically radical
That the entire manuscript be rewritten in the third person to sound less polemical
That the footnotes citing Ludwig von Mises be removed to avoid appearing derivative
That the two-volume format be compressed into a single introductory paperback
context: The cut section became a separate book eight years later. The 1962 first edition ran to 987 pages across two volumes even after the excision; the restored full text runs 1,506 pages. Source: Wikipedia, Man, Economy, and State.

question: Murray Rothbard was an American economist in the Austrian tradition. His 1962 economics treatise Man, Economy, and State was heavily cut before publication — his publisher stripped out a whole section attacking government intervention in markets. Eight years later, F.A. Harper's Institute for Humane Studies published those cut chapters as a stand-alone book, under a title that named its subject directly. What was the 1970 book called?
answer: Power and Market: Government and the Economy
choices: Power and Market: Government and the Economy
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
context: Rothbard's other books listed here are all real: America's Great Depression (1963), For a New Liberty (1973), The Ethics of Liberty (1982). Only Power and Market is the specific rescue-in-print of the excised chapters. Source: Mises Institute library, Power and Market.

question: In his 1970 book Power and Market, the Austrian economist Murray Rothbard tried to sort every possible way the state uses force in an economy into a clean taxonomy. He ended up with three groups. He grouped each act of state force by who was being forced and what they were being made to do or forbidden to do. Which three groups did Rothbard name?
answer: Autistic, binary, and triangular intervention
choices: Autistic, binary, and triangular intervention
Fiscal, monetary, and regulatory intervention
Progressive, proportional, and regressive intervention
Executive, legislative, and judicial intervention
context: The scheme is original to Rothbard and is the analytic backbone of Power and Market. The three-name scheme lets him treat drug bans, taxes, and rent control as three structurally different coercions rather than one blurry 'government activity'. The other groupings are real but describe different distinctions (kind of instrument, tax shape, branch of government). Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: The Austrian economist Murray Rothbard, writing in his 1970 book Power and Market, called it a triangular intervention when the state jumps into an ordinary deal between two private parties and forces or forbids the terms of their agreement. Two adults freely bargain, and a third party — the government — dictates how the trade must go. Which real-world policy is a textbook example of that shape?
answer: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
choices: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
A federal income tax withheld from a worker's paycheck
A statute making private possession of a drug a crime
A conscription order drafting a citizen into the army
context: Triangular intervention: state + two private parties whose exchange is dictated (rent controls, minimum wages, tariffs, licensing). Income tax and conscription are BINARY interventions (state extracts from the individual directly). A private-drug ban is AUTISTIC intervention (state forbids a solitary act, no exchange). Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: Murray Rothbard was an American Austrian-school economist. His 1962 treatise Man, Economy, and State was cut before publication, and the removed section came out as a separate book, Power and Market, in 1970. In 2004 the Ludwig von Mises Institute finally reunited both parts into one 1,500-page Scholar's Edition — the volume Rothbard had wanted in the first place. Which longtime Rothbard student edited it?
answer: Joseph Salerno
choices: Joseph Salerno
Milton Friedman
Israel Kirzner
James Buchanan
context: Salerno, a senior Mises Institute scholar and Rothbard student, restored the original architecture: pure market theory (Man, Economy, and State) plus the intervention analysis (Power and Market) in one framework. Friedman was Chicago School (Rothbard's methodological opposite); Kirzner was a Mises-seminar contemporary; Buchanan founded public choice. Source: Mises Institute, Scholar's Edition listing.

question: Milton Friedman was an American economist and 1976 Nobel Prize winner. In his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom he argued that political freedom depends on economic freedom: if the government decides your job, your rent, and the price of your bread, then voting for a new mayor changes almost nothing about your daily life. What is the core claim in one sentence?
answer: You cannot be politically free while the state controls the whole economy
choices: You cannot be politically free while the state controls the whole economy
Political freedom and economic freedom are unrelated in practice
Economic freedom is only possible under a single wise ruler
Voting is enough to protect freedom no matter who runs the economy
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago, 1962) and Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) reach overlapping political conclusions from opposite methodological traditions -- Chicago positivism vs Austrian praxeology. Samuelson (1948) is the flagship neo-Keynesian textbook; Keynes (1936) is what both books are arguing against; Galbraith (1958) is the progressive counterpoint. Source: Wikipedia, Capitalism and Freedom.

question: Imagine a law that helps 100 sugar farmers each earn one million dollars extra a year — one hundred million dollars in total. The law is paid for by charging one dollar a year to each of 100 million American taxpayers. The farmers fight fiercely to keep the law. The taxpayers barely notice they're paying at all. What is this pattern called?
answer: Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
choices: Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
Perfect competition
The invisible hand
Sunk cost
context: Mancur Olson Jr. (1932-1998) earned his PhD at Harvard and taught for most of his career at the University of Maryland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancur_Olson.

question: In 1965 a young American economist named Mancur Olson published a book with Harvard University Press that changed how people think about groups. He argued that large groups often fail to act on their shared interest because each member hopes someone else will do the work -- a puzzle he called the free-rider problem. The full title named both his topic (groups) and his central concept (the logic behind them). Which title did Olson give the book?
answer: The Logic of Collective Action
choices: The Logic of Collective Action
The Rise and Decline of Nations
Power and Prosperity
The Theory of Groups
context: The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of Groups (Harvard University Press, 1965). Source: hup.harvard.edu (Logic of Collective Action).

question: Ten million taxpayers each stand to save $10 if a certain subsidy is defeated. On the other side, a small few each stand to gain a million dollars if it passes. Olson's Logic of Collective Action predicts a clear outcome. Which side will organize a serious lobbying campaign?
answer: The hundred insiders
choices: The hundred insiders
The ten million taxpayers
Both sides organize equally
A neutral consumer coalition organizes both
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern. Each farmer has $1M at stake; each taxpayer has $10. The math of individual incentives, not moral character, produces the asymmetric lobbying. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965).

question: A middle-school class is doing a big group project. Twenty students all share one grade at the end, no matter how much each student does. Some students figure they can slack off, because the others will finish the work anyway just to protect their own grade. Economists have a name for this exact problem — a problem that shows up in taxes, unions, and international climate deals too. What is it called?
answer: Free-riding
choices: Free-riding
Regulatory capture
Adverse selection
The prisoner's dilemma
context: Free-riding is central to Olson's account: in large groups no individual has enough at stake to bear the cost of organizing, so each rationally hopes others will do it. The result is under-organization. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 1.

question: In 1965 the American economist Mancur Olson published a book called The Logic of Collective Action. It was widely misread as claiming that large groups can never organize themselves at all. Olson's actual argument was more subtle: he identified one specific mechanism that lets some large groups succeed despite the free-rider problem. What did he call this mechanism?
answer: Selective incentives
choices: Selective incentives
Coercive taxation
Charismatic leadership
Federal grants
context: Selective incentives are private benefits available only to members: union-negotiated contracts, professional certifications, discount insurance for AARP members. They give individuals a private reason to join what would otherwise be an under-organized group. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 6.

question: The American economist Mancur Olson, in his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action, showed that huge voluntary groups often hold together only because members are drawn in by private perks, not by any shared political passion. One American organization is his classic case. It has tens of millions of members who joined mainly for cheap insurance, hotel deals, travel discounts, and low-priced prescription drugs. Which American group is the standard example?
answer: AARP
choices: AARP
The American Legion
The Rotary Club
The League of Women Voters
context: AARP offers its members insurance and travel discounts as selective incentives; these private benefits sustain what would otherwise be an under-organized dispersed group of older Americans. Source: Olson, Logic (1965); Skocpol, Diminished Democracy (Oklahoma 2003).

question: The American economist Mancur Olson wrote three big books during his career. His first came out in 1965 and his last, published after his death, came out in 2000. In between, in 1982, he published a book that asked a hard question: why do some nations grow rich over generations while others slide into stagnation? What is the title of that middle book?
answer: The Rise and Decline of Nations
choices: The Rise and Decline of Nations
Power and Prosperity
The Political Economy of Growth
Sclerosis and Stagnation
context: The Rise and Decline of Nations: Economic Growth, Stagflation, and Social Rigidities (Yale University Press, 1982). It applied the Logic to macro-history. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (Rise and Decline).

question: In 1965 the American economist Mancur Olson wrote The Logic of Collective Action. He noticed a strange pattern in politics: some rules give a big benefit to a small group but spread the cost across millions who each lose only a little. The small group organizes and lobbies hard. The millions barely notice. Olson said this lopsided math explains why bad policies last even when the total cost beats the total benefit. In one word, what do these policies do?
answer: They survive
choices: They survive
They accelerate
They collapse
They rotate
context: The beneficiaries organize to defend the policy; the victims never organize to oppose it. Farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, occupational licensing, and thousands of similar policies survive for decades despite failing cost-benefit tests. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: The American economist Mancur Olson -- best known for his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action -- died in 1998, but his third book was already nearly finished. It came out in 2000 and used his ideas about interest groups and 'stationary bandits' (rulers who tax rather than plunder) to explain why some countries grow rich while others stay poor. What was Olson's posthumous 2000 book called?
answer: Power and Prosperity
choices: Power and Prosperity
The Wealth and Poverty of Nations
Institutions and Growth
Coalitions and Collapse
context: Power and Prosperity: Outgrowing Communist and Capitalist Dictatorships (Basic Books, 2000) was completed by Olson's students after his 1998 death. It introduced his 'stationary bandit' / 'roving bandit' framework. Source: basicbooks.com (Power and Prosperity).

question: Imagine the U.S. Congress passes a small tariff -- a $50-per-family tax on an imported good. Almost no one shows up at the hearings to fight it, and it sails through. The American economist Mancur Olson explained this pattern in his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action: laws that concentrate large benefits on a few and spread tiny costs across everyone are politically easy to pass. Using Olson's idea, why did this tariff pass so easily?
answer: A hundred domestic producers each gain millions; a hundred million consumers each lose a little
choices: A hundred domestic producers each gain millions; a hundred million consumers each lose a little
Congress overwhelmingly cares about consumer welfare on tariffs
The domestic producers spontaneously coordinate without lobbying
The consumers spontaneously organize but are overruled by judges
context: Olson's structural mechanism: the beneficiary side has enough per-capita stake to bear the cost of organizing; the victim side does not. The rest is arithmetic. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), applied throughout Rise and Decline (1982).

question: Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action knocked down an old assumption in political theory. Before Olson, most political scientists just took it for granted that whenever many people happened to share the same interest — workers, consumers, taxpayers, drivers — they would naturally band together and push for what they wanted. Olson showed that assumption was mostly false. Which idea did his book undo?
answer: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
choices: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
Small groups always fail against large coalitions
Politicians act from pure public spirit rather than self-interest
Voting systems always produce coherent group preferences
context: Pre-Olson pluralist theory (David Truman, Arthur Bentley) assumed shared interests produce organization. Olson showed the opposite: shared interest is not enough; you need selective incentives OR small numbers OR compulsion. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), preface.

question: On Tuesday, March 3, 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic reached the United States and financial markets began to panic, the Federal Reserve — America's central bank — did something unusual. Between its scheduled meetings, it announced an emergency cut to the federal funds rate. It was the first surprise rate cut since October 2008, at the peak of the last financial crisis. By how much did the Fed cut its rate that day?
answer: 50 basis points
choices: 50 basis points
25 basis points
100 basis points
75 basis points
context: The March 3 2020 emergency cut moved the target range from 1.50-1.75% to 1.00-1.25%. It was the first out-of-meeting emergency cut in 12 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2020 the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, made two emergency rate cuts to fight the pandemic shock. On a Sunday, twelve days after the first cut, the Fed slashed the federal funds rate down to a specific floor and left it there for two full years. What was the floor?
answer: Zero to 0.25 percent
choices: Zero to 0.25 percent
0.75 to 1 percent
0.25 to 0.5 percent
Negative 0.25 percent
context: The Sunday March 15 2020 emergency action cut an additional 100 basis points to a range of 0.00-0.25%. It also announced $700 billion in initial asset purchases. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2020 the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, promised to create as much new money as needed to buy government bonds. Chair Jerome Powell told markets there was no set limit. Critics called this 'money printing' and warned the flood of new dollars would eventually push prices in stores higher. What is one likely long-term effect of doing this?
answer: Prices in the economy rise as more dollars chase the same goods
choices: Prices in the economy rise as more dollars chase the same goods
Prices in the economy stay flat because dollars are magic
Everyone becomes richer without any cost to anyone
The government cancels all taxes because it no longer needs them
context: The March 23 2020 announcement removed any dollar cap on Treasury and mortgage-backed-security purchases. It also launched unprecedented new lending facilities. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic began wrecking the American economy, the Federal Reserve — America's central bank — did something it had never done in its entire history. It began creating new money to buy bonds issued directly by individual private companies like Apple, Ford, and AT&T. Critics like Peter Schiff and other Austrian economists said this crossed a very big line. Why did they say so?
answer: The central bank was now picking which companies to prop up
choices: The central bank was now picking which companies to prop up
The central bank ran out of gold to back its dollars
The central bank had never bought any kind of bond before
The central bank was banned by law from touching bonds
context: The Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility allowed the Fed to buy corporate bonds directly for the first time. Previously the Fed had bought only Treasuries and agency debt. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: By April 2020, the coronavirus panic had pushed the Federal Reserve into unprecedented moves. The Fed expanded its emergency bond-buying to include a new kind of debt: corporate bonds that had been rated investment-grade and safe before the pandemic but had just been cut down to junk-bond status by rating agencies like Moody's and S&P. Wall Street already had a colorful nickname for those downgraded bonds. What did people call them?
answer: Fallen angels
choices: Fallen angels
Zombie bonds
Toxic tranches
Widow-makers
context: The April 9 2020 expansion covered 'fallen angels' -- formerly investment-grade debt now trading as high yield. The Fed had crossed the line from Treasury-and-agency-only purchases into direct corporate credit allocation, including junk. Source: Grokipedia 'Fallen angel (finance)' (2026-09-05).

question: On April 9, 2020, during the COVID panic, the US Federal Reserve announced a new Municipal Liquidity Facility to buy state and city bonds. Combined with its new corporate-bond programs the same day, this pushed the central bank far past its old role of simply lending to banks. Which line did the Fed cross with these two moves together?
answer: Direct corporate and municipal credit allocation by the central bank
choices: Direct corporate and municipal credit allocation by the central bank
Guaranteeing all US mortgages
Setting long-term interest rates directly by yield-curve control
Issuing central-bank digital currency to households
context: For the first time in its history the Fed was directly choosing which private and municipal borrowers received support. This is credit allocation -- traditionally a legislative function, not a central-bank function. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: When the Covid pandemic hit in March 2020, the U.S. Federal Reserve began buying huge amounts of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities, expanding its balance sheet from about $4.2 trillion to a new peak in April 2022 -- the largest money-creation binge in Fed history. Austrian-school critics warned the flood of new dollars would show up as inflation, which it did in 2021 and 2022. Roughly how big did the Fed's balance sheet get at its April 2022 peak?
answer: About $8.9 trillion
choices: About $8.9 trillion
About $5.5 trillion
About $12 trillion
About $6 trillion
context: The Fed's assets peaked at roughly $8.9 trillion in April 2022 -- larger in dollar terms than QE1 plus QE2 plus QE3 plus Operation Twist combined. It was the largest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-22).

question: In March 2020, the Federal Reserve hired the giant Wall Street asset manager BlackRock to actually run its emergency corporate bond-buying program. Critics on both left and right pointed out an obvious problem. BlackRock is one of the very firms the Fed is supposed to regulate, and now that same firm was getting paid huge fees to help the regulator do its job. What is that cozy setup between regulators and the industries they oversee called?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Free-rider problem
Tragedy of the commons
Negative externality
context: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, was hired by the Fed to administer the corporate-bond-buying program. Critics noted BlackRock was also managing enormous corporate-bond portfolios for private clients at the same time. Source: Grokipedia 'BlackRock' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve's giant emergency lending programs of March 2020 all rested on a single legal power tucked into the original 1913 Federal Reserve Act. That section only lets the Fed lend outside its normal banking channels in what the statute calls 'unusual and exigent circumstances,' and it lets the Fed reach almost any private borrower it wants. Which section of the Federal Reserve Act is it?
answer: Section 13(3)
choices: Section 13(3)
Section 10(b)
Section 24A
Section 15
context: Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, dating to 1932, allows the Fed to lend to non-bank borrowers in emergencies. Its 2020 use was the broadest invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve's March 2020 rescue programs were far bigger than the 2008-to-2014 ones. Austrian economists at the Mises Institute warned that emergency tools rarely go back in the box after a crisis ends. They said the next crisis would begin from this new higher baseline of Fed intervention rather than from anything close to normal. What is the point the ladder is pressing?
answer: Emergency-era programs establish new institutional baselines, and next-crisis responses start from the elevated baseline rather than returning to normal
choices: Emergency-era programs establish new institutional baselines, and next-crisis responses start from the elevated baseline rather than returning to normal
Emergency-era programs are always fully unwound within two years
Emergency-era programs affect only asset prices, not consumer prices
Emergency-era programs are politically neutral and do not affect distribution
context: The Fed's 2020 balance sheet ($8.9T peak) is now the reference point. Any future crisis will be met with something at least as large. The Cantillon-effect distribution to first receivers -- asset holders, primary dealers, government contractors -- was correspondingly larger. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: In 2003, two economics professors at George Mason University in Virginia began writing a daily economics and ideas blog together. The site has kept running every single day for over twenty years, making it one of the oldest continuously updated economics blogs on the internet. Who started marginalrevolution.com?
answer: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
choices: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
Russ Roberts and Michael Munger
Bryan Caplan and Robin Hanson
Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner
context: Cowen (born 1962) and Tabarrok (born 1966) both teach economics at GMU, where they succeeded the Buchanan-Tullock generation as the public face of the George Mason public-choice and Austrian-adjacent tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_Revolution_(blog).

question: The public-choice school of economics, founded in the 1960s by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, is built on one simple idea. People who work in government — congressmen, presidents, bureaucrats, judges — react to incentives just like people working in a business or a household. They are not selfless angels once they cross into public office. What does taking this idea seriously mean for how a politician actually makes choices?
answer: The politician often picks what helps their own career, not the general good
choices: The politician often picks what helps their own career, not the general good
The politician always picks the option that helps everyone equally
The politician has no personal interests once elected to office
The politician cares only about their salary and nothing else
context: GMU became the successor institutional home of James Buchanan's Center for Study of Public Choice in 1983. Cowen directs the Mercatus Center at GMU; Tabarrok holds the Bartley J. Madden chair at Mercatus. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: In 2012 the George Mason University economists Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok launched Marginal Revolution University, a whole library of free economics video lessons. Anyone with an internet connection can watch and learn — no tuition, no admissions office, no application fee. What is the main gift of free online lessons like these to someone learning economics?
answer: Anyone with an internet connection can learn without paying college tuition
choices: Anyone with an internet connection can learn without paying college tuition
Only students already at top colleges are allowed to watch them
You must be over 30 years old to watch them
The lessons cost more than college but are shorter
context: MRU has millions of enrolled students as of the 2020s and is widely used in home-school and secondary-school economics. Its scene-led case-study style is directly modeled on Sowell's Basic Economics approach. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_Revolution_(blog).

question: In the 1800s and early 1900s, huge inventions like electricity, the automobile, indoor plumbing, and the airplane reshaped daily life. Since the 1970s, the George Mason economist Tyler Cowen argues in his book The Great Stagnation, far fewer such life-changing everyday inventions have appeared, and the economy has grown more slowly. What is this pattern usually called?
answer: A slowdown in productivity growth
choices: A slowdown in productivity growth
A trade deficit
A currency devaluation
A liquidity trap
context: Cowen followed 'The Great Stagnation' (2011) with 'Average Is Over' (2013, on labor-market polarization from technology), 'The Complacent Class' (2017), and 'Big Business' (2019, a partial defense of large corporations). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: In 2015, the George Mason economist and blogger Tyler Cowen launched a new podcast. Each episode features him interviewing a single guest for about an hour — economists, novelists, chess players, chefs, historians, and other public intellectuals. The show has now grown to more than 200 episodes and become one of the most respected long-form interview podcasts in the intellectual world. What is it called?
answer: Conversations with Tyler
choices: Conversations with Tyler
EconTalk
Freakonomics Radio
Odd Lots
context: EconTalk is Russ Roberts's older podcast (started 2006); Freakonomics Radio is Stephen Dubner's; Odd Lots is Bloomberg's Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway. Conversations with Tyler is Cowen's own long-form interview series. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: James Buchanan, an American economist who won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics, founded a whole school of economics on one blunt idea. He argued that politicians, bureaucrats, and government workers respond to incentives just like everyone else — chasing votes, budgets, and career gains — rather than acting as selfless servants of the public. What is that school called?
answer: Public choice economics
choices: Public choice economics
Behavioral economics
Development economics
Institutional economics
context: It was renamed the Mercatus Center in 1999 after a donor benefactor. The renaming came a full 16 years after Buchanan brought the center to GMU. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mercatus_Center.

question: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok teach economics at George Mason University in Virginia, the home of the public-choice tradition built by James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Vernon Smith. In 2003 they started the blog Marginal Revolution, and in 2012 they launched Marginal Revolution University with free video lessons. What did Cowen and Tabarrok add to that George Mason tradition?
answer: They moved the reasoning-move tradition online and into the popular economics conversation
choices: They moved the reasoning-move tradition online and into the popular economics conversation
They rejected the public-choice framework in favor of Keynesian macroeconomics
They took over the editorship of the American Economic Review
They served consecutively as chair of the Federal Reserve
context: Where Buchanan and Tullock built the academic apparatus, Cowen and Tabarrok made the reasoning-move tradition accessible to a general reader without a degree -- through Marginal Revolution (daily blog since 2003), MRU (free courses since 2012), Cowen's podcast (since 2015), and their principles textbook. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: In 1962 the American economist Milton Friedman published a short book making the case for free markets to a general audience. Chapter 9 went after state-issued doctor licenses, arguing they let doctors keep their numbers artificially low and their prices high. The book became one of the most-read defenses of free markets published in the 20th century. What is Friedman's 1962 book called?
answer: Capitalism and Freedom
choices: Capitalism and Freedom
Free to Choose
A Monetary History of the United States
There's No Such Thing as a Free Lunch
context: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962). Chapter 9 is titled 'Occupational Licensure.' Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo25839091.html.

question: The economist Milton Friedman, in his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom, argued that requiring a state license to practice medicine helps doctors more than it helps patients. Licensing keeps new doctors out of the profession, drives up the pay of the doctors already inside, and raises the price of care for everyone else. In each American state, who actually decides who gets a medical license and who does not?
answer: The state medical board, staffed largely by physicians
choices: The state medical board, staffed largely by physicians
The federal Department of Health and Human Services
The American Bar Association
The Federal Trade Commission
context: State medical boards, majority-populated by licensed physicians, control entry to the profession within each state. Friedman's diagnosis: this is a classic Stigler-captured licensing body. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 9.

question: In 1910 the Flexner Report, funded by the Carnegie Foundation, pushed states across America to close many small medical schools. From then on, doctors had to train at a small number of big elite schools only. Over the next decades, the number of new doctors entering the field each year fell relative to the growing population. What did this do to the price of seeing a doctor?
answer: It pushed prices higher because fewer new doctors entered the field
choices: It pushed prices higher because fewer new doctors entered the field
It pushed prices lower because doctors were more educated
It kept prices the same for a full century
It made all doctor visits completely free of charge
context: The Flexner Report (Abraham Flexner for the Carnegie Foundation, 1910) recommended consolidating US medical education on the Johns Hopkins model. Between 1904 and 1935 the number of US medical schools fell from 160 to 76. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexner_Report.

question: In 1910, a schoolteacher named Abraham Flexner published a report on American medical education. His report told state governments to shut down small proprietary medical schools that did not meet strict new standards. Over the next 30 years, the total count of medical schools in the United States dropped sharply as school after school was forced to close. About how did the number change between 1904 and 1935?
answer: From about 160 to about 76
choices: From about 160 to about 76
From about 500 to about 300
From about 76 to about 160
From about 40 to about 200
context: US medical schools dropped from about 160 in 1904 to about 76 by 1935. Enrollment fell correspondingly; physician incomes rose relative to comparable professions across the same period. Source: Starr, The Social Transformation of American Medicine (Basic 1982).

question: In many US states today, ordinary workers must get a government-issued occupational license before they can be paid to cut hair, arrange flowers, hang wallpaper, or even braid hair for their neighbors. Economists like Morris Kleiner have spent years studying what these licensing rules actually do to wages. What do studies of these rules generally find about the pay of workers who already hold a license?
answer: License holders earn more, because new competitors are kept out
choices: License holders earn more, because new competitors are kept out
Wages drop, because rules push customers away
Wages stay the same, since customers do not notice
Wages rise only during a recession
context: Morris Kleiner, Licensing Occupations: Ensuring Quality or Restricting Competition? (Upjohn Institute, 2006). His subsequent 2013 Journal of Labor Economics paper with Alan Krueger extended the analysis. Source: upjohn.org (Kleiner 2006).

question: The American economist Morris Kleiner has spent his career measuring occupational licensing in the US — laws that require a government permit to work in a job. Licensing covered about 5 percent of workers in 1950 and roughly a quarter today. His studies of hair-braider laws and interior-designer rules show that licensing mostly serves which group's interests?
answer: Existing practitioners
choices: Existing practitioners
New entrants
Low-income consumers
The uninsured
context: Kleiner estimates about a quarter of the US workforce now needs a state license to work legally. Licensed-worker wages are approximately 15% higher on average, with little measurable improvement in service quality. Source: Kleiner + Krueger, Journal of Labor Economics (2013).

question: In the United States, doctors used to be the only ones allowed to run a small primary-care clinic on their own. But by 2024, about half of US states had changed the rules — a nurse practitioner, a nurse with two extra years of medical training past nursing school, could open and run her own clinic with no doctor supervising her. Economists then compared prices and patient outcomes in those states to the old physician-only states, and they kept finding one clear pattern. What pattern?
answer: Lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference from physician-only states
choices: Lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference from physician-only states
Sharply worse patient outcomes and higher malpractice rates
Sharply higher primary-care prices and lower quality
Identical prices and quality but shorter waits
context: Multiple studies, including RAND Corporation work and AANP meta-analyses, find lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference. State medical societies routinely oppose scope expansion; state nursing associations support it. Source: rand.org (NP scope-of-practice studies).

question: In North Carolina, licensed dentists sitting on the state dental board tried to shut down cheaper teeth-whitening kiosks in shopping malls run by non-dentists. The kiosks were not hurting anyone -- they were just competition. The board used its state licensing power to run the rivals out of business. Free-market economists say this is a classic example of using government rules to shut out your competition. What is the term for that pattern?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Free trade
Comparative advantage
Creative destruction
context: North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, 574 US 494 (2015). The board had been trying to stop non-dentists from offering teeth-whitening services. The Court held that industry-majority boards without active state supervision lose Parker antitrust immunity. Source: supremecourt.gov (NC Dental 574 US 494).

question: The American economist Milton Friedman thought patients had a right to know whether their doctor was well-trained, but he did not want the government handing doctors a monopoly. He wanted a quality signal without the state-enforced barrier that lets a licensing board block newcomers from ever practicing. In place of state licensing, what did Friedman suggest?
answer: Certification rather than licensing
choices: Certification rather than licensing
Free-for-all with no state role at all
Federal licensing replacing state licensing
Direct government provision of the service
context: Friedman's certification / licensing distinction: the state may certify credentials, but should not forbid uncertified practitioners from offering services to informed adults who accept the trade-off. Quality signaling without monopoly. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962), Chapter 9.

question: The heart of the public-choice critique of medical and other occupational licensing is one default suspicion. If a state licensing board is filled almost entirely with members of the very profession it regulates — doctors regulating doctors, dentists regulating dentists, lawyers regulating lawyers — the incentives are obvious. When you see that kind of setup, what should you suspect first about the rules the board writes?
answer: That entry restrictions serve incumbent incomes more than public safety
choices: That entry restrictions serve incumbent incomes more than public safety
That the board will always adopt the safest possible rules
That state legislatures will oversee it closely
That patients enjoy full transparency into board decisions
context: The Stigler-Olson combined move: incumbents are the concentrated beneficiary organized to write the entry rules; patients are the dispersed party unable to organize. The default should be suspicion; specific safety justifications must be shown, not assumed. Source: Friedman (1962); Stigler (1971); Kleiner (2006).

question: The Austrian school of economics, founded in Vienna by Carl Menger in 1871 and carried on by Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, insists that only individual human beings can really act, choose, prefer, or decide. Countries, companies, and social classes do not literally do anything — the people inside them do. Every social outcome has to trace back to the actions of those individuals. What is this rule called?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Methodological holism
Structural functionalism
Historical materialism
context: Methodological individualism, made central to praxeology in Mises's Human Action (Yale, 1949), holds that groups, classes, and markets are useful shorthand but never literally act. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_individualism.

question: In economics, one camp says only real, individual people ever make choices, so all analysis must start from single humans. The rival camp says groups, classes, or whole societies act as units in their own right — Karl Marx's class analysis leans hard on this second move. What is the rival camp's method called?
answer: Methodological holism
choices: Methodological holism
Methodological individualism
Praxeology
Utilitarianism
context: Methodological holism (sometimes 'organicism') is the position Mises argued against. Marxist statements like 'the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat' are the paradigm case. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_holism.

question: One school of economics argues that a whole country's economy is really millions of people acting on purpose. Each is trying to make life better. Every price and every trade is one of those choices. Where does this school say the study of economics has to begin?
answer: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
choices: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
With the total amount of money in the country
With the government's official five-year plan
With the average behavior of a whole social class
context: Human Action (Yale, 1949) makes methodological individualism the foundation of praxeology in chapter 1 section 2, 'The Fundamental Task of Praxeology'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued that 'society' cannot actually make choices — only the individual people inside it can. A five-year plan that treats a whole nation like one big person will miss what real people actually want, need, and choose day by day in their own lives. What is this idea called?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Collective rationalism
Central planning theory
Social holism
context: Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies (Routledge, 1945) uses the same phrase and endorses the same doctrine from outside the Austrian tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies.

question: A Marxist writer says the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat. To an Austrian economist following Ludwig von Mises, that whole sentence hides what is really going on, because it talks in class abstractions instead of naming who is actually doing what to whom. A Misesian rewrites the sentence so the real people, choices, and incentives are easy to see. What move does the Misesian make?
answer: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
choices: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
Replace class terms with abstract aggregate demand curves
Replace class terms with statistical correlations across populations
Replace class terms with equilibrium price vectors
context: The analytical payoff of methodological individualism: 'the government intervened' hides everything; 'this senator, facing this lobby, cast this vote for this reason' opens up the incentive picture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_individualism.

question: Methodological individualism says every social outcome has to trace back to individual people acting. Some critics think this must mean every language, every market, and every custom was consciously planned by somebody in charge. But that is a misread of the idea. Friedrich Hayek, following the Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson, insisted on an important qualifier. What qualifier does the idea actually make room for?
answer: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
choices: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
Outcomes are always the intended plan of a central authority
Outcomes can be reduced to statistical population means
Outcomes emerge from unconscious biological instincts
context: The doctrine coexists with spontaneous order: a market price is not chosen by anyone yet emerges from individuals choosing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: In the 1700s the Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson, a friend of Adam Smith, coined a famous phrase. He said the great human institutions — language, common law, money, and markets — are 'the result of human action, but not of human design.' Friedrich Hayek later built a whole theory on that line. What kind of order does the phrase describe?
answer: A spontaneous order that grows without any single planner in charge
choices: A spontaneous order that grows without any single planner in charge
A carefully engineered order designed by government experts
A random order with no useful patterns at all
A dictatorship where one leader controls everything
context: Adam Ferguson's An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) contains the phrase that Hayek would use to describe spontaneous orders like markets, law, and language. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Adam_Ferguson.

question: The American Austrian economist Murray Rothbard published his own great economic treatise in 1962. It opens with the same methodological-individualist premise as Ludwig von Mises's 1949 Human Action — that all economic reasoning must start from individual human beings choosing means to reach chosen ends. What is the title of Rothbard's book?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
What Has Government Done to Our Money?
context: Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) is the postwar American restatement of the Misesian system on the same foundational premise. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: In 2020 the US Federal Reserve created huge amounts of new dollars to fight the COVID slowdown. Company treasurers watched their savings buy less each month. Some firms decided to move part of their cash reserves into Bitcoin instead of dollars. What makes Bitcoin different that would help protect a company's savings?
answer: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
choices: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
Bitcoin pays interest every month
Bitcoin is backed by the US government
Bitcoin is guaranteed by the Federal Reserve
context: MicroStrategy, headquartered in Tysons Corner Virginia and founded in 1989, was the first US public company to make Bitcoin a corporate-treasury reserve asset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroStrategy.

question: In 2020, Michael Saylor, the CEO of the software company MicroStrategy, shocked Wall Street by taking billions of dollars of his company's cash savings out of the bank and buying Bitcoin with it. Saylor explained he was guarding against one specific threat: when governments print more and more new money each year, each dollar left sitting in a company's bank account buys less and less over time. What is this money-printing problem usually called?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
Recession
Tariffs
context: Michael Saylor founded MicroStrategy in 1989 while at MIT. He stepped down as CEO in 2022 to become executive chairman but remained the public face of the Bitcoin strategy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Saylor.

question: In August 2020, the Virginia software firm MicroStrategy, run by CEO Michael Saylor, announced it would stop holding company cash in U.S. dollars and buy Bitcoin instead. Saylor said the dollar was a losing bet, and he blamed one specific pandemic-era Federal Reserve policy that was flooding the economy with new dollars. Which Fed policy did Saylor blame?
answer: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
choices: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
Setting the federal-funds rate at 5 percent
Selling off Treasury holdings under quantitative tightening
Raising bank reserve requirements sharply
context: The Fed's balance sheet grew by trillions in 2020-21 as it bought Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities to backstop pandemic markets. Saylor argued this made cash a certain loser and Bitcoin the hedge. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-21).

question: On August 11, 2020, the software company MicroStrategy -- led by CEO Michael Saylor in Tysons Corner, Virginia -- became the first big U.S. public company to move its cash reserves into Bitcoin. The money came from cash the company already had sitting on its books, not from any loan or new investors. Roughly how much did MicroStrategy spend on that first Bitcoin purchase?
answer: $250 million
choices: $250 million
$25 million
$2.5 billion
$50 million
context: MicroStrategy's August 11 2020 announcement: $250M converted from cash into Bitcoin. Subsequent purchases over 2020-2025 pushed total holdings well above 200,000 BTC. Source: microstrategy.com (August 11 2020 press release).

question: Michael Saylor's public case for holding Bitcoin sounds Austrian in almost every important way. He points to a monetary distortion in which new money benefits the first people who receive it, before market prices adjust. What is the name of that distortion?
answer: The Cantillon effect
choices: The Cantillon effect
The Fisher effect
The Balassa-Samuelson effect
The Baumol cost disease
context: Richard Cantillon's 18th-century observation: newly printed money enters the economy at specific points (banks, government contractors, financial-asset holders) and lifts those first-recipients' purchasing power before the broader price level catches up. Saylor frames Bitcoin as the escape hatch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantillon_effect.

question: MicroStrategy is a US software company whose CEO Michael Saylor turned the firm's corporate treasury into a huge Bitcoin stockpile starting in 2020. Through the 2022 crypto crash, when the stash was down billions on paper, Saylor kept buying more coins. To fund those buys, MicroStrategy issued one specific type of corporate debt again and again. Which kind of debt did they use?
answer: Convertible bonds
choices: Convertible bonds
Preferred stock
Bank revolvers
Municipal bonds
context: MicroStrategy issued multiple tranches of convertible senior notes 2020-2024 and used the proceeds to buy Bitcoin, effectively increasing its Bitcoin-per-share leverage. The stock ticker MSTR became a leveraged Bitcoin proxy. Source: microstrategy.com (investor filings 2020-2024).

question: In August 2020 the American software company MicroStrategy, led by its founder Michael Saylor, chose to store most of its cash reserves in Bitcoin instead of dollars. Saylor said he wanted to protect the company's savings from the inflation he expected after the Federal Reserve's pandemic-era money printing. What is this practice called when a company parks its cash reserves in Bitcoin?
answer: A Bitcoin treasury strategy
choices: A Bitcoin treasury strategy
Bitcoin mining
Bitcoin arbitrage
Bitcoin day-trading
context: As of early 2026 MicroStrategy is the largest CORPORATE Bitcoin holder in the world by a wide margin; other categories (individual wallets, exchange custodians, sovereign holdings) are larger overall but no single company approaches MicroStrategy's public treasury holding. Source: bitcointreasuries.net.

question: The American software company MicroStrategy, led by its founder Michael Saylor, changed its whole business identity to focus on holding Bitcoin as its main reserve. It even switched its corporate logo to Bitcoin orange and later renamed itself Strategy. Saylor tells shareholders that Bitcoin is not a short-term trading chip at all. What kind of asset does the company treat Bitcoin as?
answer: A long-term store of value
choices: A long-term store of value
A short-term trading chip
A daily payment currency only
A speculative penny stock
context: The rebrand was announced February 5 2025 and the legal name change to Strategy Inc took effect August 11 2025; the MSTR ticker was retained. Source: cnbc.com/2025/02/05/bitcoin-treasury-pioneer-microstrategy-rebrands-with-a-new-name-strategy.html.

question: Michael Saylor, the founder of the US software firm MicroStrategy, became the loudest corporate voice for putting company cash into Bitcoin. He argues the US Federal Reserve prints dollars so fast that holding cash silently steals from shareholders. In Saylor's view, protecting shareholders from that dollar debasement is not a nice-to-have or an optional choice for management. What kind of thing is it instead?
answer: A requirement of fiduciary duty
choices: A requirement of fiduciary duty
A public-relations decision
A regulatory-compliance obligation
A shareholder-vote matter
context: Saylor's move: if directors have a fiduciary duty to preserve shareholder value, and cash certainly loses purchasing power at a debasing central bank, then holding a scarce non-state asset is the fiduciary-consistent trade. It shifts the corporate-finance default. Source: saylor.org (public speeches 2020-2024).

question: Michael Saylor's MicroStrategy set off a small wave of US public companies putting Bitcoin into their corporate treasuries. In early 2021 one very high-profile carmaker joined in, buying about $1.5 billion of Bitcoin. Its CEO tweeted the news and Bitcoin's price jumped. But within months the firm sold much of the stash, spooking crypto markets. Which company made that quick retreat?
answer: Tesla
choices: Tesla
Block (formerly Square)
Marathon Digital
Coinbase
context: Tesla bought $1.5B in Bitcoin in January 2021 and sold roughly 75% of the holding within 18 months, taking the position mostly off its balance sheet. Block (formerly Square) and Marathon kept theirs. Source: sec.gov (Tesla 10-K filings 2021-22).

question: In 1976 the American economist Milton Friedman won the Nobel Prize in economics. His most famous line is that 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' -- meaning inflation is always a money problem, not a shopkeeper problem or a weather problem. What did Friedman mean by that line?
answer: Inflation is caused by printing too much money
choices: Inflation is caused by printing too much money
Inflation is caused by greedy shopkeepers
Inflation is caused by too many jobs
Inflation is caused by weather changes
context: Milton Friedman (1912-2006). His parents, Sara Ethel Landau and Jeno Saul Friedman, came from Beregszasz in Carpathian Ruthenia -- then the Kingdom of Hungary, today Berehove in Ukraine. Samuelson, Arrow and Kuznets were all real Nobel economists of the same era, which is why they make honest distractors. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Milton_Friedman); Wikipedia, 'Milton Friedman'.

question: The Chicago economist Milton Friedman and his wife Rose wrote a bestselling 1980 book called Free to Choose that also became a TV series. Its big claim about spending: letting ordinary people freely spend their own money beats which alternative arrangement?
answer: Letting government experts spend it for them
choices: Letting government experts spend it for them
Letting big companies spend it for them
Nobody spending it at all
Letting neighbors spend it for them
context: Rose Director Friedman was a Chicago-trained economist in her own right; in the mid-1930s she worked on the National Resources Committee's nationwide survey of consumer purchases. Reid and Brady were real consumption economists whose work fed into Milton's; Joan Robinson was the Cambridge economist. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rose Friedman' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Rose_Friedman).

question: A factory worker gets a one-time bonus of a thousand dollars. The Keynesian consumption rule of the 1940s predicted he spends a set fraction of it, just as he does of his wages. Milton Friedman's A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957) said that rule had missed something. What had it missed?
answer: That he plans his spending around the income he expects over years, and reads the bonus as a one-off
choices: That he plans his spending around the income he expects over years, and reads the bonus as a one-off
That he spends the bonus faster than his wages, because unearned money feels less real to him
That he cannot know whether the bonus is taxable until the spring, so he holds off spending it
That his employer set the size of the bonus knowing roughly how he was likely to spend it
context: This is the permanent income hypothesis. Friedman's charge against Keynes was precise: Keynes had related consumption to measured income without separating transitory income from permanent income. Published by Princeton University Press, 1957. Sources: Princeton University Press, 'Theory of the Consumption Function'; NBER, 'The Permanent Income Hypothesis'; Britannica.

question: By 1980 the American economist Milton Friedman had left the University of Chicago for the Hoover Institution at Stanford and was famous well beyond economics. That year he and his wife, Rose Friedman, made the case for free markets to a huge audience. It came out as both a best-selling book and a ten-part public TV series with the same title. What was it called?
answer: Free to Choose
choices: Free to Choose
Capitalism and Freedom
The Road to Serfdom
A Monetary History
context: Free to Choose (1980) was a book and a PBS series, with Rose Friedman as associate producer. Capitalism and Freedom (1962) is Milton's earlier book, The Road to Serfdom (1944) is Hayek's, and A Monetary History (1963) is the Friedman-Schwartz volume. Source: Grokipedia, 'Free to Choose' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose).

question: In 1969 President Nixon appointed a commission under Thomas Gates to study ending the draft, and Milton Friedman sat on it. General William Westmoreland, then Army Chief of Staff, testified that he did not want to command an army of mercenaries. Friedman stopped him with a single question. What did he ask?
answer: General, would you rather command an army of slaves?
choices: General, would you rather command an army of slaves?
General, what would you pay to keep the men you now command?
General, what price does your own patriotism carry today?
General, who is paying for the army you command right now?
context: Westmoreland objected that he did not like hearing patriotic volunteers called slaves; Friedman answered that he did not like hearing them called mercenaries -- 'If they are mercenaries, then I, sir, am a mercenary professor, and you, sir, are a mercenary general.' The commission's February 21 1970 report unanimously recommended ending conscription. Sources: Friedman and Friedman, Two Lucky People; Duke HOPE working paper, 'Slaves or Mercenaries'; Cato Institute centennial appreciation.

question: A famous 1963 book traced the amount of money in circulation in America year by year from just after the Civil War to 1960. It argued that the Great Depression was made much worse by the central bank letting the money supply shrink. What is the main lesson the book urged central bankers to learn?
answer: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
choices: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
Print unlimited money whenever growth slows down
Fix the exchange rate to gold once every ten years
Ignore money entirely and focus only on interest rates
context: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton, 1963) is by Milton Friedman AND Anna Jacobson Schwartz. She was a full co-author, not an assistant, spent seven decades at the NBER, and lived until 2012. Source: Grokipedia, 'Anna Schwartz' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Anna_Schwartz).

question: In 1976, the Royal Swedish Academy gave Milton Friedman the Nobel Prize in economics. The award named three of his works. Its closing line was almost a warning: it noted how hard it is for a government to steady an economy. Which three did the award name?
answer: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
choices: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
Price theory, the economics of the family, and the measurement of national income accounts
Monetary history, the theory of public choice, and the analysis of regulatory institutions
Consumption analysis, international trade theory, and the design of central-bank independence
context: The full citation: 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' The three strands map onto A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957), A Monetary History (1963), and the natural-rate argument. Sources: NobelPrize.org, Economic Sciences 1976 press release; NBER.

question: The common account of the Great Depression in 1963 was that markets had collapsed of their own accord and government had arrived to rescue what was left. Friedman and Anna Schwartz answered it with a measurement of the American money stock between August 1929 and March 1933. What had happened to it?
answer: It fell by about a third, from $26.6 billion to $17.3 billion
choices: It fell by about a third, from $26.6 billion to $17.3 billion
It rose by about a fifth, from $26.6 billion to $32.1 billion
It held almost flat, moving from $26.6 billion to $26.1 billion
It fell by about a twentieth, from $26.6 billion to $25.2 billion
context: Friedman and Schwartz's charge was not that the Fed had done too much but that it had done far too little: it let a third of the money supply disappear and turned an ordinary recession into the Great Depression. Friedman was no gold-standard partisan, which is what makes the finding so awkward for defenders of the Fed's record. Source: Grokipedia, 'Great Contraction' and 'A Monetary History of the United States'.

question: In 1967 the American economist Milton Friedman gave his presidential address to the American Economic Association. The popular idea then, called the Phillips curve, said a bit more inflation could buy a lasting drop in unemployment. Friedman told the crowd the deal would not hold up once workers wised up to it. Why not?
answer: Because once people come to expect that inflation, unemployment climbs back to where it started
choices: Because once people come to expect that inflation, unemployment climbs back to where it started
Because the extra money reaches exporters first and drives the currency down before wages move
Because no government can measure inflation fast enough to know when it ought to stop printing
Because employers meet rising prices by buying machinery, so unemployment never falls at all
context: Published as 'The Role of Monetary Policy' in 1968. Friedman called the level unemployment returns to the natural rate. The 1970s -- high inflation AND high unemployment together -- were widely read afterwards as the test his argument passed and the older view failed. Sources: American Economic Association, 'Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Milton Friedman's Presidential Address'; Bruegel.

question: Congress wants to lift consumer spending and mails every household a single rebate cheque of six hundred dollars, announced in advance as a one-time payment. A supporter predicts households will spend most of it within the quarter. An economist holding Milton Friedman's 1957 account of consumption expects much less. What is the reasoning he presses?
answer: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
choices: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
The cheque lands after the downturn has already turned, so the spending arrives unwanted
The cheque is funded by borrowing that households expect to repay in later taxes anyway
The cheque means far more to a poor household than a rich one, so the average misleads
context: This is the permanent income hypothesis doing policy work. Note what the argument is and is not: it says the rebate will move spending less than its sponsors expect, not that the sponsors are acting in bad faith. The three other choices are also real arguments made about rebates -- the lag problem, Ricardian equivalence, and distributional averaging -- each pressed by real economists. Sources: NBER, 'The Permanent Income Hypothesis'; Britannica, 'A Theory of the Consumption Function'.

question: Ludwig von Mises and Milton Friedman both concluded that central banking had made the twentieth century's worst downturns worse -- and they could barely stand each other's methods.
