Mises reasoned from principles about how acting people must behave, principles he held no statistic could overturn. Friedman thought that route unusable. What did he insist an economic claim had to do instead?
answer: Stand or fall on measured series -- money stock, prices, output -- that another researcher could check
choices: Stand or fall on measured series -- money stock, prices, output -- that another researcher could check
Rest on a written constitution that binds the central bank before any downturn actually begins
Begin from what a policymaker intends, since intentions determine which levers ever get pulled
Be reducible to a single equation, since anything not written as one cannot be argued about clearly
context: This is why Friedman must not be filed as an Austrian. He was a Chicago-school monetarist and a methodological empiricist: A Monetary History is a hundred years of data, not a chain of deductions. Austrians answer that human action is not laboratory chemistry and that the data themselves only mean anything inside a theory -- a live argument, not a settled one. Choice two is closer to James Buchanan's constitutional political economy. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Monetarism' and 'Chicago school of economics'.

question: A US Senator wants to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour to help low-wage workers. The Chicago economist Milton Friedman, following the French thinker Frederic Bastiat, taught readers to look for the person you don't see — the worker priced out when a wage floor jumps above their skill. Whose job gets priced out by the new $15 floor?
answer: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
choices: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
A senior union electrician earning $42 per hour under a long-standing collective bargain
A civil-service accountant on a fixed grade paying $58,000 per year
A hospital physician with a fellowship contract paying $190 per hour
context: Friedman's Bastiat-style worked example: at $15/hr floor, no employer can legally pay $15 for $8 of work; the 16-year-old's job does not exist, it does not appear as a fired employee, and so it is UNSEEN. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-the-minimum-wage.

question: The Chicago economist Milton Friedman wrote a Newsweek column in 1966 and a bestselling book Free to Choose in 1980 with his wife Rose. In both he gave the same blunt one-line description of what a minimum wage law actually forces employers to do. Which line did Friedman use?
answer: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
choices: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
A law saying employers must pay their workers fair market value
A law saying government fixes the price of labor for all industries
A law saying workers cannot bargain individually for wages
context: Friedman's exact 1966 Newsweek line, quoted again in Free to Choose (1980): the minimum wage forbids hiring low-skill workers at a wage that would clear the market. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-the-minimum-wage.

question: Starting in 2015 the US city of Seattle phased in a new minimum wage that hit its full $15 an hour in 2017-18, then the highest in the country. Right after the wage hit full force, three big fast-food chains — McDonald's, Panera, and Wendy's — rolled out a new piece of self-service gear inside their stores to cut labor. Which piece of gear showed up?
answer: Self-order kiosks
choices: Self-order kiosks
Robotic burger flippers
Automated deep fryers
Motion-sensor drink dispensers
context: McDonald's, Panera, and Wendy's led a mass kiosk rollout after Seattle's $15 floor took full effect; touch-screens do not need a wage, and became worth buying only once labor was made expensive by law. Source: seattletimes.com (2017-18 rollout coverage).

question: After Seattle's $15 minimum wage hit full force in 2017-18, big fast-food chains rolled out self-order kiosks in their stores to cut cashier hours. Economists point to this as a clean textbook case of one simple idea: when the price of hiring workers goes up, employers swap in more machines to do the same job. What is that machine-for-worker swap called in microeconomics?
answer: Capital-for-labor substitution
choices: Capital-for-labor substitution
Labor-supply elasticity
Income-effect dominance
Cross-price complementarity
context: Employers substitute capital equipment (kiosks) for labor (cashiers) once the relative price of labor rises above the price of the capital that can replace it. This is standard price-theory in every textbook including Sowell's Basic Economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_rate_of_technical_substitution.

question: In a famous 1994 paper, the American economists David Card and Alan Krueger checked jobs at fast-food chains sitting just across a state line. One state had recently raised its minimum wage floor. The other had not. They phoned the restaurant managers, counted workers, and reported little short-term job loss on the raise side. Which state pair did the paper make famous?
answer: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
choices: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
California vs Arizona agriculture
New York vs Connecticut retail
Texas vs Oklahoma construction
context: Card & Krueger 1994 became the standard mainstream citation for 'minimum wage does not cost jobs'; the paper is the reason Card later shared the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize. Source: American Economic Review 84(4), 1994.

question: In their 2008 book Minimum Wages, the American economists David Neumark and William Wascher pushed back on David Card and Alan Krueger's famous fast-food study. They argued that the earlier finding falls apart once you throw out phone surveys and use a much more reliable kind of employer data instead. Which kind of data did Neumark and Wascher push for?
answer: Payroll records from state unemployment-insurance filings
choices: Payroll records from state unemployment-insurance filings
Consumer-survey purchasing questionnaires
Store-window help-wanted sign counts
Chamber of Commerce membership rolls
context: Neumark & Wascher's response (2000 AER; Minimum Wages, MIT Press 2008) showed the Card-Krueger effect flips sign in long-run panels and in administrative payroll data rather than short phone surveys. Source: MIT Press catalog.

question: In his famous textbook Basic Economics, the American economist Thomas Sowell states the case against the minimum wage in a single sharp line. He argues the real cost is not paid by the boss and not by the customer at the register, but by an unseen victim — a specific young person who never even gets that first job interview because the legal wage floor has priced him out. In Sowell's own phrasing, who exactly pays the real price of the minimum wage?
answer: The chronically-unemployed teenager
choices: The chronically-unemployed teenager
The rising cost of restaurant meals
The shrinking size of retail chains
The falling profit margin of employers
context: Sowell's summary: there is no employer who 'refuses to pay a decent wage'; there are only employers who value particular workers below the floor and hire NO ONE at that skill. The unemployed teenager is the price. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics, 5th ed., chapter on price floors.

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that no distant planner can gather all the local knowledge scattered across a huge country. Free-market economists apply Hayek's 'knowledge problem' to the minimum wage: one single national wage floor cannot possibly be right for every worker in every industry in every region. What key knowledge does the local shop owner have that a distant lawmaker in the capital does not?
answer: What each specific worker is actually worth at that specific job in that specific town
choices: What each specific worker is actually worth at that specific job in that specific town
The total number of workers across the entire country
The average wage paid across every US industry
The interest rate set by the central bank
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-in-society argument applied to labor: the employer's local knowledge of a worker's productivity in a specific job is not available to a legislator setting a single national floor. This is the Hayekian bite of the minimum-wage debate. Source: fee.org/articles/hayek-and-the-minimum-wage.

question: In his 2011 book Race and Economics, Walter Williams anchors the minimum-wage debate on a single number. He points to teen unemployment in an era when the federal wage floor, in real terms, was very low. About what was the US teenage unemployment rate in the 1950s?
answer: About 10 percent
choices: About 10 percent
About 25 percent
About 40 percent
About 55 percent
context: US teenage unemployment averaged around 10% in the 1950s at a low real federal minimum wage; the rate averaged 15-20% after repeated 1970s+ increases, with especially high rates in black-teen cohorts (per Williams, Race and Economics 2011). Source: bls.gov historical LFS data.

question: The Chicago economist Milton Friedman and the two Black free-market economists Thomas Sowell and Walter Williams all wrote and spoke against minimum wage laws. Following the French thinker Frederic Bastiat, each of them ended his case with the same closing move about how a citizen should actually judge a policy like the minimum wage. What did their shared closing move say to judge?
answer: The results, not the intentions of its sponsors
choices: The results, not the intentions of its sponsors
The rhetoric, not the arithmetic of its opponents
The optimism, not the pessimism of its forecasters
The popularity, not the theory of its academic critics
context: 'One of the great mistakes is to judge policies by their intentions rather than their results' -- Friedman, restated by Sowell and Williams. The Bastiat move: the intended visible good is the SEEN; the actual outcome for the unseen victim is what matters. Source: fee.org/articles/friedman-intentions-versus-results.

question: In November 2010, a Czech coder using the name 'Slush' set up a new service. It let small Bitcoin miners join up, share their computing power, and split the payouts. Each miner got a small steady trickle instead of a rare lucky hit. What is this kind of service called?
answer: A mining pool
choices: A mining pool
A crypto exchange
A hardware wallet
A stablecoin issuer
context: The service was originally called Slush Pool and is now Braiins Pool. It solved the variance problem: as the network grew, a solo miner might wait years between block wins even with steady hashing effort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Braiins_Pool.

question: Bitcoin miners run computers that race to find a special number that unlocks a new block and its reward. Most miners team up in 'pools' so they can smooth out their income. Inside a pool, a miner gets paid for each valid partial hash they turn in — not just for finding the rare winning full hash. What is one of those partial-hash entries called?
answer: A share
choices: A share
A halving
A block reward
A dividend
context: A share is a hash that would have been a valid block at a much lower difficulty than the actual network target. It proves the miner did real work. Payout schemes like PPS, PPLNS, and FPPS all key off share counts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: Bitcoin miners run computers that compete to find the special number that unlocks the next block and its ~3.125-coin reward. The whole network only produces one block every ten minutes. Many miners with just one or two machines join large 'pools' that combine everyone's computing power and share the rewards evenly. Why does a small solo miner choose to join a big pool instead of trying to win blocks alone?
answer: Alone they may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
choices: Alone they may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
Solo mining is banned by Bitcoin's code
Pools give miners access to secret shortcuts
Solo miners must pay a fee to the government
context: Foundry USA rose to prominence after the 2021 China mining exodus. Other leaders include Antpool (Bitmain-affiliated), F2Pool (originally China, now Singapore), ViaBTC, and Binance Pool. Market shares rotate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: Bitcoin's security depends on no single player controlling most of the mining power. If any one miner or mining pool ever gained more than half of the whole network's hashing power, that player could rewrite very recent blocks, undo their own past payments, or block transactions they didn't like. Bitcoin developers give this exact concentration danger a specific name. What is this danger called?
answer: A 51-percent attack
choices: A 51-percent attack
A soft fork
A double-signature freeze
A Byzantine handshake
context: The name refers to the threshold at which a single actor's chain becomes longer than the honest network's chain. Bitcoin's security assumes the largest actor stays below 50 percent. Source: grokipedia.com/page/51%25_attack.

question: In July 2014, a Bitcoin mining pool called GHash.io briefly controlled more than 51 percent of the entire Bitcoin network's computing power. In theory, a pool that big could rewrite recent transactions and double-spend coins -- the nightmare scenario for Bitcoin's security. Bitcoin's designers had assumed no single actor would ever get that much power. What actually happened next?
answer: Individual miners voluntarily left the pool, and the pool operators publicly asked users to switch away
choices: Individual miners voluntarily left the pool, and the pool operators publicly asked users to switch away
The Bitcoin Foundation banned GHash.io from participating in the network
The US Securities and Exchange Commission ordered GHash.io to close
GHash.io launched a coordinated double-spend attack against Coinbase
context: The incident demonstrated that a mining pool's power depends on user trust. Pool operators knew that keeping >51 percent would undermine the network their own hardware depended on, so they chose to shrink. Source: grokipedia.com/page/51%25_attack.

question: A high-school student worries the 2014 GHash.io near-miss shows Bitcoin is vulnerable because a small number of pools now control most of the network. A public-choice-trained economist points out that the 2014 episode itself illustrates why the vulnerability is bounded. What is his reasoning move?
answer: Pool operators' economic value depends on the network's honesty, so they have private incentive to avoid the attack
choices: Pool operators' economic value depends on the network's honesty, so they have private incentive to avoid the attack
The US Federal Reserve directly regulates pool concentration and would prevent an attack
The 51-percent scenario is mathematically impossible because of Bitcoin's block reward
Miners are legally required by international treaty to leave any pool above 40 percent
context: This is incentive recognition -- the kind of analysis Buchanan and Tullock applied to political actors. Pool operators are not benevolent; they are self-interested actors whose interests align with network security. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: In 1982, a former congressional staffer named Lew Rockwell founded a small research institute in Auburn, Alabama, to keep alive the ideas of the Austrian-school economist Ludwig von Mises. The Mises Institute has run summer seminars, published books, and hosted scholars ever since, becoming the main U.S. home for one particular school of economics. Which school of economics does the Mises Institute teach?
answer: The Austrian school
choices: The Austrian school
The Keynesian school
The Marxist school
The Monetarist school
context: The Ludwig von Mises Institute was founded in Auburn, Alabama in 1982 and is located adjacent to the Auburn University campus. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: The US congressman Ron Paul, a doctor from Texas, ran for president three times mainly to protest what the Federal Reserve does. His campaign books and slogan repeated the same three words: 'End the Fed.' In Paul's view, the Fed's power to create new dollars out of thin air causes one big harm. What was Ron Paul's main complaint about the Fed?
answer: Printing money makes the dollar lose value over time
choices: Printing money makes the dollar lose value over time
The Fed doesn't have enough employees
The Fed's building is too small
The Fed uses old computers
context: Ron Paul, then serving as a Republican US Representative from Texas, co-founded the Mises Institute with Lew Rockwell and Murray Rothbard in 1982. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: The Ludwig von Mises Institute, founded in 1982 in Auburn, Alabama, is the main US home of Austrian economics in the Mises tradition. The moral right to use Mises's own name came from one specific person who served on the Institute's founding board until 1993. Who personally authorized the Institute's use of the Mises name?
answer: Margit von Mises
choices: Margit von Mises
Bettina Bien Greaves
Sylvia Nasar
Hazel Kyrk
context: Margit von Mises, Ludwig's widow, gave her personal blessing to the founding and remained on the board until her death in 1993. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: The Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama is the US home of Austrian economics in the tradition of Mises and his student Murray Rothbard. Since 1998 the Institute has run its own scholarly journal, the flagship outlet for research in that Rothbardian tradition, printing new economics research every quarter. What is the journal called?
answer: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
choices: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
Review of Austrian Economics
Journal of Political Economy
Public Choice
context: The Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics, edited by Joseph Salerno, is the flagship modern Mises-Institute journal. Source: mises.org/mises-university.

question: Every summer the Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama runs Mises University, a one-week intensive program on Austrian economics for college students from all over the world. Students pay their own way to fly in and give up a week of vacation. Why do they travel to Auburn instead of just taking an Austrian-economics class at their own home college?
answer: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
choices: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
It is required to graduate from any US college
It is the only program that awards college credit anywhere
Students earn a government salary after completing it
context: Mises University is the Institute's annual weeklong summer program for undergraduates, taught by senior Austrian-school faculty. Source: mises.org/mises-university.

question: Murray Rothbard was Ludwig von Mises's leading American student and the founder of a hard-money, anti-central-bank branch of Austrian economics. After Rothbard died in 1995, the Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama became the US home of his branch of the tradition. Rothbard's followers push one specific money reform above all others. Which money reform is that branch best known for?
answer: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
choices: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
A Milton Friedman k-percent money-supply rule
Explicit nominal-GDP targeting
A permanent zero-interest-rate policy
context: The Rothbardian branch is monetarily hard-line: 100% reserves and immediate abolition of the Federal Reserve. The Hayekian branch at George Mason has a different institutional emphasis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: Ludwig von Mises was the leader of the Austrian school of economics in the twentieth century and the great enemy of socialist central planning. The main modern life story of Mises came out from the Mises Institute in 2007, written by the historian Jorg Guido Hulsmann. Its full title casts Mises as a knight defending an older liberal tradition. What is the book's subtitle?
answer: The Last Knight of Liberalism
choices: The Last Knight of Liberalism
The Prophet of Vienna
The Austrian Socrates
The Chancellor's Economist
context: Mises: The Last Knight of Liberalism (2007), by Guido Hulsmann, is the definitive scholarly biography of Ludwig von Mises. Source: mises.org/library/mises-last-knight-liberalism.

question: A think tank that teaches Austrian economics puts its entire founding library online for free. Every book and every essay by its major thinkers is there for anyone with internet. Why does making the primary sources free do more for the school than any advertising ever could?
answer: A student anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
choices: A student anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
Free websites are cheaper than magazine ads
It forces every teacher to assign those books in class
Governments have to endorse whichever school offers free texts
context: Mises.org hosts freely readable editions of Menger, Bohm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Rothbard, and modern Austrian scholars. Source: mises.org.

question: By the late 1920s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had spent ten years arguing that a mixed economy of subsidies, price controls, and targeted taxes was not a stable third path between capitalism and socialism. It was, he said, an escalator that slid further left with every new fix. In 1929 he put the case in one German-language book. What is its German title?
answer: Kritik des Interventionismus
choices: Kritik des Interventionismus
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Nationaloekonomie
Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
context: Full title: Kritik des Interventionismus: Untersuchungen zur Wirtschaftspolitik und Wirtschaftsideologie der Gegenwart. Hans F. Sennholz translated the essays into English as A Critique of Interventionism, first published in 1977 by Arlington House. Source: Mises Institute, 'A Critique of Interventionism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises, the leader of the Austrian school of economics, had fled Europe in 1940 and settled in New York. On April 18, 1950, Mises spoke at the University Club in New York and gave a short, sharp version of his long case against the mixed economy — half free market, half government controls. What was that famous speech called?
answer: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
choices: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
Bureaucracy and the Free Market
The Anti-Capitalistic Mentality
context: The Commercial and Financial Chronicle first printed the address on May 4, 1950. The Libertarian Press then made it the opening essay of Planning for Freedom in 1952, and it has been the single most-quoted Mises text on the interventionist ratchet ever since. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: In a 1950 speech, Ludwig von Mises used an example to show why price caps spread. The government caps the price of one basic food to help poor families. That causes a shortage, so the government caps the price of what goes into it. Then it caps the prices of those inputs too. Which food did Mises start with?
answer: Milk
choices: Milk
Bread
Coal
Rental housing
context: Mises walked from a milk-price ceiling to feed prices, then to cattle prices, then to farm-labor wages, showing that every remedy for the previous shortage required an additional decree until the state was directing every price in the economy. He picked milk because a New York audience in 1950 remembered wartime dairy controls vividly. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: In a 1950 speech, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued that a mixed economy is not a real middle ground between capitalism and socialism. Either free markets run production, or the state does — you cannot split the steering wheel between the two. Mises put this either-or into a short three-word rule about who ends up in charge. What was that rule?
answer: Control is indivisible
choices: Control is indivisible
Prices reveal knowledge
Property implies liberty
Money is neutral
context: Mises's argument: either consumers direct production through the prices they are willing to pay, or the state does through decree. Any attempt to split the difference leaves neither mechanism doing its job; the resulting malfunction forces an escalation to full state direction. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises ended his 1950 speech, later titled 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism,' with a famous line. He said the mixed economy of price controls, subsidies, and quotas is not a lasting system at all. Instead, he said, it is a way of reaching one specific destination, step by step by step. What did Mises say it leads to, and how fast?
answer: Socialism, by installments
choices: Socialism, by installments
Poverty, in a single generation
Central banking, over a business cycle
Fascism, within a decade
context: Full sentence: 'The middle-of-the-road policy is not an economic system that can last. It is a method for the realization of socialism by installments.' The metaphor is deliberate: no single intervention looks like socialism, but the running total does. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: In a 1950 talk, Ludwig von Mises used real history to show the pattern was not just theory. He pointed to one European country. In 1914 it began with ceiling prices on a few consumer goods. By 1917 it ran a near-total war economy under one big named plan. Which case did Mises cite?
answer: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
choices: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
Britain's slide into the 1918 Defence of the Realm Act
France's move to the 1916 Loucheur decrees
Austria-Hungary's Kriegswirtschaft of 1915
context: The Hindenburg Programme of 1916-17, formally directed by General Erich Ludendorff, subordinated the whole German economy to munitions production. Mises's point was that Germany did not vote for the Hindenburg Plan in 1914; each intervening step looked reasonable given the last one, and the accumulated total was total control. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: During big wars, depressions, and panics, the size of the US federal government grows a lot. After the crisis ends, government shrinks back -- but only partway, never all the way to where it started. Which everyday tool is often used as a name for this one-way pattern?
answer: Ratchet
choices: Ratchet
Cascade
Spiral
Escalator
context: Higgs's Crisis and Leviathan: Critical Episodes in the Growth of American Government (Oxford, 1987) surveys WWI, the Great Depression, WWII, the Cold War and the post-1960s regulatory expansion, showing that the same governments that grew fastest in the emergency also grew fastest in the calm that followed. The historical documentation is the American case for Mises's 1929 prediction. Source: Wikipedia, 'Crisis and Leviathan'.

question: American farm policy is often called a textbook case of the Mises ratchet. New Deal price supports gave farmers a minimum price for corn and wheat. Harvests then piled up in surplus that Washington could not sell. Which next step did the government take to solve that surplus problem?
answer: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
choices: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
Nationalizing the grain elevators to store the surplus at cost
Declaring a temporary tariff to force domestic bakeries to buy the surplus
Rationing consumer purchases to draw down accumulated stocks
context: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 first paid farmers to plow crops under; postwar set-aside acreage programs and the 1983 Payment-in-Kind program paid producers in surplus grain not to grow more of it. Ninety years later the policy is still running -- exactly the ratchet Mises described in 1929: the intervention that fixed the last intervention's malfunction generates the next malfunction to fix. Source: Mises Institute, 'Farm Bill Folly'.

question: In 1927 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises wrote a book called Liberalismus. In it he defended an older political tradition — the one that Adam Smith, John Locke, and Thomas Jefferson had helped shape — which teaches that individual freedom, private property, and free markets are the best foundation for peace and prosperity. What is this tradition called?
answer: Classical liberalism
choices: Classical liberalism
Progressive statism
Democratic socialism
Mercantilism
context: Liberalismus (1927) argued the political and moral case for a market economy; Kritik des Interventionismus (1929) collected the economic essays showing that the halfway house between that market economy and full socialism was inherently unstable. Together they form the pair Mises's students, Hayek and Rothbard among them, later called the interventionist trilogy with Socialism (1922). Source: David M Hart, 'Ludwig von Mises: Interventionismus (1926)'.

question: By the 1930s Ludwig von Mises had argued for a decade that the mixed economy is unstable. It must either move back toward markets or forward to full state control. He used one short label to reject the idea that a real middle path exists at all. Which label?
answer: A third system
choices: A third system
A guided economy
Managed capitalism
The mixed economy
context: Mises used 'a third system' precisely because he thought it did not exist as a stable system. Either consumer sovereignty through prices rules production or the state does; the intermediate cases he documented -- rent-controlled housing, price-supported farming, tariff-protected industry, rate-suppressed banking -- were the disequilibria that generated the ratchet toward the second pole. Source: Mises Institute, 'Why Intervention Persists'.

question: In 1921 a young Austrian economist named Friedrich Hayek joined Ludwig von Mises's Vienna office as a research assistant. Decades later Hayek won the 1974 Nobel Prize in Economics. His big idea was that market prices are messages — they quietly sum up what millions of buyers and sellers know and want. What did Hayek say no central planner could ever do?
answer: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
choices: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
Print more money quickly
Set a fair tax rate
Fund a public school
context: Hayek (1899-1992) later called Mises 'my teacher' and won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: Murray Rothbard, an American student of the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, made a simple point about incentives. The more taxes a government takes and the more rules it writes, the less reward workers and inventors get for their effort. So people work less, save less, and invent less. What did Rothbard say happens when taxes and rules pile up?
answer: People produce less because their reward for effort shrinks
choices: People produce less because their reward for effort shrinks
People produce more to catch up on taxes
Nothing changes -- people always work the same
The government starts making better products
context: Rothbard (1926-1995) attended the NYU Mises seminar from 1949 and stayed for two decades, becoming the seminar's most important American product. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Israel Kirzner was one of Ludwig von Mises's own American students at New York University in the 1950s. In his 1973 book Competition and Entrepreneurship, Kirzner put one single human activity at the very center of Austrian economics — the true source of profit, of new ideas, and of the economy moving forward at all. Which activity did Kirzner put at the center?
answer: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
choices: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
Consumption as revealed preference
Saving as time preference
Central planning as knowledge aggregation
context: Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973) put alertness to unnoticed opportunities in disequilibrium at the center of Austrian microeconomics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: After World War 2, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises fled Nazi Europe and taught at New York University in America. His students carried the Austrian school's ideas into US colleges. The Austrian school had a bold view about how prices work in a free market: every price is a little signal packed with information about scarcity, demand, and cost that no single planner could ever gather in one place. What core idea did the Austrian school teach about prices?
answer: Prices carry information nobody could gather in one place
choices: Prices carry information nobody could gather in one place
Prices are set by government experts using data
Prices only reflect the cost to make each item
Prices always match the true value of a good
context: Hans Sennholz (1922-2007) held a long-tenured post at Grove City College in Pennsylvania and trained a generation of Austrian-friendly American economists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Sennholz.

question: After Ludwig von Mises had reworked Austrian economics for a European audience in the 1940s, his American student Murray Rothbard set out to restate the entire system for a postwar U.S. readership. In 1962 the publisher D. Van Nostrand released Rothbard's two-volume treatise doing exactly that -- covering choice, prices, capital, money, and cycles in one Misesian sweep. What is the title of Rothbard's 1962 treatise?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
For a New Liberty
The Ethics of Liberty
context: Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) was Rothbard's systematic treatise and the anchor of his subsequent trilogy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: In 1963 the American economist Murray Rothbard published a book that applied Austrian Business Cycle Theory -- the idea that easy money from a central bank creates fake booms -- to one big American disaster. Rothbard argued the Federal Reserve caused the 1920s boom, and then President Herbert Hoover's meddling turned the 1929 bust into a ten-year slump. Which event was Rothbard's book about?
answer: America's Great Depression
choices: America's Great Depression
The 1907 Panic
The 1970s Stagflation
The 2008 Financial Crisis
context: America's Great Depression (D. Van Nostrand, 1963) is the ABCT-and-Hoover book, published in the same year as Friedman and Schwartz's monetarist Monetary History. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: In 1946 the American journalist Henry Hazlitt wrote a short book that boiled economics down to one lesson. To judge any policy, he said, don't just count how it helps one group right now. Trace how it hits everyone else, and how it hits later. Hazlitt's book -- Economics in One Lesson -- became one of the best-selling economics books ever. What is that one lesson?
answer: Look at all the effects on all the people, not just the visible ones now
choices: Look at all the effects on all the people, not just the visible ones now
Trust whichever expert has the most college degrees
Count only the jobs created, since jobs are what matter most
Add up how a policy makes government leaders feel
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946), still in print in the same decade, has introduced more general readers to Bastiat's method than any other single book. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Hazlitt.

question: In 1996 the American economist George Reisman published a book of more than 1,000 pages, Capitalism: A Treatise on Economics, that tries to combine Ludwig von Mises's Austrian economics with the novelist Ayn Rand's Objectivist philosophy into one giant unified system. Most working economists prefer shorter, tightly-argued books to a treatise this size. Why do they prefer the shorter form?
answer: A shorter book is easier to test against reality one claim at a time
choices: A shorter book is easier to test against reality one claim at a time
Publishers refuse to print books longer than 500 pages
Long books are always historically wrong
Only university professors read long books
context: George Reisman (born 1937) came through the NYU seminar and later wrote Capitalism (Jameson Books, 1996), the only sustained attempt at a full Austrian-Objectivist synthesis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/George_Reisman.

question: Ludwig von Mises, the Austrian economist who fled Hitler's Europe and taught in New York, spent his life warning against inflation. He argued that governments should not be able to just print new money whenever they want to. What was Mises's big worry about letting governments run the printing press?
answer: Prices go up and people's savings lose value
choices: Prices go up and people's savings lose value
Factories run out of workers to hire
Trees stop growing in the country
Weather gets much colder
context: Mises accepted a professorship at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva, Switzerland in 1934. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises, the great Austrian economist, had to flee Europe in 1940 as Hitler's armies spread across the continent. He crossed to America and lived out the rest of his life in New York. From his New York classroom, Mises spent decades arguing for one specific kind of economic system. Which system did Mises defend?
answer: Free-market capitalism
choices: Free-market capitalism
Central government planning
Fascism
Communism
context: The Mises escape route ran Geneva - occupied France by train - Lisbon by ship - New York on August 2, 1940. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In the late 1930s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises took a teaching post in Geneva, Switzerland to escape rising Nazi power. There in 1940 he finished a big German-language economics treatise that he would later rewrite and expand in English as his famous book Human Action. What is the German-language title of that Geneva precursor?
answer: Nationalokonomie
choices: Nationalokonomie
Grundlegung
Wirtschaftslehre
Kapital
context: Nationalokonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens (Geneva, 1940) appeared in a Europe already at war and went almost unread. Human Action (Yale, 1949) was Mises's English rewrite. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In 1938 Nazi Germany took over Austria in the event called the Anschluss. Gestapo agents searched the Vienna flat of the exiled Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises and hauled off his private papers back to Berlin. In 1945, as the Second World War ended, Soviet troops seized the same Mises papers in Berlin. Where did the papers finally end up?
answer: Moscow
choices: Moscow
Prague
Warsaw
Leningrad
context: The Mises papers sat in a Moscow archive for 50 years and were returned to the Mises Institute in 1996. Source: mises.org/library/mises-lost-papers.

question: In 1940 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises fled Nazi-occupied Europe and reached New York City with almost nothing. He had already written a shelf of books defending free markets and sound money. Yet no major American university would put him on the payroll. Other Austrian thinkers who arrived that decade got the same cold shoulder. Why did the top US schools keep Austrian economists at arm's length?
answer: Their views clashed with the mainstream Keynesian consensus of the day
choices: Their views clashed with the mainstream Keynesian consensus of the day
Austrian economists refused to speak English
US law banned foreign professors before 1950
They demanded salaries higher than any US professor
context: Mises's NYU seminar ran from 1945 to 1969; NYU carried his Visiting Professor title but paid nothing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises, an Austrian economist who fled Hitler's Europe, taught at New York University for many years. But NYU paid him nothing. A wealthy businessman named Lawrence Fertig and a private group called the William Volker Fund paid his salary instead, so that Mises's Austrian ideas could reach American students. What role in launching ideas the mainstream refuses to support does Mises's private funding reveal?
answer: Private donors often fund ideas the mainstream refuses to support
choices: Private donors often fund ideas the mainstream refuses to support
Universities always fund every professor equally
Governments always pay the salaries of visiting professors
Only tenured professors ever receive outside funding
context: The Kansas-City-based Volker Fund covered a research fellowship; the New York advertising executive Lawrence Fertig personally supplemented Mises's NYU stipend. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises founded the modern Austrian school of economics. He said the whole subject starts from a single fact anyone can check about themselves: people choose things on purpose to reach goals they care about. Mises gave this starting point a Greek-rooted name -- praxeology -- and built all of economics on top of it. What is this starting point called, in plain English?
answer: The study of purposeful human action
choices: The study of purposeful human action
The study of animal instincts scaled up to nations
The study of random market noise
The study of whatever governments plan
context: Human Action (Yale, 1949) was Mises's English-language rewrite of Nationalokonomie (1940) and became the postwar Austrian-tradition anchor text. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: When the Austrian-school economist Ludwig von Mises fled France ahead of the German army in the summer of 1940, his wife Margit von Mises fled with him -- a bus ride across a war zone to Portugal, then a ship to New York. In 1976, three years after her husband's death, Margit published a memoir that remains the main primary source for the story of their escape. What is Margit von Mises's memoir called?
answer: My Years With Ludwig von Mises
choices: My Years With Ludwig von Mises
The Vienna I Loved
A Life With an Economist
Escape from Europe
context: Margit von Mises's 1976 memoir My Years With Ludwig von Mises is the primary source for the escape and the early American years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Margit_von_Mises.

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) is a newer idea that says a country like the United States can just print more of its own money to pay its debts and never really run out. In real life, some countries have tried heavy money-printing to pay for spending. When a government prints huge amounts of new money, what happens to prices?
answer: Prices go up and each dollar buys less
choices: Prices go up and each dollar buys less
The country becomes richer forever
People get free things forever
Nothing at all -- it works fine
context: MMT, associated with Warren Mosler, L. Randall Wray, and Stephanie Kelton, argues that a fiat-issuing government is constrained only by real resources and inflation, not by debt-service math. Source: Grokipedia 'Modern Monetary Theory' (2026-09-05).

question: A newer idea called Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) says a country that prints its own currency can never run out of money. Its supporters say the government can simply print more anytime it wants to pay for something. But when countries have actually tried heavy money-printing for long, the real world usually pushes back. What happens to a country that tries this?
answer: Prices shoot up until money is worth much less
choices: Prices shoot up until money is worth much less
Other countries send more gold to help
Nothing -- the country stays rich forever
The country's people get bigger paychecks that buy more
context: Kelton advised the 2016 and 2020 Sanders presidential campaigns and became the most visible face of MMT. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez cited MMT as economic backing for the Green New Deal. Source: Grokipedia 'Stephanie Kelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) is an idea championed by economists like Stephanie Kelton at Stony Brook University. It says a country that prints its own currency can never truly run out and does not really need to worry about deficits. Critics say the theory downplays one real-world problem that hurts the people who can least afford it. What do they say it misses?
answer: Printing extra money causes inflation, which hurts savers and the poor
choices: Printing extra money causes inflation, which hurts savers and the poor
Printing extra money makes exports too cheap for foreign buyers
Printing extra money forces banks to raise interest rates too much
Printing extra money confuses foreign investors who prefer coins
context: Kelton's The Deficit Myth: Modern Monetary Theory and the Birth of the People's Economy (PublicAffairs, 2020) reached the New York Times bestseller list. Its argument was that the traditional view of federal deficits as a constraint is a myth. Source: Grokipedia 'The Deficit Myth' (2026-09-05).

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) is an idea from economists like Warren Mosler and Stephanie Kelton. They argue a government that prints its own currency is not really held back by tax revenue or its debt level. Instead, MMT says only two forces can hold government spending back in the real world. What does the theory itself say are those only two limits?
answer: Inflation and real resources
choices: Inflation and real resources
Foreign lender willingness and gold reserves
Tax revenue and treasury solvency
Interest rates and unemployment
context: MMT says deficit financing is fine as long as excess capacity exists; taxes are for controlling inflation and redistributing resources, not for 'paying for' spending. The framing sounds new but is a modern repackaging of an old inflationist position. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020).

question: Paul Krugman, a Nobel-winning economist on the Democratic side of American politics, attacked Modern Monetary Theory -- a modern claim that a government can safely print all the money it needs. To mock the theory, Krugman reused a slogan Republican George H. W. Bush had thrown at Ronald Reagan's supply-side tax cuts back in 1980. Which nickname did Krugman reuse?
answer: Voodoo economics
choices: Voodoo economics
Trickle-down economics
Zombie economics
Snake-oil economics
context: Larry Summers's February 4 2019 Washington Post op-ed called MMT 'the new voodoo economics' -- echoing the George H.W. Bush attack on Reagan supply-side economics. Summers was a Democratic economist speaking against a left-favored school. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2019).

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) says a government can safely print new money as long as the economy has 'unused capacity' — idle workers, empty factories, machines sitting still. Austrian-school economists like Robert Murphy answer that at the scale of a whole national economy, this idea does not really hold. What do Austrians say is wrong with the 'unused capacity' claim?
answer: There is no such thing at that scale; prices rise instead of production
choices: There is no such thing at that scale; prices rise instead of production
Unused capacity only exists during wars
Capacity is measured only in barrels of oil
Only communist countries ever have unused capacity
context: The Austrian point (Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, Steve Hanke): the notion of aggregate unused capacity is a Keynesian fiction. In reality, resources are always in some use and monetary expansion always bids competing uses higher. Prices adjust to absorb the excess. Source: Murphy, Contra Krugman (podcast archive 2019-2021).

question: In early 2021 President Joe Biden's government passed the American Rescue Plan -- a huge round of new spending, most of it paid for with newly created money. Larry Summers, a well-known Democratic economist who had served in the Obama Treasury, warned that pouring in that much fresh money would push US prices up hard. Over the next two years, what actually happened?
answer: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
choices: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
Prices dropped as workers spent more freely
Nothing at all — the money vanished into savings
The dollar became the strongest currency in world history
context: The American Rescue Plan Act, signed March 11 2021 at $1.9 trillion, was an MMT-adjacent bet that fiscal stimulus of that size would not overheat prices. Summers had warned publicly against it in February 2021. Source: Grokipedia 'American Rescue Plan Act of 2021' (2026-09-05).

question: After US prices shot up sharply in 2021 and 2022, one group of economists -- nicknamed 'Team Transitory' -- blamed shipping backups and stuck ports at Los Angeles and Long Beach instead of the trillions of newly printed dollars the government had spent through the pandemic. What was Team Transitory's explanation for the inflation?
answer: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
choices: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
Store owners across the country got greedy at the same moment
Foreign oil producers alone drove up every price
Consumers suddenly switched from spending to saving
context: MMT proponents echoed the Fed's 'transitory' framing, blaming supply chains. But the core MMT claim -- that political will, not math, was the constraint -- was falsified by exactly the mechanism its critics had predicted: prices adjusted to absorb the excess demand. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: A theory called Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) said governments could print lots of money without causing much inflation. Between 2020 and 2022 many countries tried it, and prices rose fast worldwide. What did the real economy teach faster than years of debate could?
answer: A live test in the real economy can disprove a school of thought faster than years of debate
choices: A live test in the real economy can disprove a school of thought faster than years of debate
Schools of thought always survive real-world setbacks
Being popular with politicians makes a theory correct
Academic economists always predict inflation correctly
context: Twelve months of 8-9% inflation did what a decade of Austrian critique could not. The 2021-22 experience settled the empirical question and drained the political oxygen from the movement. Source: Grokipedia 'Modern Monetary Theory' (2026-09-05).

question: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) grew out of a 1990s pamphlet called 'Soft Currency Economics' by Warren Mosler, an American bond trader who ran a hedge fund. Mosler argued that a government that prints its own currency can never really run out of money. Mainstream economists later rejected the sweeping version of his claim. Why?
answer: A government can always print more money, but each new bill buys less — inflation is the limit
choices: A government can always print more money, but each new bill buys less — inflation is the limit
Governments actually do run out of paper to print money on
Only foreign countries are allowed to print more currency
Currency traders are never allowed to write about money
context: Warren Mosler's 1996 Soft Currency Economics is the founding text. The term 'MMT' itself was popularized by Australian economist Bill Mitchell at the University of Newcastle. Source: Grokipedia 'Warren Mosler' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2014 the huge Bitcoin trading website Mt Gox, based in Tokyo, Japan, suddenly went bust. It had held Bitcoins for hundreds of thousands of customers who trusted the site to keep their coins safe. About 850,000 of those Bitcoins were gone. What is the main lesson people took away from this disaster?
answer: If you don't hold your own coins yourself, someone else can lose them
choices: If you don't hold your own coins yourself, someone else can lose them
Bitcoin itself was broken and had to be rebuilt
Only rich people should be allowed to buy Bitcoin
Trading websites always pay everyone back after a crash
context: Mt Gox at its 2013 peak handled roughly 70-80 percent of global Bitcoin trading volume. The bankruptcy set the world's expectations of what could go wrong with a centralized custodian. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: A person buys Bitcoin on a big trading website and leaves the coins sitting in the website's account instead of moving them to their own private wallet. Then the website is hacked and all the coins are stolen -- this is what happened to thousands of users of Mt. Gox in 2014. What is the well-known Bitcoin saying that warns against this exact mistake?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Buy the dip, sell the top
A coin saved is a coin earned
Only the miners can lose money
context: The site was launched in 2007 by Jed McCaleb as a card-trading platform for Magic: The Gathering. He repurposed it for Bitcoin in 2010 and sold the domain to Mark Karpeles in 2011. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: In February 2014 the Tokyo-based Bitcoin exchange Mt Gox suddenly collapsed, and roughly 850,000 customer bitcoins vanished from its books -- at the time, worth about half a billion dollars. Mt Gox had been run by a French national who lived in Japan and had bought the site from its original American founder years earlier. Who was the French CEO running Mt Gox at the time of its collapse?
answer: Mark Karpeles
choices: Mark Karpeles
Craig Wright
Charlie Shrem
Ross Ulbricht
context: Karpeles had bought Mt Gox from Jed McCaleb in 2011. He was later convicted in Japan in 2019 of falsifying data (padding balance records) but acquitted of the theft charges; he received a suspended sentence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mark_Karpel%C3%A8s.

question: In February 2014 Mt. Gox -- the Tokyo-based Bitcoin exchange run by Mark Karpeles, which then handled most of the world's Bitcoin trades -- suddenly halted all Bitcoin withdrawals, blaming vague 'technical issues.' Two weeks later the site went dark, and a few days after that it declared bankruptcy. About 850,000 bitcoins had vanished. On which day did the withdrawal freeze begin?
answer: February 7, 2014
choices: February 7, 2014
January 3, 2014
December 24, 2013
March 15, 2014
context: The site went dark February 24 and the Tokyo bankruptcy petition was filed February 28. Karpeles had reassured customers that withdrawal issues were transient, but roughly 850,000 BTC were already missing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: When Mt Gox — then the world's largest Bitcoin exchange, based in Tokyo — collapsed in February 2014, it reported that roughly 850,000 customer Bitcoins had vanished. In the weeks after, staff searched old computers and found some coins forgotten in a cold-storage wallet. Roughly how many of the missing Bitcoins were recovered from that old wallet?
answer: About 200,000
choices: About 200,000
About 800,000
About 50
None -- all were permanently lost
context: The trustee retained the recovered coins for a decade of legal proceedings. Distribution to creditors finally began in 2024. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: Jed McCaleb, an American programmer, launched Mt Gox in 2007 as a website for trading Magic: The Gathering cards, then sold it in 2011 before its later Bitcoin disaster. McCaleb did not stop building — he went on to co-found two other well-known cryptocurrency projects. Which pair of projects did he help start?
answer: Ripple (XRP) in 2012 and Stellar (XLM) in 2014
choices: Ripple (XRP) in 2012 and Stellar (XLM) in 2014
Ethereum in 2015 and Cardano in 2017
Binance in 2017 and FTX in 2019
Coinbase in 2012 and Kraken in 2013
context: McCaleb had left Mt Gox by 2011. His Ripple and Stellar projects took a very different approach from Bitcoin -- centralized ledgers rather than proof-of-work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jed_McCaleb.

question: By 2024, ten years after Mt Gox collapsed in Tokyo and lost hundreds of thousands of customer Bitcoins, the court-appointed trustee finally began mailing the roughly 200,000 recovered coins back to creditors. One specific fact softened the blow for the customers who had waited an entire decade to see anything. What was that fact?
answer: Bitcoin's price had risen so much that the recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
choices: Bitcoin's price had risen so much that the recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
The trustee added a 500-percent bonus in newly minted coin
The Japanese government reimbursed all lost dollar value in yen
The Federal Reserve issued a targeted grant to Mt Gox creditors
context: Creditors who accepted repayment in Bitcoin (an option the trustee offered) received far more purchasing power than they had lost. The lesson survived: not-your-keys-not-your-coins is real, but so is Bitcoin's long-run monetary premium. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: In New York City in the 1950s, a young American student walks into a private economics seminar led by Ludwig von Mises — the great Austrian economist who had fled Vienna a decade before. The young man spends his whole life afterward fighting for free markets, sound money, and smaller government, just as his teacher did. Which school of economics is he a part of?
answer: The Austrian school
choices: The Austrian school
The Marxist school
The Keynesian school
The behavioral school
context: Rothbard entered Columbia at 16 in 1942 and took the doctorate under Joseph Dorfman. Kirzner also attended the Mises NYU seminar but took his PhD under Mises at NYU, not Columbia; Hazlitt was a journalist with no doctorate; Lachmann was an LSE-trained German Austrian. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard, the American Austrian-school economist who would later write the two-volume treatise Man, Economy, and State, was born on March 2, 1926, and died on January 7, 1995. He was born in a specific American city -- and specifically in the borough where his Jewish immigrant parents were raising him. In which American city and which of its boroughs was Rothbard born?
answer: New York City, in the Bronx
choices: New York City, in the Bronx
Chicago, in Hyde Park
Vienna, in Leopoldstadt
Boston, in Back Bay
context: Rothbard's father David was a chemist who had emigrated from Poland; the family were Jewish immigrants to the Bronx. Vienna Leopoldstadt is the classic distractor since so many first-generation Austrians (Mises, Hayek, Machlup) came from there; Chicago and Boston place two rival American economics traditions. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard was a young American economist studying at Columbia University in New York. In 1956 he finished his PhD thesis on money and banking in the young United States. Later he turned it into a book that told the money story of the first great American depression. Which depression did his book cover?
answer: The Panic of 1819
choices: The Panic of 1819
The Panic of 1837
The Long Depression of 1873
The Panic of 1907
context: Rothbard argued the Panic of 1819 followed the credit expansion of the Second Bank of the United States, a foreshadowing of his later Austrian Business Cycle Theory application to 1929. Dorfman was his adviser. The three distractors are all real 19th- and early-20th-century American financial crises. Source: Mises Institute, 'Toward a Science of Liberty' (Salerno).

question: From the mid-1950s Murray Rothbard, then a young Austrian-school economist living in New York, joined a private economics seminar that met each week in Manhattan. An Austrian scholar who had fled Nazi Europe in 1940 led the room, and the pro-market Volker Fund quietly paid his salary. Which seminar did Rothbard attend?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
choices: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
Milton Friedman's Chicago money workshop
Kenneth Arrow's Stanford theory workshop
John Kenneth Galbraith's Harvard institutional seminar
context: Mises ran the seminar at NYU from 1948 to 1969, paid for by the William Volker Fund. Rothbard became his most influential American disciple. Friedman's Chicago workshop was the methodological opposite; Arrow at Stanford and Galbraith at Harvard were mainstream mid-century venues. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard had a Columbia University PhD and was America's top Austrian-school economist. But from 1966 to 1986, no major economics department would hire him -- his libertarian politics, which called even the tax system a form of theft, were too radical for the profession. So where did Rothbard actually teach for those twenty years?
answer: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute -- an engineering school, not an economics department
choices: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute -- an engineering school, not an economics department
Grove City College's small economics program in western Pennsylvania
Auburn University's Department of Economics in Alabama
George Mason University's newly-founded Austrian economics group
context: Rothbard taught part-time at Brooklyn Poly from 1966 to 1986 -- twenty years as an engineering-school instructor while writing the Austrian tradition's flagship American treatise. Grove City housed Hans Sennholz; George Mason built its Austrian program later (1980s onward); Auburn is where the Mises Institute would later be based, but Rothbard never taught for Auburn University itself. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard, the Austrian-school economist and student of Ludwig von Mises, spent most of his career teaching at a small engineering college in New York called Brooklyn Polytechnic. In 1986 he finally left it for a named chair of economics at a desert university, where he taught until his death in 1995. Which named chair at which university did Rothbard take?
answer: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
choices: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
Ludwig von Mises Chair in Economics at Grove City College
F.A. Hayek Chair in Political Economy at George Mason University
Adam Smith Chair in Free Enterprise at Auburn University
context: UNLV hired Rothbard in 1986 into the S.J. Hall chair; he taught there until his heart attack in January 1995. The three distractor chairs are plausibly-named posts at institutions that had ties to Austrian or Chicago-adjacent economics but were not where Rothbard actually landed. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: In 1977 Murray Rothbard helped launch a Washington, D.C. libertarian think tank alongside two co-founders. Four years later a bitter dispute over strategy -- Rothbard wanted radical purity, the others wanted mainstream reach and beltway influence -- got him kicked off its board. Which think tank did he co-found and then break from?
answer: The Cato Institute, co-founded with Charles Koch and Ed Crane
choices: The Cato Institute, co-founded with Charles Koch and Ed Crane
The Heritage Foundation, co-founded with Paul Weyrich and Edwin Feulner
The Reason Foundation, co-founded with Robert Poole
The Foundation for Economic Education, co-founded with Leonard Read
context: Cato was founded 1977; Rothbard was ousted from the board in 1981 after a dispute with Crane and Koch, largely over political strategy and cultural stance. Heritage (1973), Reason (1978), and FEE (1946) are all real free-market institutions with their own real founders; Rothbard was not a co-founder of any of them. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: In 1981 the Austrian-school economist Murray Rothbard had a bitter falling-out with the Cato Institute, the libertarian think tank in Washington he had helped shape. The next year, in 1982, he teamed up with a colleague to launch a rival research institute focused entirely on Austrian economics. Rothbard would serve as its academic vice president for the rest of his life. Which institute did he co-found?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute, in Auburn, Alabama, with Llewellyn Rockwell Jr.
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute, in Auburn, Alabama, with Llewellyn Rockwell Jr.
The Independent Institute, in Oakland, California, with David Theroux
The Foundation for Economic Education, in Irvington-on-Hudson, with Leonard Read
The Atlas Economic Research Foundation, in Fairfax, with Antony Fisher
context: Rothbard, Rockwell, and Burton Blumert founded the Mises Institute in 1982 to house Austrian scholarship outside the Beltway-libertarian orbit. The three distractors are all real free-market organizations founded by the named people, but none is where Rothbard landed after Cato. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: The American economist Murray Rothbard argued in the 1960s that there should be no government at all. Instead, private property rights and voluntary companies -- courts, insurance firms, security guards -- would do everything the state now claims to do. Rothbard coined a special name for this system where the market handles even law and defense. What is it called?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism
choices: Anarcho-capitalism
Classical liberalism
Small-government conservatism
Social democracy
context: The term is Rothbard's own, distinguishing his position from Nozickian minarchism (a minimal-state night-watchman position) and from Randian objectivism (which insists on a minimal state). Classical liberalism is the older 19th-century umbrella that all three sit under. Source: Wikipedia, For a New Liberty.

question: In 1973 Murray Rothbard wrote a popular book laying out his whole political system for the general reader. It opens with a history of American liberty -- from the Revolution through the Civil War -- and ends with a plan for a fully private-property society where even courts, police, and roads would be privately run. Which book is it?
answer: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
choices: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
The Ethics of Liberty
Anarchy, State, and Utopia
The Machinery of Freedom
context: For a New Liberty (Macmillan, 1973) is Rothbard's popular manifesto. The Ethics of Liberty (1982) is his systematic philosophical case. Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is Nozick's minarchist rival. The Machinery of Freedom (1973) is David Friedman's economic-anarchist rival, published the same year. Source: Wikipedia, For a New Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard, the Austrian-school economist and libertarian writer, poured years into a huge history of the American colonies and the Revolution. He published it in four volumes between 1975 and 1979. It is his longest work of American history and it stretched from the earliest settlers to the fight against Britain. What is this four-volume book called?
answer: Conceived in Liberty
choices: Conceived in Liberty
The Discovery of Freedom
The American Testament
Empire of Liberty
context: Conceived in Liberty is Rothbard's four-volume libertarian retelling of American colonial history and the Revolution; a fifth volume was assembled posthumously from his notes in 2019. The Discovery of Freedom (1943) is Rose Wilder Lane. The American Testament and Empire of Liberty are titles of unrelated later works. Source: Mises Institute, 'Toward a Science of Liberty' (Salerno).

question: In 1940 France was falling to Nazi Germany and much of Europe was at war. Ludwig von Mises, the great Austrian economist, was teaching at a graduate institute in neutral Switzerland after fleeing Vienna. That year he printed a big new economics book in German. In which Swiss city did the book first come out?
answer: Geneva, published by Editions Union
choices: Geneva, published by Editions Union
London, published by George Allen & Unwin
New York, published by Yale University Press
Vienna, published by Julius Springer
context: Mises had been at the Geneva Graduate Institute since 1934, having left Vienna. The book, in German, was 'Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens' ('Economics: A Theory of Action and Enterprise'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1940 German-language book Nationaloekonomie was one of the great economics works of the twentieth century. It was written in Switzerland by a man widely seen as the leader of the Austrian school. But something very strange happened after it was printed in wartime Geneva. What happened to the book?
answer: It attracted almost no readership -- Germany and Austria were closed to it and Switzerland was neutral but small
choices: It attracted almost no readership -- Germany and Austria were closed to it and Switzerland was neutral but small
It sold half a million copies within its first year
It was banned by every European government
It won the Nobel Prize in Literature the year it appeared
context: Mises himself said later that Nationaloekonomie 'attracted no attention.' His works had been on the Nazi blacklist since 1933; Europe was at war; the German-speaking world was under Nazi occupation or blockade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: Ludwig von Mises fled Europe for the United States in the summer of 1940, taking his unread 1940 German book with him. Over the next nine years he rewrote and expanded it in English. In what year did the rewritten version appear, and what was its English title?
answer: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
choices: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
1945; 'The Theory of Money and Credit'
1944; 'Bureaucracy'
1957; 'Theory and History'
context: Yale University Press published Human Action in 1949. The English version was longer, more polished, and updated for the postwar American context (Keynesianism, the Cold War, the New Deal experience). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: The Austrian-school economist Ludwig von Mises published a big German-language treatise called Nationaloekonomie in Switzerland in 1940, just as war engulfed Europe and almost no one could read it. Nine years later, in America, he published Human Action (1949), which became the standard English Austrian treatise. The two books are not simply the same book in two languages. Which statement best describes how Human Action and Nationaloekonomie are related?
answer: The two cover the same terrain (praxeology, calculation, cycle, interventionism) but Human Action is longer, more polished, and updated for postwar American debates
choices: The two cover the same terrain (praxeology, calculation, cycle, interventionism) but Human Action is longer, more polished, and updated for postwar American debates
Human Action's chapters were translated word-for-word from Nationaloekonomie with no additions
Human Action rejects the arguments of Nationaloekonomie and defends the opposite conclusions
Human Action is a condensed abridgment removing more than half the German original
context: Nationaloekonomie is the tighter German-language original; Human Action is the mature English restatement. Scholars now read both to trace how Mises's arguments evolved between Geneva 1940 and New York 1949. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1940 German-language treatise Nationaloekonomie appeared in wartime Switzerland and almost immediately vanished from view — Germany and Austria were closed to it. For four decades the German original was nearly impossible to find. Then in 1980 one American group in Auburn, Alabama reprinted it so modern Austrian scholars could finally read it again. Which group did the reprint?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Cato Institute
The Foundation for Economic Education
The Hoover Institution
context: The Mises Institute, founded in 1982 by Lew Rockwell and Murray Rothbard, republished (or facilitated republication of) the German original as a scholarly reference in 1980. Jorg Guido Hulsmann's 2007 Mises biography and Joseph Salerno's introductions draw on the text. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: In 1940 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published Nationaloekonomie in German while fleeing Nazi Europe. Almost no one read it — the war was raging and the German-reading world had no market for a fat treatise defending free markets. Mises did not give up. He moved to America, rewrote the whole book from scratch in English, and published Human Action in 1949. What broader lesson about the history of books does reading both together teach a student?
answer: A great book's initial reception can be nearly nil and still be preserved by a single author's determination to rewrite it in a new language and context
choices: A great book's initial reception can be nearly nil and still be preserved by a single author's determination to rewrite it in a new language and context
A great book always finds its readership within a year of publication
A great book is best measured by its sales in the first six months
A great book must be translated by an official state translator to have influence
context: Mises's determination -- he was in his sixties, a Jewish refugee starting over in New York -- turned a nearly-unread 1940 German treatise into the 1949 English classic that shaped a whole revival of Austrian economics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: The National Collegiate Athletic Association, or NCAA, runs athletics for more than a thousand US colleges and universities. For a hundred years its rule was simple: student-athletes cannot be paid any money for playing, even though the NCAA and its member schools make billions of dollars from TV deals and ticket sales. What is a no-pay rule like that called?
answer: Amateurism
choices: Amateurism
Professionalism
Free agency
Salary cap
context: The National Collegiate Athletic Association, founded 1906, governed approximately 500,000 US college athletes across ~1,100 member institutions. Its amateurism rules held from founding through 2021. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association.

question: A big college sports group takes in around 18 billion dollars a year, mostly from TV deals. Its rule for a hundred years said the players who actually made the games could NOT be paid. About how much of that huge pile of money went to the players in cash?
answer: Basically none of it
choices: Basically none of it
About a tenth of it
About a third of it
About half of it
context: Under amateurism, athletes received scholarships, room and board, and small stipends but no cash compensation. The gap between labor value and cash compensation is the structural feature economists had long identified as cartel behavior. Source: NCAA financial reports 2018-19.

question: For decades, every major American college quietly agreed with the others: none of them would pay their student athletes a salary, no matter how much money those athletes brought in from ticket sales and television deals. Each individual school could easily have offered pay on its own to attract the best basketball or football players in the country. But they all promised each other, through the NCAA rulebook, that none of them would. Economists have a blunt name for that kind of secret agreement between employers. What is it usually called?
answer: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
choices: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
Fair-share bargaining between rival workplaces
A friendly market-sharing custom
A legal minimum-wage floor
context: Roughly 1,100 nominally competing 'employers' (universities) collectively agreed to fix the price of athlete labor at zero above standardized in-kind compensation. In any other industry this would be a per-se Sherman Section 1 violation. Source: Zimbalist, Unpaid Professionals (Princeton 1999).

question: In the mid-2000s a former UCLA basketball star named Ed O'Bannon walked into a friend's living room and saw his own face, name, and jersey number on the screen in a college basketball video game. The game had sold millions of copies. O'Bannon had been paid nothing. He decided to sue the game company for a share of the money it had made off him. Why is it fair for him to sue?
answer: A person owns their own name and likeness, so a company that sells them owes payment
choices: A person owns their own name and likeness, so a company that sells them owes payment
The company should have used a made-up player instead of a real one
Video game money always belongs half to the athletes
College sports rules ban all video games about players
context: O'Bannon v. NCAA (Ninth Circuit, August 8, 2015, upholding partial 2014 district-court ruling by Judge Claudia Wilken). Wilken held NCAA amateurism rules violated Sherman Section 1 as an unreasonable restraint of trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Bannon_v._NCAA.

question: In June 2021 the US Supreme Court ruled against the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), the governing body for American college sports, in a major antitrust case called NCAA v. Alston. All nine justices — appointed by presidents of both parties — agreed the NCAA had illegally limited what colleges could offer athletes. Why does such a unanimous 9-0 ruling matter more than a close 5-4?
answer: It signals that even judges who usually disagree see the issue the same way
choices: It signals that even judges who usually disagree see the issue the same way
It doubles the punishment for the losing side
It automatically overturns all past court rulings
It skips the appeals process forever
context: NCAA v. Alston, 594 US ___ (2021), was decided 9-0 with Justice Gorsuch writing for the Court. The decision affirmed that NCAA restrictions on education-related benefits violated Sherman Section 1. Source: supremecourt.gov (Alston 594 US).

question: In the 2021 US Supreme Court case NCAA v. Alston, all nine justices ruled against the NCAA's cap on education-related benefits for college athletes. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a separate opinion agreeing with the ruling and going further: he warned the NCAA's whole 'amateurism' setup was likely an illegal cartel. What is a cartel?
answer: A group of sellers that agree to fix prices or limit competition
choices: A group of sellers that agree to fix prices or limit competition
A single buyer with no other competitors
A government agency that reviews mergers
A tax on imported goods
context: Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence in Alston explicitly extended the reasoning: 'The NCAA is not above the law.' The concurrence signaled that the whole amateurism edifice was legally vulnerable. Source: Alston, 594 US ___ (2021), Kavanaugh concurrence.

question: Since July 2021, after a Supreme Court loss forced the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) to rewrite its rules, US college athletes can finally be paid by outside companies for the use of their name, image, and likeness (NIL). Before that, athletes were amateurs by rule and got nothing beyond scholarships. How does this NIL change usually affect how long top players choose to stay in college?
answer: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
choices: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
All players immediately drop out to play professionally
Colleges instantly become bankrupt
