The number of college teams drops to zero
context: NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) compensation became legal for college athletes on July 1, 2021. Within three years the NIL market was estimated at over $1 billion annually flowing to athletes from endorsement deals. Source: ncaa.org (NIL policy history).

question: For decades US college sports made billions in television money, but the players themselves could not be paid. In 2025 a court settlement finally set up a system to share revenue with the athletes. What basic economic idea did that settlement finally admit?
answer: The people creating the value should be allowed to earn from it
choices: The people creating the value should be allowed to earn from it
Only owners and coaches actually create value in sports
Free labor makes sports leagues fairer for fans
Athletes should pay the schools for the honor of playing
context: The House v. NCAA settlement, approved June 6, 2025 by Judge Wilken, created a revenue-sharing framework of approximately $20-22M per school per year. It effectively converted college athletes into compensated labor. Source: reuters.com (House settlement coverage June 2025).

question: Before the 1980s the NCAA -- the big group that runs US college sports -- controlled which football games could appear on television and how many. In 1984 the US Supreme Court, in NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, ruled that each university could sell its own television rights instead. What happened to the number of college football games shown after that?
answer: Many more games aired, and television money soared
choices: Many more games aired, and television money soared
Almost no games aired, because schools could not organize alone
The same number aired at the same prices — nothing changed
Fans lost interest and stopped watching college football
context: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, 468 US 85 (1984), held that NCAA control over member schools' television contracts violated Sherman Section 1. It was an earlier stage of the same antitrust unwinding. Source: supremecourt.gov (468 US 85).

question: For decades the NCAA — the body that runs US college sports — ran a business worth billions of dollars. Coaches got rich, television networks got rich, universities got rich. But the players themselves were forbidden to earn a cent for playing. The 'amateur' rule held their price at zero. Between 2014 and 2025 the rule broke — courts and states forced the NCAA to let athletes earn money from their name, image, and likeness. What tends to happen when any industry keeps a key input priced far below its market value?
answer: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
choices: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
The rule will only get stronger over time
The workers will disappear from the industry
The federal government will formally endorse the low price
context: The amateurism-as-noble-tradition framing was a cultural prop for the price-fixing structure. Once courts began applying standard antitrust analysis, the prop eroded and the cartel collapsed within about a decade. Source: Zimbalist (1999); Alston (2021); House settlement (2025).

question: During World War 2 the city of New York froze rents so landlords could not raise the price on tenants during the wartime emergency. That 'short' emergency freeze has stayed in place ever since, more than eighty years later. What is the general name for a rule that caps how much rent a landlord can charge?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Rent inflation
Free rent
Rent tax
context: November 1943 federal rent freeze on New York City marks the start of continuous US residential rent regulation. The freeze was handed off to New York State, then to NYC itself in successive laws. Source: hcr.ny.gov (rent regulation history).

question: New York City has the oldest rent-control program in the United States. It began in 1943 during World War II, when the federal government froze apartment rents as a 'temporary' wartime measure so soldiers' families would not be gouged while men were overseas. The freeze never ended. As of 2026, roughly how long has New York's rent control been running?
answer: Over 80 years
choices: Over 80 years
About 10 years
About 20 years
About 200 years
context: From November 1943 to 2026 is 82-83 years. The 'temporary' program has been extended through several successor statutes -- the Emergency Housing Rent Control Law 1946, the Rent Stabilization Law 1969, the Emergency Tenant Protection Act 1974, and the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act. Source: hcr.ny.gov.

question: In 1971 the Swedish socialist economist Assar Lindbeck, who spent his career at Stockholm University and advised Sweden's own left-leaning government, made a famous warning about one popular housing policy. He called it 'the most efficient way to destroy a city — except for bombing.' Which policy shocked Lindbeck that much even though he was a socialist?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Public-housing high-rises
Zoning height limits
Property taxes
context: Assar Lindbeck, in The Political Economy of the New Left (1971). Lindbeck was a lifelong democratic-socialist and Nobel-committee-adjacent figure, not a right-winger -- his line is cited across the political spectrum. Source: Lindbeck (1971).

question: The nineteenth-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught a lesson called 'the seen and the unseen' — an honest look at any policy counts not just the visible winners but the invisible losses no one photographs. Apply his lesson to New York City rent control, a law that caps how much landlords can raise rent. What was seen was the low rent stamped on a lucky tenant's lease. What was unseen?
answer: The apartments never built, landlords deferring maintenance, and vacant units held off market
choices: The apartments never built, landlords deferring maintenance, and vacant units held off market
The government revenue from tenant leases
The reduced traffic congestion in the borough
The higher property taxes on landlords
context: Bastiat's method: the visible benefit was to the specific rent-regulated tenant; the hidden cost was future tenants who could not find apartments, current tenants of deteriorating buildings, and landlords who warehoused units. Source: bastiat.org, mercatus.org.

question: In the 1970s New York City had an epidemic of building fires, and much of the South Bronx literally burned to the ground. The Swedish socialist economist Assar Lindbeck, who had studied New York's rent laws, later connected those fires directly to the city's decades-old rent-control system. What was the specific connection he named?
answer: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
choices: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
The lack of fire-code enforcement in regulated buildings
The higher smoker rate in rent-regulated apartments
The greater density of gas heaters in old apartments
context: Rent-controlled buildings that could not cover their mortgage and maintenance costs became liabilities. Insurance payouts on total loss exceeded the market value of an ongoing rent-controlled property. The South Bronx arson wave of the 1970s is the exhibit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx.

question: Right after World War II, in 1946, two young American economists at the University of Chicago wrote a short pamphlet called 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem.' It was published by the Foundation for Economic Education and became the first classic economic critique of rent control. Both authors would each later win the Nobel Prize in Economics. Which pair wrote it?
answer: Milton Friedman and George Stigler
choices: Milton Friedman and George Stigler
John Kenneth Galbraith and Paul Samuelson
Kenneth Arrow and Gerard Debreu
Ronald Coase and James Buchanan
context: 'Roofs or Ceilings?' by Milton Friedman and George Stigler, published by the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946, is the founding classical critique. Both won Nobel Prizes decades later (Friedman 1976, Stigler 1982). Source: fee.org (Roofs or Ceilings 1946).

question: In 2019 the economists Rebecca Diamond and Chris Palmer, working at Stanford University, published a study in the American Economic Review that examined an expansion of San Francisco's rent-control rules in 1994. Earlier studies of New York had found that rent control shrinks the housing supply -- Diamond and Palmer wanted to see whether San Francisco matched. What did they find?
answer: Housing-stock destruction and reduced supply
choices: Housing-stock destruction and reduced supply
Increased new construction of luxury units
Widespread lower rent burdens across all tenants
Rising quality of rent-regulated units
context: Diamond and Palmer's study of San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion found landlords converted, demolished, or removed roughly 15% of formerly-controlled units from the rental stock over the next two decades. Same mechanism as the New York pattern. Source: aeaweb.org (AER 2019).

question: In 2019 New York State passed the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act, known as HSTPA. The law made the city's already-strict rent rules even tighter — landlords could raise rents less, remove fewer units from regulation, and evict less easily. Within two years, economists studying the New York rental market noticed specific measurable effects. What did they find?
answer: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
choices: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
Rising landlord investment in maintenance
Faster tenant turnover across boroughs
Reduced construction permit backlogs
context: Landlords held rent-regulated units off market ('warehoused') rather than accept new indexed tenancies. New rental construction in NYC dropped. The 2019 tightening's predictable supply effects matched the seen-vs-unseen analysis. Source: Rent Stabilization Association analyses 2020-22.

question: For eighty years, economists studying rent control have kept landing on the same reasoning move -- from Milton Friedman and George Stigler's 1946 pamphlet 'Roofs or Ceilings?', through Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck's 1971 book on housing, all the way to Rebecca Diamond and Chris Palmer's 2019 San Francisco study. It is one incentive story about landlords. What does the story say?
answer: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
choices: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
Landlords with rent below cost invest more heavily in improvements
Landlords with rent below cost lower quality but expand supply
Landlords with rent below cost mostly exit but new entrants rush in
context: The core incentive story: if rent is below what maintenance and construction cost require, the rational landlord defers maintenance, warehouses units, converts to condos, or exits. Future tenants pay the invisible cost. Source: Friedman-Stigler, Roofs or Ceilings? (1946).

question: In 1996 the American computer scientist Nick Szabo had an idea. Write a contract as computer code, and it would run itself the moment its rules were met. If you paid rent, the digital door would unlock. If you missed, it would lock again. No lawyer, no judge, no court. What did Szabo call this kind of contract?
answer: A smart contract
choices: A smart contract
A legal loan
A digital receipt
A payment plan
context: Nick Szabo coined 'smart contracts' in a 1996 essay. Vitalik Buterin later built Ethereum around a smart-contract virtual machine (2015); Hal Finney built RPOW; Adam Back built Hashcash. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: In his 1998 essay, the American computer scientist Nick Szabo laid out how bit gold — his invention of software-scarce digital tokens — would be minted. A computer would solve a hard math puzzle. The answer would become a new token, and that token would then feed the next puzzle. Which cryptographic tool did Szabo chain together to mint fresh bit-gold tokens?
answer: proof-of-work
choices: proof-of-work
blind signatures
hash-based message authentication
elliptic-curve key exchange
context: Bit gold works by chaining proof-of-work: solving one puzzle produces a new token whose hash seeds the next. Blind signatures (Chaum's DigiCash), HMACs, and key-exchange are separate cryptographic primitives that bit gold did not use for issuance. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: In 1998 the American computer scientist Nick Szabo published his bit gold essay. Fiat money — dollars, yen, euros — could always be printed at a central bank's discretion. Bit gold, born from math puzzles, could not. Szabo named one money trait that no central bank could be trusted to give, but that bit gold could guarantee. Which trait did he mean?
answer: a supply whose growth rate is governed by fixed technical difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion
choices: a supply whose growth rate is governed by fixed technical difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion
an instant settlement guarantee with no per-transaction processing delay or waiting period at any point
a reversible-transaction rule for fraud protection that lets any user recall a mistaken transfer within a set window
a printed physical note that an ordinary citizen can hold in the hand and verify by touch and weight
context: Szabo argues bit gold's supply is governed by puzzle difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion; fiat has always been discretionary. Instant settlement, reversibility, and physical notes are properties the essay does not claim as the differentiator. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: Nick Szabo's bit gold system was never fully built. Szabo himself named one technical piece he could not solve, the piece that would keep a distributed record consistent when many people were solving puzzles at once. Which unsolved problem did bit gold leave open?
answer: how to reach consensus on the ordering of new bit-gold entries across a distributed network
choices: how to reach consensus on the ordering of new bit-gold entries across a distributed network
how to make the puzzles asymmetric between solving and verifying
how to encode the tokens in a portable digital format
how to sign transactions to prove ownership
context: Bit gold assumed distributed timestamping but did not specify how the network would agree on the ordering when solutions arrived from many nodes. Puzzle asymmetry, digital-format portability, and signing were already established primitives. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html; Nakamoto 2008 sec 4.

question: Nick Szabo's 1998 bit gold left one big problem unsolved: when two computers proposed different histories of the tokens, there was no rule to say which one everyone should accept. Ten years later, in 2008, the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper and closed that gap. Which mechanism did Satoshi introduce to pick the true chain of history?
answer: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
choices: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
the blind-signature bank issuance model that Chaum's DigiCash had introduced in 1989
the reusable-proof-of-work token exchange model that Hal Finney had built in 2004
the ring-signature transaction hider that later cryptocurrencies would adopt for privacy
context: Satoshi's longest-chain rule with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker specifically resolves the consensus problem bit gold left open. Blind signatures (Chaum) required a bank; RPOW (Finney) required a central server; ring signatures came later and hide senders, not resolve ordering. Source: Nakamoto 2008 sec 4.

question: The American computer scientist Nick Szabo — inventor of smart contracts and of bit gold, the closest software ancestor to Bitcoin — is also a trained lawyer. He has spent his career blending computer science, monetary history, and legal analysis in essays widely read across the cypherpunk world. From which American law school did Szabo earn his law degree?
answer: George Washington University
choices: George Washington University
Harvard University
Yale University
Stanford University
context: Szabo earned his JD from George Washington University Law School. Harvard, Yale, and Stanford Law are frequently guessed as elite law schools but none is Szabo's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: Nick Szabo is an American computer scientist and legal scholar who wrote a detailed 1998 proposal called 'bit gold,' which described almost every piece of what would later become Bitcoin. Because of his rare writing style, where he lives, his lifelong crypto focus, and that very early bit gold design, journalists and researchers have often suspected Szabo is really Satoshi Nakamoto, the mystery inventor of Bitcoin. What has Szabo always said in public when asked?
answer: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
choices: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
he has quietly confirmed the identification in later interviews
he has told journalists he cannot remember
he has been legally prohibited from discussing it
context: Szabo has denied the Satoshi identification publicly on multiple occasions. There has been no confirmation, memory-loss claim, or legal gag reported. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 Bitcoin white paper carries a short list of citations in its notes. It credits Adam Back's Hashcash, Wei Dai's b-money, and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping. But one cypherpunk project from 1998 is widely seen as Bitcoin's closest software ancestor — proof-of-work chained to mint scarce digital tokens — and Satoshi's paper leaves it off. Which project is missing from the notes?
answer: Nick Szabo's bit gold
choices: Nick Szabo's bit gold
Wei Dai's b-money
Adam Back's Hashcash
Haber and Stornetta's timestamping
context: Satoshi's white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money (Ref 1), Adam Back's Hashcash (Ref 6), and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping papers, but does not cite bit gold directly, even though the design similarity is widely acknowledged. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In 1998 the American cryptographer Nick Szabo published a blueprint called bit gold -- a proposal for digital scarce money using proof-of-work puzzles. Ten years later, in 2008, an anonymous inventor calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin. Bitcoin historians press one reasoning move about what Satoshi actually added on top of Szabo's blueprint. Which move does the argument press?
answer: That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism -- and consensus was the single hard piece the field had left open until Satoshi
choices: That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism -- and consensus was the single hard piece the field had left open until Satoshi
That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the proof-of-work mechanism -- Szabo left the puzzle chain unspecified and Satoshi added it
That bit gold is Bitcoin minus the digital signatures -- Szabo did not use signed transactions and Satoshi added them
That bit gold and Bitcoin are cryptographically unrelated designs that arrived at similar shapes by coincidence rather than lineage
context: The bit-gold-vs-Bitcoin move (Song, Antonopoulos, Ammous): Szabo had PoW, chained puzzles, digital signatures and a plan for issuance; the piece he could not close was distributed consensus, which is exactly what Satoshi's longest-chain rule solved. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html; Nakamoto white paper.

question: In one small California town, the neighbors keep voting to block new houses and apartments from being built. There are lots of jobs there and lots of people who want to move in. What is probably happening to the price of the houses that already exist?
answer: It keeps going way up -- some homes cost millions
choices: It keeps going way up -- some homes cost millions
It stays flat forever no matter what
It drops until houses are almost free
It changes only if the mayor announces a new price
context: Palo Alto's median home price approached $3M in 2024 (Zillow/CoreLogic). About 94% of its residential land is zoned for single-family detached homes; apartment construction has been effectively frozen for decades. Source: paloaltoonline.com; zillow.com.

question: In a growing town, neighbors show up at every meeting to block new apartments from being built near their houses -- they say new buildings will change the neighborhood. People joke this attitude fits the shorthand NIMBY. What three words does NIMBY stand for?
answer: Not In My Backyard
choices: Not In My Backyard
New In My Backyard
No Money Big Yield
Never In My Building Year
context: NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) describes the political pattern in which existing local homeowners organize to block new housing in their neighborhoods, even when a region's overall housing shortage produces high rents and long commutes. Source: Grokipedia 'NIMBY.'

question: In Palo Alto, California -- the wealthy Silicon Valley city that is home to Stanford University -- roughly 94 percent of residential land is zoned only for single-family homes. That effectively bans anyone from building new apartment buildings across most of the city. What term do housing economists use for zoning rules that block denser, cheaper housing like that?
answer: Exclusionary zoning
choices: Exclusionary zoning
Inclusionary zoning
Mixed-use zoning
Transit-oriented zoning
context: About 94% of Palo Alto's residential land is single-family only. This is the structural feature that makes multi-family projects require special approvals and lengthy hearings each time. Source: Palo Alto General Plan; ABAG regional data.

question: Two American economists -- Edward Glaeser of Harvard and Joseph Gyourko of the Wharton School -- coined a term for the gap between what housing costs in cities where building is hard, like San Francisco or Manhattan, and what it would cost to just build the house from lumber and labor. The gap is often hundreds of thousands of dollars per home, all created by rules. What term did they use?
answer: The zoning tax
choices: The zoning tax
The rent premium
The permitting spread
The metro markup
context: Glaeser + Gyourko, 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' (NBER Working Paper 8835, 2002) and follow-up work estimate the zoning tax at 30-60% in Bay Area cities. The wedge is a pure transfer from would-be residents to existing homeowners. Source: nber.org (Glaeser-Gyourko 2002).

question: In Palo Alto, California, homeowners who live near Stanford University benefit from strict zoning that blocks new housing. Their houses grow more valuable every year because no new ones can be built next door. The gain to them is huge and visible, but the cost spreads across many people no one sees. Who are those hidden losers?
answer: Workers priced out to Modesto, Sacramento, or out of California entirely
choices: Workers priced out to Modesto, Sacramento, or out of California entirely
Palo Alto public-school administrators
Stanford University trustees
Nearby city police departments
context: The dispersed victims cannot vote in Palo Alto, cannot attend Palo Alto hearings, and often do not know that a specific project would have housed them. That is exactly the collective-action failure Olson diagnosed. Source: Olson (1965) applied via Furman et al. (Housing Reform brief).

question: Around 2015, as housing prices in American cities climbed higher and higher, a new group of activists formed. Unlike the old Not-In-My-Backyard neighbors — the NIMBYs — who fought every new apartment building, this group did the opposite. They showed up at city council meetings pushing for more homes to be built, more density, more construction. What short name do people call this pro-housing movement?
answer: YIMBY
choices: YIMBY
SANE
PATH
HOA
context: YIMBY (Yes In My Backyard) organizations like YIMBY Action emerged around 2015-16. They served as the selective-incentive mechanism (organization, model bills, hearings turnout) that begins to solve the collective-action problem on the dispersed side. Source: yimbyaction.org.

question: In 2021 the California state legislature passed a bill letting homeowners split their lots and build a small duplex where a single-family house had once been the only option. It was a rare state-level win against the tight local zoning rules that had frozen housing supply in cities like Palo Alto and San Francisco. What short name did the bill go by?
answer: SB 9
choices: SB 9
SB 35
AB 5
AB 32
context: SB 9 (2021) allowed by-right duplex construction on many single-family lots across California, over the strenuous objections of many local governments. It attacked the rule-selection game at state level. Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (SB 9, 2021).

question: For most of the twentieth century the US city of Minneapolis -- on the Mississippi River in Minnesota, near the Great Lakes -- only allowed single-family houses on most of its residential land. In 2018 Minneapolis passed a plan called Minneapolis 2040, changing the rules so any residential lot in the city could hold up to three units. What did that change do to the supply of homes?
answer: More units per lot became legal, so more homes could be built
choices: More units per lot became legal, so more homes could be built
Every existing home was torn down overnight
People were banned from moving into the city
Everyone was forced into apartments the government owns
context: The Minneapolis 2040 Comprehensive Plan (2018) eliminated single-family-only residential zoning citywide. It was the first US big-city plan to do so, and later became a model for other cities. Source: minneapolismn.gov (2040 Plan).

question: Austin, Texas -- one of the fastest-growing cities in the United States -- let builders put up huge numbers of new apartments over about five years, from 2019 to 2024. Some people had claimed that adding new apartments always raises rents by attracting even more demand. To their surprise, what actually happened to rents in Austin?
answer: Rents fell as more apartments were built
choices: Rents fell as more apartments were built
Rents doubled as more apartments were built
Rents stayed exactly the same
Older apartments were torn down instead
context: Austin's building boom from about 2019 through 2024 produced actual measured declines in market-rate rents. It is the most-cited domestic case that supply matters. Source: apartmentlist.com; Austin American-Statesman coverage 2023-24.

question: In Palo Alto, California, decades of tight zoning that blocked new housing made the region unaffordable for workers, yet the rules never went away. The homeowners whose property values had been lifted by that scarcity turned out every election to keep them. Austrian economists lift a general rule from this story. When a bad policy hurts a region's economy but sticks around anyway, what should you look for?
answer: Existing incumbent asset-holders whose wealth was created by the policy's restriction
choices: Existing incumbent asset-holders whose wealth was created by the policy's restriction
A single hidden corrupt payment to a legislator
A federal preemption blocking local action
A recent Supreme Court decision requiring the policy
context: The zoning wedge is a multi-trillion-dollar wealth transfer to existing homeowners in constrained cities. That concentrated wealth is what organizes to defend the restrictive rule against reform. Source: Glaeser + Gyourko (2002); Olson (1965) as applied.

question: Palo Alto, California and other Bay Area cities use strict local zoning to block new housing, and their home prices have soared. Japan does housing rules differently — the national government sets zoning, and cities have little power to stop builders. Tokyo has kept growing to 37 million people, adding new apartments year after year. What has happened to Tokyo's real housing prices over the long run?
answer: They have been comparatively stable
choices: They have been comparatively stable
They have tripled over the past decade
They exceed Palo Alto's per-square-foot prices
They have collapsed to near zero
context: Japan's national zoning system permits substantial by-right housing construction, and Tokyo's real housing prices have been comparatively stable despite continued metropolitan-area growth. It is the international contrast that Bay Area reformers frequently cite. Source: Grokipedia 'Housing in Japan.'

question: North Korea has been ruled by three generations of one family since 1948. What is that family's last name?
answer: Kim
choices: Kim
Park
Lee
Choe
context: Kim Il-sung (1948-94), Kim Jong-il (1994-2011), and Kim Jong-un (2011- ) form the three-generation dynasty ruling the DPRK. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea.

question: North Korea's official state teaching, first spelled out under founder Kim Il-sung in the 1950s, is that the country must stand entirely on its own. It must not lean on outsiders — not China, not the Soviet Union, no one. What Korean word names this idea of total national self-reliance?
answer: Juche
choices: Juche
Songun
Chuche-hop
Bogus
context: Juche was formally systematized by Kim Il-sung in speeches from 1955 onward. It emphasizes political independence, economic self-reliance, and military self-defense. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juche.

question: In the 1990s, North Korea suffered a famine that killed hundreds of thousands of people. The government owned all the farms and set all the food prices. Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued this kind of failure is baked into any fully planned system. Why does the Austrian school say a planned economy so often ends in shortage?
answer: No planner can gather all the information that free prices carry
choices: No planner can gather all the information that free prices carry
Planned economies always have too much rain and not enough sun
Farmers in planned countries choose to grow only flowers, not food
Free countries always send extra food to planned countries
context: 'Gonan-ui Haenggun' (Arduous March) is North Korea's official term for the mid-1990s famine. The state has never acknowledged a death toll. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_famine.

question: In the mid-1990s, floods and the collapse of Soviet aid triggered a mass famine in North Korea, known to its own people as the Arduous March. Because Kim Jong-il's government has never opened its records, outside scholars can only estimate how many people died beyond the normal death rate. What is the standard scholarly range for those excess deaths?
answer: About 600,000 to 2.5 million
choices: About 600,000 to 2.5 million
About 6 million to 25 million
context: Andrew Natsios's The Great North Korean Famine (2001) argued for the upper end (2-3 million); Marcus Noland's demographic reconstruction argues for the lower end (600K-1M). Out of a population of about 22 million. Source: uspicedu (KEI) reports.

question: North Korea operates a set of political prison camps called kwanliso, hidden in the northern mountains and never officially acknowledged by the government in Pyongyang. Almost everything the outside world knows about them comes from escapees who made it to South Korea and from commercial satellite photos. Which American non-profit publishes yearly reports pairing those satellite images with survivor testimony?
answer: The Committee for Human Rights in North Korea
choices: The Committee for Human Rights in North Korea
Amnesty International
Freedom House
Reporters Without Borders
context: HRNK publishes The Hidden Gulag (multiple editions from 2003) and periodic camp-imagery reports. David Hawk is the lead author. Total prisoner population is estimated at 120,000-200,000 across roughly six known camps. Source: hrnk.org.

question: Inside North Korea's kwanliso prison camp system, a person accused of a political crime is not the only one arrested. The regime in Pyongyang also imprisons that person's parents, brothers and sisters, children, and even grandchildren, on the reasoning that disloyalty runs through the bloodline. What name does the regime give to this policy?
answer: Three generations of punishment
choices: Three generations of punishment
Collective correction
Family rectification
Bloodline restoration
context: 'Three generations of punishment' (san-dae) means an accused political prisoner's parents, siblings, spouse, and children are also imprisoned. The policy has been documented by defector testimony including Kang Chol-hwan's The Aquariums of Pyongyang. Source: hrnk.org.

question: In the 1920s the Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued that a socialist state cannot rationally calculate what to produce — with no market prices, planners are blind. The dispute became known as the socialist calculation debate. Decades later a single photograph turned up in every textbook telling the story: a nighttime satellite view of the Korean peninsula. What does the image show?
answer: North Korea nearly dark and South Korea blazing with light
choices: North Korea nearly dark and South Korea blazing with light
North Korea heavily forested and South Korea deforested
North Korea covered in snow and South Korea clear
North Korea flooded and South Korea dry
context: NASA and NOAA nighttime imagery show South Korea covered in urban lighting and North Korea (excluding Pyongyang) essentially dark. Same peninsula, same language, split in 1948 into planned and market economies. Source: earthobservatory.nasa.gov.

question: After World War 2, Korea was split into two countries at the 38th parallel. South Korea picked markets, trade, and private business. North Korea picked a fully planned communist economy where the state owned the factories and set the prices. The two started at similar living standards. About 75 years later, how much richer is the average South Korean than the average North Korean?
answer: About 40 times richer
choices: About 40 times richer
About 4 times richer
About 400 times richer
About the same
context: South Korea's per-capita GDP is roughly 40 times North Korea's on standard estimates (both PPP and nominal). This is one of the largest cross-border prosperity gaps ever recorded between countries with the same starting culture and geography. Source: Bank of Korea and World Bank estimates.

question: North Korea has run a near-total command economy since the 1950s — the state owns the farms and factories, and government planners set the prices. Chronic food shortages have followed the whole time. Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek offered a specific reason planned states fail this way. What is the Austrian-school explanation for why the planners cannot fix the problem?
answer: Without market prices the state cannot allocate food or resources rationally at large scale
choices: Without market prices the state cannot allocate food or resources rationally at large scale
Without oil imports the state cannot power its industry
Without foreign investment the state cannot modernize
Without democracy the state cannot legitimize taxation
context: The Mises 1920 calculation argument applied: no central planner can determine relative prices across millions of goods and inputs. The DPRK's chronic scarcity is that argument playing out in a country of 22 million for over 70 years. Source: mises.org/library/mises-planned-chaos.

question: North Korea has been running a strict command economy — every price set by planners, no free markets — since 1948. That's the longest single experiment with pure central planning still running. What broad economic result has that experiment produced?
answer: Chronic food shortages and famine, decade after decade
choices: Chronic food shortages and famine, decade after decade
Rapid economic growth that outpaces its neighbors
A booming private trading sector
A famous stock market with worldwide investors
context: The DPRK was founded September 9, 1948, one month after the Republic of Korea in the South (August 15, 1948). Kim Il-sung had returned from Soviet-army training in 1945. The Korean War (1950-53) hardened the division. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_North_Korea.

question: China's Deng Xiaoping opened Chinese markets to private business starting in 1978. Vietnam launched its own market reforms — called Doi Moi — in 1986. Cuba has cautiously started letting citizens run small businesses. All three still call themselves Communist and still have one-party rule. Which statement best describes the modern picture of command versus market-with-Party economies?
answer: Only North Korea stays pure command; China, Vietnam, and Cuba allow markets under Party rule
choices: Only North Korea stays pure command; China, Vietnam, and Cuba allow markets under Party rule
Cuba is still a pure command economy alongside North Korea
Vietnam has ended Communist Party rule entirely
China now has fully private ownership of all industry
context: China (1978), Vietnam (1986 Doi Moi), and Cuba (partial reforms from 1993) all adopted some market pricing. The DPRK remains the outlier -- the calculation-debate case that never took Mises's advice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_North_Korea.

question: In a country like North Korea, there are no regular stores selling food. The government runs shops that hand out grain, oil, and other food to each family. The amount you get depends on your job and how loyal to the party you seem. Miss a rally, and your family's ration can shrink. What is that setup called?
answer: A government rationing system
choices: A government rationing system
A free market
A farmer's market
A private grocery chain
context: The Public Distribution System (PDS) was the DPRK's principal food-allocation mechanism. Private markets were essentially banned outside a narrow set of state-approved farmers' markets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Distribution_System_(North_Korea).

question: In the 1990s, food aid from other countries stopped and a huge famine hit North Korea -- hundreds of thousands of people starved. Instead of calling it a famine, the government gave it a heroic name meaning 'a hard march we all took together.' Why do governments do that?
answer: To hide who is to blame and make the disaster sound noble
choices: To hide who is to blame and make the disaster sound noble
To warn other countries about the weather
To make sure historians write the truth
To pay the farmers back for lost crops
context: 'Gonan-ui Haenggun' (Arduous March, Kojein Haenggun) was the state's stoic official term for the 1993-98 famine. The regime has never acknowledged a death toll. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_famine.

question: In 2007 two American economists who specialize in Korea published a book called Famine in North Korea. Working from refugee interviews, satellite crop data, and Chinese cross-border trade records, they estimated that 600,000 to 2.5 million North Koreans died in the mid-1990s Arduous March famine — out of a population of about 22 million. Who were the two authors?
answer: Marcus Noland and Stephan Haggard
choices: Marcus Noland and Stephan Haggard
Andrei Lankov and Chun-Yun Yang
Robert Kaplan and Bruce Cumings
Robert Barro and Ronald McKinnon
context: Noland (Peterson Institute) and Haggard (UC San Diego) published Famine in North Korea in 2007. Their central finding: the famine was PRODUCED by the failure of the PDS itself; regions cut off from Pyongyang's distribution suffered worst. Source: piie.com Noland-Haggard.

question: During North Korea's Arduous March famine of the mid-1990s, private buying and selling of food was against the law. The state's public distribution system had collapsed, and yet ordinary Koreans still had to eat. So in vacant lots and back alleys across the country, an illegal grassroots trading network popped up anyway. It moved food between regions and saved millions of lives. What did North Koreans call it?
answer: The jangmadang markets
choices: The jangmadang markets
The rural collectives
The state grain exchange
The Kim Foundation shops
context: Jangmadang ('market grounds'), initially bicycle-basket traders selling food across regions, emerged spontaneously in defiance of the private-trade ban. By 2019 defector-survey estimates suggested ~70-80% of North Korean private consumption flowed through jangmadang markets. Source: Andrei Lankov, North of the DMZ.

question: Two young women who escaped from North Korea later wrote famous memoirs about surviving the mid-1990s Arduous March famine. Both told of watching their mothers and grandmothers walk hours to the jangmadang — the illegal street markets — to buy rice that the state had failed to deliver. Which pair of North Korean escapees wrote those memoirs?
answer: Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee
choices: Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee
Kang Chol-hwan and Shin Dong-hyuk
Lee Soon-ok and Kim Yong
Choi Jinyi and Park Sang-hak
context: Yeonmi Park's In Order to Live (2015) and Hyeonseo Lee's The Girl with Seven Names (2015) both document the jangmadang market experience. Both defected via China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeonmi_Park, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyeonseo_Lee.

question: During North Korea's mid-1990s Arduous March famine, scholars mapping the death rates found something striking. Hunger was sharpest in the northeastern provinces that Pyongyang had cut off from its central grain distribution first. Weather and international sanctions were the same across the whole country. Which pattern does this evidence establish about the mechanism of the collapse?
answer: Central-distribution failure is itself a famine mechanism
choices: Central-distribution failure is itself a famine mechanism
Weather variability was the primary cause
International sanctions caused most deaths
Chinese aid cuts were the sole trigger
context: Noland and Haggard's finding: regions closest to Pyongyang's central distribution suffered less; regions farthest and most PDS-dependent suffered worst. The mechanism is Mises 1920 in its most literal form -- central distribution cannot substitute for market allocation. Source: Noland-Haggard (2007).

question: In Seoul, a Russian-born historian at Kookmin University has spent decades interviewing North Korean escapees about daily life under the Kim family. He has written more than anyone in English about the jangmadang, the illegal street markets that saved millions of lives during the mid-1990s Arduous March famine. What is his last name?
answer: Lankov
choices: Lankov
Cumings
Oberdorfer
Myers
context: Andrei Lankov, at Kookmin University in Seoul, is the leading scholarly authority on the jangmadang system. His books North of the DMZ (2007) and The Real North Korea (2013) are standard references. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Lankov.

question: In North Korea private trade is illegal, but the government stores rarely have enough food. Over time, people set up unofficial street markets in every town. A survey of people who escaped found what share of everyday goods actually flows through those illegal markets?
answer: About 70 to 80 percent
choices: About 70 to 80 percent
About 7 to 8 percent
Less than 1 percent
About 30 to 40 percent
context: Defector-survey estimates from Kookmin University and Seoul-based think tanks suggest 70-80% of private consumption flows through informal markets. The state tolerates them because the alternative is renewed famine. Source: kookmin university surveys 2018-19.

question: In the mid-1990s, North Korea's state grain distribution system collapsed and millions of people faced starvation. In alleyways and vacant lots, private jangmadang markets sprang up without permission, and food began to move from farmers to hungry families again. Austrian economists point to this case as a live demonstration of two of their key reasoning-moves at once. Which pair does the North Korean story teach most sharply?
answer: The calculation problem in acute form plus Hayek's spontaneous order
choices: The calculation problem in acute form plus Hayek's spontaneous order
The Cantillon effect plus moral hazard
The Phillips curve plus rational expectations
The gold-standard critique plus fractional reserve
context: The calculation problem: PDS could not adapt to the 1991 aid shock. Spontaneous order: markets emerged illegally to save lives, exactly as Hayek 1945 predicted. The world's most totalitarian environment produced the sharpest confirmation of both moves. Source: mises.org/library/north-korea.

question: A woman in Mississippi wants to open a shop where she braids hair for pay. Before the state will let her, it makes her sit through 300 hours of an expensive class -- and the class does not cover braiding at all. What is this kind of 'you need a permit before you can work' rule called?
answer: An occupational license
choices: An occupational license
A sales tax
A free market
A minimum wage
context: Mississippi's cosmetology code offered no category for African-style braiding, so braiders were funneled into a 300-hour wigology license. The Institute for Justice sued for Armstrong in April 2004 (Armstrong v. Lunsford); in April 2005 the governor signed a reform letting braiders register with the Board of Health for $25 and post sanitation guidelines. More than 6,700 braiders have registered since. Sources: Institute for Justice, 'Mississippi Hair Braiding' (https://ij.org/case/armstrong-v-lunsford/); Armstrong's written testimony to the U.S. House Small Business Committee, March 26, 2014.

question: Occupational licensing is a government rule that you cannot legally do a job — cutting hair, driving a cab, arranging flowers — without a state-issued permit. In the 1950s only about one American in twenty needed such a license. By 2013 that share had grown a lot. What fraction of American workers said in 2013 that they needed a license to do their job?
answer: About three in ten
choices: About one in ten
About three in ten
About one in two
About two in three
context: Kleiner and Krueger found 29% of employees reported holding a government license, and 35% were licensed or certified. The roughly 5% baseline for the early 1950s comes from Morris Kleiner, Licensing Occupations: Ensuring Quality or Restricting Competition? (2006). Sources: Kleiner and Krueger, 'Analyzing the Extent and Influence of Occupational Licensing on the Labor Market,' Journal of Labor Economics 31(S1), 2013 (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/669060); NBER working paper 14979 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w14979).

question: Isis Brantley braided hair in Dallas since 1979. In 1997 police arrested her, because Texas made braiders take 1,500 hours of classes that never taught braiding. She fought for eighteen years and won in court in early 2015. What did Texas lawmakers do that June?
answer: Removed natural hair braiding from state licensing altogether
choices: Removed natural hair braiding from state licensing altogether
Created a shorter braiding license of two hundred classroom hours
Ordered the cosmetology course to add a natural-braiding module
Granted Brantley a personal exemption from the training rule
context: In Brantley v. Kuntz a federal court struck down the rule requiring Brantley to outfit her braiding school like a barber college. House Bill 2717 then passed the Texas House and Senate unanimously and was signed on June 10, 2015, fully deregulating natural hair braiding in Texas. Sources: Institute for Justice, 'Texas Hair Braiding Instruction' (https://ij.org/case/txbraiding/); American University Business Law Review on Brantley v. Kuntz (https://aublr.org/2015/01/brantley-v-kuntz/).

question: For years, Louisiana was the only US state that made you pass an exam just to sell flower arrangements at a shop. In 2003 the Institute for Justice, a public-interest law firm, sued Louisiana on behalf of Sandy Meadows — a widow who had lost her florist job because she was not licensed — and two other women. The lawsuit focused on how the practical test was run. What was wrong with the test?
answer: Licensed florists competing with the applicants graded the practical test
choices: Licensed florists competing with the applicants graded the practical test
The wholesale flower distributors' trade group wrote all the test questions
Applicants could sit the test only in Baton Rouge, once every second year
A year of unpaid apprenticeship under a licensed florist came first
context: Meadows v. Odom, 356 F. Supp. 2d 639 (M.D. La. 2005). The exam's subjective practical section was scored by state-licensed florists -- the incumbents an applicant would compete against. Sandy Meadows had been fired from a Baton Rouge grocery store after inspectors found her arranging flowers without a license; she died unemployed and in poverty before the case was decided. Louisiana finally repealed the florist exam in 2024. Sources: Institute for Justice (https://ij.org/case/meadows-v-odom/); Justia (https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/356/639/2573021/).

question: A state legislature takes up a bill to let hair braiders work without a cosmetology license. Consumers would pay less and more people could open shops, yet the bill dies in committee for the fourth session running, as it did the three sessions before. Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action explains why bills of this shape keep dying. Which asymmetry did Olson identify?
answer: A few who each gain a lot organize; the many who each lose a little do not
choices: A few who each gain a lot organize; the many who each lose a little do not
Voters skip the details because one vote will never change the outcome
Regulators must lean on the industry for the facts only the industry holds
Rivals burn real resources competing for a privilege, and that spending is waste
context: Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (Harvard University Press, 1965). The three distractors are also real reasoning moves, borrowed from other analysts: rational ignorance (Anthony Downs), informational capture (a strand of the capture literature), and rent-seeking waste (Gordon Tullock, 1967). Source: Olson, The Logic of Collective Action.

question: Shopping-mall kiosks in North Carolina began offering teeth whitening at a fraction of a dentist's price. The state Board of Dental Examiners -- six of its eight members practicing dentists -- mailed the kiosks cease-and-desist letters until they closed. The Federal Trade Commission sued, and the board claimed the immunity from antitrust law that states enjoy. On February 25, 2015 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against the board. What did the Court hold?
answer: A board run by active competitors keeps that immunity only under real state supervision
choices: A board run by active competitors keeps that immunity only under real state supervision
A licensing board is a private association and has never held any such immunity
Teeth whitening is not dentistry, so the board acted outside its granted authority
A board may bar competitors only after public notice-and-comment rulemaking
context: North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, 574 U.S. 494 (2015). Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote for the majority, joined by Roberts, Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan; Alito dissented with Scalia and Thomas. Where a controlling number of a state agency's decisionmakers are active market participants in the occupation it regulates, Parker state-action immunity applies only if the state actively supervises the agency. Sources: Justia (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/574/494/); Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_Board_of_Dental_Examiners_v._FTC).

question: In 1971 the American economist George Stigler — later a Nobel Prize winner at the University of Chicago — wrote a paper called 'The Theory of Economic Regulation.' It flipped the textbook view. Stigler argued that a trade group is not the victim of rules; it is the customer buying them from lawmakers. If a trade could pick one favor from the state, which favor would it want most?
answer: A rule blocking newcomers from entering the trade
choices: A rule blocking newcomers from entering the trade
A cash subsidy paid out of the state's general revenue
A guaranteed rate of return set and policed by the state
A tax on the imported goods that substitute for its own
context: George J. Stigler, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation,' Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2(1), Spring 1971, 3-21. Stigler catalogued the favors an industry can seek -- direct subsidy, control over entry, rules governing substitutes and complements, and price fixing -- and argued control over entry is worth most, because a cash subsidy draws in new entrants who compete it away while an entry barrier keeps them out for good. Stigler won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1982. Source: https://www.jstor.org/stable/3003160.

question: In his 1962 book, Milton Friedman opened his chapter on job licenses with doctors. He called the American Medical Association 'perhaps the strongest trade union in the country.' Friedman agreed a bad doctor can hurt a patient. Even so, he was against a license rule. He named a different plan. It would warn worried patients but still let them choose. What was it?
answer: State certification that a practitioner has met a published standard
choices: State certification that a practitioner has met a published standard
State registration of each practitioner's name and address before working
Compulsory malpractice insurance priced against each practitioner's record
A national entry examination written by patients rather than by physicians
context: Capitalism and Freedom, chapter 9, 'Occupational Licensure.' Friedman separated three levels of state involvement in a trade -- registration, certification and licensure -- and argued the justification weakens as you climb. Certification publishes who has met a standard while leaving the uncertified free to practice and the patient free to choose; licensure instead restricts the supply of practitioners and raises their incomes. The AMA has shaped entry into American medicine since its founding in 1847. Sources: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962), ch. 9; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism_and_Freedom.

question: Imagine a village with no money. A shoemaker wants bread. He carries his best pair of shoes to the baker and offers them for a loaf. Every trade in the village works this way: goods for goods, no coins. Which name do economists give to this system?
answer: barter
choices: barter
banking
usury
arbitrage
context: BARTER is direct goods-for-goods exchange with no medium of exchange. The obvious problem it faces is called the DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS: the shoemaker needs a baker who happens to want shoes AT THAT MOMENT. Solving that problem is what money is for. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11138-022-00600-0.

question: How did money first get started? The Austrian economist Carl Menger gave one famous answer in an 1892 essay. He said: long ago people traded goods for goods. Over time, they all began using one item like gold or silver — it was easy to carry, it did not rot, and everyone would accept it in trade. Where does Menger's idea say money came from?
answer: Regular people trading with each other, not a king or government
choices: Regular people trading with each other, not a king or government
A king who invented coins one day
A single scientist who wrote a plan for it
A big meeting of bank owners in Europe
context: Menger's essay appeared in The Economic Journal, Volume 2, June 1892, pages 239-255 -- then a very young journal, founded three years earlier by the British Economic Association (later the Royal Economic Society). The American Economic Review dates from 1911; the JPE from 1892 but published in Chicago; the QJE from 1886. Source: scispace.com/papers/on-the-origin-of-money-4ddier28ke.

question: In 1892 the Austrian economist Carl Menger — founder of the Austrian school — wrote an essay to knock down an old rival theory of money. That rival theory went back to Aristotle in ancient Greece. It said money is simply whatever the ruler stamps on metal and calls money. So the rival theory said money must come from whom?
answer: the state
choices: the state
the temple
the merchant guild
the extended family
context: Menger targeted the STATE theory of money (later formalized as Georg Knapp's 1905 Staatliche Theorie des Geldes, 'The State Theory of Money'), which said sovereign authority creates money. Menger's counter: no state stamp could get people to accept a coin unless they already thought others would too. Source: mars.gmu.edu/bitstreams/9013e402-22d7-4cb9-b937-a651fd4d1802/download.

question: A wheat farmer in a barter economy needs a plow. He finds a plow-maker -- but the plow-maker does not need wheat this month; he needs leather. The direct trade cannot happen, so the wheat farmer has to go find a wheat-hungry tanner FIRST, hoping the tanner will have leather to spare. Nineteenth-century economists gave this specific obstacle to direct trade a formal name. What is the obstacle called?
answer: the double coincidence of wants
choices: the double coincidence of wants
the tragedy of the commons
the free-rider problem
the winner's curse
context: The DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS -- both traders must simultaneously desire what the other offers -- is the obstacle barter cannot solve, and why every historical trading society has evolved SOME most-saleable good as an indirect medium. Menger's 1892 essay is the classic account of how that emergence happens. Source: moneyness.ca/2012/01/menger-and-origins-of-money.html.

question: Menger's main idea in 1892 was that some goods are easier to trade on than others. A cow trades more easily than a clay pot. Silver trades more easily than a cow. A small silver coin trades more easily than a silver bar. What English word did Menger use for this trait?
answer: saleability
choices: saleability
durability
convertibility
solvency
context: SALEABILITY (also spelled 'salability' in American English) is Menger's translation of Absatzfaehigkeit -- how easily a good can be traded away again for what the holder actually wants, at little loss of price. It is the master concept of the whole essay. Source: moneyness.ca/2012/01/menger-and-origins-of-money.html.

question: In Menger's 1892 story, nobody in the ancient world sat down and planned money. No committee met. No one wrote a plan. Yet money still showed up, from many traders each solving a local need. Hayek later named this pattern for things nobody designed but everyone uses. His three examples were money, language, and common law. What did Hayek call the pattern?
answer: spontaneous order
choices: spontaneous order
central planning
public choice
moral hazard
context: SPONTANEOUS ORDER -- Hayek's name for Menger's pattern -- captures institutions that emerge from countless individual choices without a designer. Money, language, and the common law are the three classic Austrian examples; markets themselves are a fourth. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11138-022-00600-0.

question: Menger's 1892 essay lists six traits that make a good the best fit for money. Five are: durability, portability, divisibility, sameness, and easy recognition. Gold beat copper as money because gold has more of the sixth trait. Bitcoin fans say Bitcoin has more of that trait than any physical good could. Which sixth trait is it?
answer: scarcity
choices: scarcity
beauty
warmth
colour
context: SCARCITY -- a low and predictable supply that cannot be casually expanded -- is what keeps a monetary good's purchasing power stable over time. Copper is too abundant; gold has held ~1.5%/year new-supply growth for centuries; Bitcoin's hard 21-million cap makes it (per Saifedean Ammous's Bitcoin Standard) the modern digital reinvention. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2512.07840.

question: In 1905 a German economist named Georg Friedrich Knapp wrote a book called 'The State Theory of Money.' Its famous line was 'money is a creature of law.' The book is now the founding text of a school of monetary thought. Modern Monetary Theory grew out of it. What school did Knapp start?
answer: chartalism
choices: chartalism
monetarism
bullionism
mercantilism
context: CHARTALISM (from Latin charta = token) is the doctrine that money's value comes from state issuance and tax-acceptance, not from spontaneous market emergence. Knapp founded it in 1905; today's MMT (Kelton, Wray, Mosler) is its direct descendant. Monetarism is Friedman's quantity-theory tradition; bullionism and mercantilism are early-modern doctrines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Friedrich_Knapp.

question: Ludwig von Mises built on Menger's 1892 essay in his 1912 book 'The Theory of Money and Credit.' His key move: today's buying power of a money traces back, step by step, to yesterday's buying power. You can trace it all the way back to the day before the good was money at all. On that day it had value only as a normal good. What is the name of this Mises theorem?
answer: the regression theorem
choices: the regression theorem
the impossibility theorem
the equivalence theorem
the invariance theorem
context: Mises's REGRESSION THEOREM (1912) chains money's exchange value back in time to a first day of non-monetary commodity value -- solving the circularity of 'money is valuable because it buys things and it buys things because it is valuable.' Bitcoiners argue Bitcoin's initial commodity-value was its cypherpunk demand for a censorship-resistant messaging token, which the theorem then permits. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: The Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous wrote The Bitcoin Standard in 2018. He says Bitcoin is a digital version of Menger's process. Ammous ranks money along three kinds of saleability. Two are across space (how far you can move it) and across scale (how small a unit works). What is the third kind, tied to a good's supply discipline?
answer: saleability across time
choices: saleability across time
saleability across cultures
saleability across sectors
saleability across professions
context: SALEABILITY ACROSS TIME captures whether a good stores value into the future -- and it requires supply discipline: the good's stockpile cannot be casually inflated. Bitcoin's 21-million cap and predictable halving schedule are the engineering answer. Source: jamesbachini.com/the-bitcoin-standard-summary/.

question: The Austrian economist Carl Menger published a short 1892 English essay called 'On the Origin of Money.' It was a condensed version of a longer German article he had written for the Handwörterbuch der Staatswissenschaften, a large German scholarly reference set that covered every topic in political and administrative science. What subject heading did his German entry use?
answer: Geld
choices: Geld
Kapital
Preis
Zins
context: Menger's article was the 'Geld' (Money) entry in the Handwoerterbuch der Staatswissenschaften. The 1892 Economic Journal essay condensed and translated it for the new English-language audience of British and American economists. Kapital, Preis, and Zins (capital, price, interest) were separate entries by other authors. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11138-022-00600-0.

question: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, in charge of setting interest rates. In 2011 it tried something unusual, nicknamed Operation Twist. It sold huge amounts of short-term government IOUs and bought long-term ones, pushing long-term rates down. That was a special move. What is the Fed's main everyday tool for changing interest rates?
answer: Trading government bonds to move interest rates
choices: Trading government bonds to move interest rates
Sending checks to every family
Passing laws about hiring
Building new banks
context: The 2011 program borrowed its name from a Kennedy-era Treasury-Fed program of 1961 that had first tried the yield-curve-flattening technique. Source: Grokipedia 'Operation Twist' (2026-09-05).

question: 'QE' stands for 'quantitative easing.' It is a fancy name for what a central bank actually does: create brand-new money out of thin air, then use it to buy government IOUs. In 2012 the US Federal Reserve started its third round of QE. What is the big worry many people have about it?
answer: Printing lots of new money makes prices go up
choices: Printing lots of new money makes prices go up
It slows the internet down
It makes it illegal to save money
It automatically pays off the national debt
context: QE3 initially committed the Fed to $40 billion per month in mortgage-backed-security purchases with no announced cap. Its open-ended structure was the key novelty. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: By late 2012 the Federal Reserve, led by chairman Ben Bernanke, was already buying $40 billion of mortgage-backed securities every month to hold down interest rates — the third round of what people called quantitative easing, or QE3. On December 12, 2012 the Fed added another $45 billion a month in longer-term Treasury bonds on top. What was the new combined monthly pace of Fed bond buying?
answer: $85 billion per month
choices: $85 billion per month
$40 billion per month
$120 billion per month
$25 billion per month
context: The December 2012 expansion added Treasuries to the mortgage-backed-security purchases already underway, hitting a $85B/month combined pace. The open-ended commitment meant the balance sheet grew steadily every month for two years. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: After the 2008 financial crash, the US Federal Reserve — the country's central bank — created large amounts of new money to buy government bonds. This plan was called quantitative easing, or QE. By 2014 the Fed decided the emergency was over. Rather than stop all at once, it slowly wound the bond-buying down month by month. What word does the Fed use for that slow ending of the money creation?
answer: Tapering
choices: Tapering
Deflating
Rebasing
Unpegging
context: Yellen took the chair on February 3 2014, becoming the first woman to lead the Federal Reserve. She served through February 2018. Source: Grokipedia 'Janet Yellen' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2012 the US Federal Reserve — America's central bank — announced an open-ended round of Quantitative Easing (QE), buying long-term bonds with newly created money for as long as it took to hit its goals. Unlike earlier rounds, this one had no end date. Market strategist Peter Schiff nicknamed it 'QE Infinity.' What worry does that nickname point at?
answer: Money printing might never stop, meaning the currency is being debased forever
choices: Money printing might never stop, meaning the currency is being debased forever
The Fed will pay off every American's mortgage
Interest rates will rise to 20 percent by next month
Every bank in the country will close within a week
context: Boockvar, then chief investment officer at Bleakley Advisory Group, coined 'QE Infinity' to capture the program's open-ended nature. The label stuck across financial media. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed's balance sheet had been about $900 billion before the 2008 crisis. By late 2014, after QE1 through QE3 and Operation Twist, what did it peak at?
answer: About $4.5 trillion
choices: About $4.5 trillion
About $2 trillion
About $8 trillion
About $1.2 trillion
context: The Fed's balance sheet peaked at roughly $4.5 trillion by late 2014 -- a five-fold expansion in six years. This baseline was then dwarfed by the March 2020 emergency response. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2014).

question: During the 2010s the US central bank created huge amounts of new money, but everyday store prices barely moved. Critics said this was because the new money was sitting in bank vaults instead of being spent. What is the economic word for how fast money changes hands?
answer: Velocity
choices: Velocity
Gravity
Elasticity
Density
context: Austrian analysts (Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, Jim Grant) argued the enormous base-money expansion was held in check only by depressed velocity and international dollar demand. When velocity recovered, prices would adjust. Velocity finally recovered in 2020-21. Source: Grokipedia 'Velocity of money' (2026-09-05).

question: After the 2008 financial crisis, the US Federal Reserve created trillions of new dollars through Quantitative Easing. For over a decade, everyday store prices stayed calm — but stock prices and house prices climbed fast, making asset owners much richer. Then in 2021-2023 store prices jumped too, hitting 40-year highs. What pattern does this illustrate?
answer: Cheap new money hits investment prices first and store prices later
choices: Cheap new money hits investment prices first and store prices later
Cheap new money has no effect on any prices, ever
Cheap new money causes hyperinflation within the first month
Cheap new money only makes exported goods more expensive
context: The Cantillon-effect pattern the Austrians identified fits the 2009-2023 sequence: asset prices rose first (stocks, real estate, bonds), consumer prices followed with a long lag when velocity recovered. The lag is not evidence against the mechanism; it is a feature of it. Source: Cantillon, Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en Général (1755).

question: In 2013 the US Federal Reserve — the country's central bank — was buying $85 billion of government and mortgage bonds every single month with newly created money. That is more each year than many small countries' entire economies. The Fed said this was a technical policy to steer growth. Why is a program that big fairly called political, not just technical?
answer: A program that big picks winners and losers across the economy — that is political, not technical
choices: A program that big picks winners and losers across the economy — that is political, not technical
Buying that many bonds has no effect on wealth distribution
Fed actions are always neutral because they target interest rates
Central bank programs of any size are always short-lived
context: When central-bank monthly purchases exceed the annual GDP of Bulgaria or Bolivia, the choice of which assets to buy is inescapably political. Austrian analysts press this against the Fed's self-image as a technical body making neutral adjustments. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: In 1961 President John F. Kennedy's Federal Reserve tried a bond-trading maneuver nicknamed Operation Twist — selling short-term bonds and buying long-term ones to bend the yield curve. Fifty years later, in 2011, Ben Bernanke's Fed borrowed the same name for its own program. What was the actual policy problem the 1961 Kennedy administration was trying to address?
answer: Supporting long-term investment while defending the dollar against gold outflows
choices: Supporting long-term investment while defending the dollar against gold outflows
Financing new Vietnam War operations without borrowing abroad
Reversing the effects of the 1959 steel strike
Preparing for a coming currency swap with Britain
context: The original 1961 program aimed to lower long-term yields (to encourage domestic investment) while raising short-term yields (to keep dollar deposits from moving abroad and forcing gold redemptions). The 2011 borrowing of the label was a rhetorical framing that obscured how different the two contexts were. Source: Grokipedia 'Operation Twist' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1920 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published a big claim. A country where the government owns every factory and farm cannot know how much of each thing to make. Without free market prices to reveal what buyers actually want, the planners are guessing in the dark. What is this idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The paperwork problem
The weather problem
The population problem
context: Oskar Lange, then teaching at Chicago, published 'On the Economic Theory of Socialism' in the Review of Economic Studies, October 1936 and February 1937. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: In 1936 the Polish economist Oskar Lange proposed a new kind of socialism. The state would take over all factories and mines from private owners. But it would keep markets for the consumer goods people bought day to day, and a state planning board would set the prices of tools and factory machines by copying what a real market would have charged. What is Lange's plan called?
answer: Market socialism
choices: Market socialism
State capitalism
Council socialism
Guild socialism
context: Market socialism keeps consumer-goods and labor markets while replacing private capital ownership with state ownership; the state pricing board sets capital-goods prices by trial and error. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_socialism.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had argued in a 1920 essay that without private ownership no one could rationally price steel, tools, and factory machines. In 1936 the Polish economist Oskar Lange conceded that Mises had a real point. But then, under his market-socialism plan, Lange offered a workaround for setting those prices anyway. What method did Lange propose?
answer: Trial and error by the central planning board
choices: Trial and error by the central planning board
Auction pricing on state exchanges
Prices set by worker councils
Fixed prices by moral formula
context: Lange's central planning board would announce prices, observe surpluses or shortages, then adjust up or down like a real market -- imitating market clearing without private ownership of capital. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_socialism.

question: Some modern economists say a government should set its taxes and its spending only by what seems useful for the economy at that moment. Whether the books balance or the deficit grows — that, they say, does not matter. Austrian economists at the Mises Institute and elsewhere warn hard against this rule of thumb. What warning do they give?
answer: A government freed from the balanced-budget rule tends to overspend and cause inflation
choices: A government freed from the balanced-budget rule tends to overspend and cause inflation
A government freed from the budget rule always spends less than it should
Tax collectors will refuse to work if there is no fixed budget target
Foreign countries stop trading with any nation that changes its taxes
context: Abba Lerner's The Economics of Control (1944) formalized rules by which a rational planner could set prices equal to marginal cost and achieve competitive-market allocation on paper. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abba_P._Lerner.

question: In the 1930s the Polish economist Oskar Lange argued that a socialist central planning board could copy market prices well enough to run an economy. The Austrian-British economist Friedrich Hayek pushed back — first in a 1935 book, then in a famous 1945 essay called The Use of Knowledge in Society. His counter-move shifted the whole debate. What was Hayek's key change in framing the problem?
answer: The problem is dispersed knowledge, not just price arithmetic
choices: The problem is dispersed knowledge, not just price arithmetic
The problem is enforcement, not planning
The problem is corruption, not information
The problem is speed of computation only
context: Hayek argued market prices encode dispersed knowledge (local conditions, tastes, changing circumstances) held only by millions of individuals. A trial-and-error board cannot gather that knowledge in time; the market's speed and specificity cannot be replicated by any committee. Source: aeaweb.org (AER September 1945).

question: In 1945 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published a short but famous essay in the American Economic Review journal. It argued that no central planner can gather the millions of small facts scattered across a whole society — only market prices can pull that knowledge together. The essay became the classic Austrian answer to those who said governments could plan an economy from the top down. What is the essay's title?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
The Fatal Conceit
Individualism and Economic Order
context: 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', American Economic Review 35(4), September 1945, is one of the most cited economics papers ever written. It reframed the calculation debate as being about dispersed knowledge rather than arithmetic. Source: aeaweb.org.

question: In the 1930s the Polish economist Oskar Lange tried to save socialist central planning from an Austrian critique by Ludwig von Mises. Lange said a communist government could simply copy the prices seen in real capitalist markets and use those copied numbers to plan every factory and shop. Mises and Hayek said that answer collapses on itself. What is the main problem with Lange's reply?
answer: You cannot copy prices from markets you have abolished
choices: You cannot copy prices from markets you have abolished
The copied prices would end up too accurate
The planners would have to work too many hours
Nothing — the reply solves the problem perfectly
context: Lange served as Poland's first postwar ambassador to the United States (1945-47) and later held Polish State Council positions. He died in 1965. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: For decades many economists thought Oskar Lange had answered Ludwig von Mises on paper in the socialist calculation debate. Then Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' pinpointed what central planners could not do that market prices did automatically. What did Hayek call this obstacle?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The incentive problem
The transaction-cost problem
The externalities problem
context: The 1989 collapse of the Warsaw Pact planned economies (Berlin Wall Nov 9, Ceausescu Dec 25, Velvet Revolution Dec 29) and the USSR's dissolution on December 25, 1991 shifted the calculation debate from theory to historical settlement. Lange had died in 1965. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: In the 1930s the Polish economist Oskar Lange offered a plan for 'market socialism' — planners would set prices as if they were a market. Since Lange, many new socialist plans have come out: David Schweickart's economic democracy, Elinor Ostrom's commons-management research, and forms of 21st-century socialism in Venezuela and elsewhere. Austrian economists like Friedrich Hayek said all these plans share one gap. What do they not answer?
answer: Hayek's knowledge problem
choices: Hayek's knowledge problem
Marx's labor theory of value
Keynes's liquidity trap
Ricardo's rent theory
context: Austrian critics observe that most modern socialist proposals recycle Lange's move (boards can mimic markets) without engaging Hayek's follow-up: markets encode information no board can gather in time. The knowledge problem is the load-bearing critique. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-and-anti-socialism.
