question: In 1935 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek edited a landmark collection of early European critiques of socialist central planning. The volume gathered translated essays by Ludwig von Mises, Enrico Barone, and others, plus Hayek's own opening and closing essays laying out the calculation problem. It became a founding text of the Austrian side of the socialist calculation debate. What was the book's title?
answer: Collectivist Economic Planning
choices: Collectivist Economic Planning
Individualism and Economic Order
The Pure Theory of Capital
The Sensory Order
context: Collectivist Economic Planning (1935), edited by Hayek, collected translations of Mises's 1920 essay and other early Austrian critiques for English-language readers. This is the collection Lange responded to in his 1936-37 papers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: In 1944 two Princeton scholars — the mathematician John von Neumann and the Austrian economist Oskar Morgenstern — wrote a famous book called 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior.' It launched a new branch of math and economics. It looks at how people choose when they know others are trying to outsmart them. What is that branch called?
answer: Game theory
choices: Game theory
Score theory
Random theory
Number theory
context: Oskar Morgenstern (1902-1977) took his Vienna doctorate in 1925 under Mises and Mayer, joined the Privatseminar, and eventually taught at Princeton from 1938. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: The Austrian-born economist Oskar Morgenstern spent his later career at Princeton. In 1944 Princeton University Press published a huge book he wrote with a Hungarian-American math partner. It started the whole field of modern game theory — the study of how strategic choices interact. What was its full title?
answer: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
choices: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Foundations of Economic Analysis
Value and Capital
context: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (Princeton, 1944) is the founding text of game theory and became the mathematical toolkit for economics, political science, and computer science for the next eighty years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Theory_of_Games_and_Economic_Behavior.

question: Oskar Morgenstern's 1944 game theory book was co-written with a brilliant Hungarian-American mathematician working at Princeton. This same man also worked on quantum physics, on the math of the atomic bomb at Los Alamos, and on the early digital computer architecture that most modern computers still use. Who was Morgenstern's co-author?
answer: John von Neumann
choices: John von Neumann
Kurt Godel
Norbert Wiener
Alan Turing
context: John von Neumann and Morgenstern worked on the joint book from 1940 to 1944. Morgenstern brought the economic questions; von Neumann brought the mathematics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Theory_of_Games_and_Economic_Behavior.

question: In 1928 the Austrian economist Oskar Morgenstern — later a co-founder of game theory — wrote a book in Vienna on economic forecasting. He pointed out a strange loop: once you publish a forecast, people change what they do because of it, which breaks the forecast. This puzzle got his own name. What is it called?
answer: Morgenstern's paradox
choices: Morgenstern's paradox
Arrow's paradox
Condorcet's paradox
Simpson's paradox
context: Morgenstern's 1928 Wirtschaftsprognose demolished the whole business of business-cycle forecasting; the reflexivity paradox at its core still carries his name. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: In the 1920s a young Austrian economist named Friedrich Hayek — later a Nobel Prize winner — founded a small institute in Vienna to study why economic booms are always followed by busts. Working with his mentor Ludwig von Mises, Hayek built a theory that blamed one specific culprit for the cycle. What did the Austrians say caused these boom-bust cycles?
answer: Central bank credit expansion that pushes interest rates below their natural level
choices: Central bank credit expansion that pushes interest rates below their natural level
Bad weather in Europe every seven years
A shortage of gold in world markets
Too little government spending during good times
context: Hayek founded the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research in Vienna in 1927; Morgenstern helped and took over as director when Hayek left for LSE in 1931. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Austrian_Institute_for_Business_Cycle_Research.

question: In 1938 the Austrian economist Oskar Morgenstern, a rising figure who would later co-write the founding book of game theory with John von Neumann, was away in the United States on a lecture tour. That year a huge political event handed control of Austria to a new regime in Berlin, and they promptly fired Morgenstern from his Vienna university post as politically unreliable. What was the 1938 event?
answer: The Anschluss with Nazi Germany
choices: The Anschluss with Nazi Germany
The Kristallnacht pogrom
The Munich Agreement
The Ribbentrop-Molotov Pact
context: The March 1938 Anschluss brought Austria into Nazi Germany; Morgenstern was dismissed and accepted the Princeton chair he already had an invitation for. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: Oskar Morgenstern — the same Austrian economist who co-founded game theory with John von Neumann — spent decades warning that the official economic statistics governments use to steer policy, numbers like GDP and unemployment, were riddled with far bigger measurement errors than policymakers ever admitted. In 1950 Princeton University Press published his book making this case in careful detail. What was its title?
answer: On the Accuracy of Economic Observations
choices: On the Accuracy of Economic Observations
The Nature of Statistics
Business Cycle Indicators
Measuring Business Cycles
context: On the Accuracy of Economic Observations (Princeton, 1950; 2nd ed. 1963) is often cited as an early warning against over-precision in macro policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: Oskar Morgenstern was trained in the Vienna tradition of Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, and Friedrich Hayek before moving to Princeton and co-founding game theory with John von Neumann. But Morgenstern always insisted game theory was really a formal, mathematical version of an older Austrian idea about how human beings act. Which Austrian idea did he say game theory captured?
answer: Economic outcomes emerge from the interaction of purposive choosers anticipating others' choices
choices: Economic outcomes emerge from the interaction of purposive choosers anticipating others' choices
Value is an objective property fixed by labor content
Markets always converge to full-employment equilibrium
Only central planners can compute optimal outcomes
context: The Austrian move -- purposive individual choosers acting under uncertainty and anticipating each other -- is exactly what game theory formalized. Morgenstern saw his Princeton work as the math Menger and Boehm-Bawerk never wrote for themselves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Theory_of_Games_and_Economic_Behavior.

question: By 1979 prices in the US were going up nearly 13 percent a year. A gallon of milk cost more every few months, and workers' savings were losing value fast. President Jimmy Carter picked a tall, cigar-smoking banker named Paul Volcker to run the Federal Reserve. Volcker had one bold plan to stop the inflation. What did his plan do?
answer: Push interest rates way up so people borrowed and spent less
choices: Push interest rates way up so people borrowed and spent less
Print lots more money to give to families
Ban stores from raising any prices
Give away free gasoline coupons
context: Volcker took the Fed chair in August 1979. He was tall (6 feet 7 inches), smoked cigars, and became personally identified with the inflation fight for the rest of his career. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: In October 1979 the new Federal Reserve chair Paul Volcker made a surprise move on a Saturday evening. Journalists dubbed it the Saturday Night Special. The Fed announced it would target bank reserve growth and let interest rates rise as high as necessary to break inflation. On what date did Volcker announce it?
answer: October 6 1979
choices: October 6 1979
August 15 1971
March 15 1980
November 22 1979
context: The October 6 1979 Saturday-night announcement was a monetarist experiment influenced by Milton Friedman's arguments. The Fed committed to controlling the money supply and letting rates settle wherever necessary. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1979 Paul Volcker took over as chair of the US Federal Reserve. American inflation was running near 13 percent, and Volcker decided the only cure was to crank interest rates so high that the whole economy would slow to a crawl. He knew this would throw millions of people out of work and trigger a painful downturn. What was Volcker willing to accept as the cost of killing inflation?
answer: Mass unemployment through a severe recession
choices: Mass unemployment through a severe recession
A gradual six-year adjustment with no unemployment
A currency devaluation against gold to reset expectations
A permanent freeze on wages and prices
context: Volcker's view: inflation could not be broken without accepting recession. Half-measures would simply prolong the pain. This was the opposite of Arthur Burns's political accommodation and the essential ingredient of the eventual victory. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve pushed interest rates near twenty percent in 1981 to break American inflation. The medicine worked but was brutal — factories shut, farms failed, and unemployment climbed steadily through 1982. In November 1982 the US jobless rate hit its peak. What was that peak unemployment rate?
answer: 10.8 percent
choices: 10.8 percent
6.5 percent
14.2 percent
8.0 percent
context: US unemployment peaked at 10.8% in November 1982 -- the highest rate since the Great Depression. Farmers protested outside the Fed; homebuilders mailed Volcker two-by-fours from unbuilt houses. Source: Grokipedia 'Early 1980s recession' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1980 US inflation hit 13.5 percent — the highest in decades. A tall, cigar-smoking new Fed chair, hand-picked by President Jimmy Carter, raised interest rates so high that the prime rate briefly touched 21.5 percent. That triggered a sharp recession, but inflation crashed to about 3 percent by 1983. Who was that Fed chair?
answer: Paul Volcker
choices: Paul Volcker
Alan Greenspan
Ben Bernanke
Arthur Burns
context: US CPI inflation fell from 13.5% in 1980 to 3.2% by 1983 -- a stunning victory. Volcker had destroyed the inflation expectations that had built up over 15 years and restored the Fed's credibility. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Inflation' (2026-09-05).

question: In the late 1970s the United States was suffering runaway price hikes -- gas, groceries, and rent all rising fast year after year. In 1979 Paul Volcker, the new chairman of the Federal Reserve, hiked interest rates high enough to break that inflation. From the mid-1980s until about 2007, American prices then stayed unusually calm and stable for roughly two decades. Economists gave that quiet stretch a memorable label. What is it called?
answer: The Great Moderation
choices: The Great Moderation
The Long Boom
The New Economy
The Silent Era
context: The Great Moderation (roughly 1985-2007) was the era of low inflation and low output volatility that followed Volcker's disinflation. It ended with the 2008 crisis, which some analysts trace to the excessive risk-taking the Great Moderation encouraged. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Moderation' (2026-09-05).

question: In the early 1980s a US central bank chief pushed interest rates very high to kill inflation. The medicine caused a bad recession right before an election. The sitting president refused to attack the bank in public. What economic principle does that silence support?
answer: The central bank should be free of daily political pressure
choices: The central bank should be free of daily political pressure
The central bank should always match the president's mood
Inflation is only a problem in election years
Recessions are caused only by presidential speeches
context: Reagan, though a Republican who had campaigned on ending stagflation, gave Volcker the political space to see the tightening through. Reagan reappointed Volcker in 1983 despite the recession's political cost. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: After the 2008 financial crash, the US Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010. One provision, named for former Fed chairman Paul Volcker, forbids big commercial banks from making large speculative bets with their own money while they also hold ordinary Americans' checking and savings deposits, which the government insures through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). Why does splitting those two activities matter for a bank that takes normal savings?
answer: If the bank loses its own bet, taxpayer insurance ends up covering depositors' losses
choices: If the bank loses its own bet, taxpayer insurance ends up covering depositors' losses
Bank employees would work fewer hours without the rule
Depositors would earn much higher interest without the rule
Every bank would go bankrupt without the rule
context: The Volcker Rule, adopted as part of Dodd-Frank in 2010, restricts commercial banks from engaging in proprietary trading. Volcker chaired the President's Economic Recovery Advisory Board under Obama, giving the rule its name. Source: Grokipedia 'Volcker Rule' (2026-09-05).

question: When Paul Volcker took over the Federal Reserve in 1979, US inflation ran above thirteen percent. To break it he drove interest rates near twenty percent and triggered the worst recession since the Great Depression. President Ronald Reagan, though he inherited the pain, defended Volcker publicly and refused to fire him. The whole story teaches one big lesson about what it politically takes to beat serious inflation. What move does the story point to?
answer: Breaking a serious inflation requires a Fed chair willing to accept severe recession plus a president willing to provide political cover for the recession's cost
choices: Breaking a serious inflation requires a Fed chair willing to accept severe recession plus a president willing to provide political cover for the recession's cost
Inflation can always be broken through communication and expectations management alone
The Fed can break inflation without any political cost
Presidential support is irrelevant to whether the Fed can succeed against inflation
context: Volcker's success depended on both his own willingness to see the recession through and Reagan's willingness not to attack the Fed publicly. Either failure alone would have collapsed the effort. The two-part condition is the essential lesson. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian school of economics grew out of Vienna in the late 1800s, with thinkers like Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises, and Friedrich Hayek. They defend free markets, sound money, small government, and prices set by real trades. They push back on one popular idea more sharply than any other. Which idea do Austrian economists most reject?
answer: That a small group of experts can plan a whole economy well
choices: That a small group of experts can plan a whole economy well
That people should be free to trade with each other
That saving money is a good habit
That prices are useful information
context: GMU housed both James Buchanan (Nobel 1986, public choice) and Vernon Smith (Nobel 2002, experimental economics), plus a wide bench of Austrian and public-choice-adjacent scholars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/George_Mason_University.

question: F. A. Hayek was a famous economist who won the Nobel Prize in 1974. His big idea: market PRICES are a giant signaling system, telling everyone what is scarce and what is plentiful -- information no central planner could ever gather in one place. What did Hayek call this idea?
answer: Prices are signals that carry information
choices: Prices are signals that carry information
Prices are just random numbers
Prices should be set by the government
Prices only matter for rich people
context: Peter J. Boettke is University Professor of Economics and Philosophy at GMU, and the central figure of the modern academic-Austrian scene. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: Peter Boettke edits the Review of Austrian Economics at George Mason University, continuing the Mises-Hayek tradition against central planning. What does the Austrian school call human action guided by chosen ends and means -- the starting point of all economic reasoning?
answer: Praxeology
choices: Praxeology
Behaviorism
Utilitarianism
Positivism
context: Boettke has been editor of the Review of Austrian Economics since 1998, a position from which he has shaped a generation of academic Austrian scholarship. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: In 2012 the American economist Peter Boettke, a leading voice at George Mason University, published a book defending the older tradition of Austrian and market-process economics. He argued that the profession had drifted into math-only models that miss how real markets actually coordinate people. The book laid out what he thinks economics should be. What is the book called?
answer: Living Economics: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow
choices: Living Economics: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow
Human Action
Man, Economy, and State
The Road to Serfdom
context: Living Economics (Independent Institute, 2012) is Boettke's programmatic statement: economics is the systematic study of how people coordinate plans through exchange. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: The economist Peter Leeson studied pirate ships from the late 1600s and early 1700s. He found that without any king, judge, or navy to force them, pirate crews wrote elaborate written codes of their own: how loot would be divided share by share, how a captain would be elected and could be voted out mid-voyage, and even set payments for a lost arm or a lost eye in battle. What origin of rules and order do the pirate codes reveal, given no boss was forcing them?
answer: Rules and order can grow up from the bottom without a boss forcing them
choices: Rules and order can grow up from the bottom without a boss forcing them
People always need a king to tell them how to behave
Money always corrupts the people who trade with it
Rules only matter if a government writes them down
context: Peter Leeson's The Invisible Hook: The Hidden Economics of Pirates (Princeton, 2009) is the paradigm case of GMU-Austrian analysis applied to a topic no one thought was economics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Invisible_Hook.

question: The economist William Easterly has studied two kinds of outside intervention: a foreign army trying to install a new government in another country -- as the US attempted in Iraq and Afghanistan -- and giant aid organizations flying food and medicine into disaster zones. Across both kinds of study, one finding keeps showing up. What is that common finding?
answer: Outsiders often lack the local knowledge needed to know what will actually work
choices: Outsiders often lack the local knowledge needed to know what will actually work
Outside help almost always fixes the underlying problem quickly
Local people rarely have any ideas of their own about what would help
Sending more money is always the missing piece
context: Coyne's books include After War: The Political Economy of Exporting Democracy (Stanford, 2007) and Doing Bad by Doing Good (Stanford, 2013). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Christopher_Coyne.

question: In 1990 the American economist Peter Boettke published his first book, an Austrian-school study of one country's very first years of communist central planning: from 1918 through 1928. Boettke argued that the calculation and coordination problems Mises and Hayek had warned about were visible right from the start of that experiment. Which country was Boettke's book about?
answer: The early Soviet Union
choices: The early Soviet Union
Germany after its 1923 inflation
China during the 1960s
Argentina in the 1990s
context: Boettke, The Political Economy of Soviet Socialism: The Formative Years, 1918-1928 (Kluwer, 1990) is his doctoral book, an Austrian reading of early Bolshevik economic policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: One famous economist argued that no small group of planners can ever gather all the local know-how scattered across millions of workers, shoppers, and business owners. He said this scattered know-how is what makes a market work. What is his insight called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The equality problem
The greed problem
The paperwork problem
context: The F. A. Hayek Program for Advanced Study in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics is the principal graduate training site for young Austrian scholars in America. Source: mercatus.org/hayek-program.

question: In 2010 Peter Boettke, an Austrian economist at George Mason University, edited a big reference volume for the publisher Edward Elgar. It became the standard modern one-volume introduction to the Austrian school — a book professors hand new students who want to learn the whole living tradition in one place. What is its title?
answer: Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics
choices: Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics
The Cambridge Companion to Keynes
The Palgrave Dictionary of Economics
Handbook of Monetary Economics
context: Boettke's edited Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics (Edward Elgar, 2010) collects the leading modern voices of the tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: George Mason University in Virginia runs an unusual economics department. Instead of the mainstream Keynesian and neoclassical mix, it hosts BOTH major heterodox schools that have won Nobel Prizes: one built by James Buchanan on how governments really make decisions, and one built by Vernon Smith on running economics like a laboratory experiment. Which two schools does George Mason house together?
answer: Public choice and experimental
choices: Public choice and experimental
New Keynesian and monetarist
MMT and post-Keynesian
Neoclassical macro and behavioral finance
context: James Buchanan's public-choice Nobel (1986) and Vernon Smith's experimental-economics Nobel (2002) both grew at GMU, alongside its Austrian tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/George_Mason_University.

question: Some people who love GOLD as money don't trust Bitcoin. Their main complaint: gold has been used as money for thousands of years -- you can hold it, weigh it, make jewelry from it -- while Bitcoin is just numbers on the internet. What do gold fans say Bitcoin lacks that gold has?
answer: A physical thing you can hold in your hand
choices: A physical thing you can hold in your hand
A shiny yellow color
A ticker symbol on the news
A place to store it online
context: Peter Schiff runs Euro Pacific Capital and has been a public gold-bull since the early 2000s. Michael Saylor is Bitcoin's most prominent corporate advocate; Cramer runs Mad Money on CNBC; Buffett is a Bitcoin skeptic but not from the sound-money-Austrian tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: Say an American refuses to pay federal income tax. They tell the judge the tax law is unfair or against the Constitution. What usually happens next?
answer: They lose in court and can be sent to federal prison
choices: They lose in court and can be sent to federal prison
The judge cancels the tax law immediately
Nothing happens -- federal tax is optional
The government pays them extra money for asking
context: Irwin Schiff (1928-2015) was an Austrian-economics writer whose tax-protester positions led to his imprisonment; he died in federal custody in 2015. Ron Paul, Murray Rothbard, and Lew Rockwell are separate Austrian figures unrelated by family to Peter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: In 2006 and 2007, a few economists went on television and warned that American housing prices had risen far above what people could really pay, and the whole thing would crash. Other guests laughed at them on air. Which crash did those warnings turn out to correctly predict?
answer: the 2008 US housing crash
choices: the 2008 US housing crash
the 2000 dot-com crash
the 1987 Black Monday crash
the 2020 pandemic crash
context: Schiff warned about the coming US housing crash repeatedly on 2006-07 CNBC panels; the videos went viral after the crash arrived in 2007-08. His book 'Crash Proof' (2007) laid out the argument in detail. The other crashes predate or postdate the specific prediction videos. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: In 2007 the American investor Peter Schiff published a book called Crash Proof. He warned that US house prices had been pumped up by Alan Greenspan's very low Federal Reserve interest rates, and that the bubble would end in a hard crash. A year later the 2008 financial crisis proved him right. Which older Austrian idea did Schiff's warning use?
answer: Cheap credit fuels booms that must end in busts
choices: Cheap credit fuels booms that must end in busts
Higher interest rates always mean lower house prices right away
Big banks control the whole housing market at all times
House prices only go down when the president says so
context: Peter Schiff, 'Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse' (2007). Michael Lewis wrote 'The Big Short' (2010) about the same crash from a different angle; Nassim Taleb wrote 'The Black Swan' (2007) and 'Fooled by Randomness' (2001) on general market unpredictability. Source: https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Crash+Proof-p-9780470043608.

question: Peter Schiff is an American investor and gold dealer who has been Bitcoin's steadiest critic in the sound-money world since 2013. He agrees with Bitcoiners that government fiat paper is unsound, but he says gold is real money in a way Bitcoin never can be. His main argument points to one thing gold has that Bitcoin lacks. Which thing does Schiff say Bitcoin is missing?
answer: intrinsic non-monetary value: gold has jewelry and industrial uses, Bitcoin has none of that
choices: intrinsic non-monetary value: gold has jewelry and industrial uses, Bitcoin has none of that
cryptographic security against tampering, forgery, or double-spending in the underlying ledger
portability across international borders without triggering physical searches or seizure risk
recognizability by international courts as a legally protected form of property in every jurisdiction
context: Schiff's central claim is that gold has intrinsic value (jewelry, industrial uses, 5,000 years of recognition) while Bitcoin has none, so Bitcoin is a pure speculative bubble. He does not dispute Bitcoin's cryptographic security, portability, or courtroom recognition -- he argues those are insufficient without intrinsic value. Source: https://www.schiffgold.com/; various Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: The gold-versus-Bitcoin debate has one famous matchup that keeps repeating on podcasts and TV since 2020. On one side is Peter Schiff, the gold-dealing investor who calls Bitcoin worthless. On the other side is the chairman of the software company that bought more Bitcoin than any other public firm on Earth. Who is Schiff's usual opponent in this debate?
answer: Michael Saylor of MicroStrategy
choices: Michael Saylor of MicroStrategy
Brian Armstrong of Coinbase
Changpeng Zhao of Binance
Vitalik Buterin of the Ethereum Foundation
context: Michael Saylor of MicroStrategy (renamed Strategy) is Schiff's usual debate opponent since 2020, when Saylor began the corporate treasury Bitcoin accumulation. Armstrong runs an exchange; CZ runs another exchange; Buterin runs Ethereum, not a Bitcoin-focused position. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Saylor.

question: The Bitcoin advocate Michael Saylor and the gold advocate Peter Schiff have spent years debating which is better money — gold or Bitcoin. Saylor grants that Bitcoin is new and untested by history. But he denies that having a built-in physical use (like gold's jewelry and wiring uses) is what decides whether something becomes money. What is Saylor's main move against Schiff?
answer: that monetary value comes from properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability and verifiability, and Bitcoin dominates gold on each of those measures except historical duration
choices: that monetary value comes from properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability and verifiability, and Bitcoin dominates gold on each of those measures except historical duration
that intrinsic value is entirely irrelevant to all economic reasoning about money, so gold's jewelry and industrial uses have never mattered to its role as a store of wealth
that gold has no non-monetary uses of significance and never has, so the whole gold-vs-Bitcoin debate is really about which useless object is scarcer
that only government-issued money can serve as a durable store of value, so both gold and Bitcoin will eventually be replaced by state currency systems
context: Saylor's argument: monetary properties (scarcity, divisibility, portability, verifiability, durability) determine what becomes money, not jewelry uses; on those measures Bitcoin dominates gold, with duration the one property gold currently leads on. He does not deny gold's non-monetary uses or dismiss intrinsic-value theory categorically. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts 2021-24.

question: Michael Saylor, the chairman of MicroStrategy who put his company's treasury into Bitcoin, often debates gold advocates like Peter Schiff. One of his most-repeated lines compares carrying wealth across an international border. He says a Bitcoiner can move a fortune with a memorized 12-word phrase in his head, while a person with the same value in gold cannot. What does Saylor claim gold cannot do that Bitcoin can?
answer: be transmitted over the internet
choices: be transmitted over the internet
be measured with a scale
be minted into standard units
be recognized by banks
context: Saylor's line: gold cannot be sent over the internet; Bitcoin can. This is the network-transmission property he uses to argue Bitcoin dominates gold on portability. Weighing, minting, and banking are not what the specific rhetorical move disputes. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: As of 2026 the Schiff-Saylor debate is still not settled, though both gold and Bitcoin have gone up a lot since 2020. Which specific reason does a Bitcoin teacher most often give for why the whole talk has been worth having, no matter who ends up right?
answer: That both men articulate their arguments honestly, in public, in a financial-media environment where that is unusually rare
choices: That both men articulate their arguments honestly, in public, in a financial-media environment where that is unusually rare
That the debate has convinced most governments to accept Bitcoin as legal tender
That the debate has been settled definitively by peer-reviewed economics papers
That the debate has ended with a formal apology from Schiff
context: The bank's stance (honest-debate rung): the value of the Schiff-Saylor exchange is that both men state and defend their positions publicly rather than through carefully-cropped soundbites. No government adoption cascade, definitive academic resolution, or Schiff apology has occurred. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: Peter Schiff is a well-known Austrian-school investor and a longtime Bitcoin skeptic. Michael Saylor is the CEO of MicroStrategy and one of Bitcoin's most public advocates. Their public debates keep circling one Austrian argument that Schiff hammers on -- and even Saylor treats it as a serious point, though the two men disagree on how it applies to Bitcoin. Which argument does Schiff press that Saylor takes seriously?
answer: the Mises regression theorem: a money must be traceable to a prior non-monetary demand
choices: the Mises regression theorem: a money must be traceable to a prior non-monetary demand
the Keynesian aggregate-demand model: the general price level tracks total spending
the Chicago-school efficient-markets hypothesis: prices always reflect all known info
the MMT sovereign-currency thesis: a state issuer can never involuntarily default
context: Schiff's substantive move is the Mises Regression Theorem. Saylor treats it seriously and answers with an account of Bitcoin's early cypherpunk-collectible use (following Ammous). The Keynesian, Chicago-school, and MMT frames are not Schiff's ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem; Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: In the early 1990s the US government considered banning strong ways to scramble messages. In 1991 an American programmer named Phil Zimmermann built a free tool that let anyone scramble an email so that only the intended recipient, using a matching secret, could read the message. What is that kind of scrambling called?
answer: Encryption
choices: Encryption
Deletion
Advertising
Downloading
context: Phil Zimmermann wrote PGP in 1991. Gates and Wozniak were building operating systems and personal computers; Torvalds released the Linux kernel that same year but did not write PGP. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: In 1991 an American programmer named Phil Zimmermann built a free tool that let ordinary people scramble their email so that only the recipient could read it. He gave his invention a plain, humble three-word name: an adjective meaning 'fair-to-good' plus a two-word phrase meaning 'the ability to keep things to yourself.' What are those three words?
answer: Pretty Good Privacy
choices: Pretty Good Privacy
Public General Password
Private Global Post
Perfect Guard Program
context: PGP stands for Pretty Good Privacy -- Zimmermann's deliberately modest name for a program that gave ordinary users email cryptography previously available only to governments. The other expansions are fabrications. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy.

question: In 1991 the American programmer Phil Zimmermann finished a free tool called Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) that let anyone scramble an email so strongly that even spy agencies could not read it. The US government wanted the code blocked from leaving the country. What did Zimmermann do to make sure no single government could stop the code from spreading worldwide?
answer: He uploaded it to the internet, where copies spread worldwide in weeks
choices: He uploaded it to the internet, where copies spread worldwide in weeks
He sold the rights to the US Department of Defense
He patented it and licensed only US citizens
He handed it out only on floppy disks inside the US
context: Zimmermann uploaded PGP to the internet in 1991; within weeks it was on servers in every country including US-embargoed states. Selling to DoD, patenting for US-only licensing, or floppy-only distribution are the opposite of what he did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: In 1991 the American programmer Phil Zimmermann released PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), free strong-encryption software for ordinary people. Copies quickly spread outside the United States. In 1993 the US government opened a criminal investigation of Zimmermann for exporting a weapon, using a law that treated strong encryption code as a military munition. Which law did federal prosecutors use?
answer: the Arms Export Control Act
choices: the Arms Export Control Act
the Espionage Act
the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
the Patriot Act
context: The 1993 US investigation treated strong cryptography as a munition under the Arms Export Control Act; PGP appeared on the US Munitions List alongside tanks and missiles. Espionage Act (1917) covers classified information; CFAA (1986) covers computer intrusion; Patriot Act (2001) postdates the investigation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: In the 1990s the US government classified strong email-scrambling software -- like Phil Zimmermann's free Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) tool -- as a 'munition' under the Arms Export Control Act. That meant emailing the code to a friend in another country was, by US law, the same act as sending what?
answer: A rifle or a missile
choices: A rifle or a missile
A tax form
A patent application
A public library book
context: Strong cryptography above certain key lengths appeared on the US Munitions List (USML) governed by the Arms Export Control Act. The Entity List (Commerce Department), SDN (Treasury), and OFAC country sanctions are different and specifically about persons, entities, and territories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_of_cryptography_from_the_United_States.

question: In the early 1990s the US treated Phil Zimmermann's free Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) encryption code as an export-controlled weapon: the source code could not legally be sent abroad by computer. Zimmermann's response was a piece of legal-technical theater. In 1995 MIT Press published a specific object that could not be regulated as a weapon under US law. What did MIT Press publish?
answer: a book containing PGP's entire source code, printed on paper
choices: a book containing PGP's entire source code, printed on paper
a documentary film about Zimmermann's fight
an unclassified summary of the Arms Export Control Act
a public directory of PGP users worldwide
context: MIT Press published PGP's entire source code as a printed book in 1995 -- because books, as speech, are protected by the First Amendment. A foreign purchaser could scan or OCR the pages to recover the software. The other options were not the specific counter-move. Source: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262240390/pgp-source-code-and-internals/.

question: In 1995 a group published the full source code of a strong encryption program as a printed book. Their argument was that even if the government blocked digital export, printing the same code as text should be protected. Which constitutional protection did they invoke?
answer: Freedom of speech applied to code as writing
choices: Freedom of speech applied to code as writing
The right to bear arms, applied to code as a weapon
Protection against search, applied to encrypted files
Protection against self-incrimination, applied to passwords
context: The book strategy tested whether printed source code was First-Amendment-protected speech even when the same code as an electronic download was a Munitions List item. The stunt was central to the later Bernstein v US and Junger v Daley cases that ultimately held source code as speech. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_v._United_States.

question: In the early 1990s the US Customs Service opened a criminal investigation into an American programmer named Phil Zimmermann. He had given away a free email-encryption tool called Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), and copies had spread onto foreign computers -- which the US treated the same as exporting a weapon. After nearly three years of investigation, what did the US government finally do?
answer: Dropped the case without ever filing charges
choices: Dropped the case without ever filing charges
Put him in prison for ten years
Fined him one billion dollars
Forced him to delete every copy of the software
context: DOJ dropped the investigation in January 1996 without charges. The 1993 date is when the investigation opened; the US relaxed cryptography export controls in 1999; and 2001 is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: In the 1990s US law treated strong encryption software the same as a weapon — illegal to export. A programmer printed his code as a book and sold it overseas. A court agreed that computer code is protected speech. Which US constitutional right did that ruling rest on?
answer: The First Amendment right to free speech
choices: The First Amendment right to free speech
The Second Amendment right to bear arms
The Fourth Amendment protection against searches
The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination
context: The PGP episode helped establish that source code is speech (later confirmed by Bernstein v US, Junger v Daley). Without that precedent, Satoshi's 2008 open publication of Bitcoin source code would have faced a version of the same 1993 investigation. The other options are the opposite of what the fight settled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_v._United_States.

question: A programmer in the 1990s wrote strong encryption the US government wanted to suppress. Before the government could act, he put the program on many websites worldwide so anyone could download it. Why did wide distribution first work as a defense strategy?
answer: Once software is already everywhere, the government has no way left to take it back
choices: Once software is already everywhere, the government has no way left to take it back
Petitioning legislators one by one always saves privacy tools
A well-funded lobbying group is required before shipping any code
Patenting the software is the best defense for open-source privacy tools
context: The PGP argument: releasing the software worldwide before the state could stop it removed the state's suppression leverage; you cannot un-publish a program on ten thousand servers. Legislative petitioning, lobbying groups, and patents are the opposite of the shipping-first strategy the fight vindicated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: One of the earliest groups of economic thinkers, called the Physiocrats, lived in France in the 1700s. Led by King Louis XV's court physician François Quesnay, they argued that all real wealth in a country came from just one activity. Everything else -- craft, trade, and finance -- only moved that wealth around. Which activity did the Physiocrats call the true source of wealth?
answer: Farming
choices: Farming
Banking
Shipping
Weaving
context: Francois Quesnay (1694-1774), physician to Louis XV, led the Physiocrats and published the Tableau economique in 1758. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Physiocracy.

question: In 1758 the French court doctor François Quesnay published the founding book of an early school of economics called the Physiocrats. It was the very first attempt to draw the flow of wealth through a whole economy — farmers to landlords to craftsmen and back again — as a numerical diagram, almost like a plumbing chart. What is Quesnay's famous 1758 work called?
answer: Tableau economique
choices: Tableau economique
Wealth of Nations
Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth
Principles of Political Economy
context: The Tableau economique (1758) diagrammed the circulation of wealth between farming, artisanal, and landowning classes -- the first such macroeconomic model. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tableau_%C3%A9conomique.

question: In eighteenth-century France, before Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations, a school of economists called the Physiocrats argued that land and agriculture were the true source of wealth — and that governments should get out of the way of trade and production. They coined a two-part motto in French capturing their view. What was the motto?
answer: Laissez faire, laissez passer
choices: Laissez faire, laissez passer
Liberte, egalite, fraternite
Vive la France, vive la republique
Fluctuat nec mergitur
context: 'Laissez faire, laissez passer' -- let it be done, let it pass -- is the Physiocrats' motto, later adopted more broadly as a shorthand for the classical-liberal policy stance. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Laissez-faire.

question: In 1750s France a group of economists called the Physiocrats -- led by the king's court physician François Quesnay -- argued that only one sector of the economy could create genuinely new wealth. Everyone else, they claimed, was merely rearranging wealth that already existed. Which sector did the Physiocrats call the only real source of new wealth?
answer: Agriculture
choices: Agriculture
Manufacturing
Commerce
Banking
context: The produit-net doctrine held that only agriculture produced new net wealth; manufacturing and commerce merely transformed it. The claim is now recognized as mistaken, but the free-trade policy conclusions largely stood. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Physiocracy.

question: In the 1770s the French finance minister Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot, a friend of the Physiocrats, tried to sweep away several old rules of King Louis XVI's economy: only the licensed bakers' guild could bake bread, peasants were forced to do unpaid road labor called the corvée, and every province charged its own toll on grain crossing the border. What was Turgot's point in removing those rules?
answer: To let people trade and work more freely, so more goods would get made
choices: To let people trade and work more freely, so more goods would get made
To raise the king's income by adding brand new taxes
To hand more jobs to friends of the king
To keep peasants working the same fields forever
context: Turgot's brief tenure (1774-1776) was a rare case of a Physiocrat actually running economic policy; his 1776 fall under noble pressure is a canonical example of reform blocked by concentrated interests. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anne-Robert-Jacques_Turgot.

question: In 1803 the French economist Jean-Baptiste Say published his Treatise on Political Economy. In it he argued a simple point that later became known as Say's Law: before anybody can buy something, somebody else has to make something first, because the money you spend can only come from goods and services you have already produced or been paid for. In plain terms, what does this claim?
answer: Production comes before spending; you can only buy with what you have made or earned
choices: Production comes before spending; you can only buy with what you have made or earned
Spending money is what creates jobs; making things is a side effect
Only the government can decide what should be produced
Prices always fall when the government prints more money
context: Jean-Baptiste Say (1767-1832) systematized classical-liberal economics for French readers and formulated what came to be called Say's Law. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jean-Baptiste_Say.

question: The early-nineteenth-century French economist Jean-Baptiste Say argued that producing something — building a chair, growing wheat, weaving cloth — automatically generates the income needed to buy other things in return. His idea, later shortened by English-speaking economists into a four-word slogan, became one of the most famous laws in classical economics. What is the common four-word summary?
answer: Supply creates its own demand
choices: Supply creates its own demand
Demand creates its own supply
Money multiplies through banks
Trade balances always clear
context: The compressed English form 'supply creates its own demand' was attacked by Keynes and defended by the Austrians; Say's own version emphasized that products offered on a market create the purchasing power that buys other products. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Say%27s_law.

question: The French phrase 'laissez-nous faire' -- 'let us do it' -- comes from a story told about the late 1600s. King Louis XIV's powerful finance minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert asked a merchant named Le Gendre what the crown could do to help French trade. Le Gendre's answer -- that the best thing government could do for business was simply to leave it alone -- became a slogan. What core economic idea does that phrase capture?
answer: That free markets often work better with less government meddling
choices: That free markets often work better with less government meddling
That kings should personally set all merchant prices
That every business must pay a large export tax
That only nobles are allowed to run businesses
context: Around 1680 the merchant Le Gendre reportedly answered Colbert's question 'What should we do to help you?' with 'Laissez-nous faire' -- leave us alone. The phrase then spread through economic writing via the Physiocrats around 1750-1760. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Laissez-faire.

question: Poland spent about forty years under communism. The government set every price by decree, and shop shelves were often empty. In 1989-1990, under finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz, Poland lifted price controls and switched to a free-market economy almost overnight. What is that kind of fast, all-at-once switch called?
answer: Shock therapy
choices: Shock therapy
Slow steady steps
Central planning
Farm reform
context: Leszek Balcerowicz, a Warsaw School of Economics professor, was named finance minister and deputy prime minister in the Mazowiecki government of August 1989. He assembled the reform package by end-1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leszek_Balcerowicz.

question: The Polish economist Leszek Balcerowicz served as finance minister right after communism fell. His sweeping reform package took effect on January 1, 1990, freeing prices and closing state enterprise subsidies almost overnight. The plan ended up with two nicknames — one taken from Balcerowicz's own name, and one taken from how fast and hard the change hit ordinary Poles. What is the second name?
answer: Shock therapy
choices: Shock therapy
Big bang
Cold turkey
Iron reform
context: 'Shock therapy' captured the speed of Poland's turn from central planning to market pricing overnight -- as distinct from the gradual approaches other post-communist states attempted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_therapy_(economics).

question: When Polish communism collapsed in 1989, the country was suffering empty shelves, shortages, and hyperinflation. The new finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz drew up an emergency plan to switch Poland from central planning to a market economy — not step by step, but all at once. On January 1, 1990 the Balcerowicz Plan took effect. What did Poland do to prices that day?
answer: Liberalized prices on almost all goods overnight
choices: Liberalized prices on almost all goods overnight
Introduced a state pricing board
Fixed all prices at the previous month's levels
Doubled all prices to reflect shortages
context: The immediate price liberalization was the sharpest single move. Alongside it: hard-budget constraints on state enterprises, currency convertibility, foreign trade opening, and privatization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balcerowicz_Plan.

question: On January 1, 1990, Poland ended most price controls and began selling off state-owned companies almost overnight, under a plan by finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz. Instead of communist bureaucrats setting prices, real markets set them. Shops filled with goods people had not seen in years, but wages could not keep up with the new prices. What happened to Poland's economy that first year?
answer: It contracted by about 12 percent
choices: It contracted by about 12 percent
It rose by about 12 percent
It stayed nearly flat
It doubled
context: GDP contracted about 12% in 1990 and again in 1991. Unemployment rose from nominal Communist-era full employment to over 12%. Inflation initially spiked. Political heat was intense. Source: World Bank Poland historical data.

question: After finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz dropped Poland's communist central-planning system in 1990, the country's economy then grew every single year for 16 straight years -- until the 2008 global financial crisis. No other country in Europe matched that unbroken run of growth. What is Poland's long stretch of post-communist growth often called?
answer: The Polish growth miracle
choices: The Polish growth miracle
The Warsaw compact
The Solidarity boom
The great planned expansion
context: Poland grew continuously 1992-2008, an unmatched European record. By 2019 real per-capita GDP had roughly tripled from its 1990 low. Warsaw modernized; the country joined the EU in 2004. Source: World Bank Poland data.

question: When a country switches from communist central planning to a market economy, some governments do it slowly over many years, while others rip off the whole system at once — freeing all prices and selling state companies within a few months. Poland under Leszek Balcerowicz in 1990 is the classic example of the fast approach. Economists have a memorable nickname for that rip-it-off strategy. What is it?
answer: Shock therapy
choices: Shock therapy
Slow transition
Managed decline
Soft landing
context: Jeffrey Sachs advised Poland, Russia, and other post-communist countries on stabilization. His association with shock therapy became foundational -- and controversial when Russia's later reforms produced different results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Sachs.

question: In 1989-1990 Poland used a program called shock therapy, designed by finance minister Leszek Balcerowicz: it lifted price controls, opened trade, ended most subsidies, and moved state industry into private hands almost all at once. Poles suffered a sharp short recession, then grew for decades. By 2019, how many times bigger was the average Polish person's real income than at the 1990 low point?
answer: About three times bigger
choices: About three times bigger
About twice as big
About the same
About ten times bigger
context: Poland's real per-capita GDP had roughly tripled from its 1990 low by 2019. The stretch of continuous growth 1992-2008 and steady recovery after the 2008 crisis produced the largest sustained gain among post-communist economies. Source: World Bank Poland data.

question: After the Soviet Union broke apart, Russia's economic reform was run under President Boris Yeltsin from 1992 to 1995 using a voucher privatization scheme: every citizen got paper vouchers meant to represent a share of state industry. It ended very differently from Poland's clean shock therapy — a small handful of insiders ended up owning almost everything. What is the standard critique of the Russian path?
answer: Gradual measures were captured by insiders, producing the oligarch collapse
choices: Gradual measures were captured by insiders, producing the oligarch collapse
The reforms were too fast, producing hyperinflation
The government stayed too socialist, producing shortage
The state privatized only strategic industries, producing distortion
context: Russia's voucher privatization was captured by well-positioned insiders who accumulated stakes cheaply. Without hard-budget discipline, the result was oligarch-owned enterprises rather than a genuine market. The comparison with Poland became the standard case for the coherent-package view. Source: aslund.org, Russia After Communism.

question: The socialist calculation debate between Ludwig von Mises and central planners taught that isolated reforms fail — you cannot free some prices while keeping others fixed. Poland's 1990 Balcerowicz Plan was the practical proof. Its architect Leszek Balcerowicz insisted four ingredients had to launch together, or none of them would work. What set of ingredients did Balcerowicz insist go together?
answer: Price liberalization plus hard-budget constraints plus currency convertibility plus trade opening
choices: Price liberalization plus hard-budget constraints plus currency convertibility plus trade opening
Price liberalization alone plus foreign aid
Currency convertibility plus state industrial policy
Trade opening plus continued state pricing
context: Balcerowicz's insight: nominal price liberalization without hard-budget constraints (no state bailouts of failing SOEs) does not produce market discipline. A coherent package with all four elements enables the Mises-Hayek mechanism to work. Source: Balcerowicz, Socialism, Capitalism, Transformation (1995).

question: In 1975 a young American economist at Yale University published a paper in the Review of Economic Studies. It showed with careful math that democratic leaders under reelection pressure will time their money-printing and government-spending boosts to peak right before an election, then let the bill come due afterward. The paper founded the whole field of the political business cycle. Who wrote it?
answer: William Nordhaus
choices: William Nordhaus
James Tobin
Alan Blinder
Rudi Dornbusch
context: William Nordhaus, 'The Political Business Cycle' (Review of Economic Studies, April 1975). Nordhaus later shared the 2018 Nobel for work on climate integrated assessment. Source: jstor.org (Nordhaus 1975).

question: Public choice is a branch of economics, pioneered by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, that treats politicians not as saintly public servants but as ordinary people chasing rewards, like everyone else. What is the top reward most elected politicians want?
answer: Getting elected again
choices: Getting elected again
Winning international awards
Being liked by other lawmakers
Reading more textbooks
context: Nordhaus's model: an incumbent seeking reelection benefits from a pre-election boom (voters observe strong economy, incumbent gets credit) and can defer the post-election bust past the election-day judgment. Source: Nordhaus, Review of Economic Studies (1975).

question: In the early 1970s US President Richard Nixon leaned hard on Fed chairman Arthur Burns to keep interest rates low. Nixon wanted the American economy feeling strong and jobs looking plentiful right before his 1972 reelection campaign. Burns went along. What problem does that kind of political pressure on a central bank usually cause?
answer: Inflation that shows up soon after the election
choices: Inflation that shows up soon after the election
A sudden drop in unemployment that lasts forever
Foreign countries permanently raising their tariffs
A rise in gold prices that the president can easily reverse
context: Arthur Burns chaired the Federal Reserve from February 1970 through January 1978. The Nixon White House tapes -- partially transcribed in Burton Abrams's 2006 Journal of Economic Perspectives article -- document Nixon pressing Burns for easier money before the 1972 election. Source: aeaweb.org (Abrams 2006).

question: In January 1969 Richard Nixon became US president. His hand-picked Federal Reserve chairman, Arthur Burns, then cut the federal funds rate from about 9% in mid-1969 to about 3.3% by early 1972 and let the money supply grow around 9% during 1972 itself -- a big loosening of credit right before Nixon's November reelection campaign. What was the outcome for Nixon in that November 1972 vote?
answer: A 49-state landslide reelection
choices: A 49-state landslide reelection
A narrow one-state victory
A loss to George McGovern
A defeat by a third-party candidate
context: Nixon carried 49 states on November 7, 1972 (losing only Massachusetts and DC). CPI inflation then ran ~3.2% (1972), ~6.2% (1973), ~11.0% (1974) -- the beginning of the stagflation decade Volcker would eventually crush. Source: uselectionatlas.org; bls.gov (CPI historical).

question: In June 2003 Alan Greenspan, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, cut the Fed funds rate — the interest banks charge each other overnight — down to a specific low level and then held it there for a full year. It was the lowest US short-term rate since 1958, and Austrian economists like Peter Schiff would later blame it for the housing bubble. What was that low rate?
answer: 1.00 percent
choices: 1.00 percent
0.25 percent
3.50 percent
5.00 percent
context: The Fed cut its target rate to 1.00% by June 2003 and held it there until June 30, 2004 -- when the FOMC began a slow tightening cycle just after the summer political conventions and before the November 2004 election. Source: federalreserve.gov (FOMC historical decisions).

question: From 2003 to 2004 the Fed kept interest rates very low. It began raising them only after the summer conventions, right before Bush's reelection. Austrian-school economists warned this long low-rate era would cause a big real-estate problem. Which one?
answer: A housing bubble that would eventually burst
choices: A housing bubble that would eventually burst
A permanent halt to residential construction
A boom in agricultural land prices only
A collapse in urban land values
context: US housing prices continued rising through 2006. Austrian-tradition economists like Roger Garrison (Time and Money, Routledge 2001) and Mark Thornton predicted the bubble in real time. The 2008 GFC followed. Source: Case-Shiller US National Home Price Index; Thornton, Mises Institute writings 2004-06.

question: A central bank like the US Federal Reserve is supposed to be free from the government of the day. In practice, presidents and prime ministers still lean on the chair around election time, pushing for cheap money to make voters feel wealthy. Economists who studied this — including Yale's William Nordhaus in 1975 — found a clear pattern. What does the evidence say usually happens to a central bank's policy under that pressure?
answer: Its policy tends to line up with what helps the government during elections
choices: Its policy tends to line up with what helps the government during elections
It ignores politics completely and picks the ideal policy every time
It always tightens money right before an election
Its decisions look like random noise with no pattern
context: The Alesina + Roubini + Cohen synthesis (Political Cycles and the Macroeconomy, MIT Press 1997) finds pro-cyclical bias under political pressure -- easier money before elections, tighter after -- relative to an independent counterfactual. Source: mitpress.mit.edu (Alesina 1997).

question: There is a pattern where politicians pressure central banks to keep money loose right before an election, then deal with the inflation later. In the early 1980s one central bank chief did the opposite — he tightened hard even though it cost the sitting president reelection. What does this example show?
answer: A central bank can defy the political calendar when it chooses to
choices: A central bank can defy the political calendar when it chooses to
Central banks always follow the president's wishes
Recessions never happen during election years
Fighting inflation always guarantees the president wins
context: Paul Volcker's 1979-82 tightening produced a deep recession that helped defeat Jimmy Carter in 1980. Volcker's willingness to accept that cost is the counter-example that shows independent-central-banker behavior is possible when the incentives allow it. Source: Volcker, Keeping At It (Public Affairs 2018).

question: Between 2018 and 2019, US President Donald Trump repeatedly and publicly pressured his own Federal Reserve Chair to cut interest rates faster than the Fed wanted. Trump used speeches, TV interviews, and Twitter posts to lean on him by name. Which Fed Chair received all that pressure from President Trump?
answer: Jerome Powell
choices: Jerome Powell
Janet Yellen
Ben Bernanke
Neel Kashkari
context: Jerome Powell (appointed by Trump in November 2017, sworn in February 2018) faced repeated public pressure from President Trump in 2018-19 to cut rates. It is the modern echo of the Nixon-Burns pressure documented in the tapes. Source: contemporary Wall Street Journal and New York Times coverage 2018-19.

question: The American economist James Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize for public choice theory. His slogan 'politics without romance' meant: study politicians, judges, and central bankers as ordinary self-interested people, not saints. Studies of the political business cycle are not a conspiracy theory about the Fed. So what is the real point Buchanan's approach makes about central banks?
answer: Fed independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure
choices: Fed independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure
The Fed is always corrupt regardless of who chairs it
Fed independence is a myth invented after 1913
The Fed is always politically neutral in practice
context: Buchanan's move: examine the specific chair's reappointment prospects, congressional-relationship incentives, and post-Fed career prospects. Legal independence is compatible with substantial de facto political responsiveness. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979) applied.

question: In 1979 the American economist James Buchanan traveled to Vienna to give a talk on the school of thought he had helped build called public choice, which studies politicians and bureaucrats using the same self-interested-human tools economists use for shoppers and factory owners. Buchanan wanted a memorable three-word phrase that would tell readers, in shorthand, what the school actually did. The phrase stuck and has been reprinted ever since. Which three words did Buchanan choose?
answer: Politics without romance
choices: Politics without romance
Government without illusions
Choice without benevolence
Democracy without myths
context: 'Politics without romance' is Buchanan's own three-word summary of the public-choice program. He used it as the title of a widely-cited 1979 lecture and returned to it in his Nobel-era writings. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (IHS Vienna, 1979).

question: In 1979 the American economist James Buchanan gave a talk in Vienna he titled 'Politics Without Romance.' The public-choice school he had helped found treats politicians and bureaucrats as ordinary self-interested humans, not saints. Buchanan wanted his listeners to drop one warm idea about government that many textbooks still quietly assumed. Which warm idea about government did he want to strip away?
answer: That politicians and bureaucrats act from pure public spirit
choices: That politicians and bureaucrats act from pure public spirit
That elections are decided by campaign advertising
That voters read platforms carefully before voting
That parties always keep their platform promises
context: The romance to be stripped: that political actors somehow escape the ordinary self-interest that economics assumes for consumers and firms. Public choice treats them as ordinary humans facing ordinary incentives. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: Older textbook economics arguments played a trick. They compared a real, messy, imperfect market to a perfect, imagined government that always fixes things -- and then said the government should step in. The Nobel-winning economist James Buchanan, a founder of public-choice theory, said the honest comparison had to be different. What did Buchanan say it had to be?
answer: Real market failure against real government failure
choices: Real market failure against real government failure
Ideal market outcomes against ideal government outcomes
The best market case against the worst government case
The worst market case against the best government case
context: Buchanan's move: welfare economics had compared apples to angels -- imperfect markets to perfect government. Compare like to like, and the case for intervention becomes far less obvious. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: The public-choice school of economics, built in the 1960s by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock at Virginia universities, takes seriously the rewards, votes, and punishments politicians face. It borrows the shape of a phrase economists had long used for markets that don't work well — 'market failure' — and coins a matching two-word term for policy that breaks down for the same kinds of reasons. What is the public-choice term that mirrors 'market failure'?
answer: Government failure
choices: Government failure
State breakdown
Political malfunction
Democratic deficit
context: Government failure is public choice's response to the market-failure literature: not that market failures do not exist, but that government intervention has its own systematic failure modes -- capture, rent-seeking, budget maximization, rational ignorance. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: The public-choice school, built in the 1960s by James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Mancur Olson, names a handful of ways governments fail because of the rewards leaders and voters face. The standard textbook kit has stayed roughly the same for decades. One of the choices below is a market concept from Adam Smith's tradition and does not belong to the public-choice kit at all. Which one is out of place?
answer: The invisible hand of consumer sovereignty
choices: The invisible hand of consumer sovereignty
Regulatory capture by concentrated industries
Rent-seeking by lobbyists competing for privilege
Rational ignorance by voters with low per-capita stakes
context: The invisible hand describes a MARKET mechanism, not a government-failure mode. The other three -- capture (Stigler), rent-seeking (Tullock), rational ignorance (Downs) -- are core public-choice mechanisms. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: The Nobel-winning economist James Buchanan wrote a famous short essay called 'Politics Without Romance.' In it he argued that politicians, voters, and government officials should be studied as ordinary people responding to rewards and pressures -- not as noble public servants standing above self-interest. What is Buchanan's key idea in that essay?
answer: Politicians act on their own incentives just like everyone else
choices: Politicians act on their own incentives just like everyone else
Politicians alone are immune to their own incentives
Only voters, never politicians, respond to incentives
Only businesses, never governments, waste money
context: Peter Bauer (1915-2002) was a Hungarian-born LSE development economist who spent decades attacking the romantic view of the state that underpinned post-war aid programs. Buchanan credited Bauer with the phrase. Source: Bauer, Dissent on Development (Harvard 1972).

question: The James Buchanan slogan 'politics without romance' — from his 1979 Vienna talk — points at one core move of the public-choice school he helped build. Buchanan and his colleagues Gordon Tullock and Mancur Olson insisted that economists cannot judge two groups by different moral standards: one group treated as noble stewards and the other as ordinary self-interested humans. The move behind the slogan is to apply the same tools to both. In Buchanan's view, which two groups have to be judged by the same rules?
answer: Political actors and market actors, both as self-interested humans
choices: Political actors and market actors, both as self-interested humans
Winners and losers, both as morally equivalent
Small government and big government, both as equally efficient
Voters and non-voters, both as equally informed
context: The move: if we assume ordinary self-interest for consumers and firms, we must assume it for politicians and bureaucrats too. Asymmetric assumptions (angels in government, humans in markets) built the pre-Buchanan case for intervention. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: The public-choice economist James Buchanan built his essay 'Politics Without Romance' as a test a listener can apply in real debates. When someone says 'the market has failed, so the government must act,' Buchanan's phrase forces the listener to ask one specific counter-question about the actual people who would be running the fix. Which counter-question does the test make the listener ask?
answer: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
choices: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
What percentage of GDP will the new agency consume?
Which political party currently controls the executive branch?
How much did the market failure cost in dollar terms?
context: The public-choice discipline: never compare a REAL failure to an IDEALIZED alternative. Given the actual incentive structure facing the people who would design and administer the fix, is there reason to expect improvement? Often the answer is no. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: 'Politics without romance' is the American economist James Buchanan's own three-word slogan for the whole discipline of public-choice economics, which studies how politicians and government officials respond to incentives. Below are four short slogans linked to public-choice or Chicago-school thinkers. Which one is not Buchanan's, but belongs to a different figure?
answer: There are no solutions, only trade-offs (Sowell)
choices: There are no solutions, only trade-offs (Sowell)
Politics without romance (Buchanan)
The logic of collective action (Olson)
Government-failure symmetry (Buchanan)
context: Thomas Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only trade-offs' recurs across his books. Buchanan's own slogans include 'politics without romance,' 'constitutional political economy,' and 'the samaritan's dilemma.' Source: Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (Morrow 1987).

question: Spanish miners in the New World in the 1500s dug up huge amounts of silver and shipped it back to Europe. So much silver poured in that prices for bread and cloth in Spain kept climbing year after year. What is it called when there is much more money chasing the same goods?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
A tariff
A tax cut
context: Potosi (Cerro Rico) was discovered in 1545 and by 1600 held perhaps 200,000 residents, making it larger than any European city apart from Paris and London. Source: Grokipedia 'Potosi' (2026-09-05).

question: For a hundred years after 1550, the Spanish empire ruled silver mines in Mexico and Peru. Twice a year, dozens of armed galleons gathered in Havana and sailed together across the Atlantic to Seville, carrying silver bars and gold coins back to the Spanish king. Pirates and English privateers hunted them. Historians call these convoys by a short, dramatic two-word name. What did they call these groups of ships?
answer: The Spanish treasure fleets
choices: The Spanish treasure fleets
The Portuguese caravels
The Hansa cogs
The English East Indiamen
context: The Flota de Indias sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana and then across the Atlantic, carrying the world's largest sustained cross-oceanic flow of precious metal. Source: Grokipedia 'Spanish treasure fleet' (2026-09-05).

question: Between about 1500 and 1650, Spanish galleons hauled shiploads of gold and silver from New World mines back to Europe. Over those 150 years the money supply on the continent exploded, and prices across Europe rose about five-fold -- a slow, steady inflation that puzzled kings and merchants alike. What lesson does this teach about money?
answer: When the supply of money grows much faster than goods, prices rise
choices: When the supply of money grows much faster than goods, prices rise
More silver in an economy always makes prices fall
Prices only rise when kings order them to rise
Prices rise only when trade routes are cut off
context: Modern estimates put the general European price level in 1650 at roughly six times its 1500 level, with the acceleration tracking the arrival of American silver. Source: Grokipedia 'Price revolution' (2026-09-05).

question: By 1600, thanks to the twice-yearly silver convoys from the American mines, Spain had more silver and gold coin than any nation in Europe. Any child would guess Spain was the richest country on earth. Yet Spanish workshops were closing, the royal treasury kept going bankrupt, and Spanish farmers were losing sales to Dutch and English rivals abroad. Something in that pile of silver was not making Spain rich the way people expected. What is the puzzle economists still study here?
answer: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
choices: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
The country with the most silver could not defend its ships
The country with the most silver refused to trade with its colonies
The country with the most silver banned interest on loans
context: The bullion inflow raised prices in Spain faster than in its trading partners, so Spanish goods became uncompetitive. Real wealth flowed abroad while nominal money piled up. Source: Grokipedia 'Economic history of Spain' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1556 a Spanish theologian working at the School of Salamanca in Spain watched New World silver flood European markets and shake prices across the continent. He wrote a treatise giving the first clear European version of what we now call the quantity theory of money. His simple point was that money is worth less where there is more of it. Who was this Salamanca theologian?
answer: Martin de Azpilcueta
choices: Martin de Azpilcueta
Bartolome de las Casas
Ignatius of Loyola
Francisco de Vitoria
context: Azpilcueta's 1556 Commentary on the Resolution of Money linked the arrival of American bullion to rising Spanish prices, publishing the insight roughly 220 years before Adam Smith. Source: Grokipedia 'Martin de Azpilcueta' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1500s a group of Catholic priests and law scholars in central Spain wrote about money, prices, and interest — noticing that new silver from the American mines was driving up Spanish prices year after year — 200 years before Adam Smith published the Wealth of Nations. Historians name this early group of economists after the ancient Spanish university where most of them taught. What is the group called?
answer: The School of Salamanca
choices: The School of Salamanca
The Physiocrats
The Vienna Circle
The Mercantilists
context: The School of Salamanca (Azpilcueta, Luis de Molina, Domingo de Soto, Francisco de Vitoria) is now recognized by Austrian economists such as Rothbard and Huerta de Soto as a genuine predecessor to modern economics. Source: Grokipedia 'School of Salamanca' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1556 a Spanish theologian at the School of Salamanca stated the idea plainly: more money in use raises prices, less money lowers them. Modern economists still use this Salamanca idea to warn about central banks that print money to pay for government spending, arguing the extra money simply pushes prices up. What is the modern name for that argument?
answer: The quantity theory of money
choices: The quantity theory of money
The efficient-markets hypothesis
The Phillips curve
The Ricardian equivalence
context: The quantity theory (money supply times velocity equals prices times output) was formalized by Irving Fisher in 1911, but its European roots go back to Azpilcueta and the Salamanca scholastics in the 1550s. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantity theory of money' (2026-09-05).

question: The standard textbook says economics started with Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations in 1776. Some historians of thought point to a group of Catholic scholars in 16th-century Spain who already wrote carefully about prices, money, and value. What does the 16th-century Spanish work reveal is missing from the textbook's 'economics began with Adam Smith' story?
answer: It skips real economic thinking that came centuries earlier
choices: It skips real economic thinking that came centuries earlier
It is exactly right — nothing came before Adam Smith
Adam Smith did not really exist
Economics only began in the 20th century
