Proof-of-work
Proof-of-effort
Proof-of-honor
context: Proof-of-stake (PoS): the right to propose the next block is assigned in proportion to staked collateral, not to burned electricity. Cardano, Solana, and most post-2018 chains launched with PoS from the start. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake.

question: On September 15, 2022 the Ethereum Merge switched the network from Bitcoin-style energy-hungry mining to a very different consensus method. Overnight, the network's power use dropped by more than 99 percent. What is Ethereum's new consensus method called?
answer: Proof of stake
choices: Proof of stake
Proof of work
Proof of authority
Proof of burn
context: The Ethereum Foundation's post-Merge figure is a roughly 99.95% cut in network electricity use. That is the strongest engineering argument PoS supporters make for the switch. Source: ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption.

question: Bitcoin secures its network by making miners burn electricity solving cryptographic puzzles — a system called proof-of-work. In September 2022 the Ethereum blockchain switched to a completely different rule. Anyone who wants to help validate new blocks locks up a large deposit of coins as a bond with the network. If they try to cheat, the software takes their deposit away. What is Ethereum's alternative method called?
answer: Proof-of-stake
choices: Proof-of-stake
Proof-of-work
Proof-of-labor
Proof-of-trust
context: Vitalik Buterin published the Ethereum white paper in late 2013 and has argued for proof-of-stake since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The Merge was the culmination of an eight-year design goal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin.

question: Bitcoin fans have a specific complaint about proof-of-stake — the system where whoever locks up the most coins gets the most say over new blocks. They argue proof-of-stake sneaks back in one bad feature of the old banking world, the exact feature that proof-of-work was designed to break. What feature do they say it brings back?
answer: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
choices: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
Requirement of a central government treasury for issuance
Dependence on trusted third-party settlement rails
Delegation of block production to a small licensed authority
context: The Bitcoin-community argument: whoever starts with the most tokens has the most power to add blocks, entrench their position, and shape network rules, without an external check equivalent to the electricity a PoW miner must burn. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: Bitcoin uses proof-of-work, where miners spend real electricity to add blocks. Ethereum and many newer chains use proof-of-stake instead, where validators lock up their own coins as collateral and sign new blocks. Bitcoiners point to one specific weakness of that design with a name: the nothing-at-stake problem. What does the attack say a proof-of-stake validator can do?
answer: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
choices: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
Validators can rewrite the block chain to their advantage without incurring any staking penalty
Validators can drop their staked collateral before their signatures are recorded
Validators can vote in proportion to their trading volume rather than their staked balance
context: Under PoW a miner can only mine one chain at a time (electricity is a real resource). Under naive PoS a validator can sign every fork simultaneously; the defense requires trusted checkpoints or slashing penalties that add complexity and trust assumptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake#Attacks.

question: In 2023 the chairman of the main US agency that oversees stocks and bonds argued that most proof-of-stake tokens might legally count as investment contracts under a 1946 Supreme Court test called Howey. His public speeches worried the whole crypto industry, since being called an investment contract means heavy US registration rules apply. Which US agency does he chair?
answer: The Securities and Exchange Commission
choices: The Securities and Exchange Commission
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission
The Federal Trade Commission
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority
context: Gary Gensler, then SEC chair, made this suggestion in public testimony in 2023; the SEC's PoS-token stance has since become a running legal question for Ethereum and other PoS chains. Source: sec.gov (Gensler public testimony 2023).

question: Bitcoin has never left proof-of-work — computers still burn real electricity to mint new blocks. Bitcoin's community argues this energy cost is not a bug at all. They say it is a specific kind of feature: a link that ties digital money to something outside itself, in a way that pure software promises never could. Which specific kind of feature do they say it is?
answer: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
choices: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
A regulatory-compliance cost that satisfies environmental disclosure rules
A liquidity provision that reduces short-run mining-fee volatility
A payment to network engineers who maintain node infrastructure
context: The Nakamoto-Consensus defense: the electricity is what makes Bitcoin's security depend on something outside the network's own token economics. Proof-of-stake keeps costs internal and depends on economic incentives among token holders. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: In September 2022 the Ethereum network switched from proof-of-work — miners burning electricity on puzzles, the same rule Bitcoin still uses — to proof-of-stake, where validators lock up coins as a bond and are slashed if they cheat. Ethereum bet the network on proof-of-stake, and Bitcoin stayed with proof-of-work. It is one of the largest live economic-engineering contrasts in cryptocurrency history. In one sentence, what will decide which side made the right bet?
answer: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
choices: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
Whether central banks issue their own digital currencies competing with both
Whether the SEC issues a definitive ruling on token classification
Whether major derivative exchanges list futures on both consensus mechanisms
context: The empirical verdict on PoW vs PoS security will require decades of live operation across real attacks, market crashes, and regulatory pressure. Bitcoin has fifteen years of proof-of-work data; Ethereum's proof-of-stake has three post-Merge years. Source: mises.org/library/pow-pos-empirical.

question: In September 2022 Ethereum did the Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake overnight. Two well-known cryptocurrencies stayed on proof-of-work well past that date, and both trace their technical roots back to Bitcoin — one launched in 2011 as 'the silver to Bitcoin's gold,' and the other began in 2013 as a joke coin with a Shiba Inu meme for a mascot. Which pair are they?
answer: Litecoin and Dogecoin
choices: Litecoin and Dogecoin
Cardano and Solana
Polkadot and Avalanche
Tron and EOS
context: Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee) and Dogecoin (2013, Billy Markus & Jackson Palmer) are Scrypt-based PoW coins descended from Bitcoin's codebase. Cardano, Solana, Polkadot, and Avalanche all use PoS variants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litecoin.

question: For a long time, economists imagined a strange split: bakers, farmers, and shopkeepers acted in their own interest, but politicians and bureaucrats supposedly cared only about the public good. In the 1960s a school of American economists, led by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, said this was silly — leaders want things too, like re-election, larger budgets, and better jobs. What is this school called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Public finance
Monetary policy
Central planning
context: Tullock, a lawyer by training, was one of the founders of public choice theory alongside James Buchanan. Buchanan would later win the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics for the field's development. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: In 1966 the American economist Gordon Tullock founded a new academic journal at the University of Virginia. Its first title was long and awkward. A few years later editors renamed it simply Public Choice, and that two-word name spread so widely it stuck to the whole field. What was the journal's original awkward title?
answer: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
choices: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
'Studies in Political Economy'
'Journal of Institutional Analysis'
'Constitutional Economics Review'
context: The journal renamed itself 'Public Choice' in 1969, and the new name became the label for the whole scholarly field. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: The public choice school of economics studies politicians, voters, and government workers as ordinary people who respond to incentives just like everyone else does. It was founded in the 1950s and 1960s by the economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. Their research program first grew at a state technical university, then moved down the road to a second university in the same US state, where it flourishes today. Which state was home to both schools?
answer: Virginia
choices: Virginia
Massachusetts
California
New York
context: The center was originally at the University of Virginia, moved to Virginia Tech, and then followed Buchanan to George Mason in 1983 -- an unusual case of a research center migrating with its founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Public choice is a branch of economics founded in the 1960s by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock. Its central move is refusing to treat people in government as different from people anywhere else — no halos, no special angel-status. Voters, politicians, bureaucrats, and regulators get studied the same way economists study shoppers or shopkeepers. What does the school assume about workers in government?
answer: They respond to incentives too, and often act in their own interest
choices: They respond to incentives too, and often act in their own interest
They ignore personal gain and always serve the public good
They act at random and cannot be predicted by economists
They only respond to what voters demand in each election
context: Founded 1965 as the Committee on Non-Market Decision Making. The society hosts an annual conference; the European Public Choice Society (1972) and Public Choice Society of Japan (1996) followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: Public Choice economics studies politicians and bureaucrats as ordinary self-interested people, not as selfless public servants. James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock co-founded the school at Virginia in the 1960s and wrote 'The Calculus of Consent' together. In 1986 the whole field was ratified when one of the two co-founders received one of the highest honors in economics. What was that award, and to whom did it go?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
The John Bates Clark Medal, to Gordon Tullock
The Presidential Medal of Freedom, to William Niskanen
The Manhattan Institute Hayek Prize, to Anthony de Jasay
context: The Nobel-adjacent prize (usually just called the Nobel Prize in Economics). Buchanan's citation credited his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for economic and political decision-making. Tullock never received the prize, an omission still noted by public-choice scholars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/James_M._Buchanan.

question: By 2020 the field of public choice economics — founded by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock in the 1960s — was being cited across economics, political science, sociology, and law. Its early pages had laid down a whole intellectual scaffolding: technical terms for the ways politicians, bureaucrats, and voters actually behave, rather than the pretend way old textbooks imagined them behaving. Which cluster of concepts is characteristic of the field's contribution?
answer: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
choices: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
Aggregate demand, marginal propensity to consume, Phillips curve, IS-LM
General equilibrium, comparative statics, Walrasian auctioneer, Edgeworth box
Mean-variance optimization, capital asset pricing model, efficient markets
context: Tullock coined 'rent-seeking' in 1967 in a Public Choice paper. Niskanen 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government' (1971) worked out bureaucratic behavior. Buchanan-Tullock 'The Calculus of Consent' (1962) had already introduced constitutional political economy. All worked out first in the journal before diffusing more widely. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: Imagine the workers at a shoe store go on strike. The store might lose money or even close, but nobody gets hurt — you can walk a few blocks and buy shoes somewhere else. Now imagine every police officer in a city walked off the job on the same day. Robbers, muggers, and gangs would suddenly face nobody. Who would be hurt the most by that kind of strike?
answer: The regular people who need protecting
choices: The regular people who need protecting
The bankers who lend to the police
Foreign countries
Other police departments
context: Franklin D. Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, President of the National Federation of Federal Employees, on August 16, 1937. Roosevelt considered a public-sector strike 'unthinkable and intolerable.' Source: presidency.ucsb.edu (Roosevelt letter to Steward, 1937).

question: In 1937 President Franklin Roosevelt — himself a strong champion of private labor unions — wrote a public letter to the head of a federal-workers group. In it he argued that government workers should not bargain the way private workers do. The person sitting across the negotiating table is completely different in each case, Roosevelt said. Who sits across from workers at a private company but not at a government job?
answer: A profit-maximizing private employer
choices: A profit-maximizing private employer
A voluntary industry trade association
A regulated common carrier
A cooperatively-owned enterprise
context: In the private sector, wage demands trade off against the employer's profits and the firm's competitive survival. In the public sector, the employer is a taxpayer-funded entity whose ultimate check-writer is the same voter the union spends dues to influence. Source: Roosevelt letter (1937).

question: By 2010, unions were more than four times as common in US government jobs as in private ones -- because government workers form a tight interest group bargaining against diffuse taxpayers. What did President Franklin Roosevelt himself say about public-sector collective bargaining?
answer: He opposed it
choices: He opposed it
He championed it
He was neutral
He never addressed it
context: In 2010, public-sector union density was ~36% while private-sector density had fallen to ~7%. The gap reflects both public-sector expansion after Kennedy's Executive Order 10988 (1962) and long-running private-sector decline. Source: bls.gov (union-membership historical series).

question: A state governor pushes a new labor law through the state legislature. Under the old rules, union dues had been pulled automatically from every public worker's paycheck each month, no signature needed. Under the new law, that automatic pull stops. Instead, each worker must actively choose every single year whether to send the money to the union or not. What kind of change is this?
answer: Making union dues voluntary instead of automatic
choices: Making union dues voluntary instead of automatic
Banning all unions in the state
Raising taxes on union members
Forcing every worker to join a union
context: Scott Walker's Act 10 passed in March 2011 after weeks of massive protest at the state capitol and a Democratic-senator walkout to Illinois to deny quorum. The Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the law in July 2014. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Wisconsin_Act_10.

question: In early 2011 the new Wisconsin governor Scott Walker pushed a bill called Act 10 that would sharply limit collective bargaining for most public-sector unions. Fourteen Democratic state senators fled across the border and hid in Illinois hotels. Under Wisconsin's rules, the state Senate could not vote on the bill without a certain minimum number of senators present in the chamber. What was the goal of the walkout?
answer: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
choices: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
To lobby the federal Department of Labor for intervention
To organize with unions on the Illinois-Wisconsin border
To evade personal fines imposed by Walker
context: The Wisconsin state constitution required a quorum for fiscal legislation. Democratic senators crossed the state line to make that quorum unreachable, delaying but not ultimately preventing passage. Source: madison.com and wisconsinwatch.org (2011 protest coverage).

question: In 2011 the state of Wisconsin passed a law known as Act 10. Under Act 10, public school teachers could choose each year whether to pay union dues, instead of having the money pulled automatically from their paychecks. Within a few years the biggest teachers' union in Wisconsin — the Wisconsin Education Association Council — had lost most of its dues-paying members. What does that dramatic drop tell us about many of those members before the law changed?
answer: Many were paying only because the dues were automatic, not because they wanted to
choices: Many were paying only because the dues were automatic, not because they wanted to
They enthusiastically supported everything the union did
They had never actually been union members in the first place
The law forced every teacher to quit the union at once
context: WEAC lost the majority of its members after the end of automatic dues deduction and mandatory annual recertification votes. It is the clearest measured effect of Act 10 on public-sector union density. Source: journalsentinel.com (WEAC membership coverage 2013-16).

question: On June 27, 2018 the US Supreme Court decided a case that reshaped public-sector labor law across the country. The Court held 5-to-4 that non-member public workers — teachers, clerks, prison guards, city employees — could no longer be forced to pay so-called 'agency fees' to unions bargaining on their behalf. Mark Janus, an Illinois child-support specialist who had refused to pay the fees, was the plaintiff who brought the suit and won. What is the case called?
answer: Janus v. AFSCME
choices: Janus v. AFSCME
Abood v. Detroit Board of Education
Harris v. Quinn
Knox v. SEIU
context: Janus v. AFSCME Council 31, 585 US ___ (2018), overturned the 1977 Abood decision. Mandatory agency fees to public-sector unions violate the First Amendment because all public-sector collective bargaining is inherently political. Source: supremecourt.gov (Janus 585 US).

question: The California pension fund CalPERS holds pension assets for state employees and is the largest US public pension fund. Its unfunded pension liabilities have remained a genuine long-term fiscal concern for the state. Roughly what size of assets does it manage in the mid-2020s?
answer: About $460 billion
choices: About $460 billion
About $46 billion
About $4.6 trillion
About $46 million
context: The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) manages approximately $460 billion in the mid-2020s. Its unfunded liabilities remain a fiscal concern reflecting the long-term public-sector-union bargaining pattern FDR warned about. Source: calpers.ca.gov (annual financial reports).

question: A public-sector union collects dues from its workers. Under most US state laws it also spends those dues on ads to elect governors and legislators. Those same elected officials then sit across the bargaining table from the union. What makes this different from a private union?
answer: The union helps pick the officials who then bargain with the union
choices: The union helps pick the officials who then bargain with the union
The union always represents a majority of workers by law
The union is not allowed to ever strike
The union receives federal matching funds automatically
context: Private-sector union dues cannot select the CEO across the bargaining table. Public-sector union dues can and do help select the mayor, governor, or school-board members who then negotiate. That is the circle FDR flagged in 1937. Source: Roosevelt letter (1937); Freeman + Ichniowski (1988).

question: Picture a public-sector union that spends millions of dollars in an election campaign to help elect friendly politicians into a state legislature. Two years later, the very same union sits down across the negotiating table from those same politicians to hammer out a new contract for teachers or bus drivers. In effect, the union has helped pick its own bargaining opponent. What happens to the usual idea of two independent sides at the bargaining table?
answer: It breaks down because the group is really bargaining with itself
choices: It breaks down because the group is really bargaining with itself
It becomes fairer than any private negotiation
It produces totally random outcomes
It always leaves zero benefit for both sides
context: The Olson + Stigler combined diagnosis: concentrated interest + captured counterparty gives you a single institutional structure where standard adversarial-bargaining assumptions fail. FDR saw the shape in 1937; the modern literature formalized it. Source: Olson (1965); Stigler (1971); DiSalvo, Government Against Itself (Oxford 2015).

question: In late 2008, at the height of the housing crash and banking crisis, the Federal Reserve — the US central bank — announced it would create $500 billion of new money and use it to buy up home-loan bonds from struggling banks. Nothing like it had ever been done in America. More rounds would follow in the years ahead. What do economists call this first program today?
answer: QE1
choices: QE1
TARP
PDCF
Operation Twist
context: QE1 was launched November 25 2008 and expanded in March 2009. It ran until June 2010 at a total commitment of about $1.75 trillion. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2009, as the crisis kept unfolding, the Federal Reserve — the US central bank — grew its first bond-buying program. It added $300 billion in US Treasury bonds and pushed home-loan-bond purchases up to $1.25 trillion. The program finally wound down in early 2010. Adding everything together, what total dollar figure did QE1 reach?
answer: About $1.75 trillion
choices: About $1.75 trillion
About $600 billion
About $500 billion
About $4 trillion
context: QE1's total commitment was $1.75 trillion when the program wound down in June 2010: $1.25T in MBS, $300B in Treasuries, and $200B in agency debt. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: When the Federal Reserve — the US central bank — buys a bond from a regular commercial bank, no truck full of paper cash ever leaves the Fed's vault. The Fed simply opens a computer screen and types a new, larger number into that bank's reserve account. The bond is now the Fed's, and the bank has fresh reserves. Where does the money for the purchase actually come from?
answer: The central bank creates it out of thin air by typing in the new amount
choices: The central bank creates it out of thin air by typing in the new amount
Taxpayers pay for it through this year's taxes
Other banks lend it to the central bank first
The Treasury prints paper cash and ships it over
context: When the Fed buys a bond from a primary dealer, it pays with newly created reserves credited to the dealer's Fed account -- reserves that did not exist before the purchase. This is monetary base expansion at its most direct. Source: federalreservehistory.org 'Quantitative Easing'.

question: When Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet — the pile of assets the US central bank owns — sat at roughly $900 billion. Over the next 21 months the Fed launched QE1 and bought up trillions of dollars in bonds. By the time QE1 wound down in mid-2010, the balance sheet had ballooned to a much larger figure. What size did it reach?
answer: About $2.3 trillion
choices: About $2.3 trillion
About $1.2 trillion
About $4.5 trillion
About $1 trillion
context: The Fed's balance sheet more than doubled from about $900 billion pre-crisis to about $2.3 trillion by mid-2010. This 150%+ expansion in two years was unprecedented in peacetime. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2010).

question: An Irish-born banker and merchant living in Paris in the early 1700s wrote a book called An Essay on the Nature of Trade in General. He noticed something important about newly-created money. It does not sprinkle evenly across everyone at once, like rain. It enters the economy at particular spots — a silver mine, a royal treasury, a big bank — and the people who touch it first can spend it before shop prices rise. What is the standard name for this effect today?
answer: The Cantillon effect
choices: The Cantillon effect
The Keynes effect
The Smith effect
The Bastiat effect
context: Richard Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734), an Irish-born banker who shorted John Law's bubble before it collapsed, wrote his Essai in the 1730s. It was published posthumously in 1755. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: When new money is created, it does not rain evenly across a country — it enters at one specific spot first, and whoever stands at that spot gets the fresh dollars before prices adjust. Economists call this the Cantillon effect, after the 18th-century Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon who first described it. During QE1 in 2008-09, the Federal Reserve created new reserves through a Fed-dealer window. Which group received them first?
answer: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
choices: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
Low-income wage earners on fixed hourly rates
Retirees living on Social Security benefits
Small-business owners in agricultural sectors
context: The new money enters at the Fed-dealer transaction. Asset prices (stocks, real estate, corporate bonds) rose sharply through 2009-10 while wages stagnated -- textbook first-receiver benefit. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: After the 2008 crash, mainstream defenders of QE1 — including Ben Bernanke, the Federal Reserve chairman who launched the program, in his later memoirs, and Paul Krugman on his blog — pointed to one specific effect the program had in 2008 and 2009 that, in their telling, stopped an even worse outcome from unfolding. What did they credit QE1 with achieving?
answer: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
choices: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
Directly funding the automobile-industry rescue
Preventing the collapse of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Immediately restoring pre-crisis wage growth
context: The defense: absent QE1, mortgage markets would have seized, rates would have spiked, and housing would have crashed further. Whether this defense holds up depends on counterfactuals nobody can run. Source: Bernanke, The Courage to Act (2015).

question: When the US Federal Reserve — America's central bank — creates brand-new dollars to buy government bonds, the program has a soft, technical-sounding name: 'quantitative easing,' or QE. It could just as accurately be called 'money printing,' but that is not the label officials at the Fed choose to use. If a central bank runs this money-creation program for years on end, what is the most predictable long-run effect on the real economy?
answer: Prices across the economy tend to rise -- inflation
choices: Prices across the economy tend to rise -- inflation
Interest rates fall permanently to zero on their own
Unemployment drops to zero and stays there
Exports automatically double within five years
context: The Bank of Japan ran quantitative easing 2001-2006 to fight deflation. Bernanke borrowed the label. He reportedly preferred 'credit easing' but the QE label stuck. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank of Japan' (2026-09-05).

question: Between 2008 and 2010, during the first round of the Federal Reserve's 'quantitative easing' program (QE1), a handful of Austrian-school economists appeared on cable news, radio shows, and financial newsletters warning that the Fed was really printing money to fund the federal government's giant deficits, and that price hikes would come later even if not right away. Which three Austrian voices most publicly made this call in those years?
answer: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
choices: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Ben Bernanke
Larry Summers, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz, and Alan Meltzer
context: Schiff on television, Murphy at the Mises Institute, and James Grant in Grant's Interest Rate Observer all publicly warned that the delay between monetary expansion and consumer-price adjustment did not mean the mechanism was broken. The 2021-23 wave was consistent with their long-horizon call. Source: mises.org and Grant's Interest Rate Observer archive.

question: Before 2008 the Federal Reserve — the US central bank — had never bought bonds on the scale that QE1 launched. But QE1 was followed by QE2, QE3, and a whole new round after the 2020 pandemic. Analysts now call the whole stretch since 2008 the balance-sheet era of central banking. Looking at that pattern, which claim about central banking today does this history push readers to recognize?
answer: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
choices: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
Central banks always fully unwind emergency programs within two years
Balance-sheet expansion is neutral because commercial banks control final money creation
Central-bank asset purchases affect only bond markets and never asset prices generally
context: QE1 was framed as an emergency. Seventeen years later, three additional rounds have followed, along with two massive 2020 pandemic-era expansions. Emergency practice has become standing doctrine. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: On November 3, 2010, more than a year after QE1 had wound down, the Federal Reserve — the US central bank — announced a second bond-buying program. It would create $600 billion of new money and use it to buy US Treasury bonds at a pace of $75 billion each month through June 2011. What is this second round of buying commonly called?
answer: QE2
choices: QE2
Operation Twist
TARP
TALF
context: QE2 pushed the Fed's balance sheet from about $2.3 trillion to about $2.9 trillion by mid-2011. It was the second round in what would become a multi-decade balance-sheet policy tool. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2010 the US Federal Reserve, America's central bank, launched a second round of buying government bonds with newly-created money. The plan was called QE2. One day after the November 3 announcement, Fed chairman Ben Bernanke did something unusual for a Fed chair -- he wrote an opinion piece straight to the public defending the program. Which major American newspaper printed his op-ed?
answer: The Washington Post
choices: The Washington Post
The Wall Street Journal
The New York Times
The Financial Times
context: Bernanke's November 4 2010 op-ed in The Washington Post was titled 'What the Fed Did and Why: Supporting the Recovery and Sustaining Price Stability.' Using a newspaper op-ed to defend Fed policy was itself a break from tradition of speaking only through official channels. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2010 Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke wrote a Washington Post op-ed defending QE2, a program in which the Fed would print money to buy US government bonds. Bernanke argued the bond-buying would flow through one specific market and make Americans feel richer, encouraging them to spend. Which market did he point to as the main channel?
answer: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
choices: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
The residential real-estate market, which he said would boost construction jobs
The commodity market, which he said would raise farm incomes
The auto market, which he said would help Detroit
context: Bernanke wrote: 'higher stock prices will boost consumer wealth and help increase confidence, which can also spur spending.' It was one of the first explicit public admissions that the Fed intended its policy to boost equity values. Source: Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: In his November 2010 Washington Post op-ed defending the Fed's QE2 bond-buying program, chairman Ben Bernanke argued that higher stock prices and higher home prices would make American families feel wealthier, and that feeling would lead them to spend more at stores and restaurants. Economists have a common two-word name for the idea that rising asset prices push consumers to spend. What is this idea called?
answer: The wealth effect
choices: The wealth effect
The multiplier effect
The crowding-out effect
The Balassa-Samuelson effect
context: The wealth effect is the standard economic label for higher household net worth leading to higher spending. Its invocation by Bernanke made explicit what critics had said was implicit in QE all along: the Fed was targeting asset prices. Source: Grokipedia 'Wealth effect' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2010 the US Federal Reserve announced QE2 -- a second, larger round of creating new dollars to buy US government bonds. Germany's finance minister Wolfgang Schaeuble told a newspaper that the American policy was 'clueless.' Germany had lived through hyperinflation in the 1920s and had strong opinions about money-printing. What was Schaeuble most likely worried about?
answer: That printing more dollars would push up prices and shake other countries' economies
choices: That printing more dollars would push up prices and shake other countries' economies
That the US had not printed nearly enough new money
That Germany would have to print money to catch up
That the US would lower taxes at the same time
context: Schauble, then German Finance Minister under Angela Merkel, called QE2 'clueless' in a 2010 Der Spiegel interview. He argued the program would export inflation to Europe and destabilize the emerging-market dollar bloc. Source: Grokipedia 'Wolfgang Schauble' (2026-09-05).

question: In August 2011, Texas governor Rick Perry was running for the Republican nomination for US president. On the campaign trail he warned that it would be 'almost treasonous' if the Federal Reserve printed more money between then and the 2012 election, because it might help President Barack Obama get re-elected by boosting the economy. What was Perry accusing the Fed of doing?
answer: Bending its money policy to help one side win an election
choices: Bending its money policy to help one side win an election
Refusing to obey any orders from Congress
Secretly buying gold from foreign countries
Raising interest rates too fast during a recession
context: Perry made the remark at an August 2011 campaign event in Iowa. It became one of the defining moments of Perry's brief 2012 run and marked one of the first times a Republican presidential candidate publicly attacked a sitting Fed chair by name. Source: Grokipedia 'Rick Perry' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed's QE2 program -- creating new dollars to buy US government bonds -- ran from its November 2010 announcement to its June 2011 conclusion. The Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon warned in the 1700s that new money helps whoever gets it first before prices rise. That 'Cantillon-effect' payoff of QE2 was visible on stock-market tapes during those seven months. What did the S&P 500 index of big US companies do over that window?
answer: Rose approximately 24 percent
choices: Rose approximately 24 percent
Fell approximately 5 percent
Rose approximately 5 percent
Stayed roughly flat
context: The S&P 500 gained roughly 24% from the November 3 2010 QE2 announcement through the program's June 2011 end. The wealth effect Bernanke had named publicly was operating exactly as promised -- for those who owned equities. Source: Grokipedia 'S&P 500' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2010 the Federal Reserve, chaired by Ben Bernanke, launched a second round of quantitative easing — nicknamed QE2 — buying 600 billion dollars of Treasury bonds and paying with newly created bank reserves. Austrian critics saw a classic Frederic Bastiat 'seen and unseen' problem hiding in the policy. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures QE2's structure?
answer: Seen: the recovery is strengthening; Unseen: the new reserves are flowing into asset prices, not wages or productive investment
choices: Seen: the recovery is strengthening; Unseen: the new reserves are flowing into asset prices, not wages or productive investment
Seen: full employment achieved; Unseen: currency devaluation abroad
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: rising savings; Unseen: falling consumption
context: The visible outcome (S&P 500 +24%) was framed as recovery. The invisible mechanism -- new reserves flowing directly to first-receivers who owned equities -- was the actual causal channel. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In November 2010 the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, Ben Bernanke, wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post defending a new round of 'quantitative easing' — buying long-term government bonds with newly-created money. In the piece he openly argued that a goal of the program was to lift stock prices so investors would feel richer and spend more. Once a central bank publicly says out loud that it wants to lift stock prices, what changes?
answer: It becomes a permanent, openly-admitted feature of policy, no longer a hidden side effect
choices: It becomes a permanent, openly-admitted feature of policy, no longer a hidden side effect
Op-eds by central bankers rarely reveal actual policy targets
Pushing up stock prices has no long-term effect on inequality
Central-bank asset targeting works best when kept secret
context: After the 2010 op-ed, no serious observer could claim the Fed was not targeting equity values. Every subsequent QE round openly invoked the wealth-effect channel. The distributional implications -- who owns stocks, who does not -- became visible and permanent. Source: Bernanke, Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: In November 2010 Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke wrote a Washington Post op-ed straight to the public defending QE2, the Fed's second big round of bond-buying with newly-created dollars. The piece is now cited as one of the first times a modern Fed chair broke from a long-standing tradition about how the central bank communicated. Which tradition did Bernanke break?
answer: The Fed's tradition of speaking only through official statements and formal congressional testimony
choices: The Fed's tradition of speaking only through official statements and formal congressional testimony
The Fed's tradition of publishing monthly balance-sheet reports
The Fed's tradition of holding secret FOMC meetings
The Fed's tradition of coordinating with the European Central Bank
context: Prior Fed chairs generally avoided newspaper op-eds. Bernanke's decision to argue directly to the general public via the Washington Post marked a shift toward more overt political communication. Subsequent chairs (Yellen, Powell) have all made increasing use of public commentary channels. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve System' (2026-09-05).

question: In the western Pacific Ocean, on a small island east of the Philippines, people spent hundreds of years using enormous round stone discs as money. Some of these limestone wheels were more than 12 feet across and weighed several tons -- as much as a car. Villagers would leave the biggest ones sitting outside houses or along paths. Which Pacific island is famous for using these giant stone-disc coins?
answer: Yap
choices: Yap
Guam
Tahiti
Easter Island
context: The Yap Islands are a small group in Micronesia. Their traditional currency, the rai, is one of the most distinctive monetary systems ever recorded. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: On the Pacific island of Yap, villagers used giant limestone discs called rai stones as money. But Yap itself had no limestone. Crews had to sail to another island about 250 miles away, quarry the huge discs by hand, and haul each one home strapped to an outrigger canoe. Which nearby island had the limestone quarry?
answer: Palau
choices: Palau
Guam
Bougainville
Tahiti
context: Yap has no limestone; the rai were carved from aragonite in Palau and transported by long open-ocean canoe voyage. The difficulty of transport was itself part of what made each stone valuable. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: On the Pacific island of Yap, a rai stone was a giant limestone disc used as money. Some weighed several tons. Once a really big rai was installed in a village, no one could move it again. Yet the stones still changed owners in trades. Since the physical stone stayed put, how did the transfer of ownership actually take place?
answer: By public community agreement that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed put
choices: By public community agreement that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed put
By carving the new owner's name onto the stone's surface
By moving the stone to a central marketplace once a year
By breaking off a small piece and giving it to the new owner
context: The ledger was social memory: everyone in the village simply agreed, and the transfer was complete. Physical possession and ownership were decoupled. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: On the Pacific island of Yap, giant carved limestone disks called rai stones served as money — some as tall as a house and far too heavy for one person to move. In one famous incident, a canoe crew was towing a particularly large new rai stone home across the open ocean when a sudden storm hit the boats. The heavy stone slid free of its ropes and sank to the bottom of the sea, far too deep for anyone to recover. What did the Yap islanders later decide about that lost stone?
answer: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
choices: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
They declared the crew liable for the full value in fish and taro
They dived down to retrieve fragments over the next generation
They classified it as destroyed and removed it from the record
context: The crew's testimony to the stone's exact size and quality was enough. The rai continued to circulate through community memory even though it was hundreds of feet under the Pacific. Source: William Henry Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: On the Pacific island of Yap, people used giant stone disks as money, including one that had sunk to the bottom of the sea but was still traded from owner to owner. A famous American economist said this is not so different from how the US 'owns' gold at Fort Knox. What is the similarity?
answer: Almost nobody sees the actual money, but everyone agrees who owns it
choices: Almost nobody sees the actual money, but everyone agrees who owns it
The money can be eaten if there is no food
The money is made by robots deep underground
The money is only useful for one week at a time
context: Friedman's 1991 essay 'The Island of Stone Money' was later collected in his 1992 book Money Mischief. The Yap story became one of his favorite teaching devices. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1991 the American economist Milton Friedman published an essay called 'The Island of Stone Money.' It compared the giant stone-disc money of the Pacific island of Yap to modern central-bank practice. He pointed to a real 1932-33 case: France asked to redeem its dollar deposits into gold, and clerks simply moved the gold bars from one shelf to another inside the same vault in New York. No metal ever crossed the ocean. Only the labels on the bars changed. Whose vault held that gold?
answer: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
The Bank of England in London
The Bank for International Settlements in Basel
The Bank of France in Paris
context: When France wanted to convert dollar claims to gold, staff at the New York Fed simply moved gold bars from a drawer labeled 'US' to a drawer labeled 'France' inside the same vault. National ownership changed; the metal did not move. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: The Chicago economist Milton Friedman wrote about the giant rai stones of the Pacific island of Yap in an essay called 'The Island of Stone Money.' The cypherpunks -- programmers of the 1990s who wanted digital cash -- later picked up the same story. Friedman and the cypherpunks drew the same deep lesson about what money fundamentally IS. Which claim did they draw from Yap?
answer: Money is a ledger; the physical medium is only a container for social agreement about who owns what
choices: Money is a ledger; the physical medium is only a container for social agreement about who owns what
Money must be issued by a sovereign to have value
Money is worthless unless backed one-to-one by gold in a vault
Money is fundamentally a religious or ceremonial object
context: Once you accept that the ledger is the money, the shape of the container -- stone disc, gold bar, paper note, database entry -- is a secondary engineering choice. This is the conceptual bridge from rai to Bitcoin. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: On the Pacific island of Yap, everyone in a village remembered in their own head which rai stone belonged to whom. That shared memory WAS the money system. In Bitcoin, the same job -- knowing who owns which coin -- is done not by human memory but by a shared record book, enforced by math and copied onto thousands of computers around the world. What is that shared record book called?
answer: The blockchain
choices: The blockchain
The mempool
The Merkle root
The lightning network
context: Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 design replaces trusted human memory with a chain of cryptographically linked blocks that every node holds a copy of. The rai villagers' shared verbal record becomes a mathematical public record. Source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008).

question: The economist Milton Friedman told a famous story about Yap Island in the Pacific, where huge stone disks called rai served as money — even ones that had sunk to the bottom of the sea. Everyone on the island just remembered who owned which stone. Decades later, Bitcoin arrived as a purely digital ledger every user could check. Friedman's bridge from Yap stones to Bitcoin teaches a specific recognition move about monetary innovation. Which move?
answer: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
choices: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
Only physical scarcity can back a real currency
Cryptography cannot replace the role of a sovereign
Monetary systems always fail when the physical medium is lost
context: Once money is understood as a ledger, moving from community memory to cryptographic memory is a technology upgrade, not a change in category. The Yap sunken stone is functionally the same object as an unspent Bitcoin output on the blockchain. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out: The Origins of Money (2002).

question: Most historical monies were easy to make -- kings could stamp new coins or governments could print new bills whenever they liked. But two monies stand apart. The giant rai stones of Yap had to be quarried by hand from another island 250 miles away and hauled home by canoe. Bitcoin has to be mined by computers solving hard math puzzles that burn real electricity. Which feature did both rai and Bitcoin share, that ordinary money lacks?
answer: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
choices: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
A licensed sovereign mint to stamp each unit
A physical backing in an underlying commodity
Continuous inflation to keep supply growing
context: Nick Szabo argued that a rai's cost of production (quarry, carve, canoe across open ocean) is a physical analog of Bitcoin's proof-of-work (electricity spent on cryptographic hashing). Both systems make new supply hard, and past supply cheap to verify. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out (2002).

question: A smooth-talking man promises his investors huge returns every single year. But he never actually invests their money in anything real. He simply uses the cash from brand-new investors to pay off the earlier ones, then pockets the rest. The trick only works so long as fresh money keeps rolling in the door -- and eventually the money runs dry. What is this kind of scam called?
answer: A Ponzi scheme
choices: A Ponzi scheme
A tariff
A bank run
Insider trading
context: Bernard Madoff ran the largest financial fraud in US history through his investment-advisory business. He confessed on December 10, 2008, was arrested December 11, and sentenced to 150 years in June 2009. Source: sec.gov (Madoff litigation releases).

question: In the early 2000s a Boston financial analyst named Harry Markopolos studied the trading results of a well-known New York investor named Bernie Madoff. Markopolos was a math expert, and he saw quickly that Madoff's returns could not be real -- no one in the world could earn that steady a profit every month, in every kind of market. For eight years Markopolos sent warnings to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the government's investor-watchdog agency. What happened to his warnings?
answer: The agency ignored him and the fraud kept going for years
choices: The agency ignored him and the fraud kept going for years
The agency shut the fraud down that very week
The math expert was arrested for lying
The fraud turned out to be totally legal
context: Harry Markopolos was a quantitative analyst at Rampart Investment Management. He determined by May 2000 that Madoff's steady ~1% monthly returns could not be produced by any real trading strategy. Source: Markopolos, No One Would Listen (Wiley 2010).

question: In the early 2000s the American investigator Harry Markopolos, a mathematics expert, tried year after year to warn the Securities and Exchange Commission — the SEC — that the Wall Street investment fund run by Bernie Madoff was a fraud. Madoff's reported returns went up almost every single month with hardly any dips, impossibly smooth for real markets. Markopolos ran the numbers and said no honest fund can behave that way. He was right. What kind of scam turned out to be running there?
answer: A Ponzi scheme, paying old investors with new investors' money
choices: A Ponzi scheme, paying old investors with new investors' money
Insider trading on secret news tips
Fake accounting to hide company losses
Selling stocks the seller did not actually own
context: Markopolos's November 7, 2005 submission was titled 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud,' 19 pages with 29 red flags and mathematical proofs. The SEC opened but did not adequately pursue the investigation. Source: sec.gov (Markopolos submissions).

question: In the early 2000s the American investigator Harry Markopolos sent the Securities and Exchange Commission — the SEC, the US stock-market watchdog — detailed warnings for years that the Wall Street investor Bernie Madoff was running a huge fraud. Each time SEC staff looked at the file and did nothing serious. When Madoff finally turned himself in during the 2008 crash, the losses were about $65 billion. What lesson do free-market thinkers draw from a story like this?
answer: Government watchdogs can miss huge frauds, so investors still need to think for themselves
choices: Government watchdogs can miss huge frauds, so investors still need to think for themselves
Watchdog agencies always catch fraud before regular people can
Fraud only happens when there are no rules at all
Big-name investors are always safe because the watchdog checks them daily
context: The SEC Inspector General's 2009 post-mortem report found approximately six substantive complaints raising significant red flags about Madoff between 1992 and 2008. None was adequately investigated. Source: sec.gov (OIG Report No. 509, August 31, 2009).

question: In December 2008 the New York investor Bernie Madoff was arrested after admitting his investment firm was actually a giant Ponzi scheme. Madoff had been faking his returns for decades. Afterward the US Securities and Exchange Commission -- the government agency supposed to catch this kind of fraud -- wrote its own internal report on what its staff had missed. Which of these was one of the failures the SEC report actually named?
answer: Young staff were handed cases too complicated for their training
choices: Young staff were handed cases too complicated for their training
Senior investigators were fired for asking too many questions
The whole enforcement office was shut down for a year
The person reporting the fraud refused to talk to investigators
context: The OIG Report 509 (August 31, 2009) documented junior staff assignments, missed basic verification steps (a single call to DTCC would have revealed Madoff was not actually trading the volumes he claimed), and misunderstanding of the alleged strategy. Source: sec.gov OIG Report 509.

question: Bernie Madoff, the New York man later exposed as the biggest Ponzi-scheme fraudster in American history, was not some fringe operator. In the early 1990s he had held one of the most senior positions in the American stock market world -- a position that made him a respected figure in finance long before the fraud came out. Which senior role did Madoff hold at a major US stock market?
answer: Chairman of NASDAQ
choices: Chairman of NASDAQ
President of the New York Stock Exchange
Head of the Chicago Board Options Exchange
Chief Executive of AMEX
context: Madoff served as chairman of NASDAQ in the early 1990s -- an establishment credential that made SEC skepticism of a whistleblower's complaint about him structurally harder. Stigler's capture theory predicts exactly this pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Madoff.

question: For about eight years the American investigator Harry Markopolos, a math whiz turned fraud hunter, tried to warn the Securities and Exchange Commission that Bernie Madoff's Wall Street returns had to be fake. Nobody at the agency acted seriously on his math. In the end Madoff had to turn himself in during the 2008 crash. Markopolos then wrote a book about those long years of being ignored by regulators. Which phrase became the title of his book?
answer: No one would listen
choices: No one would listen
Everyone believed me at once
The regulators were quick to act
The suspect confessed on day one
context: Harry Markopolos, No One Would Listen: A True Financial Thriller (Wiley, 2010). The book documents the whole sequence from Markopolos's side, from his May 2000 discovery through Madoff's arrest. Source: wiley.com (Markopolos 2010).

question: When Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme collapsed in December 2008, news outlets reported the fraud at $65 billion. But that figure included years of fake profits Madoff had told his clients they had earned -- money that never actually existed. When investigators added up only the REAL money that investors had handed Madoff and lost, the number was much smaller. About how much real cash did Madoff's investors actually lose?
answer: About $18 billion
choices: About $18 billion
About $65 billion
About $650 million
About $6.5 trillion
context: Actual investor cash-in losses (principal) totaled approximately $18B, while the $65B figure included years of fictitious returns credited to statements. The Madoff Recovery Fund has recovered a substantial portion of the principal for victims. Source: madofftrustee.com (Picard trustee reports).

question: The US government wants people inside big companies to report fraud, but blowing the whistle can cost you your job. To make it worth the risk, the government pays whistleblowers a percentage of the fines it collects. Why does paying a percentage work better than a flat reward?
answer: The bigger the fraud they expose, the bigger their reward -- so they speak up sooner
choices: The bigger the fraud they expose, the bigger their reward -- so they speak up sooner
A flat reward is illegal under most federal laws
Percentages are cheaper for the government in every case
Percentages are easier to spell out in a written contract
context: The SEC Office of the Whistleblower (created in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act) offers 10-30% of monetary sanctions above $1M for actionable tips leading to enforcement action. It is an institutional attempt to align incentives with fraud detection. Source: sec.gov/whistleblower.

question: Bernie Madoff ran the biggest US investment fraud in history for over a decade. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which was supposed to catch him, got detailed written warnings and ignored them again and again. What usually explains that pattern at a regulator?
answer: The staff's own career incentives pulled them away from tough fraud detection
choices: The staff's own career incentives pulled them away from tough fraud detection
Madoff's family members were secretly working at the SEC
SEC staff genuinely believed Madoff's math was correct
The SEC had zero legal power to investigate Madoff
context: Stigler's 1971 capture theory predicts that regulators tend to identify with, defer to, and hire from established regulated figures. The SEC's staff incentive structure did not reward embarrassing a former NASDAQ chairman. Markopolos, an outsider, was on the wrong side of that capture. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); SEC OIG Report 509 (2009).

question: The Bernie Madoff Ponzi scheme was reported to the US Securities and Exchange Commission for years, in detailed math from Harry Markopolos, and the agency never seriously acted. The Madoff case teaches a public-choice way of thinking about regulators. When an agency gets repeated warnings about a well-connected person like Madoff and keeps doing nothing, what specific question should you ask about the regulators themselves?
answer: Whose specific career interests are served by NOT investigating this figure
choices: Whose specific career interests are served by NOT investigating this figure
Whether the whistleblower is entitled to a share of any eventual fine
Whether the regulator's paint scheme is up to date
Whether the whistleblower's college degree is from the right school
context: Stigler-style capture analysis: work out which specific decision-makers stand to lose or gain from an investigation. When the answer is that the decision-makers see mostly downside from investigating a well-connected figure, expect systematic under-enforcement. Source: Stigler (1971); Kwak, 'Cultural Capture and the Financial Crisis' (2013).

question: For 40 years, a US agency called the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) decided which airlines could fly which routes and how much they could charge. Flying was expensive and only wealthy Americans did it much. In 1978 President Jimmy Carter signed the Airline Deregulation Act. Congress let the airlines set their own prices and pick their own routes. What happened to ticket prices for regular people after that?
answer: They dropped, and many more people could afford to fly
choices: They dropped, and many more people could afford to fly
They rose sharply for everyone
They stayed exactly the same
Only rich people were allowed to fly at all
context: The CAB, created in 1938, controlled airline routes and fares until the Airline Deregulation Act (October 24, 1978, Carter). Real airfares fell dramatically over the next two decades. Source: brookings.edu (Kahn + Deregulation history).

question: For years, the US had strict rules telling airlines what to charge and where to fly. The government removed those rules in 1978. Prices fell and many more people could afford to fly. What is it called when the government takes rules away from an industry?
answer: Deregulation
choices: Deregulation
Nationalization
Taxation
Rationing
context: Alfred Kahn (1917-2010), a Cornell regulatory economist, chaired the CAB 1977-78 and led its dismantling. He is remembered as the father of airline deregulation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_E._Kahn.

question: In 1887 the United States Congress created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the ICC, meant to protect shippers and farmers from powerful railroad companies charging them ruinous rates. Historians combing the archives later found that the railroads had quietly lobbied for the ICC themselves. They hoped a friendly regulator would freeze rates high enough for existing carriers and block new rail lines from ever entering the business. What pattern is this?
answer: Regulatory capture, when the industry ends up running its own regulator
choices: Regulatory capture, when the industry ends up running its own regulator
Free competition between many small firms
A price war between rivals
A tariff on foreign goods
context: The ICC (1887) was the first modern US regulatory agency. Kolko's Triumph of Conservatism (Free Press, 1963) argued incumbent railroads lobbied for it to stabilize rates and prevent price-cutting competition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission.

question: The Federal Communications Commission, the FCC, is the United States agency that hands out radio and television broadcast licenses. Each license can be worth millions of dollars because it grants the holder a slice of the airwaves no rival can legally use. License holders then hire lobbyists in Washington to block new stations, slow the rollout of cable TV, and delay any new technology that might compete for viewers. What does this behavior show?
answer: Government-granted licenses can turn into protected privileges the holders fight to defend
choices: Government-granted licenses can turn into protected privileges the holders fight to defend
Free markets always keep prices low for consumers
New technologies always beat old ones automatically
Consumer demand alone decides who broadcasts what
context: The FCC was created by the 1934 Communications Act, replacing the earlier 1927 Federal Radio Commission. Broadcast-license politics is a classic capture case: cable TV was delayed for years by broadcaster opposition mediated through the FCC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission.

question: In 1978 the US Congress passed the Airline Deregulation Act, which ended the strict federal rules that had held airline ticket prices artificially high for decades. Fares tumbled and many more Americans could afford to fly. Two years later, in 1980, Congress passed a similar law for another industry that moves goods across the country on highways in big rigs. Which industry got deregulated in 1980?
answer: Trucking
choices: Trucking
Passenger rail
Ocean shipping
City buses
context: The Motor Carrier Act of 1980, signed July 1, 1980, deregulated interstate trucking rates and routes, ending decades of ICC-set trucking rates. Truckload shipping costs fell substantially over the following decade. Source: brookings.edu (Motor Carrier Act history).

question: A senior worker at a government agency spends years regulating a drug company, then quits to take a high-paying job at that same company. Later, someone from the company leaves and takes a job back at the agency. What is this back-and-forth pattern called?
answer: The revolving door
choices: The revolving door
The captured cage
The regulatory bridge
The industry pipeline
context: The revolving door: senior agency officials rotate into industry positions at companies they previously regulated. GAO studies (2007 and later) documented systematic migration between FDA reviewers and the pharmaceutical industry. Source: gao.gov (FDA post-employment reports).

question: In the years before the 2008 financial crash, two US federal bank agencies were supposed to watch how safely American banks were making home loans. Both missed the enormous risks piling up in mortgage-backed securities. Later Congressional investigations found their staff regularly rotated between the agencies and the banks they were supposed to police — the so-called 'revolving door.' Which pair of agencies gets the most blame?
answer: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC
choices: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC
The Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department
The Securities and Exchange Commission and the CFTC
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and HUD
context: The OCC (chartering and supervising national banks) and the FDIC (insuring deposits and supervising state non-Fed member banks) both faced heavy post-crisis criticism for capture and revolving-door personnel flows. Source: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report (2011).

question: The Chicago economist George Stigler wrote in 1971 about a pattern he saw again and again in Washington -- an agency created by Congress to police an industry (say, banking or trucking) ends up run mostly by people from that same industry, and its rules end up helping the industry more than the public. Stigler called this 'regulatory capture.' What is the most common reason it happens?
answer: The regulators come from and go back to the industry they oversee
choices: The regulators come from and go back to the industry they oversee
The industry secretly bribes every regulator with cash
The public loses interest and stops voting for reform
The agency runs out of money and shuts down
context: Marver Bernstein, Regulating Business by Independent Commission (Princeton University Press, 1955), introduced the four-stage life cycle: gestation, youth, maturity, and old age -- with capture occurring in the maturity phase. Source: press.princeton.edu (Bernstein 1955).

question: Three US agencies show the same story: the Interstate Commerce Commission for railroads, the Civil Aeronautics Board for airlines, and the early FCC for radio. Each was built for the public but ended up serving the industry. Which line best sums that story up?
answer: Industry incumbents captured the agency and used it to restrict entry by new competitors
choices: Industry incumbents captured the agency and used it to restrict entry by new competitors
The agency's staff turned against the industry and imposed heavy fines each year
Congress abolished each agency within a decade of its founding
Consumers seized the regulatory process through mass grassroots organizing
context: The common thread across the ICC, CAB, and FCC: agencies whose original public-interest justification gradually gave way to protecting incumbent firms against new entrants. Stigler's 1971 paper formalized the pattern as theory. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kolko, Triumph of Conservatism (1963).

question: In 1971 the American economist George Stigler, later a Nobel laureate at the University of Chicago, published a famous paper arguing that regulatory agencies often get 'captured' — that they quietly stop working for the public and start working for the industry they were set up to police. Without asking opinions or reading minds, which single visible behavior of an agency is the strongest sign that it has been captured?
answer: The agency blocks new companies from entering while protecting the profits of existing firms
choices: The agency blocks new companies from entering while protecting the profits of existing firms
The agency's budget grows year over year
The agency writes detailed technical rules
The agency has a large research staff
context: Capture is measured by outcomes, not intent. If regulation systematically raises incumbent profits and blocks new competitors, the regulation is functioning like an industry-serving barrier, whatever its stated purpose. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: In 1971 the Chicago economist George Stigler published a paper called 'The Theory of Economic Regulation.' He argued that US regulatory agencies get captured by the very industries they are meant to police. Over the following decades, empirical scholars have tested his capture theory across dozens of US regulatory agencies -- from banking to trucking to airlines to communications. What has the broad pattern of that half-century of research been?
answer: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
choices: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
Stigler's theory holds only for transportation regulators, not others
Stigler's theory has been refuted by studies of environmental agencies
Stigler's theory applies only in states with weak public-service ethics
context: From transportation to broadcasting to banking to occupational licensing, empirical work has confirmed the Stigler-Peltzman pattern of incumbent-serving regulation. The theory is now standard even outside the Chicago tradition. Source: Levine + Forrence, Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization (1990); Carpenter + Moss, Preventing Regulatory Capture (Cambridge 2014).

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, writing in 1850, taught that every policy has a 'seen' effect right in front of you and an 'unseen' effect that never gets to happen. A city council plans to freeze rents on existing apartments to keep them affordable. The seen effect is that today's tenants pay less each month. What is the main unseen effect on future housing?
answer: Apartment buildings a developer would have built are never built because future rents are capped below construction cost
choices: Apartment buildings a developer would have built are never built because future rents are capped below construction cost
Apartment buildings already in place are seized by the state under compulsory-purchase orders
Apartment buildings switch to office use because commercial leases pay more per square foot
Apartment buildings raise their prices to cover a mandatory rent-control administrative fee
context: The classic price-ceiling result: capping future rents below construction cost stops the pipeline of new buildings; the units the city never gets are the Bastiat UNSEEN. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control.

question: In a large city, the government passes a strict law: 'No landlord may ever raise the rent on any apartment.' Twenty years later, the old apartment buildings are falling apart from neglected repairs, and no new apartment building has been built anywhere in the city during those twenty years. Why did no builder ever start a new apartment project?
answer: There was no way to make money building them, so no one bothered
choices: There was no way to make money building them, so no one bothered
The government forgot to let them
The city ran out of land
Builders all moved to another country
context: Lindbeck's line: 'In many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city -- except for bombing.' The bite of it is that a socialist Swedish economist said it. Source: Lindbeck, The Political Economy of the New Left, 1971.

question: A big American city passes a rent-control law that keeps apartment rents low and only lets landlords raise them a tiny amount each year, even when costs like heating oil and property taxes are rising fast. Austrian economists warned this was a classic price-ceiling mistake: fix the price below the market and shortages follow. Over many years in a rent-controlled city, what does economics predict will happen to the number of new apartments being built and to the quality of the old ones?
answer: Fewer new apartments get built, and old ones fall into disrepair
choices: Fewer new apartments get built, and old ones fall into disrepair
More new apartments get built because demand goes up
Rents fall for everyone in the whole state
Landlords compete to fix up their buildings
context: The ETPA of 1974 is the legal foundation of NYC's modern rent-stabilization regime; roughly 966,000 apartments were covered as of the 2023 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey. Source: NYC HPD 2023 Housing Vacancy Survey.

question: Sweden's capital city Stockholm has run a strict rent-control system for decades. Under the rules, a renter cannot just find an apartment on the open market -- the city keeps a public waiting list for a first-hand rental (the direct kind of lease that comes with legal rent-controlled terms). By the mid-2010s, that waiting list had grown to an astonishing average length for a first-hand rental in central Stockholm. About how long was the average wait?
answer: About 20 years
choices: About 20 years
About 5 years
About 2 years
About 6 months
context: Stockholm's Bostadsformedlingen (municipal housing office) published waits above 20 years for central-city apartments through the mid-2010s; widely reported in SVT and The Economist 2015. Source: bostad.stockholm.se.

question: A 2019 paper by Diamond, McQuade, and Qian on San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion found landlords cut rental supply by about 15 percent -- some converted units to condos, some tore them down. What did Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck famously say rent control is the most efficient known way to do to a city, apart from bombing?
answer: Destroy it
choices: Destroy it
Redistribute wealth in it
Raise its tax revenue
Attract new residents to it
context: Diamond-McQuade-Qian, 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality,' AER 2019: San Francisco's 1994 expansion caused a 15% cut in rental supply from affected landlords, deepening the shortage the policy meant to fix. Source: American Economic Review 109(9).

question: When strict rent control has been tried — in New York, Paris, and Stockholm at various points in the 1900s — a specific black-market side payment appears in every serious rent-controlled market. A would-be tenant slips upfront cash to the landlord, or to the outgoing tenant, just to secure the covered lease at the frozen rent. What is this side payment called in the rental market?
answer: Key money
choices: Key money
Cover fee
Lock deposit
Occupancy premium
context: 'Key money' is the standard term for the covert side payment used to acquire a rent-controlled lease; the Fraser Institute's 1981 collection Rent Control: Myths and Realities documents the pattern across cities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_money.

question: In 2020 the city of Berlin passed a five-year law, called the Mietendeckel or 'rent lid,' that froze rents on about 1.5 million apartments across the German capital. Germany's Federal Constitutional Court struck it down within a year, ruling that a single city had no authority to override national housing law. But suppose the court had let the freeze stand. What is the predictable long-run economic problem with a hard rent freeze?
answer: Landlords stop building or repairing apartments, so the rental supply shrinks
choices: Landlords stop building or repairing apartments, so the rental supply shrinks
Landlords raise the quality of every apartment to justify the frozen rent
Renters immediately move out to smaller cities to save money
The city instantly runs out of construction workers to build apartments
context: The Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe struck down Berlin's Mietendeckel on April 15 2021, ruling rent regulation was a federal not a state matter; Berlin tenants suddenly owed back-rent for the freeze period. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Mietendeckel.

question: Milton Friedman's Bastiat-style closing move on rent control names the specific reasoning fallacy behind the policy in one phrase. Friedman wrote: 'The most important single central fact about a free market is that no exchange takes place unless both parties benefit.' Applied to rent control, whom does the policy help and whom does it harm most?
answer: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
choices: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
Helps all tenants equally; harms only speculators and non-resident landlords
Helps first-time buyers; harms only established homeowners
Helps landlords by stabilizing income; harms the general tax base
context: This is the classic seen/unseen split for a price ceiling: the incumbent tenant is SEEN paying less; the would-be tenant who never appears on any waiting list because the building was never built is UNSEEN. Source: Friedman & Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), price-ceilings chapter.

question: The Fraser Institute's 1981 book 'Rent Control: Myths and Realities,' edited by Walter Block and Edgar Olsen, says price caps on rent lead to the same long-run results in every city that tries them. Which outcome does the book call the most damaging over decades?
answer: Collapse of new rental construction combined with deteriorating maintenance of existing stock
choices: Collapse of new rental construction combined with deteriorating maintenance of existing stock
Immediate uniform reduction in average rents across all neighborhoods
Redistribution of rental supply toward higher-income neighborhoods
Complete elimination of the private rental market within five years
context: The Fraser collection's cross-country evidence: capped future rents kill new construction, and capped current rents remove the incentive for landlords to maintain existing units. The city ends the decade with a smaller and shabbier housing stock than it started with. Source: fraserinstitute.org (Block & Olsen, Rent Control: Myths and Realities, 1981).

question: By Bastiat's method, the Stockholm 20-year waitlist and the New York cracked-plaster walk-up point at the same unseen cost -- the family that never got the apartment. What do economists call the queue-and-shortage outcome any binding price ceiling produces?
answer: Non-price rationing
choices: Non-price rationing
Producer surplus
Consumer sovereignty
Deadweight subsidy
