context: A binding price ceiling forces the market to allocate scarce units by NON-PRICE means: waiting lists, insider connections, key money, discrimination. The seen tenant paid less; the unseen family got nothing. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics, chapter on price ceilings.

question: When the US government tells the Federal Reserve to print a huge pile of new dollars, the new money does NOT magically land in every American's wallet on the same day. It flows into big banks and big companies first, through loans and bond purchases. Those first-receivers spend the new money while store prices are still old prices. By the time regular workers get their paychecks, prices at the grocery store and the rent office have already climbed. Who loses out in this chain?
answer: Regular workers, who get the money last after prices have already climbed
choices: Regular workers, who get the money last after prices have already climbed
The bankers who got the money first
The big companies that got new loans
Nobody -- everyone gets equal amounts
context: Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734) was an Irish-born banker who lived in Paris. His trading in the Mississippi Bubble made his fortune; his shorting of it made him a rare survivor. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: The Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon wrote his big economics book in French around 1730 while living in Paris. It was passed hand-to-hand among French economists for years before finally being printed in 1755, over two decades after his death. In English it is known as 'Essay on the Nature of Trade in General.' What is its original French title?
answer: Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General
choices: Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General
Traite de Politique Economique
Discours sur l'Economie Politique
Reflexions sur la Formation des Richesses
context: The essay circulated in manuscript for two decades and was finally published in 1755, twenty-one years after Cantillon's mysterious 1734 death by house fire in London. Source: Grokipedia 'Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1730s an Irish-French banker named Richard Cantillon wrote an essay explaining how new money moves through an economy. His key insight was that money creation is NOT neutral -- new gold and silver from the mines, or new bills from a printer, does not raise all prices in every corner of the country at the same moment. In Cantillon's framing, where does new money enter?
answer: At specific points, benefiting first-receivers who can spend at old prices
choices: At specific points, benefiting first-receivers who can spend at old prices
Uniformly across the whole economy in a single moment
Only in the country producing the precious metals
Only at the seasonal harvest time
context: In Cantillon's day, mines and government-favored merchants received new coins first. They could buy at old prices before prices adjusted. Late-receivers -- wage earners, savers -- paid the new higher prices with old wages. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: The Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon wrote in the 1730s that new money helps whoever receives it first -- they get to spend it while prices are still low -- and hurts savers and wage-earners who receive the money last, after prices have risen. Modern Austrian-school economists like Murray Rothbard and Jesus Huerta de Soto revived this idea and gave it a name honoring Cantillon. What do they call this pattern?
answer: The Cantillon effect
choices: The Cantillon effect
The Wicksell effect
The Fisher effect
The Balassa effect
context: The Cantillon effect is the standard Austrian label for the redistribution from late-receivers to first-receivers of newly created money. Whether the money is 18th-century Peruvian silver or 21st-century Fed reserves, the mechanism is the same. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: The 18th-century Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon noticed that new money never enters the economy evenly — it lands somewhere first, and whoever holds it first gets to spend it before prices adjust. When the Federal Reserve creates new reserves today, it does so by buying Treasury bonds from a small handpicked group of Wall Street banks known as primary dealers. Whose accounts do those brand-new reserves land in first?
answer: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
choices: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
In household checking accounts nationwide
In Treasury tax-refund payments to individuals
In the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation reserves
context: When the Fed buys a bond it credits the primary dealer's reserve account. First-receivers are banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, asset holders. Consumer prices adjust years later when velocity recovers. Source: Grokipedia 'Primary dealer' (2026-09-05).

question: Writing in Paris around 1730, the Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon noticed that when a king or a bank prints extra money, the new money does not raise all prices at once. It reaches the first borrowers and investors early, then flows through merchants, and only later shows up in what everyday shoppers pay for bread and rent. From 2020 to 2024 asset prices jumped first in 2020-21 during the pandemic Fed rescue, then consumer prices caught up in 2021-23. Which part of that modern pattern best matches Cantillon's 1730s account?
answer: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
choices: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
The complete absence of any asset-price effect
The immediate uniform response of all prices
The concentration of the effect on export prices only
context: Cantillon explicitly described the timing: new money enters at specific points, those points enjoy the old prices, prices then adjust over months and years, late-receivers pay the higher prices with wages set at the old level. The modern QE-then-CPI sequence follows the pattern precisely. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: A merchant named Richard Cantillon wrote an early economics essay around 1730. He noticed something that still bears his name: when new money is created, it does not reach everyone at the same time. Who benefits most from being closest to the new money?
answer: The people who receive the new money first, before prices have risen
choices: The people who receive the new money first, before prices have risen
The people who receive the new money last, after prices have adjusted
Everyone benefits equally, since money spreads evenly through an economy
Only foreigners benefit, because new money always flows across borders first
context: Rothbard's 1995 An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought called Cantillon 'the founder of economic science' -- an unusual honor coming from an Austrian scholar, since it displaces both Adam Smith and Carl Menger from that title. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective (1995).

question: The Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon, writing his economics manuscript in French around 1730, gave the world a new word for the risk-taking business owner. Modern economics still uses it for the person who puts up her own money right now to buy raw materials, tools, and labor, hoping to sell a finished product later — knowing she may lose everything if the market price falls before she can sell. What is that word?
answer: Entrepreneur
choices: Entrepreneur
Capitalist
Rentier
Financier
context: Cantillon's Essai introduced 'entrepreneur' as the systematic risk-bearer in the market. Modern Austrian economics -- especially Israel Kirzner -- treats this Cantillonian concept as central to how markets discover new information. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: Three hundred years ago the economist Richard Cantillon pointed out that new money always enters the economy at one specific place first — and whoever gets it first can spend it before prices rise elsewhere. Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard press this old insight hard against modern central banks like the Federal Reserve. Which pattern do they say Cantillon's idea exposes?
answer: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
choices: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
Central-bank money creation is distributionally neutral across all social groups
Central-bank money creation always causes immediate consumer-price inflation
Central-bank money creation has no effect on asset prices
context: The Cantillon-effect analysis explains why QE lifts asset prices for existing owners before consumer prices rise for everyone. It is not a bug of the modern system; it is a structural feature the Austrian tradition traces back to the 1730s. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995).

question: The Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon, who first named the entrepreneur and mapped how new money spreads through an economy, died in London in May 1734 under circumstances historians still debate. His townhouse burned to the ground, and his body was found inside so badly damaged that some investigators believed the fire had been set to hide a killing. Which unresolved suspicion has surrounded his death ever since?
answer: An insurance-fraud murder by a dismissed servant
choices: An insurance-fraud murder by a dismissed servant
A political assassination by John Law loyalists
A heart attack while asleep unrelated to the fire
A duel gone wrong on the London docks
context: Cantillon's death by house fire remains unsolved. Contemporary accounts suggest a dismissed servant may have set the fire to cover an insurance-fraud murder. The economist most famous for shorting a bubble may have been killed for money by someone who worked for him. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1960s the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) was given a stricter safety rule for new medicines. After that, the agency began taking many extra years to approve each new drug. Fewer bad drugs got through — a real gain. But the delay had a hidden cost that most people never see. What is the hidden cost of slower approvals?
answer: Sick people die waiting for medicines that would have saved them
choices: Sick people die waiting for medicines that would have saved them
Drug companies pay less tax
Doctors run out of pens
Hospitals get more crowded on Tuesdays
context: Sam Peltzman, 'An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments' (Journal of Political Economy, September 1973). Peltzman estimated lives lost from delayed approval of effective drugs significantly exceeded lives saved from blocking ineffective ones. Source: jstor.org (Peltzman 1973).

question: In the late 1950s a European sleeping pill called thalidomide was given to pregnant women in West Germany, Britain, and dozens of other countries to calm morning sickness. It caused terrible birth defects in more than 10,000 babies before being pulled in 1961. After that disaster, the United States tightened its drug approval rules sharply through the Food and Drug Administration. What is the trade-off of stricter drug rules?
answer: Fewer bad drugs get through, but good drugs also arrive much slower
choices: Fewer bad drugs get through, but good drugs also arrive much slower
Drug prices always drop
No one ever gets sick again
The government makes more money from drug taxes
context: The thalidomide birth-defect crisis (1957-62, mostly in Europe) prompted Congress to pass the Kefauver-Harris Amendments in 1962, requiring proof of efficacy for FDA approval. Source: fda.gov (Kefauver-Harris Amendments history).

question: In 1973 the American economist Sam Peltzman studied how the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendment had changed the US Food and Drug Administration. Peltzman named the seen benefit right away: fewer thalidomide-style birth-defect tragedies, because riskier drugs were now caught in longer trials. Then he named the unseen cost that no newspaper covered. What did his 1973 study identify as that unseen cost?
answer: Patients dying while safe-and-effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue
choices: Patients dying while safe-and-effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue
Pharmaceutical company profits reduced modestly
Government spending on FDA staff increased slightly
Universities hired more clinical-trial researchers
context: The Bastiat SEEN vs UNSEEN move applied to drug regulation: the prevented tragedies are visible; the patients who died waiting for approvals of drugs available in Europe or Japan are largely invisible. Peltzman argued the invisible category dominated in aggregate. Source: Peltzman, JPE (1973).

question: A dying patient wants to try an experimental drug that has passed early safety tests but is still waiting on full government approval, which can take years. A 2018 federal law finally lets patients like this try the drug. What is the moral argument for the law?
answer: A dying patient has little to lose and should get to decide the risk for themselves
choices: A dying patient has little to lose and should get to decide the risk for themselves
Only the government should ever decide what any patient may try
Drug companies should be forced to give the drug away for free
Approving drugs faster is always dangerous
context: Alex Tabarrok (George Mason University) has been a leading academic advocate for FDA reform, including chairing the right-to-try movement. The Right to Try Act was signed by President Trump on May 30, 2018. Source: fda.gov (Right to Try).

question: Some patients have a disease that will kill them and no approved treatment left to try. A newer experimental drug exists, but the Food and Drug Administration has not yet approved it. If those patients are simply told to wait for approval, what is the practical outcome for them?
answer: Death
choices: Death
Safety
Legal protection
Insurance coverage
context: The right-to-try move: absent right-to-try, a terminally-ill patient with no approved option is not being 'protected' by delay -- they are dying while decisions are made elsewhere. The default is death, not safety. Source: Tabarrok, 'Assessing the FDA via the Anomaly of Off-Label Drug Prescribing' (Independent Review 2000).

question: The California oncologist Vinay Prasad, a cancer doctor who studies how new drugs really work, argues that the Food and Drug Administration, the FDA, often approves cancer drugs through fast-track programs based only on lab-test wins — like a tumor shrinking on a scan. But those lab wins may not translate into patients actually living longer or feeling better. What is Prasad's main worry?
answer: That short-term test results are treated as proof the drug saves lives, when they are not
choices: That short-term test results are treated as proof the drug saves lives, when they are not
That the drugs are approved too slowly by the agency
That approvals are given only to old drugs, never new ones
That drug companies fund too little research on side effects
context: Vinay Prasad's book Malignant: How Bad Policy and Bad Evidence Harm People with Cancer (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2020) argues that accelerated FDA approval on surrogate endpoints has often failed to deliver actual survival improvements. Source: jhupbooks.press.jhu.edu (Prasad 2020).

question: The United States Food and Drug Administration, the FDA, sometimes okays a new drug based on a 'surrogate marker' — a lab number like a tumor shrinking on a scan, or a blood-test level dropping — that looks encouraging but has not been shown to make real patients live longer or feel better. The California oncologist Vinay Prasad has argued forcefully against this shortcut. What is the strongest case against okaying drugs on those lab numbers alone?
answer: Judge drugs by results, not by intentions or surrogate markers
choices: Judge drugs by results, not by intentions or surrogate markers
Abolish the agency and let markets rate every drug on their own
Move drug regulation into the Department of Defense
Require every doctor in the country to approve each prescription
context: Prasad's move is not 'less FDA' but 'better FDA': require the outcome that matters (survival for oncology drugs) rather than proxy measures (tumor shrinkage) that often do not translate. It is the results-not-intentions frame Friedman and Sowell repeatedly pressed. Source: Prasad, Malignant (JHU Press 2020).

question: The American economist Milton Friedman argued that a drug regulator like the US Food and Drug Administration faces two very different mistakes. It can approve a drug that turns out to hurt people — a tragedy the newspapers cover in painful detail, name by name. Or it can block a drug that would have saved lives — a tragedy no one ever sees, because the saved lives never happen. Which of those two mistakes is much harder for the public to notice?
answer: Blocking a good drug -- the people who would have been saved are never seen
choices: Blocking a good drug -- the people who would have been saved are never seen
Approving a bad drug -- patients quietly recover with no news story
Both mistakes get equal coverage in every major newspaper
Neither mistake matters, since regulators fix them within a week
context: Merck withdrew Vioxx (rofecoxib) on September 30, 2004 after evidence of increased cardiovascular risk. It became the canonical Type-I error case in FDA reform debates. Source: fda.gov (Vioxx withdrawal history).

question: Imagine a promising cancer drug that could save many thousands of lives. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) takes ten full years to approve it. During that decade the pill already exists and already works in trials, but it cannot legally reach any patient. The benefit of caution is easy to see — no bad drug slips through the review. choices: The lives lost by patients who would have been saved if the drug had arrived sooner
The paperwork burden on drug-company lawyers
The parking costs at government office buildings
The extra weekend hours for federal regulators
context: The 21st Century Cures Act was signed December 13, 2016. It broadened accelerated-approval pathways, modernized trial designs, and increased funding for the NIH and FDA. Source: congress.gov (Public Law 114-255).

question: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approves or blocks new medicines. If it approves a bad drug, people get hurt and everyone notices. If it blocks a good drug, patients die waiting — and the deaths never make the news. An honest scorecard must count what?
answer: Both the seen mistake (bad drug approved) and the unseen one (good drug blocked)
choices: Both the seen mistake (bad drug approved) and the unseen one (good drug blocked)
Only the interests of drug companies
Only the interests of currently healthy voters
Only the cost of paying the agency's staff
context: The synthesis: the SEEN cost of approving a dangerous drug is politically overwhelming; the UNSEEN cost of not approving a lifesaving drug is politically invisible. Honest cost-benefit accounts for both, which is Peltzman 1973 as a live diagnostic in 2020s FDA debates. Source: Peltzman (1973); Prasad (2020); Tabarrok (2000-).

question: In December 2020 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) let the first coronavirus vaccines reach people months before finishing its normal full-approval process. This fast-track path is called Emergency Use Authorization. What is the built-in tradeoff of using this kind of authority?

Slower access with less data than the normal path
Guaranteed complete data before any patient receives the medicine
context: Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) allowed COVID-19 vaccines to reach the population starting December 11, 2020, months before full BLA approval. It is the highest-stakes real-world case of accelerated authorization in the FDA's history. Source: fda.gov (Emergency Use Authorization).

question: Under the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, millions of Soviet citizens were sent to Gulag prison camps in Siberia or shot in political 'purges' that targeted anyone Stalin's police suspected of disloyalty. question: Under the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin, from 1936 to 1938, the secret police arrested and killed huge numbers of Soviet citizens in what became known as the Great Purge or Great Terror. Many of the victims were Stalin's own loyal Communist Party members — old revolutionaries, generals, and factory managers. The Soviet economy grew faster than every free country

question: In 1968 the British historian Robert Conquest published 'The Great Terror,' the first serious Western study of Joseph Stalin's Soviet purges. question: The British historian Robert Conquest published 'The Great Terror' in 1968, a landmark book that put Stalin's personal ambition and enormous purge death tolls at the center of Soviet history. Through the 1970s and 1980s a rival academic school in Western universities argued Conquest had overcounted the dead and given Stalin too much personal blame, saying local pressures and bureaucratic chaos mattered more. question: In 1968 the British historian Robert Conquest published The Great Terror. He estimated Stalin's execution and gulag death tolls using smuggled documents and defector accounts. question: Beyond his 1968 book 'The Great Terror' on Stalin's purges, the British historian Robert Conquest wrote a second major work in 1986 — a full history of the 1932-33 Ukrainian famine that Stalin's forced grain seizures deliberately caused, starving millions of peasants to death. The Rise of Nations
The Fall of the Kulaks
The Politics of Hunger

Conquest also wrote 'Reflections on a Ravaged Century' (1999). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: Robert Conquest was the British-American historian who exposed the true scale of Stalin's mass murder — his 1968 book 'The Great Terror' documented the millions killed in the Soviet purges, and his 1986 'Harvest of Sorrow' laid bare the Ukrainian famine Stalin engineered. question: In the United States the Federal Reserve is the central bank. It can create brand-new dollars whenever the Treasury or Congress needs more money to spend. question: Ron Paul was a Texas congressman who spent decades in Washington fighting the Federal Reserve — the central bank he blamed for the 2008 crash. Return to Gold
Money and Freedom

question: A Texas congressman named Ron Paul served in the US House on and off from the 1970s until 2013 and ran for president three times. question: In 2003 the Texas congressman Ron Paul stood on the US House floor and warned that a huge housing bubble was building across the country. question: In February 2009, just months after the 2008 financial crash, the Texas congressman Ron Paul filed a bill called the Federal Reserve Transparency Act. question: In 2009 a bill in the US House of Representatives called for a full public audit of the Federal Reserve. It picked up unusually broad support before being scaled back in the Senate. Out of 435 House members, roughly how many signed on as co-sponsors?

question: In 2009 Ron Paul, the Texas congressman and longtime critic of the Federal Reserve, published 'End the Fed'. His book made three main charges against America's central bank: that it violated the Constitution, that printing money out of thin air was morally wrong, and that it damaged the real economy. question: The Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama, is the leading center of Austrian-school economics in the United States. context: Murray Rothbard died in 1995. The Mises Institute's Rothbard Medal of Freedom is awarded to those who have advanced Austrian economics and libertarian thought. Ron Paul received it in 2011. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: The Texas congressman Ron Paul's biggest political legacy is not any single bill that passed. It is the shift he caused in what Republican politicians and primary voters treated as a normal view of the Federal Reserve. Before his 2008 and 2012 presidential campaigns, Fed-critical arguments were a tiny fringe view inside the party. Afterward, candidates who wanted to audit or rein in the Fed could win primary debates. Which recognition does this ladder press?
answer: Prior to Ron Paul, Fed-critical positions were confined to fringes; after Ron Paul, they became a mainstream Republican-primary position
choices: Prior to Ron Paul, Fed-critical positions were confined to fringes; after Ron Paul, they became a mainstream Republican-primary position
Ron Paul had no lasting effect on Republican monetary policy
Ron Paul's positions were adopted by Democrats but rejected by Republicans
Ron Paul's audit bills were fully enacted into law during the Obama presidency
context: Fed criticism before Ron Paul lived among monetarists and Ayn Rand followers. After his three decades in the House and three presidential runs, hard-money views became a normal Republican-primary stance. His son Rand Paul, a Kentucky senator since 2011, carries the campaign forward with HR 24 in the 118th Congress. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: Ron Paul's Audit the Fed campaign rested on a specific constitutional argument he made for decades. Article I Section 8 of the US Constitution gives Congress the power 'to coin money' and 'regulate the value thereof.' But the Federal Reserve, created in 1913, is an independent agency Congress cannot directly steer. Which argument did Paul press against that arrangement?
answer: Congress's Article I Section 8 monetary authority cannot legitimately be delegated to an independent agency
choices: Congress's Article I Section 8 monetary authority cannot legitimately be delegated to an independent agency
The Federal Reserve was explicitly authorized by the Constitution's Preamble
The Tenth Amendment reserves monetary authority to the states
The Sixteenth Amendment implicitly authorizes central banking
context: The constitutional case: Article I Section 8 assigns to Congress the power 'to coin Money, regulate the Value thereof, and of foreign Coin.' Ron Paul argues this authority cannot be delegated wholesale to the Federal Reserve without amending the Constitution. Source: US Constitution, Article I Section 8; Paul, End the Fed (2009).

question: In 1960 the American economist Ronald Coase argued that pollution problems can often be solved by clear property rights. Picture a big factory that keeps dumping black smoke onto a nearby farmer's field and ruining his crops each summer. Suppose the farmer legally owns the right to clean air over his own land. Under Coase's reasoning, what can he do about the factory?
answer: Sue the factory, or charge them a fee to keep polluting
choices: Sue the factory, or charge them a fee to keep polluting
Nothing -- smoke is free
Only the government can act
Move his farm to another country
context: Ronald Coase (1910-2013) won the 1991 Nobel 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: Markets and prices help millions of strangers trade and work together across the whole world. So here is a puzzle: why do companies exist at all? Why don't workers just get hired one small task at a time, in a brand new deal for every single job? The British economist Ronald Coase asked exactly this in a 1937 paper.
answer: Because it costs time and effort to keep making new deals for every task
choices: Because it costs time and effort to keep making new deals for every task
Because the government requires it
Because workers can't sell things to each other
Because prices always change too slowly
context: 'The Nature of the Firm' (Economica, November 1937), written while Coase was still at Dundee. It launched transaction-cost economics. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Coase 1937).

question: In 1937 the young British economist Ronald Coase asked a puzzling question: if markets are so good at coordinating people, why do firms exist at all? Why don't people just hire strangers by the hour for every single task? Coase noticed that using the market has hidden costs — finding partners, writing contracts, checking work, enforcing deals. A firm forms when doing a job in-house is cheaper than paying those hidden costs again and again. What did Coase call these hidden costs?
answer: Transaction costs
choices: Transaction costs
Marginal costs
Opportunity costs
Sunk costs
context: Transaction costs is Coase's coinage for the costs of using the price mechanism. Where in-house costs are lower, firms replace market transactions with command relationships. The firm's size is where the two costs meet. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase wrote a famous 1937 paper called 'The Nature of the Firm' asking why businesses exist. In 1960 he wrote a second paper that reshaped how economists think about spillover harms like factory pollution or a noisy neighbor. What is the title of that second paper?
answer: The Problem of Social Cost
choices: The Problem of Social Cost
The Federal Communications Commission
The Marginal Cost Controversy
The Nature of the Firm
context: 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960) is one of the most-cited economics papers ever written. It launched law and economics as a field. Source: chicagounbound.uchicago.edu (Coase 1960).

question: Before 1960 most economists followed Arthur Pigou, an English economist who taught at Cambridge. Pigou said that when a factory's smoke harmed a neighbor, the state should tax the harm — a 'Pigouvian tax'. In 1960 Ronald Coase, another British economist, published 'The Problem of Social Cost' and gave a very different answer, as long as the cost of bargaining between the two parties was low. What was Coase's claim?
answer: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
choices: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
The state should immediately shut down the factory
The neighbor should be forced to move at government expense
The government should build a rival factory to compete on pollution
context: Coase's insight: when parties can negotiate, they will bargain to the outcome that maximizes joint value, regardless of who initially holds the legal right. The initial rights determine WHO PAYS, not the final allocation. Source: Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960).

question: The British economist Ronald Coase studied fights between neighbors. Picture a factory whose smoke drifts onto a nearby farmer's cattle. Coase argued that the final outcome tends to be about the same as long as both sides can bargain cheaply — no matter which side the law happens to give the right to first. In Coase's view, what matters most?
answer: That the two sides can bargain cheaply, not who is given the right first
choices: That the two sides can bargain cheaply, not who is given the right first
That the government must always pick a side and force the other to obey
That the factory must be shut down no matter what
That the farmer must always move away from the factory
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase theorem' in his 1966 Theory of Price textbook. Coase himself was ambivalent about the honorific and worried the theorem was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: Ronald Coase, the British economist who wrote 'The Problem of Social Cost' in 1960, often complained that readers misread his paper. Critics claimed he had said the state should never step in when factories cause harm. Coase himself insisted that was wrong, especially when many people are affected and bargaining among them all is impossible. What did Coase actually say about cases where bargaining costs are high?
answer: Government intervention can be justified, but its own transaction costs must be included
choices: Government intervention can be justified, but its own transaction costs must be included
Nothing can be done and the parties must accept the outcome
The market always still finds an efficient solution regardless
Only judicial rulings, never legislation, are appropriate
context: Coase's actual argument: compare like to like. When private bargaining is too costly, government intervention may be superior -- provided the analysis honestly counts the transaction costs of government administration too. Source: Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960), final section.

question: The British-born economist Ronald Coase spent most of his career at the University of Chicago and won the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics. At age 100, in 2012, he co-wrote his final big book with his younger colleague Ning Wang. The book traced one huge Asian country's shift away from Maoist central planning toward markets after Deng Xiaoping's 1978 reforms. Which country's post-1978 economy did Coase and Wang cover?
answer: China
choices: China
India
Vietnam
Chile
context: How China Became Capitalist (Palgrave Macmillan, 2012), co-authored with Ning Wang. Coase was 100 at publication and 102 at his death in 2013. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase.

question: In his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm, the British-born economist Ronald Coase asked a question no one else had bothered with: why do firms exist at all? He pointed out that work happens in two very different settings. Outside a firm, prices and market bargains coordinate strangers to trade. Inside a firm, an employee mostly just does what a manager tells them to do. What mostly does the coordinating inside a firm?
answer: Command relationships between manager and employee
choices: Command relationships between manager and employee
Continuous auctions among all employees
Random assignment of tasks by lottery
Government dictate over daily operations
context: Inside a firm a manager instructs an employee what to do. Between firms, prices coordinate. Coase's question: why draw the line here rather than there? His answer: transaction costs. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: The British-born economist Ronald Coase wrote two landmark papers — The Nature of the Firm in 1937 and The Problem of Social Cost in 1960. Together they reframed debates that had seemed like a simple choice between free markets on one side and government regulation on the other. Instead of asking which side wins in theory, Coase asked something else. What common analytical move do the two papers share?
answer: They compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
choices: They compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
They assume all transaction costs are zero for tractability
They favor central planning over private ordering
They apply mathematical topology to price theory
context: The Coase move: never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative. Firms, markets, private bargains, and government all have their own transaction costs. Comparative institutional analysis must count them all. Source: Coase, Essays on Economics and Economists (Chicago 1994).

question: Around 2011 a young American named Ross Ulbricht built a hidden marketplace on the internet called the Silk Road. He put it on the Tor network, so shoppers could only reach it through a special browser that hid their location. On the site, people bought and sold drugs and forged papers with no real names and no credit cards. To keep the payments hard to trace, what kind of money did shoppers use?
answer: Bitcoin
choices: Bitcoin
US dollars
Gold coins
Personal checks
context: Ross Ulbricht (born 1984) founded Silk Road in early 2011. Charlie Shrem ran BitInstant and later served prison time on separate charges; Roger Ver was an early Bitcoin evangelist; Cody Wilson ran the 3D-printed-gun project Defense Distributed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Ross Ulbricht ran Silk Road, a hidden online marketplace where buyers used Bitcoin to shop out of sight of the police. He signed his messages 'Dread Pirate Roberts' — a name from the movie 'The Princess Bride', where one pirate name gets passed from person to person so no one can ever catch the real pirate. Why would a criminal want a name that works like that?
answer: So investigators can't be sure the person they catch is the real founder
choices: So investigators can't be sure the person they catch is the real founder
So he could win a movie-fan award
So his mom could find him easily
Because his real name was taken online
context: Ulbricht used the pseudonym Dread Pirate Roberts (DPR), from The Princess Bride (1987), where the title passes between wearers. The other names are unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Ross Ulbricht was the young American who built the Silk Road, a hidden Tor-network marketplace where people bought drugs with Bitcoin. On October 1, 2013 US federal agents in San Francisco were about to arrest him. His laptop was open and unlocked; if he closed the lid, the disk encryption would lock the whole case away forever. The agents had to grab it fast in a quiet public place. Where did the arrest happen?
answer: the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library
choices: the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library
the outdoor patio of the Bello Cafe coffee shop in the San Francisco Mission District
the third-floor entryway of his rented apartment on Hickory Street in San Francisco
the international-arrivals lobby at San Francisco International Airport terminal one
context: The arrest took place October 1, 2013 in the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library, with Ulbricht's laptop open and unencrypted. The coffee-shop and apartment guesses are common misremembers; the airport was not involved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: On October 1, 2013 US federal agents were about to arrest Ross Ulbricht, the young founder of the hidden Silk Road Bitcoin marketplace, inside a quiet San Francisco public library. His open laptop had strong full-disk encryption. If he closed the lid or locked the screen even for a moment, the agents would never read the drive or prove that he was the Silk Road boss. What did the agents do at the moment of the arrest to keep him from locking the running laptop?
answer: physically distracted him to keep him from locking the running laptop
choices: physically distracted him to keep him from locking the running laptop
used a court-ordered decryption key from Apple
captured the disk encryption key from the router
brute-forced the password over several days
context: Agents staged a couple's argument nearby to distract Ulbricht, then grabbed the running (logged-in-as-DPR) laptop before he could lock it. Apple decryption keys and router-side captures do not exist for this class of full-disk encryption; brute-force would not have succeeded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: In early 2015 a New York federal jury found Ross Ulbricht guilty on seven charges tied to the Silk Road, the hidden Bitcoin marketplace he had run on the Tor network. He was a first-time offender who had never personally used violence, though drugs had moved through his site. Judge Katherine Forrest then handed down a sentence far harsher than even prosecutors had asked for. What sentence did Ross Ulbricht receive?
answer: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
choices: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
a 20-year sentence with possibility of parole
a 10-year sentence in a minimum-security prison
a 5-year suspended sentence with community service
context: Judge Katherine Forrest sentenced Ulbricht to two life sentences plus 40 years without parole. The lesser sentences never applied. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Ross Ulbricht created the Silk Road, an online marketplace where people bought and sold things the US government had banned. In 2015 a federal judge sentenced him to two life terms in prison plus 40 years for a first-time nonviolent case. For eleven years after that sentence, one family member led the public fight to free him, arguing the punishment was far too harsh. Which family member led the push?
answer: Lyn Ulbricht (his mother)
choices: Lyn Ulbricht (his mother)
Kirk Ulbricht (his father)
Cally Ulbricht (his sister)
Judith Ulbricht (his grandmother)
context: Lyn Ulbricht ran the FreeRoss.org campaign for eleven years. Kirk (his father) and Cally (his sister) were supportive but did not lead the public campaign; Judith is not a named figure in the case. Source: https://freeross.org/.

question: In 2011 Ross Ulbricht launched the Silk Road, a hidden online marketplace where people used Bitcoin to buy and sell things the US government had banned. In 2015 a federal judge sentenced Ulbricht to two life terms plus 40 years and shut the site down. Yet within weeks, copycat marketplaces appeared. Why do black markets like the Silk Road reappear even after their operators are locked up?
answer: Buyers and sellers still want to trade, so a new marketplace opens somewhere the law cannot see
choices: Buyers and sellers still want to trade, so a new marketplace opens somewhere the law cannot see
Governments always accidentally forget to close down copycat sites
The prison sentences are usually too short to matter
Nobody wants the banned goods once the original marketplace is gone
context: Donald Trump, having promised the pardon at the Libertarian Party's 2024 national convention, signed a full pardon for Ross Ulbricht on January 21, 2025 -- the second day of his second term. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Ross Ulbricht quietly launched the Silk Road on January 27, 2011. It was a hidden Bitcoin marketplace on the Tor network where drugs and forged papers changed hands with no real names attached. It ran openly until US federal agents grabbed his unlocked laptop inside a San Francisco library on October 1, 2013. About how long did the Silk Road actually run before it was shut down?
answer: about 2 years and 9 months
choices: about 2 years and 9 months
about 6 months in operation
about 5 years in operation
about 10 years in operation
context: Silk Road ran from January 2011 until the October 2013 shutdown -- roughly 2 years and 9 months. The alternative durations do not match the actual operating window. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: In October 2013 the FBI arrested Ross Ulbricht in a San Francisco public library and shut down Silk Road, his hidden online market where buyers paid in Bitcoin. Federal agents seized the huge stash of bitcoins the site had kept in its wallets. The US Marshals Service auctioned them off in tranches starting in 2014-15. Roughly how many bitcoins did the initial takedown seizure yield?
answer: about 144,000 BTC
choices: about 144,000 BTC
about 10,000 BTC
about 1 million BTC
about 20 BTC
context: The initial October 2013 seizure at Silk Road's takedown was roughly 144,000 BTC (later seizures added more). The Marshals auctioned tranches through 2014-15, notably to buyer Tim Draper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Ross Ulbricht, the Silk Road founder who had been serving two life sentences without parole, was pardoned by President Donald Trump in January 2025. His mother Lyn Ulbricht and the 'Free Ross' campaign had spent eleven years lobbying for his release, gathering signatures and speaking at libertarian gatherings across America. Looking back on the win, one libertarian writer said the long campaign proved a big point about how a political movement should push back when its ideas run into a courtroom. Which point does the writer press?
answer: That sustained public campaigning for a specific person can succeed where abstract advocacy fails, even against the largest legal apparatus
choices: That sustained public campaigning for a specific person can succeed where abstract advocacy fails, even against the largest legal apparatus
That accepting the original sentence quietly and trusting the appeals process is the only ethical response for a movement that respects the rule of law
That armed resistance is the appropriate remedy for perceived legal injustice when the sentence appears disproportionate on nonviolent charges
That prosecutorial verdicts on nonviolent first-time offenders are always correct in retrospect and public campaigning for clemency is always a mistake
context: The libertarian argument (Rand Paul, Roger Ver, Lyn Ulbricht's own writings): the eleven-year FreeRoss.org campaign shows that specific-person advocacy is the operative pressure. The other options are the opposite of the movement's approach. Source: https://freeross.org/; Rand Paul Senate statements 2019-25.

question: Some writers call Bitcoin 'sound money' — money that no government can secretly print more of to pay its bills. Governments have watered down every paper currency in history that way. Bitcoin has one hard rule written right into its code that stops anyone, even its inventors, from ever making more. Which feature of Bitcoin makes it truly sound?
answer: Its total supply is capped forever at 21 million coins
choices: Its total supply is capped forever at 21 million coins
A committee of experts decides its price
Central banks issue new Bitcoin every year
The US government controls it
context: Saifedean Ammous holds a Columbia PhD (2011) and was for years a tenured economics professor at Lebanese American University in Beirut. Saylor runs a Bitcoin-heavy corporate treasury; Schiff is a gold advocate; Taleb writes on risk and is now Bitcoin-critical. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In 2018 the Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous published a book with the American publishing house John Wiley and Sons. The book explained why Bitcoin might be the hardest form of money ever created, and it argued that every fiat currency in history has eventually lost most of its value. It has since become the best-selling Bitcoin book of all time and has been translated into dozens of languages. What is the book's title?
answer: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
choices: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Bitcoin Way: A History of Digital Currency
The Bitcoin Manifesto: A New Financial Order
The Bitcoin Book: An Introduction for Investors
context: 'The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking' (Wiley, 2018) has been translated into 40+ languages. The other titles are fabrications. Source: https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Bitcoin+Standard%3A+The+Decentralized+Alternative+to+Central+Banking-p-9781119473862.

question: In his 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard the Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous argues that money has always formed around whichever item scores highest on one particular ratio. The ratio compares how much of the thing already exists in the world to how fast new units can be dug up, minted, or made. Gold scored highest among physical goods for most of history — which is why it kept becoming money. What is the ratio called?
answer: stock-to-flow ratio
choices: stock-to-flow ratio
debt-to-equity ratio
price-to-earnings ratio
current ratio
context: Ammous uses the stock-to-flow ratio (existing supply divided by annual new production) to argue money gravitates to whatever has the highest S2F. Debt-to-equity, P/E, and current ratio are accounting metrics with no monetary-theory role in his argument. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 1-3.

question: The Bitcoin protocol cuts its block reward in half every 210,000 blocks — roughly every four years. So fewer new coins get minted each cycle, while the total already in existence keeps growing. In The Bitcoin Standard the Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous applies his stock-to-flow ratio (existing stock divided by yearly new supply) to Bitcoin. Because of the halving schedule, what does his book say happens to Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio over time?
answer: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
choices: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
it stays flat throughout Bitcoin's existence
it falls each cycle because miners create more coins
it is set annually by a Bitcoin holder vote
context: Ammous's argument: because the halving cuts new issuance in half every four years while stock keeps accumulating, Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio approximately doubles each cycle -- heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero. The other options misdescribe the halving schedule. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: Imagine a country that cuts the last link between its money and gold. From that day on, the central bank can create as many new bills as the government asks for, and it does — for fifty straight years. Salaries and wages grow larger over time, but so do prices at every shop and grocery store, and nothing ever stops the printing press. Which of these is the most predictable long-term result of this arrangement?
answer: Prices rise steadily and savings lose value
choices: Prices rise steadily and savings lose value
Prices fall steadily and savings gain value
The government's debt shrinks on its own
The economy stops needing any money at all
context: 'The Fiat Standard' (Ammous, 2021) is the sequel to The Bitcoin Standard. The other titles are unrelated books or fabrications. Source: https://saifedean.com/tfs/.

question: Some kinds of money are easy for a country to make more of — a printing press, a keyboard entry at the central bank, or a mine that hits a rich new seam. Other kinds take real physical work to add even a little to the supply, or have a fixed number written into the code that nobody can raise. Gold and Bitcoin are the classic examples of the second kind. What is money whose supply is very hard to expand usually called by economists?
answer: hard money
choices: hard money
quick money
narrow money
helicopter money
context: 'Hard money' (money hard to produce more of) versus 'easy money' (money easy to produce more of) is the classical Austrian distinction Ammous inherits. Quick money, narrow money (M0/M1), and helicopter money are different concepts from other traditions. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 1.

question: The Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous held a tenured teaching job at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, where he taught economics and wrote The Bitcoin Standard. In 2020 the COVID lockdowns hit hard, and his university ordered every class to move to remote video teaching over the internet. That mandate became the reason Saifedean Ammous left the university that year. Why did he leave?
answer: he refused to comply with the university's online-teaching requirements during COVID lockdowns and was fired
choices: he refused to comply with the university's online-teaching requirements during COVID lockdowns and was fired
he was offered an endowed chair at Harvard's economics department and moved to Cambridge Massachusetts
he retired from academia to write books and produce his podcast full-time from Beirut
his university lost its formal accreditation during the Lebanese banking crisis and closed its doors
context: Ammous refused the mandatory online-teaching-with-lockdown regime, argued the lockdowns were themselves an example of the concentrated-power failure he had been writing about, and was dismissed from LAU in 2020. Source: Ammous public statements 2020-21; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: A well-known economics professor quit his job at a big American university. He set up his own website and began charging students directly for his lectures and writings, cutting the school out of the deal. Thousands of students followed him online. What does his move show about buyers, sellers, and middlemen on the internet?
answer: Buyers and sellers can now connect directly, cutting the middleman out
choices: Buyers and sellers can now connect directly, cutting the middleman out
Universities are legally required to bless every teacher who charges money
Direct-sales websites only work for physical products, never for lessons
Middlemen always add more value than the direct sellers who replace them
context: Ammous built saifhouse.com as a subscription platform for his Principles of Economics course and other material -- now with thousands of paying students. Khan Academy, Coursera, and Mises Institute are unrelated existing platforms. Source: https://saifhouse.com/.

question: Bitcoin's code sets a hard cap of 21 million coins that will ever exist — a rule enforced by every computer running the network. In The Bitcoin Standard the Lebanese economist Saifedean Ammous argues that this cap matters for a deep structural reason, not just as a marketing slogan about scarcity. What does the book say a truly fixed supply does to a currency over the long run?
answer: That a fixed supply removes the political discretion to debase, which historically is the mechanism by which every fiat currency has lost value
choices: That a fixed supply removes the political discretion to debase, which historically is the mechanism by which every fiat currency has lost value
That a fixed supply guarantees perpetual deflation of general prices regardless of what happens to real production or productivity growth
That a fixed supply requires a specific central authority to enforce the cap and defend it against political pressure to raise it
That a fixed supply automatically raises real interest rates in every credit market whenever borrowing demand rises against savings supply
context: The Ammous argument: fiat currencies have historically failed via political discretion to expand supply, and Bitcoin's fixed cap removes that specific mechanism. The other options misdescribe Ammous's actual claim about debasement as a political mechanism. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 4-5.

question: Saifedean Ammous is a Palestinian-Lebanese economist who wrote 'The Bitcoin Standard' in 2018, the book that pulled thousands of readers into Austrian economics through Bitcoin. He now teaches a Principles of Economics course entirely outside the university system. His students often call it the modern Austrian answer to a real economics degree. Which Austrian-school institute is his course most often compared to?
answer: the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama
choices: the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama
the London School of Economics
the Cato Institute in Washington DC
the Adam Smith Institute in London
context: Ammous's independent Austrian-economics teaching is most often compared to the Mises Institute (Lew Rockwell, Auburn AL, founded 1982), the modern American home of Rothbardian Austrian economics. The other institutions have different orientations and are not the standard comparison. Source: https://mises.org/; https://saifhouse.com/.

question: In 1994 voters in San Francisco passed Proposition I, which extended rent control to small buildings with 2 to 4 apartments. Years later, three Stanford economists used the sudden rule change as a real-world experiment on what rent control actually does to housing supply. Their study became the classic paper on the topic. Which trio wrote it?
answer: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
choices: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, and Emmanuel Saez
Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, and John Van Reenen
Milton Friedman, George Stigler, and Rose Friedman
context: The 1994 expansion created a discontinuity that let economists compare almost-identical properties on either side of the cutoff. Diamond, McQuade, and Qian are mainstream Stanford scholars, not identified with the Austrian school. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: In 1994 the city of San Francisco voted to extend its strict rent-control law to cover many older apartment buildings that had not been covered before. Twenty-five years later three economists — Rebecca Diamond, Timothy McQuade, and Franklin Qian — used detailed address-level data to study what the law had actually done to renters and to the city's housing supply. Their paper ran in September 2019 in one of the top economics journals in the world. Which journal published it?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: The American Economic Review
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
The Journal of Political Economy
The Journal of Financial Economics
context: Published as 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco.' The AER is the American Economic Association's flagship journal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian were three Stanford economists who studied San Francisco's 1994 Proposition I. That law suddenly put small older 2-to-4-unit buildings under rent control while leaving very similar nearby buildings free of it. The trio compared the two groups over the next two decades. What did they find about the number of rental units in the newly-controlled buildings?
answer: Rental supply on the newly-controlled buildings fell by about 15 percent
choices: Rental supply on the newly-controlled buildings fell by about 15 percent
Rental supply rose by about 30 percent as landlords added units
Rental supply was unchanged either way
Rental supply doubled within five years
context: Landlords converted units to condominiums, demolished and rebuilt as unregulated new construction, or undertook renovations that removed units from the rental market. Every route around rent control that the law allowed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: In 1994 San Francisco expanded rent control to older small apartment buildings, freezing rents for tenants already living there. Twenty years later three Stanford economists — Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian — pulled address-level data on every San Francisco rental and traced what happened. They found that landlords hit by the freeze converted units into condos, tore buildings down, or moved family members in, cutting the city's rental supply by 15 percent. What happened to average city-wide rents as a result?
answer: They rose by about 5 percent
choices: They rose by about 5 percent
They fell by about 5 percent
They rose by about 40 percent
They were unchanged
context: The city-wide supply reduction pushed up rents on the units that remained available to move-in tenants. The policy transferred wealth from future tenants (who face higher rents in a smaller market) to current protected tenants (who save on their own units). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: After Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian published their San Francisco rent-control study, the numbers told a mixed story: tenants already living in protected units saved billions, but the citywide rental supply shrank 15 percent, pushing rents up for everyone else. In later interviews Rebecca Diamond said clearly that the policy was not a housing fix. She used one specific way of framing the main result. Which framing was it?
answer: A wealth transfer from future tenants to current protected tenants
choices: A wealth transfer from future tenants to current protected tenants
A win-win outcome for both landlords and tenants
A vindication of increased federal housing subsidies
A demonstration that any regulation is inherently better than no regulation
context: Diamond's own framing matters: she is not an ideological opponent of the policy; she is a mainstream researcher whose finding was that the redistribution was intergenerational rather than tenant-versus-landlord. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rebecca_Diamond.

question: In 2020 a housing activist dismissed the Diamond-McQuade-Qian San Francisco rent-control study as biased. An economist trained in the Thomas Sowell tradition replied that the study's finding matched a prediction two young Chicago-school economists — Milton Friedman and George Stigler, both future Nobel laureates — had published in a short 1946 pamphlet for the Foundation for Economic Education. What was that pamphlet called?
answer: 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem'
choices: 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem'
'Capitalism and Freedom'
'The Road to Serfdom'
'Free to Choose'
context: Written by Milton Friedman and George Stigler in 1946, published by the Foundation for Economic Education. The pamphlet predicted the supply-response and quality-decay mechanisms Diamond-McQuade-Qian empirically measured 73 years later. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: In 2001 the American energy giant Enron used tricky accounting to hide huge losses for years and then went bankrupt. Thousands of workers lost their jobs and their retirement savings almost overnight. When a big company lies about its money like that and then collapses, what do lawmakers usually pass right after a scandal of that shape?
answer: New rules forcing companies to prove their money reports are honest
choices: New rules forcing companies to prove their money reports are honest
A law banning anyone from ever starting a company again
A rule requiring every worker to buy company stock
A tax break for the companies that failed
context: Named for Senator Paul Sarbanes (D-Maryland) and Representative Michael Oxley (R-Ohio), the chairs of the two committees that shaped the bill. Formally the Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: In 2002 the US Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, named for Senator Paul Sarbanes and Representative Michael Oxley. It came right after two enormous accounting scandals had shaken Wall Street: an energy-trading company that collapsed in December 2001 after hiding billions in losses, and a giant telecommunications firm that filed for bankruptcy in July 2002 after inflating its profits. Which two firms were they?
answer: Enron and WorldCom
choices: Enron and WorldCom
Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns
General Electric and Tyco
Adelphia and HealthSouth
context: Enron filed December 2, 2001; WorldCom filed July 21, 2002. WorldCom's collapse revealed roughly $11 billion in improperly capitalized expenses. Both scandals shattered public trust in audited financial statements. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enron.

question: In 2001 and 2002, giant American companies like Enron and WorldCom collapsed after top executives were caught faking their profits for years. Congress responded with a 2002 law called Sarbanes-Oxley. It forces the CEO (chief executive officer) and CFO (chief financial officer) of every big public company to personally sign a statement every quarter saying the financial numbers are true. Lying can send them to prison. What is the idea behind this rule?
answer: Making a real person legally responsible so they cannot hide behind the company
choices: Making a real person legally responsible so they cannot hide behind the company
Letting companies write whatever numbers they want
Forcing companies to publish reports only once every five years
Removing all penalties for false accounting
context: Section 302 targeted the WorldCom shape of fraud, in which senior executives had claimed ignorance of accounting irregularities. Post-SOX, that defense is legally hollow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 was passed after the Enron and WorldCom scandals to force stricter accounting at US public companies. One section of the law required company bosses to build and audit strict internal checks on their own books, and to certify them personally. It became the costliest part of the law to follow, running about $1-2 million a year for even a small public firm. Which section was it?
answer: Section 404
choices: Section 404
Section 105
Section 802
Section 501
context: The Section 404 internal-controls attestation is the compliance cost that finance professionals name first when they discuss SOX. Its cost is largely fixed per firm rather than scaling with company size. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: About 7,300 US companies were listed on public stock markets in 1996. Twenty years later many were gone — bought up in mergers, taken private by buyout firms, or simply delisted. The economist Gustavo Grullon and his co-authors published a widely cited study measuring the drop and warning that American industries were becoming much more concentrated. About how many US-listed companies were left by 2016, per the Grullon study?
answer: About 4,300
choices: About 4,300
About 6,800
About 3,100
About 5,700
context: A roughly 40 percent decline. IPO activity in the same period fell from over 300 per year in the mid-1990s to about 100 per year post-SOX. Many small-cap firms went private or stayed private rather than face Section 404 compliance costs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: A brand-new law requires every public company to file an expensive report each year. Complying costs about $1.5 million. A giant company earning $10 billion barely notices the bill. A small company earning $50 million cannot survive it. What general lesson does this show about regulations with big fixed costs?
answer: Regulations with a large fixed compliance cost fall heaviest on the smallest firms
choices: Regulations with a large fixed compliance cost fall heaviest on the smallest firms
Regulations always fail because bureaucracies are inefficient by design
Regulations succeed when their costs are widely publicized in advance
Regulations improve competition by weeding out weak firms
context: The same reasoning move that Calomiris and Haber applied to Dodd-Frank in Fragile by Design (2014). Fixed compliance costs create an anti-competitive moat around large incumbents. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: A retail investor in 2015 wants to buy shares in a promising small-cap tech firm before it grows into the next Apple. She discovers the firm has stayed private, funded instead by venture capital and later private equity. A Bastiatian critic points to the seen benefit of Sarbanes-Oxley (fewer Enron-style frauds) and names an unseen cost specific to ordinary savers. What is that unseen cost?
answer: Retail investors have lost access to early-stage growth investing, which is now reserved for accredited private-equity clients
choices: Retail investors have lost access to early-stage growth investing, which is now reserved for accredited private-equity clients
Retail investors face higher brokerage commissions on the shares that remain publicly listed
Retail investors are barred by the SEC from owning any technology stocks
Retail investors have to pay more federal tax on capital gains from private companies
context: Peter Wallison of AEI has argued that SOX plus Dodd-Frank represents the biggest capital-formation regression in US history. A firm that stays private into a multi-billion valuation delivers those gains only to accredited investors; ordinary retail buyers get the shares only after most of the growth. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Wallison.

question: On Halloween night, October 31, 2008, in the middle of the global banking crisis, a short message appeared on a small online mailing list for people who studied secret codes and privacy tools. It linked to a nine-page paper called 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' and described 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.' The writer used a pen name, not a real name. What pen name signed the post?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto
Nick Szabo
Adam Back
Hal Finney
context: The October 31 2008 post from 'Satoshi Nakamoto' to the metzdowd.com cryptography list -- run by Perry Metzger -- announced the Bitcoin white paper and linked to bitcoin.org. Source: metzdowd.com archives (October 31 2008).

question: On Halloween night 2008, someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto sent a short email to a small cryptography mailing list. Attached was a nine-page paper describing a new kind of digital money that would not need any bank or government to run it. That paper launched Bitcoin. What is its famous title?
answer: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
choices: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
A New Digital Money for the Twenty-First Century
Foundations of Distributed Cryptographic Currency
On the Cryptographic Foundations of Trustless Value
context: Nine pages, twelve sections. The paper contained no mathematics more advanced than probability theory -- deliberately readable by any competent programmer, not just cryptographers. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Before Bitcoin was invented in 2009 by a programmer using the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto, every online-cash idea had needed a trusted company — like a bank — sitting in the middle to keep track of who owned what. Without a trusted middleman, how could you stop a person from copying a digital coin and spending it twice, since a computer file can be copied endlessly? What is this old puzzle called?
answer: The double-spending problem
choices: The double-spending problem
The counterfeit-paper problem
The lost-password problem
The unreadable-code problem
context: Double-spending: how do you stop someone from spending the same digital coin twice, WITHOUT a central authority checking every transaction? Every prior digital-cash design had needed a trusted issuer (Chaum's DigiCash, e-gold, and others). Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: To keep Bitcoin honest without any central bank or trusted middleman, its inventor Satoshi Nakamoto designed a clever race. Computers around the world compete to solve a hard math puzzle. The winner adds the next page — called a block — to the shared record book of all Bitcoin transactions. Because each puzzle burns huge amounts of electricity, rewriting old pages later would be far too costly to be worth it. What is this system called?
answer: Proof-of-work
choices: Proof-of-work
Proof-of-stake
Proof-of-trust
Proof-of-purchase
context: Proof-of-work enforces the ordering: each block requires real-world computation, and the honest chain is the one with the most cumulative work. Rewriting history requires redoing all that work faster than the honest network. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In 2008 a programmer using the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper. It solved an old computer-science puzzle: how can strangers online agree on one shared list of who paid whom, with no boss and no central bank? Satoshi's answer was one sharp rule — whoever has the most compute power working honestly wins the right to add the next block of transactions to the chain. What is this design called?
answer: Nakamoto Consensus
choices: Nakamoto Consensus
Byzantine Consensus
Cascade Consensus
Delegated Consensus
context: 'Nakamoto Consensus' is the cryptography-literature name for the proof-of-work plus longest-chain rule Satoshi introduced. It is the first known solution to the Byzantine Generals Problem for open, permissionless networks. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nakamoto_consensus.

question: In late 2008 the inventor of Bitcoin, writing under the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto, first shared his design not on a big news site but on a small mailing list called the Cypherpunks list. Its members were programmers who studied cryptography — secret codes and privacy tools — and had spent the 1990s arguing about how to build digital cash without a bank. Why show it to that group first, instead of a national newspaper?
answer: They were the people most likely to spot flaws and try running the code
choices: They were the people most likely to spot flaws and try running the code
They controlled the servers that would host the new coin
They were required by law to review new money designs
They had already agreed to buy every coin in advance
context: Perry Metzger ran the metzdowd.com cryptography list, a well-known venue for reviewing cryptographic proposals throughout the 1990s and 2000s. The Bitcoin white paper appeared as a normal posting on that list. Source: metzdowd.com archives.

question: The Bitcoin white paper, written in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, is only nine pages long but is split into numbered sections that build one on top of the next. It starts with Introduction and Transactions, then walks through Timestamp Server, Proof-of-Work, Network, Incentive, Reclaiming Disk Space, Simplified Payment Verification, Combining and Splitting Value, and Privacy, before finishing with Calculations and Conclusion. How many sections does the paper have?
answer: Twelve sections
choices: Twelve sections
Six sections
Twenty sections
Three sections
context: Twelve sections: Introduction, Transactions, Timestamp Server, Proof-of-Work, Network, Incentive, Reclaiming Disk Space, Simplified Payment Verification, Combining and Splitting Value, Privacy, Calculations, Conclusion. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: No one has ever confirmed who Satoshi Nakamoto — the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin — really is, and by 2026 the mystery is still unsolved. Satoshi mined Bitcoin heavily in the very first months of the network in 2009, when almost no one else was mining and blocks were easy to win. Those early coins sit in Satoshi's known addresses to this day, never spent, never moved. About how many bitcoins are in that untouched hoard?
answer: About one million
choices: About one million
About ten thousand
About ten million
About one hundred
context: Chain analysis of the earliest-mined addresses (the 'Patoshi pattern' studied by Sergio Demian Lerner) places Satoshi's holdings at roughly one million BTC. Not one satoshi has moved from those addresses in more than fifteen years. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: When the programmer using the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper in October 2008 — in the middle of the global banking crisis — it read as a plain technical proposal: cryptography, hashing, timestamps. Nowhere did it call itself political. But over the next fifteen years, as governments printed trillions of new dollars and citizens watched their savings lose value, the paper's deeper meaning became clear to millions. What was that unseen political meaning?
answer: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
choices: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
That programming languages could enforce contracts without courts
That cryptographic proofs could replace public identity verification
That the internet could function without private-sector service providers
context: The SEEN in 2008 was a paper about digital cash; the UNSEEN was that a working solution to double-spending meant money could exist without a bank, a central bank, or any political authority. That implication took years to become visible. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin went live in January 2009. The very second computer to run on the network belonged to Hal Finney, one of the world's most respected cryptographers, whose own earlier system called Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW) had been a close cousin of Bitcoin. Finney received the first Bitcoin transaction ever sent, from Satoshi Nakamoto himself. Why does a respected expert joining early matter so much for a new open-source project?
answer: A respected expert's participation signals to other skilled people that the system is worth trying
choices: A respected expert's participation signals to other skilled people that the system is worth trying
Governments always require an expert user before allowing new software
Only open-source projects with celebrity users can ever be secure
Expert users typically demand payment before trying new software
context: Hal Finney's 2004 'Reusable Proofs of Work' (RPOW), building on Adam Back's earlier hashcash, was cited in the Bitcoin white paper. Finney ran the second-ever Bitcoin node on January 11 2009 and received the first person-to-person transaction the next day. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: From October 2008 until early 2011, the mysterious founder of Bitcoin — writing as Satoshi Nakamoto — was busy in the young Bitcoin community. He posted on internet forums, patched the software, and traded emails with the first coders. Then he wrote his last public message and went silent forever. When did he make his last public forum post?
answer: December 12 2010
choices: December 12 2010
January 3 2009
August 17 2010
April 23 2011
context: The last public bitcointalk.org post from Satoshi was on December 12 2010, on the technical topic of DDoS defenses. He never posted publicly again. Source: bitcointalk.org (Satoshi archive).

question: After launching Bitcoin in early 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto slowly stepped back from the project and vanished from the internet for good in 2010. Satoshi's very last public message on the BitcoinTalk forum went up on December 12 2010 — no goodbye, no big farewell, just a plain technical post about one small topic. Which topic was it?
answer: DDoS defenses
choices: DDoS defenses
Block-reward halving
Wallet backup procedures
Merchant integration
context: The December 12 2010 post concerned defenses against distributed denial-of-service attacks on Bitcoin nodes. Nothing in the message gave any hint that it would be Satoshi's last public communication. Source: bitcointalk.org (Satoshi's final post).

question: The inventor of Bitcoin was known only by the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto. In April 2011 Satoshi sent a short email saying he had 'moved on to other things', handed off the software keys to a developer named Gavin Andresen, and then quietly disappeared. The Bitcoin network kept humming along fine without him for the next fifteen years. Why is that a strength of Bitcoin, not a weakness?
answer: No single person needs to be alive for the network to keep working
choices: No single person needs to be alive for the network to keep working
It means Bitcoin has a secret backup owner
It proves the network cannot survive without one leader
Only the inventor knew how to fix bugs
context: The April 23 2011 email to Mike Hearn read (in essence): 'I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Hearn published the exchange years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: Bitcoin's software is open source: the full code sits on the internet where anyone in the world can read it, copy it, run their own tests, or suggest fixes. A private bank's code, by contrast, is locked inside the company and only its own employees can look at it. Bitcoin supporters say this openness makes their money system safer than one run by a single private company. Why do they say that?
answer: Thousands of eyes can spot problems, and no boss can secretly change the rules
