choices: Thousands of eyes can spot problems, and no boss can secretly change the rules
Only one hidden expert is trusted to write everything
The code is kept secret from users for safety
A single company can update the money supply any time
context: Satoshi's line: 'It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Gavin Andresen served as the lead maintainer of the Bitcoin reference client for the next several years before stepping back himself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Andresen.

question: The inventor of Bitcoin, writing as Satoshi Nakamoto, ran the software himself in early 2009 when almost nobody else did. In those first months he mined roughly a million coins — a huge pile that has sat untouched at known addresses ever since. If Satoshi suddenly returned and tried to spend all of those coins on the open market today, what would most likely happen to Bitcoin's price?
answer: It would drop sharply as buyers worried about the sudden new supply
choices: It would drop sharply as buyers worried about the sudden new supply
It would rise sharply because more coins would be in use
It would stay exactly the same because coins never change price
The network would freeze until every coin was returned
context: Chain analysis of the 'Patoshi pattern' by Sergio Demian Lerner places Satoshi's early-mined stash at roughly one million BTC. At $50,000/BTC that is $50 billion; at higher prices, far more. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto, the pen name of Bitcoin's inventor, went quiet in 2011 and has not been heard from since. Every Bitcoin address he is known to have used in the first months has been watched around the clock by thousands of researchers ever since. In fifteen years, one clear fact about those early coins has become the strongest sign that Satoshi truly walked away. What is that fact?
answer: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
choices: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
The coins have been repeatedly split across many new addresses
The coins have been used to pay Bitcoin Core developer salaries
The coins have been transferred to a charitable trust in the Cayman Islands
context: If Satoshi were alive and had access to the keys, he could have sold, borrowed against them, or moved them for privacy at any time in fifteen years. Instead, the coins sit untouched -- an unusually strong empirical signal that he truly walked away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: The person who invented Bitcoin mined about one million coins in the currency's first year. He never sold a single coin, even after they became worth tens of billions of dollars. Which temptation does that self-denial permanently remove from Bitcoin?
answer: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
choices: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
The founder's temptation to give press interviews that move the currency's price
The founder's temptation to hire successors from his own family
The founder's temptation to relocate the project to a favorable tax jurisdiction
context: A central banker profits by inflating; a company founder profits by manipulating stock; Satoshi could have sold his million BTC at any time. His non-action is a KEPT PROMISE the design's story needed. Source: mises.org/library/satoshi-kept-promise.

question: Even in 2026, no one has proven who created Bitcoin under the pen name Satoshi Nakamoto. An Australian computer scientist named Craig Wright spent years suing critics who called him a fake and trying to claim the title himself, but in March 2024 a British High Court judge formally ruled that Wright was not Satoshi. Why does Bitcoin actually work better when its true creator stays unknown?
answer: No single person can be arrested, silenced, or pressured to change the rules
choices: No single person can be arrested, silenced, or pressured to change the rules
An anonymous founder pays no taxes on any of his coins
Unknown founders are always better software programmers than famous ones
Anonymity guarantees the price of the coin will always go up
context: In the Crypto Open Patent Alliance v Wright case, the UK High Court ruled in March 2024 that Craig Wright is NOT Satoshi Nakamoto; the ruling cited his falsified documents and inconsistent testimony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright_(computer_scientist).

question: Since Satoshi Nakamoto, the pen-named inventor of Bitcoin, went silent in April 2011, many people have guessed why. Some think he died; others think he chose to disappear on purpose so no government could ever pressure him. Fifteen years on, none of the theories has ever been confirmed and no message signed with his private keys has ever appeared. In one honest line, what is the truthful answer as of 2026 to why Satoshi vanished?
answer: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
choices: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
He confirmed his retirement in a signed 2015 essay published in Wired
He handed off his private keys to Gavin Andresen in a documented ceremony
He died of a documented illness in 2013, per public medical records
context: Illness, deliberate silence, prosecution fears, or death are all live theories; none has been confirmed. What IS documented: the coins have not moved in fifteen years, and no verified message from Satoshi has appeared since April 2011. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: The unknown creator of Bitcoin, 'Satoshi Nakamoto,' mined about a million bitcoins in the first years and then vanished, never touching them. At today's prices those coins are worth tens of billions of dollars. If cashed out, what title could that person have held?
answer: The richest person on earth
choices: The richest person on earth
The chair of a major central bank
The head of a global banking group
The founder of a public company
context: At various Bitcoin price levels, Satoshi's million-BTC stash has repeatedly ranked notionally at or above the world's wealthiest documented individual. He could have sold at any point and did not. The kept promise is unusual in the history of money. Source: mises.org/library/satoshi-kept-promise.

question: In 1955 the American economist Milton Friedman wrote an essay called 'The Role of Government in Education.' He later included it in his famous 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom. Friedman argued that instead of assigning kids to one nearby public school by street address, the government should let parents choose which school to send them to. What K-12 change did the essay ask for?
answer: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
choices: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
A federally-set minimum teacher salary schedule
A single national K-12 curriculum administered by the Department of Education
Direct federal ownership of all urban public schools
context: Friedman argued government financing might be justified on externality grounds, but government production of schooling did not follow. Vouchers separated the two: public money, private (or public) provider chosen by the family. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milton_Friedman.

question: In 1970 the United States spent one amount of tax money per public-school student. Since then, spending per pupil has roughly tripled after adjusting for inflation. Meanwhile the main national test that tracks how well high school seniors read and do math — the National Assessment of Educational Progress — has been given every few years for decades. What has happened to those senior reading and math scores over that same fifty-plus-year period?
answer: They have remained essentially flat
choices: They have remained essentially flat
They have roughly doubled
They have collapsed by more than a third
They have grown steadily at a compounded 2 percent per year
context: The NAEP long-term-trend data show the flat scores. Friedman-influenced reformers cite this as the empirical anomaly a monopoly-provider hypothesis would predict: spending rose without competitive pressure to convert it into learning gains. Source: grokipedia.com/page/National_Assessment_of_Educational_Progress.

question: Milton Friedman, the Chicago-school economist and Nobel laureate, first proposed the idea in a 1955 essay called 'The Role of Government in Education'. A city government gives poor families a paper voucher they can spend at any school that will accept it — public, private, or religious. Schools now have to compete for students instead of being handed them by the district. What is this kind of program usually called?
answer: A school voucher program
choices: A school voucher program
A district assignment lottery
A tuition subsidy tax
A public option for schools
context: The Milwaukee Parental Choice Program was championed by Democratic state legislator Polly Williams, herself a former welfare mother, and signed into law by Republican Governor Tommy Thompson. The program was the model for later urban vouchers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milwaukee_Parental_Choice_Program.

question: In 2002 the US Supreme Court upheld a school voucher program running in Cleveland, Ohio — a struggling Rust Belt city where the public schools were failing badly. The court ruled 5-4 that public money could flow to religious schools chosen by parents, without violating the First Amendment's ban on state establishment of religion. What was the case called?
answer: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris
choices: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris
Everson v. Board of Education
Engel v. Vitale
Lemon v. Kurtzman
context: The 5-4 decision upheld Cleveland's voucher program on the reasoning that the aid flowed through private parental choice, not directly to religious institutions. The ruling opened the constitutional path for voucher programs to include religious schools. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zelman_v._Simmons-Harris.

question: In 2023 a school board member in a big-city district complains that families should not be free to leave for other schools, because rival charter schools and voucher programs will drain her district's enrollment. A Chicago-trained free-market economist replies with a plain grocery analogy: a store that kept 90 percent of its customers by force — not by being good — would slowly get worse, because it would face no pressure to improve. Public schools without exit, he says, are that grocery store. Which classic reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
choices: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
The externality move: education produces spillover benefits so government should fully fund it
The public-goods move: schools are non-rival non-excludable and must be publicly produced
The redistribution move: spending must equalize per-pupil funding across districts
context: This is the core Friedman-Chubb-Moe argument. John Chubb and Terry Moe developed the empirical case in Politics, Markets, and America's Schools (Brookings 1990), arguing that governance structures immune to exit block real reform. Source: grokipedia.com/page/John_Chubb.

question: Milton Friedman, the Chicago-school economist and Nobel laureate, and his wife Rose Friedman, an economist in her own right, founded an organization in 1996 during the last decade of Milton's life. It was dedicated to one specific policy application he had first proposed way back in a 1955 essay — the cause he considered his most important. The group was later renamed EdChoice in 2016. What cause did it promote?
answer: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
choices: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
The abolition of the Federal Reserve System
Universal negative-income-tax replacement of welfare programs
Repeal of federal drug prohibition
context: Milton Friedman regarded vouchers as the single application of his method with the greatest human-welfare payoff. The Friedman Foundation for Educational Choice ran advocacy, research, and litigation support until it was renamed EdChoice in 2016. Source: grokipedia.com/page/EdChoice.

question: In 2023 and 2024 a wave of US states passed Education Savings Account (ESA) laws that broadly opened K-12 school choice for the first time in American history. An ESA gives a family public money in a spendable account to pay for private-school tuition, tutoring, or homeschool supplies. Some states made their programs universal — open to every family, not only the poor. Which states did?
answer: Arizona, West Virginia, Iowa, Arkansas, Florida, and Ohio
choices: Arizona, West Virginia, Iowa, Arkansas, Florida, and Ohio
California, New York, Massachusetts, Washington, and Illinois
Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Kentucky only
Only Texas and Wyoming
context: Arizona's 2022 expansion to universal eligibility set the model; the 2023-24 wave followed. The programs give parents a state-funded account they can spend on private-school tuition, tutoring, therapy, or curriculum -- broadening Friedman's original voucher into a broader family-choice instrument. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Education_savings_account.

question: Bitcoin runs on thousands of computers called nodes, all agreeing on the same rules. Sometimes developers change those rules. One kind of change is gentle — old nodes still see new blocks as valid, so nothing breaks. Another kind is sharp — old nodes reject the new blocks and the chain splits into two. What is the gentle, backward-compatible kind called?
answer: A soft fork
choices: A soft fork
A hard fork
A soft peg
A hard peg
context: Soft forks preserve one shared chain; hard forks can create two chains if any subset of nodes refuses the change. SegWit was a soft fork; Bitcoin Cash was a hard fork from Bitcoin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fork_(blockchain).

question: Bitcoin has a rule written into its computer code: only 21 million coins will ever exist, no matter what. No single person or company can change that rule alone — the entire network would have to agree, and it never has. The US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, can print more dollars whenever it decides to. Given those two facts, how is Bitcoin fundamentally different from dollars?
answer: A central bank can create more dollars anytime, but no one can create more Bitcoin past the cap
choices: A central bank can create more dollars anytime, but no one can create more Bitcoin past the cap
Bitcoin can be printed just as fast as dollars
A central bank promises to never print more dollars
Bitcoin has no fixed rule about how many coins exist
context: SegWit had been debated since 2015. Its activation followed a User-Activated Soft Fork (UASF) push (BIP148) that pressured miners to accept the upgrade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/SegWit.

question: The 2015-2017 dispute over how Bitcoin should scale is now known as the Block Size War. When the sides could not agree, one faction hard-forked on August 1, 2017 to create a separate cryptocurrency with a much larger base block size. What was the new coin called?
answer: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
choices: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
Bitcoin Gold (BTG)
Litecoin (LTC)
Dogecoin (DOGE)
context: Bitcoin Cash launched with 8 MB blocks (vs Bitcoin's ~1 MB). Jonathan Bier's 2021 book 'The Blocksize War' is the standard chronicle of the dispute. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_Cash.

question: Bitcoin's software can be updated, but only if a large majority of miners (the people running the powerful computers that add new blocks of transactions) and users (the people running the software on their own machines to check the rules) choose to install the new version. If most refuse, the change simply does not take effect. Why must such a big group agree, instead of one boss just changing the rules?
answer: No single person or company runs Bitcoin, so a change only sticks if enough people accept it
choices: No single person or company runs Bitcoin, so a change only sticks if enough people accept it
A federal law requires a public vote before any coin can be changed
The original inventor personally signs off on every upgrade
Miners get paid extra by the government for voting yes
context: Taproot's activation was notably drama-free after the SegWit years. Over 90 percent of mining hash power signaled support during the 'Speedy Trial' window in June-August 2021. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: In November 2021 Bitcoin activated a big upgrade called Taproot. It swapped the old ECDSA signature system for a newer one called Schnorr signatures. The change had two goals: making each transaction take up less space on the chain, and making it harder for outside watchers to tell one spender from another. What are the two main reasons to upgrade the signature scheme on money software?
answer: Smaller signatures per transaction and less information leaked about the sender
choices: Smaller signatures per transaction and less information leaked about the sender
Faster mining and higher block rewards for miners
Cheaper electricity bills for every node on the network
A larger total supply of coins that can ever exist
context: Named for Claus-Peter Schnorr, a German cryptographer. Schnorr signatures allow multiple signers to combine their signatures into one, saving block space and improving on-chain privacy for multisig transactions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Schnorr_signature.

question: A high-school student notices Ethereum releases changes every few months while Bitcoin barely changes at all. She asks a veteran Bitcoin coder why. He answers that thousands of separate operators — miners, node runners, wallet makers — must all accept the new rules, so no single architect can safely rewrite them from the top. Which classic reasoning move fits his answer?
answer: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
choices: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
The efficient-markets move: any upgrade will be priced in instantly
The aggregate-demand move: upgrades should follow monetary stimulus
The revealed-preference move: users always choose the fastest network
context: Hayek's 1945 argument applies to protocol governance as well as to prices. Bitcoin's slow, consensus-heavy upgrade process is the practical embodiment of that principle. Ethereum's alternative approach takes on more coordination risk. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: From 2015 to 2017 Bitcoiners fought bitterly over whether to make blocks bigger. The dispute became known as the Block Size War, ended in a hard fork that created Bitcoin Cash, and produced a book-length postmortem. Four years later the 2021 Taproot upgrade — a genuine change to signature math — passed almost silently, with wide agreement across the community. What lesson do Bitcoin developers usually draw from the contrast?
answer: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
choices: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
Only hard forks work; soft forks always fail in the long run
The Bitcoin Foundation should have final authority over all upgrades
The US Securities and Exchange Commission should ratify each Bitcoin upgrade
context: The lesson is not that all disagreements can be avoided (Bitcoin Cash still exists) but that when the network is aligned, upgrades proceed smoothly without any central authority. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: In Bitcoin, every wallet has a secret number that only its owner should know. That number lets the owner sign a message proving the coins are theirs, so the rest of the network will accept a move. Anyone without the number cannot move those coins, no matter how much money or power they have. Anyone who steals the number can move them all, right away. What is this secret number called?
answer: the private key
choices: the private key
the block hash
the mempool ID
the nonce
context: The private key is the ~256-bit secret that authorizes spending from a Bitcoin address. The block hash is the miner-computed identifier of a completed block; the mempool is the pool of unconfirmed transactions; the nonce is the number miners adjust when hashing a candidate block. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/private-key.

question: You buy some Bitcoin on a big exchange like Coinbase, Kraken, or Binance. You leave the coins sitting in your account on their website. The private keys — the secret codes that actually move Bitcoin on the network — are held by the exchange, not by you. Then one day the exchange freezes withdrawals or goes bankrupt. What did you really own the whole time?
answer: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
choices: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
the private keys to the coins
a share of the exchange company
a government-insured deposit
context: The exchange holds the private keys; the customer holds an IOU denominated in Bitcoin. If the exchange fails, freezes accounts, or is hacked, the customer becomes an unsecured creditor. Bitcoin exchange balances are not FDIC-insured and are not equity in the exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos was a Greek-British Bitcoin teacher who wrote the textbook Mastering Bitcoin. For years he traveled the conference circuit repeating one short line to teach the self-custody rule: if someone else holds your private keys, they, not you, actually control your Bitcoin. Which seven-word line did he make famous?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins.
choices: Not your keys, not your coins.
Fix the money, fix the world.
Verify, don't trust.
Be your own bank.
context: Antonopoulos, author of Mastering Bitcoin (2014), popularized the phrase from stages in the 2010s. The other three slogans circulate in Bitcoin culture too -- 'fix the money, fix the world' is Saifedean Ammous-adjacent; 'don't trust, verify' is a general node-runner motto; 'be your own bank' is a marketing tagline -- but the pithy sovereignty rule the community drills newcomers with is Antonopoulos's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Antonopoulos.

question: The safest way to store Bitcoin is to keep the secret keys on a small physical device that never connects to the internet. Popular brands include Trezor, Ledger, and Coldcard. The owner plugs it in only long enough to sign a transaction on the device itself, then unplugs it, so hackers on the internet can never reach the keys. What is this kind of device called?
answer: a hardware wallet
choices: a hardware wallet
a paper wallet
a mining rig
a full node
context: A hardware wallet stores keys on a secure chip that signs transactions offline; the private keys never leave the device. A paper wallet is a printed key backup; a mining rig computes proof-of-work; a full node validates the whole block chain but does not by itself store spending keys. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardware_wallet.

question: Bitcoin developers propose new rules through documents called Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs). One BIP dealt with backups: if your hardware wallet is lost or broken, it lets you recover every private key from a list of plain English words. The words are drawn from a fixed dictionary of 2,048. Which BIP set this seed-phrase rule?
answer: BIP-39
choices: BIP-39
BIP-32
BIP-141
BIP-9
context: BIP-39 (2013, authored by Marek Palatinus, Pavol Rusnak, Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe) standardized the 12- or 24-word mnemonic backup. BIP-32 defines hierarchical deterministic wallet key trees; BIP-141 introduced Segregated Witness in 2015; BIP-9 covered soft-fork versioning bits. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: In February 2014 a Tokyo-based Bitcoin exchange called Mt. Gox — at the time the largest exchange in the world, handling most of all Bitcoin trades — suddenly halted withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy. About 850,000 customer coins, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, vanished with it. Savers around the world watched their balances go to zero overnight. What is the main lesson savers took from that disaster?
answer: Coins kept on someone else's website can vanish if that company fails
choices: Coins kept on someone else's website can vanish if that company fails
Bitcoin itself was broken and had to be redesigned from scratch
Only governments should be allowed to hold coins for customers
Tokyo police can always recover any coins that are lost
context: Mt Gox (originally 'Magic: The Gathering Online eXchange'), run by Mark Karpeles from Tokyo, filed for civil rehabilitation on February 28, 2014 after 850,000 BTC went missing. BitInstant had shut down earlier; Cryptsy imploded in 2016; Coinbase is still trading. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox.

question: Eight years after Mt Gox, in November 2022, a second giant Bitcoin exchange collapsed with billions of customer dollars missing. Its founder was later convicted of fraud in a New York federal court and sentenced to 25 years in prison. Which 2022 collapse taught the self-custody lesson a second time?
answer: the FTX collapse under Sam Bankman-Fried
choices: the FTX collapse under Sam Bankman-Fried
the Coinbase collapse under Brian Armstrong
the BitMEX collapse under Arthur Hayes
the Binance collapse under Changpeng Zhao
context: FTX filed for Chapter 11 on November 11, 2022; Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted in November 2023 on seven fraud counts and sentenced March 28, 2024 to 25 years. Coinbase is a public company still operating; Arthur Hayes pleaded guilty to a Bank Secrecy Act violation in 2022 but BitMEX did not collapse; CZ pleaded guilty on AML charges in 2023 but Binance did not fold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX.

question: Two of the biggest crypto exchange collapses were Mt Gox in 2014 and FTX (a large exchange) in 2022. In both, one specific group of customers kept every coin they owned while other customers lost theirs. Which decision separated the winners from the losers?
answer: holding the private keys themselves rather than leaving coins on the exchange
choices: holding the private keys themselves rather than leaving coins on the exchange
buying the exchange's proprietary token before the failure
using two-factor authentication on the exchange account
trusting the exchange's audited proof-of-reserves report
context: In both 2014 and 2022, customers who had withdrawn to self-custody wallets they controlled were unaffected by the bankruptcies. 2FA protects exchange login but does nothing when the exchange itself is insolvent; exchange tokens (FTT for FTX) collapsed alongside the exchange; proof-of-reserves reports were widely absent or misleading in both eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX.

question: A Bitcoin holder can protect against a single stolen or broken wallet by splitting the spending power across several devices. Funds can move only when a set number of them sign together -- say, two of three kept in three different places. What is this wallet setup called?
answer: a multisig wallet
choices: a multisig wallet
a hot wallet
a custodial wallet
a watch-only wallet
context: A multisig (multi-signature) wallet requires m-of-n keys to authorize a transaction (commonly 2-of-3), so no single stolen or lost device is fatal. A hot wallet is any wallet on an internet-connected machine; a custodial wallet is one whose keys are held by a service; a watch-only wallet can display balances but cannot spend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multisignature.

question: In 2022 the crypto exchange FTX, run by an American named Sam Bankman-Fried, collapsed and lost billions in customer money — the same shape of disaster that had struck the Tokyo exchange Mt. Gox back in 2014. A Bitcoin writer set the two failures side by side, eight years apart, and argued that both teach the same brutal lesson about who takes the loss when a middleman holding your coins fails. Which self-custody argument is he pressing?
answer: That an unspent output the holder cannot sign for is not the holder's money in any meaningful sense
choices: That an unspent output the holder cannot sign for is not the holder's money in any meaningful sense
That regulators should require exchanges to insure customer deposits like commercial banks do
That the Bitcoin protocol should be changed to freeze coins associated with failed exchanges
That customers should diversify across multiple exchanges to spread counterparty risk
context: The self-custody argument is a definitional one: if you cannot sign the transaction, you do not own the coin -- you own a claim on whoever can. Deposit-insurance and coin-freezing responses accept the custodial model the argument rejects; diversifying across exchanges only spreads the same counterparty risk. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX; Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.).

question: On a Friday in March 2023, a big American bank called Silicon Valley Bank failed after depositors tried to pull out billions at once. Over that weekend, worried customers at other banks that held the same kind of long-term bonds started pulling their money too. By Sunday night a second bank had been shut down by regulators. Why does one bank failing often trigger another right after?
answer: People panic and pull their money out of similar banks too
choices: People panic and pull their money out of similar banks too
Bank buildings are always in the same neighborhood
Banks all share one computer that crashes together
The government pays banks to fail one after another
context: Signature Bank, founded 2001, had grown to $110 billion in assets serving major crypto exchanges through its 24/7 payment network Signet. Its March 12 2023 seizure was the third-largest US bank failure at the time. Source: Grokipedia 'Signature Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A US lawmaker spends years in Congress writing big new rules for banks. When she retires, she takes a well-paid seat on the board of one of the very banks that must follow those rules — hired for her insider knowledge and old friendships. What is this pattern of jumping to jobs in the industries you used to regulate called?
answer: The revolving door
choices: The revolving door
Free trade
The invisible hand
The knowledge problem
context: Frank served in Congress 1981-2013 and co-wrote Dodd-Frank. His post-Congress board seat at Signature and his public criticism of the seizure created an awkward institutional twist -- the co-author of the post-2008 banking regulation defending a 2023 bank failure. Source: Grokipedia 'Signature Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: One well-known bank suddenly collapses over a weekend. Customers of a completely different bank across town see the news the next morning, panic, and rush to pull their own deposits — even though that second bank is perfectly healthy. Fear, not fundamentals, spreads the crisis from the first bank to the second. What is this kind of chain reaction called?
answer: Financial contagion, when fear spreads from one bank to the next
choices: Financial contagion, when fear spreads from one bank to the next
Regulatory capture of a single agency
A tariff on savings accounts
The knowledge problem in central planning
context: First Republic, founded in San Francisco in 1985, specialized in high-net-worth mortgage lending. It faced $100B in deposit outflows in the first quarter of 2023 alone. Source: Grokipedia 'First Republic Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: On March 16, 2023, right in the middle of the US banking crisis, eleven of the biggest American banks — including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo — teamed up in an emergency rescue for a shaky California lender called First Republic. Each of the eleven poured deposits into the failing bank, hoping to steady it and stop customers from fleeing. How much did the eleven banks put in together?
answer: $30 billion
choices: $30 billion
$5 billion
$100 billion
$300 billion
context: JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, US Bancorp, BNY Mellon, PNC, State Street, and Truist collectively placed $30 billion of deposits at First Republic. It did not work. Source: Grokipedia 'First Republic Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: In May 2023 the midsize US bank First Republic failed. Federal regulators quickly sold nearly all of it to JPMorgan Chase, already the biggest bank in the country. This is one of many mergers over the last forty years — the US had over 14,000 banks in 1984 but fewer than 4,000 by 2023. When smaller banks keep getting swallowed like this, what tends to happen over time?
answer: The biggest banks get bigger and customers have fewer choices
choices: The biggest banks get bigger and customers have fewer choices
The number of big banks stays exactly the same each year
Small banks always become the main choice for most families
The government breaks up the biggest banks after every failure
context: JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, bought most of First Republic's assets on May 1 2023. It was the second-largest US bank failure in history at that moment, surpassing Silicon Valley Bank which had held the title for seven weeks. Source: Grokipedia 'First Republic Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: From March to May 2023, three American banks collapsed in fast succession: Silicon Valley Bank in California, Signature Bank in New York, and First Republic in San Francisco. All three had been rated safe just months earlier. When analysts dug into the wreckage, they found one shared root cause tying all three failures together. What was it?
answer: Held-to-maturity bond losses from the Fed's rate-hike cycle
choices: Held-to-maturity bond losses from the Fed's rate-hike cycle
Mortgage-servicing scandals from the 2000s revival
Cross-border money-laundering enforcement actions
State-level insurance-regulation changes
context: All three banks had bought long-duration bonds at low rates during 2020-21, classified them as HTM, and watched their economic value collapse as the Fed hiked to 5.25-5.50% in 2022-23. The rate cycle that killed inflation also killed the banks that had loaded up on cheap-rate bonds. Source: Grokipedia '2023 United States banking crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2023 three US banks failed. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) normally only guarantees deposits up to $250,000, but this time it paid back everyone -- even people with much more. What is the predictable long-term problem with covering losses above the cap?
answer: Big depositors stop watching how risky their bank is, since they know they will be bailed out
choices: Big depositors stop watching how risky their bank is, since they know they will be bailed out
Banks stop failing forever, because bailouts prevent every future crisis
Small depositors immediately lose their insurance under $250,000
Insurance rates automatically fall for every bank in the country
context: The FDIC Improvement Act of 1991 allows the systemic-risk exception when a full uninsured-deposit haircut would threaten broader stability. It had been invoked rarely before 2023. The three consecutive uses in March-May 2023 established a new practical baseline. Source: Grokipedia 'FDIC Improvement Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In early March 2023 a California bank called Silvergate — whose customers were almost entirely crypto companies — quietly announced it was shutting itself down. Two days later Silicon Valley Bank, whose customers were mostly tech startups, also collapsed. Why does a bank with all its customers in one industry usually fail faster than a bank with a mix?
answer: When that one industry gets in trouble, all the customers try to withdraw at the same time
choices: When that one industry gets in trouble, all the customers try to withdraw at the same time
The bank's staff can only speak one shared industry language
Federal rules ban single-industry banks from lending money
Single-industry banks pay double the taxes of mixed banks
context: Silvergate voluntarily liquidated on March 8 2023, making 2023 a year with four US bank failures in nine weeks. Republic First (Philadelphia) also failed April 26 2024 as a lagging casualty of the same cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Silvergate Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: In May 2023 three regional US banks had already collapsed one after another. JPMorgan Chase — the biggest US bank — bought failing First Republic, and its chief said 'this part of the crisis is over.' Why does the biggest bank buying a failing bank tend to stop a chain of runs?
answer: A giant, obviously-safe bank taking over calms depositors and stops the panic from spreading
choices: A giant, obviously-safe bank taking over calms depositors and stops the panic from spreading
All depositors immediately withdraw their money once a merger is announced
Bank stocks always fall the day a merger is announced
Federal regulators automatically shut down every other bank
context: Dimon's public statement was framed as a declaration of stability but also a hint at the political-economy fact that consolidation had accelerated -- JPMorgan absorbed billions in troubled deposits from failing banks while becoming even more too-big-to-fail. Source: Grokipedia 'Jamie Dimon' (2026-09-05).

question: From March to May 2023, three US banks — Silicon Valley Bank, Signature, and First Republic — failed in quick succession, all wrecked by losses on long-term bonds they had bought when interest rates were near zero and then watched crash as the Federal Reserve, or Fed, raised rates sharply in 2022 and 2023. Bitcoin economists say the failure sequence teaches a specific recognition move about Fed monetary policy and the banking system's structural exposure. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The same central bank that creates assets during a QE cycle exposes those assets to loss during the subsequent tightening cycle
choices: The same central bank that creates assets during a QE cycle exposes those assets to loss during the subsequent tightening cycle
Bank failures are always caused by fraud rather than by policy shifts
Regional-bank stress is unrelated to Fed rate policy
Deposit insurance always prevents bank runs regardless of underlying losses
context: Banks bought long-duration bonds at 2020-21 low rates because the Fed's QE made them attractive. The same Fed's 2022-23 tightening made those bonds catastrophic losses. The whipsaw is a structural feature of a discretionary rate cycle, not a series of independent errors. Source: Grokipedia '2023 United States banking crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: Imagine a bank whose customers are almost all technology startups clustered in one small region — say, Silicon Valley in California. Business is booming when the tech industry is booming. But when tech slows down and many of those startups all pull their savings at the same time to keep paying their workers, this bank ends up in extra danger compared with a normal town bank. Why is it in extra danger?
answer: Its customers are too similar, so trouble hits them all at once
choices: Its customers are too similar, so trouble hits them all at once
Tech startups only use pennies, not dollars
The bank has no windows, so nobody can find it
Banks are not allowed to have startup customers
context: SVB was founded 1983 to serve the Bay Area tech ecosystem. Its deposit base was overwhelmingly startup companies with venture funding parked in the bank between funding rounds. Source: Grokipedia 'Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: When the Federal Reserve holds interest rates near zero, banks and big investors can borrow money almost for free. Safe things like US Treasury bonds barely pay any interest at all. So people with money to invest go hunting for anything that might pay better — including risky new startup companies. What usually happens to the money flowing into those risky startups?
answer: It floods in -- investors chase any chance of higher returns
choices: It floods in -- investors chase any chance of higher returns
It dries up -- no one wants risk at low rates
Nothing changes -- rates do not affect investing
Investors quit stocks and put every dollar in gold
context: SVB's deposits roughly tripled between 2019 and 2021, hitting about $189 billion at peak. SVB invested much of this inflow in long-duration Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities at the ultra-low rates of 2020-21. Source: Grokipedia 'Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A bank buys long-term bonds when interest rates are very low. Later, rates jump up, and those same bonds are worth much less on the open market. Under one common accounting rule, the bank does not have to write that loss down on paper. What danger does this create?
answer: The bank looks healthy on paper while quietly holding big real losses
choices: The bank looks healthy on paper while quietly holding big real losses
The bank must sell the bonds right away at any price
The bank instantly becomes richer as rates rise
Regulators know the losses long before anyone else does
context: HTM accounting hides mark-to-market losses on the balance sheet. But the economic loss is real. By year-end 2022, SVB had roughly $15 billion in unrealized bond losses -- close to its entire tangible equity of $16 billion. Source: Grokipedia 'Held-to-maturity security' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023, California's Silicon Valley Bank collapsed after depositors pulled about $42 billion in a single day using their phones. Back in the old days, worried depositors had to travel to the bank in person and stand in line for hours to pull their money out. Today anyone can tap out a huge withdrawal in seconds while reading scary posts on social media. What has this done to the speed of a bank run?
answer: Bank runs now happen in hours instead of days, giving regulators much less time to react
choices: Bank runs now happen in hours instead of days, giving regulators much less time to react
Bank runs have completely stopped happening
Bank runs now take longer because of extra online paperwork
Bank runs only happen in person and never online
context: VC Twitter -- the concentrated cluster of venture capitalists and startup founders active on Twitter/X -- lit up with 'withdraw your deposits' messages from Peter Thiel, David Sacks, and others. The digital-speed run began before most bank employees could react. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank, a California bank whose customers were mostly tech startups, had a very bad day. In just one afternoon, depositors tried to yank about $42 billion — roughly a quarter of the bank's total deposits — out through wire transfers and phone apps. What is the name for that kind of sudden rush by depositors trying to escape a failing bank?
answer: A bank run
choices: A bank run
A bank strike
A margin call
A stock split
context: $42 billion in one day was the fastest bank run in US history by a wide margin. The California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation seized SVB at 11:20 AM Pacific time that day. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 an American bank called Washington Mutual collapsed. It was the biggest bank failure in United States history. Across the country other banks were falling too, and the federal government had to step in. For years, banks had made huge loans to families to buy houses. When home prices dropped, many of those families could no longer keep up with the payments. What main problem pushed so many banks over the edge that year?
answer: They had lent against home loans that borrowers could not repay
choices: They had lent against home loans that borrowers could not repay
Customers stopped using paper checks and switched to cards
Congress passed a new tax on every checking account
Foreign banks refused to accept United States dollars
context: Washington Mutual failed September 25 2008 with $307 billion in assets, the largest US bank failure in history and larger than SVB's $209B. Lehman Brothers was an investment bank, not an FDIC-insured commercial bank. Source: Grokipedia 'Washington Mutual' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 a California bank called Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in about 48 hours. Most American bank deposits are protected up to $250,000 by a federal insurance program called the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). But at Silicon Valley Bank nearly every deposit was well above that cap -- tech startups had parked millions there. When rumors spread that the bank was in trouble, customers rushed to yank their money out. Why does a big share of uninsured deposits make a bank more likely to face a run?
answer: Uninsured depositors have a big reason to pull money out at the first sign of trouble
choices: Uninsured depositors have a big reason to pull money out at the first sign of trouble
Uninsured depositors always earn higher interest rates than insured ones
Uninsured deposits are secretly counted twice on the bank's ledger
Uninsured deposits force the bank to hold less cash on hand
context: 93% of SVB's deposits were uninsured -- one of the highest uninsured-deposit ratios in the banking system. Startups routinely park $10-100M in a single account, far above the $250,000 cap. This concentration made the bank uniquely vulnerable to a run. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: The day after Silicon Valley Bank was seized in March 2023, the US Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) held a joint announcement about depositors. Normally the FDIC only guarantees the first $250,000 in each account. But many Silicon Valley Bank customers were tech companies with millions of dollars on deposit. What did the three agencies say?
answer: Every dollar of deposit would be paid in full, even amounts above the cap
choices: Every dollar of deposit would be paid in full, even amounts above the cap
Losses of about 15 percent on deposits above the $250,000 cap
The seizure would be postponed 30 days for further review
The matter would be sent to Congress for emergency legislation
context: The Sunday March 12 2023 joint announcement guaranteed all deposits under the FDIC's systemic-risk exception. This effectively extended deposit insurance beyond the statutory cap without any congressional authorization. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: Silicon Valley Bank was a large US bank that collapsed in early 2023. For eight months before it failed the bank had no one in one senior job whose whole purpose is to spot dangerous mismatches between short-term debts and long-term holdings. Which senior role had the bank left empty?
answer: Chief Risk Officer
choices: Chief Risk Officer
Chief Executive Officer
Chief Compliance Officer
Chief Investment Officer
context: SVB's Chief Risk Officer departed in April 2022. The bank operated without a CRO for the eight months through late 2022 -- exactly the period when the rate-cycle bond losses were building on its balance sheet. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a single day. Warnings raced through Twitter, Slack, and group chats in minutes; customers used phone apps to move billions of dollars to other banks in hours. Older bank runs took days as depositors lined up on the sidewalk to reach a teller window. What does the Silicon Valley Bank collapse teach about how bank runs work now?
answer: A digital-age run can drain a bank in one day, faster than any run in earlier banking history
choices: A digital-age run can drain a bank in one day, faster than any run in earlier banking history
Digital-age runs are slower because customers deliberate longer online
Deposit insurance now completely prevents bank runs from happening
Modern banks cannot experience runs because reserves sit at the Fed
context: SVB's $42 billion in withdrawal requests in a single day is faster than any pre-2020 US bank run. When customers can move deposits by mobile app and coordinate via Twitter, the classic three-day run compresses to hours. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: From 2011 to 2013, a hidden website called the Silk Road ran on the dark web and sold illegal drugs and other contraband to customers around the world. The site refused every ordinary payment method — no bank transfers, no credit cards. It accepted only one form of payment: Bitcoin. Why would crooks running an illegal market pick Bitcoin over a bank transfer or a credit card?
answer: Bitcoin can be sent without a bank or government approving it
choices: Bitcoin can be sent without a bank or government approving it
Bitcoin is worth more than dollars in every country
Bitcoin is issued by the police
Bitcoin requires showing a driver's license to send
context: Silk Road became the first widely-known use case for Bitcoin outside of hobbyist circles. AlphaBay was a successor Tor market shut down in 2017. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Bitcoin lets anyone send money anywhere without asking a bank for permission. This has helped people escape currency controls in poor countries. It has also helped criminals sell drugs online. What honest thing must a fair defender of Bitcoin admit here?
answer: Any tool that gives people more freedom can also be used for wrongdoing

Bitcoin has never been used for anything bad
Only criminals use Bitcoin, no one else
Cash has never once been used for a crime
context: The real founder was Ross Ulbricht, a young American libertarian. He chose the name partly because in the novel it lets one Roberts retire and pass the identity along -- suggesting he could similarly step away. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Silk Road was a hidden online marketplace where people used Bitcoin to buy drugs and other illegal goods. Its founder, Ross Ulbricht, ran it under the alias 'Dread Pirate Roberts'. On October 1, 2013 agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) needed to seize his laptop while it was still logged into Silk Road's admin panel, so they staged a very careful arrest in a specific public spot. Where did they catch him?

At his apartment in Austin, Texas
At an in-person Bitcoin conference in Las Vegas
At San Francisco International Airport

question: Ross Ulbricht was found guilty in February 2015 on seven counts, including drug trafficking and money laundering. On May 29, 2015 he was sentenced. His sentence became a rallying cause for libertarians, reformers, and the Bitcoin community for a decade. What was it?

context: The prosecution cited the site's roughly $1.2 billion in sales and unproven murder-for-hire allegations; the defense argued the sentence was disproportionate for a first-time nonviolent offense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: In October 2013 the FBI arrested a young man named Ross Ulbricht in a San Francisco library. He was the secret founder of Silk Road, a hidden online marketplace where people bought and sold illegal drugs using Bitcoin. The government seized the site and sent Ulbricht to prison for life. But within weeks, copycat sites -- Silk Road 2, AlphaBay, and others -- opened for business, and customers moved right over. What does that pattern show about shutting a market by arresting the boss?

Marketplaces only reopen when the original operator is released
context: Trump had promised the commutation at the May 2024 Libertarian National Convention in Washington. It became one of the earliest acts of his second term. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Bitcoin, invented in 2009 by a person using the name Satoshi Nakamoto, was designed as digital cash that no bank or government could freeze or reverse. In the early 2010s a hidden drug market called Silk Road only accepted Bitcoin for payment. Some Bitcoiners cheered -- the payments worked exactly as designed. Others worried the drug-market link would forever taint Bitcoin's reputation. Which Bitcoin trait did Silk Road show off most?

context: The censorship-resistance was the design property Satoshi named in the 2008 white paper. Silk Road proved it functioned end-to-end at scale on an anonymous network. Whether the specific use was legitimate is separate from whether the property held. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: A high-school student in 2025 wants to know whether Ross Ulbricht's release means the underlying policy debate is settled. A public-choice-trained analyst warns her that a commutation is a specific-case decision, not a policy verdict. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Recognizing the case's argument without collapsing it into a universal endorsement of the underlying market

Enforcing a strict verdict that all Tor markets are always legitimate
Enforcing a strict verdict that all Tor markets are always illegitimate
Concluding that presidential commutations always signal a change in federal drug law
context: The bank's rule: teach a kid to see the reasoning move (proportionality of sentence, censorship-resistance as a design property), not to memorize a policy verdict. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: As the Great Depression began in 1930, the US Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, putting big new taxes on more than 20,000 kinds of imports from other countries. Angry trading partners like Canada and France hit back with big new taxes of their own. What usually happens to world trade when countries throw tariffs at each other like this?

choices: Trade shrinks and both sides get poorer
Trade grows because factories work harder
Nothing -- other countries never fight back
Only the country with the biggest army wins
context: Signed June 17, 1930, formally the Tariff Act of 1930. It raised US tariff rates on over 20,000 imported goods to their highest levels in about a century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: In 1930, just as the Great Depression was starting, the United States Congress passed a big tariff law that raised taxes on goods brought in from other countries. Historians now blame the law for making the depression worse -- other countries hit back with their own tariffs, and world trade collapsed. The act is named after the two American lawmakers who wrote it: a senator from Utah and a congressman from Oregon. What were their last names?
answer: Reed Smoot and Willis Hawley
choices: Reed Smoot and Willis Hawley
Joseph Fordney and Porter McCumber
Sereno Payne and Nelson Aldrich
Oscar Underwood and Furnifold Simmons
context: Senator Reed Smoot (R-UT) chaired the Senate Finance Committee; Representative Willis Hawley (R-OR) chaired House Ways and Means. Both later lost their seats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: In May 1930, the US Congress was debating the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a huge bill that would raise taxes on thousands of imported goods. Alarmed that this would ignite a worldwide trade war right in the middle of the Great Depression, a large group of American economists signed a public letter to President Herbert Hoover, begging him to veto it. It was one of the biggest joint statements economists had ever made. About how many names were on the letter?
answer: About one thousand
choices: About one thousand
About one hundred
About ten thousand
About fifty
context: The petition published in the New York Times on May 5, 1930 carried 1,028 signatures -- one of the largest organized economics-profession protests in American history. Hoover signed the bill anyway. Source: nytimes.com/1930/05/05/archives.

question: In June 1930, the US Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, one of the most sweeping trade laws in American history. Instead of setting one rate for all imports, lawmakers went item by item, adding a special tax on foreign goods from cheese to pocket watches to industrial chemicals. Each congressman fought to protect the industries in their own district. About how many separate goods were hit with new higher tariff rates?
answer: More than twenty thousand
choices: More than twenty thousand
About two hundred
About two thousand
More than one hundred thousand
context: The Tariff Act of 1930 set specific higher duties on over 20,000 dutiable items -- the last time Congress legislated tariff rates on that many goods directly rather than delegating to the executive branch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: In 1930 the US Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, sharply raising taxes on imported goods to protect American factories. Other big trading nations -- Canada, France, Britain, Germany -- hit back with tariffs of their own. Country after country slammed its doors on foreign trade during the Great Depression. From 1929 to 1934, by roughly how much did total world trade shrink?
answer: About two-thirds
choices: About two-thirds
About one-tenth
About one-third
About nine-tenths
context: World trade fell by roughly two-thirds between 1929 and 1934 as Canada, Britain, France, Germany, and dozens of other countries raised barriers in response to Smoot-Hawley -- the greatest peacetime contraction of international commerce ever recorded. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wanted to expose the silliness of tariffs -- taxes that block cheap foreign goods to protect local sellers. So he wrote a fake petition to the French parliament, supposedly filed by a certain trade, begging lawmakers to shut out a hated foreign rival -- the sun itself -- because its free light was ruining their business by making their product unnecessary during the day. Which trade did Bastiat pretend was filing the petition?
answer: The candlemakers
choices: The candlemakers
The winegrowers
The steelmakers
The wheat farmers
context: Bastiat's 'Candlemakers' Petition' asked the French Chamber of Deputies to block sunlight so domestic candlemakers could sell more candles -- the classic satire of a producer-protection tariff that ignores costs to consumers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlemakers%27_petition.

question: In 1930 the American government passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, putting big new taxes on goods coming from other countries. Some effects were easy to see right away — factory owners cheering, foreign goods vanishing from shelves. But the French economist Frédéric Bastiat had warned decades earlier that the biggest costs of tariffs are always the ones nobody sees at first. What was Smoot-Hawley's less-visible cost, the one that took months or years to notice?
answer: Higher prices for shoppers and lost sales for American exporters
choices: Higher prices for shoppers and lost sales for American exporters
Lower prices for shoppers and higher exports overall
A sudden drop in the size of the federal government
A rise in workers' wages faster than prices
context: Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen method: the beneficiaries of a tariff are concentrated and visible (this steel plant, this sugar planter); the costs are diffuse and hidden (every consumer pays more, every exporter loses a foreign market). Source: bastiat.org/en/twisatwins.html.

question: In 1930 the US passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, and world trade collapsed as country after country raised their own tariffs to strike back. Congress had built the mess piece by piece, with each congressman fighting to protect the industries in their own district. In 1934, Congress passed the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act, handing the president the power to lower tariffs by negotiating whole trade deals with foreign governments. Why is it usually easier for a president to lower tariffs than for Congress?
answer: A president can negotiate the whole deal at once, so no single local industry can block a line item
choices: A president can negotiate the whole deal at once, so no single local industry can block a line item
A president can print money to pay industries harmed by the change
Congress is legally forbidden from voting on any tariff bill
Foreign countries only agree to talk to a president, never to Congress
context: The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, championed by FDR Secretary of State Cordell Hull, let the president negotiate bilateral tariff cuts without going back to Congress on every rate. It began three decades of tariff liberalization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocal_Tariff_Act.

question: After World War Two, the US and 22 other countries built a shared trade deal called the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), aiming to stop another 1930 Smoot-Hawley-style tariff war. In 1995 GATT was replaced by the World Trade Organization (WTO). Why do such shared deals cut down on tariff fights between countries?
answer: Each country promises not to raise tariffs on the others, so no one has reason to strike first
choices: Each country promises not to raise tariffs on the others, so no one has reason to strike first
Each country gives up the right to trade with any non-member country
The agreement bans all imports of foreign goods
Each country agrees to use exactly the same currency
context: GATT, signed 1947 by 23 founding countries, ran successive tariff-cutting rounds through the postwar era. Its explicit institutional memory was that unilateral tariff hikes and retaliation had helped internationalize the 1930s depression. GATT became the WTO in 1995. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Agreement_on_Tariffs_and_Trade.

question: The 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act raised US import taxes on thousands of goods during the early Great Depression. Other countries hit back with their own tariffs and world trade collapsed. What lesson do economists usually draw from what happened next?
answer: Raising tariffs during a downturn usually deepens the downturn instead of fixing it
choices: Raising tariffs during a downturn usually deepens the downturn instead of fixing it
Tariffs always speed economic recovery after a stock market crash
Other countries typically ignore new tariffs and keep trading normally
Import taxes have no measurable effect on trade volumes
context: Ben Stein's economics-teacher scene in Ferris Bueller's Day Off is probably the most-watched pop-culture reference to Smoot-Hawley, delivering an accurate one-minute summary of why economists thought the tariff worsened the Depression. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferris_Bueller%27s_Day_Off.

question: Ida May Fuller was a retired legal secretary living in Ludlow, Vermont. On January 31, 1940, her mail carrier brought her Social Security check number 1 — the very first one ever paid to anyone. It was for $22.54. During her working years she had paid a total of $24.75 in Social Security taxes. Fuller lived on to age 100. What did she collect from Social Security in all across her long retirement?
answer: About $22,900
choices: About $22,900
About $2,300
About $71,000
context: Fuller collected $22,888.92 over 35 years of benefits against $24.75 paid in between 1937 and her retirement in 1939. She was born on a farm outside Rutland, Vermont on September 6, 1874. The first cohort did extraordinarily well precisely because they paid in for only a few years while a very large working generation paid the taxes. Source: Social Security Administration, 'Ida May Fuller -- The first Social Security Beneficiary' (https://www.ssa.gov/history/imf.html).

question: US Social Security works by having current workers pay taxes that fund current retirees' checks — not by saving up your own money for later. In 1950, there were 16.5 workers paying in for each retiree collecting a check, a comfortable cushion. Since then, families had fewer babies and people lived much longer. By 2024, how many workers paid in for each person receiving benefits?
answer: About 2.7
choices: About 2.7
About 5.4
About 8.1
About 1.2
context: The Social Security Administration's historical series puts the covered-worker-to-beneficiary ratio at roughly 41.9 to 1 in 1945, 16.5 to 1 in 1950, and about 2.7 to 1 today. The ratio is load-bearing because benefits are paid out of current payroll taxes rather than from each retiree's own past contributions. Sources: SSA, 'Ratio of Covered Workers to Beneficiaries' (https://www.ssa.gov/history/ratios.html); Peter G. Peterson Foundation (https://www.pgpf.org/article/the-ratio-of-workers-to-social-security-beneficiaries-is-at-a-low-and-projected-to-decline-further/).

question: The government calls the money workers must send to Social Security a 'contribution,' as if it were a gift you chose to give. But you go to prison if you refuse to send it. What did the economists Milton and Rose Friedman say was wrong with using words this way?
answer: Calling a forced tax a contribution hides what is really happening
choices: Calling a forced tax a contribution hides what is really happening
The word contribution helps workers plan their budgets
Workers really do choose whether to send the money
The word contribution is legally the same as gift
context: Free to Choose, chapter 4, 'Cradle to Grave': a company engaged in such labeling and advertising 'would doubtless be severely castigated by the Federal Trade Commission.' On the television series Friedman put it plainly: 'It has been sold as an insurance program. It's not an insurance program. It's a program which combines a bad tax, a flat tax on wages up to a maximum, with a very inequitable and uneven system of giving benefits.' Sources: Milton and Rose Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), ch. 4; Free to Choose television series, episode 4 (https://archive.org/details/freetochoose4fromcradletogravepart1).

question: Ephram Nestor came from Bulgaria in 1913. He paid Social Security tax on his US wages from 1936 to 1955. In July 1956 the government sent him back for old Communist Party ties and cut off his benefits. Nestor sued. In 1960 the Supreme Court ruled against him. What did the Court say about money paid into Social Security?
answer: It buys no property right, and Congress may change the benefits at will
choices: It buys no property right, and Congress may change the benefits at will
It buys a contract right that only a criminal conviction can extinguish
It buys a property right, but one forfeited by leaving the country
It buys a claim on the trust fund ranking behind federal bondholders
context: Flemming v. Nestor, 363 U.S. 603 (1960). The Court treated Social Security as social insurance subject to modification by Congress, not as a system of accrued property rights, and held that terminating a deported person's benefits was not punishment and so was neither a bill of attainder nor an ex post facto law. Sources: Justia (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/363/603/); Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemming_v._Nestor).

question: Each year Social Security's board of trustees publishes a report on when its trust fund — the reserve of savings — will run dry. The 2025 report moved that date one year closer, to 2034. By law, Social Security cannot borrow money to cover a gap between what comes in from payroll taxes and what it owes retirees. On the day the reserves finally run out, what does the report say happens?
answer: Incoming payroll taxes would cover about 81% of scheduled benefits
choices: Incoming payroll taxes would cover about 81% of scheduled benefits
Benefit checks would stop until Congress appropriated new money
The Treasury would make up the gap from general income-tax revenue
The retirement age would rise automatically until the books balanced
context: The 2025 OASDI Trustees Report projects the retirement fund alone depleted in 2033 with 77% of scheduled benefits payable, and the combined funds depleted in 2034 with 81% payable. Combined reserves fell $67 billion during 2024 to $2.72 trillion. SSA's June 2026 trustees release reported the combined-fund projection as consistent with the prior year. Sources: SSA press release, June 18, 2025 (https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/press/releases/2025-06-18.html); Congressional Research Service IF13045 (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13045).

question: In May 1981 Chile became the first country to let workers leave the state pension. They could send ten percent of their wages into a private retirement account instead. Jose Pinera, the labor minister, made the switch optional for those in the old plan. But one group was barred from switching. Which workers could not switch?

choices: Those within five years of retirement
Those earning below the national minimum wage
Those who had contributed for fewer than ten years
Those working for more than one employer at a time
context: Chile's AFP system began operating in May 1981, with contributions set by law at 10% of wages plus fund-manager fees. Workers eligible to retire within five years were excluded from the choice, since an account opened that late could not accumulate enough to fund a pension. Sources: SSA Social Security Bulletin 68(2), 'Chile's Next Generation Pension Reform' (https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v68n2/v68n2p69.html); OECD, 'Pension Reform in Chile Revisited' (2009).

question: George W. Bush opened his second term in January 2005 by making personal Social Security accounts his signature domestic proposal, with a White House campaign directed by Karl Rove and Ken Mehlman. Congress never brought a bill to a vote. Support collapsed once voters worked out what opening an account would do to the rest of what the program promised them. What did they conclude it would do?
answer: Cut the guaranteed benefit for all but the lowest-income recipients
choices: Cut the guaranteed benefit for all but the lowest-income recipients
Hand the investment decisions to the Treasury rather than to the worker
Force the payroll tax up to pay for the transition years
Bar a worker's children from inheriting the balance in the account
context: The traditional benefit would have been reduced in proportion to what a worker diverted into an account, which is what turned public skepticism into opposition; the transition-cost objection in the third choice was also raised, but it was the guaranteed-benefit offset that sank the initiative. Sources: Brookings, 'Why the 2005 Social Security Initiative Failed' (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/why-the-2005-social-security-initiative-failed-and-what-it-means-for-the-future/); Congressional Research Service RL32879 (https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/RL32879.html).

question: A member of Congress defends the payroll tax by pointing to the check that goes out each month to 67 million Americans, many with no other retirement income. A critic in Frederic Bastiat's tradition agrees on the facts. But the defense is incomplete, they say, because it counts only what the program did with the money and never what the money would have done otherwise. What comparison does the critic demand?
answer: What forty-five years of those same payroll taxes would have compounded to in the worker's own account
choices: What forty-five years of those same payroll taxes would have compounded to in the worker's own account
What the same revenue would have built had the state spent it on roads, ports and power instead
What retirees actually live on today in countries that never created a state pension at all
What the program costs to administer measured against a private insurer's overhead ratio
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' asks, after any law or expenditure, what does not happen because of it. The retiree's check is seen; the account the same 12.4% of a working life never built is not. This is a counterfactual and a contested one -- a private account carries market risk and no survivor guarantee, which is exactly why the reform argument is about the comparison rather than about a verdict. Milton Friedman pressed the same comparison in Free to Choose; Jose Pinera built a system around it in Chile in 1981; American voters rejected it in 2005. Sources: Bastiat (https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss.html); Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), ch. 4.

question: In 2009 the US government lent $535 million of taxpayer money to Solyndra, a California solar-panel company officials thought would win big against Chinese competitors. Two years later, in 2011, Solyndra went bankrupt and could not repay a cent of the loan. Who ends up eating that loss?
answer: Taxpayers
choices: Taxpayers
The solar-panel company's owners only
Nobody -- the government prints new money for free
Other solar companies must pay it back
context: Based in Fremont, California. The bankruptcy laid off 1,100 workers and became the signature failure of the Obama-era green industrial-policy portfolio. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: In 2009 the US government lent $535 million of taxpayer money to Solyndra, a California solar-panel firm, because officials thought Solyndra would beat both its US and Chinese competitors. Two years later the company went bankrupt and could not repay a single cent. What is the general problem with letting officials pick winning firms this way?
answer: Officials guessing which private companies will win rarely guess better than the market
choices: Officials guessing which private companies will win rarely guess better than the market
Every company the government picks always succeeds
Private investors always guess worse than officials
Solar power can never work as a business
context: The visit was a signature endorsement of the ARRA stimulus green-energy portfolio. Sixteen months later Solyndra filed for Chapter 11. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: Solyndra's tube-shaped solar panels used a rare-metal coating instead of the silicon wafers that most competitors — including cheap Chinese rivals — used. Between 2008 and 2011 one massive world price shift on a key panel material collapsed the cost gap and made Solyndra's design look far too expensive next to Chinese-made flat panels. The company went bankrupt in 2011. Which price shift was the decisive one?
answer: The world price of silicon collapsed from about $400 per kilogram in 2008 to about $40 per kilogram by 2011
choices: The world price of silicon collapsed from about $400 per kilogram in 2008 to about $40 per kilogram by 2011
The world price of copper doubled between 2008 and 2011
US import duties on Chinese solar panels rose 50 percent
The California electricity feed-in tariff was cut by 90 percent
context: Silicon is the main input for flat panels. Solyndra's whole business case rested on high silicon prices making its cylindrical alternative competitive. When silicon crashed, the case evaporated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: By 2010, private venture investors had walked away from more Solyndra funding. They had seen silicon prices crash and Chinese factories scale up. The Department of Energy backed the $535 million loan anyway. Which Austrian idea does this pattern show?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: private investors' declined bets are dispersed information a central agency lacks
choices: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: private investors' declined bets are dispersed information a central agency lacks
John Maynard Keynes's paradox of thrift: private saving reduces aggregate demand
Milton Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis about consumption smoothing
Alvin Hansen's secular-stagnation thesis about mature economies
context: Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' argued that dispersed knowledge across many private actors is irreducible to any central authority. When many private investors independently say 'no,' that revealed preference is information. A DOE loan officer facing no personal cost of being wrong lacks the same feedback discipline. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: Solyndra was an American solar-panel company. In 2009 it received a half-billion-dollar federal loan guarantee from the Obama administration to build a new factory in California. Two years later, in 2011, Solyndra went bankrupt and American taxpayers were left holding the bag. Congress opened hearings, and reporters zeroed in on one big private backer of the failed company -- an Oklahoma billionaire who had also raised campaign cash for President Obama. Who drew the heat?
answer: George Kaiser through his Argonaut Ventures firm
choices: George Kaiser through his Argonaut Ventures firm
Warren Buffett through Berkshire Hathaway Energy
T. Boone Pickens through BP Capital
Peter Thiel through Founders Fund
context: Kaiser was a Tulsa-based billionaire and Obama campaign fundraiser. The connection did not, on the public record, direct the DOE decision, but it fueled a regulatory-capture critique of the loan-guarantee program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: In 2011 a US solar-panel company called Solyndra went bankrupt after getting about $500 million from a $16 billion federal loan-guarantee program. Critics in the news focused only on Solyndra. A Bastiat-style critic says that focus misses the bigger unseen cost. What is the unseen cost?
answer: The full $16 billion could not be doing anything else, and other funded firms failed too
choices: The full $16 billion could not be doing anything else, and other funded firms failed too
The officers who approved the loans all lost their jobs
Private investors who declined Solyndra paid no taxes
California made a windfall selling Solyndra's assets
context: Bastiat's method: compare the seen benefit to the unseen alternative use of the same capital. Abound Solar (2012), A123 Systems (2012), and Fisker Automotive (2013) also went bankrupt among Section 1705 recipients. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Loan_Programs_Office.

question: The Soviet Union was a giant communist country that existed from 1922 to 1991 and stretched from Poland to the Pacific Ocean. Instead of letting shops and factories decide what to sell, the Soviets used a huge central-planning office in Moscow called Gosplan. A small committee there tried to decide how many shoes, tractors, and loaves of bread the whole country should make each year. Why is doing this well almost impossible?
answer: No small group can know what millions of people actually want
choices: No small group can know what millions of people actually want
The committee did not have enough clipboards
Russians did not want shoes or bread
There are only three products in a whole country
context: Gosplan (Gosudarstvenniy Planovyy Komitet -- State Planning Committee) coordinated Soviet five-year plans and yearly targets from 1921 through the USSR's dissolution in December 1991. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosplan.

question: In the Soviet Union, the government agency called Gosplan tried to plan the entire economy from the top down. Instead of letting prices and buyers decide what got made, Gosplan set production targets for how many boots, screws, tractors, and toothbrushes the country should produce each year. At its peak in the 1980s, Gosplan tried to set targets for an enormous list of separate products. What is the usual estimate of how many it tried to plan?
choices: About 200
About 20 billion
