About 2,000
context: Gertrude Schroeder and Alec Nove's estimates put the peak at more than 200,000 distinct product categories -- steel of various grades, screws of various sizes, textiles, consumer goods, and so on. Source: Nove, The Economics of Feasible Socialism (1983).

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that a central planner cannot possibly do the math. To coordinate an economy, he said, you have to compare each pair of prices to every other pair. If a country makes N different products, the number of comparisons is roughly N times N, divided by two. A modern economy has around 200,000 different product categories. About what size number does that formula give?
answer: 20 billion
choices: 20 billion
20 million
2 million
context: The 20-billion pairwise-price count is a heuristic teaching device (not a Gosplan-cited figure) illustrating why the calculation problem is impossible in principle, not merely difficult in practice. Each relationship shifts every day with harvests, tastes, and technology. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation.

question: In the Soviet Union of the 1900s, the state planning office Gosplan tried to decide what every factory should make. But the plan always had gaps -- a bakery might not get flour, a shop might not get shoes. Ordinary Soviets survived by trading favors with friends, cousins, and workmates who could quietly help them get scarce goods. This informal shadow system had its own Russian word, meaning 'favor-trading' or 'connections'. What is the word?
answer: Blat
choices: Blat
Kvass
Duma
Zek
context: Blat was the informal favor-trading system through which Soviet citizens obtained goods the state could not deliver. It permeated every level from consumer purchases to industrial inputs. Source: Alena Ledeneva, Russia's Economy of Favours (1998).

question: In the Soviet Union, factories were told by Gosplan -- the central planning office in Moscow -- exactly what to produce. But the plan was always short on some parts. If a tractor factory needed steel and Moscow forgot to ship any, the manager could not just call a supplier -- there was no market. So Soviet factory bosses hired traveling agents whose whole job was to go to Moscow, work every contact, and pry loose the missing supplies. What were these travelers called?
answer: Tolkachi (pushers)
choices: Tolkachi (pushers)
Kulaks
Nomenklatura
Rabkoms
context: Tolkachi ('pushers') traveled to Moscow to lobby ministries for missing components, expedite deliveries, and negotiate quotas. The role was so ubiquitous it had a name; it also illustrated Gosplan's inability to coordinate 200,000 products in real time. Source: Berliner, Factory and Manager in the USSR.

question: In the Soviet Union, nail factories were paid to hit a total weight quota by the end of each month. Near the deadline, managers rushed to finish by making only giant, heavy, nearly useless nails so the numbers came out. Elsewhere Soviet glass factories paid by square meters produced panes so thin they shattered on delivery. What is the predictable result of paying only for weight or count, never for quality?
answer: Lots of heavy, poorly-made products that nobody wants to use
choices: Lots of heavy, poorly-made products that nobody wants to use
Lighter, higher-quality products at a steady pace
Workers refuse to work in the last week of the month
The plan naturally corrects itself the following month
context: Storming (shturmovshchina) was the last-week rush to meet monthly, quarterly, or yearly plan targets. It produced low-quality output near month-end and made the phrase 'they pretend to pay us and we pretend to work' a widespread black joke. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System.

question: In 1983 a socialist economist — not a free-market thinker — published a book titled The Economics of Feasible Socialism. In it he conceded that the calculation problem, first raised by the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises against central planning, is real and cannot be waved away. Any large central-planned economy, he wrote, must face it head-on. Who wrote the book?
answer: Alec Nove
choices: Alec Nove
Oskar Lange
Michal Kalecki
Paul Sweezy
context: Alec Nove was a British socialist economist and Soviet-studies scholar at the University of Glasgow. The Economics of Feasible Socialism (1983) is one of the most honest inside-the-tradition confrontations with Mises-Hayek. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Nove.

question: The Soviet Union spent 70 years running its economy through Moscow's Gosplan office. By the late 1980s the plan was failing and shortages were everywhere. In December 1991 the Soviet parliament voted the whole country out of existence. President Mikhail Gorbachev resigned live on television, the red hammer-and-sickle flag came down over the Kremlin -- on Christmas Day, no less -- and Gosplan closed for good. What is the exact date?
answer: December 25, 1991
choices: December 25, 1991
November 9, 1989
March 5, 1953
August 19, 1991
context: The Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin on December 25, 1991; Gorbachev resigned that evening; formal dissolution followed the next day. Gosplan closed with the USSR. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union.

question: In 1920 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published a paper arguing that socialism could never work. Without real market prices, he said, a central planner cannot know what to make in what amounts. Mises's opponents countered that modern statistics and computers would solve the problem. Then, in 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed after 70 years of Gosplan trying. The West went on producing shoes, tractors, and bread by the millions with no committee at all. What did the market do that Gosplan could not?
answer: Coordinate 200,000 product categories with no committee needed
choices: Coordinate 200,000 product categories with no committee needed
Print more paper money to close deficits
Set stable exchange rates for foreign trade
Regulate monopoly pricing efficiently
context: After 1991, post-Soviet market economies coordinated the same 200,000 product categories without any Gosplan-style committee, and better. The empirical vindication of Mises 1920 was that the pricing mechanism did what no committee could. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation.

question: In 2018 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book called Discrimination and Disparities. He took aim at a common news line: if two groups end up with different outcomes, someone must have treated them differently. Sowell agreed the gap is real. But he argued the gap by itself only tells you one thing. What does he say a gap alone shows?
answer: That something differs between them, and not yet what
choices: That something differs between them, and not yet what
That the group with less has been treated worse somewhere
That the two groups began from different places
That too few years were measured for it to mean much
context: Discrimination and Disparities (Basic Books, 2018; revised and enlarged 2019) is aimed at single-factor explanation. Sowell's list of other testable causes includes age distribution, fertility rates, geography, migration history and cultural inheritance. Sources: Hachette/Basic Books title page; Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell); Independent Institute review.

question: Thomas Sowell likes to point to a group that was banned from jobs, held back by law, and hit by riots. Yet it still ended up richer than the majority that shut it out. His main case is from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines. Which group is it?
answer: The overseas Chinese
choices: The overseas Chinese
The Rohingya of Myanmar
The Ainu of Japan
The Hmong of Laos
context: The overseas Chinese communities of Southeast Asia are Sowell's most-used case. He pairs them with Lebanese traders in West Africa and Indian merchant communities in East Africa. The three distractors are real minorities of the same region who did not follow that pattern. Source: Grokipedia, 'Dominant minority' and 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'.

question: Lebanese families set up as traders across West Africa; Indian merchant families did the same across East Africa. Both arrived poor, both were resented, and both ended up running a large share of the commerce around them. Thomas Sowell says the two cases share a cause, and it is not the countries they landed in. What is it?
answer: The trading skills and business habits they brought, which kept working in a new place
choices: The trading skills and business habits they brought, which kept working in a new place
The colonial officials who preferred outsiders to locals when handing out import licences
The port cities they settled in, which were the only places open to newcomers at the time
The small size of each community, which made trust cheap and contracts easy to enforce
context: This is what Sowell means by human capital being portable: skills, work habits, commercial networks and educational traditions travel with people and go on working in a new country. It is why he studies the same group in several countries -- the surroundings change, the pattern does not. Source: Grokipedia, 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations' and 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Between 1994 and 1998 Thomas Sowell published three linked volumes -- Race and Culture, Migrations and Cultures, Conquests and Cultures -- built on fifteen years of research and travels that took him round the world twice. He gave all three the same underlying theme. What was it?
answer: That groups carry their own way of life, and their economic histories cannot be read without it
choices: That groups carry their own way of life, and their economic histories cannot be read without it
That conquest reshapes a conquered people faster than any other force in their history
That migration is the single strongest predictor of how wealthy a country will become
That national borders explain more about a group's fortunes than any inherited habit does
context: Race and Culture: A World View (1994), Migrations and Cultures: A World View (1996) and Conquests and Cultures: An International History (1998). Sowell had begun the comparative-groups argument much earlier in Ethnic America: A History (1981). Sources: FEE and Publishers Weekly reviews of Conquests and Cultures; Hoover Institution, 'Race, Culture, and Equality'.

question: Thomas Sowell argues that one English word is doing two jobs at once, and that arguments go wrong when nobody separates them. The second job is the familiar one -- treating people badly on arbitrary assumptions about their race or sex, which is what the law goes after. He labels the first job Discrimination I. What is it?
answer: Telling real differences in quality apart and choosing accordingly
choices: Telling real differences in quality apart and choosing accordingly
Preferring the group you belong to when the choice is close
Applying a rule strictly to some applicants and loosely to others
Judging a stranger by the last person you met who resembled him
context: Sowell's own wording for Discrimination I is 'an ability to discern differences in the qualities of people and things, and choosing accordingly' -- fact-based distinctions, ideally judging each person as an individual. Discrimination II is 'treating people negatively, based on arbitrary assumptions or aversions.' His complaint is that public argument uses one word for both. Sources: The Federalist, 'Thomas Sowell Explains The Economics Of Discrimination'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: Thomas Sowell wanted a case where no group-level cause could explain uneven outcomes: same parents, same house, same schools, same family income. He found one in a study of America's top scholarship finalists — kids who scored so high on national tests that they qualified for elite college scholarships — but only from families of exactly five children. What did the study show about the eldest child in those families?
answer: The first-born was the finalist more often than the other four siblings combined
choices: The first-born was the finalist more often than the other four siblings combined
The first-born was the finalist about twice as often as the youngest child was
The first-born and the youngest child together supplied nine finalists in ten
The first-born was the finalist in almost exactly one family out of every five
context: Sowell's use of the figure is careful: it is not an argument about who deserves what. It is an argument that huge disparities appear between people who share every background factor a study could control for -- so equal outcomes between whole nations would be the astonishing result, not the expected one. Sources: Walter E. Williams, 'Discrimination and Disparities II' (Creators Syndicate), quoting Sowell; Hoover Institution.

question: Chinese families in Indonesia were a small share of the country. At times they were banned from certain jobs and hit by riots. Still, Thomas Sowell picks Indonesia to make a point about what those families held. What share of Indonesia's wealth does he say they held?
answer: About eighty per cent
choices: About eighty per cent
About fifteen per cent
About thirty-five per cent
About fifty-five per cent
context: Sowell's point is not that hostility was mild -- it was severe and sometimes lethal. It is that severe hostility and economic success sat together, which is exactly what the disparity-proves-discrimination rule says should not happen. Source: Grokipedia, 'Dominant minority' and 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'.

question: A committee looks at a tough engineering program. Admits are uneven across regions, and the committee treats the unevenness as the puzzle to solve. Thomas Sowell's Discrimination and Disparities argues this kind of outcome needs many things at once: schooling, language, family, mobility, and money. What does Sowell say follows?
answer: Four of the five in place is worth nothing, so even spreading would be the astonishing result
choices: Four of the five in place is worth nothing, so even spreading would be the astonishing result
The committee should weight each of the five by how much it costs a family to supply it
Any region missing a single one of the five will catch up within about a generation
The five must be ranked, because whichever comes first will determine all the others
context: This is the prerequisites argument that opens the book: where success requires multiple prerequisites all present together, it will not be evenly or randomly distributed among individuals, groups, institutions or nations. Sources: Books At A Glance summary of Discrimination and Disparities; Shenvi Apologetics review; CultureWatch.

question: A banking regulator publishes numbers showing that applicants from one neighborhood are turned down for mortgages more often than applicants from another. The regulator concludes the lenders are biased. A reader trained by Thomas Sowell does not call the numbers wrong. Which objection does that reader press first?
answer: The two sets of applicants have to be compared on what the lender actually reads before the gap means anything
choices: The two sets of applicants have to be compared on what the lender actually reads before the gap means anything
The regulator has published only one year of figures, and a single year cannot establish a lending pattern
The lenders operating in the two neighbourhoods are different firms, so their internal rules were never the same
The applicants who expected refusal may not have applied, so the pool itself was shaped before any lender saw it
context: Note the shape of the move: the reader does not announce that the lenders are innocent. Sowell's rule is that a disparity marks the beginning of an investigation, not the end of one -- so the next step is to compare the two groups on the things the decision actually turned on. The other three choices are real objections too, each raised in actual lending-data disputes. Sources: Independent Institute review, 'Being Careful with Numbers, Words, and Visions'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: A reviewer writes that Thomas Sowell's books amount to a claim that discrimination is a myth. Sowell has answered this charge for forty years, and his answer is not that he has been misread on the details. He says the reviewer has mistaken the kind of claim he is making. What kind is it?
answer: A claim about what evidence is needed to establish a cause, not about whether that cause exists
choices: A claim about what evidence is needed to establish a cause, not about whether that cause exists
A claim about which century the worst mistreatment happened in, not about whether it happened
A claim about the motives of researchers, not about the figures those researchers publish
A claim about which level of government should collect the data, not about what the data show
context: Sowell does not deny that discrimination has existed or that it exists. His argument is methodological: unequal treatment is one candidate cause among several, and it has to be shown with evidence about treatment rather than inferred from the size of a gap. Readers who accept the method can still disagree with him about any particular case -- which is the point of a method. Sources: Independent Institute review; Shenvi Apologetics review of Discrimination and Disparities.

question: Two economists study the same wage gap. The first compares the groups as they stand this year and reads the remaining gap as the measure of mistreatment. Thomas Sowell studies the same groups across generations and across the countries they migrated to. He is not just adding detail; the second method can find something the first cannot even look for. What is it?
answer: Whether the pattern travels with the people when they move to a country with different institutions
choices: Whether the pattern travels with the people when they move to a country with different institutions
Whether the wage figures were gathered by employers or by the government's own statisticians
Whether the gap has widened or narrowed since the last time the same survey was carried out
Whether the two groups are counted in the same industry categories by the agency doing the survey
context: This is why Sowell spent fifteen years and two circuits of the globe on the culture trilogy. If a group's professional attainment holds up in Lagos, London and Chicago alike, the explanation cannot be entirely the treatment they met in any one of those places. Austrians and Chicago economists both use this move -- hold the people constant, change the institutions, and see what survives. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'; FEE review of Conquests and Cultures.

question: A legislature drafts a rule forbidding any organisation from sorting applicants by characteristics that come out unevenly across groups. An airline points out that it screens pilots on logged flight hours, and a bank that it screens borrowers on repayment records -- and both practices come out unevenly. Thomas Sowell's two-word distinction predicts exactly this collision. What does he say such a rule reaches?
answer: Fact-based sorting on real qualifications, not only sorting on arbitrary aversion
choices: Fact-based sorting on real qualifications, not only sorting on arbitrary aversion
Only the largest firms, since a small firm can rarely afford to sort applicants at all
The regulators before the firms, since the sorting rules were written by agencies first
Every industry equally, since no occupation screens applicants more heavily than another
context: This is Discrimination I and Discrimination II colliding inside one word. Sowell's claim is not that the law should permit prejudice; it is that a rule written against uneven outcomes catches the airline's flight-hours check along with the prejudice, because both produce uneven outcomes. Where to draw the line afterwards is a live political argument -- Sowell's contribution is insisting that the two things be named separately before anyone argues about it. Sources: The Federalist, 'Thomas Sowell Explains The Economics Of Discrimination'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: For decades, Thomas Sowell heard people say some market outcome -- a wage, a price, a shortage -- was too bad to accept. He said most such claims fall apart with one short question back. Almost no one had an answer ready. What was Sowell's trademark question?
answer: Compared to what?
choices: Compared to what?
At what cost?
And then what happens?
Who bears the risk?
context: Thomas Sowell (born 1930), the Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution since 1980, named 'Compared to what?' as the first of three questions he said would destroy most arguments on the left; the other two were 'At what cost?' and 'What hard evidence do you have?' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'; quotefancy.com/quote/920957.

question: At a town meeting a speaker says the market has failed this town's working families and that the council must step in and run things better. Thomas Sowell's habitual reply denies nothing the speaker has said; it simply shifts a burden onto him. What does the speaker now have to produce?
answer: The name of the institution he would put in its place
choices: The name of the institution he would put in its place
The moral case for private ownership of a business
A forecast of what local wages will do next year
A count of the families now living on credit
context: The move is a demand for a NAMED alternative. Until the speaker says which real body would run things -- a city agency, a state board, a federal programme -- there is nothing to weigh the market against, and the argument is holding a real thing up against a wish. Source: Harold Demsetz, 'Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint', Journal of Law and Economics 12 (1969).

question: Thomas Sowell's book Applied Economics rests on one idea: stage one versus everything after it. A state raises the tax on business, and the treasury does take in more money that first year. Sowell says elected officials stop thinking right there. Why?
answer: They do not think beyond the next election
choices: They do not think beyond the next election
They are never taught any economics at all
They rely on forecasts their staff invent
They believe firms cannot afford to move
context: Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One (Basic Books, 2003; 2nd ed. 2008) argues that basic economics gets misapplied because politicians think only in stage one -- the immediate result of an action -- and, in Sowell's words, 'do not think beyond the next election.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: A student compares a real, messy grocery store to an imaginary perfect one where no food is ever wasted and every shelf is always full. Then he says the real store is a failure. Economists have a name for this unfair kind of comparison. What is the mistake?
answer: Comparing a real thing to a perfect fantasy instead of to other real options
choices: Comparing a real thing to a perfect fantasy instead of to other real options
Ignoring the past when studying today
Assuming people never respond to prices
Trusting only what math models predict
context: Harold Demsetz (1930-2019) taught at Chicago from 1963 to 1971 and published 'Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint' in the Journal of Law and Economics vol. 12 no. 1 (1969), pp. 1-22. Alchian was his UCLA collaborator; Stigler and Coase were Chicago colleagues. Source: econlib.org, Biography of Harold Demsetz.

question: Harold Demsetz saw a common habit in policy writing. A writer picks a real, working setup, holds it against an ideal that lives only on paper, finds the real one worse, and calls it a failure. His 1969 paper gave the habit a name. What did he call it?
answer: The nirvana approach
choices: The nirvana approach
The scientistic approach
The aggregative approach
The positivist approach
context: Demsetz wrote that 'those who adopt the nirvana viewpoint seek to discover discrepancies between the ideal and the real and if discrepancies are found, they deduce that the real is inefficient.' Later economists relabelled it the 'nirvana fallacy.' Sources: econlib.org, Biography of Harold Demsetz; Wikipedia, 'Nirvana fallacy'.

question: Harold Demsetz granted at once that no market is perfect. His point was that no government is perfect either, so measuring one of them against a flawless standard settles nothing at all. He said policy economics therefore always faces a choice of a quite different kind. What did Demsetz say the relevant choice lies between?
answer: Between one real institution and another real institution
choices: Between one real institution and another real institution
Between short-run costs and long-run benefits
Between individual liberty and collective welfare
Between what can be measured and what cannot
context: Demsetz called this the 'comparative institutions approach': 'the relevant choice is between alternative real institutional arrangements,' not 'between an ideal norm and an existing imperfect institutional arrangement.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Nirvana fallacy', quoting Demsetz 1969.

question: In Applied Economics Thomas Sowell follows a state that has raised the tax rate it charges businesses. The treasury collects more in the first year, exactly as the sponsors promised. Sowell then asks what the state's own tax base looks like three years on. What does he say has happened by then?
answer: Firms have moved out and the revenue has fallen
choices: Firms have moved out and the revenue has fallen
Firms have raised prices and the revenue has held
Firms have cut wages and the revenue has risen
Firms have merged and the revenue has stayed flat
context: Sowell's stage-two point: businesses relocate to other states and new companies choose competitors, so the state ends up collecting less than before the increase. This is the pattern the book's subtitle names. Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: An economist demonstrates that a market might supply less of some good than would be ideal. He jumps directly to the conclusion that the government should step in and never checks whether real governments actually do that job better. What is the name for this reasoning error?
answer: Comparing a real, flawed market to a perfect imagined government
choices: Comparing a real, flawed market to a perfect imagined government
Confusing higher prices with higher costs
Ignoring the effect of taxes on producers
Assuming every consumer wants the same thing
context: Kenneth Arrow had argued the free market might provide too little innovation, then assumed government intervention would move the economy toward the optimum. Demsetz conceded that ideal intervention might improve matters, but noted Arrow had never shown that actual intervention would. Source: econlib.org, Biography of Harold Demsetz.

question: A speaker argues that American medical care is failing because millions cannot afford the treatment they need, and proposes that the federal government take the job over. A student trained on Thomas Sowell does not dispute a word of the hardship described. What does the student ask first?
answer: Which existing public system, and how does it ration care?
choices: Which existing public system, and how does it ration care?
Which private insurer profits most, and by how much?
How many people gain cover, and how soon do they get it?
What does the programme cost, and who ends up paying?
context: The point is not that public medicine is bad; it is that 'the government' is not an institution you can weigh anything against. Name Britain's National Health Service, or a Canadian province, or the Veterans Health Administration, and each has a record a student can read. Then the argument becomes an honest one, and the student decides it. Source: Demsetz 1969; Sowell, Applied Economics (2003).

question: James Buchanan told economists to study politics 'without romance.' He said officials should be modeled as ordinary self-interested people, not selfless servants. Thomas Sowell's three-word question presses the same point from the other side. What single rule are the two men enforcing?
answer: Hold every institution to the record it actually has
choices: Hold every institution to the record it actually has
Assume officials know less than they claim to know
Trust the ordinary citizen's judgement over the expert's
Judge a policy by the incentives of its authors
context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize for public choice theory, which applies economic analysis to political decision-making. Romantic politics and the nirvana approach are the same error twice over: one idealises the official, the other idealises the agency. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'; Demsetz 1969.

question: A reformer wants to replace a country's private pension market with one state fund. The fund would have independent trustees, be insulated from politics, and be audited publicly. Under a rule Harold Demsetz set out in 1969, the proposal has one specific defect as an argument, whatever its merits as a plan. What is the defect?
answer: The fund it is measured against does not yet exist anywhere
choices: The fund it is measured against does not yet exist anywhere
The fund would need more trustees than the country has
The private market it replaces has never been audited
The pensions it promises are indexed to an unknown rate
context: Demsetz's rule bites here: a design on paper has no failures, because designs never do. To argue honestly the reformer must point at a state pension fund that has actually run for decades -- Chile's, Singapore's, Sweden's -- and show its record. Source: Demsetz 1969, 'Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint'.

question: Thomas Sowell is a Black American economist who taught for many years at Stanford University in California. He is famous for writing clear, data-driven books that challenge conventional wisdom on race, poverty, and public policy. In June 2020 Sowell turned 90 years old. That same month he published a new book arguing that charter schools -- public schools run outside the teacher-union system -- were helping poor city kids learn far better than nearby traditional schools. What was the book called?
answer: Charter Schools and Their Enemies
choices: Charter Schools and Their Enemies
Vision of the Anointed
Discrimination and Disparities
A Conflict of Visions
context: Published by Basic Books. It was Sowell's 32nd book overall. He continued publishing, releasing 'Social Justice Fallacies' in September 2023 at age 93. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charter_Schools_and_Their_Enemies.

question: Thomas Sowell, an American economist who taught at Stanford, wrote a 2020 book called Charter Schools and Their Enemies. Critics of charter schools often say the students only do well because they come from richer or more motivated families. Sowell wanted to strip that objection away. So he used a clever comparison design that held income, race, and neighborhood factors steady. What exactly did he compare?
answer: Test scores of charter students vs traditional-public-school students in the SAME school buildings or same neighborhoods
choices: Test scores of charter students vs traditional-public-school students in the SAME school buildings or same neighborhoods
Test scores of charter students in affluent suburbs vs urban traditional students
Graduation rates in charter schools nationally vs public schools in Finland
College acceptance rates in private religious schools vs public magnet schools
context: The co-located comparison is important because charters and traditional schools in the same building draw from the same demographic pool -- so racial, income, and family-structure differences cannot explain any gaps. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charter_Schools_and_Their_Enemies.

question: In cities like New York, a growing network of charter schools -- free public schools run outside the traditional school district -- uses one simple rule for who gets in. Any family can apply, and when there are more applicants than seats, the seats are picked by a public lottery drawn from a barrel. No admissions tests, no interviews, no political favors, no connections. What is the main fairness argument for these lottery schools?
answer: The lottery gives every family the same shot, no matter who they know
choices: The lottery gives every family the same shot, no matter who they know
The lottery guarantees every child a top test score
The lottery is required by a federal law from the 1990s
The lottery replaces the need for teachers or classrooms
context: Success Academy operates dozens of schools in New York City, many co-located with traditional public schools in Harlem and the Bronx. Its state-test results have consistently placed it near the top of NY state rankings. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Success_Academy_Charter_Schools.

question: Thomas Sowell, in his 2020 book Charter Schools and Their Enemies, dug into New York City test-score data building by building. He looked at the top charter schools in Harlem -- a mostly Black, working-class neighborhood in Manhattan -- and compared them both to the traditional public schools right next door and to rich suburban schools far outside the city. What did his comparison show about the highest-performing Harlem charter schools?
answer: They produced test scores comparable to affluent suburban schools -- from students in the same neighborhoods as much lower-scoring traditional-school peers
choices: They produced test scores comparable to affluent suburban schools -- from students in the same neighborhoods as much lower-scoring traditional-school peers
They performed identically to nearby traditional public schools on all measures
They performed significantly worse than nearby traditional public schools on all measures
They only enrolled students already in the top 5 percent of state test-takers
context: The comparison was the load-bearing empirical finding of the book. Since charter students in these Harlem schools came from the same demographic pool as their traditional-school peers, demographic factors could not explain the gap. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charter_Schools_and_Their_Enemies.

question: Thomas Sowell, the American economist, is famous for boiling policy debates down to a handful of unavoidable questions. When someone objects to expanding charter schools by pointing at a flaw in a particular charter, Sowell insists on framing the debate with one trademark question. The point: no policy exists in a vacuum -- you have to weigh it against the real alternative these kids would otherwise face. Which question does Sowell apply?
answer: Compared to what? -- the alternative to charter expansion for these children is their current traditional-school outcome, not a hypothetical perfect public system
choices: Compared to what? -- the alternative to charter expansion for these children is their current traditional-school outcome, not a hypothetical perfect public system
How much does it cost? -- the cost per student is the only relevant metric
Who benefits? -- the answer is only teacher unions and the alternative is worse
Is it fair? -- fairness alone should determine the policy outcome
context: Sowell's 'Compared to what?' is his trademark analytical move. It reframes policy debate away from ideal-theory comparisons and toward realistic counterfactuals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Public-choice economics studies how politics really works -- how organized interest groups capture rules the general public would never vote for. In his 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action, the economist Mancur Olson showed that small concentrated groups almost always beat big diffuse ones in politics. Thomas Sowell uses Olson's idea to explain charter-school politics. Why does the political outcome tilt against charter families?
answer: Olson's dispersed-costs/concentrated-benefits: teacher unions are concentrated and organized; charter parents are diffuse and unorganized
choices: Olson's dispersed-costs/concentrated-benefits: teacher unions are concentrated and organized; charter parents are diffuse and unorganized
The Coase theorem: property rights would fully solve the problem if transaction costs were zero
Rawls's veil of ignorance: charter policy should be chosen behind a curtain of demographic knowledge
The Laffer curve: reducing charter taxation would raise total charter revenue
context: Public choice predicts that concentrated beneficiaries of the status quo will win political fights over dispersed but individually less-invested groups. UFT and AFT political spending in NY documented the concentrated-organization side. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charter_Schools_and_Their_Enemies.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell, still writing books in his nineties, has spent decades studying why groups end up with different incomes, jobs, and test scores. He argues that the 'social justice' movement -- which pushes government action to close gaps between racial and gender groups -- keeps making the same reasoning mistake, over and over, whenever it looks at those gaps. Which mistake does Sowell say it makes?
answer: It assumes any gap in outcomes between groups must be caused by unfair discrimination
choices: It assumes any gap in outcomes between groups must be caused by unfair discrimination
It assumes rich countries got rich by taking money from poor countries
It assumes small business owners are always more honest than big companies
It assumes technology always makes workers better off in the short run
context: 'Social Justice Fallacies' (Basic Books, September 2023, at age 93) applied Sowell's reasoning-move discipline to social-justice arguments. The two books together show what a sustained econ-reasoning practice looks like at the end of a career. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: In 1987 the American economist Thomas Sowell wrote a book called A Conflict of Visions. It sets out two rival pictures of human nature — one that says people can be perfected by clever policy, and one that says people are flawed and stuck with hard choices. That second picture refuses a word politicians love to promise. Sowell packed the refusal into a famous six-word sentence. What is it?
answer: There are no solutions, only trade-offs.
choices: There are no solutions, only trade-offs.
There are no free lunches, only bills.
There are no experts, only interested parties.
There are no shortages, only unpaid prices.
context: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' -- Thomas Sowell, A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles (1987). The line belongs to what Sowell calls the constrained vision, which treats human capability as limited by flaws, scarcity and incomplete knowledge. Source: A Conflict of Visions (1987), quoted at goodreads.com/quotes/1411380.

question: In his 1993 essay collection Is Reality Optional?, Thomas Sowell put two opening propositions side by side. The first, from economics, is that there is never enough of anything to satisfy everyone who wants it. Then came his line about politics that made the pair famous. What did he say politics is?
answer: To disregard the first lesson of economics
choices: To disregard the first lesson of economics
To promise more than the budget will allow
To blame the shortage on somebody's greed
To spend the money before the term ends
context: 'The first lesson of economics is scarcity: there is never enough of anything to satisfy all those who want it. The first lesson of politics is to disregard the first lesson of economics.' -- Thomas Sowell, Is Reality Optional? And Other Essays (1993). Source: goodreads.com/work/quotes/6909; libquotes.com/thomas-sowell/quote/lbc6s2i.

question: Thomas Sowell, the American economist, spent his career pushing readers to think about the trade-offs behind every policy. Free college? Universal health care? A bigger military? Each one sounds noble on its own. Sowell says that if you endorse a policy without asking one particular three-word question, you have not analyzed it at all -- you have only cheered for it. What is the question?
answer: At what cost?
choices: At what cost?
Compared to what?
For how long?
Who pays first?
context: Sowell listed three questions he said would destroy most arguments on the left: 'Compared to what?', 'At what cost?', and 'What hard evidence do you have?' The second is the trade-off question -- and 'compared to what?' is its partner, not its rival. Source: Thomas Sowell, collected at quotefancy.com/quote/920957.

question: In The Vision of the Anointed (1995), Thomas Sowell mocks the picture that smart planners carry around. On their view, every hard problem has an answer sitting somewhere, and policy just has to go get it. Sowell drew that picture with one homely image. Which image?
answer: Eggs laid out for children at an Easter hunt
choices: Eggs laid out for children at an Easter hunt
Keys lost somewhere under a lit street lamp
Weeds pulled one by one from a long border
Coins shaken loose from a locked money box
context: 'Solutions are out there waiting to be found, like eggs at an Easter egg hunt.' -- Thomas Sowell, The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (1995). His objection is not that the anointed are lazy; it is that a world of hidden answers has no trade-offs in it at all. Source: goodreads.com/work/quotes/55220.

question: A programme has run for fifteen years and has not produced what its sponsors promised. Thomas Sowell says the two rival visions read that same record in opposite ways, and that watching which reading a person reaches for tells you which vision he holds. How does the constrained vision read it?
answer: The cost of the fix exceeded its benefit, so withdraw it
choices: The cost of the fix exceeded its benefit, so withdraw it
The effort fell short of the problem, so enlarge it
The wrong agency was handed the job, so transfer it
The target was pitched too low, so raise it
context: In A Conflict of Visions Sowell contrasts a 'tragic vision of the human condition' with a 'moral vision of human intentions.' The unconstrained vision reads a failure as insufficient will or bad design and reaches for a bigger version; the constrained vision reads it as a trade-off that was miscalculated. Source: A Conflict of Visions (1987); Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In 1995 the American economist Thomas Sowell wrote a book called The Vision of the Anointed. He said a certain class of educated thinkers — the ones he called 'the anointed' — have a favorite substitute for real policy analysis. When a hard problem stumps them, they reach for something that costs nothing, commits nobody, and fixes nothing. What do they reach for?
answer: A slogan that denounces the problem
choices: A slogan that denounces the problem
A commission that studies the problem
A budget that under-prices the problem
A statistic that shrinks the problem
context: Sowell calls these 'verbal solutions' -- a public denunciation of poverty, say, standing in for any assessment of what a poverty programme costs or what it does to incentives. He treats the substitution as the signature move of The Vision of the Anointed (1995). Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A city caps what may legally be charged for a flat, and tenants in the capped flats do pay less -- that part is real, immediate and countable. Thomas Sowell's method says the sentence is only half written until a student names what the lower rent was bought with. Which cost does his analysis put first?
answer: Buildings that landlords stop maintaining
choices: Buildings that landlords stop maintaining
Taxes that homeowners must now shoulder
Wages that construction crews must accept
Mortgages that banks now refuse to write
context: Sowell's argument is about incentives, not motives: rent-capped income will not cover upkeep, so upkeep stops, and the tenant's saving is paid for in decay, queues and substandard units. Whether that trade is worth making is the reader's call; the analysis only insists that a trade is being made. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell', on his price-control analysis.

question: Thomas Sowell argues that a legal ceiling on a price does not simply push the price down; it opens a second, illegal trade beside the lawful one. He then makes a claim about the prices charged in that illegal trade which startles most people who hear it for the first time. What does Sowell say about them?
answer: They run higher than a free market's prices would
choices: They run higher than a free market's prices would
They settle at almost exactly the legal ceiling
They swing far less than lawful prices do
They fall further the longer the shortage lasts
context: 'Price controls almost invariably produce black markets, where prices are not only higher than the legally permitted prices, but also higher than they would be in a free market, since the legal risks must also be compensated.' -- Thomas Sowell, Basic Economics. The seller is being paid for the risk of prosecution as well as for the goods. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A student prices out a proposed subsidy line by line, finds the bill steep, and knocks the proposal down. Pleased with himself, he then argues that an existing programme should be abolished outright. Thomas Sowell's own rule does not let him stop where he has stopped. What must the student now do?
answer: Name what abolishing it will cost, and who bears that
choices: Name what abolishing it will cost, and who bears that
Show that the programme was unpopular when it passed
Prove that the programme's budget has grown every year
Find a country that has already abolished the same thing
context: The move is symmetric or it is worthless. Repeal is a policy too, with its own costs falling on identifiable people; a student who applies the question only to proposals he dislikes has learned a debating trick, not a method. Sowell's rail is that intentions do not settle anything, in either direction. Source: Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (1987); Applied Economics (2003).

question: A student prices out a proposed programme down to the last line item and finds the total bearable -- the country can afford it. Thomas Sowell says the analysis is still unfinished, because an affordable price proves nothing whatever on its own. What has the student still not established?
answer: That no other real arrangement buys the same thing cheaper
choices: That no other real arrangement buys the same thing cheaper
That the programme's supporters have declared their interests
That the cost will not rise once the programme is running
That the people paying the cost are the people it helps
context: Sowell treats his two questions as one test with two halves: a cost you can bear is still a cost you may not have to pay. The pairing is why he insists that a policy argument surviving only one of the questions has not been tested at all. Source: Thomas Sowell, collected at quotefancy.com/quote/920957; A Conflict of Visions (1987).

question: Thomas Sowell has never claimed the six-word line as a discovery. He treats it as a slogan for a proposition that economics has rested on since the subject began, and that every first-year textbook still opens with. Which proposition is the slogan compressing?
answer: That resources are limited, so every use forgoes another
choices: That resources are limited, so every use forgoes another
That prices carry information no planner can gather
That people answer to incentives more than to orders
That money loses value when governments issue more
context: Opportunity cost under scarcity -- the idea that using a thing one way means not using it another -- is older than Sowell by a century and more, and older than the Austrian School that sharpened it. The three distractors are the knowledge problem, the incentive principle, and the quantity theory of money: all real, all somebody else's. Source: Sowell, Is Reality Optional? (1993).

question: Every few years, a mayor of some American city announces a plan to build a shiny new stadium for the local football, baseball, or basketball team, paid for with taxpayer money. Boosters promise the stadium will bring jobs, tourists, and a booming local economy. But two American economists have spent 20 years digging into the actual data from dozens of cities. Their finding is blunt -- taxpayer-funded stadiums do not measurably grow a region's economy. Which pair?
answer: Dennis Coates and Brad Humphreys
choices: Dennis Coates and Brad Humphreys
Roger Noll and Andrew Zimbalist
Rodney Fort and James Quirk
Michael Leeds and Peter von Allmen
context: Dennis Coates + Brad Humphreys, especially their 2008 Econ Journal Watch survey 'Do Economists Reach a Conclusion on Subsidies for Sports Franchises, Stadiums, and Mega-Events?' The finding was near-unanimous across independent studies. Source: econjwatch.org (Coates + Humphreys 2008).

question: When an American city agrees to help build a new stadium for a pro football or baseball team, the deal is usually huge -- hundreds of millions of dollars, and some cross a billion. Cities can borrow that money at low interest rates because of one specific tool. This tool lets city governments raise money without their bond investors having to pay federal income tax on the interest they earn. That tax break effectively shifts costs from investors to the federal treasury, subsidizing the stadium project. Which tool provides much of that taxpayer help?
answer: Tax-exempt municipal bonds
choices: Tax-exempt municipal bonds
Federal Reserve emergency lending
Social Security trust fund grants
Medicare Part D reimbursement
context: Federal tax exemption of municipal bond interest lowers borrowing costs on stadium bonds. A 2016 Brookings analysis estimated cumulative federal cost from 1986 to 2017 of over $3 billion in foregone federal tax revenue on stadium-related bonds. Source: brookings.edu (Long + Aizenman 2016).

question: Frederic Bastiat was a French economist who in 1850 wrote a famous essay called That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Unseen. His point: when you count only the money you can see being spent on a new project, you miss the spending that would have happened somewhere else without it. Apply this to a new baseball stadium. A family spends $200 on tickets, hot dogs, and parking at the game. What most likely happens to that money across the local area?
answer: It substitutes for other local entertainment spending
choices: It substitutes for other local entertainment spending
It generates entirely new economic activity
It exports to other regions permanently
It disappears from the local economy
context: The $200 that goes to the ballgame typically comes out of what the family would have spent at a restaurant, movie, or bowling alley. The visible stadium employment is real; the less-visible offsetting decline in other entertainment employment is the substitution effect. Source: Coates + Humphreys, Journal of Sports Economics (2002).

question: In 1965 the American economist Mancur Olson wrote a book called The Logic of Collective Action. He explained why small groups often beat big ones in politics: their gain is huge and concentrated, while their opponents' costs are spread thin across millions. Apply that idea to an American pro sports stadium deal. Who is the big concentrated winner — the one who lobbies city hall, funds campaigns, and threatens to move the team to another city?
answer: The team owner
choices: The team owner
The stadium ushers' union
The city parks department
The regional bus authority
context: Team owners are typically billionaires whose franchise values rise substantially when public capital funds the stadium. They capture ticket, concession, and media revenue. Taxpayers bear the dispersed cost. Source: Olson (1965) applied; Coates + Humphreys (2008).

question: American cities that host pro football, baseball, or basketball teams face a nasty bind. When a team's owner demands a big public payment to fix up the stadium -- or threatens to move -- any city that says no risks losing its team to a city that says yes. Every city would be better off if they all refused together. But no single city trusts the others to hold the line, so they all end up paying. Game theorists have a name for a setup where each player is pushed to defect even though cooperation would help them all. Which classic setup best fits this pattern across US cities?
answer: A prisoner's dilemma
choices: A prisoner's dilemma
A coordination game with two equilibria
A zero-sum tournament
A repeated auction with cheap talk
context: The subsidy competition among US cities forms a prisoner's dilemma. Individually, each city rationally overpays because the alternative is losing the team; collectively, cities would be better off refusing to subsidize. Source: Rosentraub, Major League Losers (Basic 1999).

question: In the United States, cities often help pay for a new pro sports stadium by adding a special tax on hotel rooms instead of a direct tax on residents. Local politicians love the trick: they get a shiny new stadium without asking their own voters to pay for it. Every out-of-town visitor booking a bed for a wedding or business trip pays a little extra without noticing. Which group ends up quietly paying most of that stadium bill?
answer: Travelers and vacationers who stay at the city's hotels
choices: Travelers and vacationers who stay at the city's hotels
The football team's wealthy owners
Only the fans who actually buy game tickets
The national government in Washington
context: Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas opened in 2020 with about $750M in public subsidy funded largely by hotel-room tax revenue. The Raiders had relocated from Oakland to Las Vegas partly to capture the subsidy the Nevada government offered. Source: reviewjournal.com (Allegiant Stadium financing coverage).

question: For thirty years, US pro football and baseball teams demanding new stadiums promised huge boosts to local jobs and tax revenue. In 2008, two American economists, Dennis Coates and Brad Humphreys, published a review of every independent study on stadium subsidies -- meaning studies not paid for or commissioned by the teams themselves. They wanted to see whether the promised regional payoff was real. What did nearly all of these studies find?
answer: Near-unanimous agreement that subsidies do not produce positive net regional effects
choices: Near-unanimous agreement that subsidies do not produce positive net regional effects
Roughly evenly split between positive and negative findings
Overwhelming agreement that subsidies produce large positive effects
No independent studies had ever been conducted
context: Coates + Humphreys (2008) reviewed dozens of independent economist studies and found near-unanimous agreement that publicly-subsidized stadiums do not generate positive net economic effects. Team-commissioned studies of course reach different conclusions. Source: econjwatch.org (Coates + Humphreys 2008).

question: Almost every economist agrees that public subsidies for pro sports stadiums do not help a region overall — the promised jobs and tourism rarely materialize, and taxpayers foot the bill. Yet American cities keep handing them out, and voters keep backing them at the polls. Two structural forces, taken together, explain why. What are they?
answer: Concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost combined with a jurisdictional prisoner's dilemma
choices: Concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost combined with a jurisdictional prisoner's dilemma
Widespread economist confusion about the underlying data
Undocumented federal mandates requiring the subsidies
Unanimous voter belief in the accuracy of team-commissioned studies
context: Olson's collective-action framework (concentrated owners organize, dispersed taxpayers do not) plus the city-level prisoner's dilemma (any city that refuses loses the team) is the joint structural explanation. Source: Olson (1965); Rosentraub (1999) as applied.

question: Suppose experts on a policy nearly all agree it has bad net effects — like public sports-stadium subsidies, which economists almost unanimously call a losing deal for a city — yet the policy keeps happening everywhere. The stadium case teaches a general rule for spotting why that pattern shows up. When an analyst sees a policy like this, what should she look for first?
answer: Concentrated beneficiaries with organizational advantages
choices: Concentrated beneficiaries with organizational advantages
A single hidden constitutional prohibition on repeal
Recent shifts in demographic composition
Random voter confusion equally distributed across parties
context: The stadium-subsidies case is a clean archetype: professional consensus is against; the policy persists because organized concentrated beneficiaries have overwhelming advantages against dispersed unorganized cost-bearers. The same diagnostic applies across policy domains. Source: Olson (1965); Stigler (1971).

question: The 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat warned that people count the money visibly spent at a new stadium but forget the money families would have spent somewhere else if the stadium had never been built. That is his famous 'seen and unseen'. For decades, independent stadium studies have kept finding the same pattern: dollars spent at football games are largely dollars that would otherwise have gone to bowling, movies, or local restaurants. This is the substitution effect at the heart of the Bastiat critique. Which broad claim is honest to the literature?
answer: Sports spending substitutes for other local entertainment; the multiplier is small
choices: Sports spending substitutes for other local entertainment; the multiplier is small
Sports spending is entirely new economic activity with a huge multiplier
Sports spending has no measurable effect of any kind
Sports spending permanently exports wealth to other cities
context: The consistent independent-economist finding: sports-attendance spending is largely substituted from other local entertainment. Multipliers claimed by boosters (often 2-3x) systematically fail to appear in the data. Source: Coates + Humphreys (2008); Rosentraub (1999).

question: On January 10, 2024, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) — the federal regulator that watches over the stock market — approved eleven new investment products all at once. They finally let big investors buy real Bitcoin through an ordinary brokerage account, no crypto wallet or crypto exchange needed. What kind of product got the green light that day?
answer: Spot Bitcoin ETFs
choices: Spot Bitcoin ETFs
Bitcoin futures contracts
Bitcoin closed-end funds
Bitcoin savings bonds
context: Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds hold the actual asset rather than futures contracts. Applications had been filed with the SEC repeatedly since 2013 (starting with the Winklevoss twins) and had all been rejected until this batch approval. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: For years, buying Bitcoin meant signing up with a crypto exchange and safeguarding your own secret password. In January 2024, US regulators finally approved a spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) -- a regular stock-market fund that holds real bitcoin on behalf of its investors. Suddenly, anyone with an ordinary brokerage account could buy Bitcoin the same way they buy a share of Apple stock. Why did fans of Bitcoin see this approval as a big deal?
answer: It made buying Bitcoin as easy as buying a stock
choices: It made buying Bitcoin as easy as buying a stock
It turned Bitcoin into a government-run currency
It stopped anyone from mining new Bitcoin
It made owning Bitcoin illegal in the U.S.
context: BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (ticker IBIT) accumulated the largest ETF asset base in any category during its first year. Other issuers included Fidelity (FBTC), ARK Invest (ARKB), Bitwise (BITB), VanEck (HODL), and Grayscale (GBTC, a conversion from its existing trust). Source: Grokipedia 'iShares Bitcoin Trust' (2026-09-05).

question: For years, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) refused to let normal investment funds hold Bitcoin directly — to own any, you had to open a crypto wallet on a special exchange, a hassle most retirement savers skipped. In January 2024 the SEC finally allowed spot-Bitcoin funds, and anyone with an ordinary brokerage account could buy in. Why did Bitcoin fans cheer this change?
answer: It made owning Bitcoin much easier for ordinary savers and retirement accounts
choices: It made owning Bitcoin much easier for ordinary savers and retirement accounts
It made Bitcoin illegal for the first time
It removed Bitcoin's fixed supply of 21 million coins
It gave the government a copy of every Bitcoin wallet
context: The DC Circuit's August 2023 ruling in Grayscale v SEC held that the SEC could not consistently approve Bitcoin futures ETFs (which it had done in 2021) while denying spot Bitcoin ETFs based on the same underlying market. The ruling essentially forced approval. Source: Grokipedia 'Grayscale v SEC' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 2024, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) -- the federal agency that polices Wall Street -- voted on whether to approve funds that hold real bitcoin. Inside the five-person commission, the final vote split 3 to 2, one of the closest possible outcomes. Chairman Gary Gensler even admitted he was not personally thrilled about the result. What does such a close agency vote tell you about how officials view a new technology?
answer: Even experts inside one agency deeply disagree about whether to allow it
choices: Even experts inside one agency deeply disagree about whether to allow it
Everyone at the agency agreed it was safe
The agency vote is always exactly split by law
Public opinion outside the agency does not matter at all
context: SEC Chair Gary Gensler joined the two Republican commissioners in the 3-2 approval, over the objections of two Democratic commissioners. Gensler's own public statement made clear he was voting yes reluctantly under the court ruling's pressure. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: Bitcoin's software rules cap the total supply at 21 million coins forever. In January 2024, the US Securities and Exchange Commission approved the first spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- stock-market funds that hold real bitcoin for their investors. Money poured in far faster than skeptics predicted. By December 2024, roughly eleven months after launch, the ETFs together held about 5% of every bitcoin that had ever been mined. About how many bitcoin was that?
answer: About 1.1 million BTC
choices: About 1.1 million BTC
About 100,000 BTC
About 3 million BTC
About 250,000 BTC
context: The 1.1 million BTC accumulated by ETFs in eleven months is about 5.2% of the total 21 million cap. It is the fastest institutional accumulation of any commodity via an ETF in history. Source: bitcointreasuries.net.

question: In January 2024, the US Securities and Exchange Commission approved the first spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- stock-market funds that let big institutions buy Bitcoin without setting up their own crypto wallets. A general rule of financial markets is that whoever gets new access first benefits most, because they can buy in before prices are bid up. Small home savers with cold-storage wallets were already in. Who profits earliest from this brand-new Wall Street product?
answer: The big pension and endowment funds that can pile in on day one
choices: The big pension and endowment funds that can pile in on day one
Small savers who already keep their coins in a home safe
Bitcoin miners running computers in cold countries
Small countries using Bitcoin as their national money
context: The ETF wrapper solved a regulatory-accessibility problem for fiduciary-constrained institutions. Individual holders who wanted Bitcoin already had it. The new demand came from pools that had been prohibited by fiduciary rules from direct custody. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: Some Bitcoin supporters warn that buying Bitcoin through a big Wall Street fund is not really the same as owning it, because a bank holds the keys for you. What special feature of Bitcoin do these critics say you give up when a fund holds it on your behalf?
answer: The ability to hold your own money without needing to trust a bank
choices: The ability to hold your own money without needing to trust a bank
The chance to earn interest paid by the fund
The right to vote on new Bitcoin rules
A guarantee that the price will always go up
context: Andreas Antonopoulos is the definitive not-your-keys-not-your-coins Bitcoin educator (Mastering Bitcoin 2014); he consistently frames self-custody as the property that makes Bitcoin distinctive, and treats ETF wrappers as a return to the trusted-third-party model Bitcoin was designed to escape. Source: Grokipedia "Andreas Antonopoulos" (2026-09-05).

question: A big American company was the first to move a huge share of its cash into Bitcoin instead of dollars. Its leader welcomed the new Wall Street Bitcoin funds even though some Bitcoiners criticized them. What was his main reason for welcoming the funds?
answer: They let millions more people buy Bitcoin easily, growing its reach
choices: They let millions more people buy Bitcoin easily, growing its reach
They pay higher interest than holding Bitcoin yourself
They give the government control over Bitcoin's rules
They print new Bitcoin each year for their investors
context: Saylor has publicly framed the spot ETFs as a positive structural event -- institutional pools now have a fiduciary-safe way to hold Bitcoin exposure. He and Antonopoulos-style critics agree on the fact of institutionalization while disagreeing on whether it is a net win. Source: Grokipedia 'Michael Saylor' (2026-09-05).

question: In early 2024, U.S. regulators approved the first spot-Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- baskets big investors buy on a stock exchange. By late 2024, Bitcoin's price crossed a round-number milestone for the first time. Which milestone did it pass?
answer: $100,000 per bitcoin
choices: $100,000 per bitcoin
$60,000 per bitcoin
$250,000 per bitcoin
$40,000 per bitcoin
context: Bitcoin passed $100,000 for the first time in December 2024, roughly eleven months after the ETF approval. The ETF-driven demand was one contributor among several (the April 2024 halving, macro conditions, US election dynamics). Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the first spot-Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Overnight, big pension funds, banks, and ordinary brokerage customers could buy Bitcoin the easy legal way through the regular stock market. But the approval did not touch Bitcoin's own code — its 21-million coin cap and its open peer-to-peer network stayed exactly as designed. Which choice best describes what the approval did and did not do?
answer: It made it easier for big investors to buy in; it did not change Bitcoin's fixed supply or design
choices: It made it easier for big investors to buy in; it did not change Bitcoin's fixed supply or design
It changed Bitcoin's 21-million coin cap so ETF sponsors could mint more
It made Bitcoin only usable by big institutions from then on
It made it illegal for regular people in the U.S. to hold their own bitcoin
context: The ETF wrapper is a regulatory technology, not a monetary change. Bitcoin's fixed supply, its self-custody option, and its underlying network operate identically before and after the ETF. What changed is the demand curve from previously constrained institutional buyers. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1997, French historian Stephane Courtois and a team of European scholars published a book called The Black Book of Communism. Chapter by chapter, they added up the deaths caused by communist governments across the 1900s: Soviet gulags, the Chinese Great Leap Forward famine, the Cambodian killing fields, and more. Roughly what total did the authors find?
answer: About 85 to 100 million people
choices: About 85 to 100 million people
About one hundred thousand people
About one million people
Fewer than ten thousand people
context: Courtois was born 1947 in Dreux, France. Solzhenitsyn was a Russian dissident writer, Furet a French historian of the French Revolution, Conquest an Anglo-American historian of the Soviet purges. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: In 1968, huge student protests and worker strikes shook Paris and nearly toppled the French government. A young French student named Stephane Courtois was swept up in the movement and fired up by China's Cultural Revolution — the mass upheaval then convulsing that country. That year he picked up a hard-left cause and would spend the rest of his life writing about it. Which cause did the young Courtois adopt?
answer: Maoism
choices: Maoism
Trotskyism
Anarcho-syndicalism
Social democracy
context: The May 1968 Paris upheavals radicalized many French students; Maoism was the fashionable variant among the most zealous. Courtois grew out of it in the 1970s as reports from Cambodia and the USSR made the ideology impossible to sustain intellectually. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: Before writing The Black Book of Communism, Stephane Courtois built a career as a professional historian in France. He spent years digging through the archives of the French Communist Party and of the Comintern -- the Moscow-run organization that once directed communist parties around the world. To fund his research, France's largest state-run scientific research agency put him on staff. Which French research group hired him?
answer: The CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique)
choices: The CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique)
The Ecole Normale Superieure
The Sorbonne University
The Institut d'Etudes Politiques (Sciences Po)
context: The CNRS is France's national research funding and employment body for permanent researchers. Courtois used the position to access the archives of the French Communist Party and the international communist movement, then the newly opened Soviet archives after 1991. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: When French historian Stephane Courtois edited The Black Book of Communism in 1997, he pulled together chapters by many European scholars. Each chapter tallied the deaths under one communist government -- the USSR, China, Cambodia, North Korea, Ethiopia, Vietnam, and others. Of every chapter in the book, the one on the Soviet Union was by far the longest. Why was the Soviet chapter the longest?
answer: The Soviet system lasted the longest and killed the most people of any communist state
choices: The Soviet system lasted the longest and killed the most people of any communist state
The Soviet Union was the only communist country in the book
The chapter was longest because Russian is harder to translate
The other communist countries had lost most of their records
context: Werth was the French Sovietologist of his generation. Paczkowski covered Poland; Margolin covered Asia (China, Vietnam, Cambodia, North Korea); Bartosek covered Eastern Europe. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: When French historian Stephane Courtois published his introduction to The Black Book of Communism in 1997, two of his own co-authors -- Nicolas Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin -- were so upset that they wrote a public dissent letter to the Paris newspaper Le Monde. They accepted the book's death-toll numbers themselves; the fight was over one specific comparison Courtois had drawn in his introduction. What specifically did they object to?
answer: His equating of communist and Nazi crimes in the introduction
choices: His equating of communist and Nazi crimes in the introduction
The USSR chapter's estimate of Gulag deaths
The China chapter's estimate of Great Leap Forward deaths
The Cambodia chapter's estimate of Khmer Rouge deaths
context: Nicolas Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin agreed with the country-by-country archival totals but not with Courtois's editorial framing that put communist and Nazi crimes on the same moral plane. The country chapters have held up thirty years later. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: In 1997 the French historian Stephane Courtois edited a giant book called The Black Book of Communism. It tallied the killings of every communist regime of the 20th century — Lenin's and Stalin's USSR, Mao's China, the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, North Korea, Eastern Europe, and more. Courtois's introduction gave a topline total that has become the standard scholarly figure for the century's communist death toll. Approximately what range did he give?
answer: About 85 to 100 million
choices: About 85 to 100 million
About 5 to 10 million
About 200 to 300 million
About 1 to 2 million
context: The country breakdown: China ~65 million, USSR ~20 million, North Korea ~2 million, Cambodia ~2 million, Africa ~1.7 million, Afghanistan ~1.5 million, Vietnam ~1 million, Eastern Europe ~1 million, Latin America ~150 thousand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: French historian Stephane Courtois became famous in 1997 for editing The Black Book of Communism, a scholarly accounting of the 85 to 100 million people killed under communist regimes. What gives his indictment its unusual moral force, though, is not just the archival scholarship. It is a specific biographical fact about his own youth in Paris during the 1968 student uprisings. What is that fact?
answer: Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-historian of communism
choices: Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-historian of communism
Courtois had himself served in the KGB before defecting to France
Courtois had himself survived a Chinese labor camp
Courtois had himself fought in the Spanish Civil War
context: The trajectory from believer to counter-historian gives the introduction a particular authority. It also explains the confrontational tone that his more cautious co-authors resisted in their Le Monde letter. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: For decades, Sweden has set apartment rents by national law rather than letting landlords and renters agree on a market price. Politicians say the rule keeps housing affordable for working families. But when a rent is held below what people would freely pay for the apartment, an old economic law kicks in almost immediately. What happens next?
answer: A long waiting list forms because too few apartments get built
choices: A long waiting list forms because too few apartments get built
Everyone finds a cheap apartment fast
Landlords build extra apartments just to be nice
Rents naturally rise back to normal within a week
context: 'Bostads' means housing, 'formedlingen' means bureau or agency. The bureau runs the queue by which most first-hand rental contracts in central Stockholm are allocated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: In Sweden, apartment rents are not set by market prices. Instead, the national tenant union and the association of landlords meet each year to negotiate an official rent for each kind of apartment, based on features like age, size, and neighborhood rather than what tenants would freely pay. This unusual pricing system has a specific Swedish name written into the law. What is that name?
answer: Bruksvardeshyra ('utility-value rent')
choices: Bruksvardeshyra ('utility-value rent')
Marknadshyra ('market rent')
Kronohyra ('crown rent')
Fribyggahyra ('free-build rent')
context: Utility-value rents are set below what a market-clearing price would be, so demand for central-Stockholm rentals massively exceeds supply. Units are then allocated by time in the queue rather than by willingness to pay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: Because Sweden's rent-control law kept rents below the market price, apartments in Stockholm became bargains -- but not enough new ones got built to meet the demand. Instead of paying a higher rent, would-be renters had to sign up on a national waiting list run by the city, called Bostadsformedlingen. By the early 2020s, the average wait for a first-hand rental contract in central Stockholm reached a figure that made news around the world. About how long was that average wait?
answer: About 20 years
choices: About 20 years
About 6 months
About 5 years
About 60 years
context: The longest documented waits exceeded 30 years. Swedish parents commonly sign their children up to the queue at birth so the child has a chance of a first-hand contract by age 20. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: Because Sweden's rent-control law kept rents artificially low, too few new apartments got built and the official Stockholm housing queue, Bostadsformedlingen, stretched to a roughly twenty-year wait. Swedes quickly learned that if they wanted their child to have any chance at a Stockholm apartment as a young adult, they had to start queueing years in advance. One Swedish family practice has become the most-cited example of how deep this queue reaches into daily life. What do many Swedish parents do the day a child is born?
answer: Enter the newborn into the Bostadsformedlingen housing queue
choices: Enter the newborn into the Bostadsformedlingen housing queue
Open a national retirement savings account for the newborn
Register the newborn for compulsory military service
Reserve a place in a Nobel-affiliated preschool
context: The queue is strictly first-come-first-served. By the time a child turns 18-20 and needs their own place, roughly two decades of queue time have accumulated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: A city passes a law economists call rent control: no landlord in the city can raise the rent on an apartment, even when more people want to move in than there are apartments and would happily pay more. Over a decade or two of living under such a law, what usually happens to the number of apartments actually available to rent in that city?
answer: There are far fewer to rent, and long waiting lists appear
choices: There are far fewer to rent, and long waiting lists appear
There are many more, because landlords rush to build
The number stays exactly the same forever
Rents fall so low that everyone rents two apartments
context: Lindbeck (1930-2020) was the long-serving chair of the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences committee. His willingness to name his own country's policy publicly made his critique especially load-bearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Assar_Lindbeck.

question: Because Stockholm's official rental price does not clear the market, a specific parallel market emerged, often charging 3-5 times the controlled rent. Stockholm police reports and the housing think-tank Timbro have documented it. What is this market?
answer: An illegal second-hand sublet market
choices: An illegal second-hand sublet market
A state-run private landlord auction
A European Union subsidized rent-supplement system
