A cryptocurrency-based rental futures market
context: Sitting tenants sublet their controlled units at multiples of the controlled rent. The practice is illegal but widespread, and one of several mechanisms that emerge whenever an official price does not equilibrate supply and demand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that a market price is not just a number -- it is a signal that tells producers what to build and buyers what they truly want. Kill the price with a rent cap or a wage floor and you kill the signal, so the goods still have to be handed out somehow. A Stockholm high-school student asks her teacher how a below-market apartment ever actually gets allocated if the price does not do the work. A Hayekian economist points to a broader principle. Which is it?
answer: When a price does not clear the market, some other mechanism must -- typically queueing, connections, black markets, or exit
choices: When a price does not clear the market, some other mechanism must -- typically queueing, connections, black markets, or exit
The Swedish central bank secretly assigns units to voters of the governing party
The European Union assigns units by lottery among all EU citizens
Stockholm's climate does the allocation by discouraging most residents
context: The pattern generalizes: Soviet bread lines, US 1973 gas queues, wartime rationing, and public-housing waiting lists all illustrate the same principle. Prices carry information; suppress them and the information reappears in another form, usually less efficient. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: In 2018, the US government put a 25% tax on imported steel and a 10% tax on imported aluminum, meant to protect American metal factories from foreign competition. Steel and aluminum are the raw materials for cars, soup cans, refrigerators, and skyscrapers. When those metals get more expensive at the border, who ends up paying more for the cars, cans, and appliances at the store?
answer: Everyday buyers in the country that added the taxes
choices: Everyday buyers in the country that added the taxes
Only foreign metal companies
Only rich CEOs of car makers
Nobody -- taxes on imports are free money
context: March 8 2018 proclamations: 25% on imported steel and 10% on imported aluminum under Section 232 national-security authority; specific mill workers in Granite City IL and Ashland KY were cited by the administration as beneficiaries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_tariffs.

question: In 2018, President Trump put a 25 percent tax on steel coming into the United States. Newspapers said it would help American steelworkers keep their jobs. But the 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught a method for judging any policy: look past the obvious winners for the hidden losers that no headline names. Under Bastiat's method, which unseen group actually bears the real cost of a steel tariff?
answer: American consumers of goods that use steel as an input
choices: American consumers of goods that use steel as an input
Foreign steel exporters based in South Korea and Japan
US municipal governments that build public infrastructure
Investors in the emerging-markets exchange-traded funds
context: Bastiat's UNSEEN victim in a tariff: the American car buyer, appliance buyer, canned-food buyer, and construction customer whose prices rise because steel inputs cost more. Source: piie.com (Bown & Zhang, PIIE Working Paper 20-14).

question: In 2020 the American economists Chad Bown and Yilin Zhang studied President Trump's 2018 steel tariffs — extra US taxes on foreign steel that were meant to protect American steel jobs. They totaled the higher prices Americans paid for anything made with steel, divided that total by the number of steel jobs the tariffs actually saved, and got a per-job cost. About how much did each saved job cost per year?
choices: About $90,000
About $9,000
context: The PIIE 2020 calculation: about $900,000 spent by US consumers per steel job protected per year, because the added cost is dispersed across every buyer of steel-intensive goods. Cato and PIIE both cite the same per-job figure. Source: piie.com (Bown & Zhang PIIE WP 20-14, 2020).

question: A country adds a big tax on imported steel to save jobs at its own steel mills. Some steel jobs do come back. But other factories that buy steel to make cars and tools now pay much more, and they lay off workers. How should we honestly measure whether the tariff helped?
answer: Count the jobs saved and subtract the jobs lost at every factory that buys steel
choices: Count the jobs saved and subtract the jobs lost at every factory that buys steel
Count only the jobs saved at the steel mills
Ignore the price rise on cars and tools
Assume no other factory in the country uses steel
context: Flaaen & Pierce, FEDS 2019-086: about 1,000 primary-steel jobs added versus about 75,000 lost in steel-USING industries (autoparts, machinery, canned food, appliances) whose input costs jumped. Source: federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/2019-086.htm.

question: In the spring of 1930, more than a thousand American economists signed a public letter begging President Herbert Hoover not to sign a huge new tariff law — the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, which would raise import taxes on more than 20,000 foreign goods. Hoover signed it anyway that June. What did the other big trading countries do next that made the pain far worse?
answer: They put their own tariffs on American exports in return
choices: They put their own tariffs on American exports in return
They increased their imports from America to help out
They asked the United Nations to punish America
They dropped all their own tariffs to keep the peace
context: Smoot-Hawley (June 1930): 1,028 economists led by Paul Douglas signed a petition against it; Hoover signed anyway. Foreign retaliation followed, US exports collapsed from $5.2B (1929) to $1.7B (1933). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: In May 1930, more than 1,000 American economists signed an open petition begging President Herbert Hoover to veto a giant new tariff law -- the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, which would raise import taxes on over 20,000 goods. The signers came from every major American university. Their main warning was not about foreign policy or war but about ordinary shoppers at home. What did they warn tariffs would do to shoppers?
answer: Shoppers would pay higher prices for many everyday goods
choices: Shoppers would pay higher prices for many everyday goods
Every good in the store would suddenly become free of tax
Shoppers would refuse to buy anything American-made
Shoppers would suddenly earn twice as much money
context: Paul Douglas, University of Chicago economics professor before his Senate career, was the lead signatory; the petition ran the same day in the New York Times, May 5 1930. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Douglas.

question: In June 1930 President Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, raising US import taxes on more than 20,000 foreign goods. Other countries hit back with tariffs of their own, and world trade fell off a cliff over the next four years. Economists still cite the 1929-1934 collapse as one of the great trade-policy disasters in American history. Roughly how much did world trade fall in that stretch?
answer: About 66 percent
choices: About 66 percent
About 15 percent
About 30 percent
About 85 percent
context: World trade fell from roughly $5.3B (1929) to $1.8B (1934) -- about 66 percent. Douglas Irwin's Peddling Protectionism 2011 gives the standard modern account. Source: Grokipedia 'Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act' + Irwin 2011.

question: In 1963 the American economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published A Monetary History of the United States — a huge history of every dollar the country had printed. They settled one long-running question about why the Great Depression from 1929 onward was so unusually bad. The main cause, they argued, was not the Smoot-Hawley tariff and not the 1929 stock crash. What was it?
answer: The Federal Reserve's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock
choices: The Federal Reserve's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock
The stock-market crash of October 1929 driving consumer confidence down
European war debts pulling gold reserves out of the American banking system
The Dust Bowl reducing agricultural productivity across the Great Plains
context: Friedman & Schwartz argued the Depression's severity was monetary: the Fed let the money stock collapse by about a third, 1929-33. Smoot-Hawley made a monetary contraction worse but did not cause it. Source: Friedman & Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1963.

question: In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote his 'Candlemakers' Petition' — a satire in which the candlemakers of France beg parliament to block out the sun, since sunlight is unfair foreign competition against candles. It became the classic mockery of protectionism (the policy of using taxes to block foreign goods). When the US imposed steel tariffs in 2018, critics pointed straight back at Bastiat. In one line, what political feature does the 2018 steel tariff share with the candlemakers' argument?
answer: Concentrated benefit for a small named group; dispersed cost across every consumer
choices: Concentrated benefit for a small named group; dispersed cost across every consumer
Concentrated cost on foreign producers; dispersed benefit across all Americans
Concentrated fiscal revenue; dispersed regulatory-compliance cost
Concentrated pollution reduction; dispersed employment loss
context: Mancur Olson's Logic of Collective Action (1965) formalized this: concentrated benefits are politically loud (Granite City steelworkers), dispersed costs are politically quiet (every American who buys a car). The candlemakers' petition is the same shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentrated_benefits_and_diffuse_costs.

question: After President Trump's 2018-19 US steel tariffs took effect, Federal Reserve economists Aaron Flaaen and Justin Pierce studied the jobs impact carefully. In the Bastiat frame — count the seen jobs AND the unseen ones — the tariffs helped a small group of primary-steel workers but hurt a bigger group of downstream manufacturers whose steel inputs suddenly cost more. In one line, what ratio of jobs lost to jobs added did the Flaaen-Pierce study document?
answer: About 75 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
choices: About 75 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
About 3 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
About equal downstream losses and upstream gains
About 2 primary-steel jobs added per downstream job lost
context: Roughly 1,000 primary-steel jobs added versus roughly 75,000 downstream manufacturing jobs lost -- Flaaen & Pierce Federal Reserve FEDS 2019-086. The UNSEEN downstream employers were the Bastiat victim. Source: federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/2019-086.htm.

question: On September 20, 2008 — five days after the giant Wall Street investment firm Lehman Brothers went bankrupt and the American banking system started to seize up — US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson sent Congress an urgent request for $700 billion. The money would buy 'troubled assets' (bad mortgages and bad securities) off the banks' books. Paulson's first draft was strangely, worryingly short. How long was it?
answer: Three pages
choices: Three pages
Twenty-five pages
Two hundred pages
One page
context: The initial September 20 2008 proposal was three pages long. Its brevity became legendary; even members of Congress who supported the concept were startled by how little detail accompanied the request for $700 billion. Source: Grokipedia 'Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson sent Congress a three-page proposal asking to spend $700 billion of taxpayer money buying up bad loans from big Wall Street banks that were collapsing in the middle of a huge financial crisis. Rescuing a failing company or industry with public money has a plain, everyday name in American politics. What is that name?
answer: A bailout
choices: A bailout
A tariff
A dividend
A merger
context: Henry 'Hank' Paulson was Goldman Sachs's CEO from 1999 to 2006, then Bush Treasury Secretary June 2006 through January 2009. His Wall Street background became one of the flashpoints in the political fight over TARP. Source: Grokipedia 'Henry Paulson' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2008 US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson's first draft of the $700 billion bank bailout bill was only three pages long. Buried in it was one short clause saying that no court and no federal agency could review any decision the Treasury made spending the money — total immunity from oversight. Which numbered section of the draft carried that language?
answer: Section 8
choices: Section 8
Section 3
Section 12
Section 20
context: Section 8 of the original draft: 'decisions by the Secretary pursuant to the authority of this Act are non-reviewable and committed to agency discretion, and may not be reviewed by any court of law or any administrative agency.' Congress removed this language in the final bill. Source: Grokipedia 'Troubled Asset Relief Program' (2026-09-05).

question: On Monday, September 29, 2008, the US House of Representatives voted on an emergency $700 billion bank bailout bill during the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. To Wall Street's shock, the House rejected the bill. Traders panicked, fearing the whole banking system could collapse without government help. What was the immediate stock-market reaction that day?
answer: The Dow Jones fell 777.68 points -- the largest single-day point drop in history to that date
choices: The Dow Jones fell 777.68 points -- the largest single-day point drop in history to that date
The Dow Jones rose 200 points on hopes for a better bill
The Dow Jones fell 50 points as traders had priced in the outcome
The Dow Jones was closed early due to circuit-breaker trips
context: The 777.68-point drop on September 29 2008 was the largest single-day point drop in Dow history to that date. Congress rewrote the bill with oversight provisions and executive-pay limits, and the revised version passed October 3 2008. Source: Grokipedia 'Dow Jones Industrial Average' (2026-09-05).

question: After US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson's three-page September 2008 rescue draft was ridiculed for having no oversight, Congress rewrote the bill and added pay limits on rescued executives, watchdog inspectors, and reporting rules. Both houses passed it on Friday, October 3, 2008, and President George W. Bush signed it the same day under a new formal statutory title. What was the Act officially called?
answer: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act
choices: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act
The Financial Rescue Act
The Bank Stabilization Act
The Federal Assistance Act
context: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 authorized the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) with $700 billion in spending authority. The final bill included a Special Inspector General (SIGTARP) and a Congressional Oversight Panel chaired by Elizabeth Warren. Source: Grokipedia 'Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008' (2026-09-05).

question: During the 2008 crisis, the government first promised money to buy bad loans off big banks. Within two weeks the plan changed to hand the money straight to the nine biggest banks instead. What does that switch suggest about who the plan mostly helped?
answer: The biggest banks and their owners, more than borrowers with bad loans
choices: The biggest banks and their owners, more than borrowers with bad loans
Small local banks in every town across America
Only families who had already lost their homes
Foreign banks in Europe and Asia most of all
context: The October 14 2008 forced capital injections put $125 billion into the nine largest US banks -- whether they wanted it or not. The pivot from asset-purchase to capital-injection was made without seeking new congressional authorization. Source: Grokipedia 'Troubled Asset Relief Program' (2026-09-05).

question: In late 2008 the US government reached into a giant emergency rescue fund — Congress had built the fund that October to save collapsing banks — and used it to hand roughly $80 billion to two failing American car companies, General Motors and Chrysler. Economists have a name for the danger created when the government rescues a failing business. What is the general risk?
answer: Other companies expect a rescue too, so they stop being careful with money
choices: Other companies expect a rescue too, so they stop being careful with money
It always causes food prices to fall the next year
Foreign countries have to pay back the rescue
The rescued company's workers all lose their pensions
context: General Motors and Chrysler received TARP funds totaling roughly $80 billion. Ford declined federal assistance. The auto rescue was controversial because it stretched TARP well beyond its originally stated financial-sector purpose. Source: Grokipedia 'Automotive industry crisis of 2008-2010' (2026-09-05).

question: During the 2008 banking crisis, US Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson called the heads of the nine biggest American banks to a room and forced every one of them to take rescue money — even the careful, healthy banks that did not want it — so outsiders could not tell which banks were the weakest. Why does one-size-fits-all rescue money bother critics of the bailout?
answer: It treats careful banks the same as reckless ones, so being careful stops paying off
choices: It treats careful banks the same as reckless ones, so being careful stops paying off
It makes it illegal to open new banks
It forces banks to lend only to farmers
It doubles the salary of every bank teller
context: Sheila Bair, FDIC chair 2006-2011, argued the forced capital injections protected the too-big-to-fail structure itself by treating healthy and troubled banks identically. Her 2012 memoir Bull by the Horns tells the story from inside the crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Sheila Bair' (2026-09-05).

question: In the fall of 2008, the American housing bubble collapsed and huge Wall Street banks were suddenly worth billions of dollars less than they owed their creditors. Congress rushed a bill through and passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), which loaned around $442 billion of taxpayer money to big banks and car companies. By 2015 almost every dollar had been repaid, sometimes with interest. Even so, Austrian and public-choice economists still call TARP a costly precedent. Why do they?
answer: It taught every big bank that a large enough failure will always be met with a public rescue
choices: It taught every big bank that a large enough failure will always be met with a public rescue
It proved bailouts have no long-term effect on how bankers behave
It guaranteed no future rescue would ever be needed again
It paid back so much interest it made up for years of inflation losses
context: The dollar-for-dollar recovery is often cited as evidence TARP 'worked.' The Austrian point: the enduring effect is not financial but expectational. Every future risk-taker learned that too-big-to-fail is a real category. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012).

question: When Congress passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) in 2008, it created a small watchdog panel to check whether the banks were following the rules. Why does public-choice thinking say a watchdog is important whenever the government hands out huge sums?
answer: The people spending the money have stronger incentives to bend rules than voters have to watch them
choices: The people spending the money have stronger incentives to bend rules than voters have to watch them
Bankers cannot count large sums accurately without outside help
Watchdogs are legally required to sign every check the Treasury writes
Voters read every government report as soon as it comes out
context: Warren chaired the Congressional Oversight Panel for TARP from 2008. Her visibility on the panel launched her national political career; she was elected to the Senate in 2012 and ran for president in 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Elizabeth Warren' (2026-09-05).

question: By October 2008, the US financial system was in chaos. Big banks like Lehman Brothers had already failed after making risky home loans, and other giants like Citigroup looked ready to go under. On October 3, 2008, President George W. Bush signed a huge $700 billion program that let the Treasury Department buy troubled loans and stock from major banks to keep them alive. What is its four-letter name?
answer: TARP
choices: TARP
TALF
HAMP
QE1
context: Troubled Asset Relief Program, October 3 2008; Treasury ended up injecting preferred stock into Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley among others. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubled_Asset_Relief_Program.

question: In September of 2008, the U.S. government spent hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars to rescue big Wall Street banks that had made huge bad bets on housing loans. Economists have a name for the trap that appears when people know they will be rescued and so they take even bigger risks the next time around. What is this trap called?
answer: Moral hazard
choices: Moral hazard
Sunk cost
Free trade
Opportunity cost
context: Moral hazard: once creditors and banks expect rescue in a crisis, they demand less risk premium and take more risk, making the system more fragile for the next crisis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard.

question: In late 2008, the American government spent hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars to rescue giant Wall Street banks like Citigroup and Bank of America after they lost fortunes on bad housing loans. The visible good was clear right away — the immediate crash was stopped. But Frederic Bastiat's rule from 1850 said always to look for the unseen long-term cost as well. What is the hidden cost that Austrian critics of these rescues keep pointing out?
answer: Future bankers take bigger risks because they now expect a rescue when things go wrong
choices: Future bankers take bigger risks because they now expect a rescue when things go wrong
The paperwork cost of running the rescue program
The tax revenue lost on stock dividends the government received
The paperwork burden the rescue put on small community banks
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN in a bailout is not in the year of the bailout; it is in the next crisis. The rescued creditors' expectation of rescue changes behavior going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/tarp-moral-hazard.

question: A bank kept most of its money in long-term government bonds it had bought when interest rates were very low. When rates jumped up, those bonds were worth much less. Nervous customers heard the news and rushed to pull their cash out all at once. What is that panicked mass withdrawal called?
answer: A bank run
choices: A bank run
A margin call
A short sale
A dividend cut
context: SVB failed March 10 2023 with roughly 93% of its deposits UNINSURED, mostly tech firms and venture-capital funds. Signature Bank followed days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank.

question: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) normally protects only $250,000 in any one American bank account. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed after a bank run by frightened tech-startup depositors, most of whom had far more than that limit sitting in the bank. The federal government then announced it would cover every dollar, even the accounts far above the insurance limit. What lesson does that decision send to wealthy savers?
answer: Do not worry about the limit; the government may cover you anyway
choices: Do not worry about the limit; the government may cover you anyway
Never keep more than $250,000 in any bank, ever again
Only use cash and avoid all banks completely from now on
Move all your money to foreign banks immediately
context: The joint March 12 2023 announcement invoked the systemic-risk exception; Signature Bank got the same treatment days later. Uninsured depositors -- who had chosen to keep more than $250K in a single account -- were made whole at zero cost. Source: federalreserve.gov (joint press release, March 12 2023).

question: When Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in March 2023, many tech startups had parked tens of millions of dollars in a single account — far above the FDIC's $250,000 insurance limit — betting a full bank run would simply never happen to them. After the run hit and the bank failed, the federal government promised to make every depositor whole, insured or not. What lesson about caution does that rescue erase for the next time around?
answer: Splitting your money across many banks was the safe move; the bailout hides that lesson
choices: Splitting your money across many banks was the safe move; the bailout hides that lesson
Keeping cash under your mattress is the only safe move
Only small community banks are safe; big banks are not
Buying private insurance is required by federal law
context: The market's normal signal to a depositor over the FDIC cap: split your money across banks. The 2023 SVB rescue eliminated that signal for large uninsured depositors going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/svb-bailout-moral-hazard.

question: In 1873, the British economist and journalist Walter Bagehot published a book called Lombard Street. In it, he laid down the classic rule for how a central bank should respond during a financial panic. Bagehot said the lender of last resort should lend freely to any solvent bank, and should take only good collateral in exchange — but he added one more piece to keep bailouts from turning into free money. What sort of interest rate did he say the central bank should charge?
answer: A high, punishing rate
choices: A high, punishing rate
The prevailing market rate
A subsidized concessional rate
A rate fixed by statute
context: Bagehot's rule: 'lend freely, at high rates, against good collateral.' The punishing rate is the point -- banks would only draw the facility in true crisis, not because it was cheap. The 2023 SVB bailout gave uninsured depositors a FREE option instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street_(book).

question: The moral-hazard critique of federal bailouts has a Bastiat-shaped logic. One rescue in one crisis changes what every future actor expects. The real cost shows up in the next crisis the earlier bailout quietly invited. Which precedent-and-sequel pair does this ladder trace?
answer: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
choices: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
Continental Illinois 1984 as precedent; Long-Term Capital 1998 as institutionalization
Penn Central 1970 as precedent; Chrysler 1979 as institutionalization
Franklin National 1974 as precedent; Continental Illinois 1984 as institutionalization
context: The 2008 TARP established that the federal government would rescue major-bank creditors; the 2023 SVB action made the rescue apply to any deposit at any bank the regulators later name systemic. The UNSEEN cost of 2008 is paid in the changed behavior visible in 2023. Source: mercatus.org/publications/svb-bailout-changed-behavior.

question: Anna Schwartz co-wrote the 1963 Monetary History of the United States with Milton Friedman. Later, she offered a sharp one-line warning about the direction the Federal Reserve had taken by the 21st century. In her words, the Fed was now really in the business of doing what?
answer: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
choices: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
Fine-tuning the unemployment rate to a Phillips-curve target
Coordinating fiscal policy with the elected Treasury
Regulating derivatives markets under a systemic-risk mandate
context: Schwartz's warning, restated in her final years: the Fed's mission had drifted from monetary stability toward defending asset prices, and the moral hazard consequences would surface in the next crisis. Source: wsj.com/articles/anna-schwartz-1915-2012.

question: The government wants every child to learn to read and add, so it uses tax money to pay for schooling. But paying for school does not have to mean running every school. Instead of forcing every family into the nearest public school, the government could hand the funding to parents and let them spend it at any approved school -- public, private, charter, or religious. Which arrangement matches this school-choice idea?
answer: Parents can take the money to any approved school
choices: Parents can take the money to any approved school
The government must run every single school itself
Only rich families should get to pick a school
Schools should have no rules or funding at all
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education,' in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest (Rutgers University Press, 1955). Friedman argued for funding pupils (via vouchers) rather than school buildings. Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: Imagine the Chicago Teachers Union goes on strike three times in ten years, and every strike shuts down the city's public schools for around 300,000 kids at a stretch. Teachers are paid out of tax money, so the workers on strike are really employees of the city government. When those workers walk off the job, wealthy families can pay for a private school for a while — but who is left with no other choice?
answer: Families whose kids can only attend the public schools
choices: Families whose kids can only attend the public schools
Only the teachers themselves
The politicians who signed the contracts
Business owners in other states
context: The Chicago Teachers Union struck in 2012 (9 school days), 2019 (11 days), and 2022 (5 days) -- each closing schools for approximately 300,000 students, disproportionately low-income, whose parents cannot easily choose an alternative. Source: chicagotribune.com strike coverage.

question: A US city sets up a new program: every low-income family gets a certificate worth about $10,000 per year that they may spend only on tuition at any state-approved private school they choose for their child. If they pick a Catholic school, the certificate pays. If they pick a Montessori school, the certificate pays. If they never use it, they lose it. What is this kind of school-choice payment called?
answer: A school voucher
choices: A school voucher
A public-school tax
A tuition loan
A federal college grant
context: The DC Opportunity Scholarship Program was enacted in the 2004 DC School Choice Incentive Act. Multi-year IES / Patrick Wolf and Anna Kisida evaluations (US Department of Education 2010, 2018) found statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for scholarship recipients. Source: ed.gov (DC OSP evaluations).

question: For over a decade, the US Department of Education ran a formal study of the DC Opportunity Scholarship Program, a voucher program that helped low-income Washington families pay tuition at private schools. A research team led by University of Arkansas education professor Patrick Wolf compared students who won the voucher lottery to students who applied but did not. What clear benefit did the voucher-winning kids show?
answer: Higher graduation rates
choices: Higher graduation rates
Lower graduation rates
Higher rates of college non-attendance
Higher rates of school-year absence
context: The IES evaluations (2010, 2018) documented statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for DC OSP scholarship recipients. Congressional attempts to shut the program down have come repeatedly from the DC teachers-union's allies. Source: ies.ed.gov (Wolf + Kisida evaluations).

question: In New York City, some old public school buildings house two schools inside them at once — one run by the traditional public school district, and one an independent charter school like a Success Academy campus. Both schools take students from the same neighborhood blocks, share the same hallways, and use the same gyms and cafeterias. Why is this setup such a useful natural experiment for comparing the two kinds of schools?
answer: The neighborhood and building are the same, so those cannot explain any score gap
choices: The neighborhood and building are the same, so those cannot explain any score gap
All the kids have the same last names, so it must be genetics
The kids are picked at random by the federal government each year
The kids share the same lunches, so nutrition is the reason
context: Thomas Sowell, Charter Schools and Their Enemies (Basic Books, 2020). Sowell used NYC co-location data to compare charter and district students in the same building. In every matched-building comparison, charter students outperformed. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 2020).

question: In big American cities like New York and Chicago, two schools sometimes share a single building — a district-run public school on one floor and an independent charter school like KIPP or Success Academy on another. They share hallways, cafeterias, and gyms, and their students come from the exact same blocks. What is the biggest single advantage of comparing two schools under one shared roof like this?
answer: You can rule out the building and the neighborhood as reasons for any score gap
choices: You can rule out the building and the neighborhood as reasons for any score gap
You can force both schools to teach exactly the same lessons
You can give both schools the same teachers each school year
You can guarantee every student earns an A grade
context: NYC co-location rules place charter schools and district schools inside the same physical building, allowing direct like-for-like comparison. Sowell used this data to build his 2020 book. Source: schools.nyc.gov (co-location policy history).

question: Public choice economists study how organized groups actually behave inside a political system. One well-known argument in their studies of American public schools says that teachers' unions push very hard for higher pay, longer tenure, and stronger job protection for their own members — sometimes at the direct cost of what individual parents and taxpayers say they want for the classroom. In the language of public choice, what general pattern is this an example of?
answer: A special-interest group getting more from the system than the average voter does
choices: A special-interest group getting more from the system than the average voter does
A random side effect of holding elections every four years
A rule that automatically balances every group's power
A federal law that gives unions the final word on schools
context: Terry Moe, Special Interest: Teachers Unions and America's Public Schools (Brookings Institution, 2011). Moe applied Olson-style analysis to teachers-union political power. Source: brookings.edu (Moe 2011).

question: A US state votes on a school-choice law that would give families a check to send their kids to any school they pick, public or private. The main losers would be teachers in one big union, since some kids would switch out of public school. The union spends about ten times more money fighting against the law than parent groups spend fighting for it, even though far more families would gain than teachers would lose. Economists call this concentrated costs versus dispersed benefits. What does it show about who fights hardest in politics?
answer: A small group with a lot to lose fights harder than a big group with a little to gain
choices: A small group with a lot to lose fights harder than a big group with a little to gain
Big groups always beat small ones in every election
Money never changes the outcome of a vote
Voters always pick the option that helps the most people
context: The CTA spent tens of millions of dollars against Proposition 174 in 1993, outspending the pro-voucher side by roughly 10-to-1. The initiative failed. It is a textbook Olson concentrated-benefit case study. Source: California Secretary of State campaign-finance records; Moe (2011).

question: Mancur Olson's rule says a small group with a lot to gain will out-organize a large group with only a little to lose. Applied to American K-12 schools, one specific group fits that shape perfectly: it organizes members, negotiates contracts, backs candidates, and staffs school-board elections. Who is that concentrated interest?
answer: The teachers' union
choices: The teachers' union
State textbook publishers
Local chambers of commerce
Neighborhood parents' associations
context: The teachers' union is the concentrated organized beneficiary with the resources and staff to shape school-board and legislative outcomes. Parents and children are the dispersed victim class that pays higher taxes and receives worse outcomes but does not systematically organize. Source: Moe, Special Interest (Brookings 2011).

question: James Buchanan's public-choice school of economics teaches readers to stop asking whether individual politicians or bureaucrats happen to be good or bad people, and to ask instead which organized groups have the strongest incentive to shape the rules. In the K-12 education-policy fight in America, what is the honest structural question a public-choice reader should press, rather than the shallow 'are teachers bad'?
answer: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
choices: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
Which political party spends more per capita on schools
Which state has the highest average teacher salary
Which district uses the newest textbooks
context: The Olson-Stigler applied move: individual educators are usually decent people; the rule-selection process is dominated by whichever organized interest has resources and staff. That is a structural analysis, not a moral one. Source: Olson (1965); Moe (2011).

question: In 1955, the American economist Milton Friedman published an essay called 'The Role of Government in Education.' It launched the modern school-choice movement in the United States. Friedman argued that governments had long fused two very different jobs into one — and that separating the two would let parents choose the school their tax dollars followed. Which pair of functions did Friedman propose separating?
answer: Funding schooling versus producing it
choices: Funding schooling versus producing it
Testing students versus grading teachers
Recruiting teachers versus recruiting principals
Building schools versus stocking libraries
context: Friedman's move: the state may legitimately fund a service without also being the exclusive producer of that service. Vouchers fund the pupil rather than the building; private, charter, magnet, and district schools then compete for that funded pupil. Source: Friedman, 'Role of Government in Education' (1955).

question: In the United States, a president can serve only two terms in the White House. This rule was added to the Constitution as the 22nd Amendment in 1951, after Franklin D. Roosevelt won four presidential elections in a row from 1932 through 1944. What is the general political term for any rule that caps how many terms an elected leader may serve?
answer: Term limits
choices: Term limits
The filibuster
Judicial review
An executive order
context: The 22nd Amendment (ratified February 27, 1951) limits the president to two elected terms, passed in response to FDR's four elections. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Twenty-Second Amendment).

question: In 1995, the U.S. Supreme Court decided a 5-4 case brought against an Arkansas law that had barred long-serving members of Congress from appearing on the state ballot. The Court ruled that only a constitutional amendment — not any single state — could add new rules for who is allowed to serve in Congress. States could no longer set term limits on their federal representatives. What is the common name of this landmark case?
answer: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
choices: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
Powell v. McCormack
Roe v. Wade
Reynolds v. Sims
context: US Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton, 514 US 779 (1995), decided 5-4 on May 22, 1995. States cannot impose term limits on federal congressional service; only a constitutional amendment can. Source: supremecourt.gov (514 US 779).

question: For over thirty years, US pollsters at Gallup and Pew have kept asking Americans the same question: should there be a legal limit on how many years a US senator or House member may serve? Every survey finds Republicans, Democrats, and independents all supporting term limits by strong majorities -- one of the rare issues where partisan splits nearly vanish. What range of support do Gallup and Pew typically find?
answer: About 75 to 83 percent
choices: About 75 to 83 percent
About 25 to 35 percent
About 40 to 50 percent
Essentially split fifty-fifty
context: Congressional term-limits polling has stayed in the ~75-83% range across decades of surveys by Gallup, Pew, and others. It has never come close to the two-thirds House and Senate majorities required to send an amendment to the states. Source: news.gallup.com (term-limits polling history).

question: In 1962, the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published a book called The Calculus of Consent. In it they divided political decision-making into two very different levels. At the top level, people agree together on the rules that will bind whoever later holds office. At the lower level, sitting officeholders naturally resist those very rules. What did Buchanan and Tullock name these two levels?
answer: The constitutional and the post-constitutional
choices: The constitutional and the post-constitutional
The federal and the local
The judicial and the legislative
The elected and the appointed
context: The constitutional level is where rules are chosen behind a veil of uncertainty about your own future position. The post-constitutional level is choices made within the rules by known-position actors. Term limits are the paradigmatic case of a rule desired at level one, resisted at level two. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 6.

question: In November 1990, California voters passed the first US state law setting term limits for state lawmakers, capping how many years a senator or assembly member could serve in Sacramento. The measure came from voters who felt career politicians had grown too comfortable in office and too close to lobbyists. It passed by a narrow margin and set off a wave of copycat term-limit laws in other states. What was that ballot measure called?
answer: Proposition 140
choices: Proposition 140
Proposition 13
Proposition 209
Proposition 187
context: California Proposition 140 (November 1990) established term limits on state legislators, executive-branch officials, and staff. It launched the 1990-94 wave of state-level term-limit reforms. Source: California Secretary of State (Proposition 140 official election materials).

question: After California voters passed strict state legislative term limits in 1990, and roughly a dozen other American states soon followed, political scientists studied what actually happened inside the state capitols. Elected lawmakers now had far shorter careers and less accumulated know-how about how bills, budgets, and technical rules were actually written. Toward which groups did the real day-to-day power visibly shift?
answer: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
choices: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
The judicial branch and state constitutional officers
Political action committees only
Local school boards and city councils
context: Post-term-limits studies including Elhauge (1997) and Hansen on California pre-and-post-Proposition-140 found power shifted toward actors whose knowledge was not term-limited. The Virginia school's unintended-consequences prediction. Source: Elhauge, University of Chicago Law Review (1997).

question: A US congressman who has been in office for more than thirty years is asked at a town hall why he opposes a legal limit on how long members of Congress may serve. He brushes off the question with a familiar line: 'We already have term limits -- they're called elections. If voters don't like me, they can vote me out.' Supporters of term limits find that answer weak because of one particular fact about congressional races. Why?
answer: Long-serving incumbents almost always win, so real elections barely limit anyone
choices: Long-serving incumbents almost always win, so real elections barely limit anyone
Elections are held only once every twenty years
The Constitution bans all elections after age fifty
Voters never care who their representative is
context: Alan Grayson (D-FL), a two-term House member, repeatedly used the 'elections are term limits' line as the standard incumbent parry. The line captures the post-constitutional logic Buchanan predicted. Source: contemporary press coverage 2010-16.

question: Switzerland's national government is not run by a single president. Instead, the federal executive is a seven-member Federal Council chosen by the country's parliament. The role of president rotates among those seven every single year, so no one person can build up the perks, staff, and personal networks of the top office long enough to entrench a permanent hold on power. What does the Swiss system illustrate?
answer: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
choices: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
A recent reform in the wake of a scandal
A UN treaty obligation binding on European states
A holdover from medieval papal succession rules
context: Switzerland's rotating presidency is a constitutional-level structural rule adopted at foundation, so no sitting incumbent had to vote to shorten his own tenure. It illustrates the Buchanan point about which anti-incumbent rules can actually get chosen and stick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Council_(Switzerland).

question: The economist James Buchanan noticed that certain kinds of political reforms are almost impossible to pass, because the very officeholders whose votes are needed to enact them are the ones who would personally lose the most power. Legislative term limits are the textbook case. Which reform below shares that same shape — where the people who would lose from the change are the very ones whose votes would have to pass it?
answer: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
choices: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
Tariff repeal by consumer initiative
Interest-rate targeting by the Fed
Sunset provisions for expiring tax cuts
context: Campaign-finance reform, redistricting reform, gerrymandering reform, and term limits all share the losers-must-enact-the-reform pattern. Buchanan's constitutional-level analysis predicts these reforms will struggle regardless of majority popular support. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman + Handley on gerrymandering.

question: The public-choice study of term limits offers a general rule of thumb about political reforms in America. Whenever a proposed reform asks the current officeholders themselves to accept a personal cost — such as a shorter career — while the benefits mostly flow to future citizens or to future political challengers, what should a careful public-choice analyst expect will happen to that reform, even if a clear majority of voters supports it?
answer: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
choices: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
The reform will pass by acclamation within one session
The reform will pass automatically once polling exceeds sixty percent
The reform will pass only through executive order
context: The default is failure at the post-constitutional stage. Which is not cynicism -- it is Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy analysis of which rules survive democratic selection when the rule-writers themselves would bear the costs of the rule. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman (2006).

question: In the summer of 2022, three separate 'crypto' companies fell apart one after another in a chain reaction that spread across the entire industry. Between May and July of that year, tens of billions of dollars in customer funds were wiped out — and importantly, none of the collapses were really about Bitcoin itself. Of the three well-known altcoin projects listed below, which one collapsed first and triggered the chain reaction?
answer: Terra/LUNA
choices: Terra/LUNA
Celsius Network
Voyager Digital
FTX
context: Terra/LUNA collapsed May 9-12, 2022; Celsius froze withdrawals June 12 and filed for bankruptcy July 13; Voyager filed for bankruptcy July 5. FTX was a later collapse in November 2022 that traced back partly to the same contagion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_(blockchain).

question: In 2022, a cryptocurrency company called Terra promised that its coin, UST, would always trade for exactly one U.S. dollar. But the company did not actually hold any real dollars in reserve to back UST. Instead, an automatic computer program traded a sister coin called LUNA on the market, trying to keep UST's price steady at one dollar. What can go badly wrong with that kind of setup during a panic?
answer: If everyone tries to sell at once, the program cannot keep the price up
choices: If everyone tries to sell at once, the program cannot keep the price up
Computer programs never fail, so nothing can go wrong
The coin becomes safer than the U.S. dollar
Sister coins are guaranteed to rise in value forever
context: Do Kwon (born 1991, South Korean) co-founded Terraform Labs and led the Terra/LUNA project. SBF ran FTX; Mashinsky ran Celsius; Su Zhu ran Three Arrows Capital. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_Kwon.

question: A digital coin promised to always equal one dollar and paid huge rewards to holders. A rule tied it to a sister coin: if the coin fell below a dollar, the system printed more sister coins to fix it. In May 2022 it printed so many sisters that both crashed. Roughly how much money vanished in days?
answer: about $40 billion
choices: about $40 billion
about $500 million
about $2 billion
about $200 billion
context: The May 9-12, 2022 collapse of Terra/LUNA evaporated roughly $40 billion in nominal market value. Multiple suicides among affected retail investors were reported in South Korea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_(blockchain).

question: A U.S. 'crypto bank' called Celsius Network, run by its CEO Alex Mashinsky, had been paying customers unusually high yields on their deposits — advertising them as safer than a normal savings account. When Terra crashed in May 2022 and confidence across the whole crypto industry collapsed, worried Celsius customers rushed to pull their money out, and a full-scale run set in. On which date did Celsius freeze withdrawals and later file for bankruptcy?
answer: Celsius froze on June 12, 2022 and filed bankruptcy July 13
choices: Celsius froze on June 12, 2022 and filed bankruptcy July 13
Celsius froze on May 9, 2022 and filed bankruptcy May 12
Celsius froze on November 6, 2022 and filed bankruptcy November 11
Celsius froze on January 1, 2023 and filed bankruptcy February 1
context: Celsius Network froze all customer withdrawals on June 12, 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on July 13, 2022. The other dates correspond to unrelated collapses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius_Network.

question: Celsius Network was a US crypto lending company that promised customers eye-catching interest rates for parking their Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins with the firm. Ordinary savers, believing Celsius was safer than a bank, sent it billions of dollars. On June 12, 2022, Celsius suddenly froze all customer accounts and withdrawals, and soon filed for bankruptcy. About how much customer money was trapped inside when the freeze began?
answer: about $4.7 billion
choices: about $4.7 billion
about $50 million
about $30 billion
about $500 billion
context: Estimated customer funds locked in the Celsius bankruptcy were about $4.7 billion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius_Network.

question: In 2022 the crypto hedge fund Three Arrows Capital collapsed after its leveraged bets on the Terra ecosystem went bad. The crypto lender Voyager Digital had lent Three Arrows hundreds of millions of dollars and could not get the money back. Voyager itself then froze customer withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy weeks later. Economists have a general word for a chain reaction where one big failure knocks down the next firm, and then the next. What is that word?
answer: Contagion
choices: Contagion
Inflation
Deflation
Speculation
context: Three Arrows Capital (3AC), run by Su Zhu and Kyle Davies, was destroyed by the Terra/LUNA collapse and defaulted on Voyager's loans, forcing Voyager into bankruptcy July 5, 2022. Alameda Research was FTX's affiliated trading firm (later collapse); LTCM was a 1998 failure; Bridgewater is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_Digital.

question: A crypto coin promised to always be worth exactly one dollar without any real dollars backing it -- the promise depended on trading with a partner coin using a math formula. In May 2022 both coins collapsed to near zero in a few days. What did the crash reveal about coins backed only by a math trick?
answer: Without a real reserve of value, one bad panic can wipe the coin out
choices: Without a real reserve of value, one bad panic can wipe the coin out
Math-only coins are actually safer than Bitcoin
Only governments are allowed to create crypto coins
Coins backed by trading formulas can never lose value
context: Do Kwon was arrested at Podgorica airport in Montenegro in March 2023 with false Costa Rican documents; he was later extradited to the US in December 2024. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_Kwon.

question: Alex Mashinsky founded Celsius Network, a crypto lending firm that promised customers eye-catching returns on the coins they deposited. When crypto prices crashed in 2022, Celsius froze customer withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy, leaving depositors unable to reach their money. Mashinsky was arrested and, in December 2024, a New York federal jury convicted him. What was the substance of that conviction?
answer: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
choices: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
identity theft against Celsius customers
unregistered securities offering only
money laundering only
context: Mashinsky was convicted December 2024 of fraud and market manipulation related to the Celsius native token CEL. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mashinsky; US DOJ press releases.

question: In 2022, a whole string of major crypto companies collapsed — the stablecoin issuer Terra, the yield-lender Celsius, the broker Voyager Digital, and the giant exchange FTX run by Sam Bankman-Fried — and the users of those platforms lost billions of dollars in customer funds they had thought were safe. Yet one specific group of Bitcoin owners lost absolutely nothing across every single collapse. What one decision had they made that fully protected them?
answer: They held their own bitcoin themselves instead of trusting a company to hold it for them
choices: They held their own bitcoin themselves instead of trusting a company to hold it for them
They bought the failed company's own token first so they could withdraw before others
They turned on two-factor login and used a strong password on the company account
They paid a monthly fee to join the company's advertised insurance plan
context: In every 2022 collapse the customers who had moved bitcoin to their own hardware wallets were unaffected; those who had trusted a third party for a promised yield lost access. 2FA does not protect against custodian insolvency; native tokens (LUNA, CEL, FTT) collapsed alongside their issuers; insurance programs were widely absent or hollow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_bubble.

question: Looking back at the 2022 collapses of Terra, Celsius, Voyager, and FTX, a Bitcoin educator named Andreas Antonopoulos — famous for the phrase 'not your keys, not your coins' — pressed a point he had been teaching for years. His claim was that the failing 'crypto' companies were built very differently from Bitcoin itself. Which version of Antonopoulos's point does the argument press?
answer: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
choices: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
That all cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin eventually collapse in the same way through cascading market losses and customer runs on custodial services
That Bitcoin itself failed as a protocol in 2022 alongside Terra and Celsius and only survived because major exchanges chose to keep supporting it
That regulators should treat Bitcoin and 'crypto' identically in every jurisdiction since the underlying mathematics is the same across the whole industry
context: The Antonopoulos/Ammous move: Terra, Celsius, Voyager and FTX all had issuers or promised-yield structures with counterparty risk; Bitcoin held on a hardware wallet has neither. Bitcoin itself did not collapse; its price fell but the protocol continued operating; equating 'crypto' with Bitcoin is exactly the confusion the argument refuses. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.); Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: In 1850 the French writer Frederic Bastiat told this small parable to teach economics. A shopkeeper's front window is broken. He pays the local glazier six francs to fix it. Some townsfolk gather and say the break was actually good for the town, because the glazier now has money to spend. Bastiat says these townsfolk are forgetting something. What did they forget?
answer: The six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or bread
choices: The six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or bread
Broken windows really do create brand-new wealth
The glazier will donate his fee back to the shop
The town gets richer every time something breaks
context: Bastiat (1801-1850) published the pamphlet a few months before his December 1850 death in Rome; it is his last complete work. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: In 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short pamphlet that would define good economic reasoning for the next century and beyond. It argued that a wise economist always looks past what is obvious right in front of you — the shop rebuilt after a broken window, the workers hired by a subsidy — to the hidden effects nobody notices. The original French title names the whole method in five words. What is that title, in English?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
The Harmonies of Political Economy
The Law of Free Exchange
A Petition of the Merchants of Bordeaux
context: French original: Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas. Standard English editions since 1859 keep the literal title. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: In 1850, the French classical-liberal economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short essay in Paris just months before his death. The opening lines lay out his whole method for judging economic policies. Bastiat said that every act or law produces not just one obvious immediate effect, but a whole series of later effects that most people never notice at the time. In shorthand, what famous pair did Bastiat draw?
answer: Between the seen and the unseen
choices: Between the seen and the unseen
Between supply and demand
Between value and price
Between rent and profit
context: The whole essay's method is a single move: name the visible first effect, then name the invisible later effects the visible one hid. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote his famous 1850 essay titled "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen." Its main point is a sharp contrast between two kinds of economist. The bad economist looks only at the visible effect of a policy — the money changing hands right in front of him. The good economist looks further. What does the good economist do differently?
answer: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
choices: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
Reports the aggregate government multiplier for each proposed policy
Consults the historical record for identical policies in prior centuries
Weighs the immediate winners against a randomly-drawn sample of losers
context: This is the essay's programmatic sentence: the good economist FORESEES the effects the bad economist misses because they haven't happened yet. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen" is built as a sequence of twelve short chapters. Each chapter takes a specific French policy of Bastiat's day and works out both the visible effect and the hidden costs that visible effect conceals. The first chapter is the one everyone remembers — a small parable Bastiat uses to introduce the whole seen-and-unseen method. Which chapter opens the sequence?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The candlemakers' petition
The negative railway
The Chinese and the English
context: Chapter 1 is 'The Broken Window', built around James Goodfellow's careless son and the six-franc pane; every later chapter is another worked case. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay about a shopkeeper's broken window was written in French, so at first only French readers could read it. The first English translation did not appear until 1859 — nine full years later. During those nine years, English-speaking readers had no easy way to learn the seen-and-unseen argument. Why does a translation delay like that matter for spreading an idea?
answer: Readers in other languages cannot use the idea until someone translates it
choices: Readers in other languages cannot use the idea until someone translates it
Ideas that take longer to translate are always more true
Translated ideas lose their meaning within one year
Countries reject any book more than one year old
context: William Ballantyne Hodgson (1815-1880), Scottish educational reformer and free-trader, produced the 1859 English edition; George B. de Huszar's Liberty Fund translation (1964) is the modern standard. Source: oll.libertyfund.org/titles/bastiat-selected-essays-on-political-economy.

question: Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' was kept in continuous American print starting in 1946. The publisher was a small New York classical-liberal institute co-founded that same year by the writer Leonard Read and the journalist Henry Hazlitt, who himself wrote the classic Economics in One Lesson. What was the name of this institute?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education
The Cato Institute
The Mises Institute
The Heritage Foundation
context: FEE (Irvington-on-Hudson, 1946) has kept Bastiat's essays in print in America without a break for eighty years; Cato (1977), Mises Institute (1982), and Heritage (1973) all came later. Source: fee.org/about/our-history.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics rebrands Bastiat's 1850 seen/unseen move under a two-part label built on the same word repeated with different suffixes. The bad economist stops at the immediate effect; the good economist keeps asking 'and then what?' What phrase does Sowell teach for this second, deeper step?
answer: Stage-two thinking
choices: Stage-two thinking
Long-run analysis
General equilibrium
Rational expectations
context: Sowell uses 'stage-one vs stage-two thinking' throughout Basic Economics (2000-present) and Applied Economics; it is the same Bastiat method under a new name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay found its most famous 20th-century restatement in a short 1946 American book. That book was structured as a book-length application of the seen and unseen method to New Deal and postwar policies, and its title page was explicitly dedicated to Bastiat. Which book was that?
answer: Economics in One Lesson
choices: Economics in One Lesson
The Road to Serfdom
Free to Choose
Basic Economics

question: Milton Friedman, the twentieth-century American free-market economist, kept pointing back to one short 1850 essay by the French thinker Frederic Bastiat as the piece that shaped his own way of arguing. Bastiat, he said, taught him to always look past the shiny visible effect of a policy and hunt for the hidden costs everyone forgets. Which Bastiat essay did Friedman credit?

The General Theory of Employment
context: Friedman credited Bastiat's essay in interviews and in Free to Choose (1980); its influence on the seen/unseen habit runs through his Newsweek columns and TV series alike. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-frederic-bastiat.

question: In the late 1970s, the British government owned many of the country's biggest industries -- the coal mines, the steel mills, and the national phone company. Regulation
A tariff

The three distractors are all real prominent British women in politics of the same generation: Barbara Castle (Labour cabinet minister), Shirley Williams (Labour then SDP), Betty Boothroyd (Speaker of the House of Commons 1992-2000). None was Prime Minister. Source: Wikipedia, Margaret Thatcher.

question: In the 1980s, U.S. President Ronald Reagan cut the top federal income tax rate from a steep 70 percent all the way down to 28 percent over the course of his two terms. His supporters argued that lower rates would push people to work more hours, invest more of their savings, and start more new businesses. Central planning

Modern Monetary Theory

Carter was Reagan's predecessor (1977-1981); Ford served 1974-1977; George H. W. Bush was Reagan's Vice President and successor (1989-1993). Source: Wikipedia, Ronald Reagan.

question: At a Conservative Research Department meeting in the summer of 1975, Margaret Thatcher interrupted a speaker urging a middle way. She pulled a book from her handbag, banged it on the table, and said 'This is what we believe.' Which book did Thatcher slam on the table?

Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies

The three distractors are all real classical-liberal or conservative touchstones Thatcher admired but did not brandish that day. The Ranelagh account is the founding anecdote of the intellectual side of Thatcherism. Source: Sotheby's, 'This is what we believe: Margaret Thatcher and F. A. Hayek.'

question: In April 1947, Friedrich Hayek brought 36 free-market scholars to a hotel in a Swiss mountain village. Ludwig von Mises, Milton Friedman, Karl Popper, and Lionel Robbins were among them. They founded a society that linked free-market thinkers for the next 40 years. What is it called?

The Trilateral Commission
context: The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS) met at the Hotel du Parc on Mont Pelerin, above Lake Geneva, in the first ten days of April 1947 and has met roughly biennially ever since. The three distractors are real organisations of very different politics: the Fabian Society is British democratic socialist (founded 1884), the Bilderberg Group is a private policy conference (founded 1954), and the Trilateral Commission is a US-Europe-Japan policy body (founded 1973). Source: Wikipedia, Mont Pelerin Society.

question: In November 1984 the British government, led by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, sold shares in British Telecom -- the country's national phone company -- to the public. More than two million ordinary small savers, many of whom had never owned stock in their lives, snapped up the shares. What is the general name for a government selling a state-owned business to private owners like this?
answer: Privatisation
choices: Privatisation
Nationalisation
Regulation
Deregulation
context: British Telecom (BT) was valued at around £8 billion; the 51% flotation raised roughly £4 billion. British Rail, the Post Office, and the National Coal Board all remained in public ownership through the Thatcher years -- the coal board actively so, since it was the government's opponent in the miners' strike of 1984-85. British Gas followed in 1986 with the famous 'Tell Sid' campaign; British Airways in 1987. Source: Institute for Government, 'The Privatisation of British Telecom (1984).'

question: From March 1984 to March 1985, Britain's coal miners' union, led by Arthur Scargill, went on strike against Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's government for a full year to stop the closure of unprofitable pits. With no strike pay coming in and their savings gone, the miners eventually ran out of money and had to trudge back to work with no deal at all. What lesson does this year-long strike show about strikes as a tool?
answer: A strike only works if the workers can outlast the losses they take from not being paid
choices: A strike only works if the workers can outlast the losses they take from not being paid
A strike always forces the boss to give in eventually
A strike costs the boss money but costs the workers nothing
A strike is a peaceful way to guarantee higher pay
context: Scargill led the NUM from 1982 and was the strike's public face; the government had spent years stockpiling coal and had prepared for the confrontation. Jack Jones led the TGWU in the 1970s; Vic Feather was TUC general secretary; Rodney Bickerstaffe led NUPE and later UNISON. None led the 1984-85 miners' strike. Source: Wikipedia, 1984-1985 United Kingdom miners' strike.

question: On October 27, 1986, Britain suddenly dropped a wall of old rules on the London Stock Exchange in one dramatic overnight shake-up that was nicknamed the Big Bang. Fixed commission fees ended, foreign firms were finally allowed to join, and paper-and-shouting trading was replaced by traders staring at computer screens. What do we call this kind of policy -- removing rules like this to open up a market?
answer: Deregulation
choices: Deregulation
Nationalization
Central planning
Price control
context: The Big Bang is credited with making the City of London one of the two global financial centres of the following generation. The three distractors are all real financial-regulation events but from other countries and other decades: Glass-Steagall was a 1933 US bank-separation law; Bretton Woods was the 1944 international monetary conference; the Volcker Rule was a 2010 US restriction on bank proprietary trading. Source: Wikipedia, Big Bang (financial markets).

question: In 1979 Britain's top income tax rate was a punishing 83 percent, so a high earner kept only 17 pence of the last pound they made. Over the next decade, Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's chancellors slashed that top rate all the way down to 40 percent by 1988. What do supporters of these big rate cuts, following the American economist Arthur Laffer, argue happens when the tax rate on high earners drops that sharply?
answer: People work and invest more, so the government can still collect a lot of tax
choices: People work and invest more, so the government can still collect a lot of tax
The government collects zero tax forever after
All rich people leave the country within a week
The price of bread doubles overnight
context: Lawson was Chancellor from 1983 to 1989; the 1988 Budget is generally treated as the defining Thatcher-era tax reform. Denis Healey was Labour Chancellor (1974-1979); Geoffrey Howe was the Conservative Chancellor who cut the top rate from 83% to 60% in 1979 (Lawson took the further step to 40%); Norman Lamont was John Major's Chancellor (1990-1993), after Thatcher had left office. Source: OMFIF, 'Nigel Lawson: influential politician and architect of Thatcherism.'

question: For most of the 20th century, big-government planning was the mainstream idea in universities. A small group of Austrian-born economists kept warning that no central planner could ever gather all the price and know-how information a whole economy uses. What is that argument usually called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The velocity problem
The tax-incidence problem
The paradox of thrift
context: Hayek's health had been fragile for years; the 1974 Nobel and the Reagan-Thatcher recognition of the following decade reinvigorated him and his final book, The Fatal Conceit, appeared in 1988. Milton Friedman was Reagan's other favourite economist and a frequent White House visitor; Samuelson and Galbraith were the leading American Keynesians of the era, neither aligned with Reagan. Source: Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation, Diary Entry 11/17/1983.

question: A former fighter pilot read a book by an Austrian economist warning that big government planning leads to tyranny. He asked the author how to fight back. The advice: don't run for office; win the war of ideas from outside by starting a think tank. Why is that strategy powerful?
answer: Politicians usually only vote for what voters think is possible, so the ideas must be won first
choices: Politicians usually only vote for what voters think is possible, so the ideas must be won first
Think tanks are legally allowed to write laws that Congress must vote on
Elected officials always personally read the same books their voters read
Fighting from outside guarantees a political party will nominate you next
context: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) at 2 Lord North Street pumped out short, sharp free-market monographs from 1957 onwards and became the model for over 150 similar think-tanks Fisher would help seed worldwide. The three distractors are real organisations of adjacent politics: the Adam Smith Institute (founded 1977) was a later free-market think-tank; the Centre for Policy Studies was founded by Keith Joseph and Thatcher herself in 1974; the Fabian Society is the century-old British socialist think-tank. Source: Economic History Society, 'Waging the War of Ideas: the Institute of Economic Affairs.'

question: Through the 1920s American stocks soared as ordinary people borrowed money to buy shares. Then in late October 1929 the boom cracked. Panicked selling swept the New York Stock Exchange first on a Thursday and then, worse still, on the following Tuesday. Traders later gave those two worst days grim nicknames — each nickname pairing a color with a weekday. Which pair of days marked the crash?
answer: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
choices: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
Black Monday and Black Friday
Red Thursday and Red Tuesday
Blue Thursday and Blue Wednesday
context: Black Thursday (October 24, 1929) began the panic; Black Tuesday (October 29, 1929) broke the market. Both names have been the standard shorthand ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929.

question: In the 1920s American stock prices rose year after year. People borrowed money just to buy MORE stock, believing prices would keep rising forever. In October 1929 the whole market crashed. What is the general name for a period when prices rise on hype and cheap borrowing?
answer: A speculative bubble
choices: A speculative bubble
A tariff war
A tax revolt
A minimum wage hike
context: The Dow Jones rose from about 63 in August 1921 to a peak of 381 on September 3, 1929 -- roughly a six-fold gain in eight years. Easy credit and margin buying drove the run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roaring_Twenties.

question: America's most famous stock market index, first published in 1896 by newspaperman Charles Dow, tracks a small basket of large industrial companies. In September 1929 it reached a record high. Then the market crashed that October, and it took until 1954 — more than 25 years — for the index to climb back to its 1929 peak. Which index is this?
answer: The Dow Jones Industrial Average
choices: The Dow Jones Industrial Average
The S&P 500
The NASDAQ Composite
The Russell 2000
context: The Dow peaked at 381.17 on September 3, 1929, then bottomed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932 -- an 89% peak-to-trough decline. The S&P 500 in modern form didn't exist yet, and NASDAQ was created in 1971. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: In the roaring 1920s, ordinary Americans caught stock-market fever. Their brokers let them buy shares with borrowed money, so a buyer only had to put up a small share of the price in cash and the broker fronted the rest. This is called buying stock on margin. Roughly what minimum cash share was common at the peak of the 1929 boom, right before the great October crash?

choices: About ten percent
About half
About eighty percent
Full cash payment was required
context: Ten-percent margin was widespread by 1929 -- an investor could hold a $1,000 position with $100 down. When prices fell, brokers issued margin calls, forcing cascading liquidation. Post-crash Regulation T set higher minimum margin. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/stock-market-crash-of-1929.

question: On Tuesday October 29, 1929 — the day traders came to call Black Tuesday — panic selling on the New York Stock Exchange reached a level nobody had seen before. About one million
About one hundred million
About five hundred million
context: October 29, 1929 saw about 16 million shares traded on the NYSE -- a volume record that held for nearly 40 years. The Dow fell nearly 12 percent that day. Source: nyse.com historical trading records.

question: The Dow Jones Industrial Average hit its all-time peak in September 1929, right before the October crash. But the crash was only the start. Prices kept sliding for almost three more years as banks failed, factories closed, and unemployment soared to a quarter of American workers. The Dow finally hit bottom in July 1932.
