question: Irving Fisher was one of the most respected economists in America — a Yale professor famous for his work on interest rates and money. On October 15, 1929, just two weeks before the market crashed, he stepped to a microphone and made a public forecast about where American stock prices stood. That single sentence became the most-quoted bad call in economics. What did he say the stock market had reached?
answer: A permanently high plateau
choices: A permanently high plateau
A dangerous speculative peak
The end of its long bull run
A short-term technical top
context: Fisher's October 15, 1929 statement -- 'stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau' -- became a cautionary quote about expert overconfidence. Fisher lost most of his personal fortune in the crash. Source: New York Times, October 16, 1929.

question: The Wall Street crash of October 1929 was severe, but many economists -- most famously Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz in their landmark 1963 book A Monetary History of the United States -- have argued it should have been only a short recession, not a decade-long depression. In their view, one policy choice by America's central bank turned the crash into the Great Depression. What did Friedman and Schwartz blame?

A sudden collapse in agricultural export prices alone

Recessions had followed earlier crashes (1907, 1920-21) without becoming decade-long depressions. Source: Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (1963).

question: In 1920 America hit a brutal sharp downturn under President Warren Harding, with unemployment climbing near 12 percent. question: The date the pre-crash Dow peak of 381 was first regained by the same index -- after the 1929 fall, the Depression years, World War II, and the postwar boom -- was a landmark for anyone who had held stocks since 1929. In what decade did the Dow finally recover to its September 1929 peak?

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek argued that no government can plan a whole economy well. His reason: no small group of officials, no matter how smart, can ever know what millions of ordinary people want, need, or would pay. That information is scattered across everyone's heads and changes minute to minute. Hayek gave this problem a short name. What did he call it?
answer: The knowledge problem

Supply and demand
The gold standard
The velocity of money

Roepke, another classical-liberal continental economist, died in 1966. Machlup was Hayek's fellow Vienna Circle Austrian and later Princeton economist, but was not the 1974 laureate. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1974 press release.

question: In 1974 the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek won the Nobel Prize in Economics. He was best known for arguing that no small group of central planners, no matter how brilliant or well-meaning they were, could ever gather enough information from a desk in the capital to plan an entire country's economy for millions of people. What is this famous Hayek idea called?

choices: The knowledge problem
Comparative advantage
The invisible hand
Diminishing returns

Ohlin was another Swedish laureate (1977); Leontief won in 1973; Kuznets in 1971. All are real Nobel names of the surrounding years. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1974 press release; FEE, 'Hayek's Rejuvenating Event.'

question: In the mid-1970s the American economy did something the ruling Keynesian textbooks said was impossible. Prices at the grocery store and the gas station were rising fast — regular inflation. But at the same time jobs were disappearing, factories were closing, and unemployment was climbing. The economy was stuck and inflating all at once. Deflation

Recession

Deflation is falling prices; hyperinflation is very rapid inflation; recession is falling output. Only stagflation was the phenomenon the accepted macro model of the day said could not happen. Source: FFF, '50 Years Ago: Hayek's Nobel Lecture on The Pretence of Knowledge.'

question: On December 11, 1974 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek stepped to a lectern in Stockholm to accept the Nobel Prize in economics. The Road to Serfdom
The Use of Knowledge in Society

The three distractors are all real Hayek works of other decades: Road to Serfdom (1944), 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (an American Economic Review article, 1945), Constitution of Liberty (1960). Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Friedrich Hayek, the Austrian economist who won the Nobel Prize in 1974, warned that economics had copied physics too closely. A real physicist can measure a falling rock and predict exactly where it will land, because rocks obey fixed laws. Hayek said economists were pretending they could measure and predict the whole human economy the same way — but people are not rocks, and human choices are not falling stones. What one word do critics use for this false imitation of hard science?

choices: Scientism
Positivism
Empiricism
Rationalism

Positivism, empiricism, and rationalism are real philosophy-of-science labels for adjacent doctrines but are not the specific pejorative Hayek coined for the imitation move. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: In his December 1974 Nobel Prize lecture, titled The Pretence of Knowledge, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek warned that big economic models act as if they can predict a whole national economy but really cannot. No government agency, he said, could ever assemble the facts it would need to plan production for millions of people. Where did Hayek insist those missing facts actually sit?

In the hands of the central bank's research staff
Encoded in slowly-updating statistical time series
Inside the state's national-income accounts

The three distractors describe the sources macro forecasters actually reach for; Hayek's point is that these are precisely NOT where the decision-relevant knowledge lives. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture "The Pretence of Knowledge" attacks the view that ruled Anglo-American economics from the late 1930s through the 1970s — the idea that governments can smooth out recessions by boosting overall demand through public spending and low interest rates. The three distractors are all real texts of the Keynesian tradition -- Hansen (1941) popularised Keynes in America; Samuelson's textbook (1948) taught two generations; Robinson (1933) was a Cambridge Keynesian. Hayek's Nobel lecture is aimed at the whole tradition Keynes founded. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: The Pretence of Knowledge closes with a warning that the pretence itself has political costs. Hayek writes that the student of society must know his own limits. If he does not, he becomes a helper in the fatal push to control society, and a destroyer of a civilization that came from what?

This is Hayek's spontaneous-order doctrine restated as a moral warning. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: The Nobel Prize in Economics is not actually one of Alfred Nobel's original five prizes from his 1895 will; Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, added it in his honor much later, with the very first award handed out in 1969. Two European economists shared that first prize for building the mathematical tools economists still use to model whole economies. Who were they?

The 1974 Hayek award was thus the sixth economics prize ever given. Source: NobelPrize.org, Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

question: In 1986 the American economist James Buchanan won the Nobel Prize in Economics for a simple but bracing idea. Politicians and government workers, he showed, chase their own personal rewards -- winning re-election, growing their agency's budget, protecting their own jobs -- just as much as people running businesses in the private sector do. The three distractors are all real Chicago-tradition laureates of the same decade: Stigler (1982) for regulatory-capture theory, Coase (1991) for the theory of social cost, Becker (1992) for the economic analysis of human behaviour. All belong to the same broader turn; only Buchanan won in 1986 for public choice. Source: NobelPrize.org, all prizes in economic sciences.

question: Hayek's health had been poor in the years before the 1974 prize, and friends reported the recognition genuinely reinvigorated him. His final book, published in 1988 when he was 89, is a sustained argument against socialism as an intellectual and moral system. What is the book titled?

choices: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
The Counter-Revolution of Science
Individualism and Economic Order
The Sensory Order
context: The Fatal Conceit (1988) is Hayek's summary book of his ninth decade; it argues that socialism rests on a 'fatal conceit' -- the belief that a rational mind can design social institutions better than the trial-and-error evolution of the market order. The three distractors are all real Hayek titles from other decades: The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952), Individualism and Economic Order (1948), and The Sensory Order (1952, on cognitive psychology). Source: FEE, 'Hayek's Rejuvenating Event.'

question: In communist Poland during the 1970s and early 1980s, workers were not allowed to form their own labor unions. The government insisted that it already represented workers, so no separate voice was needed or permitted. context: Solidarnosc was founded in August 1980 at the Gdansk shipyard strikes. It was the first independent trade union in the Warsaw Pact. Banned under martial law in December 1981, it survived underground through the 1980s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union).

question: In August 1980 the workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk, Poland went on strike under the leadership of electrician Lech Walesa. They demanded the right to form their own labor union — one not controlled by the ruling Communist Party. They named the union Solidarity. Higher taxes on the poor
The government to plan even more of the economy
A total ban on all elections
context: Lech Walesa was a shipyard electrician who became Solidarity chairman, won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize, and served as President of Poland 1990-95. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lech_Wa%C5%82%C4%99sa.

question: In June 1989 Poland held its first partly free election in more than forty years. The ruling Communist Party had reserved most seats in the lower house (the Sejm) for itself, but the newly-created upper house (the Senate) was fully open to opposition candidates, and every contested Sejm seat was too. Solidarity, the once-outlawed workers' union led by Lech Walesa, ran candidates against the Party. How well did Solidarity do?

It narrowly took a small opposition foothold
It boycotted the vote
context: The Round Table Agreement allowed contested elections for the Senate and one-third of the Sejm. Solidarity won 99/100 Senate seats and swept the contested Sejm seats. The first Solidarity-led government followed in August 1989 under Prime Minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Polish_legislative_election.

question: During the Cold War, the communist countries of Eastern Europe strung a long line of fences, walls, and armed watchtowers across the continent that Winston Churchill nicknamed the Iron Curtain. Every gun barrel and locked gate on this border faced inward, toward the communist side, not outward toward the free West. What does that inward-facing design tell us about who those fences were really built to stop?

Invading Western armies
Refugees from the free West
Foreign tourists visiting
context: Hungarian border guards began cutting the barrier along the Austrian border on May 2, 1989. East Germans vacationing in Hungary began crossing on foot into Austria; the Pan-European Picnic of August 19, 1989 opened the flow to a torrent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Curtain.

question: For nearly 30 years the Berlin Wall kept East Germans from crossing into the freer West. When guards finally opened it one night in 1989, huge crowds rushed across almost at once. What does that sudden rush suggest about life under the East's planned economy?
answer: Many people had wanted out for a long time and could not say so before

Most East Germans liked the planned economy and only a few left

Only tourists on holiday crossed that night
context: Schabowski, a Politburo spokesman, botched the answer at a press conference the evening of November 9, 1989. The border guards were not warned; East Berliners walked through and danced on the Wall that night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Schabowski.

question: In November and December 1989, the people of Czechoslovakia poured into Prague's streets and forced their communist government out with peaceful marches, general strikes, and the jingling of house keys -- no shooting, no tanks, no crackdown at all. The dissident playwright Vaclav Havel became the country's new president weeks later. Because the whole change was so smooth, the events got named after a soft, luxurious cloth. Which revolution was it?
answer: The Velvet Revolution
choices: The Velvet Revolution
The Rose Revolution
The Prague Uprising
The Bohemian Turn
context: The Velvet Revolution (November 17 - December 29, 1989) was led by the Civic Forum (Czech lands) and Public Against Violence (Slovakia). The playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on December 29. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_Revolution.

question: As communist regimes fell across Eastern Europe in the final months of 1989, the collapse cascade reached Romania. Its long-ruling dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and his wife Elena tried to flee the country, were captured, and were given a hasty military trial. A firing squad shot them the same day the verdict was read. Of all the 1989 Eastern European revolutions, only Romania's ended with the leaders' execution. On what specific date were the Ceausescus shot?
answer: December 25, 1989
choices: December 25, 1989
November 9, 1989
December 29, 1989
January 1, 1990
context: The Christmas Day execution at Targoviste military barracks made Ceausescu the only communist leader shot during the 1989 collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Nicolae_and_Elena_Ceausescu.

question: On December 25, 1991 the Soviet Union was formally dissolved, and its last leader Mikhail Gorbachev resigned live on television. The red hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered for the last time above the ancient walled fortress in the heart of Moscow that had served as the seat of Russian government since the days of the tsars. What is that famous walled complex of palaces and cathedrals called?
answer: The Kremlin
choices: The Kremlin
The Bolshoi Theater
The Moscow History Museum
The Duma Building
context: On December 25, 1991 the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin flagpole and the Russian tricolor raised. Gorbachev resigned as USSR President that evening; the Union formally ceased to exist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union.

question: Robert Heilbroner was a lifelong American democratic-socialist economist at the New School who had spent his career favoring economic planning over free markets. In his September 1990 New Yorker essay 'After Communism,' he stunned his readers by admitting that the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had been right all along in the old socialist calculation debate. What three-word verdict did Heilbroner write?
answer: Mises was right
choices: Mises was right
The plan failed
Socialism has died
Prices always win
context: Heilbroner's September 10, 1990 New Yorker essay 'After Communism' delivered the three-word verdict from a witness who had spent his life on the other side of the calculation debate. It became the epitaph of the debate. Source: The New Yorker, September 10 1990.

question: The year 1989 gave history one strange ironic coincidence. On June 4, Poland held its first partly free elections in decades and the Solidarity movement crushed the ruling communists at the ballot box. That very same day, on the other side of the world, a communist government in China rolled tanks and opened fire on unarmed pro-democracy protesters in its capital's most famous central square. What was that other June 4, 1989 event?
answer: The Tiananmen Square killings
choices: The Tiananmen Square killings
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Iran-Iraq ceasefire
The Reykjavik summit
context: June 4, 1989 saw both Solidarity's Polish election sweep and the People's Liberation Army's crackdown in Beijing. The two events on the same day frame Chinese and European responses to their 1980s reform pressures. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre.

question: When the Soviet Union collapsed between 1989 and 1991, nearly every Western Sovietologist was caught flat-footed -- most had assumed the system would grind on for decades yet. But one small school of economists, led by Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, had predicted decades earlier that a planned economy must eventually fail, because with no real market it could not price anything and its planners would flying blind. Which school made that call?
answer: The Austrian economists
choices: The Austrian economists
The Keynesian macroeconomists
The rational-expectations theorists
The New Keynesians
context: Mises (1920, 1922), Hayek (1935, 1945), and Rothbard (1962) all argued the Soviet-style economy was calculation-impossible and therefore ultimately unsustainable. Robert Conquest, on separate grounds, made similar predictions. Most Western sovietology missed it. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: After the 2001 recession, America's central bank -- the Federal Reserve, chaired by Alan Greenspan -- held its main short-term interest rate, the federal funds rate, at a very low 1 percent for a full year to help the economy recover. Then on June 30, 2004 the Fed finally began raising rates in what became a long tightening cycle, Greenspan's first hike in four years. By how much did the Fed raise the rate in that very first move?
answer: 25 basis points
choices: 25 basis points
50 basis points
100 basis points
10 basis points
context: The June 30 2004 quarter-point hike moved the funds rate from 1.00% to 1.25%. It began a tightening cycle that would prove one of the most consequential -- and most predictable in its consequences -- in Fed history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: From June 2004 to June 2006, the American Federal Reserve — led first by chairman Alan Greenspan and then by Ben Bernanke — raised its main short-term interest rate at every single meeting. That was seventeen small hikes in a row, each of 0.25 percent. By the June 2006 meeting the rate reached its peak, and the Fed held it there for over a year before cutting again. What was that peak rate?
answer: 5.25 percent
choices: 5.25 percent
3.5 percent
6.5 percent
2 percent
context: The last hike, June 29 2006, was Greenspan's successor Ben Bernanke's -- Bernanke had taken the chair February 1 2006. The seventeen consecutive quarter-point hikes ended at a 5.25% federal funds rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve, usually just called the Fed, is the central bank of the United States, and its policy committee meets about every six weeks to decide interest rates. When the committee plans to leave rates unchanged, it often reuses the exact same coded phrase in its short public statement, meeting after meeting. This slow, deliberately predictable language is on purpose. Why does the Fed use these repetitive code words?
answer: To signal its next move without surprising markets
choices: To signal its next move without surprising markets
To hide policy from investors
To keep Congress out of the loop
To satisfy legal reporting rules
context: The phrase 'measured pace' meant '25 basis points per meeting.' It became a Wall Street cliche through 2004-06 as traders learned to expect the predictable quarter-point cadence. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: From 2003 to 2004 American banks handed out home loans called adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs. These loans opened with very low "teaser" interest rates for the first two or three years, then reset upward to whatever the market rate was on the reset date. When the Federal Reserve raised rates seventeen times from 2004 to 2006, those teaser loans began resetting into a much higher-rate world. What happened to many families' monthly payments overnight?
answer: They doubled or tripled
choices: They doubled or tripled
They dropped by half
They stayed flat
They increased by about 5 percent
context: Adjustable-rate mortgages with 2-year teaser periods reset in 2006-07 to the new market rates. Many households saw payments double or triple. Subprime foreclosure notices climbed sharply in the second half of 2006. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: Normally banks charge a higher interest rate to lend money for 10 years than to lend it for 2 years, because more time means more risk of things going wrong. But sometimes short-term rates rise above long-term rates -- lenders start charging more for a 2-year loan than a 10-year one. That strange flip is called an inverted yield curve, and in United States history it has been the single most reliable warning sign of what?
answer: A recession within the next year or two
choices: A recession within the next year or two
A stock-market boom in the next few months
A big rise in the value of the dollar
A crash in commodity prices
context: The yield-curve inversion signal comes from Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 New York Fed research paper. Every US recession since 1968 has been preceded by a sustained inversion. The 2006 signal was accurate: NBER dated the recession start December 2007. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1996 two economists working at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published a paper showing that a very specific bond-market signal -- the inverted yield curve, where short-term interest rates rise above long-term ones -- is the best statistical warning sign of a coming U.S. recession. Later financial-crisis writers cited their paper again and again. Who wrote that landmark paper?
answer: Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin
choices: Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin
Ben Bernanke and Alan Blinder
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Krugman and Maurice Obstfeld
context: Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 paper 'The Yield Curve as a Predictor of US Recessions' documented the empirical reliability of the signal across every US recession since 1968. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2006, the US yield curve inverted — short-term interest rates rose higher than long-term ones. This is a warning sign because banks make money by borrowing short-term and lending long-term, and an inverted curve means they can no longer earn from doing that. The inversion held through most of 2007. The National Bureau of Economic Research is the private body that officially dates when US recessions begin and end. When did NBER later date the start of what became the Great Recession?
answer: December 2007
choices: December 2007
September 2008
March 2007
January 2009
context: The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee later fixed the recession start at December 2007. Bear Stearns's hedge funds had collapsed July-August 2007; Lehman failed September 15 2008. The Fed's own recession-warning tool had rung the bell for two years before the crisis fully arrived. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Recession' (2026-09-05).

question: Through 2007 alarming news kept piling up about American subprime mortgages — the risky home loans that banks had given to borrowers with poor credit. Delinquencies rose, hedge funds tied to subprime bonds collapsed, and two of Bear Stearns' internal funds imploded that summer. Yet Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke and other officials kept repeating one calming phrase about the stress in these loans. What phrase did they use?
answer: The problems were contained
choices: The problems were contained
The situation was transitory
The turbulence would soon pass
The stress was normal seasonal noise
context: Bernanke and other Fed officials used 'contained' repeatedly through 2007 to describe subprime stress. The phrase would join 'transitory' in the museum of Fed forecasting errors. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: The person who ran the U.S. bank-insurance agency (the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC) through the 2008 crash later called it 'the most predictable financial crisis in American history.' Which two warning signs had been visible for years before the crash?
answer: A rapidly rising housing bubble and a huge boom in loans to people who could not repay them
choices: A rapidly rising housing bubble and a huge boom in loans to people who could not repay them
A sudden shortage of oil combined with a war in the Middle East
A drop in immigration combined with a colder-than-normal winter
A jump in software company failures combined with a stock split
context: Bair's phrase captured what many observers had warned about in real time: the yield curve had inverted, subprime foreclosures were climbing, and Fed officials were dismissing both signals. Source: Bair, Bull by the Horns (2012).

question: Between 2004 and 2006 the US Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate seventeen times in a row. By late 2006 the yield curve — which normally slopes upward from short-term to long-term rates — had inverted, meaning short-term rates were paying more than long-term rates. In market history that shape has almost always signaled a coming recession. The Fed watched its own inverted signal for over a year and did nothing before the 2008 crash landed. Taken together, what recognition move about central banks does this teach?
answer: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
choices: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
The Fed always acts immediately on yield-curve inversion signals
Yield-curve signals are unreliable in modern markets
Central banks always respond correctly to market-based recession warnings
context: The full pattern is comic if it were not so damaging: cheap money 2003-04 built the housing bubble; tight money 2004-06 popped it; the yield-curve inversion warned of recession from late 2006; Fed leadership called the stress 'contained' through 2007. The tool rang the bell; the institution ignored the bell. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In September 2008 the huge, 158-year-old Wall Street investment bank Lehman Brothers ran out of money. It had loaded up on risky bonds tied to American home loans, and when those loans defaulted the bank's books collapsed. Lehman owed more than it could pay, and it had to shut down under a special court process for insolvent firms. What is the general word for that legal shutdown?
answer: Bankruptcy
choices: Bankruptcy
A dividend
A merger
An IPO
context: Lehman had 25,000 employees worldwide and was the country's fourth-largest investment bank. Bear Stearns had already been swallowed by JPMorgan in a rescue that March; Merrill Lynch was sold to Bank of America on the same weekend Lehman failed; Goldman Sachs converted to a bank holding company a week later to survive. Only Lehman was allowed to fail outright. Source: Wikipedia, Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers.

question: From about 2003 to 2006 American banks handed out cheap home loans to buyers who often could not truly afford them. When lots of new buyers can suddenly bid on houses, home prices jump fast — not because the houses got any better, but because more borrowed money is chasing them. Economists have a special word for this kind of unsafe, air-filled price jump in an asset. What is it called?
answer: A bubble
choices: A bubble
A boom
A rally
A correction
context: The three distractors are all real 2008-crisis callers, but from other backgrounds: Roubini was an NYU economics professor, Shiller a Yale housing-index economist, and Burry the physician-turned-hedge-fund manager of The Big Short. Schiff was the Austrian-influenced STOCKBROKER whose television appearances -- and the mocking laughter of the panelists sharing his studio -- became the viral post-crash montage. Source: NPR, 'The Man Who Predicted the Economic Meltdown.'

question: Peter Schiff is an American investment broker who warned publicly for years that the mid-2000s American housing boom was unsustainable and doomed. In 2007, just before the meltdown hit, he published a book predicting three specific disasters: a housing crash, a banking crisis, and a falling US dollar. Within about a year of the book's release, all three were unfolding. What is the book called?
answer: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
choices: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
Too Big to Fail: The Inside Story of How Wall Street and Washington Fought to Save the Financial System
House of Cards: A Tale of Hubris and Wretched Excess on Wall Street
context: Crash Proof appeared in early 2007 and reads today as an eerie sequential forecast of the events of 2007-08. The three distractors are all real 2010-11 books ABOUT the crisis after the fact -- Michael Lewis (The Big Short, 2010), Andrew Ross Sorkin (Too Big to Fail, 2009), William Cohan (House of Cards, 2009). Only Schiff wrote his book BEFORE the crash. Source: Wikipedia, Crash Proof.

question: In 2006 and 2007, a small handful of investors -- Michael Burry, Peter Schiff, and a few others -- went on financial TV shows and warned that American house prices were going to crash and that big Wall Street banks would fail. The other guests and hosts mostly laughed at them on air, calling them cranks. When the 2008 financial crisis proved those warnings right, what did that laughter really show?
answer: Even experts can miss huge risks that a few outsiders see
choices: Even experts can miss huge risks that a few outsiders see
Crashes are impossible to predict at all
TV pundits are usually correct
The government always warns people first
context: 'Peter Schiff Was Right' was uploaded in late 2008 and racked up millions of views. The three distractors are real 2009 documentary films about the crash -- Frontline's Inside the Meltdown, Frontline's The Warning (on Brooksley Born and derivatives), Niall Ferguson's The Ascent of Money -- all serious, but none is the specific mockery-then-vindication YouTube montage. Source: NPR, 'The Man Who Predicted the Economic Meltdown.'

question: After the dot-com bust, Alan Greenspan's Fed cut its main interest rate to a low level. It held the rate there for a full year, from June 2003 to June 2004. That fed the housing boom that peaked in 2006. What did Greenspan cut the rate to in June 2003?
answer: 1 percent
choices: 1 percent
3 percent
5.25 percent
Zero percent
context: One percent was, at the time, the lowest federal funds rate in nearly half a century; it made adjustable-rate mortgages and long-duration housing bets look permanently affordable. 3 percent was closer to the Taylor-rule level economists like John Taylor said would have been appropriate; 5.25 percent was the peak the Fed later raised to in 2006; the ZIRP era of a zero-percent rate arrived only after the 2008 crash. Source: FEE, 'A Tale of Two Bubbles.'

question: From June 2004 the Fed raised the funds rate in seventeen quarter-point steps, reaching 5.25% by June 2006. The rate rises reset tens of billions of dollars of adjustable-rate mortgages upward, and by 2006 housing prices began to fall and mortgage default rates rose sharply. Which Austrian-tradition mechanism does this pattern illustrate?
answer: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
choices: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
The Keynesian liquidity trap
Minsky's financial-instability hypothesis of endogenous fragility
Real business cycle theory of exogenous technology shocks
context: The Austrian claim: cheap credit made long-duration projects (in this case housing developments and mortgage assets) look profitable; when rates returned to something like the natural rate, the mismatch between the projects started and the saving to sustain them was revealed and collapsed. The three distractors are real rival cycle theories from Keynes (liquidity trap), Hyman Minsky (financial instability), and Kydland-Prescott (real-business-cycle) -- all applied to the same crisis by their proponents. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations.'

question: In March 2007 a top American central banker told Congress that trouble in the risky home-loan market seemed 'likely to be contained.' Eighteen months later a huge bank failed and the whole financial system nearly crashed. What lesson does this remark leave about central bankers?
answer: Even the top experts often cannot see a crisis coming
choices: Even the top experts often cannot see a crisis coming
Central bankers always predict crashes months in advance
One expert opinion is enough to prevent any bank from failing
The central bank causes every recession on purpose
context: Bernanke chaired the Fed from February 2006 to January 2014. Greenspan retired in January 2006 (a month before the housing peak); Yellen chaired the Fed 2014-2018 after the crash; Volcker had been Fed chairman 1979-1987, a generation earlier. Only Bernanke was in the chair on 28 March 2007. Source: Yahoo Finance, 'This Day in Market History.'

question: In 2003 a Texas congressman warned Congress that two huge home-loan companies with quiet government backing were helping blow up an artificial bubble in house prices. Five years later the housing market crashed. Why does a quiet government backup for a private company help create a bubble?
answer: It lets the company take huge risks because taxpayers will cover the losses
choices: It lets the company take huge risks because taxpayers will cover the losses
It forces the company to build only tiny houses
It makes the company invest only in gold
It causes new houses to be finished twice as fast
context: Paul introduced the Free Housing Market Enhancement Act that year to strip Fannie and Freddie of their government sponsorship; the bill went nowhere. Barney Frank was the ranking Democrat on the same committee and defended the GSEs against Paul's warnings. Sanders was a House member during those years but was not the author of this specific testimony; Schumer was a senator, not a House committee witness. Source: RonPaulQuotes, 2003 testimony.

question: In 1931, an Austrian-school economist gave famous lectures in London. He said that when a central bank pushes rates too low, firms start big long-term projects that real savings cannot support. What usually happens to those projects when the cheap money ends?
answer: Many of them cannot be finished and are abandoned as wasted investment
choices: Many of them cannot be finished and are abandoned as wasted investment
They all finish much faster than planned
They always get turned into government offices
They become permanently profitable no matter what
context: Hayek delivered the four LSE lectures in January 1931 at Lionel Robbins's invitation; George Routledge published them the same year. Mises founded the theory in his 1912 Theory of Money and Credit; Rothbard wrote the mature Austrian textbook Man, Economy, and State (1962); Friedman was the Chicago monetarist, not Austrian. Only Hayek wrote Prices and Production. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations.'

question: After the 2008 crash, the Fed cut rates to zero and began buying huge amounts of bonds. It ran three rounds of buying from 2008 to 2012. The Fed's balance sheet grew from under $1 trillion to over $4 trillion by 2014. What is the one-phrase name for this buying program?
answer: Quantitative easing
choices: Quantitative easing
Open-market operations
The discount window
Reserve-requirement adjustment
context: Quantitative easing (QE) was the label the Fed adopted for buying long-dated Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities directly with newly-created reserves, once the funds rate had hit its zero lower bound. The three distractors are all real, older Fed policy tools: open-market operations (routine short-Treasury buying and selling), the discount window (direct emergency lending to banks), and reserve-requirement adjustment (changing the fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves). QE was the historically new instrument. Source: Brookings, 'The Fed's Balance Sheet.'

question: After the 2008 stock market crash and financial panic, Americans wanted to know what had gone wrong. The historian Thomas Woods, working at the Mises Institute in Alabama, wrote the main Austrian-school reply. His 2009 book blamed easy Federal Reserve money and government-pushed housing loans, not free markets. It shot to number one on the New York Times bestseller list and became the standard free-market story of the crash. What did Woods call the book?
answer: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
choices: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
Stress Test: Reflections on Financial Crises
context: Thomas E. Woods Jr.'s Meltdown (February 2009) frames the crash as a straight Austrian-Business-Cycle case study -- Fed cheap credit, malinvestment in housing, inevitable liquidation, bailouts prolonging the disease. The three distractors are all real bestsellers about the crisis: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010), Reinhart and Rogoff's This Time is Different (2009), and Timothy Geithner's Stress Test (2014). Only Woods's book is the Austrian one. Source: Wikipedia, Meltdown (Woods book).

question: In the years just before the COVID-19 pandemic, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet -- the assets it holds against the dollars it has issued -- stood at roughly $4.2 trillion. In the 27 months from March 2020 to June 2022, that number more than doubled. Roughly what size did the Fed's balance sheet reach at its 2022 peak?
answer: About $8.9 trillion
choices: About $8.9 trillion
About $5.1 trillion
About $12.4 trillion
About $6.3 trillion
context: The Fed balance sheet peaked at $8.97 trillion as of June 8, 2022, up about $4.25 trillion from March 18, 2020. Source: Peter G. Peterson Foundation summary of Federal Reserve data (https://www.pgpf.org/article/the-federal-reserve-will-begin-reducing-its-holdings-of-treasury-notes-and-bonds/).

question: M2 is a way to count the dollars in the US, like checking, savings, and money markets. In early 2020 M2 stood at about $15.4 trillion. By April 2022 it had jumped by about 40 percent. About what did M2 reach at its 2022 peak?
answer: About $21.7 trillion
choices: About $21.7 trillion
About $17.2 trillion
About $28.5 trillion
About $19.0 trillion
context: M2 rose from about $15.4T in February 2020 to a peak near $21.7T in April 2022 -- a 40%+ jump in about two years, the fastest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2023/may/the-rise-and-fall-of-m2).

question: In early 2021, US consumer prices were rising only 1.4 percent a year, close to normal. Then as the country reopened after COVID and the Federal Reserve kept its money-printing high, prices began climbing fast. Jerome Powell, the head of the Fed, kept telling Americans in press conferences that any jump in prices would be short and fix itself. He used one word again and again in 2021 to describe the rise. Which word did Powell use?
answer: transitory
choices: transitory
cyclical
structural
endemic
context: Powell used 'transitory' repeatedly through 2021; on November 30 he told Congress it was 'probably a good time to retire that word.' At his August 2021 Jackson Hole speech he used 'transitory' and 'temporary' five times each defending the call. Sources: Federal Reserve press conference transcripts; Bloomberg 'Powell Ditches Transitory Inflation Tag' (Nov 30 2021).

question: By spring 2020, a small group of American analysts warned that lasting inflation was coming in about two years. Peter Schiff and the hard-money crowd said the same thing: grow the money supply that fast and prices must follow. Which school of economics did they draw on for that call?
answer: The Austrian school (Mises, Hayek, Rothbard)
choices: The Austrian school (Mises, Hayek, Rothbard)
The Keynesian school (Samuelson, Krugman)
The Modern Monetary Theory school (Kelton, Wray)
The New Classical school (Lucas, Sargent)
context: Schiff and other hard-money analysts used Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1931) to argue in 2020-21 that the Fed's monetary expansion would produce persistent inflation on a two-year lag. Milton Friedman's monetarist tradition, though not strictly Austrian, made a parallel prediction. Source: SchiffGold podcast archive 2020-21 (https://www.schiffgold.com/peters-podcast/peter-schiff-2021-the-year-of-inflation).

question: In February 2020, before the pandemic, the M2 dollar supply was about $15.4 trillion. Twenty-six months later, in April 2022, it peaked near $21.7 trillion -- a roughly 40% expansion. Milton Friedman, in a famous 1963 talk in India, had summarized his answer to what happens next in a single sentence about inflation and money. What conclusion does Friedman's sentence draw about what causes persistent inflation?
answer: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output
choices: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output
It is always the result of workers demanding wages ahead of productivity
It is always driven by corporate market power and price gouging
It is always the consequence of oil shocks and other supply disruptions
context: From Friedman's 1963 talk 'Inflation: Causes and Consequences' delivered in India: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon in the sense that it is and can be produced only by a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output.' Source: Wikiquote / Hoover Institution reprints.

question: By June 2022 US yearly consumer inflation hit its highest since 1981, following trillions in pandemic-era money creation. For months the Federal Reserve and Treasury had insisted the price rise would be short-lived. What single word did they use to describe the inflation that kept climbing anyway?
answer: Transitory
choices: Transitory
Structural
Cyclical
Imported
context: US CPI peaked at 9.1% year over year in June 2022, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics -- the largest 12-month increase since November 1981. Source: BLS, 'Consumer prices up 9.1 percent over the year ended June 2022' (https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2022/consumer-prices-up-9-1-percent-over-the-year-ended-june-2022-largest-increase-in-40-years.htm).

question: Once the June 2022 inflation reading came in, the Federal Reserve reversed course and began raising its policy rate faster than at any time since the early 1980s. Between March 2022 and July 2023, the fed funds target rose from 0-0.25% to 5.25-5.5% -- 525 basis points in roughly sixteen months. Which earlier Federal Reserve chair's tightening cycle -- the only comparable one in modern history -- was Powell's 2022-23 campaign most often compared to?
answer: Paul Volcker's 1979-1982 campaign
choices: Paul Volcker's 1979-1982 campaign
Alan Greenspan's 1994-1995 campaign
Arthur Burns's 1972-1974 campaign
Ben Bernanke's 2015-2018 campaign
context: The FOMC raised its target 525 bp between March 2022 and July 2023, the fastest tightening cycle in four decades -- rivalled in pace only by Paul Volcker's 1979-82 campaign, which pushed rates near 20% to crush inflation. Sources: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter June 2024; Richmond Fed Economic Brief 23-26.

question: In March 2020 the COVID pandemic shut down the American economy and stock markets crashed. The Federal Reserve responded by buying bonds at a pace it had never used in its 107-year history — Treasuries the government issues, plus mortgage bonds tied to home loans. In April 2020 alone the Fed made purchases that were a huge chunk of everything it would print during the whole crisis. Roughly what dollar amount did the Fed buy in that one month?
answer: Over $1 trillion
choices: Over $1 trillion
About $150 billion
About $80 billion
About $400 billion
context: April 2020 Treasury and agency-MBS purchases by the Federal Reserve exceeded $1 trillion in that single month -- a single-month pace that the previous eleven decades of the Fed's history had never approached. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (July 2020, 'A New Reserves Regime? COVID-19 and the Federal Reserve Balance Sheet').

question: One theory says a government can safely print money for programs. It says the only real limit is running out of workers and factories, not rising prices. From 2021 to 2023 the Fed roughly doubled the money it had made, and prices jumped from about 1 percent to over 9 percent a year. What did that jump most clearly prove wrong?
answer: Printing lots of new money really does drive up prices
choices: Printing lots of new money really does drive up prices
Governments must balance their budget every single year
Only regular banks decide how much money exists
Central banks should target only the exchange rate
context: Kelton's 2020 book argued the binding constraint on federal spending was not deficits but real resources and inflation; critics point to 2021-23 CPI running 1.4% -> 9.1% as real-time falsification of the practical judgment that the resource constraint was not yet close. Source: 'The Deficit Myth' (2020); Mises Institute review (https://mises.org/mises-wire/review-stephanie-keltons-deficit-myth).

question: For most of 2021, Jerome Powell used one calming word to describe inflation. Then on November 30, 2021 he told the Senate it was 'probably a good time to retire that word.' In the same hearing he began warning that big rate hikes were coming. In which month's testimony did Powell drop the word?
answer: November 2021
choices: November 2021
March 2022
August 2021
January 2023
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30, 2021 that it was 'probably a good time to retire that word' -- formally dropping the earlier framing. The FOMC began its rate-hike campaign in March 2022. Source: Bloomberg 'Powell Ditches Transitory Inflation Tag, Paves Way for Rate Hike' (Nov 30 2021).

question: In 2020-21 the Federal Reserve about doubled the money supply. It told the public any price jump would be brief supply-chain stuff. Instead the Consumer Price Index (CPI) climbed from 1.4% to 9.1% two years later. Which money argument did the critics get right?
answer: A big enough increase in the money supply pushes prices up on a lag, whatever else is going on
choices: A big enough increase in the money supply pushes prices up on a lag, whatever else is going on
Bank regulators always control prices better than markets do
Farm subsidies survive because their costs fall on many taxpayers at once
A central planner cannot set correct relative prices without money
context: The Austrian and monetarist critics pressed Friedman's line -- persistent inflation is a monetary phenomenon -- against the Fed's supply-chain framing. Supply and demand shocks can shift the SHAPE of the inflation but a 40% M2 expansion drives the general price level on a lag. Powell dropped 'transitory' Nov 30 2021; CPI peaked at 9.1% June 2022. Sources: Friedman 1963; SchiffGold; BLS; Bloomberg Nov 30 2021.

question: Around 2018, hedge-fund manager Jesse Felder made a phrase popular. It means prices rising at the same time in many things: homes, stocks, art, and more. The same money cause drives them all. What is the phrase?
answer: The everything bubble
choices: The everything bubble
The Goldilocks economy
The great moderation
The productivity boom
context: Felder popularized the 'everything bubble' label to distinguish the modern QE-era pattern from single-asset bubbles like the dot-com or 1980s Japan. It was expanded by Vincent Deluard and Grant Williams. Source: Grokipedia 'Everything bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: From January 2020 through June 2022, the Case-Shiller US home price index, built by economist Robert Shiller and his colleague Karl Case, rose about 45 percent. That was the fastest 30-month climb since the index began in 1987, part of the post-pandemic housing boom driven by low interest rates. What was the top yearly gain in that stretch?
answer: About 20.8 percent in April 2022

About 8 percent in March 2021
About 35 percent in June 2022
About 3 percent in December 2021
context: The 20.8% year-over-year gain in April 2022 is the highest reading in the Case-Shiller series. Housing was the single most visible of the everything-bubble asset classes. Source: S&P/Case-Shiller US National Home Price Index (fred.stlouisfed.org).

question: When the COVID-19 pandemic hit in March 2020, US stocks crashed as businesses shut down. The S&P 500 index, which tracks America's 500 largest companies, hit a low on March 23, 2020. Then the Federal Reserve pumped trillions of new dollars into the economy through emergency programs, and stock prices rocketed upward. The S&P 500 peaked in December 2021. About 30 percent
About 200 percent
About 15 percent

question: When the COVID-19 pandemic crashed markets in March 2020, Bitcoin's price fell to about $4,000. Then the US Federal Reserve printed trillions of new dollars to fight the pandemic recession, and Bitcoin's price rocketed upward — since only 21 million bitcoins can ever exist, its supply cannot be printed to match. The price peaked in November 2021. About how high did it go?
answer: About $69,000
choices: About $69,000
About $30,000
About $20,000
context: Bitcoin peaked at roughly $69,000 in November 2021 -- a 17-fold rise from the March 2020 low. It was among the most extreme moves in the everything-bubble asset complex. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin' (2026-09-05).

question: In early 2021, a Reddit forum called WallStreetBets rallied millions of small investors to buy shares of two struggling US companies. Their share prices shot far above what the real businesses could justify. One was a mall-based video-game store; the other was a large movie-theater chain. answer: GameStop and AMC Entertainment

Netflix and Peloton
Zoom and DocuSign
Tesla and SolarCity
context: GameStop surged in January 2021 after r/wallstreetbets coordination against short-sellers; AMC Entertainment followed later that year. Both episodes were symptoms of the broader liquidity flood into speculative assets. Source: Grokipedia 'GameStop short squeeze' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2021 a new market exploded: 'non-fungible tokens', or NFTs — digital art pieces whose ownership was recorded on a blockchain like Bitcoin. Buyers spent huge sums on cartoon apes, pixel portraits, and one-of-a-kind image files. Then over the next couple of years the whole NFT market crashed by more than 90 percent. choices: About $25 billion
About $2 billion
About $100 million
About $150 billion
context: Total NFT sales hit about $25 billion in 2021. By 2023 volumes had fallen 97% from peak. The rise-and-collapse pattern is a textbook Cantillon-first-receiver liquidity spike. Source: Grokipedia 'Non-fungible token' (2026-09-05).

question: During the 2020-21 stock-market boom, a special kind of Wall Street shell company let hundreds of private startups skip the usual public listing process and go public just by merging with the shell. These cash-shell vehicles raised over 160 billion dollars in 2021 alone, then nearly vanished by 2023 once the Federal Reserve raised interest rates and the boom broke. What are they called?
answer: SPACs -- special-purpose acquisition companies
choices: SPACs -- special-purpose acquisition companies
REITs -- real-estate investment trusts
ETFs -- exchange-traded funds
IPOs -- initial public offerings
context: SPACs raised about $162 billion in 2020-21, matching the entire prior decade combined. Volumes collapsed as rates rose in 2022. The SPAC boom was a paradigmatic Cantillon-effect speculative excess. Source: Grokipedia 'Special-purpose acquisition company' (2026-09-05).

question: During the boom of 2020-21 a famous American fund manager became a star by betting big on trendy tech companies. Her fund rose sharply, then fell about 80 percent when the boom ended. What is the general lesson when a fund concentrates on hot stocks during a boom?
answer: The same concentration that made it rise fast can make it crash just as hard
choices: The same concentration that made it rise fast can make it crash just as hard
Concentrated funds always outperform diversified ones
Government insurance covers all the losses in a fund
Hot stocks are guaranteed to keep rising forever
context: Cathie Wood's ARKK peaked in February 2021 and lost about 80% peak-to-trough by 2022-23. It was the poster-child of long-duration growth-stock cycle exposure to rate policy. Source: Grokipedia 'ARK Investment Management' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1730s the Irish-French banker Richard Cantillon wrote that fresh money does not spread evenly through an economy: whoever gets it first benefits, while those who get it later pay higher prices for everything. The 2020-24 US cycle fit this shape almost exactly. In 2020-21 asset prices — stocks, homes, art — rose first. In 2021-23 everyday consumer prices rose. In 2022-23 a bust hit. Which framework, from the Austrian tradition, names this pattern?
answer: The Cantillon-effect pattern of first-receiver benefits followed by later-receiver adjustment
choices: The Cantillon-effect pattern of first-receiver benefits followed by later-receiver adjustment
The Keynesian animal-spirits framework of investor sentiment
The efficient-markets hypothesis of neutral price discovery
The random-walk model of stock-market behavior
context: The Austrian intellectual contribution to the 2020s: identifying the pattern as a Cantillon-effect sequence rather than as 'irrational exuberance' or 'animal spirits.' The specific rise-then-fall timing across asset classes tracks the theory precisely. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: After a decade of near-zero interest rates, by 2021 what critics called the 'everything bubble' had pushed the most speculative assets to record highs. When the Federal Reserve hiked rates hard in 2022 to fight inflation, the crash hit hardest in a few specific corners -- the assets that had risen most on cheap money. Which trio saw the sharpest peak-to-trough drops during the 2022-23 bust?
answer: Bitcoin -78%, ARK Innovation ETF -80%, and the meme-stock complex -90%+
choices: Bitcoin -78%, ARK Innovation ETF -80%, and the meme-stock complex -90%+
S&P 500 -70%, Case-Shiller Home Price Index -60%, and Treasury bonds -50%
Gold -85%, silver -80%, and platinum -75%
Investment-grade bonds -75%, corporate credit -70%, and municipal bonds -65%
context: The speculative-asset tier -- long-duration growth stocks, crypto, meme stocks -- corrected hardest as rates rose. Real estate and broad equities were stickier because Powell's 2022-23 hikes came after the peak and did not fully unwind earlier gains. Source: Grokipedia 'Everything bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: A government runs out of money. It seizes land from a big organization inside its own country and prints paper money saying 'this money is backed by that land.' What is the danger of this kind of paper money?
answer: The government can just print more whenever it wants, so the money loses value
choices: The government can just print more whenever it wants, so the money loses value
The land will always keep the money valuable
Only the organization loses out, not regular people
Paper money is always safer than gold
context: The Assembly's November 2 1789 decree nationalized the property of the Church in France to serve as backing for a new currency. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1789, the new revolutionary government of France seized huge tracts of land owned by the Catholic Church. To pay its bills fast, it issued a paper currency backed by claims on that seized property. Each note was, in theory, a legal ticket to a piece of Church land. The paper money had one name. What was it called?
answer: The assignat
choices: The assignat
The livre tournois
The louis d'or
The franc
context: The name came from the French verb 'assigner' -- each note was assigned against specific land parcels for redemption. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: France's first paper money, the assignats, came out in late 1789. The first batch was 400 million livres, and the Assembly swore it would be the only one. By 1795 the total in use was a very different figure. What did the total reach?
answer: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
choices: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
About 2 billion livres, roughly 5 times the promised limit
About 800 million livres, roughly double the promised limit
Just under 400 million livres, exactly the promised limit
context: Every subsequent Convention and Directory added new issues to cover expenses. By late 1795 the outstanding stock exceeded 40 billion livres of face value. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: In revolutionary France, the assignat was the paper money the National Assembly had issued starting in 1789, supposedly backed by land it had seized from the Catholic Church. By the mid-1790s French farmers and traders had lost trust in the assignats and were asking for gold coin instead. The revolutionary state did not cut back on printing. Instead it raised the legal penalty for treating gold as worth more than paper. What was the top penalty for doing that?
answer: Death
choices: Death
Prison for one year
A fine of 100 livres
Public flogging
context: The Convention's 1793-94 anti-hoarding laws carried capital punishment for those who refused assignats at face value or hoarded specie. Legal coercion did not restore confidence in the paper. Source: Andrew Dickson White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: The assignat, France's revolutionary paper currency issued from 1789 and supposedly backed by seized church lands, had lost almost all its value by 1796. One assignat was worth about one thousandth of its face amount. The Directory — the government running France at the time — pulled the assignats out of use and tried a fresh start with a new paper money, again supposedly backed by the same land. What was the replacement currency called?
answer: The mandat territorial
choices: The mandat territorial
The new assignat
The livre revolutionary
The franc germinal
context: The mandats territoriaux were introduced in March 1796 and collapsed even faster than the assignats they replaced, losing 97% of value within months. Napoleon later restored specie-based currency with the franc germinal in 1803. Source: Grokipedia 'Mandat territorial' (2026-09-05).

question: The Assignat crash was France's second try at a national paper money in less than a hundred years. The first try ended in a 1720 crash in Paris, run by a Scottish schemer. Whose plan was that first try?

Jean-Baptiste Colbert's royal treasury
Cardinal Richelieu's tax edicts
Necker's compte rendu

question: In 1912 the American historian Andrew Dickson White, a co-founder of Cornell University, wrote a short but forceful book called Fiat Money Inflation in France. question: During the French Revolution in the 1790s, the new government printed paper money called assignats, supposedly backed by land seized from the church. Officials printed more and more of the paper to pay the government's bills, until the currency collapsed and shopkeepers refused to accept it. Paper money can succeed if backed by patriotic sentiment
Only unlimited legal-tender enforcement can preserve currency value
The failure of paper money in France was due to foreign interference
context: White's book documented every mechanism the Revolution used -- legal tender laws, price controls, capital punishment for speculators -- and their uniform failure once the paper supply outran the backing. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: During the French Revolution, the government printed huge amounts of paper money. When it lost value, they tried price controls, made refusing the paper illegal, and even executed 'hoarders.' Prices kept climbing. The 1944-1971 Bretton Woods system

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to look for 'the seen and the unseen' -- the visible near-term gain that hides a slow-moving destruction. Applied to the assignat, the paper money France issued in 1789 against seized Church land, the state printed more and more notes until prices exploded and savings were wiped out. context: Bastiat's frame: the visible policy tools look decisive; the invisible costs -- black markets, empty shelves, evaporated savings -- are the actual result. The Assignat is a textbook illustration published 40 years after Bastiat's death. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In a 1912 book on money, an Austrian economist made this claim. Money must have had some other use before it became money. If not, no one could know what it was worth on its first day. Which Austrian economist made this claim?

choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Friedrich Hayek
Murray Rothbard

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued in 1912 that money does not just appear as money out of thin air. the Calculation Debate
the Praxeological Axiom
the Time-Preference Theorem

question: Some Austrian economists said Bitcoin should never have caught on as money. They said money must start as a useful item first, like gold or salt. Bitcoin had no prior use. What did Bitcoin end up showing about that idea?

Money always needs a government to declare it legal

Robert Murphy later took the opposite (pro-Bitcoin) side; Peter Boettke is at George Mason; Israel Kirzner works on entrepreneurship not monetary theory. Source: https://mises.org/profile/frank-shostak.

question: In the 2010s, the Austrian economist Frank Shostak analyzed Bitcoin using Ludwig von Mises's Regression Theorem. Since Bitcoin has no such physical history, Shostak drew a direct conclusion — one that many other Austrians and Bitcoin supporters strongly dispute. What did Shostak predict about Bitcoin's future?

that Bitcoin would become the world's dominant reserve currency by 2020
that Bitcoin should be adopted by central banks as a reserve asset
that Bitcoin's value was purely a matter of government regulation
context: Shostak's conclusion from applying the Regression Theorem as he read it: Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that must eventually collapse. He did not predict reserve-currency status, central-bank adoption, or a regulation-only explanation. Source: Shostak Mises Wire articles 2013-15.

question: The Austrian economist Frank Shostak argued that Bitcoin could not really be money. Younger Austrians pushed back. Saifedean Ammous, Peter St Onge, and others led the reply. What did the Ammous side claim?

that Bitcoin had an implicit government-backing guarantee from the start through federal law-enforcement action
that Mises himself would have retracted the Regression Theorem if he had lived to see Bitcoin's first two years
context: The Ammous/St Onge response: in Bitcoin's earliest days it functioned as a cypherpunk collectible whose non-monetary use was the technical curiosity itself; that initial demand satisfied the theorem's requirement. The other options are not what the pro-Bitcoin Austrians argued. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8-9.

question: The economist Saifedean Ammous, author of the 2018 book 'The Bitcoin Standard,' defended Bitcoin against Austrian critics who said it violated Mises' Regression Theorem -- the rule that money must have had an earlier non-money use. the January 3, 2009 genesis block
the October 31, 2008 white paper
the January 2013 Cyprus banking crisis

The genesis block and white paper are pre-money events; the Cyprus crisis (March 2013) is later. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: For most of the 2010s, Austrian economists rejected Bitcoin, arguing it violated Mises' Regression Theorem -- the rule that money must first have had a non-money use. question: Some Austrian economists argue that anything used as money must have started with some other use first -- like gold, which was valued for jewelry long before it became coins. Why does Bitcoin make people debate this old rule?

Sowell is not an Austrian and does not run a Bitcoin podcast; Friedman was a monetarist, died 2006; Samuelson was a Keynesian, died 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_P._Murphy.

question: For years the Austrian economist Frank Shostak had insisted Bitcoin could not be true money — it had no earlier use, so Mises's Regression Theorem should rule it out. Looking back at this Shostak-Ammous debate, one writer said the real lesson goes past Bitcoin. answer: That even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record

That any internal disagreement inside a school of thought discredits the whole tradition and reveals its foundational theorems as unable to survive scrutiny
That founding texts should be treated as fixed and never re-examined against new empirical cases, since re-examination undermines the tradition's authority

question: Austrian economists spent a century arguing that governments always debase paper money, and that only a truly scarce, hard-to-counterfeit asset (once, gold) protects savers. Bitcoiners say the same case now fits a new asset. Which property of Bitcoin carries that Austrian case?

choices: Its fixed 21-million cap plus proof-of-work makes it costly to create and impossible to inflate
Its friendly logo makes people want to save in it rather than spend it
Its use of the internet makes it faster than paper checks in the mail
Its price rises whenever the Federal Reserve prints more dollars

Shostak took the opposite position; Block and Hulsmann have been publicly ambivalent. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_St._Onge.

question: A bunch of banks made bad bets on bonds that lost value. To keep them from failing, the country's central bank started a program that let them borrow money using those bad bonds as collateral. What is this kind of central-bank rescue usually called?

question: A bank owns bonds only worth 80 cents on the dollar right now. The central bank lets the bank borrow using those bonds as collateral -- but counts them as worth the full 100 cents. Why do critics call this a hidden bailout?

question: When the Federal Reserve loans money to a bank, it takes bonds from the bank as collateral. Normally the Fed looks at what those bonds could actually sell for today, then trims that number a bit more for safety. What is this normal practice called?

question: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed and several other US banks looked wobbly. The Federal Reserve set up an emergency program called the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP). Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failed after their bond holdings lost value when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates fast. question: The Fed can only set up special emergency loan programs when things are very bad. That was the case in March 2020 and again in March 2023. When the Fed reaches for that power, what does it usually tell the country?
