context: Section 13(3), dating to 1932, permits Fed lending to non-bank borrowers in 'unusual and exigent circumstances.' Its 2020 and 2023 uses established the highest cadence of invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023, after Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank suddenly collapsed, the Federal Reserve set up a new short-term loan program. It let banks borrow cash using their bonds as backup — even bonds whose market price had dropped sharply after the Fed raised interest rates. Why does a new rescue program like this one worry critics of the Federal Reserve?
answer: Banks may take bigger risks in the future, expecting another rescue
choices: Banks may take bigger risks in the future, expecting another rescue
Emergency programs cause every bank to close down
It forces the Fed to sell off its office buildings
It makes banks raise interest rates on savings accounts
context: BTFP expired on March 11 2024, one year after its launch. Outstanding balances continued to be paid down, but no new borrowings were permitted after that date. The precedent, however, stands. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: In several crises the Fed has taken bonds from banks as loan backup at a price higher than the bonds could sell for. What is the risk when a central bank acts like shaky assets are worth more than they really are?
answer: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
choices: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
It doubles the value of every bond overnight
It shrinks the money supply on purpose
It forces all banks to sell their buildings
context: The 2008 Term Auction Facility (TAF) was the previous precedent for accepting collateral at above market value. BTFP was in effect a re-run of that mechanism, calibrated to bond-loss stress rather than to broader liquidity strain. Source: Grokipedia 'Term Auction Facility' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 2023 the Federal Reserve started a lending program (the Bank Term Funding Program, or BTFP) that let banks borrow using bonds worth less than face value -- but the Fed accepted them at full face value. Which 'seen vs unseen' reading best captures what that program really did?
answer: Seen: it steadied the banks. Unseen: it subsidized losses the Fed's own low-rate policy had caused.
choices: Seen: it steadied the banks. Unseen: it subsidized losses the Fed's own low-rate policy had caused.
Seen: rising interest rates. Unseen: falling exports.
Seen: growing employment. Unseen: shrinking productivity.
Seen: a broad recovery. Unseen: a narrow crisis in one region.
context: The banks had bought long bonds at low rates because the Fed's earlier policy made them attractive. When the same Fed's tightening exposed those bonds to loss, the BTFP quietly reimbursed the losses. The whole cycle -- create the incentive, expose the loss, cover the loss -- was internal to Fed choices. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In March 2023, after Silicon Valley Bank collapsed on losses from long-dated Treasury bonds, the Federal Reserve launched the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP). It let banks post their underwater bonds as collateral at face value and borrow cash against them at par. The Fed formally shut the program down in March 2024. Why do Austrian critics say ending BTFP does not undo the precedent it set?
answer: Every bank now knows the Fed will lend against bad bond portfolios in the next crisis too
choices: Every bank now knows the Fed will lend against bad bond portfolios in the next crisis too
The Fed announced it will never offer another emergency loan to any commercial bank
Interest rates will never rise again, so bank bond losses cannot recur
Ending the program proves the Fed has given up on all rescue tools forever
context: The BTFP ran its course but its precedent is now baked into every bank's implicit risk framework. Duration mismatch is less risky when the central bank has demonstrated willingness to cover the loss. Moral hazard accumulates one precedent at a time. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: Imagine the US federal government starts giving every college student a new $10,000 grant to help pay for tuition. Colleges know almost exactly how much extra money each student now has to spend on school. The economist William Bennett noticed a pattern in what happens next, year after year, whenever federal aid increases. What tends to happen to tuition prices in the years after such a grant?
answer: Tuition prices go up by about the same amount
choices: Tuition prices go up by about the same amount
Tuition prices fall because students have more money
Tuition prices stay exactly the same forever
Colleges refund the extra aid to families
context: William Bennett was Reagan's Secretary of Education (1985-88). His 1987 NYT essay 'Our Greedy Colleges' launched what came to be called the Bennett Hypothesis. Source: nytimes.com/1987/02/18 (Bennett op-ed).

question: In 1987, William Bennett was the US Secretary of Education under President Ronald Reagan. He wrote a New York Times opinion piece accusing colleges of raising their tuition to swallow up whatever extra federal aid Congress gave to students. His claim now bears his name as the Bennett Hypothesis. According to Bennett, extra federal college aid mostly flows in the end to which group?
answer: Colleges, through higher tuition
choices: Colleges, through higher tuition
Students, through lower net cost
Federal loan servicers, through fees
State governments, through matching grants
context: The Bennett Hypothesis: subsidies to a demand-side party (student) can be substantially captured by the supply-side party (college) when supply is constrained and demand is inelastic. Source: Bennett, NYT (1987).

question: US federal student loan debt exploded from the early 1990s through 2023, as college tuition kept rising faster than family incomes and Congress kept lending more to close the gap. Millions of former students now carry loan balances they may never fully repay. Total student loan debt is now one of the largest categories of household debt in America, larger than credit card debt or auto loans. About what dollar total does US federal student loan debt stand at in the mid-2020s?
answer: About $1.7 trillion
choices: About $1.7 trillion
About $170 billion
About $17 trillion
About $170 million
context: Total federal student loan debt grew from ~$100B in the 1990s to ~$1.7T in the early-to-mid 2020s. The debt is largely the mirror image of the tuition inflation the Bennett Hypothesis predicts. Source: newyorkfed.org (Household Debt and Credit Report).

question: From 1978 to 2018, US public four-year college tuition rose about 213% in real terms, and private four-year tuition rose about 129%. That was faster than almost any other price in the economy — much faster than groceries, cars, or houses. Over those same forty years, one type of federal money kept expanding to help students pay, and its growth matched the tuition climb almost exactly. Which type of federal money was it?
answer: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
choices: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
Federal defense procurement contracts
Federal highway trust fund grants
Federal agriculture price supports
context: The tuition rise tracks federal aid expansion tightly -- the 1965 Higher Education Act reauthorizations, the 1992 direct-loan program, and the 2010 elimination of private-lender intermediation each expanded federal aid. Source: nces.ed.gov (tuition historical series); collegeboard.org (Trends in Student Aid).

question: The New York Federal Reserve Bank has a research team that studies how public policy shapes prices. In 2015 that team, led by economist David Lucca, examined what happens each time Washington makes more federal student loans available to college students. They compared each dollar of new federal loan money to changes in colleges' published sticker tuition. When federal loans went up by a dollar, what did the researchers find happened to sticker tuition?
answer: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
choices: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $0.05 decrease in tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $2 decrease in net cost
A $1 increase in loans produced no measurable tuition change
context: Lucca + Nadauld + Shen, New York Fed Staff Report 733 (2015, revised 2019). The 60-cent tuition pass-through is a direct market-mechanism confirmation of the Bennett Hypothesis using discontinuities in loan-limit rules. Source: newyorkfed.org (staff report 733).

question: Two American economists, Grey Gordon and Aaron Hedlund, built a detailed computer model of the entire US college tuition market from 1987 to 2010. They used it to test how much of the huge tuition rise came from Washington making more federal student aid — Pell Grants and subsidized loans — available to students. When they ran their simulation, roughly what share of the tuition rise did the model blame on this aid expansion?
answer: Essentially all of it
choices: Essentially all of it
About one-quarter
About half
None of it
context: Gordon + Hedlund's model attribution was approximately 106% of the observed rise -- essentially all of it, with a slight overshoot other model features offset. Note the model dependency in interpreting the exact number. Source: NBER Working Paper 21967 (Gordon + Hedlund 2016).

question: In 1987 William Bennett, the US Secretary of Education under President Reagan, wrote a famous New York Times op-ed. He argued that federal student loans do not really make college more affordable — instead, colleges quietly raise tuition every time Washington offers more loan money, because students can now borrow more, so schools will simply charge more. The more Washington lends, the more schools charge. What is this idea called in economics today?
answer: Bennett Hypothesis
choices: Bennett Hypothesis
Baumol effect
Cantillon effect
Rent-seeking loss
context: The Delta Cost Project and GAO documented administrative-staff growth of ~87% from 1987 to 2011, well ahead of the ~50% student-enrollment rise. The aid revenue built bureaucracy rather than classrooms. Source: deltacostproject.org (Trends in College Spending reports).

question: For decades in the United States, college tuition has risen far faster than most other prices -- outpacing wages, medical care, and general inflation. In 1987, US education secretary William Bennett published a New York Times essay giving a famous answer: cheap federal student loans meant colleges could keep raising the sticker price and let taxpayers cover the gap. What is the most common explanation critics still give for the runaway costs?
answer: Cheap government-backed student loans let colleges keep raising tuition
choices: Cheap government-backed student loans let colleges keep raising tuition
Fewer people wanting to attend college each year
Falling wages for professors and staff
A shortage of paper for printing textbooks
context: Richard Vedder, Going Broke by Degree: Why College Costs Too Much (AEI Press, 2004). Vedder's book presented the tuition-inflation / administrative-bloat pattern years before the Lucca and Gordon-Hedlund quantitative work. Source: aei.org (Vedder 2004).

question: The Bennett Hypothesis, named for US education secretary William Bennett, says a government subsidy paid to buyers gets captured by suppliers whenever supply is tight -- the price simply rises to soak up the new money, and the buyer ends up no better off. The pattern shows up in more than college costs. Where else does the same idea appear in US policy: a subsidy to buyers that gets eaten by tight supply?
answer: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
choices: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
Federal wildlife-refuge acquisitions
National Park entrance fees
Federal snow-plowing grants
context: Section 8 vouchers substantially raise landlord rent capture in constrained markets. Similar mechanisms operate in health-insurance subsidies (premium inflation) and the 2008-10 first-time homebuyer credit (largely captured in seller prices). Source: Collinson + Ganong on Section 8; Zwick + Malani on homebuyer credit.

question: The Bennett Hypothesis, named for US education secretary William Bennett, says a buyer-side subsidy in a tight market flows straight through to suppliers as higher prices instead of helping the buyer. That gives an analyst a check to run before any new buyer-side subsidy gets approved. What question should the analyst ask about the supply side?
answer: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
choices: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
Whether the supplier's headquarters is unionized
Whether the supplier accepts credit cards
Whether the supplier files its taxes electronically
context: The reasoning move: when a subsidy is proposed, ask whether the supply side is constrained and whether the specific suppliers have pricing power. If yes, expect substantial subsidy capture through prices. Source: Bennett (1987); Lucca + Nadauld + Shen (2015).

question: Since William Bennett's 1987 claim that colleges raise tuition to swallow federal aid, economists have refined the Bennett Hypothesis into three specific effects. First, aid raises the sticker price colleges can charge. Second, colleges spend the extra revenue on climbing walls, fancy dorms, and thick layers of administrators rather than on more classrooms. Third, the number of students actually taught per professor barely changes. Which one sentence best captures what federal student aid does overall?
answer: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
choices: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
It reduces the total price paid per credit hour
It shifts students into cheaper community colleges
It eliminates the need for private philanthropy
context: The three-part mechanism: demand-side pricing effect, administrative expansion of aid-funded revenue, and amenity-competition arms race in place of price competition. All three point in the same direction. Source: Gordon + Hedlund (2016); Vedder (2004); Delta Cost Project reports.

question: On the night of August 12-13, 1961, the East German communist government sealed the border between East and West Berlin to stop its citizens from fleeing to the free West. Soldiers first rolled out barbed wire in the dark. Then workers built a concrete barrier that would stand for 28 years, splitting families and a city in two. What did they build?
answer: The Berlin Wall
choices: The Berlin Wall
The Iron Curtain
The Elbe Line
The Warsaw Line
context: Walter Ulbricht's East German government built the initial barrier overnight August 12-13, 1961. It grew into a concrete wall encircling West Berlin, standing until November 9, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: After World War II, Germany was split in half — the free western part and the communist East Germany controlled by the Soviet Union. The old capital, Berlin, was also split. In 1961, the East German communist government built a huge concrete wall completely around West Berlin to stop its own citizens from escaping into the free western half of the city. The Berlin Wall became the most famous symbol of communist rule keeping its own people trapped. Roughly how long was the full barrier around West Berlin?
answer: About 155 kilometers
choices: About 155 kilometers
About 15 kilometers
About 1,550 kilometers
About 500 kilometers
context: The Wall was roughly 155 km (96 miles) long, encircling West Berlin -- not running along the East-West German border. It included concrete, watchtowers, a 'death strip', anti-vehicle trenches, and patrol roads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: The Berlin Wall stood in the middle of Berlin, Germany, from 1961 to 1989. It divided communist East Germany from free West Germany during the Cold War. Along the Wall, East German soldiers manned tall concrete watchtowers armed with machine guns. Those guns were not aimed westward at the free countries at all. They were aimed the opposite way. Which direction did the watchtower guns actually point?
answer: East, at East Germans
choices: East, at East Germans
West, toward free Berlin
Straight up, at aircraft
Both directions equally
context: The Wall's fortifications faced INWARD -- guns and mines directed at East Germans trying to leave, not westward at any invading force. The design fact is the argument: the state had to wall its own citizens in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: After World War II, Germany was split in two — communist East Germany on one side, free West Germany on the other. The city of Berlin sat inside East Germany but was itself split, and until 1961 people in East Berlin could simply walk across into West Berlin. So they did. Between 1949 and 1961 huge numbers of East Germans walked out this way, more than a fifth of the entire country. About how many people had left by the time the East German government finally built the Berlin Wall to stop them?
answer: About 3.5 million
choices: About 3.5 million
About 350,000
About 35 million
About 35,000
context: About 3.5 million East Germans left through Berlin between 1949 and August 1961 -- roughly a fifth of the country's population. The Wall was built to stop the flow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: After the 1961 Berlin Wall closed the last escape route out of communist East Germany, people still tried to cross -- swimming rivers, climbing fences, digging tunnels, and racing across the border strip. Guards were ordered to shoot to kill. Over the 28 years the Wall stood, the Berlin Wall Memorial in Germany has confirmed a documented death toll at the Wall itself. What is that figure?
answer: About 140
choices: About 140
About 14
About 1,400
Over 14,000
context: The Berlin Wall Memorial documents about 140 confirmed deaths at the Wall itself; several hundred more died at the wider inter-German border. The first was Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961); the last was Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989). Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: East Germany's communist government ran a huge secret police force called the Stasi, based in East Berlin. To keep tabs on its roughly 16 million citizens, the Stasi employed one uniformed officer for every 180 people, and it also recruited about twice as many unpaid civilian informants — neighbors, friends, even spouses reporting on each other. What does that enormous amount of spying tell us about how the East German rulers actually held on to power?
answer: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
choices: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
Most citizens loved the government and rarely needed watching
The police mainly caught foreign spies from the West
The system worked because everyone freely volunteered to inform
context: Ministerium fuer Staatssicherheit -- Ministry for State Security -- gave East Germany the highest surveillance-to-population ratio of any modern state. Source: bstu.de (Stasi Records Archive).

question: The Berlin Wall split communist East Berlin from the free West for nearly 30 years. Within days of its being built, people started dying trying to escape -- some by jumping from apartment windows in the border zone. What does that very first escape death show?
answer: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
choices: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
Escape attempts were actually very rare from the start
The wall was quietly popular with most East Berliners
The wall stopped nobody from crossing in either direction
context: Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961) died jumping from her fourth-floor Bernauer Strasse apartment on the border. She is the first of the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented victims. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: The Berlin Wall was built by communist East Germany in 1961 and stood for 28 years. It was designed and guarded to stop people from moving in one direction only. In February 1989, only months before the Wall finally fell, East German border guards shot 20-year-old Chris Gueffroy — the last person killed trying to cross. In which direction were people like Gueffroy trying to escape?
answer: From communist East Berlin to free West Berlin
choices: From communist East Berlin to free West Berlin
From free West Berlin into communist East Berlin
From East Berlin north into Denmark
In both directions about equally at all times
context: Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989) was shot trying to cross to West Berlin. His death drew international protest and East German policy shifted; his was the last shooting fatality at the Wall. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: After East Germany's communist government fell in 1990, its secret police, the Stasi, left behind millions of pages of files spying on ordinary citizens. Germany passed a law called the Stasi Records Act, giving every East German the right to read the file the state had kept about them personally — and to see which friends, coworkers, and family members had informed. Why does opening these kinds of files matter after a police state falls?
answer: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
choices: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
It makes the old spies work harder in the future
It automatically arrests everyone named in the files
It hides the truth so the country can move on faster
context: The Stasi Unterlagen Gesetz (Stasi Records Act, December 1991) established the office administering the archive and gave individuals the right to read their own files. The former ministry headquarters at Normannenstrasse is now the Stasi Museum. Source: bstu.de.

question: In the 1920s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued that a fully planned socialist economy could not calculate prices rationally, because without real markets there is no way to know what people truly want. His student Friedrich Hayek carried on the debate for decades. The Berlin Wall — 3.5 million East Germans having already fled before it went up in 1961, and machine guns aimed inward at the East — illustrated the Austrian point at physical scale. Which core Austrian argument did the Wall's design demonstrate?
answer: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
choices: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
The market side always subsidizes the planned side
Planning works well as long as walls are built early
Cold War rivalry drove all migration flows
context: The argument is exit-as-verdict: given free comparison across an open border for twelve years, the population had voted with its feet. The Wall's inward-facing design is the calculation-debate answer made physical. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: The Berlin Wall was the concrete and barbed-wire barrier the East German communist government built completely around West Berlin, to keep its own citizens from fleeing to the free western half of the city. It stood for exactly 28 years. When the communist regime finally collapsed, ordinary Germans from both sides rushed the gates with hammers and pickaxes and tore the wall down with their own hands. In what years did the Berlin Wall stand?
context: The Wall was built August 12-13, 1961 and fell November 9, 1989 -- 28 years and 3 months. The demolition was completed by the early 1990s; small segments remain as memorials, and a double-cobblestone line traces the former path across the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: Around 2019 on Bitcoin Twitter, a short three-word slogan took over as the standard reply to any headline about a bank freeze, a country's money-printing binge, or a currency crash. Fans typed it under news stories again and again until it became the defining Bitcoin meme of the era, part of an argument that sound money could cure many modern financial ills. Which phrase was it?
answer: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
choices: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
'To the moon'
'Diamond hands'
'When Lambo?'
context: Popularized by Michael Saylor and thousands of others. Half meme, half genuine argument that most modern financial pathologies trace to monetary debasement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: Bitcoin fans often insist they want nothing to do with the much larger online scene of thousands of copycat coins, scam tokens, and centralized cryptocurrency projects. They argue Bitcoin -- launched anonymously in 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto -- is a separate thing, sound digital money, while the wider label lumps it in with speculative junk that mostly ends in losses. What broader label do they try to distance Bitcoin from?
answer: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
choices: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
The traditional-finance industry
The federal-reserve academic literature
Central-bank digital currencies
context: Bitcoin advocates argue Bitcoin is monetary infrastructure with a specific design; altcoins are, in their view, mostly speculative tokens or venture-capital exit vehicles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A 'sat' or satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest divisible unit. How many satoshis make up one Bitcoin?
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC. Named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto. Naming the smallest unit for the creator is analogous to naming a small currency unit for a founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Satoshi_(unit).

question: Bitcoin is a digital currency created in 2009 that trades at a wildly changing price. Some fans do not try to time the market. Instead they buy a small fixed amount on a regular schedule — every week, every payday, or every month — no matter whether the price is up or down. The smallest unit of a bitcoin is called a satoshi, or 'sat' for short. In the online Bitcoin community, what slang phrase describes this steady buying habit?
answer: Stacking sats
choices: Stacking sats
Rebalancing the portfolio
Hedging the position
Rolling the futures
context: Formally this is dollar-cost averaging. The community identity built around stacking emphasizes the discipline of not trying to time the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: In Bitcoin online communities on sites like Twitter and Reddit, there is a well-known dismissive slogan that Bitcoin holders throw at people who refuse to buy any Bitcoin at all. The slogan is 'Have fun staying poor.' It is snarky, but the community means it as a serious economic prediction, not just a joke. What is the slogan's core claim about people who keep their savings only in regular government dollars?
answer: Inflation slowly eats dollar savings, so refusing Bitcoin leaves them poorer over time
choices: Inflation slowly eats dollar savings, so refusing Bitcoin leaves them poorer over time
Bitcoin owners are legally required to give money to skeptics
The government pays Bitcoin owners a monthly bonus
Only rich people are allowed to buy Bitcoin
context: Cobie is the pseudonym of Jordan Fish, a British Bitcoin and altcoin trader who co-hosts the UpOnly podcast. The slogan expresses the impatience of holders who have watched skeptics predict Bitcoin's death for years while the network keeps functioning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: The Bitcoin community has developed its own habits and rituals without anyone in charge: stacking sats each payday, running personal computer nodes at home, meeting up in local city groups, holding giant yearly conferences. No committee designed any of this — it grew from the bottom up. A Nobel-winning Austrian economist decades earlier had a name for exactly this kind of unplanned pattern, where useful order emerges from many separate free choices. Which economist and which idea?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
choices: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
John Maynard Keynes's animal spirits
Milton Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis
Paul Samuelson's revealed preference
context: Spontaneous order is Hayek's term for shared norms and institutions -- like language, common law, and open-source software -- that arise without any central planner. Bitcoin culture emerged with no central architect. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather at big Bitcoin conferences in Nashville, Miami, Prague, and Riga. To an outsider they might look like typical Wall Street investment events with speakers offering quick-profit stock tips. In fact they feel very different. The keynote speakers on the main stage rarely talk about short-term price forecasts or trading strategies at all. What subject actually dominates those keynote talks?
answer: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
choices: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
Presentations of specific-price Bitcoin forecasts by regulated broker-dealers
Panels on hedge-fund short-selling strategies
Endorsements of specific altcoins by government regulators
context: The culture's emphasis on long time preference (deferring consumption today for a stronger monetary position later) and monetary-history education distinguishes the Bitcoin conference circuit from the mainstream investment-conference culture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_conference.

question: In May 2010, a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz offered 10,000 bitcoins to anyone who would send him a meal. What simple food did he ask for?
answer: two large pizzas
choices: two large pizzas
a hamburger and fries
a case of beer
a bucket of fried chicken
context: Hanyecz wrote 'I'll pay 10,000 bitcoins for a couple of pizzas... like maybe 2 large ones so I have some left over for the next day.' The transaction settled on May 22, 2010. Source: https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=137.0.

question: In May 2010, a Florida programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two Papa John's pizzas delivered to his home. At the time each bitcoin was worth less than a penny, so the whole meal cost about forty dollars. It was one of the very first real-world purchases made with Bitcoin. Why is that trade now famous?
answer: Those 10,000 bitcoins would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars
choices: Those 10,000 bitcoins would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars
The pizzas were the best pizzas ever made
The bitcoin transaction failed
The programmer got the pizzas for free
context: The pizzas were ordered from Papa John's through its normal website by a UK forum user with the handle 'jercos'; Papa John's had no direct involvement with the crypto side of the deal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: On May 22, 2010, in Jacksonville, Florida, a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz completed the first known real-world purchase using Bitcoin. He paid 10,000 bitcoin for two Papa John's pizzas delivered to his door. Bitcoin was so new and untested that a single coin was worth only a tiny fraction of a penny. Roughly what were his 10,000 bitcoin worth in US dollars that day? (Bitcoin fans still celebrate the anniversary every year as 'Pizza Day.')
answer: about $41
choices: about $41
about $8,000
about $2
context: 10,000 BTC at the prevailing rate of roughly $0.004 per BTC came to approximately $41 -- so Hanyecz paid about $20 per pizza in dollar terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: On May 22, 2010, the Florida programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas -- one of the earliest known uses of Bitcoin to buy anything real. Bitcoiners now treat that date as a milestone. It was not the very first Bitcoin trade ever -- earlier trades had swapped Bitcoin for cash between users -- but it was the first of a special kind. Which milestone did Hanyecz's pizza order set?
answer: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
choices: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
the first Bitcoin mined by a home computer
the first Bitcoin exchange listing
the first Bitcoin transaction between two people who had never met
context: Bitcoin had been mined, sent between hobbyists, and traded for other cryptocurrencies before May 22, 2010 -- but Hanyecz's pizzas were the first documented exchange of BTC for a real physical good, marking Bitcoin's crossing from experiment to money. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Before the 2010 pizza order made him famous, the programmer Laszlo Hanyecz had already changed Bitcoin forever. In the early days, Bitcoin mining ran on ordinary computer processors (CPUs) and produced only a trickle of new coins. In 2010, Hanyecz posted a piece of code on the bitcointalk online forum that changed how mining worked from that day on. What did the code do?
answer: the first software that let a graphics card (GPU) mine Bitcoin
choices: the first software that let a graphics card (GPU) mine Bitcoin
the first mobile Bitcoin wallet
the first mixing service to anonymize transactions
the first Lightning Network channel implementation
context: Hanyecz worked out that a GPU could hash far faster than any CPU and wrote and shared the code, inadvertently starting the mining arms race that led to FPGAs, then ASICs. Mobile wallets came later; mixing services and Lightning are unrelated projects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: On May 22, 2010, the Florida programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas -- one of the first real-world purchases with Bitcoin. Every year on that same date, Bitcoin holders around the world order pizzas, post lunch pictures online, and celebrate the trade that turned Bitcoin from a hobby into money you could actually spend. What is this fan holiday commonly called?
answer: Bitcoin Pizza Day
choices: Bitcoin Pizza Day
Genesis Day
Satoshi Day
The Halving Anniversary
context: The community holiday Bitcoin Pizza Day is celebrated every May 22. Genesis Day (January 3) marks the mining of Block 0; Satoshi has no official birthday; the halving happens roughly every four years, not annually. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: In 2010 a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas. At bitcoin's cycle highs years later, what would that same 10,000 bitcoins have been worth?
answer: over one billion US dollars
choices: over one billion US dollars

question: In 2022, Austrian economists argued about whether Bitcoin fit Mises's Regression Theorem — the rule that money must start with some non-money use. question: In 1997 the French publisher Robert Laffont put out a huge 900-page book by six European historians, edited by Stephane Courtois. question: In 1997 a team of European historians published The Black Book of Communism, a country-by-country count of deaths under communist rule during the 1900s. question: The China chapter of the Black Book of Communism counts deaths from three major disasters: the Great Leap Forward famine of 1959-61, the Cultural Revolution of 1966-76, and the ongoing laogai prison-labor camps. What total does the book give for China?

question: In 2003 the American journalist Anne Applebaum won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for a book called 'Gulag: A History.' question: China's 'Great Leap Forward' from 1958 to 1962 tried to leap ahead of the West through forced collectivization of farms and backyard steel furnaces. The result was the largest famine in human history. Roughly how many people are now estimated to have died?

question: In 1997 a team of European scholars led by Stephane Courtois published Le Livre noir du communisme (The Black Book of Communism). question: At the end of World War II the United States demobilized fast — over 8 million American soldiers came home by June 1946. Alvin Hansen, a Harvard economist often called the 'American Keynes,' made a bold public prediction about what would happen once wartime government spending was pulled back. What did he say the economy would do?

choices: Slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn
Sustaining wartime full employment for at least another decade
Entering a mild recession that would end within six months
Experiencing runaway inflation as pent-up demand met limited supply
context: Hansen and other 'secular stagnation' Keynesians argued the war had 'lifted' the US out of the 1930s and removing wartime spending would collapse it back. Every major Keynesian forecast in 1945-46 predicted renewed depression. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Hansen.

question: In 1945 World War II ended. Federal spending in Washington fell fast, and 8 million American soldiers came home looking for civilian jobs all at once. Many famous economists at the time predicted a huge slump — even a second Great Depression. What actually happened to the US jobless rate in 1946 and 1947?
answer: Stayed around 4 percent
choices: Stayed around 4 percent
Rose to about 15 percent
Rose to about 25 percent as in 1933
Stayed exactly at wartime levels near 1 percent
context: Despite the Keynesian prediction of depression, unemployment averaged around 4% in 1946-47 as private demand and investment absorbed the released wartime resources within months. Source: bls.gov historical LFS series.

question: In his 1946 book Economics in One Lesson, Henry Hazlitt said the end of World War II proved one Bastiat argument in the real world. All that wartime spending had not been what kept the country rich. Which Bastiat argument did Hazlitt say the postwar drop proved?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The candlemakers' petition
The negative railway
The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: The postwar experience was Bastiat's broken-window in reverse: the destruction (of massive government spending) did not impoverish the country because the released resources were used privately. Hazlitt makes this the anchor chapter of Economics in One Lesson. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Right after the September 11, 2001 attacks on New York and the Pentagon, the New York Times economist Paul Krugman wrote a column suggesting the vast destruction might do some economic good, since so much would have to be rebuilt. Economists pointed out that this misses a classic warning the Frenchman Frederic Bastiat had made back in 1850. What thinking mistake did that column make?
answer: The broken window fallacy
choices: The broken window fallacy
The sunk cost fallacy
The law of supply and demand
The tragedy of the commons
context: Krugman's September 14 2001 NYT column, and follow-ups on Hurricane Katrina and the 2011 Japan earthquake, applied broken-window logic to disasters and terrorist attacks. He later walked the framing back. Source: nytimes.com (Krugman archive, September 14 2001).

question: Bastiat teaches you to look for the hidden cost that a 'destruction helps the economy' claim ignores. Hurricane Katrina cost about $100 billion to rebuild. What did people in Louisiana and Mississippi end up with by late 2006, compared to before the storm?
answer: The same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries

Better houses than before, thanks to the stimulus multiplier on federal spending
The same houses they had before, plus a year of higher aggregate income
Fewer houses than before, but with matching insurance-industry compensation
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN: the resources that rebuilt destroyed homes could not build new homes elsewhere. The Gulf ended 2006 no better off in housing stock than it had been in mid-2005, minus everything the same labor and capital could have produced instead. Source: cato.org/commentary/broken-window-fallacy-still-fooling-people.

question: When the September 11 attack destroyed the Twin Towers in New York, huge quantities of steel, concrete, and skilled workers were pulled in to rebuild them. Bastiat's method asks a critical question. What did the country lose the chance to build with all those same workers and materials?

The federal defense programs Congress passed later in 2001
The airport-security jobs the government hired for after the attacks
The insurance-industry reserves for covering future attacks
context: The classic seen/unseen split for reconstruction: the WTC rebuild used labor and materials that would otherwise have built new offices in Queens or new homes on Long Island. The rebuild is SEEN; those other buildings are UNSEEN because they never got built. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/broken-window-fallacy-and-911.

question: The end of World War II is the biggest peacetime drop in federal spending ever recorded. About how much did federal spending fall from 1945 to 1946?

The Austrian-Bastiat prediction (private demand absorbs the released resources) beat the Keynesian one on the largest peacetime test available. Source: whitehouse.gov OMB historical tables.

question: In 1946, as 8 million American soldiers came home from World War II and federal wartime spending collapsed, most economists feared a huge slump. It did not come. Human Action
Bureaucracy

question: The general Bastiat lesson from the 1946 postwar demobilization can be stated in one sentence about released resources and private demand. Empirically, 1946-47 US private consumption and private nonresidential investment surged as government spending fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-World_War_II_economic_expansion.

question: A whole family of claims -- 'the September 11 attacks help the economy,' 'World War Two ended the Great Depression,' 'Hurricane Katrina will boost the Gulf Coast' -- all share the same Bastiat-style error. What two things are they wrongly treating as equal?

Consumption and inflation

question: A boy throws a rock through a shopkeeper's window. Some people say, 'at least this creates work for the window-maker!' What are they forgetting?

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a famous parable. A shopkeeper's careless son smashes a windowpane in his father's shop. Ten francs
Twenty francs

question: In Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen,' a French shopkeeper's window is smashed by his careless son. question: In Bastiat's broken-window story, the shopkeeper has to spend six francs replacing the glass. Bastiat's whole point is that this money was already planned for something else the shopkeeper now cannot buy. What is the name for that other, invisible purchase?

question: Bastiat ends his broken-window chapter with a plain accounting summary. Before the break, the shopkeeper had a window and six francs; after the break, he has only a window. What single-sentence summary does Bastiat give about the community as a whole?

The community has traded consumption for investment

question: In 1850 the French writer Frédéric Bastiat published a famous essay called 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen.' In it, a shopkeeper's window is smashed by his careless son. question: On September 14, 2001, three days after the 9/11 attacks destroyed the World Trade Center in New York City, the Nobel-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote a column in The New York Times suggesting the terrorist attacks might 'do some economic good' by forcing massive rebuilding. question: In 2009 the federal government paid buyers a cash rebate to trade in older vehicles for newer ones. But the trade-ins had to be destroyed by pouring sodium silicate directly into the engine. Which 2009 program is now the textbook broken-window example?

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat's 1850 broken-window essay was titled 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen.' question: In 1980 the American economist Milton Friedman — already famous for winning the Nobel Prize — published a bestselling book called 'Free to Choose' with his wife Rose, and hosted a popular ten-part PBS public television series by the same name. Only bank executives' hands
Government economists' hands, since they see the big picture

question: In 1962, the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published the book that founded public choice as an academic field — the study of how self-interested people actually behave inside government, not just in markets. The Logic of Collective Action

question: For a long time most economists assumed that everyone working inside government — voters at the ballot box, elected politicians, and career civil servants — always tried to do what was best for the whole country. choices: Voters, politicians, and bureaucrats
Only wealthy business owners
Only foreign leaders
Only judges

question: In the 1960s the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock founded a school of thought called public choice economics. They said politics really has two levels. What did Buchanan and Tullock call that upper level?

choices: The constitutional level
The judicial level
The bureaucratic level
The electoral level
context: The constitutional level is where individuals choose the rules that will bind all subsequent political choices. Buchanan's whole later career built out this idea as 'constitutional political economy.' Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: In their 1962 book The Calculus of Consent, the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock argued that when citizens sit down to pick constitutional rules, they cannot know whether they will later end up on the winning or losing side of the votes those rules produce. What phrase did they use for this rule-choosing mindset?

choices: The veil of uncertainty
The veil of ignorance
The original position
The natural condition
context: The 'veil of uncertainty' is Buchanan-Tullock's term. Individuals reasoning about future political outcomes rationally consent to rules that limit majority power. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: A philosopher asked a challenging question. What rules would you pick for your society if you did not yet know whether you would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick, popular or friendless? Choosing rules without knowing your own future spot is called reasoning from behind what?

choices: A veil of ignorance
A curtain of doubt
A wall of silence
A cloud of neutrality

Buchanan reached the parallel constitutional move nine years earlier from an independent starting point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Theory_of_Justice.

question: In 1962, two American economists — James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock — published a book called 'The Calculus of Consent.' The natural convergence of common purposes

question: In The Calculus of Consent (1962), the American economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock argued that people picking constitutional rules from behind their 'veil of uncertainty' would demand higher-than-majority thresholds for some especially big decisions — because a bare 51 percent could too easily strip a losing minority of rights. Proportional rules

Supermajority rules for consequential choices minimize expected total cost. Source: Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: The economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock met at the University of Virginia after Tullock left the US Foreign Service in 1958. question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's 1962 book 'The Calculus of Consent' laid down most of the founding ideas of public choice — the economics of politics. The veil of uncertainty behind rule choice
Vote-trading and logrolling analysis
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern comes from Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965) -- three years after the Calculus. The other three are all in the Calculus. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Olson (1965).

question: The book Calculus of Consent became famous in public-choice theory because it drew one crucial distinction between two kinds of political question. That distinction is at the center of the book's whole analysis. Which distinction does the book emphasize?
answer: The distinction between the RULES of the game and the choices WITHIN the rules
choices: The distinction between the RULES of the game and the choices WITHIN the rules
The distinction between right-wing and left-wing voters
The distinction between economic policy and social policy
The distinction between elected and appointed officials
context: The constitutional / post-constitutional distinction is Buchanan's most enduring contribution. Individuals may agree on the rules (constitutional consent) while disagreeing on the choices made under the rules (post-constitutional politics). Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), preface and Chapter 6.

question: Half a century after James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published The Calculus of Consent — the founding text of public choice, which helped win Buchanan the 1986 Nobel in economics — its influence extended far beyond formal scholarship. In one sentence, how is the book's abiding lesson best summarized?
answer: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
choices: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
The bigger the majority, the wiser the decision
Politicians are always more knowledgeable than voters
Economic policy should never be constrained by any constitution
context: Buchanan's whole later career built out this insight. Constitutional rules that bind majorities are the deepest form of consent, because they are agreed to when the future distribution of winners and losers is still unknown. Source: Buchanan, The Reason of Rules (Cambridge 1985).

question: In 1821 Britain formally committed that its central bank would redeem paper pound notes for gold at a fixed price -- about 4.86 pounds per troy ounce, the informal rate since 1717. This launched a monetary system that would become the model for the industrial world. What is that system called?
answer: The gold standard
choices: The gold standard
The silver standard
The bimetallic standard
The gold-exchange standard
context: The 1821 resumption of gold payments by the Bank of England is the conventional start of the classical gold standard, a system Britain led until 1914. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Before 1914, the world ran on the classical gold standard. Each major country's currency — the British pound, the American dollar, the French franc — was tied to gold at a fixed weight. Because every currency locked to gold, the exchange rates between currencies were locked too. For most of the years before 1914, one British pound was worth about how many US dollars?
answer: About 4.86 dollars
choices: About 4.86 dollars
About 2.20 dollars
About 10 dollars
About 1.60 dollars
context: The pound-dollar rate stayed at 4.8665 for decades before 1914, held there by the two currencies' independent gold parities. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1871, the newly-unified Germany of Otto von Bismarck adopted the gold standard, switching from silver. The switch demanded enormous sums of gold. Germany paid for it out of a huge war indemnity extracted from a European power it had just defeated in a short, decisive war. Which payment funded Germany's move to gold?
answer: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
choices: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
The Austrian tribute after the Austro-Prussian War
The Ottoman payment for the Berlin conference
The Danish settlement over Schleswig-Holstein
context: France paid Germany 5 billion francs in gold after its 1871 defeat, giving Chancellor Bismarck the reserves he needed to move Germany to the mark on a full gold basis. Source: Grokipedia 'Franco-Prussian War' (2026-09-05).

question: The classical gold standard tied paper money to gold at a fixed weight. Under that system in Britain, prices in 1914 were roughly the same as prices in 1821 — a full century apart. Britain industrialized massively over those hundred years, but the price of bread or coal barely drifted. What single word describes prices that stay flat over the long run like that?
answer: Stable
choices: Stable
Hyperinflationary
Deflationary by two-thirds
Volatile in a wide upward trend
context: The British price level fluctuated within a range but showed no sustained trend across the 93 years of the classical gold standard. A pound in 1914 bought roughly what a pound in 1821 bought. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Under the classical gold standard before 1914, a working-class Italian family in Naples could receive money from a son laboring in London without worrying about the exchange rate. If he mailed home five pounds sterling, the equivalent value in Italian lira arrived — the same worth across the whole trip, nothing eaten by shifting rates. What feature of the system made that possible?
answer: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
choices: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
The Bank of England guaranteed all foreign remittances at face value
The Italian government subsidized the Lira-Pound conversion
International trade unions negotiated the exchange rates
context: The pound was fixed to gold at one ratio, the Italian lira at another; their cross-rate followed mechanically. A worker's remittance kept its purchasing power across borders because both currencies shared a real anchor. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, writing after World War II, looked back on the classical gold standard — the 1870s-to-1914 arrangement in which each currency was legally fixed to a real weight of gold. He read its meaning as political, not merely economic, because it bound governments' hands. How did Mises describe it?
answer: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
choices: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
The unavoidable relic of a pre-industrial economy
A middle-class conspiracy against wage earners
A technical convenience of no political significance
context: Mises argued that gold discipline restrained state power more effectively than any written constitution. Governments unable to inflate had to persuade taxpayers or lenders to fund their projects. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: Under the classical gold standard (1870s to 1914), every paper dollar or pound was legally redeemable for a fixed weight of real gold held in a vault. That put a hard limit on how much money a government could print, and therefore on how much it could spend without raising honest taxes. What did those honest gold-backed budgets make too costly to fund?
answer: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
choices: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
Building public schools and hospitals
Maintaining diplomatic embassies abroad
Sponsoring scientific expeditions
context: Under gold, wars had to be paid for by taxes or borrowing. Neither scaled to modern industrial slaughter. Governments could inflate only by first suspending convertibility -- which is what all major belligerents did within days in August 1914. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: Between 1871 and 1914 most of Europe ran on gold-backed money. What is one big economic feature people remember from that time?
answer: Rising trade, a growing middle class, and long stretches of stable prices
choices: Rising trade, a growing middle class, and long stretches of stable prices
Constant inflation that quietly shrank most family savings
Rapid money printing used to pay for many small wars
Bank collapses in almost every country every few years
context: The Belle Epoque -- 'beautiful era' -- runs from roughly 1871 to 1914. Its economic character (free capital movement, stable prices, mass migration funded by private savings) was inseparable from the shared gold basis of world money. Source: Grokipedia 'Belle Epoque' (2026-09-05).

question: For nearly a hundred years, most European currencies had been redeemable for gold at fixed weights — the classical gold standard. Then in the first week of one specific month in 1914, every major belligerent in Europe suspended gold convertibility so its government could print new money to pay for the coming Great War. That month ended the classical gold standard forever. Which month was it?
answer: August 1914
choices: August 1914
January 1914
November 1914
October 1918
context: Germany suspended gold payments August 4 1914; Britain effectively followed within days; France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary within the week. The century of stable prices ended not because gold discipline failed but because states wanted to fight a war that gold discipline would have made unaffordable. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian economists praised the classical gold standard for a political reason, not a monetary one. Because the money supply could not expand at will, governments had to live within their budgets, and paying for a war with printed money became painful. Which specific effect do they emphasize most?
answer: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
choices: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
It prevented all business-cycle fluctuations
It ensured full employment across the developed world
It equalized income across social classes
context: The Austrian point: the value of gold discipline is not perfect stability -- there were still recessions and shocks -- but the constraint it placed on government power. Every 20th-century abandonment of gold was driven by governments that wanted to be freed from that constraint. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: There is a famous story from British-ruled India about colonial rulers who tried to solve a snake problem in one big city by offering a cash reward for every dead cobra. The plan backfired so badly that economists still use the story to name a whole class of well-meaning policies that produce perverse results — the Cobra Effect. In which Indian city is the original story set?
answer: Delhi
choices: Delhi
Bombay
Calcutta
Madras
context: The parable is traditionally set in British colonial Delhi in the late 19th century. The historical base is disputed; Siebert used it as an illustrative parable in 2001 for the general perverse-incentive pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: The British rulers wanted fewer cobras in the city. They set up a payment plan to get people to help. What did the government offer?
answer: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
choices: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
A tax rebate for landowners who eradicated cobras from their plots
A trained mongoose delivered to each household that requested one
A public-works job for anyone willing to clear cobra dens
context: The bounty was the seen policy: kill more cobras, get paid, cobra population should fall. Straight, intuitive, and completely wrong once the incentive was actually running. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: In British-ruled Delhi, colonial officials worried that cobras were killing too many people, so they offered a bounty: bring in a dead cobra, get paid. Poor Delhiites quickly found a way to work the system that never crossed the government's mind. This is the origin of the 'Cobra Effect' — good-intentions policy that produces the opposite of what leaders hoped. What did the locals start doing to cash in on the bounty?
answer: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
choices: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
Began smuggling cobras in from neighboring provinces
Began stealing cobras from public zoo enclosures
Began falsely reporting non-cobra snakes as cobras
context: Farming dead cobras in the back yard was more profitable than hunting wild ones. The bounty had created a farming operation, not a hunting one -- exactly the unseen behavioral response the policy did not price in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: In British-ruled Delhi, colonial officials worried about the cobras in the streets and offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra brought to the authorities — the story that gave the 'Cobra Effect' its name. Locals soon began breeding cobras just to collect the reward. When the government caught on and stopped paying, what did the breeders do with all their now-worthless snakes?
answer: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
choices: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
Petitioned the government for a compensation payment
Killed and buried their cobra stock privately
Sold the cobras through underground exotic-pet markets
context: Delhi's cobra population ended the program HIGHER than it started; the released breeder-stock hit the streets after the bounty ended. The parable's whole punch is this cancellation-worse-than-nothing outcome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: A very similar bounty story is well-recorded from French colonial rule in Southeast Asia. In the early 1900s the French administration in one of its capital cities wanted to cut the rat population and paid a bounty per severed rat tail. Locals promptly started breeding rats — or clipping the tails off live rats and releasing them to breed again. Which city was this?
answer: Hanoi
choices: Hanoi
Saigon
Phnom Penh
Vientiane
context: The French Hanoi rat-bounty (1902) is better historically documented than the Delhi cobra story. Rat-catchers began FARMING rats and turning in the tails while releasing the tail-less rats to breed more. Source: Michael Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race,' French Colonial History 4 (2003).

question: In 1975, the British economist Charles Goodhart was studying how the Bank of England tried to control the money supply. He noticed something strange: the moment officials picked a specific number to grade themselves against, that number stopped working as an honest measurement — people gamed it. His short rule is now paraphrased everywhere as: 'When a measure becomes a ___, it stops being a good measure.' What word fills in the blank?
answer: A target
choices: A target
A budget item
A regulation
A subsidy
context: Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Originally a Bank of England paper on monetary aggregates, it generalized to name the whole pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law.

question: In the mid-2010s, Wells Fargo — one of the biggest banks in America — told every teller: hit your monthly quota for opening new customer accounts, or lose your bonus. Tellers responded by opening millions of fake accounts customers had never asked for. Whole families got credit cards they'd never signed up for. Economists call this a textbook case of Goodhart's Law. What is the lesson from the story?
answer: Reward a target instead of the real goal and people will hit the target in harmful ways
choices: Reward a target instead of the real goal and people will hit the target in harmful ways
Bonuses always make workers more honest with their customers
Extra accounts do no real harm since customers rarely notice
Big banks are usually the fastest to spot their own fraud
context: Wells Fargo's 2016 cross-sell fake-accounts scandal: employees hit incentive targets by opening real accounts customers had not requested. The bounty on 'accounts opened' produced accounts, not customer value. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo_cross-selling_scandal.

question: From 2001 to 2015, a US federal education law tied school funding partly to standardized test scores. Critics complained schools started teaching only what appeared on the standardized test, and they called that pattern 'teaching to the test.' What was the popular name of that law?
answer: No Child Left Behind
choices: No Child Left Behind
Race to the Top
Every Student Succeeds
Elementary and Secondary Education
context: NCLB (2001), signed by George W. Bush, made federal funds contingent on test-score improvements; schools optimized on the specific tested items, sometimes at the expense of everything else. The 2015 Every Student Succeeds Act replaced it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act.

question: The Cobra Effect, Goodhart's Law, and the Hanoi rat bounty all illustrate the same hidden pattern of unintended consequences. When policy creates a reward, people respond in ways nobody planned. In 2010, a US health law fined hospitals when patients returned within 30 days of discharge, and some hospitals responded creatively. What did they do to avoid the fine?
answer: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
choices: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
Refused to accept transfers from other hospitals with high readmission rates
Reduced the length of stay for all admitted patients uniformly
Charged patients directly for care that would trigger a readmission classification
context: The ACA's CMS 30-day-readmission penalties incentivized hospitals to keep returning patients in ED observation status (which is not counted as an admission), reducing the measure without necessarily improving the outcome. Standard Cobra-Effect / Goodhart pattern. Source: healthaffairs.org/do/10.1377/hpb20180216.35660.

question: In the 1950s, most experts said the government should run more of the economy. One economist wrote a big book to defend an older idea. He said free people making their own choices is better than a small group planning for all. What is that older idea called?
answer: Classical liberalism
choices: Classical liberalism
Socialism
Mercantilism
Fascism
context: F. A. Hayek completed the manuscript in May 1959; University of Chicago Press published it as 'The Constitution of Liberty' in February 1960. Source: Wikipedia article on The Constitution of Liberty (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constitution_of_Liberty).

question: Friedrich Hayek — the Austrian-born economist and 1974 Nobel laureate — wrote his big 1960 book 'The Constitution of Liberty' while teaching at the University of Chicago. But he was not in Chicago's famous economics department. He was in a small interdisciplinary program that also housed the novelist Saul Bellow and the philosopher Allan Bloom. What was that program called?
answer: The Committee on Social Thought
choices: The Committee on Social Thought
The Chicago School of Sociology
The Cowles Commission
The Committee on Human Development
context: Hayek held the Committee on Social Thought chair at Chicago from 1950 through the late 1950s; The Constitution of Liberty was written there. Source: University of Chicago Press catalog listing (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo9253956.html).

question: In his 1960 book 'The Constitution of Liberty,' the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek insists that liberty means one specific, narrow thing. Liberty is NOT wealth. It is NOT political voice. It is NOT economic power. Liberty, Hayek says, is simply not being forced to serve another person's will. What single condition does Hayek call true liberty?
answer: The absence of coercion by another person
choices: The absence of coercion by another person
The satisfaction of one's most fundamental preferences
The equal exercise of political voice in the public sphere
The material means to pursue one's chosen ends
context: Hayek: liberty is the absence of coercion by another person -- being made to serve another's will. Not power, not wealth, not political participation. Source: Cato Institute review and Online Library of Liberty essay by Ronald Hamowy (https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/hamowy-s-critique-of-hayek-s-concept-of-freedom).

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1960 book 'The Constitution of Liberty' is organized in three named parts. Part I sets up the philosophical foundations — what freedom is and why it matters. Part II covers the legal framework: the rule of law, the constitution, and private property. Part III applies the ideas to specific policies like taxation and welfare. What title did Hayek give to Part I?
answer: The Value of Freedom
choices: The Value of Freedom
The Meaning of Liberalism
Between Instinct and Reason
The Origins of Order
context: The book runs Part I 'The Value of Freedom,' Part II 'Freedom and the Law,' Part III 'Freedom in the Welfare State.' Source: BiblioVault edition listing (https://www.bibliovault.org/BV.book.epl?ISBN=9780226315393).

question: In 'The Constitution of Liberty,' the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek says two fines feel very different in kind. Being fined for running a red light — a rule that was written down beforehand and applied the same way to everybody — feels like justice. But being fined because a police officer decided on the spot, 'you owe me because I said so,' feels tyrannical. Same money out of your pocket. Very different systems. Which classical legal contrast is Hayek pointing to?
answer: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
choices: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
Private property versus common ownership
Positive freedom versus negative freedom
Judicial review versus legislative supremacy
context: Hayek's core Part II thesis: the rule of law -- general, prospective, equal, published in advance -- is a distinct kind of political order from administrative discretion, even when the practical results coincide. Source: True North Ideas summary (https://truenorthideas.org/the-constitution-of-liberty-hayeks-lessons-for-today-and-tomorrow/).

question: In 'The Constitution of Liberty,' Hayek does not claim people are always wise. He says a free society will make discoveries in law, science, and culture that a planned one never could. His whole case rests on one key claim about knowledge. Which one?
answer: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
choices: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
That elected representatives are systematically better informed than administrators
That most citizens correctly rank their long-term interests over short-term ones
That common law judges reason more reliably than legislators about complex trade-offs
context: Hayek's argument: freedom matters because we do not know in advance what discoveries a free society will make; only a free order can produce them, precisely because a planner would have to know them already to permit them. Source: Cato Institute Regulation review (https://www.cato.org/regulation/spring-2026/book-review-constitution-liberty).

question: At the very end of his 1960 book on liberty, Hayek rejects a political label that many readers had assumed applied to him. Instead he claims an older British label, the same one Edmund Burke had famously claimed for himself. What is the title of Hayek's closing chapter?
answer: Why I Am Not a Conservative
choices: Why I Am Not a Conservative
The Errors of Progressivism
The Old Whig's Defense
Beyond Left and Right
context: The postscript is titled 'Why I Am Not a Conservative.' Hayek identifies himself as an 'Old Whig,' the term Burke had used for himself. Source: Hayek, postscript, reprinted at Cato (https://www.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/articles/hayek-why-i-am-not-conservative.pdf).

question: In the 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' postscript to his 1960 book, Hayek explains why conservatism cannot be a genuine alternative to socialism. Conservatives, he says, want to keep things as they are; he himself wants to move somewhere. Which reasoning move against the conservative label is Hayek pressing?
answer: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
choices: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
That conservatism has always been captured by throne-and-altar aristocracy and cannot be democratized
That conservatism confuses the value of tradition with the value of the particular customs it inherits
That conservatism is incompatible with the constitutional limits on royal power the Whigs defended
context: Hayek: conservatives want to keep things as they are; he wants to move toward greater freedom -- so conservatism cannot be a real alternative to socialism, only a brake on it. Source: Hayek, 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' (https://soonersentinel.substack.com/p/fa-hayek-why-i-am-not-a-conservative).

question: In 1975 a new British political leader interrupted a speaker urging a 'middle way' between free markets and government planning. She pulled a thick book by an Austrian economist out of her bag, slammed it on the table, and said 'This is what we believe.' What was the core belief that book pressed?
answer: Individual liberty and free markets are what makes a free society possible
choices: Individual liberty and free markets are what makes a free society possible
The government should own every large business in the country
A single wise leader is the best long-term ruler for any country
Trade between countries always hurts the poorer country
context: The anecdote is told in John Ranelagh's 'Thatcher's People' (1991); the Margaret Thatcher Foundation itself calls it 'perhaps a little too perfect to be actually true,' so it should be treated as reported testimony rather than settled fact. Sources: Sotheby's essay (https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/this-is-what-we-believe-margaret-thatcher-and-f-a-hayek); Margaret Thatcher Foundation archive note.  (Legend.)

question: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation tells a famous story: in 1975 Thatcher slammed Hayek's book on a table and said 'this is what we believe.' But its own archive note calls the story 'perhaps a little too perfect to be actually true.' What rule about historical sources does that warning point to?
answer: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
choices: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
That John Ranelagh's 1991 book was later fully retracted by its publisher
That Margaret Thatcher denied the anecdote in her own memoirs
That Hayek himself in the 1980s explicitly denied ever meeting Thatcher
context: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation records the anecdote as beloved-of-biographers but cautions it may be too perfect to be true; Ranelagh 1991 is the source, not a contemporaneous document. Neither Thatcher's memoirs nor Hayek's biography retracts the story -- the Foundation simply flags it as unverified testimony. Source: Margaret Thatcher Foundation Hayek archive (https://www.margaretthatcher.org/archive/Hayek).  (Legend.)

question: In June 1775, the Second Continental Congress voted to fight Britain for American independence. But Congress had no power to tax the people — only the thirteen individual states could tax. To pay for soldiers, muskets, and gunpowder, Congress started printing a new paper money of its own that had nothing backing it but the promise of a future country. What was this Revolutionary-War paper money called?
answer: Continental currency
choices: Continental currency
The greenback
The Spanish milled dollar
The Massachusetts note
context: The June 22 1775 resolution authorized $2 million in bills of credit -- soon known as 'Continentals' -- to fund the Revolutionary War effort. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: During the Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the Continental Congress had no power to tax, so it paid for the war by printing paper money called Continentals — about $241 million in all. At the start of the war, the thirteen colonies together held only a much smaller stock of real gold and silver coins to back that paper. About how much?
answer: About $6 million
choices: About $6 million
About $80 million
About $200 million
About $600 million
context: Estimates of specie in the colonies at 1775 hover around $6 million. Printing $241 million against a $6 million specie base guaranteed collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: By the summer of 1781, one paper dollar printed by the Continental Congress to fund the Revolutionary War was worth about one cent in silver. By the end of that year, it was worthless — the printed paper had less value than firewood. A folk saying about worthless things came out of that collapse and stayed in common American English for a whole century. Which phrase?
answer: Not worth a Continental
choices: Not worth a Continental
Broke as a Yankee
Cheap as tobacco
Poor as a Whig
context: The phrase 'not worth a Continental' became the standard American idiom for anything valueless. Barbers reportedly papered their shops with unwanted Continentals as decoration. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: During the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the Continental Congress paid its soldiers in paper Continentals. As Congress kept printing more, each Continental bought less and less — the phrase 'not worth a Continental' entered American English. When the paper finally collapsed to near-zero value, one group was hit hardest. Who suffered most?
answer: Soldiers' families and small savers who held Continentals as savings
choices: Soldiers' families and small savers who held Continentals as savings
British creditors resident in London
Wealthy Philadelphia merchants
French officers on Rochambeau's staff
context: Soldiers who earned in Continentals watched the paper their families held evaporate. Farmers who accepted Continentals for grain became poor; those who insisted on gold were denounced as gougers. This asymmetric destruction became a Founding-era grievance. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: In 1777 and 1778, the Continental Congress watched its own paper money — the Continental — losing value fast as it printed more of it to fund the Revolutionary War. Instead of stopping the printing, Congress tried to force merchants and farmers to keep selling their goods at old, low prices. Anyone charging more could be punished by the local authorities. What are legal ceilings on prices and pay like these called?
answer: Wage and price controls
choices: Wage and price controls
Import quotas
Excise taxes
Legal-tender waivers
context: Congress and several state governments imposed wage and price controls in 1777-78, hoping to freeze the visible collapse. The controls were widely evaded and abandoned within about a year. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).
