context: Bruce Caldwell has argued textual evidence points to 'a product more of [Bartley's] pen than of Hayek's' -- so scholars should treat specific passages as uncertain while acknowledging the core argument (extended order, cultural evolution, fatal conceit) is unmistakably Hayek's mature synthesis. The book remains Volume 1 of the Collected Works. Source: Wikipedia; Alan Ebenstein biography review (https://www.independent.org/tir/2001-fall/friedrich-hayek/).

question: In December 1913 President Wilson signed the law creating a new US central bank two days before Christmas. What is that central bank called?
answer: The Federal Reserve
choices: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
The World Bank
The Mint
context: The Federal Reserve Act was signed on December 23, 1913, after most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/federal_reserve_act_signed.

question: In 1913, the US created its own central bank. It decides how much money exists and where interest rates go. What is this US central bank called?
answer: The Federal Reserve
choices: The Federal Reserve
The World Bank
The Treasury Department
The Bank of America
context: Wilson (Democrat, 28th president 1913-21) signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, ten months into his first term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: In 1913, the US Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act, creating a central bank system for America. To keep any single city — like New York — from hoarding all the banking power, the law spread the new central bank across the country. Each region got its own Reserve Bank branch. How many regional Reserve Banks did the Act create?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
One
Fifty
Six
context: Twelve regional Reserve Banks: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas, San Francisco. Each was owned by its member commercial banks, not by the federal government. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-banks.htm.

question: On December 23, 1913 President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act, creating a new central bank for the United States and ending decades of arguments over who should print American money. Only this new bank was allowed to issue the green paper bills that Americans still carry in their wallets today. What are those bills formally called?
answer: Federal Reserve Notes
choices: Federal Reserve Notes
Treasury Notes
United States Notes
National Bank Notes
context: The dollar bills in circulation are Federal Reserve Notes, backed by the Fed's assets rather than by gold. Before 1913, national banks issued their own notes backed by Treasury bonds. Source: federalreserve.gov/faqs/currency.htm.

question: In 1913, one congressman warned that the new Fed would become 'the invisible government by the money power.' What was he warning about?
answer: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
choices: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
That paper money would replace gold coins in daily use
That most private banks would go out of business quickly
That the federal government would soon take over all factories
context: Rep. Charles Lindbergh Sr. (R-MN) opposed the bill from the House floor in December 1913, warning it would create 'the most gigantic trust on earth'. His son the aviator was 11 years old at the time. Source: Congressional Record, House, December 22, 1913.

question: In November 1910, a handful of America's richest bankers boarded a private train down to Jekyll Island, Georgia, disguising themselves as duck hunters so no one would recognize them. In secret they drafted a plan for a giant new central bank that would lend emergency money to other banks. Three years later that plan became the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. What is the biggest worry with a plan made that way?
answer: The bank might quietly serve those few insiders more than ordinary people
choices: The bank might quietly serve those few insiders more than ordinary people
The bank cannot legally exist without a public vote first
The public will refuse to spend the new money at all
The bank will forget to hire anyone to run it
context: The Jekyll Island meeting (November 1910) at the private hunting club of J.P. Morgan and other Wall Street bankers produced the Aldrich Plan, whose essential mechanisms were adopted (with Democratic rebranding) as the Federal Reserve Act. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jekyll_Island.

question: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 became known by a short nickname taken from its two main sponsors in Congress: a Democratic senator from Oklahoma, and a Democratic House member from Virginia. Both had spent years arguing for a more elastic paper currency that could expand and contract with the needs of American businesses. What were their last names?
answer: Owen and Glass
choices: Owen and Glass
Aldrich and Vreeland
Sherman and McKinley
Bland and Allison
context: Senator Robert Owen (D-OK) chaired Senate Banking; Representative Carter Glass (D-VA) chaired House Banking. The Act is sometimes called the Owen-Glass Act. Glass later co-sponsored the 1933 Banking Act (Glass-Steagall). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, controls how much money is sloshing around in the American banking system. To add money it buys securities from banks, and to drain money it sells securities back to them. This buy-and-sell process is called open-market operations. Which single main type of security does the Fed use for it?
answer: Treasury securities
choices: Treasury securities
Corporate bonds
Mortgage-backed securities
Foreign-currency reserves
context: Open-market operations are the Fed's day-to-day tool: buying Treasuries adds reserves and pushes rates down; selling Treasuries drains reserves and pushes rates up. The NY Fed desk executes them. In 2008-09 the Fed extended purchases to mortgage-backed securities under emergency authority. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

question: On December 23, 1913, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act into law, creating America's central bank. December 23 is unusually late in the year for a major bill — most substantive laws are wrapped up earlier. Historians say the timing was chosen on purpose. What was the practical effect of scheduling the signing so close to Christmas?
answer: Most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays
choices: Most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays
The stock exchanges were closed for holiday trading
European banks could not open new gold accounts
The federal budget deadline forced an immediate signature
context: The Senate passed the bill December 19; the conference report was finalized December 22; Wilson signed December 23. Many members had already headed home. Critics like Lindbergh treated the timing as evidence that debate had been foreshortened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: President Woodrow Wilson, who had signed the 1913 Federal Reserve Act, died in 1924. A quotation began circulating decades later in which a dying Wilson supposedly regretted creating the Fed, saying he had 'unwittingly ruined my country.' Historians who later hunted for the source have found the sourcing shaky. Which statement best describes the actual documentary status of the quote?
answer: The 'unwittingly ruined my country' portion has no verified primary source and is likely apocryphal
choices: The 'unwittingly ruined my country' portion has no verified primary source and is likely apocryphal
The full quote is documented in Wilson's collected papers at Princeton
The quote was published in the New York Times the week Wilson died
The quote comes from Wilson's 1913 book 'The New Freedom'
context: Historians (including Wilson biographer John Milton Cooper) have been unable to locate the 'unwittingly ruined' language in Wilson's papers. A separate passage about 'the invisible government by the money power' is authentic and appears in Wilson's pre-signing 1913 book 'The New Freedom'. Honesty rail: cite only what is verifiable. Source: princeton.edu/~mudd (Wilson papers).

question: The 1913 law creating the Federal Reserve gave it no specific number goals -- only vague language about 'furnishing an elastic currency.' Congress did not add explicit goals until 1978. Which two goals did that later law tell the Fed to pursue at the same time?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Zero inflation and the abolition of paper money
Full public ownership of every commercial bank
A fixed exchange rate with the British pound
context: The 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act added the explicit dual-mandate language (maximum employment plus stable prices) to the Federal Reserve Act. Before 1978 the Fed's goals were essentially self-defined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey%E2%80%93Hawkins_Full_Employment_Act.

question: A 1978 US law gave the Fed two goals at once -- one about jobs and one about the value of the dollar. What is this pair usually called?
answer: The dual mandate
choices: The dual mandate
The single mandate
The gold anchor
The Bretton Woods rule
context: The Fed's 'dual mandate' is a shorthand for maximum employment plus stable prices, established by the Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm.

question: In 1978 the US Congress passed a law called the Humphrey-Hawkins Act that told the Federal Reserve — America's central bank — to do two things at once: keep prices steady, and keep as many people working as it can. What is one problem with giving a single group two big goals?
answer: The two goals can pull against each other, so the bank has to choose
choices: The two goals can pull against each other, so the bank has to choose
Neither goal really matters at all
One agency should have many more goals
The bank always ignores both goals
context: Full title: Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978; sponsors Senator Hubert Humphrey (D-MN) and Representative Augustus Hawkins (D-CA). Humphrey died in January 1978 and the Act was named in his honor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey%E2%80%93Hawkins_Full_Employment_Act.

question: The two policy goals assigned to the Fed by the 1978 law are usually stated as a pair. What are the two goals in the pair?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Maximum growth and low taxes
Trade balance and currency reserves
Balanced budget and low national debt
context: The Federal Reserve Act (as amended in 1978) directs the Fed to 'promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates'. The third goal is treated as derivative. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm.

question: The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, was told by a 1978 law to chase two goals at once: keep prices steady, and keep as many people employed as possible. When European countries set up the European Central Bank (ECB) in 1998 to run the new euro currency, they wrote its rulebook differently — one main goal only. What is that single goal?
answer: Keep prices steady
choices: Keep prices steady
Get everyone a job
Hold lots of gold
Grow the economy fast
context: Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union makes price stability the ECB's primary objective; other goals may be supported only 'without prejudice' to it. This single-mandate design was influenced by the German Bundesbank's inflation-fighting record. Source: ecb.europa.eu/mopo/intro/objective.

question: In 1967-68, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps showed that any long-run trade-off between inflation and jobs would break down. Once workers learn to expect higher prices, they adjust. Then in 1978 Congress passed the dual-mandate law. What was awkward about the timing?
answer: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
choices: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
The trade-off had just been confirmed by a decade of Keynesian success
The natural-rate concept had not yet been proposed
The Phillips curve was a brand-new discovery
context: By 1978 stagflation (simultaneous high inflation and unemployment) had made the naive Phillips-curve trade-off untenable. The dual mandate embedded the trade-off in statute at the very moment academic economics was walking away from it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: Austrian-school economists like Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises argued that a central bank asked to chase two goals at once — stable prices and high employment — will feel a steady political pull toward one side. Politicians, they said, see the goal that grabs voters at the ballot box. Which side does the Austrian critique say tends to win in practice?
answer: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
choices: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
The price side, because inflation directly hurts bond markets that lobby the Fed
Both sides equally, since the mandate is symmetric on paper
Neither side, since the Fed is technically independent of politics
context: The Austrian public-choice reading: unemployment produces immediate political pressure; a couple of extra points of inflation is diffuse and delayed. A Fed with both goals therefore leans easy over time, producing persistent low-grade inflation and asset-price booms. Source: mises.org/library/case-100-percent-gold-dollar.

question: The Federal Reserve — America's central bank — publicly aims for 2 percent yearly inflation. But 'inflation' can mean many things: housing prices, stock prices, the M2 money supply, or the price of the groceries a family actually buys. The Fed chose one specific consumer index and has steered policy by it since 2012. It excludes wild food and energy swings and reflects what US households really spend. Which measure does the Fed track for its 2 percent target?
answer: The core PCE price index
choices: The core PCE price index
The Case-Shiller housing price index
The S&P 500 total return
The M2 money supply
context: The Fed's 2% target is stated on core Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation. Austrian critics note that this leaves asset-price inflation (housing bubbles, stock booms) formally uncounted -- a lever the employment side of the mandate exploits. Source: federalreserve.gov/faqs/economy_14400.htm.

question: Through 2021, prices in America climbed fast — gasoline, groceries, rent. Fed Chair Jerome Powell repeatedly called this inflation 'transitory,' meaning it would soon pass on its own. It did not. In 2022 the Fed reversed course and hiked interest rates sharply. Austrian critics of the Fed's dual mandate — the legal job of fighting BOTH inflation AND unemployment — saw a pattern in the miss. What pattern did this show?
answer: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
choices: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
The unusually rapid market response to Fed guidance
The success of forward-guidance communication tools
The dominance of monetary versus fiscal policy in modern practice
context: Fed leadership held rates near zero through most of 2021 while inflation ran above 5 percent, using the labor-market recovery as reason to delay. When the pivot came in March 2022, the Fed had to tighten unusually fast. Austrians treat this as the mandate's incentive structure playing out on schedule. Source: federalreserve.gov press releases 2021-22.

question: Milton Friedman, the Chicago-school economist and Nobel laureate, spent decades arguing that the Federal Reserve should not sit in a room picking interest rates by hand. He wanted a mechanical rule — one simple number, held steady year after year, that the Fed could not override on a whim. What was Friedman's proposed rule?
answer: A constant money-supply growth rate
choices: A constant money-supply growth rate
A constant unemployment target
A constant real wage index
A constant nominal exchange rate
context: Friedman's 'k-percent rule' would have set money-supply growth at a low, constant percentage annually, removing Fed discretion over the employment-inflation trade-off entirely. Rothbard argued Friedman's rule was still fiat and preferred a gold-anchored money. Source: Friedman, A Program for Monetary Stability (1960).

question: The 1978 U.S. law that gave the Federal Reserve its 'dual mandate' -- maximum employment and stable prices -- was named after a senator who died before it passed. Austrian critics argue those two goals often clash directly. Which clash do they point to?
answer: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
choices: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
Lower taxes always cause both goals to fail together
Full employment automatically causes deflation, which raises prices
Stable prices are always achieved without any change in employment
context: Hubert Humphrey (D-MN, former Vice President under Johnson and 1968 Democratic presidential nominee) died January 13, 1978. Augustus Hawkins (D-CA), the House co-sponsor, lived until 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey.

question: In 1980 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book called Knowledge and Decisions. It took Friedrich Hayek's famous 1945 essay on how scattered pieces of knowledge get used in an economy, and stretched the idea far beyond markets. Three years later Hayek himself reviewed the book in Reason magazine. What did Hayek say about it?
answer: That it was the best book on general economics in years
choices: That it was the best book on general economics in years
That it restated his own argument and added nothing new
That its examples were American and would not travel
That it belonged to sociology rather than to economics
context: Hayek's 1983 Reason review said the book expanded admirably on his own concepts and made them clear to lay readers through real-world examples. Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) also took the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Thomas Sowell is an American economist at Stanford's Hoover Institution who has written about politics for over fifty years. He says that when people fight over one law after another — welfare rules, gun rules, tax rules, school rules — they are not really arguing about the laws. Deep down, he says, both sides hold two very different views of one thing. Different views of what?
answer: What human beings are capable of
choices: What human beings are capable of
Who ought to hold political power
How wealth ought to be divided up
Which rights the law must protect
context: Sowell's constrained vision treats human capacities as permanently limited by flaws, scarcity and incomplete knowledge, so every arrangement buys one thing by giving up another. The unconstrained vision treats those limits as artifacts of bad institutions that clear-sighted people could redesign away. Sowell's most quoted sentence belongs to the first: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell taught readers to ask five hard questions before believing any policy claim: 'Compared to what?', 'At what cost?', 'What hard evidence?', 'And then what?', and 'What do you mean?'. One newspaper column claims a new government program is working. Its whole proof is three heart-warming interviews with people who say the program changed their lives. No statistics, no comparison group, no numbers at all. Which of Sowell's five questions does that column beg?
answer: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
choices: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
context: Sowell's complaint in The Vision of the Anointed is that a claim gets accepted 'even though evidence is seldom asked or given'. Three people who feel helped tell you nothing about the people the programme missed, harmed, or would have helped anyway -- and those are the ones no reporter interviews.

question: The economist Thomas Sowell taught that any political claim should be pressed with five hard questions before you believe it. Picture a city that boasts its new housing program built 4,000 apartments and moved 4,000 families in. Every proud number counts what the program made. Not one number counts what it used up, or what it crowded out. Which of Sowell's five questions was skipped?
answer: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
choices: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: The money, the land, the timber and the builders' hours all had other employments, and those employments are now gone. Sowell's point is that a benefit figure standing alone is not analysis -- it is advertising. The cost is real whether or not anybody publishes it.

question: A writer lists real failures at a private insurer -- claims denied, customers stranded -- and says the state should take over. Sowell replies that the insurer is real, but the state in the writer's head is not. Which of Sowell's five questions is he pressing?
answer: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
choices: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
context: This is the move at the heart of Knowledge and Decisions: markets and governments are both ways of deciding, and both are staffed by real people with limited knowledge. Comparing a real market with an ideal government is not a comparison at all. Sowell's question does not settle who wins -- it insists that both contestants show up.

question: A state caps the rent a landlord may charge. In the first year the tenants in those flats pay less, exactly as promised, and the cap is declared a success on that evidence. Landlords, builders and would-be tenants have not yet had time to do anything about it. Which of Sowell's five questions has been skipped?
answer: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
choices: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
context: Applied Economics carries the subtitle Thinking Beyond Stage One for exactly this reason. A landlord who cannot raise the rent can still stop maintaining, convert the building, or sell it; a builder can put his capital somewhere else entirely. None of that shows up in year one, and all of it lands on the tenants the cap was written for.

question: The economist Thomas Sowell had a list of five questions to press against any political promise. Imagine a candidate promising to end homelessness for good, with zero downside for anyone. Sowell would say no such plan can exist — not because this one is flawed, but because of what policy always is: a choice among costs, never a free lunch. Which of his five questions does he press?
answer: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
choices: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' -- A Conflict of Visions (1987). The trade-off question is not the same as the cost question: cost asks what the resources gave up, trade-offs asks which problems you have agreed to accept in exchange for the ones you are removing. A programme with no downside is not a bargain a human being can strike.

question: Thomas Sowell's Applied Economics (2003) draws a line between the way a politician evaluates a policy and the way an economist does. His charge is not that politicians are stupid; it is that their analysis reliably halts at one particular point. Where does it halt?
answer: At the policy's first, immediate result
choices: At the policy's first, immediate result
At the point where the money runs out
At the next general election in the cycle
At the boundary of their own department
context: Hence the subtitle: Thinking Beyond Stage One. Sowell's chapters run housing, medical care, discrimination and national development through the later repercussions, which he says are often very different from the immediate effects and much longer lasting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: In 1945 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published a famous essay showing how market prices carry scattered knowledge from stranger to stranger — no one person has to know everything for the system to work. Thomas Sowell agreed with Hayek, then extended the idea. Sowell asked a further question about every institution he studied: markets, courts, firms, families, legislatures. What further question does he ask?
answer: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
choices: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
How each one distributes the gains among the people taking part
How much each one costs the taxpayer to administer in a year
How quickly each one can be replaced when the public turns on it
context: This is Sowell's extension of Hayek and the reason 'compared to what?' is an institutional question rather than a debating trick. A firm that misjudges its customers loses money and has to change; an agency that misjudges its clients may get a larger budget. Both make mistakes. What separates them is what happens next. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A government proposes to cancel all outstanding student debt. Thomas Sowell would grant that the first effect is exactly what its authors promise: today's borrowers stop owing. His fifth question asks what follows. Which second-round effect does it put first?
answer: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
choices: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
Banks tighten lending to every borrower who is not at a college
Graduates who repaid early petition Congress for equal treatment
States cut their own university funding by the amount forgiven
context: All four are second-round effects worth tracing; Sowell's question puts the incentive change first because it is the one that alters what people do from now on, rather than redistributing what has already happened. Note what the question does not do: it does not tell you the policy is wrong. It tells you which column of the ledger the proposal has left blank.

question: A student learns Sowell's five questions and runs them on rent control, tariffs and the minimum wage -- and ends up disagreeing with Sowell about all three. The questions have still done their work. What is it that the five questions actually deliver?
answer: An account of what a policy costs and causes, which you then weigh yourself
choices: An account of what a policy costs and causes, which you then weigh yourself
A ranking of policies from the most harmful down to the least harmful
A test that every sound policy passes and every unsound one fails
A method for predicting which policies a legislature will adopt
context: The five-question distillation -- trade-offs, at what cost, compared to what, what hard evidence, and then what happens -- is a reader's compression rather than a list Sowell packaged in one book; the questions appear across A Conflict of Visions, Knowledge and Decisions, The Vision of the Anointed, Applied Economics and dozens of columns. They yield a full account and no verdict. Two people can run all five honestly on the same policy and still weigh the answers differently, because what a society should trade for what is not an economic question.  (Legend.)

question: Inside the Federal Reserve, one committee votes to raise, lower, or hold the target interest rate. What four-letter name is that committee known by?
answer: FOMC
choices: FOMC
OCC
FDIC
CFPB
context: The Federal Open Market Committee sets the Fed funds rate target and directs open-market operations. Every 6-8 weeks its policy statement is the market-moving output. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The US central bank's rate-setting group holds a set number of regular meetings each year. About how many meetings does it hold?
answer: Eight
choices: Eight
Two
Twenty
Fifty
context: The FOMC meets eight times a year on a published calendar, roughly every 6-8 weeks. Each meeting yields a policy statement, a chair press conference, and minutes released three weeks later. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm.

question: The Federal Open Market Committee sets US interest rates. Its voters come from two Fed groups. How many voting seats are there at each meeting?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
Seven
Five
Nineteen
context: Twelve voting seats: seven Board of Governors members in Washington plus five regional Reserve Bank presidents. Nineteen officials attend and speak, but only twelve vote. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The Federal Reserve — America's central bank — has twelve regional banks scattered across the country, from Boston to San Francisco. Their presidents take turns voting on interest rates, but one regional bank is different: it holds a permanent vote at every single meeting of the rate-setting committee. It sits in the country's biggest money city, home to Wall Street and the New York Stock Exchange. Which city hosts this permanent-voting Fed bank?
answer: New York
choices: New York
Chicago
San Francisco
Dallas
context: The New York Reserve Bank president holds a permanent FOMC vote; the other 11 regional presidents rotate through four voting seats on annual cycles. NY's permanent seat dates to the 1913 founding when it was the largest district. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: The Federal Reserve — America's central bank — is run by a seven-member Board of Governors that sits in Washington DC. The President of the United States picks each Governor and the Senate approves them. To keep the Board out of daily politics and party swings, Congress in 1935 gave each Governor a single very long term — much longer than the President's own four-year term. How long is one Governor's term?
answer: Fourteen years
choices: Fourteen years
Four years
Six years
Life
context: Fourteen-year non-renewable terms are the longest fixed terms of any federal position other than Supreme Court justices (who have life tenure). The length is set by the Federal Reserve Act to insulate governors from short-term political pressure. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-board.htm.

question: A central banker has a habit. Every time stocks drop hard, he cuts rates to save the investors. After years of this, how do big investors act?
answer: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
choices: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
They stop investing entirely and buy only gold coins
They lend only to farmers and small shops
They demand higher interest rates on every loan
context: Greenspan chaired the Fed 1987-2006 across the Black Monday 1987 crash, the 1998 LTCM rescue, the 2000 dot-com bust and the 2004-06 rate cycle. His dominance of FOMC agenda-setting became a case study in chair-driven committee dynamics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan.

question: The Federal Reserve — America's central bank — does not personally set the interest rate on your mortgage, your credit card, or your savings account. Instead the Fed targets one single rate: the overnight rate that banks charge each other when they need to borrow reserves from one another for just a few hours. Moving that one rate ripples out through every other rate in the economy. What is this key rate called?
answer: The federal funds rate
choices: The federal funds rate
The mortgage rate
The credit card rate
The savings account rate
context: The FOMC votes a target range for the federal funds rate -- the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other. The New York Desk then conducts open-market operations to keep the effective rate in that range. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' makes a point Austrian critics apply to central banks that set rates. No group, however smart, can gather up the scattered facts held by billions of borrowers, savers, and firms. What is this move usually called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The free-rider problem
The principal-agent problem
The tragedy of the commons
context: Hayek argued that the price system distributes knowledge no central board could gather in time -- the 'knowledge problem'. Applied to the FOMC: twelve people cannot know the 'correct' interest rate for an economy of hundreds of millions. Source: Hayek, American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: The Federal Reserve has twelve regional banks — in New York, Chicago, San Francisco, Dallas, and eight other cities. Unlike the seven Governors in Washington, the twelve regional bank presidents are not picked by the President and are not approved by the Senate. Instead, the private commercial banks in each district have a hand in choosing them, through a special group of local directors set up under the 1913 Federal Reserve Act. Which group actually chooses each regional Fed president?
answer: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
choices: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
The Senate Banking Committee
The full Board of Governors alone
The President of the United States
context: Each regional bank has nine directors (three classes); the non-banker directors (Class B and C) select the regional president, with Board of Governors sign-off. There is no Senate confirmation. Public-choice critics call this a governance gap. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-banks.htm.

question: The Chair of the Federal Reserve — currently Jerome Powell — holds a press conference and issues a short written statement after every rate-setting meeting. Traders read these lines so closely that changing one word — say from 'patient' to 'measured' — can move billions of dollars in stocks and bonds within seconds. A whole profession of reporters and analysts has grown up around this word-by-word reading. What nickname do we give the people who do it?
answer: Fed watchers
choices: Fed watchers
Reserve auditors
Rate scouts
Balance-sheet analysts
context: 'Fed watcher' names an entire subprofession -- economists at investment banks, journalists at Bloomberg and Reuters, and think-tank analysts whose full-time job is reading FOMC statements, minutes, and chair speeches for subtle shifts. Adjective changes ('appropriate', 'patient', 'accommodative') routinely move markets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fedspeak.

question: For most of the 1800s, the United States had no central bank at all. President Andrew Jackson had killed the Second Bank of the United States in 1836. From then until Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913 — about 77 years — American banks operated with no central authority above them, printing their own state-chartered notes. What do economists call this period?
answer: The free-banking era
choices: The free-banking era
The gold-standard era
The Progressive Era
The Populist era
context: Roughly 1837-1863, the 'free-banking' period followed Jackson's veto of the Second Bank in 1832 and his refusal to renew its charter. State laws let anyone meeting capital rules charter a bank. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_banking.

question: Before the American Civil War, the United States had no single national dollar. Each state-chartered bank printed its own paper notes, and hundreds of different bills moved through the country. A shopkeeper in New York might be handed notes from a Georgia or Ohio bank he had never heard of. He needed to know whether that faraway bank was still open, and what its notes were really worth. What printed guide did he use?
answer: Printed banknote reporters
choices: Printed banknote reporters
Federal exchange rates
Treasury bulletins
Chamber-of-commerce circulars
context: Banknote reporters were subscription publications listing every known bank and the current discount at which its notes traded. A note from a distant bank might sell at 90 cents on the dollar; from a failed bank at zero. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_banking.

question: During the American Civil War of the 1860s, the Union government in the North needed enormous sums to pay for the fighting against the Confederacy. Congress passed the National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864, letting new federal banks print one uniform paper dollar backed by government war bonds. Before this, every state bank had printed its own private notes and no two looked alike. What problem did those laws mainly solve?
answer: The country had no single trusted paper currency
choices: The country had no single trusted paper currency
Banks charged too much interest on farm loans
Coins were being melted down for jewelry
Silver mines had run out of ore
context: The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 created federally-chartered national banks that could issue a uniform note backed by Treasury bonds held as reserves. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/national-banking-acts.

question: In 1865, right after the American Civil War, the US Congress wanted to kill off state-chartered bank paper notes and push every bank into the new National Banking system that President Lincoln and Treasury Secretary Salmon Chase had set up during the war. Congress did not ban the state notes outright. Instead it slapped a heavy tax on them — heavy enough that state-bank notes vanished within a couple of years. What was the tax rate?
answer: 10 percent
choices: 10 percent
1 percent
50 percent
3 percent
context: The 10 percent tax on state-bank notes made state-note issue commercially impossible. State banks that survived had to shift to deposit banking rather than note issue. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_bank.

question: Old American textbooks used to say the free-banking era — the years between the 1830s and the Civil War, when states let banks operate without a federal central bank overseeing them — was pure chaos, with failures everywhere. In 1983 the economists Arthur Rolnick and Warren Weber, working at the Minneapolis Federal Reserve, took a fresh look at the actual failure records. What did they find about bank failures in states with good free-banking rules?
answer: They were modest and comparable to later regulated eras
choices: They were modest and comparable to later regulated eras
They ran to five times later loss rates
They wiped out about half of all deposits nationally
They caused a permanent gold outflow
context: Rolnick and Weber studied bank failure rates and noteholder losses in the leading free-banking states (New York, Massachusetts) and found them modest. This is now standard revisionist scholarship. Source: minneapolisfed.org/research/qr/qr731.pdf.

question: The Bank of England was created in 1694 to help King William III borrow money for his long war against France. The First Bank of the United States was chartered in 1791 partly to fund debts left by the Revolutionary War. Time and again through history, long wars have pushed governments to create one big central banking system with a national currency. Why do wartime rulers push so hard for a central bank?
answer: To make it easier to borrow the huge sums a war costs
choices: To make it easier to borrow the huge sums a war costs
To lower the price of bread for city families
To prevent farmers from planting new crops
To force citizens to save more of their allowance
context: Salmon Chase (Treasury 1861-64, later Chief Justice of the United States) designed the National Banking system to help finance the Union war effort by creating a captive market for Treasury bonds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase.

question: In the 1800s some banks in Michigan and Indiana printed paper money that could, in theory, be swapped back for gold or silver coins — but only at the bank's redemption office. To dodge ever paying out, some banks hid those offices deep in remote woods where hardly any human could reach them. People joked that a certain wild forest creature was more common at the counter than customers were. What was the term for these banks?
answer: Wildcat bank
choices: Wildcat bank
Fly-by-night bank
Ghost bank
Backwoods trust
context: 'Wildcat bank' comes from the 1830s-40s midwestern banks whose redemption offices were placed in wooded locations far from ordinary commerce, on the theory that wildcats outnumbered actual noteholders. The colorful term outlived the era. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildcat_banking.

question: After the American Civil War, Congress built the National Banking system: uniform paper notes, federal charters, and reserve rules. But it deliberately left one crucial feature out, because critics feared it would concentrate too much power in one spot. When bank panics hit in 1873, 1893, and 1907, that missing feature became the main political argument for creating a permanent central bank — the Federal Reserve, born in 1913. What was missing from the National Banking system?
answer: A lender of last resort
choices: A lender of last resort
A gold standard
Uniform paper currency
Federal chartering of banks
context: National banks could issue a uniform currency but no institution stood ready to supply emergency liquidity in a panic. Every major panic (1873, 1893, 1907) had to be handled by ad-hoc private rescues, culminating in Morgan's 1907 intervention. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/national-banking-acts.

question: During the American Civil War of the 1860s, the US Treasury had to pay Union soldiers and buy weapons but did not have enough gold on hand to do it. So the Treasury printed a brand-new kind of paper money not backed by any metal at all — just by the federal government's promise. The ink on the back of the bill was bright green. What nickname did people give those notes?
answer: Greenbacks
choices: Greenbacks
Federal Reserve Notes
Silver Certificates
Continental dollars
context: Greenbacks were the fiat US Notes issued by the Treasury under the Legal Tender Acts starting 1862. They circulated at a discount to gold during the war and returned to par when convertibility was restored in 1879. They are distinct from national-bank notes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenback_(money).

question: In America's free-banking era, roughly 1837 to 1863, hundreds of state-chartered banks each printed their own paper notes with no federal regulator watching them. Note-holders still had to know which banks were sound. Merchants solved this without any government body by pricing risky banks' notes at a steep discount, and printed 'banknote reporters' listed the going rate. The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek would later point to setups like this as classic examples. What kind of solution was it?
answer: An emergent-order solution -- prices carrying reputational information
choices: An emergent-order solution -- prices carrying reputational information
A form of government price-fixing
A quota system administered by the Treasury
A gold-standard arbitrage arrangement
context: The Hayekian reading: the banknote-reporter system was a decentralized market for reputation and risk information; discount prices carried the signal. This is a small-scale example of the price-system-as-knowledge-aggregator that Hayek 1945 would later theorize. Source: minneapolisfed.org/research/qr/qr731.pdf.

question: In April 1947, right after World War II, most university professors around the world backed big government plans and central control. A small group led by the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek gathered at a Swiss mountain village called Mont Pelerin. They spoke up for individual freedom, private property, and free markets. What older intellectual tradition were they defending?
answer: Classical liberalism (limited government plus free markets)
choices: Classical liberalism (limited government plus free markets)
Socialism
Fascism
Anarchism
context: Hayek convened the founding conference of the Mont Pelerin Society, April 1-10, 1947, at the Hotel du Parc in the village of Mont Pelerin near Vevey. Mises, Friedman and Robbins were all in the room; Hayek organised it and served as the society's first president, 1947-1961. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'; Grokipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: The 1947 Swiss group almost named their new society after two 1800s liberal writers. Frank Knight called them 'two Catholic aristocrats.' Mises worried their old mistakes would stick to the group. So they used the village's name. Which two writers had been proposed?
answer: Lord Acton and Alexis de Tocqueville
choices: Lord Acton and Alexis de Tocqueville
Adam Smith and David Ricardo
John Stuart Mill and Herbert Spencer
Edmund Burke and Benjamin Constant
context: The group was to have been the Acton-Tocqueville Society. Knight's objection and Mises's carried the day, and the name of a Swiss hillside above Lake Geneva went instead onto the most influential classical-liberal association of the century. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society', citing Alan Ebenstein, Friedrich Hayek: A Biography (2014), ch. 18.

question: In April 1947, thirty-nine economists and thinkers gathered at a Swiss mountain hotel above the village of Mont Pelerin. Central planning was rising fast around the world — in Stalin's Soviet Union, in Mao's new China, and in the growing welfare states of Western Europe. The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek called the group together to defend one idea against that tide. Which idea?
answer: Free markets and individual liberty
choices: Free markets and individual liberty
Higher tariffs on all imports
A single world government
Strong labor unions everywhere
context: Friedman, born July 31, 1912, had joined the Chicago economics faculty in 1946 and was thirty-four at Mont Pelerin. He would serve as the society's president from 1970 to 1972 and win the Nobel Memorial Prize in 1976. Buchanan and Becker were later members and presidents; Samuelson never joined. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman'; Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: When the Mont Pelerin Society first met in April 1947, its thirty-nine members — including Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, and Milton Friedman — signed a Statement of Aims. Its opening lines warned that three things were disappearing across large parts of the Earth, swallowed by Communist and fascist states and by growing government planning in the West. Two of the three were personal liberty and voluntary teamwork. What was the third?
answer: Private property
choices: Private property
Freedom of religion
Representative government
The rule of law
context: The Statement of Aims warned that 'the central values of civilization are in danger,' naming individual liberty, human cooperation by voluntary agreement, and private property, 'together with the institutions necessary to maintain these.' It went on to blame a decline of belief in private property and the rule of law. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: The ten days at Mont Pelerin in 1947 came to 18,062.08 Swiss francs, and 93 per cent of that bill was settled not by the scholars, nor by their universities, nor by any of the American foundations that chipped in, but by one institution alone. What kind of institution paid the overwhelming share?
answer: A Swiss commercial bank
choices: A Swiss commercial bank
An American charitable foundation
A British government department
A Vatican educational trust
context: The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt -- today Credit Suisse -- paid 93 per cent of the conference costs. Smaller sums came from the William Volker Fund via Harold Luhnow, from the Bank of England via Alfred Suenson-Taylor, and from the Foundation for Economic Education. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society', citing Mirowski and Plehwe (2009), p. 15.

question: In 1950 Friedrich Hayek left the London School of Economics for the University of Chicago, where Milton Friedman had been teaching since 1946. For the twelve years that followed the two men worked on the same campus -- yet Hayek never held a post in Friedman's department. Where at Chicago was Hayek appointed?
answer: The Committee on Social Thought
choices: The Committee on Social Thought
The Law School faculty
The Graduate School of Business
The Department of Philosophy
context: Hayek was Professor of Social and Moral Science on the Committee on Social Thought from 1950 to 1962 -- an interdisciplinary body, not the Economics Department -- and his salary was funded in part by outside grants including the Volker Fund. Aaron Director, another Mont Pelerin founder, was the one at the Law School. Source: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: In his 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics,' the Chicago economist Milton Friedman argued that a theory should be judged only by whether its predictions come true — even if its starting assumptions look completely fake or unrealistic. The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek refused to accept that test for economics. What was Hayek's main objection?
answer: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
choices: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
That predictions in economics can never be made short-run enough
That an economist's assumptions matter more than any test can show
That economics should be studied as a branch of law and history
context: Hayek attacked what he called scientism in The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) and returned to it in his 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretence of Knowledge': an economics that counts only what it can count will quietly drop the dispersed, local, tacit knowledge that makes markets work at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Milton Friedman wrote the introduction to the fiftieth-anniversary edition of Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom, and admired the man for half a century. On one piece of Hayek's economics he was blunt to the point of rudeness, and said so in print more than once. Which part of Hayek's work did Friedman call false?
answer: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
choices: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
Hayek's account of how prices carry information
Hayek's account of how legal rules evolve
Hayek's account of how planning erodes liberty
context: 'The Hayek-Mises explanation of the business cycle is contradicted by the evidence. It is, I believe, false.' Friedman first pressed the objection in a 1964 NBER article and again in Economic Inquiry in 1993, examining U.S. cycles from 1879 to 1988 and finding no significant link between the length of an expansion and the severity of the contraction after it. Source: Mark Skousen, 'Economics on Trial', The Freeman (FEE), March 1, 1995.

question: Both men wanted money taken out of politicians' hands, and each published an answer. Milton Friedman's, set out in 1959, was a rule for the central bank: raise the money supply by a fixed few per cent a year and stop meddling. Friedrich Hayek's answer of 1976 was more radical still. What did Hayek propose?
answer: Letting private banks compete to issue currencies
choices: Letting private banks compete to issue currencies
Fixing the currency's value to a basket of goods
Returning the currency to a gold coin standard
Handing note issue to an international authority
context: Friedman's k-percent rule appeared in A Program for Monetary Stability (1959): fix money growth at roughly 3 to 5 per cent a year. Hayek's Denationalisation of Money (1976) would not tie the monopoly down but abolish it, letting users walk away from any currency being debased. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman'; Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: In 1974 the economics Nobel committee gave one prize to a thinker who argued central planning could never work, and split it with a thinker who had spent his career arguing for planning. What does that shared award show about the state of the field at that time?
answer: Serious economists still disagreed at the deepest level about whether planning was possible
choices: Serious economists still disagreed at the deepest level about whether planning was possible
Every top economist had come to agree that planning worked well
Every top economist had come to agree that planning could never work
The committee refused to pick a side because the two men were personal friends
context: The 1974 prize went jointly to Hayek and the Swedish social-democrat Gunnar Myrdal 'for their pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations and for their penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena.' Tinbergen won in 1969, Kuznets in 1971, Leontief in 1973. Eight Mont Pelerin members have taken the prize in all: Hayek, Friedman, Stigler, Allais, Buchanan, Coase, Becker and Vernon Smith. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: On January 3, 2009, a person named Satoshi Nakamoto mined the very first Bitcoin block on his own computer. What is that first block called?
answer: the genesis block
choices: the genesis block
the coinbase block
the halving block
the segwit block
context: The first block is 'the genesis block' or 'Block 0'; it was mined January 3, 2009. 'Coinbase' names the special transaction inside each block that mints new coins to the miner; the halving is a recurring reward-cut event; SegWit was a 2017 protocol upgrade. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: On January 3, 2009, a programmer using the name Satoshi Nakamoto mined the very first block of Bitcoin — the genesis block. It paid a 50-coin reward to the address written into the software. Due to a quirk in the very first version of Bitcoin's code, those 50 coins have a strange fate that separates them from every other reward mined since. What can never happen to them?
answer: it can never be spent or moved to another address
choices: it can never be spent or moved to another address
it can never be seen by other nodes
it can never be used as a mining reward
it can never be counted in the total supply
context: By a quirk of the original code, the genesis-block coinbase output was written such that it is unspendable -- the 50 BTC exists in the chain but can never be moved. Every full node sees it; miners still get later rewards; supply totals do include it. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: On January 3, 2009, an anonymous coder using the name Satoshi Nakamoto mined the very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, called the genesis block. Inside that block's coinbase transaction — the birth record of the whole chain — Satoshi hid a short line of text that served no technical purpose whatsoever. It was a message meant to be read by whoever came looking. What did that message quote?
answer: a January 3, 2009 headline from The Times of London
choices: a January 3, 2009 headline from The Times of London
a Bible verse from the book of Revelation
a passage from Ayn Rand's Atlas Shrugged
Ludwig von Mises's 1920 socialism-calculation essay
context: The embedded text reads 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' -- the actual front-page headline of the London Times that day. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: On January 3, 2009, the anonymous creator of Bitcoin — known only as Satoshi Nakamoto — mined the very first block of the new currency. Into that block Satoshi permanently embedded a real newspaper headline from The Times of London printed that same day. He wanted the world to see why he had built a currency no government could inflate. What did the headline talk about?
answer: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
choices: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates
the European Central Bank launching the euro
the Bank of Japan announcing quantitative easing
context: The Times, January 3, 2009 front page: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' referred to Alistair Darling, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, preparing to rescue major British banks a second time following the 2008 financial crisis. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Times archive.

question: The Times headline Satoshi embedded in the genesis block was doing two jobs at once. The first was cryptographic: because the block hash includes that text, the block could not possibly have been mined earlier than the day the headline was printed. What was that first function called?
answer: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
choices: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
an encryption key preventing later modification
a mining-difficulty target for Block 1
a signature identifying Satoshi's private key
context: Including a January 3, 2009 headline proves the block could not have been mined earlier -- the same trick newspaper hostages hold up dated papers to prove the video is current. The Bitcoin protocol has separate difficulty and signature machinery. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: When Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's very first block in January 2009, he embedded a headline from The Times of London: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.' The headline did two jobs at once. One was to prove the block was mined that very day, not earlier. The other was purely political — a message about what Bitcoin was fighting against. What stance does the community read into that choice?
answer: a direct protest against the 2008-09 bank-bailout culture
choices: a direct protest against the 2008-09 bank-bailout culture
a celebration of British monetary tradition
a warning about Chinese currency manipulation
an endorsement of European monetary union
context: The headline referenced a second bailout of failing UK banks weeks after the first; embedding it in Bitcoin's founding block was widely read as naming the political enemy: a monetary system in which banks fail and the state prints to rescue them. The other options are not supported by the text. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: The anonymous coder Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's genesis block on January 3, 2009. But he did not immediately mine block 1 right after. He paused first — presumably to be sure his new software actually worked correctly on a live network before letting the chain grow past a single block. Roughly how long was the gap before Block 1 appeared?
answer: about six days
choices: about six days
about six hours
about six weeks
about six minutes
context: Block 0 was mined January 3, 2009; Block 1 was mined January 9, 2009 -- a gap of about six days. From that point on, blocks arrived on roughly the ten-minute schedule that has held ever since. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Bitcoin block chain.

question: No modern government currency before Bitcoin was launched with a news headline about the ruling class baked permanently into it. When Satoshi Nakamoto embedded The Times of London's January 2009 bailout headline into Bitcoin's very first block, forever, Bitcoin writers began comparing that gesture to one famous kind of document. Which comparison do they use most?
answer: a declaration of independence naming the adversary in one sentence
choices: a declaration of independence naming the adversary in one sentence
a corporate mission statement filed with regulators
a monetary policy target set by a central bank
an academic dedication to a favorite teacher
context: The comparison in the Bitcoin literature (Ammous, Antonopoulos, Song, others) is to a declaration of independence: an act that both timestamps itself and names its adversary explicitly. No corporate filing, central-bank target, or academic dedication had ever served that purpose in a monetary system. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) chapter on Bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin's very first block, mined by Satoshi Nakamoto on January 3, 2009, paid its miner the standard block reward of 50 bitcoins. But because of a small quirk in Satoshi's original code, those particular 50 coins were never entered into the spendable ledger the way normal block rewards are. They can never be moved by anyone, ever. What effect does that have on how many bitcoins will ever really circulate?
answer: Fifty coins are permanently locked out of the circulating supply
choices: Fifty coins are permanently locked out of the circulating supply
The next block's reward is doubled to make up for it
The first supply halving is delayed by 210,000 blocks
The overall 21-million cap is lowered by 50 coins
context: The 50 BTC of the genesis reward can never be moved, so the coins nominally exist in the chain but can never enter circulation. The supply cap arithmetic is not adjusted (21M is a mathematical limit from halving geometry); block-reward and halving schedule are unchanged. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Austrian-school writers — economists in the tradition of Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek — often treat Bitcoin as a major monetary invention. When they analyze the Times of London bailout headline that Satoshi Nakamoto embedded permanently in Bitcoin's very first block, they press one particular point about what it signals. It says Bitcoin can do something no government-issued fiat money can. Which move does the argument make?
answer: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule at issuance and refuse the political discretion to rescue any subsequent bank failure
choices: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule at issuance and refuse the political discretion to rescue any subsequent bank failure
That a monetary system can be democratically voted into and out of existence each cycle
That a monetary system's founder must remain publicly known to legitimize it
That a monetary system requires state backing to be trusted
context: The genesis-headline argument (Ammous, Song, Antonopoulos) is a rules-vs-discretion move: Bitcoin binds itself at issuance to a fixed schedule with no bailout discretion. Democratic overturning, publicly-known founder, and state backing are precisely what Bitcoin does NOT rely on. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Between 1958 and 1962 the Chinese communist leader Mao Zedong ordered a national program he called the Great Leap Forward. Every family farm in China was forced to join a giant government-run collective farm. Peasants were pulled away from planting rice and grain and ordered to melt down their own tools to make cheap iron in their backyards. In just four years, about 30 million Chinese people starved to death. What was the main cause of that famine?
answer: Farmers were forced off their own plots and had no reason to work hard
choices: Farmers were forced off their own plots and had no reason to work hard
A hurricane wiped out the harvest three years in a row
Foreign countries blocked all food imports
A new plant disease killed most of the rice
context: The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) was Mao's attempt to overtake Britain in steel output within 15 years through people's communes and backyard industrial furnaces. It produced the deadliest famine in history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward.

question: The Great Leap Forward pushed rural Chinese families into huge farming groups. Each group held thousands of households. What were the groups called?
answer: People's communes
choices: People's communes
Village councils
Farm brigades
Rural collectives
context: People's communes of 5,000 households or more replaced smaller cooperatives in 1958. Private plots, tools, and cookware were absorbed. The commune was both economic unit and local government. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_commune.

question: From 1958 to 1962, Mao Zedong pushed China through the Great Leap Forward — a five-year sprint to overtake Britain in steel production. The industrial side of the plan asked ordinary peasants to melt down their own cookware, farm tools, and door hinges in tiny village kilns to meet local steel quotas. Almost none of the metal came out usable. What were those village-scale kilns called?
answer: Backyard steel furnaces
choices: Backyard steel furnaces
Rural blast plants
Village steel mills
Communal foundries
context: Backyard furnaces (tulufeng) produced mostly unusable pig iron. The destruction of farm implements happened exactly as collectives needed them for the harvest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward.

question: During China's Great Leap Forward, launched in 1958 by Chairman Mao Zedong, farmers were ordered to plant seeds crammed close together and plow the soil super deep. Mao trusted the Soviet scientist Trofim Lysenko, who had claimed these methods would boost harvests to record levels. Lysenko's ideas were pseudoscience, not real biology — and in Mao's China no one dared say so publicly. What happened to the harvest?
answer: It collapsed, and tens of millions starved
choices: It collapsed, and tens of millions starved
It doubled, feeding the whole country
It stayed the same as before
It grew slowly for a decade
context: Lysenko's rejection of Mendelian genetics had been imposed on Soviet agriculture by Stalin. Chinese agriculture adopted Lysenkoist close-planting and deep-plowing techniques during the Great Leap, with disastrous results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysenkoism.

question: During Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward in China (1958-1962), local commune leaders were terrified of being punished if they missed harvest quotas. So they lied and reported far more grain than the fields had actually produced. Beijing believed the paper numbers. What did the Chinese state do with all this pretend 'extra' grain that existed only in the reports?
answer: Exported it to earn foreign currency
choices: Exported it to earn foreign currency
Stored it in national reserves
Distributed it back to the communes
Fed it to livestock
context: Beijing exported grain based on the inflated commune reports, drawing on 'reserves' that did not exist. This continued as village granaries emptied and peasants starved. Source: Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (2008).

question: In 1959, during Chairman Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward in China, one of Mao's own top generals — Peng Dehuai — wrote him a private letter admitting the giant farm-reorganization plan was failing and Chinese peasants were starving in huge numbers. In a one-party state, where no one is allowed to publicly challenge the ruler, what usually happens to that critic?
answer: He is punished, purged, or silenced
choices: He is punished, purged, or silenced
He is promoted for his honesty
He is asked to redesign the plan himself
He is given a raise and a public medal
context: Peng Dehuai's private letter at Lushan warned of the campaign's failure. Mao circulated it publicly, had Peng denounced and purged; Peng was later beaten to death during the Cultural Revolution. The moment Mao chose to defend the campaign over fixing it cost tens of millions more deaths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Dehuai.

question: The Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng spent years secretly reading local Chinese Communist Party archives, county by county, to count the dead from the Great Leap Forward famine of 1958-62. His book Tombstone became the most-cited modern estimate outside of the Chinese government's own tally. About how many people died in that famine?
answer: About 36 million
choices: About 36 million
About 3 million
About 300,000
About 300 million
context: Yang Jisheng's Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962 was first published in Hong Kong in 2008; the English edition (FSG) appeared in 2012. Yang was a longtime Xinhua journalist who accessed provincial archives across China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tombstone_(book).

question: The Dutch-born historian Frank Dikötter spent years reading local Communist Party archives inside China that had only just been opened to outside researchers. In his 2010 book 'Mao's Great Famine', he argued that deaths from Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward (1958-1962) reached about 45 million people. Why do modern historians now say the toll was far higher than earlier Cold War guesses?
answer: Local Communist Party archives, once opened, showed the true numbers were hidden for decades
choices: Local Communist Party archives, once opened, showed the true numbers were hidden for decades
Foreign newspapers of the 1960s already listed exact death numbers
Chinese families had to report every death to Beijing while it happened
The World Health Organization ran the Chinese census in 1960
context: Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine (Bloomsbury, 2010) drew on party archives to argue for a 45-million total. It won the Samuel Johnson Prize for non-fiction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao%27s_Great_Famine.

question: The Great Leap Forward was Mao Zedong's disastrous 1958-1962 push to leap China into industrial socialism. Grain requisitions, forced communes, and fake harvest reports triggered the deadliest famine in human history. Different demographic methods give different totals, but modern scholarly studies — by Yang Jisheng, Frank Dikötter, and others — cluster in one broad range. What is the standard scholarly range for excess deaths?
answer: About 15 to 45 million
choices: About 15 to 45 million
About 1.5 to 4.5 million
About 150 to 450 million
context: Yang Jisheng estimates ~36 million; Dikotter ~45 million; Jasper Becker's Hungry Ghosts (1996) synthesized earlier work in a 15-30 million range. The lower bound is ~15M, the upper ~45M. Source: aggregation of Yang, Dikotter, Becker.

question: In 1920 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published an essay arguing that a socialist economy could not calculate rationally: without private property in the means of production, there are no real market prices, so planners have no way to know which uses of steel or grain are wasteful. For Mises's calculation argument, Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward in China (1958-1962) is the largest single vindication in history. What mechanism did it demonstrate?
answer: Without market prices there was no signal that the commune grain reports were fantasy until the granaries were empty
choices: Without market prices there was no signal that the commune grain reports were fantasy until the granaries were empty
Without market prices industrial planning was more efficient than under capitalism
Without market prices agricultural output naturally rose
Without market prices international trade solved local shortages
context: Mises's 1920 argument at the largest possible scale: no market prices meant no way to correct commune-level lies about production before the empty stomachs did the correcting. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: In communist China, Chairman Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward -- his 1958 push to rush the country into modern industry overnight -- ended in mass famine and collapse. Party leaders formally shut it down in January 1961. Two more moderate men then ran a partial retreat from 1961 to 1965, letting peasants sell some crops and reopening small markets to feed the country. Mao would answer them five years later by unleashing the Cultural Revolution to purge them. Who were the two men who ran that retreat?
answer: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping
choices: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping
Zhou Enlai and Chen Yun
Lin Biao and Kang Sheng
Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao
context: Liu Shaoqi (as state president) and Deng Xiaoping led the 1961-65 recovery, restoring some private plots and market allocation. Mao's answer was the 1966 Cultural Revolution, which purged both. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931976).

question: In 1937 and 1938 the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin ordered his secret police to arrest and shoot huge numbers of his own people. Even loyal party members, army generals, and factory bosses were killed. Historians now call this the Great Terror. What is a sudden mass roundup and killing of your own people by their own government called?
answer: A purge
choices: A purge
A protest
A recall election
A boycott
context: The Great Terror (Bolshoy terror), July 1937 - November 1938, executed about 750,000 people in 18 months. Also called the Yezhovshchina after NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge.

question: In the Soviet Union in the 1930s, dictator Joseph Stalin ran a special police force called the NKVD. Its agents could pound on a family's door in the middle of the night, drag someone away, and hold them for months with no trial. Then they shipped the prisoner to a work camp in freezing Siberia. What do we call a police force like this -- one that answers only to the ruler, not to any court?
answer: Secret police
choices: Secret police
Traffic police
Court bailiffs
Border guards
context: Nikolai Yezhov ran the NKVD 1936-38. He was replaced by Lavrentiy Beria in November 1938, arrested in April 1939, and shot on February 4, 1940. His name was erased from photographs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Yezhov.

question: In 1937 the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin's secret police -- the NKVD -- sent a secret order to every local office in the country. The order told each office an exact number of people it had to shoot and an exact number to ship to labor camps. Local police then rounded up whoever was handy to fill their numbers. What kind of instruction is that?
answer: A quota to fill, whether or not people were guilty
choices: A quota to fill, whether or not people were guilty
A budget to spend on new prisons
A list of specific traitors caught in the act
A cap on how many arrests they were allowed
context: NKVD Order 00447 (July 30, 1937) established 'first category' (execution) and 'second category' (10-year camp) quotas by region. Local officers were rewarded for exceeding the quota. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NKVD_Order_No._00447.

question: During the Soviet Great Terror of 1937 and 1938, the secret police carried out mass shootings for about 18 months. When Soviet archives opened after 1991, historians got a firm figure. Roughly how many people did the secret police shoot in that year and a half?
answer: About 750,000
choices: About 750,000
About 75,000
About 7,500
About 7.5 million
context: About 750,000 shot -- roughly 1,000 per day for 18 months. About 1.5 million total were arrested. Figures are from opened NKVD archives after 1991. Source: memo.ru (Memorial archives).

question: Time and again, after a revolution wins, the new dictator turns on the very friends who helped him seize power. Joseph Stalin shot most of Lenin's old Bolshevik comrades in the 1930s. Mao Zedong purged the men who had marched with him on the Long March. Robespierre sent his fellow French revolutionaries to the guillotine in 1794. Why does the new ruler keep doing this to his oldest allies?
answer: They know his weaknesses and might replace him
choices: They know his weaknesses and might replace him
They refuse to eat the same food as the workers
They lost too many chess matches at the palace
They are the only ones who can read foreign languages
context: Bukharin was tried in the March 1938 Trial of the Twenty-One and shot. He had been Lenin's designated 'darling of the party'. Trotsky had already been exiled (1929) and was assassinated in Mexico in 1940. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_the_Twenty-One.

question: In 1968 the British historian Robert Conquest published a book called 'The Great Terror,' showing that Joseph Stalin's Soviet regime had killed millions of its own people in the 1930s. Many Western professors mocked the book and defended the Soviet record. When the Soviet archives finally opened after 1991, they proved Conquest right down to the numbers. Why do some scholars fight bad news about a system they like?
answer: They are more loyal to the theory than to the facts
choices: They are more loyal to the theory than to the facts
They cannot read documents written in foreign languages
The archives were sealed by an international law
The evidence had not been discovered anywhere on earth
context: Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (Macmillan, 1968) was the pioneering account. A 1990 revised edition (Oxford UP) folded in the archival numbers. Conquest reportedly suggested titling the new edition 'I Told You So, You Fucking Fools'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Conquest.

question: In 1937 and 1938, Joseph Stalin launched what historians now call the Great Terror. He accused his own senior Red Army officers of secretly plotting with Nazi Germany and put them on trial. The purge tore through every level from marshal down to colonel and broke the Soviet military just before World War II began. Stalin had five top Marshals of the Soviet Union at the start. How many of those five were killed?
answer: Three of five
choices: Three of five
One of five
All five
None
context: Three of five marshals (Tukhachevsky, Blyukher, Yegorov) were shot; also 13 of 15 army commanders, 8 of 9 fleet admirals, and roughly half the officer corps. The Red Army was still recovering when Germany invaded in June 1941. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_of_Trotskyist_Anti-Soviet_Military_Organization.

question: In the Soviet Union during the late 1930s, the head of the secret police who ran the mass arrests and shootings was himself executed by his replacement soon after. This pattern repeated with each new chief. What lesson does this teach about a totalitarian regime?
answer: Even the enforcers get killed once their work is done, so no one is ever safe
choices: Even the enforcers get killed once their work is done, so no one is ever safe
Secret police chiefs almost always retired peacefully
The regime rewarded its most loyal servants for life
Only ordinary citizens were ever in danger under the terror
context: Beria replaced Yezhov in November 1938 and ran the NKVD (later MVD) through Stalin's death in 1953. Beria himself was arrested and shot in December 1953. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria.
