question: During Joseph Stalin's Great Terror in the late 1930s, whole ethnic communities living near the Soviet Union's borders -- Poles, Koreans, Germans, and Finns -- were arrested wholesale and either shot or deported as suspected foreign spies. Nobody had to have done anything wrong; sharing an ancestry with a neighboring country was enough. What does this pattern show about how sweeping communist state terror could get?
answer: It could target people just for who their grandparents were, not for anything they had done
choices: It could target people just for who their grandparents were, not for anything they had done
It only ever punished people who committed real crimes
It applied the same standard of evidence as an ordinary court
It never touched families of ordinary factory workers
context: NKVD Order 00485 (August 11, 1937) targeted ethnic Poles across the USSR. About 111,000 were shot in the Polish Operation. Similar orders targeted Germans, Latvians, Greeks, and other border-nation communities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Operation_of_the_NKVD.

question: The American historian Timothy Snyder's 2010 book 'Bloodlands' studies Joseph Stalin's and Adolf Hitler's mass killings side by side. The same stretch of Eastern Europe -- Ukraine, Belarus, and Poland -- was crushed first by Soviet communism and then by Nazi Germany between 1933 and 1945. Together the two regimes killed around 14 million civilians there, one after the other. What does looking at both death tolls together show?
answer: Two very different ideologies can produce a similar scale of slaughter of ordinary people
choices: Two very different ideologies can produce a similar scale of slaughter of ordinary people
The two regimes always cooperated as friendly allies
Only one of the two regimes actually killed civilians
Civilian deaths were rare in that region during those years
context: Bloodlands: Europe Between Hitler and Stalin (Basic Books, 2010) covers the 14 million civilians deliberately killed in the region between 1933 and 1945. It won the 2013 Hannah Arendt Prize. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodlands.

question: Bitcoin was invented by an anonymous programmer using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. He switched the network on for the first time on January 3, 2009, in a block called the genesis block. Every time a miner solved the network's puzzle and added a new block of transactions, the code paid the miner a fixed number of brand-new bitcoins as a reward. How many bitcoins did that very first block reward pay?
answer: 50 BTC
choices: 50 BTC
25 BTC
6.25 BTC
1 BTC
context: The initial block reward was 50 BTC per block. 25 BTC was the reward after the first halving in 2012; 6.25 BTC applied 2020-24; 1 BTC has never been a block-reward value. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: In 2009 the anonymous programmer Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin. He wrote a rule right into the code: miners earn new bitcoins as a reward for each block of transactions they secure, but every 210,000 blocks -- about every four years -- that reward is automatically cut in half. Bitcoin fans have a short name for this scheduled event. What do they call it?
answer: the halving
choices: the halving
the fork
the airdrop
the burn
context: 'The halving' (early forum slang 'halvening') is the scheduled event that cuts the block reward in half. A fork is a protocol change or chain split; an airdrop is a token giveaway on other networks; a burn is destroying tokens by sending them to an unspendable address. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by an anonymous inventor calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto. He built the schedule of new coins into the software itself, not on any calendar. A 'halving' event cuts the mining reward in half after a set number of blocks have been mined. Since blocks come about every ten minutes, that works out to roughly one halving every four years. How many blocks pass between halvings?
answer: 210,000 blocks
choices: 210,000 blocks
21,000 blocks
1,000,000 blocks
50,400 blocks
context: The halving happens every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years at ~10-minute block times). Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin was designed in 2008 by an anonymous inventor named Satoshi Nakamoto so that the reward miners earn for adding a new block gets cut in half about every four years. This event is called a halving. The very first Bitcoin halving happened in November 2012. Before it, each mined block paid the miner 50 new bitcoins. After the halving, how many bitcoins did each block pay?
answer: 25 bitcoins
choices: 25 bitcoins
10 bitcoins
5 bitcoins
Zero bitcoins
context: The first halving cut the reward from 50 BTC to 25 BTC in November 2012. The second (25 -> 12.5) came July 2016; the third (12.5 -> 6.25) May 2020; the fourth (6.25 -> 3.125) April 2024. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by an anonymous inventor named Satoshi Nakamoto. He designed it so only 21 million coins will ever exist. Every four years or so, the reward miners get for adding new coins is cut in half -- this is called a halving. Eventually the reward will fall all the way to zero, and no more new coins will ever be created. What is the main point of this shrinking reward?
answer: To keep new supply scarce and predictable forever
choices: To keep new supply scarce and predictable forever
To force miners to give up and go home
To make each transaction cost more to send
To let the government print extra coins later
context: The April 2024 halving cut the reward to 3.125 BTC per block. The 2028 halving is expected to cut it to 1.5625 BTC. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin is a digital money invented in 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto. Its rules give miners new coins as a reward for adding blocks, but every four years that reward is cut in half — an event called a 'halving.' Because each halving shrinks the payout, the total coins ever created add up to one fixed limit written into the code from day one. What is Bitcoin's final total cap?
answer: 21 million bitcoins
choices: 21 million bitcoins
100 million bitcoins
1 billion bitcoins
210 million bitcoins
context: The geometric halving series sums to 21 million BTC -- the fixed hard cap, expected to be effectively reached around 2140. After that miners earn only transaction fees, not new coins. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by an anonymous programmer known only as Satoshi Nakamoto. A whole bitcoin can be split into one hundred million tiny units, and those tiny units were named in his honor so his contribution would live on inside the currency. What is this smallest denomination called?
answer: a satoshi
choices: a satoshi
a bit
a wei
a millibit
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC (10^-8 BTC), named for Satoshi Nakamoto. 'Bit' and 'millibit' are informal larger sub-units (1 bit = 100 satoshis); 'wei' is Ethereum's smallest unit, named for cypherpunk Wei Dai, not a Bitcoin unit. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Units.

question: Bitcoin was designed by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2009 with a hard supply cap of 21 million coins. Every 210,000 blocks the mining reward is cut in half, and this halving pattern shrinks toward zero on a mathematical curve set by the code itself -- no committee or vote can change it. Following that curve, around what year will the very last new bitcoin be mined?
answer: around 2140
choices: around 2140
around 2050
around 2200
around 2028
context: The geometric issuance schedule -- 50 -> 25 -> 12.5 -> ... -- exhausts at approximately the year 2140 assuming the ~10-minute average block time holds. From that point on miners are compensated only by transaction fees. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: The American economist Milton Friedman argued for decades that if a country's money supply grows faster than its goods do, prices must rise -- this is his monetarist line on inflation. When Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin in 2009, he built in a hard cap of 21 million coins as the sharpest possible reply to Friedman: money that literally cannot expand no matter what. What property of Bitcoin's 21-million cap makes it different from every past money system?
answer: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
choices: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
the cap doubles automatically whenever the block-time drifts
the cap adjusts based on global GDP growth
the cap is set by an annual vote of Bitcoin holders
context: The 21M cap is enforced by every node's software; raising it would require every user to accept a protocol change that would fork Bitcoin. It cannot be adjusted for GDP, drift, or voter preference. Every fiat central bank has discretion to expand; Bitcoin has none. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Austrian-school economists like Friedrich Hayek celebrate Bitcoin's fixed 21-million-coin cap as its greatest strength, echoing Milton Friedman's warning that unlimited money causes inflation. Keynesian economists disagree; they see the very same fixed cap as a serious flaw. Their concern is not about inflation but about what a rigid money supply does during a recession, when spending is already falling. What is the main Keynesian complaint about a fixed cap?
answer: That a truly fixed supply forces the general price level to adjust downward during a recession, worsening debt burdens
choices: That a truly fixed supply forces the general price level to adjust downward during a recession, worsening debt burdens
That a fixed supply automatically triggers hyperinflation whenever velocity falls
That a fixed supply cannot be divided into small enough units for retail commerce
That a fixed supply requires a central bank to enforce it
context: The standard Keynesian critique -- Krugman, DeLong, Summers -- is that a fixed-supply currency has no elastic response to demand shocks, so nominal prices and wages must fall (Fisher's debt-deflation). Hyperinflation is by definition monetary expansion, not fixed supply; Bitcoin divides to 10^-8; a fixed cap is what removes any need for a central issuer. Source: Ammous vs Krugman debates; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_deflation.

question: In August 1931 a young Austrian economist teaching in London wrote a long two-part review essay in the journal Economica. It attacked the newest big book from Cambridge University's most famous living economist. The pairing sparked one of the biggest arguments in twentieth-century economics. Who was the reviewer, and who was his target?
answer: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
choices: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
Ludwig von Mises reviewing Alfred Marshall
Murray Rothbard reviewing Paul Samuelson
Milton Friedman reviewing Joan Robinson
context: Hayek published Part I of his review of Keynes's A Treatise on Money (1930) in the August 1931 issue of Economica; Keynes replied and Hayek rejoined in November 1931; Hayek's Part II appeared in February 1932. Source: The Coolidge Review, 'Why the Keynes-Hayek Clash Endures' (https://www.coolidgereview.com/articles/keynes-hayek-debate-endures).

question: In the early 1930s, during the Great Depression, two famous economists argued in newspapers and journals about how to save the economy. Friedrich Hayek was Austrian; John Maynard Keynes was English. Their fight was about what a government should do during a slump, when businesses were failing and workers were losing their jobs by the millions. What was the core disagreement between Hayek and Keynes?
answer: Keynes said governments should spend more; Hayek said that would make things worse later
choices: Keynes said governments should spend more; Hayek said that would make things worse later
Both agreed governments should print money without limit
Both agreed governments should shut down all banks
Keynes said abolish money; Hayek said abolish farms
context: Economica was the LSE journal that ran the Hayek review, Keynes's reply, and Hayek's rejoinder across four issues from August 1931 to February 1932. Keynes's own Cambridge-based Economic Journal ran a separate front in the debate (Sraffa's 1932 review of Hayek). Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: By 1931 Friedrich Hayek had moved from Vienna to teach at the London School of Economics. Cambridge's John Maynard Keynes had just published a big book called Treatise on Money. Hayek tore it apart page by page in a long two-part review. His main charge: Keynes ignored an older European school of thought on interest rates and what it called the natural rate. Which school did Hayek say Keynes had skipped?
answer: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
choices: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
The Marshall-Pigou tradition on partial equilibrium welfare economics
The Marx-Engels tradition on the falling rate of profit
The Walras-Pareto tradition on general equilibrium mathematics
context: Hayek's central technical charge against Keynes's Treatise was that Keynes had a monetary theory disconnected from capital theory and had ignored the continental (Knut Wicksell in Sweden, Ludwig von Mises in Vienna) tradition on the natural rate of interest -- the foundation Hayek's own business-cycle theory was built on. Source: Mises Institute, Hayek's 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J. M. Keynes.'

question: When John Maynard Keynes replied to F. A. Hayek's 1931 Economica review of his Treatise on Money, he mostly refused to answer Hayek's technical points. Instead he pivoted to attack Hayek's OWN 1931 book on business cycles, calling it 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read.' Which book of Hayek's was Keynes attacking?
answer: Prices and Production
choices: Prices and Production
The Pure Theory of Capital
The Road to Serfdom
Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle
context: Keynes wrote that Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) was 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read' and 'an extraordinary example of how, starting with a mistake, a remorseless logician can end up in Bedlam.' Keynes's move -- attack the OTHER book rather than defend his own -- became famous for its aggression. Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: In 1931 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published a book called 'Prices and Production,' arguing that easy money from central banks caused booms and busts. His rival, the English economist John Maynard Keynes, quietly arranged for a Cambridge colleague named Piero Sraffa to write a harshly critical review of Hayek's book. Sraffa's review appeared in 1932 and professional opinion swung against Hayek's theory for a generation. What kind of power over a whole field's views does the Sraffa review reveal a single well-placed critique can have?
answer: A well-placed critical review can shift a whole field's views
choices: A well-placed critical review can shift a whole field's views
Only the most mathematical theory ever wins the debate
Book reviews never affect which theories professors teach
Whoever writes the longest book always wins the debate
context: Piero Sraffa was an Italian-born Cambridge economist and a Keynes ally. His hostile 1932 review argued that without money there is a MULTIPLICITY of commodity own-rates and no unique natural rate of interest can be identified -- the concept of the 'own-rate of interest' was introduced (unnamed) in that review. Hayek replied in the Economic Journal in June 1932 with 'Money and Capital: A Reply to Mr. Sraffa.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Sraffa-Hayek debate' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sraffa%E2%80%93Hayek_debate).

question: In the 1930s one big rivalry shaped British economics. At one university, John Maynard Keynes and his students argued that governments should spend heavily to fight downturns. At another, Friedrich Hayek and Lionel Robbins argued markets and sound money worked best when governments stayed out. Their feud became the century's central economics debate. Which two schools were behind the fight?
answer: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
choices: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
Cambridge and Oxford
Oxford and the London School of Economics
Cambridge and Manchester
context: Keynes was at King's College, Cambridge; Hayek had arrived at the London School of Economics on Houghton Street in 1931. The 1930s Cambridge-vs-LSE feud framed the whole landscape of British economics until the war. Source: Adam Smith Institute review, 'Keynes Hayek: The Clash That Defined Modern Economics' (https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/thinkpieces/review-keynes-hayek-the-clash-that-defined-modern-economics).

question: In 1936 John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money -- the book that would reshape twentieth-century macroeconomics. F. A. Hayek, Keynes's most technical Austrian critic, made a choice about the General Theory that he later called one of the great professional regrets of his life. What did Hayek do?
answer: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
choices: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
He wrote a hostile Economica review that Keynes never answered
He co-authored a rebuttal book with Ludwig von Mises
He challenged Keynes to a public debate at Cambridge
context: Hayek chose not to review the General Theory in 1936. He gave several reasons later, including that Keynes was notorious for changing his mind, so Hayek expected the position would soon be revised again; by the time it was clear Keynes was serious, the Keynesian revolution had swept the profession with no serious Austrian rebuttal in print for a generation. Source: Bruce Caldwell, 'Why Didn't Hayek Review Keynes's General Theory?' Duke University (https://public.econ.duke.edu/~bjc18/docs/Why%20Didn't%20Hayek%20Review%20General%20Theory.pdf).

question: In 1936 the English economist John Maynard Keynes published 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money,' the book that would define twentieth-century macroeconomics. Friedrich Hayek, the leading Austrian economist and Keynes's chief rival, chose not to write a formal review of it. Years later Hayek explained why: he had watched Keynes swing to a new position twice already, and he expected another swing was coming. Which recurring habit of Keynes did Hayek cite?
answer: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
choices: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
Keynes refused to engage in print with any Austrian economist
Keynes had privately told Hayek the General Theory was a joke
Keynes had already promised a full retraction in a coming article
context: Hayek said in interviews that Keynes had a well-known propensity to change his positions, so writing a long technical review of one Keynes book seemed likely to be answered by yet another Keynes book that revised everything -- as had partly happened with the Treatise on Money after Hayek's 1931 review. Source: Caldwell, Duke University essay.

question: The 1931-1932 Hayek and Keynes review essays, later correspondence between the two men, and Piero Sraffa's 1932 attack were collected together and published as one volume of the University of Chicago Press's Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. Bruce Caldwell edited the collection in 1995 under a pointed title. What is the volume titled?
answer: Contra Keynes and Cambridge
choices: Contra Keynes and Cambridge
The Trend of Economic Thinking
Individualism and Economic Order
Studies in Philosophy Politics and Economics
context: Contra Keynes and Cambridge, edited by Bruce Caldwell, was published in 1995 as Volume 9 of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. Its three parts cover Hayek's 1930s arrival at LSE, the direct exchanges with Keynes and Sraffa, and later essays -- including Hayek's previously unpublished 1963 memoir 'The Economics of the 1930s as Seen from London.' Source: University of Chicago Press catalog (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo3614356.html).

question: Two economists in 1930s Britain argued furiously in journals about how economies really work. But when war came in 1940, one of them personally helped the other find a place to live and stood fire-watch duty with him at night. What does this friendship show about honest disagreement?
answer: People can differ deeply about ideas without becoming personal enemies
choices: People can differ deeply about ideas without becoming personal enemies
Anyone who criticizes your ideas is your true enemy
Intellectuals never actually mean the criticisms they write in journals
Personal friendship always changes what people write in their journals
context: Keynes was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge; when LSE was evacuated to Cambridge in 1940, Keynes found Hayek a place at King's and Hayek's son Laurence a place at King's College School. Hayek and Keynes shared night fire-watch duty on the King's chapel roofs, and Hayek later called the wartime Cambridge hospitality one of the pleasantest memories of his life -- a striking coda to the 1931-1932 attack in Economica. Source: University of Cambridge Alumni magazine, 'City of refuge' (https://www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/magazine/issue-98/city-of-refuge).

question: In 1932 and 1933 Joseph Stalin's Soviet government sent collection squads into Ukraine. Their job was to take grain from every peasant farmer. The squads took almost everything — even the seeds farmers needed to plant the next spring's crop. Villages had nothing left to eat. What happened to the people of Ukraine that winter?
answer: Millions starved to death
choices: Millions starved to death
They became the richest region of the Soviet Union
They received free bread from the government
The population grew quickly
context: Holodomor combines the Ukrainian holod (hunger) and mor (mortality, plague). It is used specifically for the 1932-33 famine as a policy-driven catastrophe distinct from natural crop failure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: The Holodomor was the man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine in 1932 and 1933. It was not just a bad harvest. Joseph Stalin's government set a grain quota so high that no village could meet it, then sent search crews into peasant homes to enforce it. What did the crews take?
answer: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
choices: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
Only the marketable surplus
Only mid-quality grain
Only what was above household needs
context: Requisition brigades searched houses and took stored food, cured meat, and seed grain. Peasants with no reserves and no seed for next year starved by early 1933. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: In January 1933 Joseph Stalin signed an order that sealed the borders of Soviet Ukraine during the Holodomor famine. Starving villagers could no longer walk to nearby Russian regions to buy or beg for food. Guards were posted on every road and rail line to check travel papers. What happened to Ukrainians who tried to leave anyway?
answer: They were turned back or arrested
choices: They were turned back or arrested
They received travel permits and rations
They were resettled in Siberia with food
They were allowed passage but taxed heavily
context: The January 22, 1933 order sealed Ukraine and the Kuban internally, stopping the peasant escape that had helped during earlier famines. It converted a policy-caused shortage into a policy-caused mass death. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: During the Holodomor famine in 1932 and 1933, Joseph Stalin's officials had a special punishment for Ukrainian villages that missed their impossible grain quota. The village was put on a state list. All trade with it was cut off, the last food was seized from every shelf, and no resident was allowed to leave. What were these villages called on the state list?
answer: Blacklisted villages
choices: Blacklisted villages
Suspended communes
Under-quota settlements
Restricted zones
context: 'Blacklisted villages' (chorna doshka villages) were targeted for full economic isolation and starvation. Signs marked the boundaries. The mechanism killed by community, not by household. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: The Holodomor was Joseph Stalin's man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine in 1932-33, when Communist Party grain quotas stripped villages bare and troops sealed the borders so starving peasants could not escape. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, historians finally opened the party and secret-police archives and counted the dead in earnest. What is the standard range they now give?
answer: About 3.5 to 7.5 million
choices: About 3.5 to 7.5 million
About 35 to 75 million
context: Most peer-reviewed studies (Snyder's Bloodlands 2010, Ukrainian government 2008 study, Andriewsky, Graziosi) cluster at 3.5-5 million; the upper bound reaches ~7.5 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: The Holodomor was the man-made famine that killed millions of Ukrainians under Joseph Stalin in 1932 and 1933. For decades the Soviet Union denied it happened. Then, in November 2006, Ukraine's own parliament — the Verkhovna Rada — passed a law that finally named the famine as a specific kind of state crime. What did the Verkhovna Rada officially call it?
answer: A genocide
choices: A genocide
A humanitarian catastrophe
A policy failure
A wartime atrocity
context: The Verkhovna Rada's November 28, 2006 law recognized the Holodomor as a genocide of the Ukrainian people. The European Parliament followed with a similar resolution in December 2022 during Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor_genocide_question.

question: The Holodomor was Joseph Stalin's man-made famine that killed millions of Ukrainian peasants in 1932-33. For decades Soviet authorities denied it had happened at all, and Western newspapers like the New York Times helped bury the story. In 1986 the British historian Robert Conquest published the first major Western scholarly account, released by Oxford University Press. What was its title?
answer: The Harvest of Sorrow
choices: The Harvest of Sorrow
The Great Terror
Bloodlands
Red Famine
context: Robert Conquest's The Harvest of Sorrow: Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine (Oxford UP, 1986) was the first major Western scholarly synthesis. It was funded partly by the Ukrainian diaspora and treated with skepticism by academic sovietology until the archives opened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvest_of_Sorrow.

question: In the early 1930s the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin decided to break Ukrainian peasant resistance to his forced collective-farm policy. He sent armed grain squads into Ukrainian villages that seized not only the year's harvest but even the seed grain farmers needed for next year's crop. Millions of Ukrainians starved to death in their own farmhouses while grain sat guarded in Soviet warehouses. What is that engineered famine called in Ukraine today?
answer: The Holodomor
choices: The Holodomor
The Great Leap
The Cultural Revolution
The Great Purge
context: Anne Applebaum's Red Famine: Stalin's War on Ukraine (Doubleday, 2017) is the standard modern reference. Serhii Plokhy's The Man with the Poison Gun and other work cover adjacent Ukrainian history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Famine.

question: Soviet Kazakhstan's 1932-33 famine, the Asharshylyk, came from forced collectivization — the state seized the nomads' herds and banned private slaughter. Historians count roughly 1.5 million dead. That toll erased about what share of the entire ethnic Kazakh people?
answer: About 40 percent
choices: About 40 percent
About 4 percent
About 15 percent
About 80 percent
context: About 1.5 million Kazakhs died (roughly 40% of the ethnic Kazakh population). The famine transformed Kazakhstan's demographic balance for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakh_famine_of_1930%E2%80%931933.

question: The Holodomor killed roughly four million Ukrainians in 1932 and 1933. Historians distinguish it from ordinary famines caused by bad weather or a locust plague. They point to a specific mix of state actions by Joseph Stalin's Soviet government that turned a crop shortfall into deliberate mass death across the countryside. Which combination best describes that policy mechanism?
answer: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
choices: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
An early frost combined with a locust plague
A blockade by Western powers restricting food imports
A Ukrainian nationalist boycott of Soviet economic institutions
context: The three-step policy mechanism -- impossible quotas, sealed borders, blacklisting -- converted a policy-induced shortage into targeted mass death. This is what distinguishes the Holodomor from natural famine. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: The Holodomor was a famine engineered on purpose by Joseph Stalin's Soviet grain-seizure policies in Ukraine in 1932 and 1933. Armed squads stripped Ukrainian villages of every last kernel while the government blocked peasants from leaving the region to find food. Millions starved. Many European legislatures -- Germany, Poland, Ireland and others -- have since voted to formally recognize the Holodomor as a genocide. Why does that formal recognition matter?
answer: It records the deaths as a deliberate crime, not an accident of bad weather
choices: It records the deaths as a deliberate crime, not an accident of bad weather
It pays money to the surviving families of the victims
It reverses the Soviet Union's own censorship of the event
It criminally prosecutes surviving Soviet officials
context: The European Parliament passed a December 15, 2022 resolution recognizing the Holodomor as genocide. The timing during Russia's invasion of Ukraine added political weight to the recognition. Source: europarl.europa.eu (2022/2988 RSP).

question: In April 1975 a communist group called the Khmer Rouge, led by a man named Pol Pot, took over the country of Cambodia in Southeast Asia. They emptied every city at gunpoint, banned money and private property, closed all schools, and killed anyone who seemed educated -- even people who wore glasses. In just four years, about a quarter of all Cambodians were dead. What is the main lesson?
answer: Trying to erase a whole society and start over causes mass death
choices: Trying to erase a whole society and start over causes mass death
Banning money always makes a country richer
Emptying cities makes farms produce more food
Killing educated people helps the economy grow
context: The Khmer Rouge (Communist Party of Kampuchea), led by Pol Pot (born Saloth Sar), captured Phnom Penh April 17, 1975. Their rule ended with a Vietnamese invasion in December 1978 - January 1979. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Rouge.

question: When Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge took power in Cambodia in April 1975, they announced it was 'Year Zero.' They said history was starting completely fresh from their victory -- Cambodian tradition, Buddhist religion, family bonds, and all schooling would be erased and rebuilt from scratch. What is the danger of a government that thinks it can wipe the slate clean?
answer: It usually has to destroy the people and traditions that do not fit its plan
choices: It usually has to destroy the people and traditions that do not fit its plan
It always doubles the country's wealth in one year
It never affects normal families
It only changes flags and holidays, nothing else
context: Year Zero meant every trace of the previous urban-professional society was to be erased. Money was abolished, the central bank building blown up, private property abolished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Zero_(political_notion).

question: In April 1975 the Khmer Rouge, a communist guerrilla movement led by Pol Pot, captured the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh and ended a long civil war. Within three days of taking the city they did something no modern regime had ever attempted against its own capital of roughly 2 million people. What did they do?
answer: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
choices: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
Executed all professional-class residents immediately
Confined them to reeducation blocks by street
Deported them by rail to Vietnam
context: Hospitals were emptied of patients, monasteries of monks, universities of professors -- all forced out on foot within days. This is the first act of the Year Zero policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Phnom_Penh.

question: In April 1975 a communist group called the Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, seized power in Cambodia. Over the next four years they tried to erase every city-educated person from the country. They hunted teachers, doctors, engineers, and clerks. Wearing one everyday item was enough to be marked for execution because it suggested you could read. Which item?
answer: Glasses
choices: Glasses
A wristwatch
Leather shoes
A hat
context: Wearing glasses marked a Cambodian as educated. Speaking French, having soft hands, or having worked in a profession similarly marked people for execution or death by forced labor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_genocide.

question: After Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge took over Cambodia in 1975, they emptied the capital Phnom Penh at gunpoint and turned a former high school called Tuol Sleng into a secret prison. Inside its old classrooms, guards tortured and killed roughly 15,000 ordinary Cambodian citizens -- teachers, doctors, factory workers, even children. What does turning a school into a torture site tell you about that regime?
answer: It sees ordinary life and learning as threats to its power
choices: It sees ordinary life and learning as threats to its power
It needs the building because no others exist in the city
It is trying to teach the prisoners a new job skill
It is running short of workers to build fresh prisons
context: S-21, in a former Phnom Penh high school, was chief Kaing Guek Eav ('Duch')'s facility. The photographic and confession archive he kept became the evidence base for later trials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuol_Sleng_Genocide_Museum.

question: After taking Cambodia in 1975, Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge emptied the cities and trucked millions of citizens to work camps and to hundreds of rural execution sites now known as the Killing Fields. Around a quarter of the country's people -- roughly 1.7 million out of 7 million -- were murdered in only four years. What does mass killing on this scale usually require?
answer: A government with total power and no check on its rulers
choices: A government with total power and no check on its rulers
A short-term food shortage caused by bad weather
A small group of unhappy soldiers acting alone
A neighboring country secretly funding the killings
context: The Killing Fields at Choeung Ek is the most-visited memorial site. Hundreds of similar sites across Cambodia together hold the remains of roughly 1.5-2 million victims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_Fields.

question: Historians studying Cambodia under Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979 estimate how many died. The best modern figures come from Yale's Cambodian Genocide Program and from Ben Kiernan's careful death-toll studies, out of a pre-1975 Cambodian population of about 7 to 8 million. Proportionally it is the worst genocide of the 20th century. What is the standard death-toll range?
answer: About 1.5 to 2 million
choices: About 1.5 to 2 million
About 15 million to 20 million
context: About 1.5-2 million Cambodians died -- roughly a fifth to a quarter of the entire population. Nazi Germany killed a smaller fraction of its own population than the Khmer Rouge killed of theirs. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: The top leaders of the Khmer Rouge — the communist group that killed roughly two million Cambodians in the late 1970s — all knew each other from their student years in one European capital in the early 1950s. Pol Pot, Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, and Son Sen studied there together on French scholarships and absorbed hardline Marxist ideas from the local left. Which capital shaped them?
answer: Paris
choices: Paris
London
Moscow
Rome
context: The Cercle Marxiste-Leniniste in Paris in the early 1950s included Saloth Sar (later Pol Pot), Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, and Son Sen. They returned home with the pure-agrarian-utopia idea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Pot.

question: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge killed roughly a quarter of Cambodia's own people in the late 1970s. Their rule ended not from an internal revolt but from a neighboring communist country invading -- Vietnam sent its army across the border in December 1978 and toppled the Khmer Rouge within weeks. Two communist regimes had gone to war with each other. What claim about shared communist ideology preventing war does the Vietnam–Cambodia war actually disprove?
answer: Being communist did not prevent wars between them
choices: Being communist did not prevent wars between them
Communist countries always joined together against outside threats
Only western countries ever attacked communist regimes
Cambodia's own army overthrew the Khmer Rouge without outside help
context: The Vietnamese invasion began December 25, 1978 and captured Phnom Penh on January 7, 1979. Vietnam installed the Kampuchean People's Republic and occupied the country until 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian%E2%80%93Vietnamese_War.

question: Kaing Guek Eav, known as 'Duch,' was the chief of the Khmer Rouge's S-21 torture prison in Phnom Penh, where roughly 14,000 Cambodians were killed in the late 1970s. In 2010, more than three decades after the regime fell, a specific UN-backed hybrid tribunal seated inside Cambodia convicted him of crimes against humanity. What was the tribunal called?
answer: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
choices: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
The International Criminal Tribunal for Cambodia
The Phnom Penh War Crimes Court
The UN Cambodia Commission
context: The ECCC (Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia) convicted Duch (Kaing Guek Eav) in July 2010 and later convicted senior leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan. Pol Pot died under house arrest in 1998 without trial. Source: eccc.gov.kh.

question: In August 1982 Mexico, one of the biggest countries in Latin America, told the world's banks something scary: it could not pay back the huge loans it had taken from them during the 1970s oil boom. Banking has a specific word for when a country or person cannot pay back what they owe. What is that word?
answer: A default
choices: A default
A discount
A dividend
A donation
context: Finance Minister Jesus Silva Herzog called the US Treasury on August 12, 1982 to say Mexico could not service its dollar debt. Brazil, Argentina, and others followed within months. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: In the 1970s Walter Wriston, the chairman of the huge US bank Citibank in New York, was famous for a bold line about lending to foreign governments. He repeated it in an opinion piece in the New York Times in September 1982, right before Latin American countries began stopping payment on their debts and threw the world into a debt crisis. What was Walter Wriston's line?
answer: Countries don't go bankrupt
choices: Countries don't go bankrupt
Currencies always float
Dollars always come home
Banks never fail
context: Walter Wriston, Citibank chairman 1967-84, argued sovereigns could always repay because they could tax and print. His September 1982 op-ed in the New York Times crystallized the doctrine -- just as the crisis was breaking. Source: nytimes.com Wriston 'Banking Against Disaster', September 14 1982.

question: In 1979 the US Federal Reserve's new chairman, Paul Volcker, pushed short-term interest rates above 19 percent to break America's runaway inflation. Poor Latin American countries -- Mexico, Brazil, Argentina and others -- had borrowed billions of dollars from big US banks at floating rates that would shift with US policy. When Volcker's rate hikes hit, their monthly interest bills exploded. What happened to those countries?
answer: Their debt payments exploded and many countries went bust
choices: Their debt payments exploded and many countries went bust
They got a big grant from the World Bank to pay it off
The dollar collapsed, wiping out their debts
Nothing much, their loans were in local money
context: Volcker (Fed chair 1979-87) pushed the fed funds rate above 19 percent in 1981 to break US inflation. The rate spike also blew up dollar-denominated foreign loans across Latin America. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/anti-inflation-measures.

question: On August 12, 1982, Mexico's finance minister told US banks his country could not pay back its foreign loans. Big American banks had loaned so much to Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina in the 1970s that the debts topped the banks' own capital — a collapse would have wiped them out. The near-crisis launched a long regional slump across Latin America. What was that slump named?
answer: The Lost Decade
choices: The Lost Decade
The Long Depression
The Marshall Plan
The Great Society
context: The FDIC's 'History of the Eighties' documents the exposure. Marked to market, several of the largest US banks would have been technically insolvent had the Latin American loans been written down at the time. Source: fdic.gov/bank/historical/history.

question: A group of poor countries cannot pay back giant loans. Instead of letting them default, big banks are pressured to keep the loans on the books and stretch the payments out for many years. What is the main effect of pretending a bad loan is still good?
answer: The pain is spread out but the bad loan never really goes away
choices: The pain is spread out but the bad loan never really goes away
The borrower pays the loan off in half the time
The banks earn far more interest than they would have
The country suddenly becomes rich enough to repay everything
context: 'Concerted lending' meant banks were pressured to keep extending fresh credit so that old loans could technically stay current. This bought time for bank balance sheets at the cost of years of Latin American recession. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: In the 1980s, country after country in Latin America — Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile — sank into the same trap. Prices ran wild. Jobs vanished. Banks failed and had to be rescued. For ten straight years, regular families barely saw life improve. Historians looking back gave this whole stretch of the 1980s a nickname to mark how much time was wasted. What nickname did they give it?
answer: A lost decade
choices: A lost decade
A golden decade
A quiet recovery
A steady climb
context: Per-capita GDP in Mexico did not regain 1981 levels until the mid-1990s. Inflation ran into the thousands of percent in Argentina, Brazil, and Peru during the 1980s. The World Bank and IDB use 'Lost Decade' as the standard term. Source: World Bank data.

question: In the late 1980s, Mexico, Brazil, and other poor countries owed enormous sums to US commercial banks. They could not pay. In 1989, US Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady proposed a clever swap. The banks would trade their bad, unsellable loans for new tradable bonds, and the US Treasury would partly back them. What was the main economic idea behind this Brady Plan?
answer: Turn a bad loan you cannot sell into a bond you can sell to spread the loss
choices: Turn a bad loan you cannot sell into a bond you can sell to spread the loss
Cancel every debt and start over from zero
Force poor countries to hand over natural resources instead
Have the US taxpayer directly pay off every foreign loan
context: Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady's 1989 plan converted the old loans into new tradable bonds partially backed by zero-coupon US Treasuries as collateral. This finally let banks acknowledge and market-price losses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: The 1989 Brady Plan needed something rock-solid to back the new country bonds so investors would buy them. US Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady picked a special type of US Treasury bond. This bond pays no interest along the way. It just quietly grows and pays back its full face value at the end. What kind of Treasury bond was used as the backing?
answer: US Treasury zero-coupon bonds
choices: US Treasury zero-coupon bonds
Federal Reserve deposits
US gold reserves
SDRs from the IMF
context: Countries bought long-dated US Treasury zeros with a portion of new-loan proceeds; the zeros' face value at maturity guaranteed the principal on the Brady bonds. This gave holders a hard collateral floor while letting the coupon on the sovereign portion trade at deep discount. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: Austrian and moral-hazard economists — writers in the tradition of Ludwig von Mises and later Robert Higgs — argue the 1980s Latin American debt workout revealed a classic pattern of privatized gains and socialized losses. The 1970s dollar loans from Citibank and other US banks made huge profits for years, but when Mexico defaulted in 1982, the workout arrangement protected one group and hurt another. Who paid the price, and who was let off the hook for the loans they made?
answer: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
choices: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
Latin American publics bore currency gains; US banks paid full losses
European banks bore the losses; US banks were untouched
The IMF absorbed the losses through direct grants
context: The Austrian reading: the workout socialized the costs of bad lending onto Latin American publics via the Lost Decade, while US bank creditors were rescued from the market discipline that would have failed several of them. This is the template that repeated in 1998, 2008, and 2010. Source: mises.org/library/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: In the 1970s Citibank chairman Walter Wriston famously declared 'countries don't go bankrupt' and pushed his bank into massive foreign lending to Latin American governments. When Mexico defaulted in August 1982, the pain was extreme because of one specific feature of those Citibank loans that Austrian critics later flagged as the root of the damage. Which foreign-lending practice made the damage so bad?
answer: Dollar-denominated loans to sovereign borrowers
choices: Dollar-denominated loans to sovereign borrowers
Local-currency loans with fixed exchange rates
Gold-backed loans with hard collateral
Loans indexed to consumer prices
context: The Latin American loans were mostly dollar-denominated. When US rates spiked under Volcker, sovereign borrowers owed more dollars in interest than their export earnings could cover, and had no domestic monetary tool to help. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: In the 1840s the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short book called The Law. He argued that the proper job of law was to protect three things: a person's life, their freedom, and the property they had earned. Then he warned about what happens when law is used instead to take from some people and hand what they earned to others. What did he say the law becomes?
answer: The law becomes a tool for legal robbery
choices: The law becomes a tool for legal robbery
The economy always grows twice as fast
Everyone becomes richer at the same time
Nobody notices any difference
context: French original: La Loi. Published June 1850, six months before Bastiat's death in December; his most widely-read work in English by a wide margin. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat, dying of tuberculosis, wrote a short pamphlet called The Law. In it he argued that the law's one legitimate job is to defend three basic rights that every person is born with -- rights that exist before any government does. Which three rights did he name?
answer: Life, liberty, and property
choices: Life, liberty, and property
Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
Life, health, and safety
Speech, assembly, and conscience
context: 'The law is the collective organization of the individual right to lawful defense.' Bastiat's triad is nearly Lockean; he says these three exist BEFORE any law and give the law its purpose. Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: In 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a short pamphlet called 'The Law.' In it he warned about what happens when the government uses the law itself to take from some people and hand it to others. His French term for this was 'spoliation legale' — two words, sharp and blunt. What are those two words in English?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Public spoilage
Common transfer
Social equalization
context: Bastiat's spoliation legale becomes 'legal plunder' in every standard English edition since Hodgson 1859; the term is Bastiat's own coinage for the phenomenon. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: In his 1850 pamphlet The Law, Frederic Bastiat, a French economist and member of the National Assembly, gave readers a simple test to spot what he called 'legal plunder.' The test was a single question one could ask about any proposed law to check whether it was really robbery in disguise. According to Bastiat, one asks whether the law does what?
answer: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
choices: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
Fails to secure a positive right to housing or employment for every citizen
Was passed by a majority smaller than two-thirds of the elected assembly
Diverges from the natural-law tradition articulated by medieval theologians
context: Bastiat's second test in the paragraph: 'See if the law benefits one citizen at the expense of another by doing what the citizen himself cannot do without committing a crime.' Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: A French writer argued that government taking from some to give to others is legal plunder. One form is socialism — guaranteed jobs paid for by taxing everyone. What is the other big form, where the government blocks foreign goods to help favored home industries?
answer: Protectionism
choices: Protectionism
Free trade
Volunteer charity
Private savings
context: The two French policies Bastiat names as legal plunder: PROTECTIONISM (tariffs transferring wealth from consumers to sheltered producers) and SOCIALISM (transfers from taxpayers to National Workshop beneficiaries). Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: When a government constantly uses the law to take from some people and give to others, ordinary citizens slowly stop asking whether something is right or wrong. They only ask whether it is legal. What is that shift in a country's moral sense usually called?
answer: Corruption
choices: Corruption
Progress
Balance
Freedom
context: Bastiat treats moral CORRUPTION as the largest unseen cost of legal plunder: legality replaces morality in the citizen's daily judgments. Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: In his 1850 pamphlet 'The Law,' the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote one sentence that libertarian readers ever since have quoted like scripture. It describes what the state becomes when politicians use the law to take from some people and give to others — Bastiat's 'legal plunder' turned into a whole system. Which sentence of Bastiat's carries that line?
answer: The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else
choices: The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else
Society exists for the benefit of its members and not the members for society
Politics is the art of the possible in an age of impossible expectations
The government is best which governs least, because the people discipline themselves
context: French: L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde. From Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' and echoed inside The Law. Source: bastiat.org/en/state.html.

question: Since 1950, the standard American edition of Frederic Bastiat's 1850 pamphlet 'The Law' has stayed continuously in print. It comes from a small New York classical-liberal group that the businessman Leonard Read and the journalist Henry Hazlitt helped found in 1946 to teach free-market economics. Which group has kept 'The Law' in print for more than seventy years?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education
The Cato Institute
The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Heritage Foundation
context: FEE (Irvington-on-Hudson) has issued The Law without a break since 1950; Cato (1977), the Mises Institute (1982), and Heritage (1973) came later. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: In 1850, the French economist Frederic Bastiat published a short, fiery pamphlet called 'The Law.' In it he argued that when a government uses the law itself to take from one group and give to another, it is committing what he called 'legal plunder.' What is the pamphlet's main claim about the proper job of law?
answer: Law exists to protect life, liberty, and property, not to redistribute them
choices: Law exists to protect life, liberty, and property, not to redistribute them
Law exists mainly to redistribute wealth from rich to poor
Law should set every price and wage in the economy
Law should force every citizen to work in state-run jobs
context: Paul's Liberty Defined (2011) cites The Law as the single best entry point; the pamphlet is, by wide margin, the first Austrian-adjacent text most American libertarian teenagers ever read. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Defined.

question: Frederic Bastiat wrote in French, so English-speaking readers needed translators. For most of the 1900s only three short works of his — The Law, Economic Sophisms, and Selected Essays on Political Economy — were available in English. All three were published by one small liberty-minded educational group based in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Which group put them out?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
The Cato Institute
The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: FEE was founded 1946 by Leonard Read in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Its editions were excellent for their day but covered only a fraction of Bastiat's actual output; most of his correspondence, journalism, and Assembly speeches had never been translated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: A rich businessman starts a private foundation. Its mission is simple: reprint and hand out old books by dead economists who defended free markets — thinkers like Frederic Bastiat and Adam Smith. He wants students centuries from now to still be able to read them, without needing any government program to make it happen. What does this quiet, generous project show about how ideas survive?
answer: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
choices: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
A government-run textbook program
A public library system paid by taxes
A university tenure system
context: Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat is projected to run to six volumes. Goodrich, an Indiana lawyer and businessman, endowed the foundation specifically to sustain the classical-liberal scholarly tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Imagine a French shopkeeper in a small town. A stray rock breaks his front window. He pays a glazier six francs to replace it. A crowd gathers and cheerfully claims the accident was actually good for the town, because it gave the glazier six francs of new work. Frederic Bastiat used this story in 1850 to teach a famous lesson about hidden costs. What is the crowd missing?
answer: The shopkeeper cannot now spend that money on something else
choices: The shopkeeper cannot now spend that money on something else
The glazier will refuse to accept the payment
The window was actually fine and did not need fixing
The shopkeeper will get his money back from the town
context: Hart works alongside general editors Jacques de Guenin and Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean. He also maintains the Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org), a free online archive of classical-liberal texts that includes all the Bastiat volumes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: The Liberty Fund began publishing a six-volume Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat, translating the French economist's writings into modern English. Volume 3, released in 2017, contains his most famous 1850 essay — the one where he introduces the idea of hidden effects versus visible effects using the story of a shopkeeper's broken window. What is that essay called?
answer: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
choices: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
'The General Theory'
'The Wealth of Nations'
'Das Kapital'
context: 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas' (1850). Volume 3 also contains the Economic Sophisms, Bastiat's satirical essays including the Petition of the Candlemakers demanding a law against the sun. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Frederic Bastiat's most famous essay, published in France in 1850, opens with a shopkeeper whose front window is smashed by his own careless son. The shopkeeper pays a glazier to fix it. Neighbors gather and say cheerfully, 'well, at least the glazier gets work — a broken window is actually good for the economy.' What does Bastiat say the neighbors are missing?
answer: The shopkeeper would have spent that money on something else, so nothing new is created
choices: The shopkeeper would have spent that money on something else, so nothing new is created
The glazier will hire more workers, so the town is truly richer
Breaking things is a hidden way to grow the economy
Insurance companies cover the loss, so nobody is really hurt
context: The Liberty Fund Collected Works (7 volumes, 2011-) added scholarly apparatus the earlier FEE translations lacked: introductions locating each essay in 1840s French political context, glossaries of French figures, and modern translations that restored passages 19th-century English editions had toned down. Source: Grokipedia 'Frederic Bastiat' + Liberty Fund catalog.

question: David M. Hart, the Liberty Fund's English editor for the Bastiat Collected Works, has also built and maintained a free online resource that makes the whole Bastiat corpus (and hundreds of other classical-liberal texts) available at zero cost to any 21st-century reader with internet access. What is the resource called?
answer: The Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org)
choices: The Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org)
The Ludwig von Mises Institute online archive
The Cato Institute policy library
The Federal Reserve archival collection
context: Any curious kid with internet access can now read every essay Bastiat ever wrote, in modern English, on a free website funded by a classical-liberal foundation. The tradition is being actively cultivated, not just preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: In the United States, lobbying is when companies and interest groups pay professionals to try to shape federal laws, rules, and regulations. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets has tracked total federal lobbying spending every year since 1998, and the number has climbed steadily for a quarter century. About how much did federal lobbying cost in 2023?
answer: About $4.1 billion
choices: About $4.1 billion
About $410 million
About $41 billion
About $41 million
context: Federal lobbying spending grew from ~$1.44B in 1998 to ~$4.1B in 2023 per opensecrets.org (Center for Responsive Politics). Registered federal lobbyists number ~11,000-14,000. Source: opensecrets.org (Lobbying Data).

question: Instead of making better products, some businesses spend their money chasing favors from the government. They pay lobbyists in Washington, give money to political campaigns, and file lawsuits trying to change the rules in their favor. Economists have a specific name for the wasted resources this activity burns up — resources that could have built something real. What is this kind of loss called?
answer: Deadweight loss
choices: Deadweight loss
Sunk cost
Transfer payment
Opportunity income
context: Tullock's move: resources burned in the competition for privilege produce no goods or services; they only reshuffle existing wealth. The whole rectangle of resources burned is deadweight loss to society. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (June 1967).

question: In the United States, lobbying is the paid business of pressing federal lawmakers and regulators for favorable rules. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets tracks who spends the most each year. In 2023 one single industry topped every other, laying out about $385 million on federal lobbying by itself. Which industry led the list?
answer: Pharmaceuticals and health products
choices: Pharmaceuticals and health products
Defense contractors
Motion pictures and television
Iron and steel
context: Pharmaceuticals/health products led at ~$385M in 2023, followed by electronics manufacturing and equipment (~$228M) and insurance (~$164M). Source: opensecrets.org (Top Industries 2023).

question: In the United States, lobbying is the paid business of pressing federal officials for rules and spending that favor a particular group. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets tracks the biggest single spenders every year. One large business federation has come out on top in most recent years, and in 2023 it spent about $68 million lobbying the federal government. Which group is it?
answer: The US Chamber of Commerce
choices: The US Chamber of Commerce
The National Rifle Association
The American Bar Association
The American Legion
context: The US Chamber of Commerce has been the largest single-organization federal lobbying spender for most recent years -- ~$68M in 2023. National Association of Realtors (~$52M) and Meta Platforms (~$20M) round out the top individual spenders. Source: opensecrets.org (Top Organizations 2023).

question: In a 2014 study, three economists — Marianne Bertrand, Matilde Bombardini, and Francesco Trebbi — dug through US lobbying records to answer a sharp question: does a lobbyist earn her big fees because she knows the policy issue deeply, or because she personally knows the right politician? Their working paper had a memorable title that put the two theories side by side. What was it?
answer: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
choices: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
The Price of Access
Do Lobbyists Matter?
Money and Influence
context: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi, 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? An Empirical Assessment of the Lobbying Process' (American Economic Review, December 2014). Answer: mostly whom. Source: aeaweb.org (Bertrand et al. 2014).

question: In Washington DC there is a well-known pattern called the 'revolving door.' A member of Congress or a top congressional staffer works in government for years on a modest federal salary that is capped by law. Then they leave and take a job at a K Street lobbying firm, cashing in on their inside contacts and knowledge of the rules. Which range best fits the pay bump they usually get when they walk through that door?
answer: 500 to 1000 percent
choices: 500 to 1000 percent
10 to 25 percent
0 to 5 percent
Pay cuts of 30 to 50 percent
context: Ex-Members and ex-senior staffers who become lobbyists command salary premiums of ~500-1000% over their government pay, consistent with a market pricing their capture-value. Source: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi (2014); Blanes i Vidal + Draca + Fons-Rosen, American Economic Review (2012).

question: In 1938, as Nazi Germany's propaganda agents worked inside America to shape public opinion before World War II, the US Congress passed a law. It required anyone who lobbied on behalf of foreign governments, foreign political parties, or foreign companies to publicly register and disclose the money. If you took cash from Berlin, Moscow, or Beijing to sway US opinion and policy, you had to say so. Prosecutors still use this law today. What short name is that 1938 law known by?
answer: FARA
choices: FARA
FLDA
USRA
FIDA
context: The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), passed 1938, requires disclosure of foreign-government-directed lobbying. FARA disclosures in recent years total ~$500M/year, on top of the ~$4B/year in domestic-lobbying disclosure. Source: justice.gov/nsd-fara.

question: In Washington DC, a single downtown street runs a few blocks near the White House and the Capitol. So many lobbying firms and trade groups keep offices along it that the street's name — K Street — has become shorthand in the news for the whole American lobbying industry. What does the clustering of firms along K Street teach about how policy actually gets made?
answer: Lobbyists cluster near power because access to lawmakers is valuable
choices: Lobbyists cluster near power because access to lawmakers is valuable
Lobbying firms are legally required to share one office building
Lobbyists usually prefer to work far from all elected officials
The federal government owns all the offices near Congress
context: K Street NW in downtown Washington DC hosts many of the largest lobbying firms and trade associations. 'K Street' has become synonymous with the lobbying industry as an American shorthand. Source: Grokipedia 'K Street (Washington, D.C.)'.

question: In 1967, the American economist Gordon Tullock published a paper on the welfare costs of tariffs, monopolies, and theft. He argued something new: when the government has power to hand out favors, people spend real resources chasing those favors — hiring lobbyists, wining and dining lawmakers, funding think tanks. Today, roughly four billion dollars a year flows into federal lobbying in Washington. Which sentence best fits Tullock's view of what that spending actually buys?
answer: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
choices: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
Money is spent purely to educate legislators about general policy tradeoffs
Money is spent on ceremonial political events with no material effect
Money is spent solely to comply with existing legal disclosures
context: Tullock's rent-seeking framework: $4B/year is not being spent to persuade Congress of general truths. It is being spent to capture concrete, industry-specific policy outcomes. The stated purpose (democratic participation) is not always false; the aggregate spending is not consistent with it either. Source: Tullock (1967); opensecrets.org.

question: Public choice economists like James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock noticed a repeating pattern in Washington. Concentrated industries — sugar, banking, defense contractors — fund armies of lobbyists to shape one narrow law that helps them. The costs get spread thinly across millions of taxpayers and consumers who never notice they are paying. When a complex new law suddenly targets one industry, what should a careful policy watcher suspect by default?
answer: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
choices: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
The beneficiaries are always the retail voters who elected the sponsors
The statute is copied verbatim from a Nordic model
The statute was drafted overnight by a single ideologue
context: When a proposed statute is complex, industry-specific, and heavily lobbied, the Tullock-Olson default is that the concentrated organized interests are the primary beneficiaries. The First Amendment protects petition; the ladder analyzes the aggregate incentive structure. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: You are dying of thirst in a desert. Someone offers you a glass of water and you would trade almost anything for it. But if they offer you a fifth glass after four, you barely care. Why does the fifth glass feel less valuable than the first?
answer: You need it much less than the first one
choices: You need it much less than the first one
The water changes chemistry after four glasses
The seller has to lower the price by law
The government taxes extra glasses
context: Menger's Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre insisted that value is subjective, ranked by an individual chooser, and always applies to a specific additional unit rather than to a good as a class. That single move dissolved a hundred years of classical puzzles. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger and the Sesquicentennial Founding of the Austrian School'.

question: Two people find identical gold coins on the beach. One is a rich collector who already has thousands of them. The other is a poor kid who needs bus fare home. Who values that one coin more?
answer: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
choices: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
The rich collector, because he understands gold
They value it equally because it is the same coin
Neither, because gold has no real value
context: Jevons's The Theory of Political Economy appeared in London in 1871, the same year as Menger's Grundsaetze. Marshall would not publish his Principles until 1890; Mill and Senior belonged to the earlier classical generation. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: In 1871 an English economist argued that a thing's value depends not on the whole pile you own, but on how useful one more unit would be to you right now. If you have zero apples, one more is huge; if you have twenty, one more is small. What is this idea called?
answer: Marginal utility
choices: Marginal utility
Labor theory of value
Cost of production
Fair market price
context: Jevons was Professor of Political Economy at Owens College, Manchester -- the institution that later became the University of Manchester. He wrote The Theory of Political Economy while holding that chair. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: In the 1870s, a French economist named Leon Walras, working at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland, went further than the other founders of modern economics. He built a mathematical model where every price in every market is set at the same time, all linked together like one giant system of equations. What did Walras call this idea?
answer: General equilibrium
choices: General equilibrium
Partial equilibrium
The gold standard
Central planning
context: Walras published in Lausanne, using the French word 'rarete' for what English readers called marginal utility. Cournot preceded him with 1838 mathematical duopoly; Pareto succeeded him in the Lausanne chair after 1893; Bastiat was of an older generation and no marginalist. Source: Britannica, 'Leon Walras'.

question: In the 1870s, the French economist Leon Walras dreamed up 'general equilibrium' — modeling a whole economy at once, with every price, every buyer, and every seller tied together in one huge system of mathematical equations. Modern computers can crank those equations for hours. But the real economy does not sit still while the equations run. What is the biggest real-world problem with Walras's dream?
answer: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
choices: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
Computers today are still too slow to add up any prices
There is a law against writing equations about markets
Economists refuse to share their equations with each other
context: Walras held the chair of political economy at the Academie de Lausanne (later the University of Lausanne) from 1870; his book was printed there in 1874. The Lausanne School of general equilibrium takes its name from the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Between 1871 and 1874, three economists in three countries -- Menger, Jevons, and Walras -- each landed on the same new idea. Historians of economic thought call it one of the tightest cases of parallel invention ever. What name do they give this cluster?
answer: The marginal revolution
choices: The marginal revolution
The neoclassical synthesis
The Methodenstreit
The Keynesian revolution
context: The Methodenstreit was the later Menger-Schmoller quarrel over historicist versus analytic method; the neoclassical synthesis was the mid-twentieth-century Samuelson fusion of Keynes and Walras; the Keynesian revolution was the 1930s reversal against neoclassical orthodoxy. Only the 1871-1874 cluster is called the marginal revolution. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: In the 1870s, three economists in three different countries hit on the same idea at almost the same time. Carl Menger in Austria, William Stanley Jevons in England, and Leon Walras in Switzerland all said the same thing: the value of one more slice of pizza depends on how many slices you have already eaten. What do economists call this idea?
answer: Marginal utility
choices: Marginal utility
The labor theory of value
The invisible hand
Comparative advantage
context: Marshall married Jevons's marginal-utility insight to partial-equilibrium supply-and-demand diagrams, adding elasticity of demand, consumer surplus and the representative firm. The Cambridge School he founded dominated English-speaking economics for the next half century. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alfred Marshall'.

question: Carl Menger, the Austrian economist who founded the Austrian school in Vienna in 1871, read Leon Walras's plan to model the whole economy as one giant system of equations. Menger thought Walras was wrong at the deepest level, not just as a matter of technique. To Menger, economics was not like physics — it was about people making purposeful choices in real time. What was Menger's core objection to Walras?
answer: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
choices: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
The mathematics of 1874 was not yet advanced enough for the task
General-equilibrium models understate the importance of labour-time in value
Walras had rejected marginal utility in favour of pure cost-of-production
context: Menger accepted the marginal-utility insight the three founders shared; his disagreement was about method. This methodological gap between the Austrian and Lausanne roads persists to the present day and underlies the Austrian critique of modern DSGE modelling. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: The idea that each extra unit of a good is worth less than the one before had already been written down years before Menger, Jevons, and Walras made it famous in the 1870s. A German scholar named Hermann Heinrich Gossen laid it out in a book in 1854. Almost nobody noticed at the time. What does Gossen's earlier, ignored discovery show about big economic ideas?
answer: Big ideas often show up in more than one place before the world is ready to hear them
choices: Big ideas often show up in more than one place before the world is ready to hear them
Only one person can ever discover any economic idea
Economic ideas always come first from the most famous universities
Nobody thought about value at all before the year 1870
context: Gossen's 1854 Entwickelung der Gesetze des menschlichen Verkehrs laid down what are still called Gossen's Laws of diminishing marginal utility and equimarginal allocation. Robert Adamson of Manchester found the surviving copy in 1878 and Jevons publicly acknowledged Gossen's priority in the second edition of his own book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gossen's laws'.

question: In the 1870s, three economists working separately — Carl Menger in Vienna, William Stanley Jevons in England, and Leon Walras in Switzerland — all landed on the same insight. Value depends on the marginal unit, not the total. This became known as the Marginal Revolution. Once that move was on the table, an entire class of older classical value theories collapsed at one stroke. Which theory did it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
choices: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
The quantity theory of money later revived by Milton Friedman
The theory of comparative advantage stated by David Ricardo
The Malthusian population principle
context: Every rung of the labour-theory chain assumed value was a property of the good, fixed by its cost or labour input. The marginalist move denies the assumption: value is a ranking of the next unit by a specific chooser. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus were unaffected -- each addressed a different question. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: Three economists in three countries hit the same core insight within three years. That suggests the marginal idea was ripe by 1870. But the three roads split sharply into the Austrian, Cambridge, and Lausanne schools -- with different methods, styles, and reach. What does that split suggest about economics?
answer: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
choices: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
It is primarily an empirical laboratory science like chemistry
It is settled by mathematical proof once its axioms are stated
It has no genuine intellectual disagreements after 1874
context: The Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools agreed on the marginal-utility insight but disagreed sharply about whether economics should be prose-based praxeology, partial-equilibrium diagrams, or systems of simultaneous equations. Those methodological choices still divide the profession. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: In the 1800s, some economists in Germany said the only way to know an economy was to gather piles of historical facts and numbers from one particular country. This group was called the German Historical School. The Austrian economist Carl Menger and his followers in Vienna said no — collecting facts alone was not enough. What did the Austrians say you also needed?
answer: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
choices: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
The exact weight of every coin in circulation
A list of every farmer's birthday
A map of every road in the country
context: The book was Untersuchungen ueber die Methode der Socialwissenschaften (Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences, with Special Reference to Political Economics), 1883. Schmoller held the chair at the University of Berlin from 1882 and led what economists call the 'younger' German Historical School.
