Suddenly there was much more money chasing the same amount of bread, cloth, and grain, and prices in many European towns roughly doubled over a lifetime. What do we call it when lots of new money chases the same goods and drives prices up?
answer: Inflation
choices: Inflation
Deflation
A depression
A trade surplus
context: The School of Salamanca was a group of Dominican and Jesuit theologians at the University of Salamanca who wrote on price, money, labor, and just conduct in the context of the Spanish empire. Source: grokipedia.com/page/School_of_Salamanca.

question: In the 1500s, a group of Catholic scholar-priests at the University of Salamanca in Spain worked out early ideas about price, money, and just trade -- long before Adam Smith. Historians call them the School of Salamanca. Their leading founder was a Dominican friar who lived from 1483 to 1546. Who was he?
answer: Francisco de Vitoria
choices: Francisco de Vitoria
Thomas Aquinas
Duns Scotus
Bartolome de Las Casas
context: Francisco de Vitoria (1483-1546) led the Salamanca faculty during the crucial New-World-collision decades of the 1530s and 1540s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Francisco_de_Vitoria.

question: In 1556, a Spanish priest teaching at the University of Salamanca -- nicknamed Doctor Navarrus -- noticed that Spanish silver flooding in from the New World was pushing prices up all across Europe. He argued that more money chasing the same goods must mean higher prices. This idea later became known as the quantity theory of money. What was his real name?
answer: Martin de Azpilcueta
choices: Martin de Azpilcueta
Luis de Molina
Domingo de Soto
Tomas de Mercado
context: Martin de Azpilcueta (1491-1586), also called Doctor Navarrus, wrote Manual de Confesores y Penitentes (1556), which contains the earliest clean statement of the quantity theory of money. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: Martin de Azpilcueta was a Spanish priest and scholar teaching at the University of Salamanca in the 1500s. He noticed that silver flooding into Spain from one enormous mine high in the Andes had roughly doubled Spanish prices within his lifetime. That observation pushed him toward a money-based theory of inflation: more silver in circulation meant higher prices for the same goods. Which South American mine did the silver come from?
answer: Potosi
choices: Potosi
Zacatecas
Cerro de Pasco
Guanajuato
context: The Cerro Rico mine at Potosi (in modern Bolivia) was the largest source of the Spanish silver that flooded Iberian markets after 1545. Azpilcueta traced the price rise directly to that inflow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: In 1963, the American economist Milton Friedman published a famous one-line rule about money and prices -- that when the money supply grows faster than the amount of goods, prices rise, everywhere and always. Austrian economists like to point out that a Salamanca scholar, Martin de Azpilcueta, had made the same argument back in 1556 after watching American silver double Spanish prices. Which Friedman line did Azpilcueta beat him to by four centuries?
answer: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon
choices: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon
There is no such thing as a free lunch
Only government can create true monopoly
The natural rate of unemployment is exogenous
context: Friedman's famous dictum restated the same insight Azpilcueta had made four hundred years earlier while writing a confessor's manual. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: In sixteenth-century Spain, Catholic theologians at the University of Salamanca — later called the School of Salamanca — worked out early ideas about market prices, money, and just exchange. One Jesuit scholar of the school published a six-volume treatise from 1593 to 1609 arguing that a just price emerges from what buyers subjectively value a good at, not from the labor or cost that went into it. Who was he?
answer: Luis de Molina
choices: Luis de Molina
Francisco Suarez
Robert Bellarmine
Domingo Banez
context: Luis de Molina's De Iustitia et Iure (1593-1609) argued the just price is the price willing buyers and willing sellers would trade at in a normally functioning market, an early subjective-value move that anticipated Menger 1871. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Luis_de_Molina.

question: In 1995, the Austrian economist Murray Rothbard published a two-volume history of economic thought. He argued that the standard textbook story starts too late -- it begins with Adam Smith in 1776, as if nobody had thought carefully about prices, money, and fair exchange before then. Rothbard showed that a rich tradition of writing on these questions had gone on for centuries earlier. Which group did the book restore to the story?
answer: Medieval scholars who studied prices and money in monasteries and universities
choices: Medieval scholars who studied prices and money in monasteries and universities
Ancient Egyptian tax officials who ran the pharaoh's grain stores
Chinese silk-road merchants who first invented paper receipts
British factory owners of the 1800s industrial towns
context: Rothbard's An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (2 vols, Edward Elgar, 1995) argued that the classical story starting with Adam Smith in 1776 had overwritten the earlier Salamanca contributions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/An_Austrian_Perspective_on_the_History_of_Economic_Thought.

question: Modern historians now know that Spanish scholars in the 1500s -- men like Martin de Azpilcueta and Luis de Molina, working at the University of Salamanca -- worked out important ideas about prices, money, just wages, and fair trade. They did this more than two centuries before Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776. What does this earlier discovery show about the history of economic thought?
answer: Market ideas were being worked out for centuries before they became famous in English
choices: Market ideas were being worked out for centuries before they became famous in English
Adam Smith invented every economic idea from scratch by himself
Nobody thought seriously about money at all before the year 1700
Spanish scholars in the 1500s had no interest in trade or prices
context: Grice-Hutchinson's The School of Salamanca: Readings in Spanish Monetary Theory 1544-1605 (Oxford, 1952) was the first major English-language scholarly recovery of the tradition, from which Rothbard and Chafuen later drew. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marjorie_Grice-Hutchinson.

question: Public choice economists study the people who work in government — presidents, senators, agency staff, city clerks. Like everyone else, these people want things: re-election money, bigger department budgets, better jobs after their term ends. Public choice says we should assume they respond to those rewards, not to pure 'the public good.' What is the main idea?
answer: People in government act on incentives like everyone else
choices: People in government act on incentives like everyone else
People in government always put the public first
Voters always pick the best leaders
Bigger government always means better results
context: MacLean's book, 'Democracy in Chains: The Deep History of the Radical Right's Stealth Plan for America,' was published by Viking. It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist that year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: In 2017, the historian Nancy MacLean published Democracy in Chains, a book about the Nobel-winning public choice economist James Buchanan. MacLean argued Buchanan led a hidden right-wing project against American democracy -- a claim many economists and historians disputed on sourcing grounds. Even so, major book-industry institutions gave the book prominent recognition. Which of these did it earn?
answer: It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist
choices: It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist
It received the Pulitzer Prize for History in 2018
It was awarded the National Humanities Medal in 2019
It was chosen as the Book of the Year by the Financial Times
context: The mainstream-media reception shaped Buchanan's public image in the months after publication. That reception drove the intensity of the scholarly rebuttal that followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: A branch of economics called public choice, developed by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock in the 1960s, studies how politicians, judges, and bureaucrats respond to incentives — the same way grocers and shoppers respond to prices and profits. Public choice warns against one lazy view that many older civics textbooks used to take for granted. Which view is that?
answer: That government officials always act in the public interest
choices: That government officials always act in the public interest
That grocery shoppers pay attention to prices
That teenagers try to save some of their allowance
That farmers understand how crop rotation works
context: Munger's article documented specific instances of systematic misreading of Buchanan's correspondence and published work. He is a Duke political scientist who has worked in public-choice theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: James Buchanan was a Nobel-winning economist who co-founded public choice theory. In 2017 the historian Nancy MacLean published a book called Democracy in Chains, arguing that Buchanan's work was really a secret plot against democracy for wealthy donors. In December 2018, two economic-thought scholars took her book apart line by line. Their long rebuttal ran in one of the field's top journals. Which journal published that essay?
answer: The Journal of Economic Literature
choices: The Journal of Economic Literature
The American Economic Review
The Journal of Political Economy
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
context: The essay, 'The Sound of Silence: A Review Essay of Nancy MacLean's Democracy in Chains,' was written by Jean-Baptiste Fleury and Alain Marciano. It is often cited as the definitive scholarly response. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: After Nancy MacLean's 2017 book Democracy in Chains accused the Nobel economist James Buchanan of a secret plot for wealthy donors, scholars pushed back hard against her method. Reviews by Michael Munger, by Fleury and Marciano, by Peter Boettke, and by Bernstein and Adler all landed on one shared, specific charge about how MacLean had treated Buchanan's own writings and letters. What was that charge?
answer: That MacLean quoted Buchanan and his correspondents systematically out of context
choices: That MacLean quoted Buchanan and his correspondents systematically out of context
That MacLean invented fictional interviews with living historians
That MacLean plagiarized substantial portions from a rival author's work
That MacLean failed to disclose funding from a partisan advocacy group
context: Several key quotations were shown to reverse the actual meaning of Buchanan's writing; the alleged Buchanan-segregationist connection was not supported by the archival record MacLean cited. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: Imagine a high-school student in 2025 reading two books side by side. First: Nancy MacLean's 2017 Democracy in Chains, which won wide media praise and reached the National Book Award finals, arguing that the Nobel economist James Buchanan's public-choice work was a secret plot for wealthy donors. Second: the long detailed rebuttals in the Journal of Economic Literature and elsewhere, from scholars across the ideological spectrum, all pointing at the same textual and quotation problems. What broader analytical lesson does the pair teach about intellectual-history writing?
answer: When a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across ideological lines, that pattern is itself diagnostic
choices: When a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across ideological lines, that pattern is itself diagnostic
Any book on a Nobel-winning economist should be treated as automatically true
Any book criticized by libertarians must be presumed to be correct
Any book that reaches the National Book Award finals cannot contain systematic errors
context: The MacLean case is not one of 'both sides disagree.' Non-libertarian scholars who knew the primary sources (Munger, Fleury, Marciano) documented consistent misrepresentation. The pattern of rebuttal from experts across ideological lines is the relevant epistemic signal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: In November 1990, President George H.W. Bush signed Clean Air Act Amendments that included the world's first big cap-and-trade market. Power plants got a fixed number of tradable allowances they could buy and sell. Which pollutant did the Acid Rain Program target?
answer: Sulfur dioxide
choices: Sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen oxides only
Particulate matter
context: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments created a cap-and-trade market in sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions from coal-fired power plants. It was the first large national environmental market of its kind. Source: epa.gov (Acid Rain Program history).

question: In 1960, the British-American economist Ronald Coase wrote a paper called The Problem of Social Cost. It led, decades later, to a new way to fight pollution: instead of the government telling each factory exactly what to do, factories buy and sell rights to release a set amount. Cheap cleaners sell spare permits to expensive cleaners. What did that trading plan use, that regulators sitting in an office could not gather on their own?
answer: The dispersed knowledge utilities have about their own abatement costs
choices: The dispersed knowledge utilities have about their own abatement costs
The consumer preference rankings of household electricity buyers
The private lobbying strategies of trade associations
The confidential financial ratios of individual firms
context: Coase's insight: no central regulator can know every utility's marginal abatement cost. A market in emission rights routes reductions to whoever can achieve them cheapest -- using dispersed knowledge no bureaucrat can gather. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (October 1960).

question: In 1990, the US Congress updated the Clean Air Act. Coal-fired power plants were pouring out sulfur dioxide, and rain downwind was turning acidic and killing forests and fish. Instead of ordering every plant to install the same scrubber, the law set a national cap on total sulfur and issued tradable permits. Plants that could cut cheaply sold their spare permits to plants where cutting was expensive. What is this approach called?
answer: Cap-and-trade
choices: Cap-and-trade
Command-and-control
Pigouvian tax
Nationalization
context: US power-plant SO2 emissions fell approximately 40% below 1990 levels by 2005 -- meeting the statutory targets. Ellerman, Joskow et al., Markets for Clean Air (Cambridge UP 2000), gave the standard economic evaluation. Source: epa.gov (Acid Rain Program compliance reports).

question: The 1990 Clean Air Act launched America's Acid Rain Program, a cap-and-trade system where power plants bought and sold rights to release sulfur dioxide. Once running, it cost about $1 billion a year -- much less than anyone expected. Before the program started, budget analysts had estimated the older fixed-rule command-and-control plan would cost far more each year. What was their estimate?
answer: $4-6 billion per year
choices: $4-6 billion per year
$100 million per year
$40-60 billion per year
About the same as the actual program
context: CBO pre-program estimates were $4-6B/year under command-and-control. Actual market-based compliance came in near $1B/year -- 1/4 to 1/6 of the projected cost. The efficiency gain is what the Coase framework predicts. Source: Ellerman + Joskow et al., Markets for Clean Air (Cambridge UP 2000).

question: Ronald Coase was a British economist who won the Nobel Prize in 1991. He showed that clear property rights plus bargaining could handle pollution problems better than sweeping government rules. Applying his idea to green policy, the real choice designers face is not 'rules versus no rules.' What is the actual choice?
answer: Command-and-control versus property-rights-plus-trading
choices: Command-and-control versus property-rights-plus-trading
Federal versus state jurisdiction
Public versus private ownership
Voluntary compliance versus criminal enforcement
context: Both are forms of regulation. Command-and-control tells firms which technology to use; property-rights + trading sets a cap on total emissions and creates a market in the right to emit. The second uses dispersed knowledge; the first assumes the regulator has it. Source: Coase (1960); Ellerman + Joskow (2000).

question: A group of countries wants to lower factory pollution without simply banning things or setting one flat tax. Instead, their governments agree on a total limit -- a cap -- on how much a group of factories together can pollute each year. Each factory gets a share of permits under that cap. A factory that pollutes less than its share can sell its leftover permits to a factory that needs more. What is the general name for this kind of policy?
answer: Cap-and-trade
choices: Cap-and-trade
A carbon tariff
A production quota
A currency peg
context: The EU ETS launched January 1, 2005, covering CO2 emissions from power generation and heavy industry. It is the largest carbon market in the world and carries the same Coasean logic as the 1990 US Acid Rain Program. Source: ec.europa.eu (EU ETS overview).

question: A state passes a new climate law. It sets a legal ceiling on how much greenhouse gas its factories together can release each year, and that ceiling shrinks a little each year to force pollution down over time. Companies that cut their pollution below their share can sell their leftover permits to companies that go over. The state has effectively created a market in pollution rights. What kind of program is this?
answer: A cap-and-trade market
choices: A cap-and-trade market
A flat carbon tax
A total ban on all factories
A cash subsidy paid to polluters
context: California's AB 32 (the Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006) authorized the state cap-and-trade program that launched January 1, 2013. The program covers about 85% of state emissions. Source: ww2.arb.ca.gov (AB 32 history).

question: In 2009, US Representatives Henry Waxman of California and Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote a bill that would have set up a national cap-and-trade market for carbon dioxide, letting companies buy and sell permits to emit greenhouse gases. The bill passed the House but died in the Senate. Its collapse showed a specific weakness that cap-and-trade develops when the government hands out permits for free to well-connected industries. What is that weakness?
answer: Free-permit allocation attracts rent-seeking capture
choices: Free-permit allocation attracts rent-seeking capture
Cap-and-trade physically prevents any emissions reductions
Markets in emissions cannot be enforced under any circumstances
The Federal Reserve refuses to clear such transactions
context: Who gets the free initial allowances (rather than buying at auction) is a rent-seeking prize in the Tullock 1967 sense. Waxman-Markey allocated most permits free to incumbents; the Senate fight over allocation contributed to the bill's death. Source: Tullock (1967) applied; Congressional Research Service (Waxman-Markey history).

question: In the late 1980s, acid rain from coal-burning power plants was killing forests and lakes across the American Northeast. A Harvard economist named Robert Stavins helped design a new kind of plan for Congress. The federal government would cap total sulfur dioxide pollution from power plants and hand out permits equal to that cap. Plants that cleaned up faster could then sell their leftover permits to plants that lagged behind. The 1990 Clean Air Act wrote it into law. What is this plan called?
answer: Cap-and-trade
choices: Cap-and-trade
A pollution tariff
Direct government cleanup by hired crews
A total ban on all factory emissions
context: Project 88, led by Senators Timothy Wirth (D-CO) and John Heinz (R-PA) and drafted by Harvard's Robert Stavins, proposed cap-and-trade and other market-based instruments. Its influence shaped the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments. Source: hks.harvard.edu (Stavins bibliography).

question: In 1960, the British-American economist Ronald Coase published The Problem of Social Cost. Textbooks later boiled it down to a slogan called the Coase Theorem — that if property rights are clear and bargaining costs nothing, private parties will settle pollution and other spillovers on their own. Coase himself repeatedly said this missed his real argument. What is the accurate one-sentence characterization of the reasoning move he actually made?
answer: Compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
choices: Compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
Government should never intervene in any market failure
All externalities disappear if you draw the diagram correctly
Property rights should always be assigned to the wealthiest party
context: Coase's move: never compare a REAL institution to an IDEALIZED alternative. Command-and-control, property-rights + trading, and private bargaining all have their own transaction costs. Comparative institutional analysis counts them all. Source: Coase, 'The Firm, the Market, and the Law' (Chicago 1988).

question: The 1990 US Clean Air Act launched an emissions market for sulfur dioxide, the pollutant behind acid rain. Rather than order each coal plant to install identical scrubbers, the law capped total sulfur nationwide and let plants buy and sell tradable permits. The reasoning move at the heart of that design is a specific claim about who has the relevant knowledge for cheap abatement. Which best captures that move?
answer: Utilities know their own abatement costs; the regulator does not
choices: Utilities know their own abatement costs; the regulator does not
The regulator has access to superior technical modeling of every plant
The utilities' knowledge is irrelevant to cost-minimization
Only universities can properly estimate abatement costs
context: The Hayek-adjacent knowledge-problem insight: cheap abatement information is dispersed across thousands of plants and cannot be gathered centrally. A market in emissions permits routes the information into the allocation via prices. Source: Coase (1960); Hayek AER (1945) as background.

question: In 1920, right after the First World War, an Austrian economist in Vienna sat down to write a long essay. Many people around Europe were saying socialism would soon replace the market. He answered no — a fully socialist state, where the government owns all farms and factories, can never make smart choices. No private property means no trading, no trading means no real prices, and without prices no one can compare the cost of one plan against another. Who wrote it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Rudolf Hilferding
Joseph Schumpeter
Werner Sombart
context: 'Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen' appeared in Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik volume 47, 1920. Mises first delivered the argument at the Nationaloekonomische Gesellschaft in 1919. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: When Ludwig von Mises published his 1920 essay saying socialism could not calculate costs without market prices, other economists fired back. What followed was a forty-year argument between two camps: the Austrians on Mises's side, and socialists like Oskar Lange on the other. They fought over whether central planners could ever do the math that markets do when comparing costs. What is this famous fight usually called?
answer: The socialist calculation debate
choices: The Cambridge capital controversy
The socialist calculation debate
The Methodenstreit
The Keynes-Hayek exchange
context: The phrase covers the entire arc from Mises 1920 through the 1930s Lange-Lerner reply, Hayek's 1935 volume and 1945 essay, Mises's 1949 Human Action restatement, and the empirical verdict in 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: In the 1930s an economist tried to answer a big charge. Critics said socialism could not work with no real prices. His fix: a planning office could set prices by trial and error. Raise them when shortages hit. Lower them when there is a surplus. What was his big claim?
answer: Central planners can copy what markets do for prices
choices: Central planners can copy what markets do for prices
Central planning is impossible in principle
Only religion can guide an economy correctly
Trade with other countries is unnecessary
context: Oskar Ryszard Lange (1904-1965) taught statistics and economics at Chicago from 1938 to 1945; after the war he returned to Poland to serve its Stalinist government and try to prove his ideas in practice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: In the mid-1930s the Polish economist Oskar Lange wrote a reply to Ludwig von Mises. Mises had said socialism could not work without real market prices. Lange said a socialist state could copy the math of markets. A central board would guess a starting price for each good, watch to see if warehouses filled up or shelves went bare, and then adjust the price up or down. Because it borrowed the price-adjusting trick from real markets, this hybrid system got its own name. What is it called?
answer: Market socialism
choices: Command economy
Market socialism
Guild socialism
State capitalism
context: Lange's blueprint kept public ownership of the means of production but grafted on a trial-and-error price mechanism performed by planners rather than by exchange between owners. Abba Lerner refined it in 'The Economics of Control' (1944). Source: www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Lange.html.

question: In 1920 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises pointed out a hidden flaw in any fully socialist state. Real prices, he said, only appear when many buyers and sellers trade freely and haggle. In a country where the government owns every farm and factory, there are no traders and no real prices. Without them, planners cannot tell what to make, how much to make, or which way of making it wastes the least. What is this puzzle called?
answer: The socialist calculation problem
choices: The socialist calculation problem
The overproduction paradox
The trade-deficit puzzle
The wage-lag effect
context: Published by George Routledge & Sons in London in 1935, with Hayek's own introductory essay 'The Nature and History of the Problem' and Barone's 'Ministry of Production in the Collectivist State' as an appendix. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: Hayek's most famous essay said the facts you need to run an economy live in millions of minds. The tin miner's local rock, the shopper's list, the machinist spotting a faster tool. Prices, he said, pull all of it together on their own. Which journal ran the September 1945 essay?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: Economica
The American Economic Review
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
The Journal of Political Economy
context: 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' ran in AER volume 35, number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. It was written as a direct rebuttal of Oskar Lange's market-socialist proposal, reframing the argument from prices to knowledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: In 1945 the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek published a short essay called 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.' The Polish socialist Oskar Lange had argued that a central planning board could guess prices and adjust them like a market. Hayek granted the point — a board could make guess-and-check work on paper. But he said this missed something markets do that planners cannot copy at all. Which ability did Hayek give to markets alone?
answer: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
choices: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
Enforcing binding property rights against politically-connected insiders
Predicting long-run structural shifts in industry composition
Maintaining stable purchasing power across the business cycle
context: The market process is not primarily a calculating device; it is a knowledge-discovery device. The 'knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- who has a spare truck, which mine seam thinned out, which customer is ready to try a substitute -- exists only in the heads of the people on the spot. Prices summarise it. Source: fee.org/articles/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/.

question: The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises fled Vienna in 1934 to escape the coming Nazi rule and eventually settled in New York. There in 1949 he published a huge, thousand-page book called Human Action. It restated the argument he had been making since 1920: without real market prices set by real trading, no central planner can figure out how much of each good the country should make. What is the core problem he named?
answer: The economic calculation problem
choices: The economic calculation problem
The tax revenue problem
The population growth problem
The trade deficit problem
context: 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics' (Yale, 1949) devoted a full section to the impossibility of economic calculation under socialism, drawing on the twenty-nine years of debate since 1920. Hayek's parallel restatement came in 'Individualism and Economic Order' (1948). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: For decades, mainstream economists thought Lange's guess-and-check board had beaten Mises on paper. Austrian economists said no, but had to wait on history. What single event in November 1989 made even friendly mainstream economists reopen the question?
answer: The fall of the Berlin Wall
choices: The signing of the Maastricht Treaty
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Plaza Accord devaluation of the dollar
The passage of the Single European Act
context: On November 9 1989 East German official Guenter Schabowski, at a press conference, mistakenly announced immediate opening of the border; the wall was breached that night. Within two years every planned economy in Eastern Europe had collapsed and begun a market transition. Source: www.archives.gov/news/topics/berlin-wall-anniversary.

question: After the Soviet Union fell in the early 1990s, one long-time socialist economist wrote an essay. He had spent decades defending planning. But he admitted the free-market side of the 1920 planning debate had turned out to be right. What does this admission show?
answer: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
choices: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
Socialist economists never admit anything, no matter what happens in the world
The 1920 debate about planning was never actually settled by any evidence
Central planning worked well and only the Soviet version of it failed
context: The line was: 'It turns out, of course, that Mises was right.' Heilbroner (1919-2005) had held the Norman Thomas chair at the New School and had, in the 1953 first edition of 'The Worldly Philosophers', omitted Mises, Hayek and Friedman entirely. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right.

question: One Austrian economist argued central planners could not calculate real prices without markets. A second Austrian economist pushed the point deeper: even if planners had every price already, they still could not gather all the local knowledge that ordinary people use every day. What did the second thinker add to the first?
answer: The knowledge problem, that no central office can collect all the scattered facts guiding daily choices
choices: The knowledge problem, that no central office can collect all the scattered facts guiding daily choices
The tax problem, that planners cannot collect enough taxes
The voting problem, that planners cannot count votes accurately
The transport problem, that planners cannot ship goods on time
context: Don Lavoie (1951-2001) coined the modern phrase 'the knowledge problem' in this book and its companion 'National Economic Planning: What Is Left?' (both 1985). Peter Boettke and Virgil Storr edited the 2016 reissue. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: From 1930 to the mid-1950s the Soviet Union ran a huge system of forced-labor camps, scattered across Siberia and the far north. Prisoners — many of them arrested for saying the wrong thing or belonging to the wrong class — worked in freezing mines and forests, cutting timber and digging ore. Millions died of cold, hunger, and overwork. What Russian word is the name for this camp system?
answer: Gulag
choices: Gulag
Kolkhoz
Duma
Politburo
context: Glavnoye Upravleniye Lagerei (Main Camp Administration) ran the Soviet camp system. At peak it comprised over 400 camps and held several million prisoners at any given moment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag.

question: The Russian writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn had been a prisoner in the Soviet forced-labor camps himself. Back home he secretly wrote a huge book about what he had seen, kept the pages hidden from the secret police, and had friends smuggle them out on tiny rolls of film. When The Gulag Archipelago finally appeared in the West in 1973, it shook the world. What did his book give the world?
answer: The truth about the Soviet camps
choices: The truth about the Soviet camps
A love story from wartime Russia
A guide to Russian cooking
The plans of the Soviet space program
context: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (1918-2008) spent eight years in the camps (1945-53) after his arrest for a private letter mocking Stalin. His The Gulag Archipelago was published in Paris in three volumes 1973-75. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Solzhenitsyn.

question: In 1973 a Russian writer who had spent years inside the Soviet labor camps published a huge three-volume book in Paris exposing the whole camp system. His book broke the West's belief that the camps were a small problem. What did the book mostly reveal?
answer: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
choices: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
That the camps were actually schools of arts and crafts
That the camps held only convicted violent criminals
That Stalin had personally freed most of the prisoners
context: The Gulag Archipelago combined Solzhenitsyn's own experience with hundreds of survivor accounts he had collected. English translation appeared 1974-78 in three volumes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gulag_Archipelago.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Soviet writer who had survived Stalin's labor camps and secretly documented their horrors. In December 1973, the first book of his masterpiece The Gulag Archipelago was smuggled out and published in Paris. Two months later, in February 1974, the furious Soviet state hit back at him. What did they do?
answer: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
choices: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
Sentenced him to a new 15-year camp term
Placed him under indefinite house arrest in Moscow
Sent him to internal exile in Kazakhstan
context: Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the USSR on February 13, 1974. He lived in Vermont from 1976 to 1994 and returned to Russia in May 1994 after the USSR's fall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Solzhenitsyn.

question: In the late 1930s, the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin launched what became known as the Great Purge. He ordered mass arrests, staged show trials in Moscow, and executed generals, party members, poets, and ordinary citizens he thought disloyal. Soviet archives opened after the Soviet Union fell showed roughly how many people this campaign killed. What was that number?
answer: Well over a million people
choices: Well over a million people
Only a few hundred people at most
About ten thousand people in total
Zero people, since the trials were peaceful
context: Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (Macmillan, 1968) was pioneering. A 1990 revised edition (Oxford UP) folded in the archival numbers. Conquest reportedly suggested titling the new edition 'I Told You So, You... Fools' (an expletive softened for a family bank). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Terror.

question: From the 1920s through the 1950s, under Lenin and then Stalin, the Soviet government sent millions of people to forced-labor camps. Many were arrested for so-called political crimes — a joke about a leader, a friend abroad, a spoken doubt. The camps were scattered across Siberia and other freezing regions, and prisoners cut timber and mined gold in temperatures far below zero. What was this camp system called?
answer: The Gulag
choices: The Gulag
The Peace Corps
The Marshall Plan
The Warsaw Pact
context: Anne Applebaum's Gulag: A History (Doubleday, 2003) drew on newly opened Soviet archives. Her later work includes Iron Curtain (2012) on postwar Eastern Europe and Red Famine (2017) on Ukraine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag:_A_History.

question: The Gulag was the Soviet Union's vast network of forced-labor camps, running from Stalin's rise through his death in 1953. In her 2003 book Gulag: A History, the historian Anne Applebaum tallied every prisoner known to have passed through those camps between 1930 and 1953. What was her total figure?
answer: About 18 million
choices: About 18 million
About 1.8 million
About 180,000
About 180 million
context: About 18 million prisoners passed through the Gulag between 1930 and 1953, with roughly 1.5-1.7 million documented camp deaths. Further mortality in the deportation-settlement system for kulaks and deported peoples adds to the associated total. Source: Applebaum, Gulag: A History (2003).

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Russian writer who survived a Soviet labor camp himself and then spent years secretly interviewing more than two hundred other survivors. In 1970 the Nobel Prize in Literature honored his testimony against Soviet tyranny. His most famous work, a three-volume book, mapped the entire Soviet slave-labor camp system, camp by camp, region by region. What is that book called?
answer: The Gulag Archipelago
choices: The Gulag Archipelago
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
Cancer Ward
The First Circle
context: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1970 cited 'the ethical force with which he has pursued the indispensable traditions of Russian literature'. Solzhenitsyn could not travel to accept in Stockholm and finally received the medal at the 1974 Nobel ceremony after his expulsion. Source: nobelprize.org (Solzhenitsyn 1970).

question: In 1974, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's three-volume book The Gulag Archipelago appeared in the West and documented the Soviet labor-camp system in devastating detail. It hit the French intellectual left, which had long defended the Soviet Union, with real moral force. A group of former Maoist students in Paris broke with communism and began arguing that Marxist regimes produced camps, not paradise. What was this group called?
answer: The Nouveaux Philosophes
choices: The Nouveaux Philosophes
The New Left
The Frankfurt School
The Situationists
context: The Nouveaux Philosophes (New Philosophers) -- Andre Glucksmann, Bernard-Henri Levy, and others -- publicly renounced Marxism partly under the impact of Solzhenitsyn's book. The moment marked the French intellectual left's break with communist theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouveaux_philosophes.

question: In 1968 the British-American historian Robert Conquest published The Great Terror, a book about Stalin's mass killings of the 1930s. Working from letters, memoirs, and refugee accounts, he estimated the death toll far above the Soviet Union's official figures. For years many Western critics attacked his number as wildly too high. Then in 1991 the Soviet Union collapsed and the archives opened — and the numbers matched Conquest almost exactly. What does the opened archives matching Conquest reveal about honest outside estimates versus a closed regime's official numbers?
answer: Honest outside estimates can be closer to the truth than a closed regime's official numbers
choices: Honest outside estimates can be closer to the truth than a closed regime's official numbers
Historians outside a country can never estimate that country's deaths accurately
Soviet official statistics on the Terror were always accurate all along
The Great Terror actually caused very few deaths
context: The editor did not use the suggested title -- the 1990 revised edition was still called The Great Terror -- but the anecdote captured the intellectual settlement. Sovietologists who had dismissed Conquest's 1968 count as Cold War inflation found the archives confirmed his numbers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Conquest. (Original quote used an expletive; softened for a family bank.)

question: In 1995 the American economist Thomas Sowell wrote a book attacking a group he called 'the anointed' — people in universities, newspapers, and government who treat their own good intentions as proof that a policy worked, even when the real results are terrible. The book's main title was The Vision of the Anointed, and its subtitle named the habit outright. What was it?
answer: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
choices: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
Ideological Origins of Political Struggles
A Common Sense Guide to the Economy
The Decline, the Deception, the Dogmas
context: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic Books, 1995). The three rejected subtitles are also Sowell's own: A Conflict of Visions (1987), Basic Economics, and Inside American Education. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell).

question: In 1999 the American economist Thomas Sowell wrote a book about two very different ideas of fairness. One says everyone plays by the same rules and lives with the outcome. The other says that isn't enough — society must reach back and fix the unfair hands life deals so that outcomes come out even in the end. What did Sowell call this book?
answer: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
choices: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Discrimination and Disparities
A Conflict of Visions
Knowledge and Decisions
context: Published by the Free Press in 1999, with sections titled 'The Mirage of Equality', 'The Tyranny of Visions' and 'The Quiet Repeal of the American Revolution'. Sowell's word 'cosmic' is doing real work: the second standard is what someone would choose if he were designing the universe from scratch, and it is therefore not a standard any human institution can be held to. Source: Simon and Schuster publisher page (https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Quest-for-Cosmic-Justice/Thomas-Sowell/9780684864631).

question: Thomas Sowell's 2010 book on intellectuals opens by refusing the everyday meaning of the word. He does not mean a clever person, and he does not mean a person with degrees. His definition is narrower than that, and turns on the job itself. Whom does Sowell count as an intellectual?
answer: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
choices: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
Someone who holds a university post in the humanities
Someone who advises governments on questions of policy
Someone whose writing reaches a large popular audience
context: Sowell's phrase is that 'an intellectual's work begins and ends with ideas, not the practical application of ideas to real world problems.' The narrowness is deliberate and load-bearing: it is what lets him make the accountability argument later in the book, and it is why a surgeon or an engineer, however brilliant, is not an intellectual while doing his own job. Intellectuals and Society (Basic Books, January 5, 2010); a Revised and Expanded Edition followed in 2011.

question: In The Vision of the Anointed Thomas Sowell set out a four-stage pattern he says repeats through social policy. Stage one: a situation is proclaimed a crisis. Stage two: the anointed propose a remedy promising result A, while critics warn it will produce result Z. Stage three: result Z arrives. What does Sowell say stage four looks like?
answer: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
choices: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
The remedy is quietly repealed and its authors move on to a fresh crisis
Congress commissions an independent review that settles the disagreement
The critics are invited to draft the replacement legislation themselves
context: Sowell's line on stage four: 'No burden of proof whatever is put on those who had so confidently predicted improvement.' The champions may also argue that things would have been worse still without the remedy -- a claim that cannot be checked, and is not offered to be checked. Source: Mises Institute, 'How The Vision of the Anointed Explains Every Crisis in America' (https://mises.org/power-market/how-vision-anointed-explains-every-crisis-america).

question: Suppose a political campaign wants the government to pay back every group for wrongs done to their ancestors, so that outcomes finally come out even. In his 1999 book The Quest for Cosmic Justice, the American economist Thomas Sowell says the wish behind such a plan is decent. Still, he objects. Which objection does he press hardest?
answer: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
choices: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
That voters would never approve the taxes such a programme has to raise
That the agencies running the programme would capture most of the money
That courts, not legislatures, must settle questions of historical wrong
context: This is Hayek's knowledge problem carried into the moral realm: redressing disadvantage across ethnicities, generations and geographies would require knowing what every group's circumstances actually were and what each owes the others -- knowledge that is scattered, contested and in most cases gone. The rejected choices are real objections too (public choice, regulatory capture, constitutional), but they are not Sowell's move here.

question: Sowell compares the intellectual to a surgeon, an engineer, and a battle commander. A commander who fails at the wrong moment can pay with his own life. Sowell says the intellectual's work is judged by a very different test. Whose vote decides if an intellectual has done well?
answer: The peers who read the work and praise it
choices: The peers who read the work and praise it
The voters who elect politicians who adopt it
The publishers and editors who paid for it
The students who are taught it at university
context: Sowell's point is not that intellectuals are stupid or wicked; it is that the feedback loop that disciplines a surgeon or a bridge-builder is missing. Ideas are judged by whether they sound good to other people in the same trade. Whether they 'make life better or worse for others', Sowell writes, 'is another question entirely.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: In his 1995 book The Vision of the Anointed, the American economist Thomas Sowell described a four-stage pattern he saw again and again in modern policy. Stage one is 'the crisis' — a problem is announced as urgent, unbearable, requiring immediate action. Sowell's complaint about this stage is not that the trouble described is pleasant. It is that one particular check almost never gets run before the crisis is declared. Which check?
answer: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
choices: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
Whether a foreign country has already tried the proposed remedy
Whether the people affected were ever asked what they wanted
Whether the money to pay for the remedy exists anywhere at all
context: Sowell's wording: such a situation is 'routinely characterized as a crisis, even though all human situations have negative aspects, and even though evidence is seldom asked or given to show how the situation at hand is either uniquely bad or threatening to get worse. Sometimes the situation described as a crisis has in fact already been getting better for years.' A remedy introduced onto an improving trend can then claim credit for the trend.

question: Thomas Sowell's charge that intellectuals pay no price for being wrong leans on historical cases, and the one he presses hardest concerns Britain between the wars. British intellectuals of the 1930s campaigned hard on a question of national defence, and the country paid for their position within the decade. What did they campaign for?
answer: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
choices: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
For handing the navy's budget to the new air force
For a defence union with France and the Low Countries
Against keeping a garrison east of the Suez Canal
context: Sowell's wider claim in Intellectuals and Society is that during the twentieth century intellectuals 'have on balance made the world a worse and more dangerous place', often lending support to dictators. The interwar British case is his cleanest illustration of the accountability gap: none of the writers who argued against rearming lost their standing when the war came. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: In his 2010 book Intellectuals and Society, the American economist Thomas Sowell gave the word 'intellectual' an unusually narrow meaning: someone whose end-product is only ideas. That definition rules out many people the word normally covers. For example, an engineer who publishes brilliant papers on bridge design is not, by Sowell's test, working as an intellectual when he designs bridges. Why not?
answer: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
choices: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
Because he is paid by a firm rather than by a university
Because bridge design rests on physics rather than argument
Because he publishes for other engineers, not for the public
context: The test is not the subject matter, the employer or the audience -- it is whether the work terminates in ideas or in something the world can break. This is why Sowell's definition matters for the argument: the same person can be an intellectual on Tuesday, writing on social policy, and not one on Wednesday, signing off a span.

question: A campaigner defends a proposal by saying that all the experts agree with it, so obviously the country should do what they say. In his 2010 book Intellectuals and Society, the American economist Thomas Sowell argues that people whose only product is ideas usually face no personal cost when those ideas go wrong. His whole argument turns that expert-appeal into a question the listener ought to ask back. What is the question?
answer: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
choices: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
Which experts, and who paid for the studies they are citing?
How many experts disagree, and where has their work appeared?
How long have the experts held this view, and what changed it?
context: The rejected questions are worth asking too -- funding, dissent, and the history of a consensus all bear on it. But Sowell's specific contribution is the accountability question, because it sorts experts by the one variable his definition isolates: whether being wrong costs them anything. An epidemiologist, an actuary and a bridge engineer answer it very differently.

question: Sowell's 1995 book describes what policy elites do; his 2010 book asks why they can keep doing it, decade after decade, without the pattern ever breaking. The explanation he gives is structural rather than a claim about anyone's character. What is it?
answer: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
choices: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
Their credentials shield them from having to argue with outsiders
The press shares their politics and declines to report the failures
Voters forget quickly and rarely reopen an argument about old policy
context: This is the spine of the trilogy: The Vision of the Anointed (1995) records the pattern, The Quest for Cosmic Justice (1999) examines the standard that licenses it, and Intellectuals and Society (2010) supplies the mechanism. Note what the argument does not claim -- not that the anointed are dishonest, and not that their conclusions are always wrong. It claims that the occupation carries no cost for being wrong, so nothing in it corrects the error. A reader can accept the mechanism and still disagree with Sowell about any particular policy.

question: In the 1840s the French writer Frédéric Bastiat wrote short, funny essays defending free trade. His most famous point came in an essay called 'That Which is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen.' When the government does something — smash a window, hire workers, hand out a subsidy — you notice the visible result. But you also have to think about the hidden costs, the things that never got made because the money went elsewhere. What did he call this pair?
answer: The seen and the unseen
choices: The seen and the unseen
Supply and demand
The invisible hand
The gold standard
context: Bastiat was elected to the Constituent Assembly on April 23, 1848 as one of seven deputies from Landes, served on the finance committee, and generally voted with the center-left; his term ran until his death on December 24, 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat, writing in the 1840s, loved short and biting lines. One of his most famous defined the government this way: 'a big story where everyone tries to live at the cost of everyone else.' What was his point?
answer: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
choices: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
Government can print free money for everyone
Government workers pay their own salaries
Government spending never requires taxes
context: The essay 'The State' (L'Etat) appeared in near-final form in the Journal des Debats on September 25, 1848 after a shorter draft had run in Bastiat's own revolutionary paper Jacques Bonhomme in June. It was reprinted as a booklet by Guillaumin later the same year. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' contains the single most-quoted line he ever wrote: a compact one-sentence definition of what a government actually is. Fill in the blank: 'The state is the great ______ by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else.'
answer: fiction
choices: fiction
leviathan
machine
market
context: The French original reads 'L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde.' The Dean Russell English translation renders 'grande fiction' as 'great fictitious entity,' but 'great fiction' is the version that circulates in almost every 20th-century classical-liberal citation. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/frederic-bastiat-on-the-state-as-the-great-fiction-by-which-everyone-seeks-to-live-at-the-expense-of-everyone-else-1848.

question: Frédéric Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' opened with a joke prize. Not five hundred francs — a whole million, plus crowns, crosses, and ribbons of honor. It was offered to anyone who could give a clear, honest definition of one single word. Then Bastiat gave his own famous one-line entry, which mocked how everyone expects the government to feed them at everyone else's expense. Which word was the prize for?
answer: The word 'the State'
choices: The word 'the State'
The word 'liberty'
The word 'property'
The word 'the People'
context: The essay opens: 'I would like to see a prize founded, not of five hundred francs, but of a million, with crowns, crosses and ribbons, for the person who gives a good, simple and intelligible definition of this word: the State.' The mock contest was rhetorical -- Bastiat never had to pay out because, as he framed it, no non-mystical definition could avoid collapsing into the transfer-shape his own line named. Source: https://www.panarchy.org/bastiat/state.1848.html.

question: Frederic Bastiat was a French economist and pamphleteer in the 1840s. In one famous line he summed up bad government this way: the state is 'the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else.' What key insight about voting and public spending is he pointing at?
answer: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
choices: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
Voters can lower taxes just by voting for more spending
Governments always spend money on exactly the right things
Every citizen already produces enough to fund all programs
context: Jacques Bonhomme was Bastiat's short-lived revolutionary paper founded during the 1848 Paris moment; a draft of 'The State' ran there in June 1848 before the fuller version appeared in the Journal des Debats on September 25. 'Jacques Bonhomme' is the traditional French nickname for the rural common man -- the audience Bastiat pitched the essay to. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: In 1850 the French economist Frederic Bastiat published a pamphlet called The Law. He warned about a specific trick: get lawmakers to pass a law that makes taking property from your neighbor legal, and once it's on the books, the taking even looks respectable and orderly. What did Bastiat call this trick?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Free exchange
Voluntary trade
Simple charity
context: The Law (La Loi) was published in June 1850. It repeats and sharpens the 'great fiction' insight of the 1848 essay, casting the same claim as a critique of the perversion of legal force. Bastiat died on December 24, 1850. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: In 1848, revolution broke out in Paris and a wave of new state programs was on the table. The French economist Frederic Bastiat printed his essay The State in the Journal des Debats, one of the top Paris daily newspapers, aimed at a very specific slice of French society — the people he wanted his 'great fiction' warning about state benefits to reach. Which readership was that?
answer: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
choices: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
The Bonapartist Catholic peasantry
The Marxist Parisian workers' clubs
The Legitimist rural nobility
context: The Journal des Debats was historically the paper of liberal-Orleanist bourgeois opinion under Louis-Philippe and remained an influential centrist daily under the Second Republic. Bastiat chose it deliberately -- his target reader was the propertied liberal, not the barricade fighter. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: In 1986 the American economist James Buchanan won the Nobel Prize in economics. Together with Gordon Tullock he had built a whole school on one plain observation. Voters, politicians, and bureaucrats are people too. They use government power to help themselves — winning votes, expanding their agencies, steering benefits to friends and donors — and they respond to incentives like anyone else. What is the field they founded called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Labor economics
Behavioral finance
Game theory
context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for his work founding public choice theory -- the formal analysis of politics using economic tools -- with his 1962 book The Calculus of Consent, co-authored with Gordon Tullock, as the flagship text. Buchanan repeatedly cited Bastiat as the classical statement of the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: Two French essays published within eleven days in September 1848 both attacked the Provisional Government's promises. One was Bastiat's 'The State,' with its 'great fiction' line. The other, published in the same paper, was an article by Alexis de Tocqueville. The two men held one seat between them on the same committee of the Constituent Assembly that autumn. Which committee was that?
answer: The finance committee
choices: The finance committee
The judiciary committee
The military committee
The colonial committee
context: Bastiat served on the Constituent Assembly's finance committee through 1848-1849 -- the committee handling the tax and spending questions his 'great fiction' line directly framed. Tocqueville, elected the same April, served in the Assembly as well and would soon join the government as foreign minister. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: In 1848 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote that the state is 'the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else.' Free-market thinkers have quoted that line for more than a hundred and fifty years. But the real payoff for a reader today isn't the quotable slogan — it's the underlying reasoning move it presses on the reader. Which move does the line press?
answer: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
choices: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
That any government is a criminal conspiracy against its own population
That representative democracy is preferable to monarchy on efficiency grounds
That the free market always produces the best possible distribution of wealth
context: The 'great fiction' Bastiat is naming is the illusion that the state has some independent fund of wealth of its own; the reasoning move is that every promised benefit must in fact come from someone -- the tax-payer, the money-holder, the excluded competitor. The reader can accept or reject Bastiat's evaluation; the MOVE is the transfer-recognition. James Buchanan's public choice theory, honored with the 1986 Nobel, formalized the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: For a long time economists like Adam Smith and Karl Marx thought a thing's price should equal the hours of work put into making it — ten hours of labor should sell for twice as much as five. Then in the 1870s, three economists working separately in different countries — Carl Menger in Vienna, William Jevons in England, and Léon Walras in Switzerland — noticed something completely different. Where does a thing's value actually come from?
answer: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
choices: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
From how many hours the worker spent making it
From how much the raw materials cost
From the average price it usually sells for
context: Menger's move was to relocate value from the OBJECT to the SUBJECT: the same loaf of bread ranks high to a hungry man and low to a full one, so value is not a property of the loaf. The labor theory (Smith 1776, Ricardo 1817, Marx 1867) had made value inhere in the good; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced it in 1871-1874 with subjective valuation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book); mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: In 1871 the Austrian economist Carl Menger gave this famous example. A farmer has 5 sacks of grain and no way to buy or trade for more. He uses sack 1 for his own food, sack 2 for extra food, sack 3 to feed chickens, sack 4 to brew whisky, and sack 5 to feed his pet parrots. Then robbers steal just one sack. Which use does he drop first?
answer: The least important one -- parrot feed
choices: The least important one -- parrot feed
The most important one -- basic food
He splits the loss across every use equally
The oldest use -- whisky-brewing
context: Menger's core marginal move is right here: the value of ONE sack is not the average across all uses and not the most important use, it is the LEAST important use the farmer would sacrifice on losing one. This is why the SAME grain is worth different amounts to a well-supplied farmer and a starving one -- their marginal uses differ. The example is from Book 3 of the 1871 Grundsaetze. Source: ecaef.org/carl-menger-and-the-idea-that-broke-economics-open/.

question: Adam Smith noticed a strange puzzle in 1776. Water is needed for life yet almost free. Another substance is not needed for life at all yet sells for a fortune. This puzzle took about 95 years to solve. Which substance was the expensive one in Smith's puzzle?
answer: Diamonds
choices: Diamonds
Salt
Tulips
Silk
context: Smith wrote: 'Nothing is more useful than water, but it will purchase scarce anything... A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' Smith moved on rather than solving it; the resolution waited for the 1871 Marginal Revolution. Salt was famously scarce in some ancient economies but not Smith's example; the tulip mania (1637) is a bubble story, not the paradox; silk was expensive but not paradoxically so. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: In the early 1870s something strange happened in economics. Three different economists in three different countries — Carl Menger in Austria, William Stanley Jevons in England, and Léon Walras in Switzerland — all independently figured out the same key idea about how value really works, each on his own within a few years of the others. None of the three had read the others' papers. Historians later gave that whole cluster of near-simultaneous discoveries a single name. What is it called?
answer: The Marginal Revolution
choices: The Marginal Revolution
The Keynesian Revolution
The Industrial Revolution
The Neoclassical Synthesis
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of the clearest cases of parallel discovery in intellectual history. The Methodenstreit was Menger's later 1883 quarrel over method with the German Historical School; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Paul Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Source: economicsandhistory.substack.com/p/the-marginal-revolution-and-neoclassical.

question: How can water, which we need to live, be nearly free while diamonds cost a fortune? An economist named Menger said the puzzle disappears once you stop comparing all the water in the world with all the diamonds. What is a person actually ranking when they choose?
answer: The next unit added to what they already have
choices: The next unit added to what they already have
The average price over the last ten years
The total amount produced worldwide each year
The moral worth of the person who wants it
context: A city-dweller with a full tap ranks the NEXT glass of water near-zero -- his thirst is already met; the NEXT diamond added to a collection nobody has still ranks high because it is scarce. Total utility of water is enormous and of diamonds tiny; the MARGINAL utility is the reverse, and price tracks the margin. This is Menger's founding move: value is set at the margin, not by the class. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: Carl Menger, the Vienna economist who founded the Austrian school in 1871, said that some things meet real human wants but are still not 'economic goods.' Mountain air and seawater are there in unlimited supply, so nobody ever has to choose between one breath and another. Something must be true of a good before a chooser has to rank one unit against the next. What does Menger require?
answer: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
choices: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
The good must have taken labor to produce
The good must be legally recognized as property
The good must have a market price above zero
context: For Menger, an unlimited good has utility but no VALUE, because no chooser is ever forced to give up one use to serve another -- there is no ranking at the margin. Only when the good is scarce relative to the wants it could satisfy does a chooser have to rank the marginal unit, and only then does the subjective theory generate a price. Labor-cost, legal recognition, and positive market price are consequences of scarcity, not its cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: A tailor spends 10 hours making a badly-cut, badly-sewn suit that hangs poorly. A second tailor spends 5 hours making a well-cut, well-sewn suit that fits beautifully. On the labor theory of value the first suit should be worth about twice the second. On the subjective theory that Menger pressed against the classical tradition, which comparison actually holds?
answer: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
choices: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
The two suits are worth the same, because labor is labor
The 10-hour suit is still worth more, because it embodies more work
Neither suit has any value until a market price is quoted
context: This is the sharp edge of Menger's move against the labor theory: labor-hours cannot GENERATE value if a chooser ranks the badly-made product lower. Value flows one way only, from the ranking down to the price; labor spent producing something no one ranks highly is labor wasted, not value created. If the labor theory cannot survive this simple case, then Marx's entire theory of surplus value and exploitation -- built on the labor theory -- has no floor to stand on. Source: mises.org/articles-interest/subjective-theory-value.

question: David Ricardo's 1817 Principles said the value of a good comes from the labor put into it. Fifty years later, a German exile in London built a whole theory of capitalist exploitation on that base. He said 'socially needed labor time' was the source of every good's value, and the gap between that value and the worker's wage was surplus taken by the boss. Menger's subjective theory tears the whole thing apart by showing labor cannot make value at all. Whose 1867 book carries the exploitation argument the subjective theory undoes?
answer: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
choices: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
John Stuart Mill, in Principles of Political Economy
Thomas Malthus, in An Essay on the Principle of Population
Jean-Baptiste Say, in A Treatise on Political Economy
context: Marx's 1867 Das Kapital vol. 1 inherits Ricardo's labor theory and refines it as 'socially necessary labor time'; the entire theory of surplus value, exploitation, and the falling rate of profit depends on labor being the source of value. If Menger's subjective account is right, this foundation is gone: value comes from the chooser's ranking, not from labor-hours. Boehm-Bawerk drove the point home explicitly in Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896). Mill (1848), Malthus (1798), and Say (1803) all predate Marx and do not carry the exploitation theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_theory_of_value.

question: In the 1870s, Austrian economists like Carl Menger developed the subjective theory of value: the price a buyer will pay for the next unit lives inside his own head, set by how he ranks that unit against every other use only he knows. A central planning board trying to set a rational price hits a wall no dataset can fix, because the key fact is not written down anywhere. Which later Austrian argument does this feed straight into?
answer: Mises's socialist calculation argument
choices: Mises's socialist calculation argument
Ricardo's comparative advantage argument
Friedman's monetarist quantity theory
Coase's transaction-cost theorem
context: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth runs directly out of subjective value: if value lives in individual choosers' rankings, then a central planning board without market prices has no way to know how to allocate scarce means -- the information it would need is dispersed across millions of heads and revealed only through the choices those choosers actually make. Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' extends the same point. Ricardo, Friedman, and Coase pressed unrelated arguments. Source: mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Carl Menger's 1871 Principles launched the Marginal Revolution — but no English edition appeared for 79 years, so the ideas reached America through Mises's students, not the book. What core Menger insight explains why the fourth glass of water is worth less to you than the first?
answer: Diminishing marginal utility
choices: Diminishing marginal utility
Comparative advantage
Labor theory of value
Rent-seeking loss
context: The 1950 Free Press edition appeared 29 years after Menger's death (1921), 79 years after the German original (1871), and only after Menger's pupil Hayek had already moved from Vienna to LSE (1931) and then Chicago (1950). Frank Knight -- Milton Friedman's teacher at Chicago -- wrote the introduction. The gap is a measure of how far the Austrian tradition had traveled inside German-speaking economics before English-speaking economics noticed the founding text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In 1912 in Vienna, a 31-year-old economist finished his first big book. It was called The Theory of Money and Credit, and he also handed it in as the thesis he needed to be allowed to teach at the University of Vienna. In it he traced the value of money all the way back to its non-money beginnings, and founded what became known as Austrian money theory. Who was the young author?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Carl Menger
Ludwig von Mises
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Friedrich Hayek
context: Ludwig von Mises (born Sep 29 1881) was 31 when 'Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel' appeared. He submitted it as his Habilitationsschrift to obtain the venia legendi, the license to lecture at university level. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; mises.org/library/book/theorie-des-geldes-und-der-umlaufsmittel.

question: Ludwig von Mises was an Austrian economist who wrote a landmark book about money in German in 1912. In English it is called 'The Theory of Money and Credit.' What was the original German title?
answer: Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen
Menschliches Handeln
context: 'Umlaufsmittel' literally means 'means of circulation'; Batson translated it as 'fiduciary media' inside the text, but the publisher chose the cleaner 'Money and Credit' for the English title. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: A shopkeeper asks: why does a silver coin have any value at all? People say, because it buys stuff today. But it only buys stuff today because it bought stuff yesterday, and the day before, and back and back. If you keep going back in time, what did the coin's value first come from?
answer: A time when silver itself was a useful thing people wanted for jewelry, tools, and trade
choices: A time when silver itself was a useful thing people wanted for jewelry, tools, and trade
A government law that ordered everyone to accept it
A magic property built into the coin at the mint
A promise from a bank to trade it for something else
context: Mises's move: today's demand rests on yesterday's known purchasing power, and you can trace the chain back through time until you reach a moment when the money-good had a non-monetary use (gold as jewelry, silver as ornament, cattle as food). The circularity dissolves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: Economists in the early 1900s noticed a pattern. When a central bank makes loans very cheap, businesses build lots of new factories and houses. A few years later, many of those projects turn out to be losers and shut down. What did the economists call this up-then-down cycle?
answer: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
choices: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
The natural rhythm of the seasons
The result of workers asking for higher pay
A punishment sent by foreign competitors
context: Hayek's LSE lectures 'Prices and Production' (1931) built the roundabout-production capital theory of Boehm-Bawerk together with Mises's monetary seed into the full ABCT: artificially low interest rates from bank credit expansion distort the structure of production, generating an unsustainable boom that must end in a bust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: Back in 1871 Carl Menger had left a puzzle unsolved: where does money's value come from in the first place, when its whole use is just to buy other things? In his 1912 book The Theory of Money and Credit, Ludwig von Mises answered him. Mises traced money demand back in time, one day at a time, deeper and deeper. It had to land on a moment where the chain could finally close. What kind of moment was that?
answer: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
choices: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
A day when a sovereign first stamped his image on a coin and decreed its face value
A day when a chartered private bank first issued notes payable to bearer on demand
A day when a joint-stock company first offered redeemable shares in a public market
context: Gold jewelry and dentistry, silver ornament, cattle used for food and traction, salt for preservation. Once the chain lands on a real barter-good with real demand for its own sake, the value it later carries as money is grounded in something outside the circular loop. Source: mises.org/online-book/man-economy-and-state-power-and-market/5-marginal-utility-money/b-money-regression.

question: In 1912 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published a book called The Theory of Money and Credit. He argued that when a central bank prints a lot of new money, prices don't rise evenly across the whole economy — the new money enters at specific points and reaches different people at very different times. Who, Mises said, gets hurt first and worst by this uneven rise?
answer: Savers and people on fixed incomes
choices: Savers and people on fixed incomes
Bankers who receive the new money first
Government officials who set the policy
Owners of gold and silver mines
