context: The 1953 Yale edition added Part Four -- Mises's direct response to the Keynesian orthodoxy that had swept postwar Anglo-American economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: In 1963 the American economist Murray Rothbard, one of the leaders of the Austrian school, published a short, punchy book called What Has Government Done to Our Money? In it he explained that governments all through history have quietly cheated the people who use their currency — either by shaving down the amount of gold or silver in each coin, or by printing extra paper notes that dilute what already exists. What is that practice called?
answer: Currency debasement
choices: Currency debasement
Free banking
The gold standard
A trade surplus
context: Rothbard packed the case for commodity money and against government-run currency into a booklet aimed at the general reader. Fifty years on it remains the standard introduction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Has_Government_Done_to_Our_Money%3F.

question: In January 2009 a new digital money called Bitcoin was mined for the first time. It was only digital. No state backed it. It had never traded as anything else. Some Austrians said Mises had ruled it out. They pointed to one part of his 1912 argument. Which part did they use against Bitcoin?
answer: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
choices: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
The quantity theory's requirement of stable velocity of circulation
The state theory's requirement of tax-driven acceptance
The real-bills doctrine's requirement of short-term commercial backing
context: The debate raged in Austrian circles from about 2011. Critics argued Bitcoin was born as pure money and therefore was ruled out on Misesian grounds; defenders had to find the prior demand Mises's chain required. Source: mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bitcoin-regression-theorem-and-emergence-new-medium-exchange.

question: In 2013 the writer Konrad Graf answered an old Austrian objection to Bitcoin. Critics said Bitcoin broke Ludwig von Mises's 1912 rule that any money must grow out of an earlier non-money use. Graf answered that the earliest Bitcoin users — cypherpunks and cryptography hobbyists — already valued Bitcoin for a real, direct use, even before anyone treated it as money. What use did Graf point to?
answer: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
choices: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
Its use as a store of value with a predictably fixed twenty-one-million supply cap
Its use as a settlement layer for high-frequency exchange trading
Its use as programmable collateral for decentralised lending contracts
context: The first buyers wanted the tokens because the underlying protocol did something no other technology could -- move digital value across a network without a trusted third party. That utility, present before any market price, was the non-monetary demand the regression theorem required. Source: www.konradsgraf.com/blog1/2013/2/27/in-depth-bitcoins-the-regression-theorem-and-that-curious-bu.html.

question: Not every Austrian thought Mises's regression theorem needed defending against Bitcoin. Robert Murphy and Silas Barta split from Konrad Graf and Peter Surda. They refused to hunt for a prior non-money use at all. They said Mises's 1912 argument answered a different question than Bitcoin poses. How did they read the reach of the theorem?
answer: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
choices: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
As overturned by Milton Friedman's 1956 restatement of the quantity theory
As applying only to commodities Menger's 1892 essay classified as saleable
As already refuted by Georg Knapp's 1905 state theory of money
context: Murphy and Barta treated the theorem as a historical explanation of how commodity monies emerged, not a constraint on future ones. Konrad Graf, Peter Surda, and Jeffrey Tucker took the other route -- accept the theorem, find the prior non-monetary demand. Source: stephankinsella.com/2025/07/austrians-bitcoin-impossible/.

question: A Wall Street bank boss becomes the Treasury Secretary (top government money job) for a few years, then quits and goes right back to Wall Street as a top-paid banker. Later his bank gets in trouble and the government bails it out. What is this move called?
answer: The revolving door between government and Wall Street
choices: The revolving door between government and Wall Street
An arm's-length transaction
A pure free market
A public works project
context: Robert Rubin, Goldman Sachs 1966-1992, Treasury Secretary 1995-99 under Clinton, Citigroup executive committee 1999-2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rubin.

question: In late 2008, big US banks like Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers were failing or on the edge of failing. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson rushed a $700 billion rescue plan through Congress, using taxpayer money to keep the surviving banks alive. What do we call it when the government spends tax money to save a private business from failing?
answer: A bailout
choices: A bailout
A tariff
A tax cut
A stimulus check
context: Henry 'Hank' Paulson joined Goldman in 1974, became CEO in 1999, and served as Treasury Secretary July 2006 to January 2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulson.

question: In September 2008 the giant American insurance company AIG was about to collapse from a wave of bad housing-linked bets. The US Treasury put up roughly 180 billion dollars to rescue AIG, and much of that money then flowed straight out to the big Wall Street banks that had done business with AIG. Economists call the danger that grows out of rescues like this 'moral hazard.' What is the worry when the government rescues big banks like this?
answer: Banks will take even bigger risks next time, since they expect another rescue
choices: Banks will take even bigger risks next time, since they expect another rescue
Small savers will suddenly earn much higher interest
Ordinary shoppers will pay less for groceries
Banks will start refusing to lend to anyone at all
context: Goldman received approximately $12.9B as an AIG counterparty via the ~$182B AIG rescue. The AIG-Goldman payments became a focal point of revolving-door criticism of the 2008 crisis response. Source: fcic.gov (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report, 2011).

question: Timothy Geithner had a long career moving between finance and government. From 2003 to 2009 he led the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the arm of the Fed closest to Wall Street. From 2009 to 2013 he served as Treasury Secretary under President Obama, running the bank bailouts of the financial crisis. After he left the Treasury, what kind of private firm did he join as president?
answer: A private-equity firm
choices: A private-equity firm
A hedge fund
A public university
A commercial airline
context: Geithner joined the private-equity firm Warburg Pincus as president in March 2014. His 2014 memoir Stress Test explicitly defends the 2008-09 bailouts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Geithner; warburgpincus.com.

question: Janet Yellen chaired the US Federal Reserve, the central bank that sets American interest rates, until 2018. After she stepped down she spent the next two years traveling and giving paid speeches to bankers and investors, pulling in about $7 million before President Biden made her his Treasury Secretary in 2021. Who paid most of that speaking money?
answer: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
choices: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
European central banks
US public school districts
Nonprofit advocacy groups
context: Yellen's financial disclosures documented approximately $7M in Wall Street speaking fees over the two-year interval. The pattern -- top financial-regulator role followed by high-fee industry advisory -- matches the earlier three Treasury secretaries. Source: US Office of Government Ethics disclosures 2020-21.

question: In 2009 the American economist Simon Johnson, a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), gave a public warning about big Wall Street banks. He said they had grown so powerful that they helped write the very rules meant to regulate them -- lawmakers took their advice, hired their people, and copied their language. What is this pattern called?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Free-market competition
Proof-of-work mining
Voluntary exchange
context: Simon Johnson, 'The Quiet Coup' (The Atlantic, May 2009). Johnson, MIT professor and former IMF chief economist, applied his IMF-era capture-diagnosis toolkit to the US financial-crisis response. Source: theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2009/05.

question: In 2012 the University of Chicago economist Luigi Zingales, an Italian-born free-market thinker, published a book aimed at American readers. He argued that America's finance industry had drifted away from real competitive capitalism into what he called 'crony capitalism' -- a system in which big firms use political connections to bend the rules in their favor. He asked for pro-market reforms to take the country back. What did he name the book?
answer: A Capitalism for the People
choices: A Capitalism for the People
The Wealth of Nations Revisited
The Bailout State
Free Markets Under Fire
context: Luigi Zingales, A Capitalism for the People: Recapturing the Lost Genius of American Prosperity (Basic Books, 2012). Zingales -- Italian-born, teaching at Chicago Booth -- became a mainstream-economics voice against financial-sector regulatory capture. Source: basicbooks.com (Zingales 2012).

question: In 2019 the head of a US agency that regulates drug companies stepped down. Soon after, he took a paid seat on the board of a big drug company he had just been regulating. What is this pattern of moving between regulator and regulated industry called?
answer: The revolving door
choices: The revolving door
Insider trading
A market corner
A public buyback
context: Scott Gottlieb, FDA Commissioner 2017-19, joined the Pfizer board in June 2019. It is a parallel modern case of the pattern documented across finance, defense, and pharmaceutical regulation. Source: pfizer.com (board announcement June 2019).

question: Simon Johnson and Luigi Zingales are two American economists who study why regulators so often end up defending the very industries they oversee. Both point to the revolving door -- an official leaves a big bank to work at the Treasury or the Fed, then leaves government to return to a big bank. They call it a form of regulatory capture. What feature of the setup makes the capture work?
answer: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
choices: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
Regulators are secretly bribed with cash payments
Federal law requires all regulators to work in industry first
The industry has hidden veto authority over hiring decisions
context: The Stigler-capture-via-revolving-door mechanism: the career incentives of every serving official partly align with the industry regardless of individual character, because the qualified pool has this shape by construction. This is institutional-incentive selection, not corruption. Source: Johnson (2009); Zingales (2012); Stigler (1971).

question: From 1988 to 2013 four US Treasury secretaries -- Nicholas Brady, Robert Rubin, Henry Paulson, and Timothy Geithner -- all came out of Wall Street firms or the New York Federal Reserve before taking the top financial-regulation post in the US government. Public-choice economists use this Wall-Street-to-Treasury pattern to illustrate a general reasoning move about who ends up in top financial regulation. The move is not the claim that these individuals were personally corrupt. What is the actual claim?
answer: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
choices: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
The pattern is criminal conspiracy prosecutable under federal statute
The pattern is entirely random and requires no explanation
The pattern is imposed by international treaty obligations
context: Each of the four served legally and by presidential appointment. The critique targets the STRUCTURAL pattern that produces the pattern: the pool of qualified candidates comes from and returns to the industry. Source: Zingales (2012); Johnson (2009); Stigler (1971).

question: In 2014 three economists -- Marianne Bertrand, Matilde Bombardini, and Francesco Trebbi -- published a paper that tried to put a dollar figure on Washington's 'revolving door.' They tracked former Members of Congress and senior congressional staffers who quit public service and went to work as lobbyists for private clients. When they compared the new lobbying salaries with the old government pay, they found a large jump. What pay jump over the old government salary does their research usually find?
answer: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
choices: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
10 to 20 percent premiums
Essentially no premium over public pay
Pay cuts of 30 to 50 percent
context: The Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi 2014 AER paper 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?' documented substantial premiums for connected lobbyists, consistent with a market pricing capture-value. Source: aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.12.3885.

question: In the 1800s some economists, like the Frenchman Antoine Cournot, wrote in heavy mathematics that only trained scholars could follow. Frederic Bastiat, a French classical liberal of the same era, took the opposite path on purpose. What kind of writing did he choose?
answer: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
choices: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
Formal mathematical proofs
Latin scholastic disputation
Long-form academic treatises
context: Bastiat wrote so that a French farmer could follow the argument, deliberately unlike Cournot's 1838 Recherches that used calculus to model demand curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Antoine_Augustin_Cournot.

question: Frederic Bastiat was a French economist and writer in the 1840s who taught economics through short, punchy essays. He almost always started each essay with something the reader could actually picture -- a broken shop window, a new railway, a debate in the French chamber of deputies -- before drawing any lesson. What is this opening move called?
answer: Starting with a concrete scene
choices: Starting with a concrete scene
Starting with a mathematical equation
Starting with a historical statute
Starting with a syllogism
context: Part one of the Bastiat method: put a scene in front of the reader before you make the argument. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Frederic Bastiat, the French economist of the 1840s, taught a rule for arguing well against opponents. Before you answer someone's argument, he said, you must first restate that argument in a certain form -- not the sloppy version but the best possible version, so your reply is fair. In what form must you state the other side?
answer: In its strongest form
choices: In its strongest form
In its weakest form
In caricature form
In its shortest form
context: Part two: state the opposing view sympathetically and at its strongest. This is Bastiat's 'ineptly defended' discipline, later renamed 'steelmanning' in 21st-century rationalist writing. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Frederic Bastiat, the 1840s French economist, had a three-step method for demolishing bad economic arguments. First, describe what people see and applaud. Second, name what the opposing view is missing. Third, drag into the light what the opposing view has hidden. This last step is the surprise turn that surfaces what a policy actually costs. What does the third step trace?
answer: The unseen consequences
choices: The unseen consequences
The historical antecedents
The mathematical proof
The alternative equilibrium
context: Part three: trace the unseen -- the tailor whose sale was lost when the shopkeeper repaired his broken window, the worker priced out by the minimum wage, the consumer who paid more for domestic goods. Source: bastiat.org.

question: In 1946 the American journalist Henry Hazlitt published a slim book with Harper & Brothers. Chapter by chapter, he used Frederic Bastiat's seen/unseen method to test New Deal policies like price controls, rent control, tariffs, and public-works spending. It became the most-read popular Austrian economics book in English. What is the book's title?
answer: Economics in One Lesson
choices: Economics in One Lesson
Basic Economics
Free to Choose
The Wealth of Nations
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) is a chapter-by-chapter application of the seen/unseen method to mid-20th-century American policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: In 1980 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book that used the same seen/unseen method Frederic Bastiat had used a century earlier. Sowell applied it to modern policy, testing big political claims against the small everyday choices real people make with the limited knowledge they have. What is the book's title?
answer: Knowledge and Decisions
choices: Knowledge and Decisions
A Conflict of Visions
Basic Economics
The Vision of the Anointed
context: Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) is the most sustained modern application of the classical-liberal knowledge-and-decision framework to policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Frederic Bastiat's method -- the seen, the not-seen, the hidden -- is powerful for arguing about tariffs, government make-work schemes, and his famous broken-window parable. But it is not built for every classical-liberal topic. Which topic does Bastiat's method not by itself give the tools for?
answer: Monetary theory and business-cycle analysis
choices: Monetary theory and business-cycle analysis
Public-facing argument about tariffs
Public-facing argument about make-work schemes
Public-facing argument about the broken window
context: For monetary theory the tradition needs Menger, Mises, and Hayek; for capital theory Bohm-Bawerk; for public choice Buchanan and Tullock. Bastiat's method is the first tool, not the only one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote almost his entire published output in a short burst at the end of his life. His book The Law, his Economic Sophisms, and Economic Harmonies were all packed into the years just before he died of tuberculosis in 1850. Roughly how many years did his major writing career span?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Twenty-five
Fifteen
Two
context: Bastiat farmed at Mugron in the Landes for most of his adult life, publishing his first major essays in 1844-1845 and dying December 24, 1850. The pamphlets, sophisms, and Harmonies were all produced in that five-year window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: For decades the United States has kept the price of one common food at about twice the world price. It does this by strictly limiting how much of that food can be brought in from other countries and by giving low-interest loans to American growers of the crop. Kids taste this price every time they buy candy or soda. Which food is it?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Coffee
Cocoa
Vanilla
context: The US Sugar Program, established by the Sugar Act 1934, still runs under each Farm Bill; typical US price in the 2010s was about 35 cents per pound against a world price of about 17 cents. Source: gao.gov/products/rced-00-126.

question: The US government puts a big tariff -- a tax on imports -- on sugar brought in from Brazil, Mexico, and other countries. Because of that tariff, sugar in America costs about twice as much as sugar sold on the world market. Millions of families notice it every time they buy candy, soda, or baked goods. Who is hurt most?
answer: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
choices: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
American sugar farmers -- they lose sales
Foreign sugar growers -- they gain a bigger market
No one -- everyone pays the same price
context: The Sugar Act 1934 first structured the quota, loan, and allotment system that still supports US sugar prices today under the 2018 Farm Bill's re-authorization. Source: grokipedia.com/page/United_States_Sugar_Program.

question: In 2003 the candy company Kraft closed the Michigan factory that made Life Savers, the famous ring-shaped hard candy that kids have chewed for a century. Kraft moved production to Montreal, Canada, because US sugar cost about twice as much as Canadian sugar -- and sugar is the main ingredient of a Life Saver. Why was American sugar so pricey?
answer: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
choices: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
American sugar tastes different from Canadian sugar
Sugar cannot grow anywhere in the United States
The US mint uses sugar to make coins
context: Kraft Foods moved Life Savers production from Holland, Michigan to Montreal in 2003 because Canadian sugar was about half the US price under the US Sugar Program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Life_Savers.

question: American sugar tariffs and import quotas keep US sugar prices at roughly double the world price. Candy makers who rely on cheap sugar have to buy at that inflated price. In the 2000s, two big Chicago-area candy makers moved much of their production overseas, saying they could no longer afford to buy sugar inside America. Which pair of companies moved?
answer: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
choices: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
Hershey and Mars
Wrigley and Tootsie Roll
See's and Ghirardelli
context: Ferrara Pan Candy Company moved much of its Chicago-area production to Mexico in the 2000s; Brach's Confections closed its Chicago plant in 2003 and moved to Mexico. Both cited US sugar prices. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ferrara_Candy_Company.

question: The US Sugar Program is a law that keeps American sugar prices about twice the world price. Every few years Congress votes on a new Farm Bill, and every time the Sugar Program stays in -- even though hundreds of millions of American shoppers pay more for candy, soda, and baked goods because of it. A small group of sugar growers gains millions; each shopper loses only a few dollars. Which economic idea best explains why the program keeps winning?
answer: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
choices: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
John Rawls's veil of ignorance
Ronald Coase's transaction-cost bargaining
John Kenneth Galbraith's countervailing power
context: Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965): about 4,000 sugar farms get large concentrated payoffs and organize politically; about 330 million consumers each pay a few dollars extra a year and do not. The smaller organized group wins. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: US sugar lobbyists often say American sugar growers must be shielded from cheaper foreign sugar or they will go out of business. In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a famous satire mocking that exact kind of argument. In his tale, French candlemakers petition the government to block the sun -- because the sun gives away free light and unfairly hurts their industry. What is this satire called?
answer: The Petition of the Candlemakers
choices: The Petition of the Candlemakers
The Broken Window fallacy
The Negative Railway argument
The Petition of the Vintners
context: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat's Petition of the Candlemakers had French makers of candles and lamps demand a law blocking sunlight to protect them from unfair sun-powered competition. Source: bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught the 'seen and unseen' method: don't just look at the workers a law protects, look at the industries that quietly buy that same good as an input. When the US doubles the price of sugar to help sugar growers, Bastiat's method points at the downstream industries that use sugar as an input -- candy factories, bakeries, soda bottlers. What outcome does his method predict for those industries when a domestic law doubles their input cost against the world price?
answer: They move production to where sugar is cheap
choices: They move production to where sugar is cheap
They automate away all remaining sugar workers
They keep US production and absorb the input cost
They petition congress to raise consumer prices further
context: The predicted move played out in 2003 when Life Savers relocated from Michigan to Montreal, in the 2000s when Ferrara Pan and Brach's moved much production to Mexico. Higher US input costs pushed candy jobs across the border. Source: trade.gov/employment-changes-us-food-manufacturing-impact-sugar-prices.

question: The US Sugar Program is a set of federal price supports and import quotas that keep American sugar prices at about double the world price. Most of the multi-billion-dollar gain flows to a single Cuban-American family in Florida -- the owners of Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals, two of the largest sugar companies in the country. What is the family's name?
answer: The Fanjul family
choices: The Fanjul family
The Hershey family
The Mars family
The Coca-Cola Candler family
context: The Fanjul brothers of Florida own Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals; they are the paradigm case of a small, politically-organized beneficiary group that has kept the Sugar Program in every Farm Bill. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fanjul_brothers.

question: No single person in a country knows where every apple is, how many nails a factory needs, or what shoe size Aunt Judy prefers. That knowledge is spread across millions of people. What tool lets all of that hidden knowledge get used, without any boss having to know it?
answer: Prices in a free market
choices: Prices in a free market
A government planning committee
A national computer running the whole economy
A single wise king
context: F. A. Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4, September 1945, pages 519-530 -- eleven pages that became one of the most-cited economics papers of the 20th century. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society).

question: In 1945, the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek published his most-cited paper, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' arguing that markets aggregate scattered local knowledge no central planner can gather. It appeared in the top journal of the American Economic Association. Which journal was that?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: The American Economic Review
The Journal of Political Economy
The Economic Journal
Econometrica
context: The essay appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London (LSE had by then returned from its Cambridge evacuation). Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In 1945 the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek, then teaching at the London School of Economics, wrote a short essay called 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.' He said the real problem of running an economy is not how to share out things we already have -- the 'blackboard planners' of the 1930s had been busy solving that puzzle with equations. Hayek said they were solving the wrong problem. So what did Hayek say the real problem is?
answer: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
choices: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
How to equalize the marginal productivity of capital across all industries
How to compute the aggregate demand curve for a whole national economy
How to eliminate the fluctuations of the business cycle through fiscal policy
context: Hayek's reframing was the essay's central move: the socialist-calculation debate was not about better arithmetic; it was about the unavailability of the underlying data to any single mind or committee. The knowledge that a market uses to allocate resources is scattered across millions of heads and cannot be gathered up to a central board in usable time. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago hosted PDF (https://home.uchicago.edu/~vlima/courses/econ200/spring01/hayek.pdf).

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay draws a sharp line between two kinds of knowledge. On one side is the scientific knowledge in textbooks that a central board could in principle collect. On the other side is a different kind of knowledge -- inherently dispersed, held by individuals about their particular jobs, ships, warehouses, and customers. What does Hayek call this second, load-bearing kind of knowledge?
answer: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
choices: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
The general theory of aggregate demand and supply
The rational expectations of forward-looking agents
The universal grammar of market institutions
context: Hayek's phrase: the important knowledge in an economy is 'the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- that a certain ship is half-empty, that a warehouse has a surplus, that a foreman on the third shift has spotted a way to save two hours. This knowledge is inherently local and inherently dispersed. Source: Hayek 1945, Econlib version (https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html).

question: In 1945 the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek published an essay called The Use of Knowledge in Society. He used one metal as his running example. When a new use for it appears or a mine somewhere closes, its price rises. Every user around the world then cuts back on the metal -- even people who have no idea why the price moved. Which metal did Hayek use?
answer: Tin
choices: Tin
Copper
Iron
Silver
context: The tin example on page 526 of the American Economic Review version is the paragraph everyone quotes. Hayek's point: a single number -- the tin price -- carries the whole world's changing knowledge about tin (mine closures, new uses, war coming) to every user of tin, without any user needing to know the underlying cause. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF.

question: In 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' F. A. Hayek gave a famous metaphor for the price system: it works like a piece of machinery for registering change, a system where each producer watches only the movement of a few pointers. To which modern technology did Hayek compare the price system?
answer: A system of telecommunications
choices: A system of telecommunications
A national railway timetable
A wartime radar screen
A newspaper printing press
context: Hayek's phrase: the price system is 'a kind of machinery for registering change, or a system of telecommunications which enables individual producers to watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials.' Prices carry knowledge no single mind holds. Source: Western Sydney Pressbooks critical-analysis version (https://westernsydney.pressbooks.pub/criticalanalysis/chapter/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/).

question: Mises said that without market prices, planners cannot figure out what to make. A younger Austrian added a sharper point: even trying hard, planners cannot gather all the little bits of local know-how that markets pull together every day. What is this idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The tax collection problem
The public goods problem
The population problem
context: Mises 1920 said no exchange, no prices, no rational allocation. Hayek 1945 added: even if a benevolent, honest planner had perfect intentions, the dispersed knowledge that market prices summarize is not gatherable in usable time by any central agency. The Austrian critique of planning is not about will or motive -- it is about knowability. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF; Mises Institute critical commentary.

question: In 1945 Friedrich Hayek published his famous essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' arguing that no central planner can gather all the scattered local knowledge that markets use every day. Three years later, in 1948, the University of Chicago Press collected that essay together with Hayek's other pieces on individualism, spontaneous order, and the socialist calculation debate into a single volume. What is that 1948 book called?
answer: Individualism and Economic Order
choices: Individualism and Economic Order
The Constitution of Liberty
Studies in Philosophy Politics and Economics
The Counter-Revolution of Science
context: Individualism and Economic Order (University of Chicago Press, 1948) collected Hayek's essays from the 1930s and 1940s including 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937), and 'The Meaning of Competition.' The Constitution of Liberty (1960), Studies (1967), and The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) are all real Hayek works of later or different focus. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In December 1974 F. A. Hayek delivered the Nobel Memorial Prize lecture in Stockholm on the failures of the mathematical macroeconomics of the day. The title of the lecture was a direct descendant of the 1945 essay's argument about what a central mind cannot hold. What was the title?
answer: The Pretense of Knowledge
choices: The Pretense of Knowledge
The Fatal Conceit
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Road to Serfdom
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretense of Knowledge' argued that the postwar economics profession had adopted the manner of the physical sciences while imitating something it could not actually deliver -- the pretense that macroeconomic aggregates and models could substitute for the dispersed knowledge the price system aggregates. The lecture is the direct descendant of the 1945 essay. Source: Econlib version of Hayek 1945.

question: The reasoning move at the heart of Hayek's 1945 essay is one a critic of central planning can carry into any policy debate -- rent control, minimum wages, wage-price controls, ration schemes. It is NOT a moral verdict; it is a claim about knowability. Which move does the essay actually press?
answer: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
choices: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
That central planners are always corrupt and always self-interested
That a planned economy must eventually generate hyperinflation of the consumer price index
That workers in planned economies are forbidden from changing jobs by law
context: The essay's argument is a claim about the STRUCTURE of economic knowledge, not a moral or motive claim. Even a saintly, brilliant planner cannot hold the knowledge the price system aggregates because that knowledge lives in millions of individual heads about local circumstances. The student can accept or reject the move, but the essay actually presses this reasoning move, not the corruption or hyperinflation charges. Source: Hayek 1945.

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay closes with a striking image of what a market economy accomplishes: without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause of a raw-material scarcity, tens of thousands of people are made to use the material more sparingly. What one word from the essay best names this achievement Hayek was praising?
answer: A marvel
choices: A marvel
A miracle
A machine
A market
context: Hayek writes: 'The marvel is that in a case like that of a scarcity of one raw material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' The word MARVEL carries the essay's astonishment -- that a system no one designed does what no committee could. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In Vienna in the late 1920s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises ran a famous private seminar in his office at the Austrian Chamber of Commerce. Many young Austrian economists attended, and Friedrich Hayek was the first of them to leave for a permanent job abroad. Which British school asked Hayek in 1931 to give four lectures that ended in a permanent chair?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Cambridge
The University of Oxford
The University of Edinburgh
context: Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding LSE's economics department, brought Hayek over from 27 to 30 January 1931 to give the lectures published later that year as Prices and Production. The talks landed so well that LSE offered Hayek the Tooke Chair the following year. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek was invited to the London School of Economics (LSE) in 1931 and stayed almost twenty years, before moving on to the University of Chicago in 1950. From 1932 onward he held one particular endowed chair at the LSE, named after a nineteenth-century English economist. Which chair did he hold?
answer: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
choices: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
The Cassel Chair of Economics
The Drummond Chair of Political Economy
The Marshall Chair of Political Economy
context: Named for the 19th-century monetary theorist Thomas Tooke, the Tooke Chair was LSE's senior economics professorship. Hayek held it from 1932, became a British subject in 1938, and finally left in 1950 for a position in Chicago's Committee on Social Thought. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Fritz Machlup was an Austrian economist who had studied under Ludwig von Mises in 1920s Vienna. In 1933 he took a Rockefeller grant that carried him across America -- to Columbia, Harvard, Chicago, and Stanford. In 1935 he settled into a full American teaching job that lasted the next twelve years. Where did he take that long teaching post?
answer: The University of Buffalo
choices: The University of Buffalo
The University of Chicago
Princeton University
Cornell University
context: Machlup held his Buffalo chair from 1935 to 1947, later moving to Johns Hopkins and then Princeton. He was one of the first of Mises's Vienna circle to make a fully American career. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fritz Machlup'.

question: Gottfried Haberler was another Austrian economist trained by Ludwig von Mises in 1920s Vienna. From 1934 to 1936 he worked as an economist for an international body based in Geneva, Switzerland on the shore of Lake Geneva. That job produced his famous survey of business-cycle theories, 'Prosperity and Depression.' Which international body hired him for those Geneva years?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The Bank for International Settlements
The International Chamber of Commerce
The International Labour Office
context: Haberler served in the economic administration of the League of Nations in Geneva from 1934 to 1936. In autumn 1936 he moved to a Harvard professorship that lasted until his 1971 retirement. Source: Britannica, 'Gottfried von Haberler'.

question: Oskar Morgenstern was an Austrian economist who ran the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research in Vienna and belonged to Mises's private seminar. On March 13, 1938 the German army rolled into Austria in the event called the Anschluss, ending Austrian independence. Morgenstern happened to be out of Europe that day. Where was he, and what did he do?
answer: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
choices: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
In Zurich on sabbatical; he returned home the following month
In London consulting for the Bank of England; he moved on to Cambridge
In Stockholm at a conference; he stayed and took a Riksbank post
context: Morgenstern was travelling in America as a Carnegie Visiting Professor when the Anschluss occurred. From six invitations he chose a three-year appointment as Class of 1913 Lecturer in Political Economy at Princeton, and simply did not return home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar Morgenstern'.

question: Ludwig von Mises, the leader of the Austrian School of economics, left Vienna in 1934 for a paid teaching chair that his own home city had never offered him despite his fame. He taught at this foreign institution for the next six years, until the German army's advance across Europe forced him to flee again. Which institution did he move to?
answer: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
choices: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
The London School of Economics
The Sorbonne in Paris
The University of Zurich
context: Vienna had recognised Mises with only an unpaid Privatdozent title. The Geneva institute (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) gave him his first paid professorship. He held the chair from 1934 until 1940. Source: Mises Institute, 'Ludwig von Mises: The Logician of Freedom'.

question: In July 1940 the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises and his wife Margit fled Geneva as the German army swept through France. Spain turned them back three times before they finally got a Spanish visa at Toulouse. They crossed Spain by train, reached the Atlantic coast of Portugal, and boarded a ship bound for America. From which Portuguese port did they sail?
answer: Lisbon
choices: Lisbon
Bilbao
Barcelona
Vigo
context: Portugal's neutrality made Lisbon the great escape port for European refugees in 1940. Mises and Margit sailed from there and docked in New Jersey on 2 August 1940, where their Viennese friend Alfred Schutz met them on the pier. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Celebrating the Arrival of Ludwig von Mises in America'.

question: When Ludwig von Mises, the leader of the Austrian School of economics, stepped off the ship in New Jersey on August 2, 1940, he had already fled Vienna and then Geneva ahead of the Nazi advance. Many economists ranked him among the greatest minds of his time. American universities knew his name. How old was he then, and what US university chair awaited him?
answer: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
choices: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
Forty-four, and a full Harvard professorship awaited him
Sixty-seven, and a Yale endowed chair had been arranged in advance
Fifty-two, and a Chicago professorship followed within the year
context: Mises was born on 29 September 1881. He turned 59 the month after his arrival. From 1945 to 1969 he taught at New York University as an unpaid Visiting Professor; the William Volker Fund paid his stipend until 1962, and a consortium including the businessman Lawrence Fertig, who sat on the NYU board, took over afterwards. Source: FEE, 'Ludwig von Mises: A Prophet Without Honor in His Own Land'.

question: Karl Menger was a mathematician and the son of the founder of the Austrian School. He left Vienna a full year before the Anschluss for a visiting job at an American Catholic university. He then resigned his Vienna chair in March 1938. Which US university took him in?
answer: The University of Notre Dame
choices: The University of Notre Dame
Georgetown University
Fordham University
The Catholic University of America
context: Menger arrived in South Bend, Indiana in autumn 1937 and stayed until 1946. His father Carl Menger had founded the Austrian School with the 1871 Grundsaetze; the son carried the family name into American mathematics. Source: MacTutor, 'Karl Menger'.

question: Seven years after the Nazis fell, a small group of scholars met on a mountain above Lake Geneva. They wanted to see if classical liberal thought could be rebuilt after the war. Hayek called the meeting on 10 April 1947. Thirty-six came, including Mises, Machlup, Friedman, Stigler, Popper and Robbins. What group was founded there?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Cato Institute
The Institute of Economic Affairs
The Foundation for Economic Education
context: The Mont Pelerin Society took its name from the hotel above Lake Geneva where the founding meeting was held. Hayek served as its first President until 1961. Half a dozen of the founders were direct veterans of Mises's old Vienna Privatseminar. Source: montpelerin.org, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: In 1974 the Nobel Prize in Economics went to a former member of Ludwig von Mises's private seminar in 1920s Vienna. He shared the prize with the Swedish social democrat Gunnar Myrdal -- an unusual pairing of a free-market economist and a welfare-state economist that shocked observers. Which Vienna emigre took home the free-market half of the prize?
answer: Friedrich von Hayek
choices: Friedrich von Hayek
Fritz Machlup
Gottfried Haberler
Oskar Morgenstern
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel citation named his work on money, credit and interdependence between economic, social and institutional phenomena. Machlup, Haberler and Morgenstern each made major contributions in America but Hayek alone of the Vienna diaspora was Nobel-honoured. Source: Britannica, 'F. A. Hayek'.

question: In 1920s Vienna, a group of Austrian economists led by Ludwig von Mises argued that no small committee -- no matter how smart -- could plan a whole country's economy the way a family plans its weekly budget. Why not, according to Mises's argument?
answer: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
choices: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
Committees are always lazy
Committees don't have enough computers
Committees never agree with each other
context: The Vienna Circle of logical positivists, gathered around Moritz Schlick and Rudolf Carnap, was the leading interwar philosophy-of-science movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: In the 1930s the Austrian mathematician Kurt Godel proved something startling: no math system can prove every true fact that lives inside it -- some truths always sit beyond the rules. Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek made a similar-shaped point about the whole economy itself. What did they say?
answer: No small group can ever plan a whole economy -- they can't know enough
choices: No small group can ever plan a whole economy -- they can't know enough
The economy runs on pure luck
Only the smartest person should set every price
Math cannot describe money
context: Kurt Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorems were presented partly through Menger's Vienna colloquium, one of the most famous mathematical results of the 20th century. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Godel%27s_incompleteness_theorems.

question: In early 1900s Vienna the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises argued against socialists who wanted the state to plan the whole economy from the top down. Mises said no central planner, however clever, can copy one everyday tool that quietly guides millions of people to work together without any single person in charge. What is that everyday tool?
answer: Market prices
choices: Market prices
Government orders
Newspaper editorials
Weather reports
context: Moritz Schlick was shot dead by Johann Nelbock on the University of Vienna's Philosophenstiege on June 22, 1936, an early hammer-blow to the interwar Vienna intellectual scene. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moritz_Schlick.

question: In 1920s Vienna, Ludwig von Mises led a free-market circle of Austrian economists. Against them stood the Vienna Circle, a rival group of philosophers and scientists who wanted society run on scientific plans. Its leading thinker was Otto Neurath, who championed a 'planned economy.' Which political tradition is Neurath tied to?
answer: Socialism
choices: Socialism
Classical liberalism
Traditional conservatism
Anarcho-capitalism
context: Otto Neurath combined logical-positivist philosophy with Austro-Marxist socialism; the Vienna Circle formally endorsed physicalism and rejected metaphysics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Rudolf Carnap was a leading philosopher in the Vienna Circle, a group that argued only claims testable by logic and observation had real meaning. In 1935, as Nazi power rose across Europe, Carnap emigrated to the United States and joined a major American university. That school then became a main home of logical positivism in North America. Which school did he join?
answer: The University of Chicago
choices: The University of Chicago
Harvard University
the University of California, Berkeley
Columbia University
context: Carnap took a chair at the University of Chicago in 1935 and taught there until 1952 before moving to UCLA. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: The Austrian mathematician Kurt Godel fled Vienna in early 1940 by a strange, roundabout route -- east across the Soviet Union on the Trans-Siberian Railway, then Japan, then across the Pacific by ship. He arrived in the United States and joined a famous research institute where he stayed the rest of his life, becoming a close friend of Albert Einstein. Where did he end up?
answer: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
choices: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
MIT
Harvard University
the University of Chicago
context: Godel fled via the Trans-Siberian Railway and Japan in 1940, arriving at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he became a colleague of Einstein and von Neumann. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kurt_Godel.

question: For decades before 1938 Vienna had been home to a brilliant scene -- coffeehouse thinkers, mathematicians like Kurt Godel, economists like Ludwig von Mises, novelists like Stefan Zweig. Within months of one political event in 1938 the whole scene was scattered, its members exiled, silenced, or killed. What kind of political change usually makes free thinkers flee a country?
answer: A dictator takes over and shuts down free debate
choices: A dictator takes over and shuts down free debate
The country holds a peaceful election
The country lowers its taxes
A new stock exchange opens for business
context: The March 1938 Anschluss brought Nazi Germany into Austria and expelled Jewish intellectuals from Vienna's universities. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anschluss.

question: In 1934 the Viennese philosopher Karl Popper, in his book 'The Logic of Scientific Discovery,' proposed a simple test for whether an idea should count as real science. He said the idea must make a risky prediction -- it has to be possible to state exactly what evidence would prove the idea wrong. Popper argued that Marxism and Freudian psychology failed this test, while Einstein's physics passed it. What is the name of this test?
answer: Falsifiability
choices: Falsifiability
Verification
Consensus
Repeatability
context: Karl Popper's Logik der Forschung (1934) put falsifiability at the center of scientific method, in opposition to Vienna Circle verificationism. He shared the classical-liberal politics of Mises without belonging to the Circle. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Popper.

question: At lunchtime two kids trade lunch items -- your apple for their cookie. Both of you smile and walk back to the table happy with the swap. Nobody forced you, and nobody tricked either of you. From an economist's view, why did that simple little trade make both of you better off at the same time?
answer: Each of you valued what you got more than what you gave up
choices: Each of you valued what you got more than what you gave up
One of you must have tricked the other
The apple and cookie cost exactly the same to make
Trading always makes one person lose
context: Menger took the chair in 1873 in the Faculty of Law and Political Economy (economics was then taught inside the law faculty) and held it for thirty years, until 1903. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Carl_Menger.

question: Carl Menger founded the Austrian School of economics in 1870s Vienna. He had two great first-generation students. One of them took the University of Vienna's economics chair in 1904, right after quitting his job as the Finance Minister of Austria-Hungary. He held the chair and taught seminars in Vienna until his death in 1914. Who was he?
answer: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
Karl Menger the younger
context: Bohm-Bawerk held a parallel Vienna chair from 1904 until his death in 1914, giving Vienna both leading Menger students teaching side by side for a decade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: In early 1900s Vienna, Ludwig von Mises's famous private seminar taught many young economists who later split apart on politics. Some, like Friedrich Hayek, grew up to defend free markets. Others, like Otto Bauer, grew up to lead the socialists. The two sides then argued for years over one big question about how an economy should be run. What big question did they argue about?
answer: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
choices: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
Whether numbers should be written left to right or right to left
Whether spring or fall is a better time to sow wheat
Whether German or French makes a better first language
context: The 1905-1914 Bohm-Bawerk seminar had the future greatest Austrian liberal (Mises), the future Austrian Social Democrat foreign minister (Otto Bauer), and the future Marxist finance minister of Weimar Germany (Hilferding) sitting together. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: Ludwig von Mises, the Austrian economist writing in the 1920s, argued that a small group of central planners can never run a whole country's economy the way a family plans a weekly budget. His reason was that free markets constantly generate millions of tiny pieces of local information that planners have no way to invent from a central office. What are those pieces of information?
answer: They lack the millions of local price signals that markets produce
choices: They lack the millions of local price signals that markets produce
Central planners always cheat and steal from ordinary citizens
Central planners refuse to work more than four hours a day
Central planners are not allowed to use computers
context: Mises took his Vienna doctorate in 1906 and habilitated in 1913 as a Privatdozent -- an unpaid lecturer with the right to teach -- while working full-time for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Picture a country that ends all its private markets and lets a small state committee set every single price by government rule -- no bargaining, no bidding, no shopping around. Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek said one important tool that normally guides what gets made, and how much, then vanishes overnight. What tool is lost?
answer: Prices that reveal what people really want
choices: Prices that reveal what people really want
The postal service and its mail carriers
The alphabet used to write down new laws
The soldiers who patrol the country's border
context: Hans Mayer held the Vienna chair from 1922 to 1938; the paid chair thus passed out of the front-rank Austrian tradition just as the private-seminar tradition became the school's main institutional home. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Mayer_(economist).

question: In the early 1920s Rudolf Hilferding, a Marxist economist, served as Finance Minister of Germany under the Weimar Republic. During that period the German central bank printed huge amounts of new paper marks to pay government debts and war reparations. A loaf of bread that cost a few hundred marks in early 1923 cost hundreds of billions of marks by that November. What happens to prices in a country that prints a lot of new money very fast?
answer: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
choices: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
Prices fall because there is more money to spend
Prices stay the same because printing is invisible
Prices only rise on goods brought in from abroad
context: Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910) was a leading Marxist analysis of banking; he later served twice as Finance Minister of Weimar Germany. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rudolf_Hilferding.

question: Vienna had been the world capital of Austrian economics from the 1870s through the 1930s -- the university seminars, the coffeehouse debates, the private library of Ludwig von Mises. Then in one year a political event brought foreign troops in, arrested opponents, and forced Jewish and dissenting professors out. The last members of the school had to emigrate, most to the United States. Which event ended Vienna's role?
answer: The 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany
choices: The 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany
The 1919 Treaty of Saint-Germain
The 1927 July Revolt
The 1934 Austrian Civil War
context: Mises had already left Vienna for Geneva in 1934. The 1938 Anschluss ended the Vienna institutional tradition; the remaining figures (Hayek at LSE from 1931; Haberler at Harvard 1936; Morgenstern at Princeton 1938; Machlup in America 1933) had all emigrated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: On October 31, 2008, an anonymous author calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto posted a short paper to a small cypherpunk email list. The paper described a new kind of digital money called Bitcoin, sent person-to-person with no bank in the middle. For a math-heavy proposal it is famously brief. About how long is the main body of the paper, not counting the notes at the end?
answer: About nine pages
choices: About nine pages
About one page
About fifty pages
About two hundred pages
context: Nine pages of body text, organized into twelve numbered sections plus an abstract and references. That is the length of a typical computer-science conference paper of its era. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper, written under the name Satoshi Nakamoto and posted to a cypherpunk email list on October 31, 2008, begins with an abstract that names the exact problem Satoshi wants to fix. In that opening sentence, Satoshi is describing how internet buying and selling has come to rely on banks and payment companies sitting in the middle of every purchase. Which of these is the actual opening line?
answer: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
choices: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
'Money is a social construct that will be replaced by decentralized applications.'
'The Federal Reserve is the enemy of every honest saver.'
'This paper introduces a new consensus mechanism called proof-of-stake.'
context: The opening sentence identifies the trusted-third-party dependency as the problem to eliminate. The rest of the paper explains the peer-to-peer solution. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: To add a new block of transactions to the Bitcoin blockchain, a computer called a miner must first solve a very hard math puzzle that eats real electricity. This design, laid out in Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 Bitcoin white paper, makes cheating extremely expensive -- any attacker would have to redo all the puzzle work for every block they wanted to change. What is the name of this security method?
answer: Proof-of-Work
choices: Proof-of-Work
Proof-of-stake
Free banking
Legal tender
context: Section 3 introduces the timestamped chain concept; Section 4 shows how to secure it. The section explicitly cites Adam Back's Hashcash as prior art. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In 2008, an anonymous programmer using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper, proposing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system with no central bank behind it. The paper carefully cites specific earlier work in cryptography and digital cash. Which pair of predecessors does its reference list name?
answer: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
choices: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
David Chaum's DigiCash and Nick Szabo's bit gold
Vitalik Buterin's Ethereum and Charlie Lee's Litecoin
Ralph Nader's Public Citizen and Milton Friedman's Free to Choose
context: Both Hashcash and b-money were cypherpunk-lineage proposals from the 1990s that Satoshi combined and extended. DigiCash and bit gold are historically related but are not cited in the paper's references. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In section 7 of the 2008 Bitcoin white paper, Satoshi Nakamoto describes a data trick that lets old spent records be trimmed away from the chain while still leaving a compact fingerprint that proves the whole history has not been tampered with. Each block keeps only a short summary of its transactions, arranged so that any single record can be checked without storing them all. What is that tree-shaped hash structure called?
answer: A Merkle tree
choices: A Merkle tree
A linked list
A hash table
A relational database
context: Named for Ralph Merkle, who patented the structure in 1979. Each block header commits to the Merkle root of its transactions, so nodes can discard old bodies and keep only proofs. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In October 2008 the anonymous author Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper. In it Satoshi describes a way for a phone wallet to check that a payment really happened without downloading the whole history of every Bitcoin transaction. Instead the wallet keeps only tiny summary headers of each block plus a short cryptographic proof of inclusion. What is the point of this shortcut?
answer: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
choices: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
It makes every bitcoin transaction completely private
It removes the need for any miners at all
It changes bitcoin's fixed supply cap
context: SPV enables phone-and-laptop wallets to check that a payment is in the longest chain by requesting Merkle proofs from full nodes. It is what made mobile Bitcoin wallets practical. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In October 2008 the anonymous author Satoshi Nakamoto emailed a cryptography mailing list a nine-page paper titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System.' The paper is broken into twelve numbered sections that cover the network, mining, incentives, and privacy. The twelfth and final section is unusually short for a technical paper -- just a brief summary of the coin-as-chain-of-signatures idea and the proof-of-work security argument. Which title does the twelfth section carry, and how long is it?
answer: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
choices: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
Discussion, roughly two pages
Bibliography, roughly one page
Appendix A, roughly three pages
context: The paper is famously terse. Satoshi said what needed saying and stopped. The Conclusion recaps the peer-to-peer solution and the assumption that honest miners hold more hashing power than any attacker. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell -- a Chicago-trained free-market thinker at Stanford's Hoover Institution -- likes to boil his view of economics down to one line: 'There are no solutions, only trade-offs.' What does he mean?
answer: Every choice gives up something else -- you can't get all good and no cost
choices: Every choice gives up something else -- you can't get all good and no cost
Smart leaders can fix every problem at zero cost
Only the government can solve real problems
If you try hard enough, no one has to lose anything
context: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930, Gastonia, North Carolina) was adopted and raised by his great-aunt Molly and her two adult daughters after his father died shortly before his birth and his mother died a few years later; the family moved to Harlem when he was nine. Walter Williams taught at George Mason, Glenn Loury at Brown, and W. Arthur Lewis won the 1979 Nobel Prize. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell was born in 1930 in Gastonia, North Carolina and grew up poor in a small wooden house. His family had no electricity and no running water. In his memoir 'A Personal Odyssey' Sowell told about one ordinary everyday thing he had simply never learned as a young boy in that isolated home. What was it?
answer: That blond was a hair color
choices: That blond was a hair color
That milk came from cows
That the ocean was salt water
That radios carried live music
context: Sowell wrote in A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) that his childhood encounters with white people were so limited that he did not know blond was a hair color. He recalled a small wooden house in Charlotte on an unpaved street with no electricity or running water. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell', citing A Personal Odyssey.

question: As a boy Thomas Sowell won a spot at Stuyvesant, a top public high school in New York City. He was the first person in his family to study past sixth grade. At seventeen, running short on money and living in a home that fought too often, he quit school and went to work. Which job did young Sowell take?
answer: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
choices: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
Sorting mail at the main post office
Loading freight on the Brooklyn docks
Running an elevator in a midtown tower
context: Sowell dropped out of Stuyvesant at 17 because of financial difficulties and family quarreling, then worked long hours in a machine shop and as a delivery man for Western Union. He also tried out for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1948. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell later became a famous economist. One of his best-known points is about a rule that sounds nice but ends up hurting the very people it's supposed to help: a minimum wage set higher than what a beginner's work is worth. Who does he say gets hurt most?
answer: Young workers with no experience, who can no longer get their first job
choices: Young workers with no experience, who can no longer get their first job
Rich business owners who lose most of their money
Older workers who have been employed for decades
Farmers who grow food for city customers
context: After basic training in South Carolina, Sowell was sent to a photography school in Florida and served as a Marine photographer; he was discharged in 1952 and never rose above private first class. Photography remained his lifelong hobby. Sources: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: The economist Thomas Sowell grew up poor in 1940s Harlem. Each day he rode the bus home from his downtown high school, past rich stores, past a concert hall, past comfortable blocks, then over a bridge to his own tenement neighborhood. The gulf between the two worlds puzzled him. In his early twenties, which thinker did young Sowell first turn to for an answer?
answer: Karl Marx
choices: Karl Marx
Adam Smith
Frederick Douglass
Benjamin Franklin
context: Sowell has said he was a Marxist through his twenties. Of the bus ride he wrote: 'The contrast between that and what I'd been seeing most of the trip really baffled me. And Marx seemed to explain it.' He wrote a Harvard senior thesis on Marxian economics and a Columbia master's thesis on Marxian business cycle theory. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: In 1959 the young African-American economist Thomas Sowell moved to the University of Chicago to study for a graduate degree. He went there to learn from famous free-market economists like Milton Friedman and George Stigler. The Chicago school taught that one everyday tool guides an economy better than any state plan drawn up in a ministry. What tool did they mean?
answer: The price of goods and labor in a free market
choices: The price of goods and labor in a free market
A list of quotas set by lawmakers
A yearly government printout of who should produce what
A vote every month on what should cost how much
context: Sowell chose Columbia in order to study under George Stigler, later a Nobel laureate; on learning Stigler had moved to Chicago he followed him there in the fall of 1959 and took his PhD at Chicago in 1968, with a dissertation on Say's Law and the general glut controversy. Friedman, Knight and Becker were all Chicago economists. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In 1980 the American economist Thomas Sowell, a Chicago-trained scholar famous for his free-market columns, left teaching at UCLA (the University of California, Los Angeles) to write books and columns full time. He joined Stanford's Hoover Institution, a research group that studies public policy from a free-market and classical-liberal viewpoint. What is the general name for an organization like Hoover that hires scholars to publish policy studies?
answer: A policy think tank
choices: A policy think tank
A trade union
A stock exchange
A credit union
context: Sowell joined the Hoover Institution at Stanford as a fellow in April 1977 and became a senior fellow in September 1980, holding the title Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow on Public Policy. He had earlier been at the Urban Institute (1972-74) and the American Enterprise Institute (1975-76), which is why those are live answers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the summer of 1960 Thomas Sowell, whose first year of graduate school at Chicago had left his politics untouched, took a summer job at the U.S. Department of Labor studying Puerto Rico's sugar industry, where Washington set the wage floor. He saw that as that floor rose, the sugar payrolls shrank. He brought the finding to the office he had joined. What would his colleagues not do?
answer: Test whether the law was helping the workers
choices: Test whether the law was helping the workers
Release the employment figures he had assembled
Compare Puerto Rico with mainland sugar growers
Let an intern brief the division chief directly
context: Sowell has said his colleagues were surprised by his questioning and that 'they certainly weren't going to engage in any scrutiny of the law' -- their job was to enforce it, not to check it. He called this 'the beginning of the erosion of my faith in government programs.' Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Britannica 'Thomas Sowell'; New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell reached Harvard by an unlikely road -- dropout, Marine, night classes at Howard -- and graduated magna cum laude in 1958. Asked long afterwards to name the best thing about having gone there, he gave an answer that had nothing to do with the teaching. What did he say?
answer: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
choices: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
That nobody there ever asked where you had gone to high school
That you learn how fast a reputation starts doing your arguing for you
That it teaches you to distrust every credential, beginning with your own
context: Sowell's line: 'One of the best things about going to Harvard is that, for the rest of your life, you are neither intimidated nor impressed by people who went to Harvard.' He finished high school by equivalency after the Marines, took a civil service job in Washington and studied nights at Howard University before transferring. Source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: After graduating, Thomas Sowell was asked to teach a college course on the Soviet economy. Prepping the class finally made Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' click for him. He saw why Soviet central plans kept failing and put the whole thing in one sharp line about who held what -- power versus knowledge. Which line did Sowell use?
answer: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
choices: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
Those who wrote the plans never had to live under the plans they wrote
Those who owned nothing were told every day that they owned everything
Those who waited longest in the queue were always served last
context: Sowell: 'There was a knowledge problem that was inherent in that system. In a nutshell, those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power.' Hayek's essay is 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Knowledge and Decisions (1980) is the book where Thomas Sowell carried Hayek's idea about scattered information into real courts, firms, schools, and lawmaking. He traded graphs for real places a reader could picture. Hayek reviewed it himself, and his title was not modest. What did Hayek call it?
answer: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
choices: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
A Worthy Successor to The Road to Serfdom
An American Answer to the Planners
The Case Against Expertise, Made at Last
context: Hayek titled his review of Knowledge and Decisions 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'; the book also won the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. Sowell has called it a book-length application of Hayek's 1945 essay to specific American institutions. Sources: Wikipedia 'Knowledge and Decisions'; FEE, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; New Criterion.

question: Thomas Sowell has said the summer of 1960 began the erosion of his faith in government programs -- not because the sugar numbers alone convinced him, but because of how the people around him received the numbers. He compressed that summer into one sentence he has been applying to institutions ever since. Which sentence?
answer: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
choices: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
That good intentions and good results are different things, and only results can be counted
That every program grows until it costs more than the problem it was built to solve
That the people a program is meant to help are the last whose interests anyone counts
context: Sowell's own words: 'It forced me to realize that government agencies have their own self-interest to look after, regardless of those for whom a program has been set up.' This is public-choice reasoning arrived at by observation, before Sowell had read the public-choice literature. Option two is close to Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions', a genuinely different move. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the 1990s a loose group of programmers, mathematicians, and privacy fans in California and beyond began calling themselves the cypherpunks. They said ordinary people should be able to send private notes, and one day private money, that no bank, boss, or government could read, trace, or block. What computer tool did they insist would make that possible?
answer: Strong encryption -- math that scrambles the message
choices: Strong encryption -- math that scrambles the message
Louder microphones
Faster mail trucks
Better paper envelopes
context: Timothy C. May was the retired Intel physicist. Gilmore was Sun's fifth employee; Hughes was a Berkeley mathematician; Chaum was an American cryptographer at a different company. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: In 1988 a computer scientist named Timothy May, who worked as a physicist at the chip company Intel in California, wrote a short essay making a bold guess. He said that if regular people ever got hold of strong math to scramble their messages, no state would be able to spy on their letters or block their payments. What did May think would grow up as a result?
answer: Private communication and private trade between strangers
choices: Private communication and private trade between strangers
Only more junk mail
Nothing -- people wouldn't care
Bigger post offices
context: May's 1988 essay is 'The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto'. 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' was Eric Hughes's separate March 1993 essay; 'The Cyphernomicon' was May's later 1994 book-length FAQ; 'The Sovereign Individual' is a 1997 book by Davidson and Rees-Mogg. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: In 1988, the American engineer Timothy May helped start the cypherpunk movement -- computer people who thought strong encryption could give ordinary citizens privacy from governments and banks. That year May wrote the Crypto Anarchist Manifesto. To open it, he grabbed the famous first line of an 1848 European pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, and swapped the word 'communism' for 'crypto anarchy.' Which opening line did May borrow and rewrite?
answer: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
choices: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.'
'Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent...'
'When in the course of human events, it becomes necessary for one people...'
context: May's opening deliberately echoes the 1848 Communist Manifesto's 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' The other openings are Declaration of Independence (1776) and Gettysburg Address (1863). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May, an Intel physicist writing in 1988, opened his short essay The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto with a line borrowed from Karl Marx: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.' He said the specter stood for a bundle of powers he believed strong computer codes would soon give ordinary people. Which powers did May predict in that essay?
answer: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
choices: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
cheap global manufacturing and rapid international logistics for goods moving across every continent
solar power and unlimited clean energy sufficient to end civilization's fossil-fuel dependence permanently
artificial intelligence sophisticated enough to replace most human labor across every category of employment
context: May's specter was strong cryptography enabling anonymous communication, contracting, and trade beyond state surveillance.
