The other categories are separate technological forecasts May did not centrally address in the manifesto. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May was an Intel physicist in California who quit his day job young and spent his time writing about what math and computers would do to politics. His 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto has one striking line about what individuals and groups would soon be able to do together in perfect secret, without any government able to watch. Which prediction does that line make about anonymous action?
answer: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
choices: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
'The internet will soon make all of human knowledge free of charge and instantly available to every person on the planet regardless of their nation.'
'Computers will one day think and feel as humans do, and will eventually claim rights of their own from the human governments that built them.'
'Every citizen of every industrial nation will one day own a personal computer more powerful than anything a national laboratory possesses today.'
context: The exact quote from May's manifesto. The other statements are broadly attributed to different figures (Stallman on knowledge freedom, Minsky/Kurzweil on AI, various early PC forecasts). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: In his 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto, the Intel-physicist-turned-writer Timothy May named several concrete tools he believed the math of strong encryption would soon make possible. Over the following thirty years, other cypherpunks -- Adam Back, Wei Dai, Hal Finney, and eventually the anonymous Satoshi Nakamoto -- actually built most of them. Which set of tools did May sketch back in 1988?
answer: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
choices: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
smartphones, social media, video streaming, and cloud storage
gene therapy, artificial hearts, brain implants, and space elevators
hydrogen fuel cells, fusion power, and orbital solar arrays
context: May specifically anticipated remailers, pseudonyms, smart contracts, and untraceable payments -- all built between 1990 and 2010. The other technology lists are unrelated. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto did not name any specific project, because none existed yet. But May did describe the shape of a future untraceable digital cash: money sent person-to-person, with no bank sitting in the middle and no state able to see or stop the transfers. Almost exactly twenty years after his essay, on Halloween 2008, an anonymous author released a short white paper that matched May's sketch almost point for point. Which event was that?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
the Federal Reserve's 2008 quantitative easing program
the launch of Facebook in 2004
the introduction of chip-and-PIN credit cards
context: Bitcoin's 2008 white paper realized in engineering form the untraceable-payments capability May had forecast in 1988. QE, Facebook, and chip-and-PIN cards are unrelated technologies. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In the early 1990s in the San Francisco Bay Area a small group of programmers, cryptographers, and privacy activists began meeting in person and mailing one another on an email list. They called themselves 'cypherpunks,' and members included Eric Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore. They shared one core belief about what ordinary people should be able to use freely, without government permission or bank approval. What did they think ordinary people needed?
answer: Strong encryption for private messages and digital cash
choices: Strong encryption for private messages and digital cash
Only government-approved chat apps
Only paper money, never any digital money
Only bank-issued forms of communication
context: 'The Cyphernomicon' (1994) by Timothy May is a book-length FAQ. 'The Crypto Handbook' is a fabrication; 'The Anarchist Cookbook' (William Powell, 1971) is a separate unrelated pamphlet; 'A Cypherpunk's Grimoire' does not exist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: In 1988 Timothy May, a retired Intel physicist, wrote a short essay he called 'The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto,' which he later read aloud at the first cypherpunks meeting in the San Francisco Bay Area. At the time there was no code and no working system -- none of the tools May described actually existed yet in software. A modern cypherpunk historian says the essay is best read not as a report on what already existed but as a special kind of intellectual work. How does the historian describe it?
answer: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
choices: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
a summary of already-shipping cryptographic tools that had reached ordinary consumers by the late 1980s
a proposal for a specific new company that May intended to found using his Intel stock-option wealth
a legal brief prepared for a specific US court case involving the export of cryptographic software
context: The essay was pure forecast in 1988 -- no working code, no infrastructure. Every specific technology May named would be built over the next thirty years by the movement he named. It was not a shipping summary, corporate proposal, or legal brief. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: When the cryptographer, essayist, and cypherpunk co-founder Timothy May died in 2018 at age 66, obituaries in the crypto press had to describe his place in the chain of ideas that eventually produced Bitcoin -- a project May did not build, but whose whole surrounding movement he had helped invent thirty years earlier. Which role did the crypto world settle on giving him at his death?
answer: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
choices: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
the actual person behind the Satoshi pseudonym
the founder of the Bitcoin Foundation
the CEO of the first Bitcoin exchange
context: May's 2018 obituaries credited him as a co-founder of the cypherpunk movement from which Satoshi wrote. He never claimed the Satoshi identity, did not found the Bitcoin Foundation, and did not run an exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A child is offered one cookie today or two cookies tomorrow, and grabs the one today. A lender is offered $100 back today or $100 back next year, and asks for $105 for the wait. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk gave a name to this plain fact in his 1889 book. What did he call it?
answer: Time preference
choices: Time preference
Marginal utility
Opportunity cost
The endowment effect
context: Boehm-Bawerk's time preference is the ranking every chooser puts on a present good above the SAME good in the future -- two apples today over two apples next year, dinner tonight over dinner tomorrow. Marginal utility (Menger 1871, Wieser 1884) is a different concept about the LAST unit; opportunity cost (Wieser again) is about the next-best forgone use; the endowment effect (Thaler 1980) is a modern behavioural finding about ownership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: Imagine a friend offers you one candy bar right now, or two candy bars a whole year from today. Most kids -- and most adults -- reach for the one candy bar today. Economists have a name for this deep human tendency to prefer stuff-sooner over stuff-later, and it shapes everything from interest rates to saving habits. What is the preference called?
answer: Time preference
choices: Time preference
Inflation
A tariff
A subsidy
context: Mises attended Boehm-Bawerk's celebrated Vienna seminar 1905-1913 and inherited both the time-preference framework and the general Austrian method. Hayek was Mises's own student at Vienna in the 1920s (Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914 when Hayek was 15); Rothbard was Mises's American student in the 1950s at NYU; Kirzner was another Mises student at NYU. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: A hedge-fund analyst asks a plain question: WHY should anyone pay interest? If I lend you $100 for a year and you give me back exactly $100, I'm no worse off -- I got my money back. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference account says the lender IS worse off, because being made whole after a wait is not being made whole at all. What has the lender given up that must be compensated?
answer: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
choices: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
The labor-hours he spent earning the money
The physical wear on the coins from being handled
The cost of writing up the loan contract
context: This is the pure time-preference theory of interest in its cleanest form: interest is the price of WAITING, not a payment for risk or wear or paperwork. The lender defers a year of spending; only a promise of MORE than the original sum next year compensates him for that deferral. Mises would call the pure-time-preference component 'originary interest' in Human Action (1949); Rothbard would build his entire interest theory on this alone in Man, Economy, and State (1962). Source: econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html.

question: Time preference varies wildly between choosers. A child grabs the cookie NOW. A monk under vows may live indifferent to whether the meal comes today or next week. A grandmother forgoes a cruise to leave money for a grandchild who will spend it decades from now. What does the Austrian tradition say every chooser -- however patient -- still has some of?
answer: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
choices: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
A precise numerical discount rate they can state on request
A moral obligation to prefer later over sooner
A market-determined interest rate identical to everyone else's
context: Even the patient monk still prefers a good NOW to the same good in the infinite future -- a promise of an apple in a thousand years is worth zero today to anyone who will not be alive to eat it. Time preference is positive for every actor with a finite horizon; only the SIZE varies. The child has a very high time preference (cookie now); the grandmother has a very low one; both have some. Source: mises.org/library/brief-defense-misess-conception-time-preference-and-his-pure-time-preference-theory-interest.

question: In Human Action (1949), Ludwig von Mises argued that time preference is not a quirk some people have and others do not. It is built into every human choice, because we always rank sooner against later. Mises gave a special name to the interest that comes from pure time preference. Which name?
answer: Originary interest
choices: Originary interest
Nominal interest
Compound interest
Marginal interest
context: Mises separated three components in market interest: (1) originary interest, the pure time-preference core; (2) an entrepreneurial component covering business risk; (3) a price premium covering expected inflation. Only the originary interest is praxeological -- built into human action itself -- and would remain in Mises's evenly rotating economy where risk and inflation are removed by assumption. Nominal, compound, and marginal are unrelated finance terms. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: In the early 1900s, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises studied why interest rates exist at all. He said any real-world rate has extra pieces added on for business risk and expected inflation. But if you strip those add-ons away, the pure base rate that remains comes from just one thing about human nature. What does Mises say sets that base rate?
answer: How much people prefer having money now over later
choices: How much people prefer having money now over later
How productive machines and factories currently are
How much new gold is dug out of the ground each year
How high wages get pushed by big labor unions
context: Rothbard's is a Pure Time-Preference Theory of interest (PTPT) -- the productivity-of-capital account (going back to Boehm-Bawerk's own THIRD reason for interest, and to Fisher) is rejected as confused; risk and inflation get modelled as separate premiums added on top. The market rate you actually see is time preferences plus those premiums. Frank Fetter's 1904 Principles gave the pure account first; Mises and Rothbard both credit him. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf.

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 book pushed a next step. A people who save more, on the whole, can build things a spend-it-all people cannot. They can support long work chains, tools that make tools, and projects that take a decade. A people who eat what they make as fast as they make it cannot. What did he call these long chains where saved goods are patiently rearranged to make more later?
answer: Roundabout production
choices: Roundabout production
Comparative advantage
Aggregate demand
Full employment equilibrium
context: Roundabout production is Boehm-Bawerk's central capital-theory concept: instead of catching fish with bare hands, first make a net; instead of walking, first build a car factory; instead of a car factory, first build a machine-tool industry to build the factory. Each step adds waiting time and requires deferred consumption. Comparative advantage is Ricardo 1817 on trade; aggregate demand and full employment are Keynesian macroeconomic constructs from the 1930s. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: Two countries start with the same people and resources. Country A saves hard and puts off spending for a generation. Country B spends every dollar right away and borrows to spend more. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference theory says which country ends up with the more capital-heavy economy?
answer: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
choices: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
Society B -- higher spending drives more investment
Both equally -- time preferences do not affect capital structure
Society B -- consumption is what stimulates growth
context: Deferred consumption is what FREES real resources for long-term projects: workers and materials not consumed today can be used to build tools, factories, and infrastructure whose payoff comes years out. Society B's aggressive present consumption leaves nothing for the long projects. This is why Austrians (Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek) argue that SAVING -- not spending -- is the engine of a capital-intensive economy, directly against the Keynesian priority given to aggregate demand. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: A central bank pushes short-term interest rates well below the rate that would balance actual saving against actual borrowing. Entrepreneurs looking at the low rate start long-term projects -- factories, subdivisions, mining operations -- on the reading that lots of long-term saving is available. But consumers have not in fact deferred any consumption; the low rate was a policy choice, not a signal from real saving. Which Austrian move names what the low rate has done?
answer: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
choices: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
It efficiently reallocates resources to their highest-value use
It cures the shortage of aggregate demand
It permanently raises the economy's growth rate
context: This is the time-preference core of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929-1931): when the central-bank rate is held below the market-clearing rate, entrepreneurs get a false signal that consumers have saved more than they have. Long projects get started that cannot in fact be finished with the real resources available. The bust is the market discovering the truth -- capital gets written down, malinvested projects are liquidated, workers laid off, and the economy returns to a structure the real time preferences will support. The other three options describe Keynesian, Chicago-neoclassical, and stimulus-permanence claims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: The Austrian economist Hans-Hermann Hoppe wrote a book called Democracy: The God That Failed in 2001. In it he argued that elected leaders think only about the next election, not the next generation. They promise big spending now — pensions, subsidies, wars — knowing the bills will fall on leaders and children not yet born. Hoppe called this pattern 'high time preference.' Over generations, what did he say the short-term thinking produces?
answer: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
choices: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
A permanent rise in the standard of living
A stable long-run balance in the political system
A gradual return to hereditary monarchy
context: Hoppe's central thesis links rising time preference to decivilization: short-horizon political incentives crowd out long-horizon private planning, borrowing-against-the-future replaces saving, and the visible symptoms are rising crime, degenerating standards, and swelling public debt. The book is controversial and Brandon's bank presents it as one named critic's argument. Time preference is Hoppe's master variable; the argument runs straight out of Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Boehm-Bawerk gave three reasons for positive interest in his 1889 book: (1) future goods will be more plentiful; (2) people undervalue future needs from carelessness; (3) present goods work better for starting production. Frank Fetter, Mises, and Rothbard later said only one of these truly belongs to the pure interest rate. The other two are separate effects. Which reason is the pure-time-preference core?
answer: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
choices: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
The greater physical productivity of tools made today
The larger future supply of goods
The scarcity of gold-based money
context: The Fetter-Mises-Rothbard purification argues that Boehm-Bawerk's first reason (larger future supply) collapses back into the second (it works only via preferences), and the third (productivity of present goods) is a productivity effect, not a time-preference effect. What is left as the ROOT of interest is the pure ranking of present over future -- reason two, in Boehm-Bawerk's numbering. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: In 2021 prices in America started climbing fast — food, gas, and rent all going up. The Federal Reserve (America's central bank), led by chairman Jerome Powell, kept saying the same thing: don't worry, this will fade on its own soon. Instead of admitting that too much new money had been printed, officials picked one calming word to describe the rising prices. What single word did they use?
answer: Transitory
choices: Transitory
Permanent
Explosive
Runaway
context: Jerome Powell, Janet Yellen, and most Federal Open Market Committee members publicly called the 2021 inflation 'transitory' at press conferences and hearings from April through November. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank, based in Washington DC. It can create new dollars out of thin air and lend them to big banks. When it creates a lot of new dollars very fast, more money ends up chasing the same food and toys on store shelves. What usually happens to the prices you pay at stores?
answer: Prices go up -- your money buys less
choices: Prices go up -- your money buys less
Prices go down -- your money buys more
Prices stay exactly the same
Only rich people's prices go up
context: Powell was appointed by President Trump and reappointed by President Biden. He led the FOMC through the pandemic response, the transitory-inflation call, and the 2022-23 tightening cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: Through most of 2021 the US Federal Reserve, led by chairman Jerome Powell, told the country that a rising wave of price increases would fade on its own within months. Fed officials called the inflation 'transitory' and rested the argument on three supports: pandemic base effects, tangled global supply chains, and one more claim specifically about the American job market. What was that third supporting claim?
answer: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
choices: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
Higher productivity would offset any wage pressure
Immigration would keep wage growth low
Automation would eventually replace scarce workers
context: The 'transitory' case argued that with unemployment still elevated, workers lacked bargaining power for the wage gains that would sustain price inflation. Critics pointed out that a 25%+ expansion in the M2 money supply is not absorbed by labor-market slack. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: In February 2021, the well-known Democratic economist Larry Summers — who had served as Treasury Secretary under President Bill Clinton — warned that President Biden's huge new $1.9 trillion Covid spending bill would push American prices up sharply. Most of his own party ignored him. Within a year, food, gas, and rent were rising at the fastest rate in about 40 years. What was Summers warning about?
answer: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
choices: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
A sudden shortage of paper for printing books
A drop in the number of people going to college
A rise in the price of internet service alone
context: Summers's February 4 2021 Washington Post op-ed argued that the size of the Biden fiscal package created substantial inflation risk. Fed officials publicly dismissed the warning. He was largely proven right within twelve months. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2021).

question: Through 2021 the US Federal Reserve, led by chairman Jerome Powell, kept calling the rising prices 'transitory,' meaning the problem would fade on its own soon. Prices climbed all year anyway — gas, groceries, rent. By late 2022 the Fed finally admitted the story was wrong and raised interest rates in a rush. What lesson do many critics draw from that episode?
answer: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
choices: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
Central banks always predict inflation perfectly ahead of time
Prices only rise when the weather is unusually bad
Rising prices are always the fault of everyday shoppers
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30 2021: 'I think it's probably a good time to retire that word.' CPI was already at 6.8% year-over-year that month. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2021, US Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell finally admitted that the word 'transitory' had become misleading and retired it in front of Congress. Roughly six months later, US year-over-year consumer price inflation hit its cycle peak in a specific month. What did that peak reading come in at, and in which month?
answer: 9.1% in June 2022
choices: 9.1% in June 2022
5.4% in June 2021
12.3% in September 2022
6.8% in November 2021
context: The June 2022 CPI print of 9.1% was the highest US year-over-year inflation since November 1981. It came six months after the transitory framing was abandoned and marked the peak that Powell then aggressively tightened to reverse. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: After the Covid crisis of 2020, the US government and the Federal Reserve created trillions of new dollars in stimulus checks, bond purchases, and bank loans. When prices began rising sharply in 2021, White House and Fed officials blamed supply-chain trouble that would soon pass. Austrian-school critics, including followers of Milton Friedman and Ludwig von Mises, pointed to a different cause. What was their main point?
answer: When the money supply grows a lot, prices eventually rise no matter what supply chains do
choices: When the money supply grows a lot, prices eventually rise no matter what supply chains do
Supply-chain trouble only affects services, never physical goods
Higher interest rates were already fixing the problem quickly
Prices always fall three months after any shock
context: The monetarist point: transitory factors resolve, but a large one-time expansion in the money supply flows through prices over a lag of 12-24 months. The Fed was staring at the monetary cause and offering a supply-side explanation. Source: Steve Hanke, Johns Hopkins Money and Growth papers (2021).

question: By late 2021 US prices were rising over 6 percent a year — the fastest in about 40 years. Yet the Federal Reserve, still led by chairman Jerome Powell, kept its main interest rate at zero and kept buying billions of dollars of bonds each month. Austrian-school critics said this was still far too loose. What term describes keeping money cheap and plentiful while prices are already rising?
answer: Easy money
choices: Easy money
Tight money
Neutral money
Balanced money
context: The Fed maintained QE and zero rates through November 2021 despite inflation already at 6.2%. The critique: the Fed was pouring gasoline on the very fire it was calling a mirage. Source: federalreserve.gov (FOMC statements November 3 2021).

question: The 'transitory inflation' story that US Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell repeated through 2021 is now widely cited as the modern Fed's worst forecasting error -- the peak reading eventually came in at 9.1 percent by June 2022, more than four times the Fed's own 2 percent target. What lesson does the Austrian tradition of economics, following Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, draw about how central banks predict inflation?
answer: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
choices: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
Central banks always over-tighten in response to inflation forecasts
Central bank models correctly predict inflation trajectories within two years
Central bank forecasts are unbiased on average and only occasionally wrong
context: The transitory episode is a case study in institutional motivated reasoning: the Fed had run enormous QE and preferred an explanation that did not implicate its own actions. A recognition move about how central banks talk about inflation. Source: George Selgin, Cato Institute commentary (2022-23).

question: Before the big 2021-2022 inflation hit, an economist who backed hard money was nominated to the Federal Reserve's board but rejected by the Senate. Critics said she was too skeptical of easy money. What does that rejection show about how the Fed picks its leaders?
answer: Nominees who challenge the Federal Reserve's usual easy-money views often fail confirmation
choices: Nominees who challenge the Federal Reserve's usual easy-money views often fail confirmation
Only nominees who oppose all Federal Reserve policy ever get confirmed
Nominees are picked at random from a lottery of American economists
The Senate rubber-stamps every Federal Reserve nominee without a hearing
context: Shelton's 1994 book Money Meltdown and later writings argued that unrestrained Fed discretion produced asset inflation and currency debasement. Her November 2020 Senate cloture defeat is often cited by Austrian analysts as a lost hard-money oversight opportunity. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: In the 1920s and 1930s, the Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek asked a hard question about socialism. Could a full state-planned economy actually work if a government committee had to set the price of every single good in the country -- bread, steel, shoes, tractors, everything -- without a real market of buyers and sellers giving those prices? What did Mises and Hayek argue?
answer: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
choices: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
Yes -- committees always know best
Yes, if the committee has enough computers
Yes, as long as the leader is smart
context: Hoff (1895-1982) took his doctorate at the University of Oslo. Ohlin, Frisch, and Myrdal were other Nordic economists of the same generation but on different sides of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: The Norwegian economist Trygve Hoff wrote his doctoral dissertation in 1938 on the great socialist calculation debate — the argument over whether central planners could set prices for a whole country without any real market to guide them. Eleven years later, in 1949, the translator M. A. Michael turned the book into English, and William Hodge of London published it. What was the English title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Human Action
context: The Norwegian original was 'Okonomisk kalkulasjon i socialistiske samfund.' The 1949 English edition brought Hoff's argument to a wider audience just as Human Action was appearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Through the 1920s and 30s, economists across Europe and America argued fiercely about whether central planners could ever price goods as well as a real market -- the socialist calculation debate. In 1938 the Norwegian economist Trygve Hoff published a big survey book, 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society,' that tried to gather up the whole argument in one place. Which bodies of writing did Hoff draw on for his survey?
answer: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
choices: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
The German Marxist literature alone
The Anglo-American Marshallian tradition alone
The French general-equilibrium school alone
context: Hoff defended Mises against Oskar Lange in careful detail, marshalling the German, English, and Soviet evidence. The book was in a real sense the definitive 1938 statement of the Austrian side of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: The Norwegian economist Trygve Hoff was not primarily an academic; he ran a family business and edited a widely-read free-market magazine called Farmand from Oslo. When Nazi Germany occupied Norway during World War II, Hoff's outspoken editorials made him a marked man, and he paid a specific personal price for his other career. What happened to him during the war?
answer: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
choices: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
He fled to neutral Sweden and taught at Stockholm University for the duration
He served as economic advisor to the Norwegian government-in-exile in London
He worked as a translator for the Allied forces in Iceland
context: Hoff edited the anti-Nazi magazine Farmand. Nazi occupation authorities arrested him for the editorship. He survived; after the war Farmand became a leading Nordic classical-liberal publication and Hoff a major figure in the small postwar European liberal revival. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In April 1947, the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek called together 39 scholars from around the world at a mountain resort above Lake Geneva in Switzerland. Their aim was to defend classical liberal ideas -- free markets, private property, the rule of law, limited government -- from the twin postwar threats of communism and central planning. The Norwegian businessman-economist Trygve Hoff was one of the founding members. What was the group they founded called?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Chicago School Society
The Vienna Circle
The Fabian Society
context: Named for Mont Pelerin above Vevey, Switzerland, where the founding meeting was held April 1-10, 1947. Hoff joined Mises, Hayek, Friedman, Ropke, Rustow, Robbins, Popper, Polanyi, Stigler, Machlup, and Knight in the founding cohort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: Trygve Hoff's 1938 doctoral book Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society had gone out of print by the 1970s. In 1981 an American economics institute dedicated to reviving the Austrian tradition of Mises and Rothbard reprinted it, with a fresh foreword by a leading Austrian-tradition scholar. Which group brought Hoff's book back into circulation?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Cato Institute
The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
The Bank for International Settlements
context: The foreword was written by Karl Brunner, the Swiss-born monetarist. The reprint made Hoff's careful pre-Hayek-1945 defense of Mises available to modern Austrian scholars for the first time in decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In 1967 the American economist Gordon Tullock wrote a short nine-page paper for a small journal called Western Economic Journal. In it, Tullock argued that the usual textbook cost of monopoly -- the little shaded triangle drawn in every intro economics book -- was way too small a number for the real harm monopolies, tariffs, and even ordinary theft do to a society. What title did he give the paper?
answer: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
choices: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
The Political Economy of Redistribution
The Vote-Trading Machinery of Congress
The Calculus of Public Choice
context: Gordon Tullock, 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' (Western Economic Journal, June 1967, later renamed Economic Inquiry). It was initially rejected by more prestigious journals before finding a home. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Tullock 1967).

question: Imagine a US steel firm sees Congress about to pass a tariff worth $100 million a year to it -- protection from foreign competition, plus almost guaranteed profits. In his 1967 paper on tariffs and monopolies, the American economist Gordon Tullock asked a sharp question: how much of that $100 million would the firm be willing to spend on lawyers, campaign gifts, and Washington lobbyists to make sure Congress hands the tariff its way?
answer: Up to $100 million per year
choices: Up to $100 million per year
About $1 million per year
About $10 million per year
Whatever the median firm spends
context: Tullock's insight: firms will burn real resources on the competition for privilege up to the full value of the privilege sought. If competing firms fight the tariff, they will burn resources on the other side. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: A monopolist earns big profits. Rival companies and lobbyists know those profits are up for grabs. So they spend huge amounts of time and money lobbying politicians, filing lawsuits, and running ads to either grab the monopoly or defend it. What does an economist call this waste?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Fair competition
Consumer surplus
Cost-benefit balance
context: The 'Tullock rectangle': resources spent competing for the monopoly rent equal in expectation to the full monopoly-profit rectangle. Later scholars named it after him. Source: Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975) formalized the Tullock rectangle.

question: The American economist Gordon Tullock spent his career studying rent-seeking -- the wasted effort people spend chasing a government-granted privilege instead of producing anything real. To show what he called the Tullock rectangle, he used a homespun example: theft. Tullock argued the value of what a thief actually steals is only a transfer from one pocket to another. The true drag on society, he said, was something else entirely. What did Tullock say was the real social cost of theft?
answer: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
choices: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
The dollar value of stolen goods
The lost tax revenue from unreported income
The cost of judicial trials for accused thieves
context: Tullock's illustration: theft merely TRANSFERS wealth from victim to thief -- the total is unchanged. The real deadweight loss is the whole edifice of prevention and preparation on both sides. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967), section on theft.

question: A big American car company hires expensive lobbyists in Washington DC. Their job is to push Congress for a new rule that blocks foreign rivals from selling cars in the United States. The company spends millions on lawyers, ads, and dinners for congressmen — instead of building better, cheaper cars for its customers. Economists have a general name for this pattern. What is it called?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Regulatory capture
Moral hazard
Adverse selection
context: Tullock originated the concept in 1967; Krueger's 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' (American Economic Review, June 1974) coined the phrase 'rent-seeking' and cemented the term. Source: jstor.org (Krueger 1974).

question: In 1974 the American economist Anne Krueger took Gordon Tullock's 1967 idea about wasted lobbying effort and tested it on one big developing country. She showed how the country's government import licenses were worth huge sums, and how firms spent nearly as much money on lobbying, gifts, and paperwork to win the licenses as the licenses were themselves worth. Which country did Krueger study?
answer: India
choices: India
Brazil
Turkey
Egypt
context: Krueger studied India's License Raj -- the elaborate system of import and industrial licenses that allocated the right to operate certain businesses. Her estimates suggested rent-seeking losses of a large percentage of Indian GNP. Source: Krueger, American Economic Review (1974).

question: In his 1967 paper The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft, the American economist Gordon Tullock put three very different-looking things under a single analytical roof: a firm being granted a legal monopoly, a Congress-granted tariff on foreign steel, and even an ordinary burglar breaking into a house. What shared feature makes all three of them create the larger deadweight loss Tullock was pointing to?
answer: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
choices: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
Each involves foreign parties competing with domestic firms
Each requires central-bank money-printing to sustain
Each is prohibited by the US Constitution
context: Whenever there is a REDISTRIBUTIVE prize on offer -- a rent -- real economic inputs get burned competing for the prize rather than producing value. The productive economy loses those inputs. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: In 1967 the American economist Gordon Tullock studied a puzzle: some very smart, well-paid, skilled workers spend all day helping one group grab money from another group by working the rules of government. They produce nothing new — no crops, no houses, no medicine — just paperwork and favors. Tullock later called this pattern rent-seeking. Which job is the classic example?
answer: Lobbyists
choices: Lobbyists
Farmers
Teachers
Truck drivers
context: Tullock argued that talented lawyers and lobbyists whose entire work was securing regulatory privilege were engaged in a socially wasteful zero-sum contest. The productive economy loses their talent. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Baumol, Journal of Political Economy (1990) on productive vs unproductive entrepreneurship.

question: The American economist Gordon Tullock's whole 1967 argument leans on a strong claim about what firms and lobbyists actually do when they compete for a government-granted rent -- a tariff, a special license, an exclusive monopoly grant, or a subsidy. What does Tullock say the competition among rival seekers uses up, on average, before the rent is even awarded?
answer: The full value of the rent being sought
choices: The full value of the rent being sought
Half the value of the rent being sought
Only a small fraction of the rent
None of the rent, since competition is impossible
context: Under free entry into the competition for rents and constant returns to lobbying, expected dissipation equals the full rent. Later scholarship (Posner 1975, Rogerson 1982) explored conditions under which dissipation is less than full. Source: Tullock 1967; Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975).

question: The American economist Gordon Tullock's 1967 paper The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft is now widely regarded as one of the founding texts of the public-choice subfield of political economy -- the study of what happens when self-interested behavior operates inside government too, not just in markets. Which single sentence best captures the enduring reasoning move at the heart of Tullock's argument?
answer: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
choices: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
Monopoly profits are always immediately competed away
Foreign tariffs impose no domestic welfare cost
Theft has no social cost because it merely transfers wealth
context: The rent-seeking move: whenever a redistributive prize is on offer, real economic resources will be burned competing for it, and society loses the value of those resources. This is a general result, not a partisan claim. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Buchanan + Tollison + Tullock, Toward a Theory of the Rent-Seeking Society (Texas A&M 1980).

question: Rent-seeking is when a company spends money lobbying government for a special favor — a subsidy, a license, a tariff — instead of making better products for customers. The public-choice economists James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock argued in the 1960s that some kinds of policy invite far more rent-seeking than others. Which policy design tends to reduce this waste the most?
answer: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
choices: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
Elaborate industry-specific carve-outs and case-by-case licenses
Discretionary agency waivers granted by senior political appointees
Rotating tax preferences renegotiated each Congress
context: Broad rules leave nothing worth lobbying over; carve-outs and discretion create rents. This is why constitutional political economy favors general rules and why Buchanan named 'generality' as a core principle. Source: Buchanan + Congleton, Politics by Principle, Not Interest (Cambridge 1998).

question: In the 1960s, the American economist Milton Friedman said the tangle of US welfare programs could be replaced with one clean idea. Instead of many offices deciding who qualified for which check, everyone would file a normal tax return. If your income fell below a set line, the IRS would send you a check -- the reverse of paying tax. Friedman's idea has a name that economists still use. What is that kind of tax called?
answer: A negative income tax
choices: A negative income tax
A luxury tax
A sales tax
A tariff
context: Friedman's motivation was administrative simplification and preservation of work incentives via a gradual known phase-out. It differed structurally from the modern UBI concept, which typically adds a universal payment on top of the existing safety net. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: The American economist Milton Friedman proposed the Negative Income Tax -- a plan where the government would simply mail cash to families below a set income line, replacing dozens of separate welfare programs. From 1968 to 1979 the United States and Canada ran four big real-world experiments to test it. Critics warned that once the checks started arriving, people would quit their jobs in droves. What did the trials actually find about work hours?
answer: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
choices: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
A total 80 percent reduction in work hours across all recipients
No measurable change in work hours in any subgroup
A doubling of work hours as recipients gained financial security to seek new jobs
context: The New Jersey/Pennsylvania (1968-72) and Seattle/Denver (1970-77) US experiments and the Manitoba MINCOME (1974-79) Canadian experiment all found modest work-hour declines with substantial administrative-cost savings over the multi-program comparison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: During the 2020 US presidential race, the Democratic candidate Andrew Yang, a New York entrepreneur, built his whole campaign around one big idea: give every adult American one thousand dollars a month, with no strings attached. He called it the Freedom Dividend, and he would pay for it partly with a new national sales tax. What is the general name for this kind of policy?
answer: Universal basic income
choices: Universal basic income
A progressive income tax
Payroll tax withholding
A tariff on imports
context: Yang, a tech entrepreneur, made UBI the signature of his campaign. His proposal was a universal flat payment with no income phase-out, structurally different from Friedman's NIT. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Andrew_Yang.

question: The largest recent US trial of no-strings cash transfers was funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch. It gave $1,000 a month to 1,000 people in Illinois and Texas for three years. When results came out in August 2024, what did the study find about work hours?
answer: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
choices: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
Recipients doubled their work hours on average
Recipients quit the labor force entirely at a rate of 80 percent
Recipients showed no change in work hours whatsoever
context: The study also found modest health improvements and no clear positive employment outcomes despite proponent hopes. The findings largely echoed the 1970s NIT experiments' pattern of moderate labor-supply reductions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Two plans send everyone a monthly cash check. The older plan, proposed by the Chicago economist Milton Friedman in the 1960s as a Negative Income Tax, would first cancel food stamps, housing aid, and most other welfare — so the check is the whole safety net. A newer plan from the 2020 candidate Andrew Yang usually keeps every existing program and adds the cash on top. What is the key difference?
answer: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
choices: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
One is paid weekly and the other is paid once a year
One is funded by tariffs and the other by property taxes
One is only for citizens and the other includes tourists
context: Friedman would have supported replacing programs with an NIT and opposed adding a UBI on top of them. The two proposals share a label but have opposite structural implications for the state's role and for the effective marginal tax rate facing the recipient as income rises. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: In his 2006 book In Our Hands: A Plan to Replace the Welfare State, the American libertarian scholar Charles Murray proposed sending every adult American 10,000 dollars per year. His plan would end nearly every existing welfare program — Social Security, Medicare, food stamps, housing aid, unemployment insurance — and use that money instead to fund the flat cash grant. What makes his plan different from an add-on plan?
answer: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
choices: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
It adds monthly payments on top of the existing programs
It applies only to people over 65 years of age
It is paid in food stamps rather than cash
context: The Murray design is a UBI in label but an NIT in structure -- a flat universal payment that eliminates the existing multi-program stack. Same-label proposals with different phase-out and replacement structures produce very different outcomes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: In 1976 a Republican governor of one American state convinced voters to set aside a big share of the state's oil-royalty money in a special investment fund. Starting in 1982, the fund began paying every one of that state's residents — men, women, and children — an annual dividend of one to two thousand dollars per person. It has paid out every single year since, making it the longest-running cash-dividend program in the country. Which state runs it?
answer: Alaska (the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend)
choices: Alaska (the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend)
Texas (the Texas Oil Trust Distribution)
California (the California Resident Dividend)
Wyoming (the Wyoming Mineral Royalty Payout)
context: The Alaska Permanent Fund was created in 1976 and the Dividend program began payouts in 1982. Every Alaskan resident (regardless of income) receives the annual share. It is the closest real-world US analogue of a UBI. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Alaska_Permanent_Fund.

question: A student asks a public-choice economist whether a Universal Basic Income — a monthly government check to every adult — is 'obviously a good idea.' The economist refuses to answer yes or no. Instead he compares two same-name plans: Charles Murray's UBI, which would replace nearly every welfare program with cash, and Andrew Yang's UBI, which would add cash on top of every program. Two plans with the same label, opposite results. Which reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
choices: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
Any cash transfer to households below the middle income is always good
Any cash transfer to households above the middle income is always harmful
Policy details never matter because people never change their behavior
context: This is Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only tradeoffs' at the policy-design level. A UBI on top of existing programs has different effects from an NIT that replaces them. The kid learns to look under the label at the actual mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: In 1949, right after World War II, the US Congress passed the Agricultural Act. It ordered the federal government to prop up prices for one favorite farm product by buying up any surplus and storing it -- sometimes as huge stockpiles of cheese and butter aging in warehouses. That program has kept running for over 70 years, protecting one specific industry. Which farm product does the US government prop up?
answer: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
choices: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
Wheat only
Corn only
Soybeans only
context: The federal purchases were made largely as butter and processed cheese, which stored better than fluid milk. The program has been renamed and modified many times but the above-market-support core has persisted for 75+ years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: By 1981, after decades of the federal dairy price-support program buying up all the extra milk American farmers made, the US Department of Agriculture owned a mountain of one processed dairy product. It sat aging in giant refrigerated caves and warehouses across the Midwest — Wisconsin, Missouri, Kansas. President Reagan later ordered much of it given away to the poor. Which item did the government have, and roughly how much?
answer: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
choices: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
About 10,000 pounds of yogurt
About 5 million pounds of ice cream
About 100 million pounds of powdered milk only
context: The stockpile became a national embarrassment. Congressional hearings and press coverage forced action; the Reagan administration began a distribution program the same year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: In 1981, President Ronald Reagan's team faced a strange problem: the US dairy price-support program had bought so much surplus milk that federal warehouses were overflowing with cheese wheels aging into inedible bricks. Rather than throw the cheese away, the Reagan administration handed out huge yellow blocks of it to food banks for free. The blocks became so common in poor neighborhoods that a new phrase entered American speech. What did the phrase become?
answer: 'Government cheese'
choices: 'Government cheese'
'Federal butter'
'Reagan powder'
'The white brick'
context: The loaves were shelf-stable pasteurized processed cheese food. The distribution continued through the 1990s and became a cultural touchstone in low-income neighborhoods (referenced in hip-hop and stand-up comedy). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: In their 1980 book Free to Choose, the Chicago economists Milton and Rose Friedman studied the US dairy price-support program. Around 100,000 dairy farmers pocket most of the benefit — sometimes tens of thousands of dollars each per year — while over 300 million American shoppers pay a little more for milk, cheese, and butter. The dairy lobby fights hard for the program; ordinary shoppers barely notice the cost. Which public-choice framework fits this pattern?
answer: Concentrated benefits with dispersed costs
choices: Concentrated benefits with dispersed costs
The tragedy of the commons
Adverse selection in insurance markets
Ricardian equivalence in fiscal policy
context: The concentrated beneficiaries organize (dairy lobby, state-level dairy compacts) because the per-household benefit is large. The dispersed victims do not organize because the per-household cost is small enough not to warrant political effort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: The American economist Milton Friedman spent years attacking the US dairy price-support program. His argument leaned on a bigger political-economy idea: small, tightly organized groups (like a few thousand dairy farmers) usually beat big, scattered ones (like millions of milk drinkers) in political fights, because the small group has more to gain from each vote and can coordinate. That theory got its most famous statement in a 1965 book by an American economist named Mancur Olson. Which book laid it out?
answer: 'The Logic of Collective Action' by Mancur Olson
choices: 'The Logic of Collective Action' by Mancur Olson
'The Calculus of Consent' by Buchanan and Tullock
'The Road to Serfdom' by Friedrich Hayek
'Capitalism and Freedom' by Milton Friedman
context: Mancur Olson (1932-1998) was an American economist at Maryland. His 1965 book (Harvard University Press) argued that concentrated beneficiaries face lower coordination costs than dispersed victims, explaining why regulated industries can capture their regulators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: By 2014, the US government had been buying up surplus milk under the 1949 Agricultural Act for 65 years. The 2014 Farm Bill kept dairy farmers protected above market prices, but replaced the old direct-purchase machinery with a new insurance-style mechanism that paid farmers whenever their profit margin -- milk price minus feed cost -- dropped below a chosen level. What did the 2014 Farm Bill replace the older program with?
answer: The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) system
choices: The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) system
A federal ban on all dairy subsidies
A privatized dairy futures exchange
A European-Union-style quota auction
context: DMC pays farmers when the margin between milk price and feed cost falls below a chosen threshold. The mechanism is different from bulk purchase but the underlying above-market income guarantee for dairy producers persists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: In 1999, Hugo Chavez took power in Venezuela promising 'socialism for the twenty-first century.' One of his first economic moves was to freeze prices for food, fuel, and everyday goods at levels the government chose. Store owners were told: sell for the state's price or go to jail. But the mandated prices were often lower than what it cost to produce or import the goods, so every sale meant a loss. What happened next in Venezuelan shops?
answer: Shelves went empty -- shops stopped stocking things that lost money
choices: Shelves went empty -- shops stopped stocking things that lost money
Shelves stayed full -- shopkeepers gladly sold at a loss
Many new stores opened
Prices dropped to zero everywhere
context: Chavez ruled Venezuela from 1999 to 2013 and built the model his successor Maduro inherited. Source: Grokipedia 'Hugo Chavez' (2026-09-05).

question: By the mid-2010s the Venezuelan government's price controls had emptied store shelves — bread, milk, and medicine all gone. To keep paying its bills, the government under President Nicolás Maduro printed enormous amounts of new bolivar money. A loaf of bread that once cost a few pesos was soon millions of pesos, then billions. People carried cash in shopping bags. What is this called?
answer: Hyperinflation
choices: Hyperinflation
Deflation
Recession
A trade surplus
context: Maduro won a disputed April 2013 election and remains in power. His tenure saw hyperinflation, mass emigration, and near-total dollarization of the informal economy. Source: Grokipedia 'Nicolas Maduro' (2026-09-05).

question: Through the 2010s, Venezuela's socialist government -- Hugo Chavez and then Nicolas Maduro -- set legal top prices on food and basic goods, prices far below what shops needed to charge just to restock. Producers stopped shipping at a loss. Walk into a Caracas supermarket or a drug store and shelves that used to be full were bare. What did shoppers keep finding was missing?
answer: Widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine
choices: Widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine
A boom in domestic manufacturing
A rapid rise in real wages
Falling emigration as living standards improved
context: Producers facing prices below their costs cut output. Shelves emptied. The government blamed a 'capitalist conspiracy' and sent soldiers to force shops to sell at controlled prices. Source: Grokipedia 'Crisis in Venezuela' (2026-09-05).

question: By 2018 Venezuela's economy was in freefall. Years of Chavez and Maduro's price controls, oil-industry seizures, and money-printing had unleashed hyperinflation on the same scale as Weimar Germany in 1923, when Germans burned marks in their stoves for heat. That year the International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its official estimate of Venezuela's yearly inflation rate. About how high did the IMF say prices were rising?
answer: About 130,000% per year
choices: About 130,000% per year
About 500% per year
About 25% per year
About 3,000,000% per year
context: The IMF's 2018 estimate of Venezuelan annual inflation was roughly 130,000%. By 2019 a wheelbarrow of banknotes was needed for basic groceries -- the Weimar image replayed a century later, in Latin America. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Venezuela' (2026-09-05).

question: After two decades of socialist rule under Hugo Chavez and Nicolas Maduro, Venezuela's economy was in ruins -- hyperinflation, empty grocery shelves, medicine shortages, a broken oil industry. Ordinary Venezuelans packed what they could carry and walked out, crossing into Colombia, Peru, Brazil, and beyond. By 2024 the United Nations was tracking one of the largest peacetime exoduses in modern history. About what share of the country had left?
answer: About one quarter, some 7.7 million people
choices: About one quarter, some 7.7 million people
About one tenth, about 3 million people
About half, about 15 million people
About one twentieth, about 1.5 million people
context: The 7.7 million displaced Venezuelans make this the largest displacement crisis in modern Western Hemisphere history -- larger than any war-driven displacement in Latin American history. Neighbors like Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, and Chile have absorbed the majority. Source: Grokipedia 'Venezuelan refugee crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: By the early 2020s, Venezuela's hyperinflation had wrecked the bolivar so completely that people invented their own solution -- not from any government decree, but from millions of individual choices. Shopkeepers started listing prices in a foreign currency they trusted more. Meanwhile millions of Venezuelans working abroad wired money home to family through a US digital-payment app. Together these two moves gave Venezuela a partial economic recovery. What did Venezuelans start doing with prices and wages?
answer: Pricing goods in US dollars and receiving remittances via Zelle from relatives abroad
choices: Pricing goods in US dollars and receiving remittances via Zelle from relatives abroad
Bartering exclusively for gold coins minted before 1999
Reintroducing a fixed exchange rate to the Argentine peso
Adopting the Ecuadorian sucre as everyday money
context: Bodegas quietly priced goods in USD; salaries were paid via Zelle transfers from relatives in Miami. The Venezuelan economy dollarized from below, without any legal change. Source: Grokipedia 'Economy of Venezuela' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1920, an Austrian economist published a paper called 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' His argument was blunt: without private property in factories and land, there are no real markets; without markets, no real prices; and without prices telling planners that steel is scarcer than sand, central planners must guess in the dark. This paper opened what economists still call the 'socialist calculation debate.' Who wrote that 1920 paper?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Murray Rothbard
Israel Kirzner
context: Mises's 1920 paper 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' argued that without market prices for capital goods, socialist planners have no way to know whether a proposed use of resources creates or destroys value. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: In 1920, just after Russia's Bolshevik revolution turned into full-scale central planning, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises published a paper called 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' Economists today call his argument the 'socialist calculation problem,' and it launched a decades-long debate. Mises said socialism could not work, for a reason baked into its design. Which deep flaw does the calculation problem point to?
answer: Central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices would signal about scarcity and value
choices: Central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices would signal about scarcity and value
Central planners always cheat and skim revenues for personal gain
Central planners cannot enforce laws without the consent of unions
Central planners fail because workers refuse to work for low wages
context: The calculation problem is epistemic, not moral. Even honest, well-intentioned planners cannot substitute for a working price system because prices aggregate dispersed knowledge that no central authority possesses. Source: Mises, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920).

question: The Soviet collapse of 1991 and Mao's famines of 1958-62 happened before smartphones, in closed countries a Cold War away from most Americans -- their reality was hard to see even for the people living through them. Venezuela's collapse is different: it is unfolding right now, being filmed on cell phones and posted to social media, in a Spanish-speaking country close to the United States. That closeness gives the Venezuelan case something the older cases lack. What does Venezuela have that older socialist collapses do not?
answer: It is happening now, on smartphone video, in a Western Hemisphere country a plane ride from Miami
choices: It is happening now, on smartphone video, in a Western Hemisphere country a plane ride from Miami
It happened in a country with no oil resources or export commodities
It happened without a preceding period of price controls
It happened under a government that publicly renounced socialism
context: Old newsreels of Soviet or Maoist collapse are historical footage. Venezuela is on YouTube in Spanish that Google Translate handles instantly. A Western middle-schooler can watch the calculation problem play out in real time. Source: multiple English-language documentaries 2018-2024.

question: In 1920, Ludwig von Mises argued that a socialist economy cannot rationally allocate resources without market prices to signal scarcity. For most of the twentieth century, Mises's critics dismissed this as theoretical hand-waving -- an untestable claim from an old Austrian. Then Venezuela ran the experiment in slow motion, on live video, with hard economic data anyone can read. Which move does the Venezuelan case sharpen?
answer: The socialist calculation problem is not an abstract academic dispute; it is an observable, current phenomenon
choices: The socialist calculation problem is not an abstract academic dispute; it is an observable, current phenomenon
Price controls always eventually work if enforced hard enough
Central planning is a good idea in principle but hard to execute in practice
Modern digital tools solve the calculation problem central planners once faced
context: The Mises argument that seemed like a theoretical dispute in 1920 is now a public fact playing out on smartphone video. The empirical case makes the theory unavoidable for any honest student. Source: Mises, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920).

question: During Venezuela's collapse in the late 2010s, prices for most goods rose thousands of percent a year -- but one resource stayed extremely cheap because the government kept its consumer price far below what it actually cost the state to produce. Clever Venezuelans plugged in cryptocurrency mining rigs, drew huge amounts of this cheap resource, and used it to earn Bitcoin, which held its value while the bolivar died. Which resource were they using?
answer: Electricity, whose domestic price was set far below production cost
choices: Electricity, whose domestic price was set far below production cost
Coffee, whose export price was set by state marketing boards
Petroleum, whose retail gasoline price was heavily subsidized
Cocoa, whose government purchase price was above world levels
context: By 2018 Venezuela had one of the largest per-capita Bitcoin-mining populations in Latin America. Cheap electricity plus hyperinflation made mining locally-generated sound money one of the most rational responses available to a Venezuelan saver. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: As Bitcoin mining spread across Venezuela's cheap-electricity homes and warehouses, President Nicolas Maduro's government did not free the market or celebrate the innovation. Instead, starting in 2018, it treated the miners as a political threat because Bitcoin let people store savings outside state control. In 2023 Maduro banned mining outright. What did his regime do to Venezuelan Bitcoin miners in the meantime?
answer: Sent political-intelligence police to raid mining operations and seize rigs
choices: Sent political-intelligence police to raid mining operations and seize rigs
Signed a free-trade agreement with the United States
Legalized Bitcoin as a second national currency alongside the bolivar
Distributed government-owned mining equipment to every household
context: SEBIN (the political intelligence service) and later SUNACRIP raided mining operations, seized rigs, and eventually banned mining outright in 2023 citing 'electricity grid stability.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: As Venezuela's economy fell apart in the late 2010s, private stores could not stock food at the mandated prices. The state stepped in to hand out subsidized food boxes -- rice, oil, flour, canned tuna -- and for millions of families they became the only reliable source of calories. The boxes were distributed by neighborhood committees loyal to the ruling party, and they took their name from those committees. What is the four-letter Spanish acronym?
answer: CLAP (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion)
choices: CLAP (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion)
PSUV (Partido Socialista Unido de Venezuela)
SEBIN (Servicio Bolivariano de Inteligencia Nacional)
PDVSA (Petroleos de Venezuela SA)
context: 'Local Committees for Supply and Production.' The boxes typically contained rice, cornmeal, oil, sugar, and canned goods. Distribution was tightly controlled by neighborhood collectives loyal to the ruling PSUV party. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comit%C3%A9_Local_de_Abastecimiento_y_Producci%C3%B3n.

question: When Venezuela ran out of food under socialist central planning in the 2010s, President Nicolás Maduro's government began handing out subsidized grocery boxes to poor families through a program called the CLAP (Local Committees for Supply and Production). Reporters and neighbors soon found that families whose block did not vote for Maduro's ruling party quietly stopped receiving their boxes. What political use of government-controlled food does Venezuela's CLAP program reveal?
answer: It can be used as a tool to force people to support the ruling party
choices: It can be used as a tool to force people to support the ruling party
It always reaches families faster than private stores could
It costs the government less than letting people shop for themselves
It ends up giving every family the same amount of food
context: Opposition figures Maria Corina Machado and Leopoldo Lopez, and journalists Anatoly Kurmanaev and Anibal Sanchez in Reuters and NYT reports 2016-2019, documented the loyalty conditionality. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comit%C3%A9_Local_de_Abastecimiento_y_Producci%C3%B3n.

question: In Venezuela today, some young people quietly mine bitcoin on home computers while the government hands out food boxes based on which party you support. A student asks what idea explains why the government-run side works so badly. The answer comes from the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises in his famous 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' What was Mises's argument?
answer: Without real market prices, a planner cannot figure out what to make
choices: Without real market prices, a planner cannot figure out what to make
Governments should always print more money during a crisis
Farmers should collectively own all the country's factories
Free trade always hurts the poorest workers in a country
context: Mises's 1920 essay predicted that an economy without market prices would 'grope in the dark' -- unable to compute rational allocation. Venezuela's fall-back to Bitcoin (for those with technical skill) and to political loyalty (for everyone else) is what that groping looks like at national scale. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: In 2019 the Human Rights Foundation, a US-based nonprofit, published a case study called 'The Venezuelan Cryptocurrency Boom.' It documented how ordinary Venezuelans -- not speculators or day traders -- used Bitcoin to escape hyperinflation, receive help from relatives abroad, and hold savings the government could not seize or inflate away. Two authors wrote it: a Venezuelan software engineer and an American economist. Who wrote that report?
answer: Alejandro Machado and Jill Carlson
choices: Alejandro Machado and Jill Carlson
Michael Saylor and Cathie Wood
Vitalik Buterin and Charles Hoskinson
Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison
context: The report catalogued how Bitcoin (and Ethereum) let Venezuelans preserve savings, receive remittances, and transact outside the bolivar. It became one of the standard cited sources on the Venezuelan case in Bitcoin policy debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that when a government destroys market prices, something else has to decide who gets what -- goods do not allocate themselves. Venezuela's split economy showed exactly what that 'something else' looks like in practice. On one side stood an underground digital marketplace where people traded and saved outside the state's reach. On the other side stood state food boxes handed out based on loyalty to the ruling party. Which two things filled the gap that prices used to fill?
answer: The underground global market via Bitcoin, and political loyalty via CLAP
choices: The underground global market via Bitcoin, and political loyalty via CLAP
The World Bank's grants program, and remittances from Venezuelans abroad
A restored gold standard, and barter networks in coffee
Chinese state loans, and Colombian food aid
context: Two allocation mechanisms for a country whose market prices had ceased to function: hard-money exit for the technically skilled, party-loyalty allocation for everyone else. The Austrian-tradition prediction was that suppressed prices would reappear as SOMETHING; Venezuela made the something visible. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: Imagine a government tells every grocery store: you must sell milk for one dollar a gallon. But the farmer's costs -- feed, labor, refrigerated trucks -- already add up to more than a dollar per gallon before the store even puts it on the shelf. If a store obeys, every gallon sold is a loss. Store owners are not stupid. What happens to the milk supply on the shelves?
answer: There will be a shortage -- milk will disappear from shelves
choices: There will be a shortage -- milk will disappear from shelves
There will be a huge surplus of milk
Milk quality will improve
Nothing at all will change
context: Nicolas Maduro won the April 14, 2013 special election following Chavez's death on March 5, 2013. He extended and later expanded price controls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Maduro.

question: In 2014, Venezuela's president Nicolas Maduro pushed through a law that set legal top prices on many everyday goods. Shopkeepers who charged even a little more could be arrested, their inventory seized and their store shut down. In English the law is usually called the Fair Price Law. What is its Spanish name?
answer: Ley Organica de Precios Justos
choices: Ley Organica de Precios Justos
Ley de Solidaridad Social
Ley de Alimentacion Popular
Ley de Justicia Comercial
context: The Fair Price Law (Ley Organica de Precios Justos, January 2014) created a new agency (SUNDDE) to enforce maximum retail prices. Overcharging carried criminal penalties. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela.

question: In late 2013, Venezuela's government passed the Fair Price Law, capping prices on hundreds of everyday goods below what stores paid to import them. Within weeks the shelves emptied -- and one basic household product became the global symbol of Venezuela's crisis. News crews in 2013 and 2014 filmed lines that stretched around the block just to buy this one item. What were Venezuelans queueing for?
answer: Toilet paper
choices: Toilet paper
Coffee
Sugar
Salt
context: The 2013 Venezuelan toilet-paper shortage became a symbol of the price-control-induced supply collapse. Flour, cooking oil, milk, rice, and soap also disappeared -- but toilet paper became the political news story. Source: reuters.com Venezuela shortage coverage 2013.

question: The nineteenth-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to look for two things in any policy: what is seen, and what is unseen. Apply Bastiat's rule to Venezuela's 2014 Fair Price Law. The seen was easy: the cheap mandated prices printed on packages in state supermarkets, right there where the TV cameras could film them. What was the unseen consequence of the same law?
answer: The shelves themselves -- basic goods disappeared and Venezuelans queued for hours
choices: The shelves themselves -- basic goods disappeared and Venezuelans queued for hours
The tax revenue lost on capped items
The state supermarkets' opening hours
The government's cost of enforcement
context: The visible low price hid the invisible cost: flour, cooking oil, milk, rice, toilet paper, and soap disappeared as suppliers withdrew rather than sell at a loss. Queuing filled the gap. Source: bastiat.org, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela.

question: By 2014, Venezuela's black market -- called 'bachaqueo' by Venezuelans -- had swallowed most everyday shopping. People bought capped items at state stores and immediately resold them outside at their real prices. The Maduro government's answer was not to raise the caps but to install a biometric machine at every state-store checkout, so a shopper could only buy their monthly quota once. What kind of body-scan system did Venezuela install?
answer: A fingerprint-indexed rationing system
choices: A fingerprint-indexed rationing system
A retinal-scan purchase system
A voice-recognition allocation tool
A national ID card with QR codes
context: The Sistema Biometrico used fingerprint scanners at state supermarket checkouts to limit each household to weekly quotas of basic goods. It was the government's response to the bachaqueo secondary market. Source: bbc.com Venezuela biometric rationing.

question: After hyperinflation and shortages shattered Venezuela's regular grocery system in the mid-2010s, the Maduro government began handing out cardboard boxes of subsidized food through neighborhood committees run by the ruling party. If your household stayed loyal to Maduro's party, a box of rice, flour, and cooking oil arrived. If not, you were quietly skipped. What did Venezuelans come to call these boxes?
answer: The CLAP boxes
choices: The CLAP boxes
The Chavez packs
The Maduro rations
The Solidario baskets
