context: The December 1978 Third Plenum is treated as the birth of the reform-and-opening-up era. From 1978 to 2019 China's per-capita GDP rose more than fifty-fold -- but only where and when the market replaced planning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up.

question: In 1986 Vietnam's Communist Party copied China's 1978 reforms: they let farmers sell their crops, ended most price controls, and welcomed foreign investors. Vietnam's per-person income has since grown about eight times. What big change did these reforms make?
answer: They moved the country from central planning toward a market economy
choices: They moved the country from central planning toward a market economy
They doubled the size of the government's central planning office
They ended all foreign trade to protect Vietnamese jobs
They banned private ownership of farmland forever
context: 'Doi Moi' means 'renovation'. Vietnam went from about $422 per-capita GDP in 1986 to nearly $3,700 in the following decades. Central planning was quietly abandoned; the Party stayed in charge but stopped setting most prices. Source: thediplomat.com/2023/01/the-myth-of-doi-moi-in-vietnam/.

question: In 1985 the American economist Don Lavoie published 'Rivalry and Central Planning.' He said the mainstream had answered Mises's point about prices but never engaged Hayek's deeper point about dispersed knowledge. Modern Austrians like Joseph Salerno, Peter Boettke, and Guido Huelsmann then drew a lesson about how the field handled the 1989 collapse. Which pattern did they name?
answer: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
choices: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
The profession quietly withdrew all remaining market-socialist proposals by 1995
The profession credited the Austrians in its textbooks by the mid-1990s
The profession dropped comparative-systems economics from graduate curricula
context: Lavoie, Salerno, Boettke, and Huelsmann observed the same pattern Thomas Kuhn described in 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' -- a discipline can accept the outside facts while continuing to teach the old textbook framing. That, they argued, is why market-socialist proposals keep reappearing in every generation. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: Robert Heilbroner was one of the 20th century's best-selling American socialist economists -- his book The Worldly Philosophers taught economic history to millions of students. In a 1990 New Yorker essay he made a famous public admission: Ludwig von Mises had been right about socialism all along. Heilbroner said his admission accepted the verdict of a 69-year experiment, the biggest test in social-science history. What deep question had planned economies been forced to answer with hundreds of millions of lives?
answer: Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
choices: Whether Marx's labour theory of value could be salvaged with better mathematics
Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
Whether socialist countries could avoid dependence on world trade
Whether workers' councils could substitute for private firms as legal owners
context: The 1920 essay had said no -- not because central planners lacked good intentions, but because the information needed to compare production plans exists only in the dispersed heads of the people doing the producing and consuming. The 20th-century death toll of Communism, put by the Black Book of Communism at roughly 100 million, was the price of running the experiment. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: A short 1920 German essay argued central planners could not calculate real prices without markets. Its ideas only reached most Western economists in 1935, when a fellow economist edited an English-language volume built around it. What effect did that translation and editing have?
answer: It set the terms of the whole planning-versus-markets debate for decades
choices: It set the terms of the whole planning-versus-markets debate for decades
It settled the debate immediately with no further argument anywhere
It caused every economist to abandon market economics forever
It had no effect at all outside of Germany
context: 'Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism', edited by F.A. Hayek (Routledge, London, 1935). Hayek's own introductory essay 'The Nature and History of the Problem' framed the debate for a whole generation. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: Imagine a government department that gets a bigger budget every year no matter how well its workers actually do their job. The boss of the department gets a bigger corner office and a larger staff each time the budget grows, and unlike a private business he never has to compete for paying customers. Year after year he sits down to fill out next year's budget request. What is the boss most likely to ask for?
answer: An even bigger budget
choices: A smaller budget so taxpayers save money
An even bigger budget
The same budget every year
No budget at all
context: William Niskanen (1933-2011) was a Chicago-trained economist who served in Nixon's OMB, chaired Reagan's CEA (1981-85), and chaired the Cato Institute from 1985 until his death. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Niskanen.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen published a book that used economic reasoning to explain how public offices -- government agencies staffed by career bureaucrats -- actually behave when nobody is watching them closely. The book became a foundation of public-choice economics, the branch of economics that studies how officials respond to incentives. What did Niskanen title it?
answer: Bureaucracy and Representative Government
choices: Bureaucracy and Representative Government
The Politics of Bureaucracy
Inside Bureaucracy
Bureaucracy
context: Bureaucracy and Representative Government (Aldine-Atherton, 1971). It built directly on Gordon Tullock's earlier Politics of Bureaucracy (1965). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Niskanen.

question: Niskanen made a bold move. Instead of assuming bureaucrats work for the public good or their agency's mission, he asked what they actually gain personally over a career. Salary, prestige, staff, and promotions all rise with one thing. Which thing did he say they really maximize?
answer: The size of their agency's budget
choices: The size of their agency's budget
The public opinion of their agency
The number of press releases per year
The judicial rulings favoring their agency
context: Niskanen's model: salary, staff, prestige, perquisites, agency power, and promotion prospects are all positively correlated with agency budget. A bureaucrat rationally advancing his or her career therefore fights for a bigger budget. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 4.

question: The American public-choice economist William Niskanen studied why federal agencies keep growing year after year. His answer never accused bureaucrats of being bad people or corrupt individuals -- many were dedicated civil servants trying hard to serve the country. Instead, Niskanen pointed to something impersonal, built into the design of the job itself, that shaped their behavior. What is his real claim?
answer: The career incentive structure REWARDS budget-expanding behavior
choices: The career incentive structure REWARDS budget-expanding behavior
Bureaucrats are corrupted by contact with lobbyists
Bureaucrats consciously conspire to defraud the public
Bureaucrats are less ethical than private-sector employees
context: Niskanen models an INCENTIVE STRUCTURE, not a moral failing. Whatever an agency's official mission, the structure that rewards its staff systematically favors expansion. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface.

question: The public-choice economist William Niskanen's model of bureaucracy makes a striking prediction: a federal agency will almost never announce that its mission is finished. Even when a problem seems solved -- a disease pushed back, a program completed -- the agency finds new mission statements, new priorities, and new problems to grow into. Niskanen's model explains this pattern with a single reason. What is that reason?
answer: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
choices: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
Federal law prohibits announcing mission completion
The agency cannot legally hire external consultants to certify completion
Congress passes laws to keep agencies alive regardless of mission
context: A completed-mission announcement is against every staff member's career interest. The predictable behavior is instead mission creep -- redefining the mission as new problems the agency must address. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 5.

question: When Ronald Reagan took office as US president in January 1981, his administration promised to shrink the federal government. His team fought hard for budget cuts, agency reorganizations, and hiring freezes, and Reagan personally attacked government bloat in dozens of speeches. Over his two full terms, from 1981 to 1989, what actually happened to the total number of federal civilian jobs?
answer: It barely moved despite the political pressure
choices: It barely moved despite the political pressure
It fell by roughly forty percent
It rose by roughly a hundred percent
It fell to Depression-era levels
context: Federal civilian employment stayed essentially flat under Reagan (1981-89) despite aggressive rhetoric. Individual agency budgets fluctuated modestly; the total was very sticky. Niskanen predicts exactly this stickiness. Source: OPM historical federal civilian employment data (bea.gov, opm.gov).

question: In 1967 the American economist Anthony Downs published a book called Inside Bureaucracy, a close study of how government offices actually work. After watching officials for years, Downs sorted the people inside every bureau into personality types — climbers chasing promotion, conservers protecting their safe posts, zealots devoted to one cause, plus advocates and statesmen. From these patterns he drew one big teaching about a large bureaucracy. What is it?
answer: People inside government act on their own goals, just like people outside it
choices: People inside government act on their own goals, just like people outside it
People inside government always put the public first
Government offices always shrink to the smallest useful size
Government offices only hire people who agree with the mayor
context: Anthony Downs, Inside Bureaucracy (Little Brown, 1967). Downs classifies bureaucrats by mix of self-interest and mission-interest; Niskanen models the aggregate effect. The two frameworks fit together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: The public-choice economist William Niskanen served on Ronald Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, the president's inner circle of economic policy advisors. In 1985 Niskanen resigned in frustration. He never accused Reagan of any personal wrongdoing, but one specific policy fight had driven him out -- Niskanen felt the White House had quietly abandoned a promise Reagan had made in every campaign speech. What was the immediate cause?
answer: The administration's abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda
choices: The administration's abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda
The administration's tariff on Japanese steel
The administration's monetary policy under Volcker
The administration's income-tax reform of 1986
context: Niskanen resigned in protest of the administration's growing deficits and its failure to pair tax cuts with a serious spending-cut program. He then moved to chair the Cato Institute for the rest of his career. Source: Niskanen, Reaganomics (Oxford 1988).

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen published a book called Bureaucracy and Representative Government. He built a model treating government agency chiefs as self-interested people who want bigger budgets, more staff, and larger turf — not as selfless servants of the public. His model predicts patterns you would not expect if agencies just served the public good. Which pattern below is NOT one of Niskanen's predictions?
answer: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
choices: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
Agencies rarely announce that their mission is complete
Agencies with unclear performance metrics tend to grow fastest
Agencies grow during friendly administrations and shrink little under opposition
context: Niskanen predicts the OPPOSITE: agencies with UNCLEAR performance metrics grow fastest, because failure cannot be measured. Where failure IS measurable, budget increases become harder to justify. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 6.

question: In 1971 the American economist William Niskanen published Bureaucracy and Representative Government. His argument: if you assume bureau chiefs are just as self-interested as businessmen — chasing bigger budgets, more staff, and larger turf — you predict real agency behavior far better than the old assumption that they simply serve the public. Niskanen's whole argument can be summed up in one sentence about what economics adds when applied to public employees. Which sentence best captures the payoff?
answer: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions about agency behavior
choices: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions about agency behavior
Bureaucrats are morally worse than other workers
All federal agencies should be abolished
Bureau chiefs are always incompetent
context: Niskanen's contribution: give up the benevolent-planner assumption and predictions about bureau behavior become far more accurate. This is the symmetric application of standard economic reasoning to political actors. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface and Chapter 12.

question: In early August 1914, the great powers of Europe — Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Austria-Hungary — mobilized for what would become the First World War. Each government needed to pay for guns, shells, and soldiers with new paper money it did not have gold to back. Almost overnight, every side did the same thing to its currency. That move ended the classical gold standard, the century-old system that had let anyone trade paper bills for real gold coins at a fixed rate. What did every side do?
answer: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
choices: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
Devalued its currency by 50%
Nationalized its central bank
Adopted a fixed foreign-exchange peg
context: Germany suspended convertibility on August 4 1914; Britain effectively followed within days; France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary all did the same within the week. The gold standard died in one week. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: In August 1914 the First World War broke out across Europe. Every major country that entered the war -- Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Austria-Hungary -- immediately stopped letting citizens trade paper money for physical gold at the bank, because a full gold standard would have strictly limited how much money a government could raise to pay for the war. Under a real gold standard, there were only two honest ways to fund a war. What were they?
answer: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
choices: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
Requisitioning goods or issuing bonds
Selling colonies or licensing trade monopolies
Devaluing the currency or issuing new coins
context: Under gold, states could raise money only by taxing (unpopular, slow) or borrowing (limited by lender willingness). Once off gold, they could print paper and defer the reckoning until after victory. Source: Grokipedia 'World War I reparations' (2026-09-05).

question: When the First World War began in 1914, the German government could not raise enough tax revenue to pay for the fighting. So it began printing paper marks by the ton. Between 1914 and 1918 the total quantity of German paper notes in circulation grew massively, planting the seed for the hyperinflation that would explode after the war ended. About how many times bigger did the paper stock get over those four years?
answer: About 12 times
choices: About 12 times
About 2 times
About 60 times
About the same
context: Germany's monetary base grew roughly 12-fold between 1914 and 1918, seeding the postwar hyperinflation. Britain's price level roughly doubled; France's roughly tripled; Russia's ruble collapsed entirely in the 1917 revolution. Source: Grokipedia 'Papiermark' (2026-09-05).

question: In every major war of the 20th century -- the First World War, the Second World War, the Korean War, Vietnam -- governments printed massive amounts of brand-new paper money to pay for soldiers, guns, tanks, and supplies. Prices in the shops rose quickly as a result, because factories and farms could not fill up store shelves any faster than before. What is the name for this rise in prices caused by too much new money chasing the same goods?
answer: Inflation, because more money is chasing the same amount of goods
choices: Inflation, because more money is chasing the same amount of goods
Deflation, because there are more goods than money
Full employment, because everyone has a job
A permanent boom, because factories keep growing
context: The US entered the war in April 1917, roughly two and a half years after the European powers. Its shorter war and smaller relative commitment kept dollar inflation modest compared to the belligerents already fighting since 1914. Source: Grokipedia 'United States home front during World War I' (2026-09-05).

question: In early 1919, just after the First World War ended, an Austrian economist in Vienna published a book called Nation, State, and Economy. In it he argued the war could never have dragged on for four bloody years under a full gold standard — governments would have run out of real gold to pay soldiers within months and been forced to make peace. Only unlimited paper printing, freed from gold, let the killing continue. Who was that Austrian economist?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Joseph Schumpeter
John Maynard Keynes
context: Mises's 1919 book Nation, State, and Economy argued that gold discipline would have forced belligerents to a negotiated settlement within months. The four-year industrial slaughter (~17 million dead) was economically possible only because paper-money printing had been unleashed. Source: mises.org/library/nation-state-and-economy.

question: In 1925 Britain went back to the gold standard, meaning the government would once again let people trade paper pounds for physical gold coins on demand. Chancellor of the Exchequer Winston Churchill picked a specific old rate to fix the pound at. It made the pound too strong on world markets and forced painful deflation, wage cuts, and unemployment on British coal miners and factory workers. At what rate did Churchill fix the pound?
answer: The prewar 1914 parity
choices: The prewar 1914 parity
The 1918 wartime peak
Twenty percent below 1914
A floating market rate
context: On advice from Bank of England officials, Churchill returned sterling at the 1914 rate of $4.86, even though the pound's real value had fallen. British exports became uncompetitive; unemployment stayed high through the late 1920s. Source: Grokipedia 'Return to gold' (2026-09-05).

question: In April 1925 Winston Churchill, then Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, made the fateful decision to put the British pound back on the pre-war gold standard -- and at the pre-war exchange rate, which many economists said was too high. The economist John Maynard Keynes was furious. Keynes wrote a short pamphlet attacking the decision, and its title named Churchill personally as the man responsible for what Keynes predicted would be a national disaster. What did Keynes call his pamphlet?
answer: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
choices: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
The Return to Gold: A Warning
The End of Sterling
The Twenty-Fifth of April
context: Keynes's 1925 pamphlet echoed the title of his 1919 attack on the Versailles Treaty, 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'. Keynes and the Austrians agreed about the 1925 decision (both thought it wrong) though for different theoretical reasons. Source: Grokipedia 'John Maynard Keynes' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1922 Genoa Conference tried to ease pressure on world gold reserves. It proposed a weaker version of the classical system. Only central banks would hold real gold, and commercial reserves would be foreign currencies backed by gold. What is this weaker system called?
answer: The gold-exchange standard
choices: The gold-exchange standard
The bimetallic standard
The Bretton Woods system
The special drawing rights system
context: The gold-exchange standard emerged from the 1922 Genoa Conference and became the interwar norm. It was already collapsing by 1931 when Britain permanently abandoned gold; it died fully with WW2. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold exchange standard' (2026-09-05).

question: When money is backed by gold or has a fixed supply, the government cannot just print more when it needs to pay for something huge. Austrian economists say this is why states that want to fight big wars have always wanted to break that link. What is their thesis?
answer: Sound money limits state power, and war-making states always want to escape that limit
choices: Sound money limits state power, and war-making states always want to escape that limit
Sound money is just a technical rule with no effect on politics or wars
Sound money encourages military spending by making wars cheaper to fund
Sound money is preferred by governments and only opposed by private banks
context: Every 20th-century abandonment of gold discipline was driven by governments that wanted to expand spending -- usually war spending -- beyond what taxpayers would voluntarily fund. The pattern is not incidental; it is structural. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: Austrian-school economists read the political and monetary catastrophes of the 20th century -- the two World Wars, the abandonment of the gold standard, the great hyperinflations, the Cold War -- as one connected story rather than as two independent tragedies (war on one side, money on the other). In this Austrian reading, industrial-scale war and monetary breakdown are bound together at the deepest level. Which pairing best captures that link?
answer: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
choices: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
The wars caused monetary collapse and the collapse then caused more wars
Monetary experiments and wars were independent 20th-century phenomena
The wars were entirely funded by taxes on wealthy citizens
context: The Austrian counterfactual: no four-year Great War without paper-money printing; no paper-money printing without abandoning gold discipline. The 20th century's political catastrophes and its monetary catastrophes have a shared root cause. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: In China from 1958 to 1962, Chairman Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward campaign forced peasant farmers off their family plots and onto giant government-run collective farms called people's communes. Village grain was hauled off to feed the cities and to sell abroad for machinery. What was the main result out in the countryside where the food had been grown?
answer: The worst famine in history -- tens of millions starved
choices: A big harvest that fed everyone
The worst famine in history -- tens of millions starved
Farmers became rich for the first time
No change -- country life stayed the same
context: Yang was born 1940 in Hubei province. Dikotter, Banister, and Ashton are Western scholars of the same famine; Yang was the insider-journalist who counted from within. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: In 1958 China's Chairman Mao Zedong ordered the country's farms merged into huge state-owned collectives called people's communes as part of his Great Leap Forward campaign. Peasants were pulled off the fields and told to melt down iron pots in tiny backyard furnaces to make steel, instead of growing food. Grain output crashed. What was the result across China over the next four years?
answer: A famine that killed tens of millions of Chinese peasants
choices: A famine that killed tens of millions of Chinese peasants
A record harvest that ended hunger in Asia
A short strike that lasted only a few weeks
A minor delay in factory building
context: Tombstone (Mu Bei in Chinese) referred to the author's father, to whom the book was dedicated, and to the millions unnamed in Chinese public memory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: The Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng spent decades secretly gathering evidence about the Great Leap Forward famine of 1958 to 1962, when Mao Zedong's forced collectivization killed an estimated 36 to 45 million Chinese peasants through starvation. Yang eventually published his findings as the massive book Tombstone. His entire life project was triggered by a specific personal event during the famine. What was it?
answer: His own father, a rural schoolteacher, died of starvation in April 1959
choices: His own father, a rural schoolteacher, died of starvation in April 1959
His own village was destroyed by a Red Guard raid
His own mother was denounced as a class enemy
His own house was seized by the local commune
context: The party had denied there was a famine; the young Yang, then a high-schooler and Communist Youth League member, believed them. Discovering later that his father had been one of tens of millions became his life's work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: In 2008 the Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng published a book called Tombstone, based on seven years of secretly digging through provincial Communist Party archives. He was counting excess deaths from the Great Leap Forward — Mao Zedong's forced collectivization drive from 1958 to 1962, in which Chinese peasants starved by the tens of millions after their grain was seized to feed cities and export markets. Yang added up county death records the Party never wanted foreigners to see. Roughly what figure did he arrive at?
answer: About 36 million
choices: About 36 million
About 3 million
About 3,000
About 300 million
context: Prior Western estimates (Judith Banister 1987, Basil Ashton 1984, both around 30 million) had been top-down demographic estimates from national census gaps. Yang's was the first bottom-up count from actual provincial records. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Great_Chinese_Famine.

question: In 2008 the Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng published Tombstone, his massive study of the Great Leap Forward famine of 1958 to 1962 that Mao Zedong's forced collectivization had caused. In the 1980s the demographers Judith Banister and Basil Ashton had already estimated tens of millions dead by subtracting expected births from later census counts. Yang did something they could not. What was his methodological breakthrough?
answer: He counted from actual provincial party records rather than inferring from national census gaps
choices: He counted from actual provincial party records rather than inferring from national census gaps
He interviewed exactly 100,000 survivors in a randomized survey
He used a computer model of Chinese demography from 1949 to 2000
He worked entirely from published Chinese government White Papers
context: Yang's Xinhua credentials and personal connections gave him access to provincial archives that had never been available to Western scholars. The bottom-up method vindicated the older top-down estimates and added specificity province by province. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: In 2008 the Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng published Tombstone, his archive-based count of the tens of millions of Chinese peasants killed in Mao Zedong's 1958-1962 Great Leap Forward famine. Four years later, the American publisher Farrar, Straus and Giroux released an abridged English edition that made Yang's numbers reachable in the West. Who did the translation, and what was the abridged English title?
answer: Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian; 'Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962'
choices: Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian; 'Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962'
Perry Link and Andrew Nathan; 'The Tiananmen Papers'
Wu Ningkun and Li Yikai; 'A Single Tear'
Ha Jin and Yan Lianke; 'The Four Books'
context: The two-volume Chinese original was abridged to one English volume. Wu Ningkun and Li Yikai wrote a different memoir (A Single Tear); Ha Jin and Yan Lianke are novelists of adjacent Chinese trauma but not Yang's translators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: In 2008 the Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng published Tombstone, his archive-based history of the tens of millions killed in Mao Zedong's 1958-1962 Great Leap Forward famine. The English edition came out in 2012, and in 2013 the Manhattan Institute in New York awarded Yang the Hayek Prize for it. Three years later, in 2016, the Chinese Communist government took a specific step regarding Yang and the prize. What did the government do?
answer: Denied him permission to leave China to accept the prize in person
choices: Denied him permission to leave China to accept the prize in person
Allowed him to travel and receive the prize in New York
Awarded him a competing state honor to counterbalance the Hayek Prize
Rescinded the Hayek Prize under diplomatic pressure
context: Tombstone remains banned for mainland Chinese publication. The prize is named for Friedrich Hayek and is the Manhattan Institute's annual award for a book that best reflects Hayek's principles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: In the 1960s the American economist Milton Friedman studied the Great Depression, the terrible slump that began in 1929 when the American stock market crashed. Banks closed by the thousands, workers lost jobs, and families went hungry through the 1930s. Friedman argued the crash never had to get that bad. He blamed America's central bank — the Federal Reserve — for standing by while banks failed and the country's money supply shrank by a third. What did Friedman say went wrong?
answer: The central bank made the crash worse instead of stopping it
choices: Farmers refused to grow food that year
The central bank made the crash worse instead of stopping it
Businesses stopped wanting profit
Workers didn't want jobs anymore
context: The University of Chicago hosted a two-day conference in November 2002 to mark Milton Friedman's 90th birthday. Friedman (born July 31 1912) sat in the audience for Bernanke's remarks. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2008 many of the biggest American banks were about to collapse. They had made huge loans on houses that were suddenly worth far less than the borrowed money — the housing bubble had burst. To stop the banks from failing, the central bank of the United States, called the Federal Reserve, created brand-new money and used it to buy up the banks' bad debts. That kept the banks running while ordinary homeowners lost their houses. What is that kind of rescue called?
answer: A bailout
choices: A tax cut
A bailout
A recession
A tariff
context: Bernanke had joined the Fed Board in 2002 after two decades as an academic at Princeton. His scholarly work focused on the monetary history of the 1929-33 downturn -- exactly the topic of his apology. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002, at Milton Friedman's 90th birthday party, Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke made a public apology. He said the Fed had caused the Great Depression by letting the money supply shrink about 33 percent between 1929 and 1933 — exactly the case Friedman and his coauthor Anna Schwartz had laid out in a heavy 1963 book of economic history. What is that book called?
answer: A Monetary History of the United States
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
Free to Choose
Capitalism and Freedom
The Great Contraction
context: The full title is A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960, coauthored with Anna Schwartz and published by Princeton University Press in 1963. Chapter 7, 'The Great Contraction,' contained the specific argument. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: In their 1963 book A Monetary History of the United States, economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued that the Federal Reserve had turned an ordinary 1929 downturn into the decade-long Great Depression. In 2002, Fed governor Ben Bernanke publicly accepted their charge on the Fed's behalf. What did the Fed actually do between 1929 and 1933 to make the collapse so much worse?
answer: Allowed the money supply to contract about 33% by failing to act as lender of last resort during bank failures
choices: Allowed the money supply to contract about 33% by failing to act as lender of last resort during bank failures
Deliberately raised interest rates to attack speculators
Devalued the dollar against gold in coordination with Britain
Printed money to bail out farmers hit by drought
context: Bank failures cascaded 1930-33, wiping out deposits and shrinking the money supply. Friedman and Schwartz argued a competent central bank should have flooded the system with liquidity -- exactly what Bernanke did in 2008. Source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History (1963).

question: In November 2002 the Federal Reserve official Ben Bernanke spoke at a University of Chicago birthday party for the economist Milton Friedman, who was turning 90. Friedman and his co-author Anna Schwartz had spent decades arguing that the Fed itself caused the Great Depression of the 1930s by letting thousands of banks collapse. In his closing sentences Bernanke turned to Friedman and Schwartz in the audience and made a direct concession. Which sentences captured it?
answer: You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
choices: You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
You were wrong, but we forgive the theoretical mistake
We agree partially, but the fiscal side matters equally
You may be right but the evidence is not yet decisive
context: Bernanke abused (his word) his official status as a Fed representative to deliver the extraordinary concession directly to the 90-year-old Friedman. The full text is on federalreserve.gov. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 2002 the future Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke -- then a Fed governor -- spoke at a birthday celebration for the economist Milton Friedman, who had long argued that the Federal Reserve caused the Great Depression by letting the money supply collapse in the early 1930s. Bernanke closed his talk with a rare public admission on behalf of his own institution. What did his speech say the Federal Reserve had caused?
answer: The worst economic catastrophe in modern American history
choices: The worst economic catastrophe in modern American history
The dot-com stock-market bubble of the 1990s
The 1970s inflation of the Great Inflation era
The 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital Management
context: The Great Depression (1929-33) was the deepest and longest downturn in US history. An official Fed representative publicly conceding institutional responsibility for it was unprecedented. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: In 2002, Fed governor Ben Bernanke stood at Milton Friedman's 90th birthday party and apologized on the Federal Reserve's behalf for causing the Great Depression. Six years later, Bernanke — now Fed chair — was in charge during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Austrian-school economists said his crisis response completely contradicted the humility of that 2002 speech. What did Bernanke do at the Fed that his Austrian critics attacked?
answer: Launched massive quantitative easing and zero interest rates that his critics argue mispriced capital and seeded a later inflation wave
choices: Launched massive quantitative easing and zero interest rates that his critics argue mispriced capital and seeded a later inflation wave
Allowed bank failures to cascade unchecked through the whole system
Raised interest rates aggressively into the recession to protect the dollar
Publicly refused to serve as lender of last resort in September 2008
context: The Austrian critique: in avoiding the 1930s error, Bernanke committed an opposite error -- keeping rates artificially low for years, mispricing capital across the economy, and setting up the 2020-24 inflation wave. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012, updated 2014).

question: Milton Friedman died in November 2006, before he could see how Fed chair Ben Bernanke would handle the 2008 crisis. Friedman's longtime coauthor Anna Schwartz, however, lived until 2012, and in October 2008 the Wall Street Journal published a candid interview with her about Bernanke's response to the collapse. What was Schwartz's assessment?
answer: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
choices: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
That he was implementing exactly the policy she and Friedman had recommended
That his intervention would restore price stability within a year
That she supported his aggressive rate cuts unreservedly
context: Schwartz's October 2008 Wall Street Journal interview sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response, effectively reversing the endorsement Bernanke had claimed six years earlier. Source: Wall Street Journal, 'The Fed and the Financial Crisis' interview (October 18 2008).

question: In 2002 the Federal Reserve official Ben Bernanke publicly apologized to the economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz for the Fed's disaster during the Great Depression — the mistake of letting banks and the money supply collapse in the 1930s. Six years later, when Bernanke ran the Fed during the 2008 crisis, Anna Schwartz sharply criticized him from the opposite direction: this time the Fed flooded markets with new money and rescued failing banks in ways she said stored up new problems. Together these two moments form a specific recognition about central-bank learning. Which move does the ladder press on the reader?
answer: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next crisis
choices: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next crisis
Central banks steadily improve their forecasting record over decades
Public apologies from central bankers reliably predict better future policy
Academic historians consistently produce better central-bank chairs than practitioners
context: Bernanke avoided the 1930s mistake and possibly caused a 2020s one. The pattern is not incidental. Every crisis-forged lesson becomes doctrine that the next crisis violates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In November 2002, the Federal Reserve official Ben Bernanke spoke at a University of Chicago birthday party for the economist Milton Friedman. Bernanke stood before Friedman and his co-author Anna Schwartz and admitted, on behalf of the Fed, that their famous critique of the central bank was correct — the Fed itself caused a huge disaster in the 1930s, not private markets or greedy speculators. Which critique of the Fed was Bernanke agreeing with?
answer: The Fed caused the Great Depression by failing to lend to banks in the crisis
choices: The Fed caused the Great Depression by failing to lend to banks in the crisis
Import tariffs caused the Great Depression by strangling international trade
Rigid wage rules under President Hoover caused the Great Depression
Foreign countries devaluing their currencies caused the Great Depression
context: The Friedman-Schwartz thesis is now standard even inside the Fed. The remaining dispute is not whether the Fed failed but what the correct alternative response would have been -- which is where Austrian critics part ways with the monetarist prescription. Source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History (1963); Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In the year 2000 Zimbabwe's government, led by Robert Mugabe, seized farms from the experienced commercial farmers who had run them for decades. It handed the land over to political supporters -- many of whom had never grown a crop in their lives. What was the likely result for the country's food supply in the years that followed?
answer: The country goes from feeding itself to needing food aid
choices: Food gets cheaper for everyone
The country goes from feeding itself to needing food aid
Farms become more productive
Exports of grain increase
context: Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017. The fast-track land-reform program of 2000 onward is the direct fiscal cause of the later hyperinflation. Source: Grokipedia 'Land reform in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: By 2008 the government of Zimbabwe was broke. Tax revenue had collapsed, so to keep paying soldiers and civil servants, President Robert Mugabe's Reserve Bank kept printing more and more Zimbabwean dollars. Prices rose faster and faster. In November 2008 the monthly inflation rate hit one of the two highest figures ever recorded in world history. What was that November 2008 monthly rate?
answer: About 79.6 billion percent
choices: About 79.6 billion percent
About 1,300 percent
About 250 million percent
About 4.6 trillion percent
context: November 2008 Zimbabwean monthly inflation is officially estimated at 79,600,000,000% -- prices doubling roughly every 24 hours. Only Hungary's July 1946 pengo (41.9 quadrillion percent) was worse in recorded history. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: By January 2009, Zimbabwe's hyperinflation under President Robert Mugabe had spun completely out of control -- prices were doubling every 24 hours or faster. That month the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe printed a single banknote whose face value broke the world record for the largest number ever printed on a piece of paper money. What was its face value?
answer: 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
choices: 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
1 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
10 billion Zimbabwe dollars
1 quintillion Zimbabwe dollars
context: The 100,000,000,000,000-Zimbabwe-dollar note is the highest-denomination banknote ever issued by any government in monetary history. When issued in January 2009 it bought roughly three eggs. Source: Grokipedia 'Zimbabwean dollar' (2026-09-05).

question: By 2008 the southern African country of Zimbabwe had crashed. Prices doubled every day because President Robert Mugabe's government kept printing new money to pay its bills — a runaway printing spree called hyperinflation. Farmers refused to sell food for Zimbabwean dollars because the paper was worthless by evening. So ordinary Zimbabweans stopped using the local money entirely and switched to foreign currencies for daily buying and selling. Which foreign currencies did they pick up?
answer: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
choices: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
The British pound and the euro only
The Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan
The Kenyan shilling and the Egyptian pound
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans used whichever foreign currency they could get. The government formally accepted the dollarization; the Zimbabwe dollar was demonetized in June 2015. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: By 2009 Zimbabwe's own currency, the Zimbabwe dollar, had been destroyed by years of runaway money-printing under President Robert Mugabe. People had already stopped using it for daily shopping, but old leftover balances still sat frozen in bank accounts. In June 2015 the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe formally killed the Zimbabwe dollar. It offered to swap those remaining bank balances for US dollars at a single blunt exchange rate. What was that rate?
answer: 175 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
choices: 175 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
1 billion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
10 trillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
1 million Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
context: The demonetization rate was Z$175,000,000,000,000,000 for USD 1 -- the government's formal admission of the currency's collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Zimbabwean dollar' (2026-09-05).

question: After Zimbabwe finally abandoned its own currency in 2015 and switched to using US dollars for everyday trade, the country's famous 100-trillion-dollar banknotes did not disappear. Instead, tourists, collectors, and internet shoppers around the world began buying them as novelty items -- the most famous surviving artifact of hyperinflation gone wild. What is the new role of these banknotes today?
answer: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
choices: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
Legal tender in Zimbabwe's tourist areas
Reserve assets held by African central banks
Backing for a new Zimbabwean cryptocurrency
context: A Zimbabwean 100-trillion-dollar note now sells for roughly $2 to $15 USD on collector sites -- a physical, cheap, permanent reminder of what fiat-currency collapse looks like. Source: collector-market listings on eBay and specialist numismatic sites (2020-2025).

question: In the mid-2000s, Zimbabwe's economy collapsed after president Robert Mugabe seized productive farms and gutted the country's tax base. The Austrian school of economics has a simple story for how a hyperinflation is born, and Zimbabwe followed it exactly. First a government's tax revenue falls apart. Then the central bank steps in to cover the gap by printing new money. Which two things combined to cause Zimbabwe's money crash?
answer: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
choices: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
A trade deficit from failed exports plus a currency peg to gold
A shortage of labor plus a rise in wages
A political crisis plus a foreign embargo
context: The land-seizure program destroyed the productive tax base. The Reserve Bank was ordered to fund the state anyway. Money-printing without a growing real economy produces the Cantillon-effect destruction of savers, then hyperinflation, then abandonment. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: When Zimbabwe's money crashed in the late 2000s, prices doubled every few days and old bills became wallpaper. Many Western economists were caught off guard, because a comfortable idea had settled in during the quiet postwar decades. They had assumed something about hyperinflation itself. Which comfortable Western guess did Zimbabwe's collapse correct?
answer: That modern hyperinflations are relics of the 1920s and no longer happen
choices: That modern hyperinflations are relics of the 1920s and no longer happen
That all hyperinflations end quickly through spontaneous market recovery
That hyperinflations are always the result of foreign invasion
That hyperinflations always require the presence of gold reserves
context: Zimbabwe is not history; it is a live monetary experiment students can watch on YouTube today. The same mechanism runs identically in Africa, Latin America, and the modern world whenever it is unleashed. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation' (2026-09-05).

question: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation destroyed the Zimbabwe dollar in the late 2000s, just as the German mark had died in 1923 Weimar Germany. Every hyperinflation in history has ended the same way -- not by government decree, but by people below simply refusing to hold the collapsing bills any longer. Zimbabwe's ending shows what money really is at bottom: something people choose, not something a state forces. What did Zimbabwe's money system actually do at the end?
answer: Ordinary people spontaneously adopted foreign currencies from below, before the government formally allowed it
choices: Ordinary people spontaneously adopted foreign currencies from below, before the government formally allowed it
The government successfully re-anchored the Zimbabwe dollar to gold
The IMF imposed a new central-bank currency by treaty
A regional currency union in Southern Africa absorbed the Zimbabwe dollar
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans were already pricing goods in USD, rand, and pula in the informal economy. The government then formalized what citizens had already done. Money is what people accept; the government simply catches up. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: The 19th-century French economist Frederic Bastiat taught readers to compare what is seen from a government policy with what quietly stays unseen. In 2008 Zimbabwe's Reserve Bank was printing money at a runaway pace to pay soldiers and officials, and monthly inflation climbed to about 79.6 billion percent. Which pairing best captures the seen-and-unseen structure Bastiat would draw for the Zimbabwean episode?
answer: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
choices: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
Seen: land redistributed to landless workers; Unseen: rising urban employment
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: an independent central bank; Unseen: rising foreign reserves
context: The visible policy achievement (paying the army and civil service) hid the invisible destruction (every existing bank balance and cash holding in the country evaporating). The Cantillon effect on a national scale. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: Imagine a country where prices are rising 100% a day because the government prints new money nonstop to pay its bills. A loaf of bread costs twice as much tonight as it did this morning. To 'fix' the problem, the president orders every shop to cut prices in half — or the shopkeepers go to jail. Shopkeepers now face selling bread for less than the flour cost them. Very quickly, what happens in the stores?
answer: Shelves empty because selling below cost bankrupts stores
choices: Prices stay low and everyone shops happily
Shelves empty because selling below cost bankrupts stores
Stores make bigger profits than ever
The government's money becomes worth more
context: Zimbabwe's president since 1980. Police and army units enforced the order in Harare and Bulawayo supermarkets, arresting shopkeepers who did not comply. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: On June 26, 2007, Zimbabwe's president Robert Mugabe blamed shopkeepers for the country's runaway inflation and ordered every price in the country cut in half. Store owners obeyed at gunpoint. Shoppers rushed in to buy meat, bread, and milk at the new bargain prices. Almost immediately the shelves went bare. About how long did it take for stores across Zimbabwe to run empty?
answer: About 48 hours
choices: About 48 hours
About six months
About two years
About a decade
context: Consumers rushed to buy at below-cost prices; merchandise vanished into private hoarding or black markets. The collapse happened at time-lapse speed compared to normal economic-policy failures. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: On June 26, 2007, Zimbabwe's president Robert Mugabe ordered every price in the country cut in half to fight the country's runaway inflation. Within 48 hours the shelves went bare as shoppers bought up everything at bargain prices. But a bigger downstream effect began within days, spreading up the supply chain past the empty shelves themselves. What began happening across Zimbabwe's producers?
answer: Factories (meat processors, dairies, bakeries) began shutting down because they could not produce at below-cost mandated prices
choices: Factories (meat processors, dairies, bakeries) began shutting down because they could not produce at below-cost mandated prices
The Zimbabwean central bank raised interest rates to defend the currency
The IMF signed an emergency lending program with Harare
Neighboring Botswana closed its border to prevent smuggling
context: The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries reported that hundreds of manufacturers closed operations or laid off staff within the first two weeks of the order. The reasoning: no firm can produce a loaf of bread at a mandated price below the cost of the flour and fuel to bake it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: On June 26, 2007, Zimbabwe's president Robert Mugabe ordered every price in the country cut in half to fight hyperinflation. Store shelves emptied in 48 hours. Factories shut down within days. The order was never formally cancelled with a big announcement -- it was quietly abandoned once even loyal officials could see the wreckage on the streets. About how long did Mugabe's price-halving order stay on the books before it was dropped?
answer: About three months
choices: About three months
About one week
About one year
About five years
context: The order was not formally rescinded; enforcement simply lapsed as the visible collapse of shelves and factories made it politically impossible to sustain. The underlying hyperinflation continued. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: In June 2007 the president of Zimbabwe, Robert Mugabe, ordered every shopkeeper in the country to cut prices in half — or go to jail. Shelves emptied within days because stores could not sell bread and meat below the cost of buying them. But Mugabe was aiming his order at the symptom (rising prices) while ignoring what was actually driving them. What was the underlying cause of Zimbabwe's inflation?
answer: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget
choices: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget
Global commodity prices had risen because of Chinese demand
Zimbabwean workers had gone on strike for higher wages
The US Federal Reserve had raised interest rates
context: The classic Friedman monetary diagnosis: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. The price ceiling attacked the symptom (visible prices) while the disease (money creation) continued and accelerated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: By January 2009 Zimbabwe's currency had been destroyed by years of nonstop money-printing under President Robert Mugabe. Prices doubled every day, and shoppers hauled bricks of cash in wheelbarrows just to buy a single loaf of bread. That month the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued a physical banknote — one piece of paper — that became the world's most famous illustration of hyperinflation, photographed in economics textbooks ever since. What was the note's face value?
answer: 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars
choices: 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars
500 Zimbabwean dollars
1,000 Zimbabwean dollars
10 billion Zimbabwean dollars
context: The country formally adopted the US dollar as its functional currency the same year 2009, abandoning the Zimbabwean dollar entirely. Cato senior fellow Steve Hanke had tracked the Zimbabwean hyperinflation in real time and published widely-cited estimates through the collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: In June 2007 the president of Zimbabwe, Robert Mugabe, ordered every shop in the country to cut prices in half — or go to jail. Shelves emptied within days. Years later, a high-school student in 2025 asks a Hayekian economist (a follower of the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek, who studied how price signals coordinate an economy) what makes this Zimbabwe episode uniquely useful for teaching how price controls fail. The economist points to one specific property of the case. Which property?
answer: The whole seen-versus-unseen chain from order to visible collapse ran in about 48 hours
choices: The whole seen-versus-unseen chain from order to visible collapse ran in about 48 hours
The order was rescinded by international treaty within one day
The Zimbabwean parliament unanimously vetoed the president's order
The affected supermarkets sued the government and won
context: Most price-control failures unfold over years and can be argued about. Zimbabwe compressed the entire chain -- decree, seen legal price on labels, unseen goods disappearing, shortages, factory closures -- into a single school-week. It became the fastest, cleanest demonstration in modern economic history. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: In 1926 the small Ohio village of Euclid had passed rules telling landowners what kinds of buildings — houses, shops, or factories — could go on each lot. A real-estate firm called Ambler Realty sued, arguing the village had no right to control private land that way. The US Supreme Court ruled for the village, and that decision still gives every American city the power to write zoning codes today. What is the case called?
answer: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty
choices: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty
Kelo v. City of New London
Penn Central v. New York City
Berman v. Parker
context: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926) upheld comprehensive municipal zoning against a Fourteenth Amendment challenge and became the constitutional backstop for every US zoning code since. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Village_of_Euclid_v._Ambler_Realty_Co..

question: In most big American cities, the city government draws lines on a map to decide which land can hold homes, which land can hold stores, and which land can hold factories. This rule is called zoning. But a few places, like most of Houston, Texas, have no zoning at all. Neighborhoods there still need some way to keep, say, a smelly chemical plant from moving next to a school. What might a no-zoning neighborhood use instead?
answer: Private agreements written into each home's deed
choices: A vote by all the people in the state
Private agreements written into each home's deed
Random dice rolls each year
Whatever the mayor's family wants
context: Houston, Texas is the largest US city without a conventional zoning code. Land-use control there is done through private deed restrictions, not city ordinance. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zoning_in_Houston.

question: In 2002 two American economists studied why apartments in big cities like New York and Boston cost so much more to buy than they cost to build. They compared the actual brick-and-mortar cost of putting up an apartment with the price it eventually sold for. The gap — sometimes 50 percent or more — showed how much strict zoning laws cost city renters, since those laws stop builders from adding new homes on scarce land. Which pair of economists wrote that paper?
answer: Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko
choices: Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Krugman and Enrico Moretti
Raj Chetty and John Friedman
context: Glaeser (Harvard) and Gyourko (Wharton) published 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' as NBER working paper 8835 in 2002 and in the FRBNY Economic Policy Review in 2003. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: In the early 2000s, the economists Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko studied Manhattan's housing market. They measured what it actually cost to build a new apartment there and compared that with the price the same apartment sold for. The huge gap, they argued, was money that zoning restrictions had piled on top — and they called it the 'zoning tax'. About how big was that zoning tax per Manhattan apartment?
choices: $5 million
context: Their 2002 paper found a zoning tax of roughly $500,000 per apartment in Manhattan; by the 2010s the Manhattan figure was well over a million. Loose-zoning cities such as Houston and Atlanta showed essentially zero zoning tax. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: A homeowner argues that zoning — the city rules that say only single-family houses can go on this street — protects the neighborhood's character from apartments and duplexes. The 1800s French economist Frédéric Bastiat had a famous method for questions like this. He always asked: what does a rule cost that nobody actually sees, because those things never come into existence? Applied to zoning, which unseen cost does Bastiat's method point to?
answer: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
choices: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
The published municipal permit fees
The construction jobs on the buildings that were built
The listed prices of the homes that already exist
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): existing homes and their prices are visible; the never-built housing, the families priced out of the metro area, and the 2-hour commuters are the invisible casualties. Source: bastiat.org.

question: In many growing American cities, strict zoning codes keep housing scarce and expensive. Economists point out that the people hurt most are workers who would move in from cheaper places if more apartments existed — but they don't live in the city yet. Meanwhile the codes stay tight for decades. What pattern of local politics best explains why zoning stays this restrictive in city after city?
answer: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
choices: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
Cities lack the legal authority to change zoning codes at all
Construction companies uniformly oppose new residential building
Federal law preempts almost all local land-use decisions
context: Concentrated benefit + dispersed cost with a franchise twist: existing owners benefit from constrained supply and vote for it; the priced-out do not live in the city yet, so their preferences carry no votes. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: A growing American town has a zoning code that says only single-family houses can go up on most streets — no apartments, no duplexes, no townhouses allowed on the same lots. Meanwhile, hundreds of new families move in each year, drawn by jobs, schools, and safe streets. As more people arrive over the decades while the rule stays in place, what usually happens to home prices in that town?
answer: They go up, because the rule blocks builders from adding more homes
choices: They go up, because the rule blocks builders from adding more homes
They stay flat, because zoning rules do not affect prices
They fall, because the rule scares builders away for good
They fall, because single-family houses are always cheap to build
context: The Minneapolis City Council adopted the Minneapolis 2040 plan in December 2018, ending citywide single-family-only zoning. Every residential lot became eligible for up to a triplex. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Minneapolis_2040.

question: In 2021, California passed a law called SB 9 that let the owner of a single-family lot split it and build up to four homes on the same piece of land — overriding city zoning codes that had banned anything but a single house per lot. Using the ordinary logic of supply and demand, what should this law do to housing prices in the cities where multi-unit building had been banned?
answer: Push prices down over time by allowing more homes to be built where demand is highest
choices: Push prices down over time by allowing more homes to be built where demand is highest
Push prices up because each new unit adds demand for land
Have no effect on prices, since zoning rules do not affect the market
Push prices down only in rural areas where lots are already large
context: California SB 9 (signed September 2021, effective January 2022) plus SB 10 gave the YIMBY movement its first big statewide preemption win. Source: grokipedia.com/page/California_Senate_Bill_9.
